Manuscript: NGMCP Reel No. B 181/1, Manuscript No. 5-1922. Description: An extensive liturgical manual for the worship of Tripurasundarī.

Composed by Prāṇamañjarī, the wife of the scholar Śrī Premanidhi.
(Folio 1a) Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati! Homage to the illustrious Kārtavīryārjuna!

Victorious is Kārtavīryārjuna, who has risen from the Sudarśana; he is Arjuna because he is the supreme cause of the Sudarśana’s emergence. By whose grace the two goals—the eternal and the desired—are now ready to manifest, their course having been made firm by the Sudarśana.
The manual. || 1 ||

Here, the King of Tantras named *Svanirmitasudarśana*, definitively established with an excellent commentary and intended for the purpose of various desired rites, is clearly presented by Kamalā; likewise, the *Tripurasundarīpaddhati*, which is like a sister to the *Sudarśana*, is proclaimed by her. || 2 ||

O Mind, if Lakṣmī has departed for that abode of skin, bone, and blood belonging to Śrī Hari, it is only right; let there be no path for grief upon her being placed there. Standing before you is a fresh composition, its words of various colors and its meaning profound and far-reaching;
it is already given, yet it is quickly being fashioned anew.
She whose mother was the illustrious Harṣamatī, daughter of King Harṣadeva;

whose birthplace was Kūrmāñcala, renowned throughout the directions; she who is the beloved wife of the treasure-house of scholars, Śrī Prāṇamañjaya; and who is independent by nature—[to her] belongs this *Śrīsundarī-paddhati*. 4.

When the worship of Tripura is performed according to the true rule even without the stainless Kamalā, then why should that worship of Tripura not be [complete] without this very stainless Kamalā? (5)

Thus, for those who perform these obligatory, occasional, and occasional rites— preceded by a comprehensive collection of various meanings that are mutually dependent and emanated from the independent Tantras— their status as a portion of Me is attained.
At the conclusion of the *Prasrutatantra*, because that [practice] was favored by the Blessed One and because such a desire exists in all people,

[this work] is a new manual named *Kamalā*, composed in accordance with the *Svatantratantra* alone, preceded by a compendium of its subject matter for the benefit of all people, and accompanied by the complete daily rite (*nityā*) of the venerable *Tripurasundarī-nityā*.
The manual is being manifested.

A practitioner (sādhaka), desiring to perform the worship of the mantra of Śrī Tripurasundarī by relying solely on the venerable *Śrī Tantrarāja*, due to the diversity of inclinations toward existence arising from the power of karma accumulated in successive previous births, [proceeds as follows].
If one does not find a teacher endowed with the nine characteristics— such as being faultless and having traveled [to various lands]— in a nearby region,
then even if such a devotee is heard of in a distant or very remote region, one should go there and take refuge in that teacher. Furthermore,
the teacher should not be one whose nature consists of demonstrating various other deities or describing the great majesty of their respective worshippers.

By whatever means possible, one should lead [the seeker] toward devotion directed toward that supreme deity, mantras, and so forth; and having examined their possession of firm and healthy faith, freedom from great poverty, and being devoid of defects such as mental instability,
one should graciously accept as one's own disciple every person who has come for refuge, provided they are not born of a *pratiloma* (inverse) or *saṃkara* (mixed-caste) union.
Among those previously described who possess the characteristics of teacher and disciple, one should specifically seek out,

above all others, those who possess the characteristics shown to a higher degree in both the present time and place and in the respective places suitable for their own departure at that time; otherwise, they should not be followed as such.

Nor does this entail the consequence of severing the traditional lineage; nor is this definition restricted solely to another age, since there is a requirement for a definition applicable to the age currently under discussion; nor is the practice restricted solely to another age, given the various statements in the current tantras that would otherwise be inexplicable without reference to this present age.

Because it would lead to the logical fallacy of impossibility. Do not fear that how could there be an examination of those two, given that the qualities belonging to another are inaccessible to another; for it is possible to infer those qualities through cohabitation and other such means.
In that regard, for the Brāhmaṇas and others, [the temperaments] are respectively, for the most part: *ṛju* (straight), *kaṭhina* (hard), and *kaṭhinatarakaṭhina* (extremely hard).
The *mahākaṭhina* [vow] is by its very nature for a Brahmin after one year, for a Kṣatriya after two years, and for a Vaiśya after three years; [it is not for a Śūdra].
For those born of anuloma mixtures, the period for testing—consisting of living together and so forth—is fixed at four years; for those born of pratiloma mixtures, it is five years.
Their women should also be tested according to the time since their respective husbands, and unmarried girls according to the time since their fathers.
And it has been stated that the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for all the aforementioned castes, as well as for their women and those of mixed (*anuloma*) origin,
is unimpeded with respect to the sixteen *Nityā* Vidyās— even when they incorporate the *Praṇava*— as well as with respect to the other Vidyās and mantras taught in this independent Tantra.

Having thus examined [the student], if immediately after the instruction there is a perception of his bad qualities— characterized by the fact that the fruits of his actions are unseen, his being deficient in merit, his misconduct, and so forth—
then an expiation (prāyaścitta) is required from the teacher.

Regarding both the expiation and the renunciation of a disciple: if it is perceived that he possesses negative qualities such as pride in the fruits of visible actions, laziness, poverty, and so forth,
then there is neither expiation nor renunciation for him.

Furthermore, do not suspect that even the first alternative— the sacrifice of the wings— is encompassed by the scriptural statements regarding transgression (*pratyavāya*); for these two [alternatives] lack the characteristics prescribed by the scriptures,
since even the scripture concerning transgression upon renunciation does not mention them, following the method previously described even after examination.

Furthermore, in order to perform an examination of one's own devotion to the chosen deity and so forth, he should, on the tenth lunar day (tithi), instruct the Nityānityā-vidyā— consisting of five or six syllables— according to the prescribed method of instruction.
And the disciple, having acquired that knowledge, should practice that science for some time, preceded by service to the teacher as previously described.
The examination is not only for the teacher alone, nor for the disciple alone, nor even for both together; rather, the mantra itself must also be examined before it is taught.

The methods for examining that [debt] are divided into five types: purification by the five nights (*pañcarātri-śuddhi*), purification by the storehouse (*koṣṭha-śuddhi*), purification by wealth and debt (*dhana-ṛṇa-śuddhi*), and purification by enmity (*vaira-śuddhi*). Furthermore, this examination is necessary for the purpose of instructing those who are to be corrected.

In applications for the purpose of suppressing enemies, having ascertained their hostility, and for the sake of employing them in the task of suppressing those [enemies] through that very science, an examination of the assets and liabilities of all practitioners— whether they be those currently striving (*sādhya*), those who have attained success (*siddha*), or those of the third kind— is also necessary for everyone.

In that regard, the method for purifying the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*) is as follows: the forty-eight letters, namely the four groups of four beginning with *a* (excluding the nasal dot, the visarga, and the letter *kṣa*), are respectively the letters of the signs starting from Aries through Capricorn. Thus, those whose names begin with the letter *pa* and so forth belong to the signs beginning with Sagittarius.
One should personally infer the zodiacal signs (rāśis) for mantras such as "Arjunāya namaḥ" based on one's own birth sign;

a mantra whose first syllable falls in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth sign from one's own sign should not be adopted for the purpose of worship for one's own benefit. However, for the purpose of worship intended to subdue an enemy, one should consider the enemy's sign.
One should adopt a mantra that is favorable to one's own [natal] sign, such as the sixth, eighth, or other signs; furthermore,

it should be understood that if there is mutual friendship or enmity between the lord of one's own sign and the lord of the sixth, eighth, or other signs, the resulting defects or virtues do not apply.
The nature of the retrograde motion of the zodiac signs is as follows:
The method for purifying the *tārās* is as follows: having divided each of the twenty-seven lunar mansions, beginning with Aśvinī,
into sixty-six parts each, one assigns thirty-three and three-quarter units to each of the forty-eight syllables beginning with *a*.
A quarter [of a sign] is not thirty-four degrees; rather, the portions of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) should be applied sequentially.

Thus, it is established that the zodiacal signs, beginning with Aries, are formed by the sequentially obtained degrees of the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī, numbering one hundred and thirty-five. And so it is.
Just as in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), here too in this tantra, each zodiac sign beginning with Aries is [treated] by means of nine quarters (*pāda*) each.
It is established that within the twenty-eight constellations (*nakṣatras*) beginning with Aśvinī, there are four letters each—starting with *a* and so on—for every one and a quarter constellation;

this is because of the traditional recollection: "cu, ce, co, la for Aśvinī; li, lu, le, lo for Bharaṇī; a, i, u, e for Kṛttikā. Thus, the fact that [the names] Cumbana, Cūḍāmara, and others belong to the sign of Aries (*meṣarāśi*) is obtained from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*).

The regulation of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) follows the sequence: *ā* for Aśvinī, *i* for Bharaṇī, *ī* and *u* for Kṛttikā, and so forth; whereas the assignment of the zodiac signs (*rāśi*) to the consonant groups follows another system, such as *a* and *ā* for Aries (*meṣa*), *u* and *ū* for Taurus (*vṛṣabha*), and so on—this is the method of other Tantras.

And according to the method of the present tantra, which is distinct from both of those, here the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā belongs to one whose name begins with the letter *pa*, while for mantras beginning with the letter *a*, the constellation is Aśvinī; thus,
the mantra-constellation becomes the ninth counting from the subject's constellation, and so forth— one should understand this for oneself.
From the asterism of the person for whom something is to be accomplished (*sādhya-nakṣatra*), the first syllables of the third, fifth,

and seventh asterisms are not to be adopted for mantras intended for one's own worship; however, for mantras intended for the subjugation of enemies (*nigraha*), the first syllables of the third, fifth, and seventh asterisms from the asterism named Svāti must certainly be required.

Mantras such as "Bhairavāya namaḥ" and others consist of two lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). For those whose names begin with the letter *pa*, these mantras are not to be accepted, because according to the aforementioned method, their own *nakṣatra* is Śravaṇa—the third from their [name's] *nakṣatra*—and even though their second from their own *nakṣatra* is Uttarāṣāḍhā, [the mantra] still does not apply. For it is stated in the root text that there is a group of four *nakṣatras* beginning with the third.
The first syllables of the mantras beginning with *pā* are not to be adopted; rather, those beginning with *nakṣatra* are to be adopted.
Here in this tantra, the birth-star (*janmatārā*) is indeed to be taken. The nature of the wheel of stars is as follows:

(4a) Just as is the manner of purifying the interior, so there are five [lines] extending east-west and north-south.

Having drawn five lines intersecting one another with equal intervals, one constructs a wheel consisting of sixteen squares; therein, the square in the northeast, the square to its south, and the two squares below it— these four squares together constitute one group.

The fourth group of four squares starting from the northeast (īśāna) square—namely the third, fourth, seventh, and eighth—is the second group; the four squares located directly below the squares of the second group is the third group; and the fourth group of four squares starting from the northeast—namely the ninth, tenth, thirteenth, and fourteenth—is the fourth group. Thus are the four groups.
They are to be conceptualized.
In whichever class one should count from this square in a clockwise direction, the method of writing the letters therein is as follows:
in the first square of all, namely the northeast (Īśāna) square, the letter *a* is to be written because it is the first of all;
in the first square of the second class, the long form of *ā*; and in the first of the third class, the short *i*.

In the first [cell] of the fourth group, there is the long vowel *ī*. Then, having placed the respective first letter of each of the four groups starting from the first in the second cell of each of those four groups,
one should write the fifth letter of each group— namely the four beginning with *u*— according to the letters, as well as in the third cell of each of the groups.

From the letter placed in the second square of each respective class (*varga*), one should write the fifth letter, and so on, for the four letters beginning with *ḷ*. Likewise, in the fourth squares of the classes,
from the letter placed in the third square of each respective class, one should write the fifth letter, and so on.
Having filled sixteen squares with the sixteen vowels by repeating [the sequence] once, one should again [fill] the first four groups of consonants, etc.,
on page 4b.

Having written the thirty-two syllables from *ka* to *sa* by repeating each one once in the sequence of the first of the first, the second of the second, the third of the third, and the fourth of the fourth squares; then,
the remaining three syllables [are placed] in the first of the first squares of the first, second, and third groups.

"One should write"—thus, in all the squares, starting from each respective first letter placed therein, the second and subsequent letters become the seventeenth, the seventeenth, and so on; this is the final conclusion.
By writing in this manner, in the first square of the first group, [one finds] that which consists of *a*, *ka*, *tha*, and *ha*.
The four castes fall [into this]; the elders teach that the very nature of this wheel is that which expresses the word *kathaha*.
In the second [section], however, three groups of five should follow each of those;
in the third, nine from them, and then in the fourth, as many as twenty-one.
In the first [verse] of the second section, there is the second letter of the second [group];
in the second [verse] of that same [section], the sixth and sixth [letters] shall become the tenth and tenth.
In the third [case] it is that, but in the fourth, O Śakra, it consists of the syllables "Śakra-śakramita. || 2 ||
In the first cell of the third group, there are three letters from those [preceding ones];
in its second [cell], seven syllables; and in its third, the syllables of Śiva.
In the fourth [square], however, there should be letters numbering fifteen (15) in sequence;
in the first cell of the fourth group, the fourth [letter] from 'a' onwards [is placed].
In the second [case], it is eight less than twice that number; in the third, it is equal to the number of the suns (twelve).
The summary is as follows: that which is measured most abundantly in the fourth [group] consists of two syllables;
the group beginning with the first letter of one's own name is the "Siddha" group; and the second group, following in clockwise order from there, is the "Sādhya" group.
The third is *susiddha* (well-accomplished), and the fourth is *ari* (enemy). Furthermore, within that same grid (*koṣṭha*) of the *siddha*-group [of letters] on page 5a,
if there is a letter of the mantra associated with the first letter of one's own name, it is *siddhasiddha*.

If the letters of the mantra are present in that same group in the second square, it is *siddhasādhya*; if they are present in that same group in the third square, it is *siddhasusiddha*; if they are present in that same group in the fourth square, it is *siddhāri*. In the [number of] squares corresponding to the *siddha* group, [the result is determined by] the name.

If the letter of the mantra is in the same square as the letter of the name within the *susiddha* group—that is, in a square belonging to the *siddha* group—then the objective (*sādhya*) is accomplished. If it is in the second [square], the *sādhya* is difficult to accomplish (*sādhyasādhya*). If it is in the third, the *sādhya* is easily accomplished (*susiddha*). If it is in the fourth, the *sādhya* is an enemy (*ari*). If the letter of the name is in the same square as the letter of the mantra within the *susiddha* group, then [the result is] likewise according to that very square.

Then, in the first mantra-syllable, it is *susiddhasiddha*; in the second mantra-syllable, *susiddhasādhya*; in the third mantra-syllable, *susiddhasusiddha*; and in the fourth mantra-syllable, *susiddhāri*.

In the enemy group (arivarga), if a letter of the mantra exists in the same numbered square as the letters of the name belonging to the Siddha group, it is "enemy-Siddha" (arisiddha); in the second [square], it is "enemy-Sādhya" (arisādhya); in the third, it is "enemy-very-Siddha" (arisusiddha); and in the fourth, it is "enemy-enemy" (aryari). These designations apply specifically to those squares because they reside therein; their application to the mantras is secondary (gauṇa).

The application of "Siddha" and so forth is a designation for the mantras themselves; alternatively, due to their connection with those [mantras], the application is figuratively used for the squares (*koṣṭha*). This is another matter. Now, regarding their results: a "Siddha-Siddha" mantra yields its fruit from the recitation (*japa*) and other rites as prescribed in the ritual manual (*kalpa*), provided that success is not achieved through a single attempt; in such a case, the procedure must be performed three times.
Following such scriptures, it follows that a *siddha* [mantra] grants its fruit through twice the number of recitations (*japa*) and so forth as the number stated in the *Kalpa*;
however, a *susiddha* [mantra] grants its fruit by mere attainment, without requiring recitation and the like. (p.

The *siddhāri* (enemy that is successful) awaits its opportunity in easy tasks; the *hativāndhava* (destroyer of kinsmen) yields results through the great hardship of following many repetitions of *japa* and other rites once the goal has been achieved; the *sādhyasādhya* (difficult to achieve and difficult to master) yields results with extreme difficulty;

the *sādhyasusiddha* (difficult to achieve but easy to master) yields results by doubling the number of *japa* and other rites prescribed for a *kalpa*; and the *sādhyāri* (difficult to achieve and an enemy).
It robs the practitioner of all his prosperity. A *susiddhasiddha* [mantra] grants its fruit through the recitation (*japa*) prescribed in the ritual manual (*kalpa*), just like a *siddhasiddha*;

however, one need not follow the various branches of scripture such as "if success is not attained with one [recitation]," nor is it necessary to increase the number according to the current age (*yuga*). A *susiddhasādhya* [mantra] [grants its fruit] through the aforementioned recitation and so forth, in accordance with the qualities of the age.

One who is well-perfected (*susiddha*) and well-kindled (*sudīpta*), being dependent on [factors] such as prosperity (*vṛddhi*) for the bestowal of fruit, has attained such a state through the exertions of various kinds of recitations (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), and so forth performed in previous lives; he should be employed in tasks that are difficult, let alone those that are easy.

A mantra becomes effective only when it was given as a gift in a previous birth; however, that is not necessarily the case. If, upon examining the initial letter of the enemy's name, the mantra is found to be *susiddha* (well-accomplished) for that enemy, then if it were employed by him for purposes such as killing (*māraṇa*), his own death or other misfortune would not occur; rather, [the harm] would fall upon the one who employs such a mantra against him.
Therefore, only a mantra that has become an enemy should be employed against an enemy in such an action, and certainly not one that is otherwise.
One who has fully mastered the enemy is a destroyer of the lineage of the practitioner.

An *ari-siddha* [planet] causes the destruction of the practitioner’s son; an *ari-sādhya* causes the destruction of his wife; an *ari-su-siddha* gradually brings about the total annihilation of his lineage; and an *ari-ari*, by its mere arrival, kills the practitioner. In this context, even by the second and subsequent syllables of the practitioner’s name, the mantra becomes subject to the influence of the [planetary] states.
p.
6a) The investigation of the *siddha* and other [categories] should be performed according to the respective order for all four classes of letters (*varṇa*), not merely for the first two;
therein, too, the vowels presented in sequence [are to be applied] to the vowels presented in sequence, and the consonants [to the consonants].

The mantra associated with the first, second, third, and so on [syllables] must be performed together with those first, second, third, and subsequent consonants; it is not to be done according to one's own whim. Therefore, as in other systems (*tantrāntara*), the rule of *tantra* (the simultaneous application) is to be observed here as well.
Furthermore, the Lord has indicated by the fact that the dot (*bindu*) and the visarga are neither written nor mentioned in this wheel (*cakra*).
In the case of the mantra syllables beginning with *hṛt-prāṇa* and so forth,

as well as the practitioner’s syllables such as *Valabhadra* and others, one should not include the first vowel (*a*) when considering the consonantal correspondence for each individual syllable. However, in the mantra "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*), the letter *ja* is associated with its subsequent vowel (*ai*).

And the Blessed One indicated by means of two doors that there is no opening [of the door] in such cases. Therefore, in a place where there is no opening, the first vowel must be determined as either favorable or unfavorable.

When this discrimination has been made, if there is an abundance of enemy letters (*arivarṇa*) and letters to be accomplished (*sādhyavarṇa*), there is the state of being to be abandoned; however, if there is an abundance of accomplished (*siddha*) and well-accomplished (*susiddha*) letters, [it is not so].

Furthermore, even when there is equality [of alternatives], the state of being acceptable depends on following the first letter; therefore, its primary acceptance is the well-established position—this should be reflected upon. Moreover, the Lord, by indicating that one must also consider conformity with letters other than the first syllable, has [thereby] shown what is stated in other tantras as well.
Furthermore, that which is taught as being to be followed even after deliberation is as follows:
where the first and last letters are established and accompanied by the mantra, it yields fruit quickly. (1)
If it occurs at the beginning or end of the syllables of the person to be accomplished, it yields fruit with great difficulty.
Perfectly accomplished at the beginning and the end, it bestows the fruits of all desired objects. || 3 ||
One whose first letter is 'r' must be avoided as an enemy. || 4 ||
First, that which is already accomplished and last, that which is yet to be accomplished, becomes fruitful through double recitation and other means. || 5 ||
That mantra which is "Siddha" at the beginning and "Susiddha" at the end bestows success inevitably through the recitation as prescribed.
One for whom there is a Siddha at the beginning and an enemy at the end must be abandoned, even if accompanied by a mantra.
That mantra whose first syllable is the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and its last syllable is the established (*siddha*), bestows success through three-fold recitation.
He is to be accomplished at the beginning, perfectly established at the end, and bestows success according to the path described in the Kalpa.
A mantra whose beginning is the thing to be accomplished (sādhya) but whose end is its enemy must be avoided with great effort. || 10 ||
The established doctrine, beginning with "well-accomplished" (susiddha) and so forth, yields its fruit through recitation as previously described. || 11 ||
But that which begins with the "well-accomplished" (susiddha) and ends with the "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) brings success through fourfold recitation. || 12 ||
A mantra that begins with *susiddha* and ends with *ari* is middling. || 13 ||
A mantra whose first syllable is *ari* (a semivowel) and whose last syllable is *asiddha* (an unaspirated stop), even if it is otherwise effective, must be abandoned.
A mantra whose phonemes are well-established in its beginning, middle, and end bestows auspicious results. || 15 ||
In the beginning, middle, and end, the one who describes the goal remains indifferent. || 16 ||
One who is well-perfected in these three places certainly accomplishes all goals. || 17 ||
The mantra located in the three places is death; of this there is no doubt. || 18 ||
A mantra that begins with a *siddha* [syllable] and ends with a pair of *sādhya* [syllables] becomes useless. || 19 ||
Beginning with Siddha and ending with Dvisusiddha, it accomplishes all desired aims and purposes. || 20 ||
A mantra beginning with *siddha* and ending with the pair of enemies (*ari*) is destructive. || 21 ||
If [the planet] is an enemy at the beginning, a Siddha in the middle, and a Sādhya at the end, there is accomplishment of the task with difficulty;
its fruit will indeed be of its own nature. || 22 ||
If the enemy [number] occurs at the end, the first, and the middle, it is a "sādhya-yuga" [configuration]; the task will be delayed, yet it shall be pacified very quickly. || 23 ||
When the first and third [syllables] are to be accomplished and the second is already accomplished, then success comes to one who recites the additional [syllable]. || 24 ||
When the [mantra] is established at the beginning and the end, and is being accomplished in the middle, even then the attainment of the fruit occurs through an increase in recitation. || 25 ||
Where the syllables of the Siddha-mantra are encapsulated by the syllable *ari*, that mantra brings about destruction. || 26 ||
Even a mantra whose syllables are well-established but are encircled by enemies (ari) brings about destruction. || 27 ||
Where the syllables of the sādhya are encapsulated by the siddha along with the mantra, that bestows swift accomplishment. || 28 ||
A mantra in which the syllables of the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya) are encapsulated by the syllables of the well-accomplished one (susiddha) also bestows swift success. || 29 ||
Wherever the enemy [mantra] is encapsulated by the *siddha* [mantra], that mantra is not an enemy; rather, it performs its function from the very end of its difficulties. || 30 ||

Wherever there is an enemy letter encased by a *susiddha* [letter], that too is not an enemy in every respect, but rather performs its function with difficulty; one that is *siddha* and encased by a *sādhya* brings about success only with extreme difficulty. || 32 ||
Even one who is well-accomplished, when encased by the object of accomplishment (sādhya), bestows success only with great difficulty. || 33 ||
Where a mantra is mastered while being encircled by enemies, it is difficult to perform even with distant sacrificial fuel.
Wherever a mantra is well-accomplished but encircled by its enemy, that mantra too is extremely distant [from success] and must be avoided. || 35 ||

And here, the name characterized by such [Vedic] definitions as "He who, though asleep, is awake" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.11) and so forth, should be adopted in all cases. When there is a plurality of such names, that uttered by the father is used. If even that is not uniform, then for women, that which was designated by the father and others at the time of initiation in the husband's house is used; if initiated in the father's house, that which was designated there is used.

Many authorities maintain that the distinction between the letter *va* and the letter *la*, as well as the letters at the end of the *pa*-group (*pavarga*) and the semivowels (*antastha*), should be understood from other texts.

It occurs to me that the intention of the Blessed One is this: having first established the caste corresponding to the birth-star (*nakṣatra*) at which one was born, one should consider compatibility based on the mere letters of the conventional name alone.

Otherwise, how could it be said that "this mantra is well-accomplished, well-accomplished, born from the exertion performed in previous births"? And how could it be said that "due to the exhaustion of the worship performed in previous births, the mantra becomes a debt for practitioners in this life by not yielding its fruit"? For it has been stated by the Blessed One himself in this very tantra:

The name uttered by the father and others is likewise used in the ritual; for one who is not himself learned in the Tantric scriptures, such knowledge may be obtained through the instruction of the father or others, since it is possible for them to establish a convention for the son or other child using a name that accords with the desired mantra. Birth under a specific portion of a particular constellation is not dependent on anything else; therefore—

The contingency of violating one's own independence by resorting to another tantra for the sake of discerning the distinction between the two *vakāra*s and two *lakāra*s has already been addressed; therefore, even though she is adorned with independence—characterized by not depending on other systems—she resorts to another tantra, thinking, "I shall adopt that [tantra] alone by which she, while sleeping, awakens. Thus, she is independent (*svatantra*).
In this present tantra, the removal of doubts has been made delightful; even the objection regarding the destruction of sins has been answered.

According to the method stated in this tantra, one must rely on considerations such as compatibility based on names corresponding to the specific birth asterism (*nakṣatra*), because for one born in the latter part of Aśvinī, [the name] Bharaṇī [would not apply].
In the eastern portion of Pūrvaphalgunī, both [types of births] shall have names such as Ānandaśarman; likewise,
for one born in the northern portion of Bharaṇī and for one born in the eastern portion of Kṛttikā,
there shall be names such as Īśvaraśarman.

If it is the case that this applies to subsequent instances as well, how could there be a determination of a single name based on birth under a specific asterism? According to the method of the *Jyotiḥśāstra*,
those born in the latter half of Aśvinī have names such as Cauramardana, Lakṣmīnidhi, and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "līlādhara," it should be stated that the assertion that [the child] will be born under the first half of Bharaṇī is not as authoritative as it appears,

because it depends upon other scriptures concerning the wife. This is because, when examining the compatibility of the two names mentioned— such as "Ānandaśarman" and so forth— in the Siddhādicakra and other such systems, there is no deficiency.

If one considers the compatibility of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), then that specific [result] which is desired follows; for this very reason, it is said in the *Saṃhitā* that [the result] is according to the name of one's own asterism (*svarkṣa*).

Furthermore, in another tantra, it is stated that one should examine [the matter] from the syllable of the birth asterism (*janmarkṣa*), where the first syllable of the name is used. If it is asked, "What is the recourse for such statements as 'he sleeps' or 'he wakes'?"—listen: in the case of knowledge, [it refers to] the zodiac sign (*rāśi*) and the asterism (*nakṣatra*).

Based on the statement from the *Nārāyaṇīya*, "beginning with the first letter of one's own name," and the citation by Palapādācārya, "the birth asterism begins at birth and ends with the star of the mantra," it is clear that for one whose birth asterism is manifest, the procedure is according to the birth asterism; but for one whose birth asterism is lost, Piṅgalā says one should speak according to the letters of the name.

And because of the scriptural statement, "He is born under his own star," the expansion of his knowledge occurs precisely at that time. Without deliberation, for what reason would there be such an impulsion?

This mantra is well-established by its designated name, and its state of being "well-accomplished" (susiddha) and so forth is possible only for one who has exerted effort in a previous birth. However, in the case of those names designated through a process preceded by the consideration of auspiciousness, one cannot infer the exertion of a previous birth.

It cannot be said that compatibility with everything is possible solely by means of a well-known name; for since there are many such [names], why might the opposite not also be the case—that [compatibility] exists through the birth-star (*janmarkṣa*)? This is because of the statement beginning with "unknown," etc.

Since it is possible for *praṇaścam* and so forth to serve as the deciding factor (*vinigamaka*), one might ask: "If this is the method, how is the second and subsequent syllables of names to be known once the first syllable has been determined? The answer is: no; because when establishing the names by placing the asterism's syllable at the beginning, one must simply consider what is consistent with the single-syllable [name]. This is the summary.

The method for purifying wealth and debt is as follows: according to the aforementioned direction, starting from the letter of one's own birth-star (janmanakṣatra) or name, and proceeding through the sequence of the Mātṛkā letters up to the first letter of the mantra, one should calculate the resulting number and multiply it by three. Then, by dividing the resulting number by seven, the remainder is known as the "name" (ko nāma).

The "heap" (*rāśi*) is the number obtained by counting from the first letter of the mantra up to the letter corresponding to one's own birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*); this number is then tripled, and the resulting total is divided by seven— the remainder is the "mantra-heap," starting from whichever letter [of the alphabet] it corresponds to.

The remaining number resulting from the calculation and so forth is its "ruling factor" (*vāśi*). In that regard, if the numerical mass of the mantra is a higher number, then that mantra is excellent; it must necessarily be practiced by a practitioner whose numerical mass is lower, even if they have failed to attain their desired goal despite the exertion of worship through recitation, fire-offerings (*homa*), and other means in previous births.

This very [type of] mantra is called "debt-bearing" (*ṛṇin*). As for that mantra which has fewer syllables, it is accomplished by this practitioner through the grace of the Guru; or else, having attained the state of being debt-bearing even from a mantra obtained in a previous birth merely by receiving it, he fails to practice it due to being intoxicated with the pride of power over all his desired goals.
That which is denoted by the word "wealth" (dhanin) is not to be adopted when one desires what is wished for in this very life; however,

if the desired object is common to future lives as well, or if it is something to be accomplished through enemies and so forth, then [one may adopt] a mantra and the like beginning with that syllable.
We neither exclude nor include such cases; for in this system, even a remainder of zero is equivalent to a remainder of seven, and a remainder of six is indeed equal to a remainder of zero.
Furthermore, in this system, it is prohibited for a remainder to terminate as a remainder of seven.

The manner of resolving enmity (*vairaśuddhi*) is as follows: there is mutual opposition between the fiery (*āgneya*) letters and the earth (*bhauma*) letters on the one hand, and the watery (*jalīya*) letters on the other; likewise, there is mutual opposition between the airy (*vāyavya*) letters and the watery letters, as well as the earth letters;
however, no letter has opposition with the ether (*ākāśa*) letters. Thus, [the letters] beginning with *sa*, *ra*, and *k* are fiery.

The practitioner should not adopt such things as the water-born syllables (*jalīyākṣara*), the divisions (*bhāgaka*), the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) of the Uttarāṣāḍhā constellation, or mantras such as "Obeisance to the Lord of Sītā" (*sītāpataye namaḥ*). This concludes the discussion.
Likewise, there is a mutual contradiction between mantras dedicated to male deities and those dedicated to female deities; therefore, neither of these two [classes] may be primary.

Since the *mādeya* (the object to be attained) is primary, there is no harm even in the worship of mantras such as those of the Guru, Mantra-kiṅkara, and others, which serve as ancillary (*aṅga*) components.

Likewise, there is mutual opposition between fierce (*krūra*) and gentle (*saumya*) mantras; similarly, there is mutual opposition between the *Tvaritā* and *Nṛsiṃha* mantras, as well as between weapon-mantras (*astra-mantra*) such as the *Sudarśana* and others. Therefore, those two [types of mantras] are not one.
That it is to be worshipped by practitioners—this is the general direction [of the teaching].

Thus, following the acceptance of the primary knowledge (*pradhānavidyā*) in accordance with [the disciple's] suitability, [the teacher should initiate] the well-examined disciple on the fourteenth lunar day (p.

One should then impart the *Jvālāmālinī* mantra. Furthermore, for the sake of his own mastery (*yogyatā*) and accomplishment (*siddhi*), the disciple should himself practice that mantra even after it has been mastered by the Guru.

Thereafter, the first consecration (*prathamābhiṣeka*) must be performed for the initial instruction regarding the principal deity. The procedure for this is as follows: vermilion (*darada*), red lead (*sindūra*), and so forth.

In a temple dedicated to one’s own chosen guru— which is colored with red ochre and other pigments, perfumed with the incense of sandalwood and other fragrances, illuminated on all sides by rows of lamps and the like, and adorned with canopies, flower garlands, and so forth— when the birth of the disciple occurs under any of the signs of Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, or Aquarius,
provided it is endowed with the auspicious planetary conjunctions and qualities such as being the eleventh house [from the ascendant], or otherwise...
Starting from sunrise until the end of the next sunrise, on a full moon day in the form of the Perfectly Awakened One (*saṃbuddha*),

or on a day favorable to oneself under the auspices of a benefic planet and in any zodiac sign or ascendant, or on a day when the three syllables characterized as will be described later coincide, or on the fifth or tenth lunar day.

On a full-moon day that corresponds to one of the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*), or on the birthday of one's own teacher (*nātha*), or on the day of one's teacher’s rest (*virāma*), or on the birthday of one's own preceptor, or during the four final *ghaṭikās* of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)— on any such occasion, having fixed the time for the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*),
one should, on the day preceding it, pay homage to the Guru, Gaṇapati, and the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), and remember Śrī Viṣṇu.
Immediately after performing my daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), having received the command of my guru, and having recorded the place, time, my own lineage (*gotra*),

zodiac sign (*rāśi*), name, and desire, I shall perform the first instruction according to the prescribed ritual for the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, in accordance with her royal decree and as best as my intellect permits; as an ancillary part of that, [for one] of such-and-such a lineage...

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "I shall perform the selection of the Brahmin named so-and-so, born under such-and-such a zodiac sign, preceded by worship with the nine coverings," [one proceeds].

One should pour the water for the *arghya* and other offerings held in the right hand onto the ground; then, having prepared the general *arghya* according to the directions to be described below, one should worship the Guru with the ninefold offerings (*navopacāra*) characterized by the horse and so forth, using the verse-mantra beginning with "For me, blinded by the darkness of ignorance... and these rings.

Having first made the formal declaration: "O [Name], of [Gotra] and [Zodiac Sign], I choose you, a Brāhmaṇa, as my Guru for the purpose of the first instruction in the Śrī Mahātripurasundarī Vidyā," the candidate should offer this to him according to the ritual procedure of selection (*varaṇasāmayī*). The Yoginīs and Yogins should do likewise.

Having first performed worship with materials of slightly less value, one should choose [the preceptor] individually, stating the formula: "I choose you for the purpose of assisting in the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) to be performed by the Guru. And the chosen Guru, having donned the materials for the choice upon his respective limbs as appropriate, [should perform] the previously mentioned...

On a patch of ground measuring three cubits within the temple, having drawn the Śrīcakra— centered with a dot suitable for the placement of the jar's base— using a paste of camphor, sandalwood, saffron, agallochum, and musk, or else with sandalwood mixed with red sandalwood and vermilion; then, in its central portion, [one should prepare] with twenty māṣakas and palas...
The measure of a *khārī* consists of twenty-five thousand and sixty (*25,060*) *pala*s, which is equivalent to four thousand and ninety-six (*4,096*) *pala*s multiplied by six.

One should fill [the vessel] with water from the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, or other such sources that flows upward, mixed with any one of the following decoctions: a decoction of all the medicinal herbs of every color, a decoction of the medicinal herbs of the specific mantra taught for that purpose, a decoction of medicinal herbs consisting of a mere emission (*visarga*), or a decoction of milk-soaked [herbs];
and [the vessel] should be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, each subsequent material being superior to the preceding.

Having placed the pitcher as a secondary element with the root mantra, one should deposit within it the nine gems, gold, copper, and sandalwood using the root mantra alone; having likewise cast rice and other grains as they are available, one should place upon its mouth sprouts of *induvallī*, mango, jackfruit, and *aśvattha* trees, as well as a *mātuliṅga* fruit, and then [settle] that [pitcher].

Having wrapped the *kalaśa* at its base and at its neck with two red cloths—one for each—therein, within that *kalaśa*, one should visualize the goddess Sarvamaṅgalā in the form of a *bindu*. This consists of a double-walled *bhūpura* (fortress) with four gates and supporting pillars; inside that, a thirty-two-petalled lotus; inside that, a sixteen-petalled lotus; and inside that, an eight-petalled lotus.

Having visualized the wheel of daily worship (*nityapūjācakra*), one should there— following the sequence of sitting on the seat, sipping water (*ācamana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and so forth as described in the introduction— worship Sarvamaṅgalā with the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*) beginning with the foot-bath (*pādya*) and ending with betel (*tāmbūla*). Then, in the locations to be described, in the form of petals and so forth, [one should worship] Bhadrā and the others.

Having worshipped the fourfold enclosure (varaṇacatuṣka) in the center—each successive enclosure beginning with the first—preceded by the offering of flowers and the presentation of the worship, one should then worship the three enclosures of the couples of deities (mithunadevatā). The procedure for this is as follows:
just as in the consecration of the Śrīcakra, fire [is employed] to remove defects such as burning or striking the image.

The form of worship consisting of the sequence of the digits of the sun and moon is the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); likewise, even in the first initiation, the object of the fundamental withdrawal extends from fire (*vahni*) up to the moon (*soma*).
The very sequence of Kalās alone must be followed as the method of worship; this is indeed the path approved even by the Nidhi-kāras.

Therefore, here, in twenty locations—consisting of the tips of eight petals of the fire [lotus], sixteen petals, and twelve petals—one couple of deities is assigned to each pair of locations, such that there is one couple deity for every two places.

One should worship with their respective mantras as follows: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Yaṃ*, I worship the sandals of Agnidhūmnārcis; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Raṃ*, I worship the sandals of Vahāṣmā; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Laṃ*, I worship the sandals of Śucijvalinī; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vaṃ*, I worship the sandals of Tejojvālinī; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Śaṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Prabhāvisphuliṅginī.

"I worship Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṣaṃ Dāva, O auspicious sandals; I worship Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Saṃ Śikhī, O sandals whose form is fire; I worship Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Haṃ Dyuti, O tawny-colored sandals; I worship Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Laṃ Dā, O carrier of oblations; I worship Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kṣaṃ Grāsaka, O carrier of offerings—I worship. Then...

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra: "I worship the Root-Vidyā, the All-Auspicious (Sarvamaṅgalā), the Eternal (Nityā) Pādukā," one should offer the worship of the fourth enclosure to those deities with a handful of flowers, saying: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the fourth enclosure—the All-Auspicious, the Eternal—accept this worship. Thus, the worship of the fourth enclosure should be offered to those very deities.

Furthermore, since the prayer is primarily addressed to the presiding deity in every instance, one should thereafter worship the twelve *mithuna* deities of the Sun in the twenty-four locations consisting of the sixteen-petaled [lotus], the four [petals] of the [remaining] circle, the thirty-two-petaled [lotus], and the twenty petals at the tips; their mantras are as follows: *hrīṃ śrīṃ kaṃ*.
Maṃ dhātṛ (p. 11b) tapinī pāduke pūjayāmi 2 | Khaṃ vaṃ aryamatāpinī pāduke pūjayāmi 2 | Gaṃ phaṃ |

Mitra, with Dhūmrā and Apādukā—Pūjā. 2 Ghaṃ Paṃ, Varuṇa and Mahīcī—Pādukā—Pūjā. 2 Ṅaṃ Naṃ, Aṃśu and Jvālinī—Pādukā—Pūjā. 2 Caṃ Dhaṃ, Bhaga and Ruci—Pādukā—Pūjā. 2 Chaṃ Daṃ, Vivasvat and Suṣumṇā—Pādukā—Pūjā. 2 Jaṃ Thaṃ, Indra and Bhogadā—Pādukā—Pūjā. 2 Iṃ Taṃ, Pūṣan and Viśvā—Pādukā—Pūjā. 2 Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ñaṃ Ṇaṃ.
Parjanya and Bhoginī, worship the sandals (pādukā). 2 Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṭaṃ Ḍhaṃ, Tvaṣṭṛ and Dhāriṇī, worship the sandals.

2 Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṭhaṃ Ḍaṃ, Viṣṇu and Kṣamā, worship the sandals. Having thus worshipped all the deities of the Sūrya-mithuna, at the end of the root-mantra (mūlavidyā), [one should say]: "I worship the sandal of the eternal Sarvamaṅgalā," while standing in the center.

Having worshipped the Goddess, one should offer the *puṣpāñjali* for the presentation of worship, saying: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these eternal goddesses of the sixth enclosure, Sarvamaṅgalās, accept this worship. Then, one should worship the eight petals starting with Bhadrā, the sixteen petals starting with the powers (Śaktis) such as Pūraṇī, and the thirty-two petals starting with Kāminī.
Because it is occupied by Svecchā and the others, worship is prescribed at the tips of those respective petals;
likewise, because the locations of the square (catur-asra) are occupied by the twenty deities beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Kālaśakti,
[worship] is performed in those very locations according to the rule within the thirty-two-petaled lotus, leaving a remainder for the twelve-petaled [lotus].
Having worshipped the six pairs of deities, one should worship the ten pairs of deities related to the Moon who are presided over by Vasiṣṭha.
Their mantras are as follows: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṃ, I worship the sandals of Amṛta; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Āṃ, I worship the sandals of Mānada; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Iṃ, I worship the sandals of Pūṣan; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Īṃ...

Pāduke-pūjā: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṛṃ, worship of the sandals of Śaśin; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ḷṃ, worship of the sandals of Candraka; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ḷṃ, worship of the sandals of Kānta; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Eṃ, worship of the sandals of Jyotsnā; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aiṃ, worship of the sandals of Śrī; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ, worship of the sandals of Prīta; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Auṃ, worship of the sandals of Aṅgada.

Having worshipped the deities of the lunar digits (candrakalā) and the couples (mithuna-devatās) with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ pūrṇapādukāyai pūjayāmi* and *hrīṃ śrīṃ aḥ pūrṇāmṛtapādukāyai pūjayāmi*, and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the root mantra (mūlavidyā) with: *sarvamaṅgalāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, [one should worship] these eternal Sarvamaṅgalās with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*.

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the words, "May the deities of the seven lineages accept this offering," and having performed the remaining three services consisting of hymn (*stotra*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), and prostration (*namaskāra*), one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony with camphor-filled wicks and the like at the conclusion of the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) and daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*), and repeatedly ask for forgiveness.

Having visualized the goddesses of the letters (varṇadevatās), beginning with Śakti and Uṣāpanī, as dissolved into the principal limbs [of the deity], one should dissolve Sarvamangalā into one’s own self by means of the Khecarī-mudrā. Then, although the Śrīcakra has been drawn below, one should contemplate it within the water of the pitcher (kalaśa) because the place of the Bindu is occupied by the pitcher; therein, [one should meditate on] that which is to be described, neither deficient nor excessive.

One should worship Śrī Tripurasundarī according to the mode of worship with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) following the system of nine enclosures (*navāvaraṇa*). However, there is this specific distinction here: because the Bindu is occupied by the Kalaśa, one should first worship the form of the Bindu within the primary deity’s own Cakra, and then perform the worship of Aṇimā and the other Siddhis in the Cakra situated below the Kalaśa.
The ritual action must be performed in those very locations that are perceptibly present, and not merely in those locations as they are imagined;
thus, even the purpose of hearing the sound of the *cakra* in the lower location is lost there in the absence of worship.
It would have only an unseen (transcendental) purpose; thus, having performed the daily recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*) at the conclusion of the worship,
and having offered three circles of food and so forth with the *Kuru Kullā* mantra divided into three parts, and having asked for forgiveness for the kingdom with camphor and other substances,
one should satisfy the previously invited *yoginīs* and *yogins* with garments, ornaments, food, and other offerings.
One should pass the night with festivities such as dancing and singing.
Thus ends the section on latent impressions (vāsanā).

Then, in the morning, having performed his daily and occasional obligatory rites, the Guru should again worship the deity of the Vidyā with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra). Then, while touching [the disciple] with the "life-giving hand" (jīvakara) and reciting the mantras of the deities of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga),
he should contemplate the identity of the Goddess and the water, and as before, perform the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) of the Śakti.

Having dismissed the principal goddess and asked for her forgiveness, while conchs, horns, and other instruments are being sounded, the Guru— accompanied by his wife and surrounded by yoginīs and yogis— raises the water-pot and places it upon the head of the disciple, who is seated facing east upon a pure, well-decorated, square diagram of the *mātṛkā* letters situated in the north-eastern corner.

Having placed a fruit upon the mouth of the water-pot, the Guru, facing eastward and situated in his own station, should sprinkle the disciple— who is likewise situated in his station— with the water from the pot containing the cast-in sprouts three times, in such a way that [the disciple] becomes like a student; then, that water [should be visualized as flowing] through the path of the pores of the skin from the *brahmarandhra* down to the *mūlādhāra*.

While contemplating that [the water] enters within the body and performs the cleansing of all defects, one should perform the sprinkling with the entire water from the jar, leaving only what remains for personal use. (p.

Having bathed his entire body, he should sit upon his own seat. The disciple, wearing a pure white upper garment and adorned with perfumes, garlands, and the like, should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the water from the jar. He should then offer to the Guru perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and betel leaf, followed by prostrations, the recitation of hymns, and the act known as the surrender of one's own self.

Having worshipped with the nine services (navopacāra) according to the Master’s wish, one should offer everything—one's entire possession—as a fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru, whether collectively or individually, according to one's wealth: elephants, horses, a queen (mahiṣī), rams, cows, female slaves, land, gold, ornaments, garments, houses, villages, and so forth; uttering "tada huṃ tada huṃ," and reciting "Obeisance to You, O Blessed Master," and so on.

Having praised [the deity] three times with five verses, offered three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and prostrated three times with the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*), he should stand silently before the Guru with palms joined in reverence (*baddhāñjali*). Then, having caused the disciple to enter the *Jvālāmālinī* wheel, the Guru should perform the piercing (*vedha*) to be described hereafter; thereafter, the Guru, having extracted the principles (*tattva*) and so forth from the vase (*kalaśa*)...
Having seated the disciple directly beneath the *kalaśa* (vase), and having meditated upon himself as non-different from the Goddess,

he gazes at the disciple with a compassionate, unblinking gaze. He [visualizes] the syllable *Saṃ*, accompanied by the letters beginning with *Ā* and ending with *Ta*, residing within the deity Sākinī, who is golden-hued and situated at the base of the staff-like *suṣumṇā* channel, which begins from the central region between the anus and the genitals.
The external light situated within the triangle inside the pericarp of the four-petaled lotus-base;

the staff of the *suṣumṇā* located in the region of the heart; the deity Rākinī, red as vermilion, situated within the triangle inside the pericarp of the twelve-petaled lotus joined with the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*.

The solar radiance situated in the center, located at the region below the *brahmarandhra* within the stalk of the *suṣumṇā*, existing as a white luster at the tip of the staff, residing within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus, and positioned in the middle of a triangle.

Having meditated upon this very Śrīcakra, which is the splendor of the Moon and composed of light itself, within one's own heart; and having meditated upon that same cakra as it has emerged from one's own nostril through the path of the outgoing breath and entered the heart of the disciple via the disciple's incoming breath; and having meditated there upon the Goddess, red in color and of graceful form—one should worship her.

Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (vitalization) of the Goddess— of this very Goddess Tripurasundarī— with the mantra beginning "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of the Goddess... [are] here, in the wheel located in the heart of the disciple," and having performed the fourfold rites beginning with installation (*sthāpana*) preceded by the display of their respective mudrās, one should worship the Goddess there with the five mental offerings (*pañcopacāra*), followed by the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*).

Having performed the *nyāsa* of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the expansion (*vyāsa*), and the *nyāsa* of the goddess of speech (*vāgdevatā*)— which are denoted by the three stages of *nyāsa*— upon the body of the disciple in such a manner that the disciple does not hear those mantras, and having caused dancing, instrumental music, and so forth to be performed, the Guru, standing in the left position at the level of the disciple's ear, should remain in such a place that the disciple may become [one with] the Guru.

Having first taught nineteen vidyās— the vidyā of hand-purification (karaśuddhi), the vidyā of ritual placement (nyāsa), the vidyā of the fourfold seat (āsana), the vidyā of the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), and the vidyā of the eight goddesses of speech (vāgdevatā)— whose essential forms will be described hereafter, one should then teach the primary vidyā as the thirtieth; thereafter follows the contemplation of the oneness of the deity, the mantra, and the guru.

The disciple should be instructed on the procedure as follows: preceded by the contemplation of the non-duality of the mantra, the deity, and the guru, he should recite the principal vidyā one hundred times within that very cakra. Then, rising at the command of the Lord (nātha), he should perform, as before, the recitation of hymns, the offering of handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali), and prostrations; thereafter, he should feed the yoginīs, the yogis, and the brahmins.
Having further gratified [the preceptor] with food and other offerings, one should conclude this rite by means of the recollection of Viṣṇu and other such practices.
(p. 14a) And the disciple who has received initiation should reside in the preceptor’s house for three full days, performing service to the preceptor; he must not [leave].

If it were not so— that is, if [the disciple] were neither in his own home nor in another’s house— there would be no attainment of identity with the mantra-deity through the Guru. Consequently, the disciple, having purified his self through the aforementioned recitation and meditation preceded by the contemplation of identity with the Guru, the mantra, and the deity, and having obtained the qualification for the Full Initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) and so forth, [proceeds] based on that to the second [initiation].
One should follow the procedure for initiation.
Thus concludes the procedure for the first initiation, which has as its fruit the removal of impurities.
Now follows the procedure for the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), which constitutes the preliminary limb of the second instruction.

The *pūrṇābhiṣeka* (full initiation) is indeed threefold, distinguished by the categories of superior, middling, and inferior. Even if one has attained progressively higher stages among the preceding positions due to being incapable [of the former], this very position is indeed the superior one; for if it were inferior, there would be no connection to the fruit resulting from its performance, even when one possesses the capacity for each of the preceding positions.

Therein, the method for the supreme *pūrṇābhiṣeka* is as follows: during the fifteen lunar days (*tithis*) beginning from the first day (*pratipadā*) after the full moon day (*pūrṇimā*) and ending with the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), one should mentally select any one of those days within the fortnight consisting of sixteen solar days (*sāvana-dina*).
Then, on the preceding full moon day, the disciple—having performed the daily and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*) in the morning—[proceeds].
Having prostrated before the Guru and the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), and after performing the worship of Vināyaka and the remembrance of Viṣṇu, one should receive the permission of the Guru.

Then, having specified the place, time, one’s own lineage (gotra), zodiacal sign (rāśi), name, and desired object, according to the application of one’s intellect and in accordance with the prescribed ritual:
"Because, by this first instruction, the status of being a Guru has arisen for me, [O you] of such-and-such lineage, such-and-such zodiacal sign, and such-and-such name..."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with the highest option of the door of existence (*bhāvadvāra-uttamapakṣa*), "I shall perform the second initiation preceded by the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*)," one should again, as before, inscribe the second [initiation] as being prior to the morning of the initiation.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Preceded by worship, I shall perform the investiture (*āvaraṇa*) with the materials for the investiture as they have been prepared for the venerable Guru and for the Yoginīs and Yogins," and having worshipped the Guru with the nine services (*navopacāra*) beginning with scents as previously shown, [one should worship] with these rings, earrings, garments, and the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*.

Having declared, "I choose you as my guru to perform the preliminary rite of initiation," and having presented the various materials for that selection to the guru, one should also choose the Yoginīs and others, preceded by the statement, "I choose them for the purpose of assisting in the consecration performed by the venerable guru. Once chosen, the guru should say, "I am chosen."

Having accepted those materials, he should wear them upon the respective limbs as appropriate. Then, in the Nātha-maṇḍala described for the full moon day and other such occasions, he should worship each of the nine Nāthas with the ninefold offerings (navopacāra).
Then, at dawn, having performed the daily rites and so forth pertaining to the first day of the fortnight consisting of sixteen days, [he should proceed].

On a smooth and level ground measuring nine cubits in length and breadth, one should draw the Śrīcakra of the nature to be described hereafter; then, having fashioned a single circle within each of all the ninety-nine locations of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-sthāna*), one should [draw] equal intervals within each of those circles.

Having established fifteen marks by casting lines, one should produce fifteen triangles in sequence— starting from the first mark to the second, from the second to the third, and so on up to the fifteenth— within each circle, together with a pericarp.
Together with the sixteen completed triangles, when one thousand five hundred and thirty-six triangles have been constructed,
[one should place] heaps of rice equal in number to those triangles, so that they are mutually intermingled.
In such a manner that they do not come into being, [one should prepare] for each of them a vessel made of either gold, silver, copper, or earth,

possessing its own respective primary elemental form as previously described, filled with the aforementioned decoction of medicinal herbs and the like, or with the water of a river, or with water measured according to one's own capacity, [and containing] the nine gems, gold, and copper.

Having established the jars with the root-mantra— jars which are filled with sandalwood and the seven grains, whose mouths are adorned with sprouts of *indravallī*, *vahnī*, mango, jackfruit, and *aśvattha* trees, along with the fruit of the citron, and whose necks and mouths are each wrapped with a single cloth— one should first [perform the rite] over the jar situated in the very center of all.

One should worship Sarvamaṅgalā by means of the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra), preceded by the visualization of her discus; the procedure for this shall be explained clearly in the section on Sarvamaṅgalā.

This, however, is the *smaraṇasūtra*— the meaningful collection of topics beginning with that worship: sitting on the seat, ritual sipping (*ācamana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), salutation to Gaṇeśa, recollection of Śrī Viṣṇu, prostration to the Guru, requesting his permission,
the worship of the nine lords (*navanātha*) based on the head, the hymn to the Guru, the extraction of the *pādukā*, and that which pertains to the *śrīcakra*.
The ritual procedure consists of: placing a heap of rice in thirty-six thousand five hundred locations;
establishing an equal number of water-jars; pouring an amount of water equivalent to one *khārī* measure into each jar;
wrapping them with two red cloths; and [placing] gold, copper, the nine gems, and the seven types of grain.

Having performed the rites beginning with the throwing of sandalwood and ending with the throwing of sprouts from the *vallī*, mango, breadfruit, and *aśvattha* trees, as well as the offering of *mātuluṅga* fruit, one should perform the daily worship of Sarvamaṅgalā within the water of that jar.

The preliminary rite of meditation (*cintana-pūjā-pūrvāṅga*), the worship of the sacrificial pedestal (*vali-pīṭha-pūjā*), the placement of the general offering vessel (*sāmānyārghya-pātra*) made of gold or another material and filled with water together with the five substances such as *gorocanā*,

the visualization of fire, sun, and moon by means of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Kulasundarī concerning the triad of its base and so forth, and [the visualization] concerning *gorocanā* and the other substances.

The meditation on the five elements; the meditation on the wheel of worship that is all-auspicious; the meditation on the distinction between that water and those substances; the consecration of the eyes with the mantra of ten syllables using those vidyās; the worship of the deities of its six limbs;
and the ritual materials for worship, including water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), a vessel for mental bathing, and perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and so forth.

At the conclusion of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), having performed *prāṇāyāma* with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) preceded by the mention of place, time, lineage (*gotra*), zodiac sign (*rāśi*), name, and desired object, and at the end of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the procedure of initiation (*dīkṣā*) preceded by the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), [one performs] the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) for the sake of establishing the fitness for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) of the principal deity, as well as [the purification of] one's own self (*svātma*).

"One should perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). Regarding this, any ritual action for which no mantra has been specified should be performed with the *Nityā* mantra. However, it should be understood that even when performing another deity's ritual—such as one's own daily (*nitya*) rite—if the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other such rites have already been performed, then since the self has already been consecrated by them, they need not be performed again; for indeed...

Since actions differ according to their purpose, which is the purification of one's own self, one engages even in other rites; what then to say of the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*) and so forth?

As for the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, because it is specifically prescribed as the placement (*nyāsa*) of the respective phonemes preceded by the specific *nityā-vidyā* [of each deity], it must be repeated for each individual daily worship (*nityārcana*). This does not apply to the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* concerning other deities, such as Kākadhā.

Regarding the phrase "tatratvasya" (in that case, however): following that, one should proceed with the sequence of four steps— namely, the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* preceded by the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) assignment, the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* together with the *vidyā*, the aforementioned six-limbed assignment, the phoneme assignment (*varṇanyāsa*), the pervasive assignment (*vyāpakanyāsa*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), meditation (*dhyāna*), the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhāpana*), the visualization of the deity as having the form of radiating rays, the contemplation of the powers (*śakti*) of the corresponding form and its surrounding enclosures, and the formal establishment (*sthāpana*).

The twelve-fold service (dvādaśopacāra), the auspicious worship (maṅgalāpūjana), the worship of the Lord (nāthapūjā), the worship of the weapons (āyudhapūjā), the worship of the seven enclosures (saptāvaraṇapūjā),

and the worship of each individual enclosure (pratyāvaraṇapūjā) should be performed; then follows the principal worship (pradhānapūjā), its dedication (tadarpaṇa), the recitation of the remaining [mantras],

the three services consisting of libation (tarpaṇa), prostration (praṇāma), and the offering of the mouth (karasā), as well as the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), the placement of the letters (varṇanyāsa), and the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa).

The daily recitation (*nityajapa*) performed with the *sampuṭita* method, the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*), the waving of lights (*ārārtika*), the offering of oblations (*validāna*), preceded by the worship of the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatāpūjana*); the contemplation on the unification of all auspiciousness within the water (*jala-sarvamaṅgalaikya-bhāvanā*), the dismissal of the enclosure (*āvaraṇavisarjana*), the ritual withdrawal of all auspiciousness (*sarvamaṅgalodvāsana*), the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*), the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), the ritual placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*), the pervasive ritual placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*), the recitation of the hymn to the Guru (*gurustotra*) and the hymn to the Goddess (*devīstotra*), and prostration before the Guru.

One should perform all rites ending with the remembrance of Viṣṇu; having worshipped Sarvamaṅgalā in the central pitcher, one should sprinkle its drops into the fifteen remaining pitchers situated around it. In this very manner, without deficiency or excess, [one should do so] for the ninety-five pitchers beginning with Oṇimā.
Having worshipped Sarvamaṅgalā, one should cast drops from each of those pitchers into fifteen pitchers situated around each of them. Thus ends the ritual for the first day.
p.

16b) Then, on the second day, having performed his daily rites, the Guru should worship the principal Nityā upon the decorated wheel there with the twelve offerings; the procedure for this shall be clarified further below, and it is to be performed here.
The thread that connects the collection of ritual items included within that worship is as follows: sitting on the seat, performing the *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water),
*prāṇāyāma* (breath control), the worship of one’s own guru based upon the head, the recitation of his hymn of praise, the request for his permission,
the worship of Vārāhī, the worship of Kurukullā, the request for her permission, and the *śrīcakra* based upon the *kalaśa* (vase).

Contemplation upon each respective place, time, and so forth; the worship of all the secret and manifest Yoginīs and the deities of the thirty-eight sacred seats (pīṭhas); the establishment of the general arghya vessel;

and the offering of water for the feet, the arghya, water for sipping (ācamana), the bathing vessel, garments, ornaments, perfumes, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (naivedya).

The arrangement of offerings such as betel-leaf and the like; the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of all those [materials] again; the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), purification of the hands (karaśuddhi), ritual placements (nyāsa), the fourfold seat-mantras (āsana-mantra-catuṣka), the worship of one's own seat (svāsana-pūjana), the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), the removal of obstacles (vidhmotsādana), the ritual placement of the goddess of speech (vāgdevatā-nyāsa), the ritual placement of the phonemes of the mantra (mantravarṇa-nyāsa), the pervasive ritual placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa), and the human redness (lauhitya-mānava).

The worship of the Ghaṭikā-cakra, the worship of the Mithuna-cakra, the Śrīcakra which effects the unity of one's own self, the performance of the Nyāsa, the invocation (āvāhana), the mantras for the seat (āsana), the worship of the Goddess’s seat, meditation,

the visualization of the mass of her splendor as rays radiating from that location, the visualization of the deities of the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇa-devatā) as they spread forth, and their installation (sthāpana).
The binding, veiling, and summoning, preceded by the recitation of their respective mantras,
followed by the display of the seventeen mudrās (p.

One should perform the offering of the twelve services beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) up to betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*), followed by the dismissal (*utsarjana*) and the presentation of those offerings. Then, one should perform the worship of the fifteen Nityās based on the body of the Goddess, using the sixteen-syllable mantra of the nine Lords (*navanātha*) as the instrument and the body of the Goddess as the locus; these constitute the sixteen acts of worship of the Nityās. Thus it is.

Having worshipped the principal goddess, one who has attained the state of *aṇimā* should worship the power of form (*rūpaśakti*)— in the form of *hrīṃ śrīṃ a ā ī*— and her sandals (*pādukā*) within the central of the sixteen pitchers by means of the five services consisting of perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, using the mantra to be described for that [pitcher]. Then, having worshipped the accomplishment of *aṇimā* in the central pitcher, [one should worship] in the pitcher to its west...
Thinking "I worship," one should worship the Śakti known by the names *a*, *ā*, and *ī* with the sixteen-syllable Vidyā;

then, following the sequence of circumambulation, one should worship the other fourteen Śaktis who constitute the enclosure of the *aṇimā*-siddhi. In all of their mantras, there should first be the two seed-syllables (*bīja*), and at the end, the four syllables *rūpa-śakti*.
"I worship the sandals" (*pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*)—this seven-syllable mantra has the name of the respective Śakti in the middle;
it is given as three syllables, and thus the Śakti-mantras are identical in structure, differing only in their names.
Therefore, that mantra is written clearly below; the remainder is indicated by [the numbers] two and eleven: *akāī* (2) and *asvāī* (11).

Then, having attained the power of levitation (*laghimā-siddhi*), one should worship that [power] in the water-pot (*kalaśa*) by means of that mantra, and [perform the ritual] with the water-pot and other items placed before it in a clockwise direction.

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis with these mantras: *haṃ vā ī* (11 times) 2, *haṃ śā ī* (11 times) 2, *haṃ ṣā ī* (11 times) 2, *haṃ sā ī* (11 times) 2, *haṃ hā ī* (11 times) 2, *haṃ lā ī* (11 times) 2, *haṃ kṣā ī* (11 times) 2, *haḥ ā ī* (11 times) 2, *haḥ kā ī* (11 times) 2, *haḥ khā ī* (11 times) 2, *haḥ gā ī* (11 times) 2, *haḥ ghā ī* (11 times) 2, *haḥ ṅā ī* (11 times) 2; then, [worship] at the Bhagamālinī jar.
Having worshipped her with that mantra, one should [place] around it fifteen pitchers, [inscribed] with: 2 *haḥ cāī* 11, 2 *haḥ chāī* 11,
2 *haḥ jāī* 11, 2 *haḥ jhāī* 11, 2 *haḥ ñāī* 11, 2 *haḥ ṭāī* 11,
2 *haḥ ṭhāī* 11, 2 *haḥ ḍāī* 11, 2 *haḥ ḍhāī* 11, 2 *haḥ ṇāī* 11, 2 *haḥ tāī* 11, 2 *haḥ thāī* 11, 2 *haḥ dāī* 11, 2 *haḥ dhāī* 11.
Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis with the Vidyās beginning with *haṇnāī* (11),
and having worshipped the Goddess Tripurāntā, who is the form of the Mistress of the Cakra (*cakreśī*), with the Root-Vidyā using the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra*).
Having offered the worship of the eighth enclosure as in the daily worship, one should display the seed-syllable and the mudrā of the offering. Thus ends the ritual for the ninth day.

Then, on the tenth day, following one's daily obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, one should worship the principal Goddess in the primary jar— which is situated in the center of all and surrounded by a triangle within the *bindu*-cakra— by first worshipping the seat of Śiva in the form of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*) with the mantra "Oṃ saṃvid-āsanāya namaḥ," and then [worship] with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ saṃvid-āsanāya namaḥ."

Having worshipped with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should [recite] around those [deities] in fifteen jars: 2 *haḥ pāī* 11, 2 *haḥ phāī* 11, 2 *haḥ vāī* 11, 2 *haḥ bhāī* 11, 2 *haḥ māī* 11, 2 *haḥ yāī* 11, 2 *haḥ rāī* 11, 2 *haḥ lāī* 11,
2 *haḥ vāī* 11, 2 *haḥ śāī* 11, 2 *haḥ ṣāī* 11, 2 *haḥ sāī* 11, 2 *haḥ hāī* 11, 2 *haḥ lāī* 11.

Having worshipped the fifteen specific Śaktis with the fifteen Vidyās, each consisting of sixteen syllables beginning with *haḥ kṣā ī*, one should worship the Mistress of the Cakra (Cakreśī) in the form of Tripurasundarī with the root-vidyā using the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). Then, having offered the worship of the ninth enclosure (*navamāvaraṇa-pūjā*) according to the very method prescribed for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).

"One should display the *yonimudrā*" means that from the second day up to the tenth, having performed the worship of the Goddess distinguished by each of the nine enclosures along with their respective retinues over those nine days, on the tenth day itself, one should [worship] the principal *Nityā* within her own body using each of her own *Nityā-vidyās* from among the fifteen *Nityā-vidyās*.

Having worshipped the fifteen Nityās with their respective name-mantras, one should worship each of them individually with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). Then, having performed the fourteenth offering in the form of reciting the hymn of praise (*stotra-pāṭha*), one performs the fifteenth offering in the form of libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Having performed [the ritual] together with its ancillaries, one should arrange the sixteenth service, which consists of prostration. Thus ends the duties for the tenth day.
