Then, on the eleventh day, following the daily obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) and others, one should worship with the root mantra (*mūla-vidyā*) and the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) in the midst of the principal daily worship. Within the sixty-two and six hundred jars established upon the emanation wheel (*sṛṣṭi-cakra*), which consists of a square, a sixteen-petaled lotus, and an eight-petaled lotus, one should [worship] *aṇimā* and the other powers (*śaktis*) in their respective order.

Having worshipped those respective Śaktis with the five types of offerings (pañcopacāra), one should present the worship of the first, second, and third enclosures (āvaraṇa) just as before. Thus ends the ritual for the eleventh day.

Then, on the twelfth day, following the daily obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) and others, having worshipped with their respective *vidyās* the five hundred and forty-four *śaktis* established in the wheel (*cakra*) consisting of two sets of fourteen spokes,
one should offer the worship of the fourth, fifth, and sixth enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) according to the method described for the daily worship, presenting the offerings given by each of them.
Thus concludes the ritual duties for the twelve days.

There, on the thirteenth day, having worshipped with their respective mantras the thirty-three hundred and thirty śaktis placed in the jars within the *saṃhāracakra*— which consists of the *ādhāracakra*, the *trikoṇacakra*, and the *binducakra*— as well as their weapons,
one should perform the worship of the seventh, eighth, and ninth enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) there according to the method prescribed for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).
One should offer it.
Thus concludes the ritual duties for the thirteenth day.

Then, on the fourteenth day, at the conclusion of his daily obligatory rites, in a secluded place at night, having gratified the principal deity— who is accompanied by all the [retinue] classes— according to the procedure to be described with the offering of libations (*tarpaṇa*) as the fifteenth service (*upacāra*), he should perform the sixteenth service, which consists of prostration (*natirūpa*).

Thus concludes the ritual for the fourteenth day. Then, on the fifteenth day, after performing one’s daily rites and so forth (p. 31b), one should consecrate the central flask with all the *kāanityā* vidyās.

Having recited the root mantra one thousand times— interspersed with the *aṅguṣṭhādi-nyāsa*, the *hṛdayādi-nyāsa*, the *varṇa-nyāsa*, and the *vyāpaka-nyāsa*— and having performed the offering consisting of the contemplation of non-difference [between the mantra and the deity], he should offer oblations according to the procedure for the daily fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*). Then, he should unite the visualized radiant energy (*tejas*) within the fire-drop (*bindu*).

Having worshipped with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) and offered a bali-oblation with the Kurukullā-vidyā, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with a wick containing camphor and other substances, and then ask for forgiveness. During all these days,
one should hold a great festival with dance, song, and so forth, regarding them as being identified with the Yoginīs.
One should satisfy the married women—who have been determined to be yoginīs—and the devoted servants with garments, ornaments, food, and so forth. Thus ends the ritual for the fifteenth day.

Then, in the sixteenth [day], immediately after the daily and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*), one should worship the principal goddess in the central vessel (*kalaśa*) with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), preceded by the installation of the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*). While touching the central vessel itself, one should recite the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*) and contemplate the identity (*aikya*) of the water in the vessel and its presiding deity.

Having visualized all the obscuring powers (*āvaraṇa-śakti*)— whether directly or through a lineage— as dissolved into the principal deity by means of the *śaktyutthāpana-mudrā*, and having visualized even the principal deity as having entered into one's own self by means of the *khecarī-mudrā*, one should recite the Guru-stotra and Devī-stotra at the conclusion of the three types of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Thereafter:
On that very same day, having first performed the consecration with the water from the Vārāhī flask, one should impart the Vārāhī mantra.
Now, in connection with that initiation (dīkṣā), all that pertains to it—such as the obligatory (nitya) and optional (kāmya) rites—is here described.
Having produced one very large circle by rotating the compass at the desired radius,
one should draw ten lines therein from the southeast corner to the northwest corner, and then from the southwest corner to the northeast corner.

Having laid down ten threads intersecting it, one hundred and twenty-one squares are produced; there, having written the name of the practitioner and others— such as "O Devadatta, perform [the rite], O Vārāhī, grant your grace"— in the very center square, starting from the square immediately below that...

Having written, in a clockwise direction following the order of exit, the ten syllables in their respective forms— u, ū, o, ga, ja, ḍa, da, va, la, and la— as the foundation, one should then write at its end: *ainamo bhagavati vāttāli vāttāli vārāhi vārāhi varāhamukhi varāhamukhi andhe andhinyai namaḥ stambhini stambhinyai namaḥ jambhe*.
Homage to Jambhinī! Homage to Mohinī, the Deluder! Homage to Stambhinī, the Paralyzer! Paralyze, paralyze so-and-so!

Paralyze all the wicked and malicious ones! Cause the paralysis of the tongues of all! Act, act quickly to bring them under control! Aiṃ glauṃ ṭhaṭha huṃ phaṭ svāhā! Thus is the characteristic [of the mantra].
One method is to write the vidyā as it stands; or else, having drawn sixteen lines each extending east-west and sixteen lines each extending north-south, intersecting one another at equal intervals,
one should produce two hundred and twenty-five squares, and within those, in the four directions starting from the east—
Having omitted the eighth square located at the very center of the outer path,
[place] the seventh, eighth, and ninth squares in the second path, and the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth,
and tenth squares in the third path.

In the fourth row, having omitted the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh squares, one proceeds in order: thirteen in the first row, nine in the second row, and [nine] in the third row.
In the fifth and fourth rows, one [square] each— having thus cleared twenty-eight squares per corner,
a total of one hundred and twelve squares have been cleared; then, among the remaining one hundred and thirteen squares, having made the lower portions of each of the four directions [blank],...
In the central square, the verb—denoted by the term *karma* (object)—is to be placed because it effects the accomplishment of the action.

In the square above that, the word for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) ending in the genitive case is to be placed; in the square below that, the word for the object (*sādhya*) ending in the accusative case is to be placed. Thus, among the remaining one hundred and ten squares, including the four triangular squares, [the arrangement is as follows].

The second method is as follows: beginning from the front triangle and proceeding clockwise by way of entry, one should write the letters of the mantra, equal in number to the [triangles], one by one. Alternatively, having drawn twelve lines each extending east-west and twelve lines extending north-south, intersecting one another at equal intervals;

Having prepared one hundred and twenty-one squares, having written the name of the practitioner and others in the very center of the central square, and having written the syllables of the mantra starting from the square below that, proceeding clockwise in a counter-clockwise direction (nirgamagatyā), one should write the syllables representing the elements and the earth as previously described in the remaining ten squares.

The third method: among these, according to the instruction of one's own guru, having placed a water-pot (*kalaśa*) upon any one of those aforementioned yantras— which has been raised from the ground with vermilion (*darada*) and other substances, and whose center is covered with rice (*vrīhi*)— in accordance with the prescribed rite, [one should worship] Vārāhī within it.
One should contemplate the wheel of daily worship as follows: having drawn two circles with equal intervals between them, one should mark six points at equal intervals within the inner circle;
then, leaving a space between each of those marks, one should produce a six-pointed wheel by drawing six lines from mark to mark.

Having fashioned a six-cornered figure within that [circle], with its corners touching and not touching the pericarp, one should then form a triangle within it facing oneself; thus, in the *nityapūjācakra*, one should worship Vārāhī, the deity under discussion.
However, in the case of the *nityārcācakra*, which is an ancillary part of initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should extract [the deity] directly without regard for a ritual jar (*kalaśa*).
The manner of that [practice] is as follows: having first anointed oneself with fragrant oil and bathed with scented water,

and having likewise performed the morning rites thereafter, the practitioner— whose body and face are thus purified and who is adorned with red sandalwood paste and garlands— having entered the sacrificial pavilion, [should sit upon] the red [seat] worshipped with the prescribed seat-mantra (āsana-vidyā).
Having assumed either the Svastika or Padma posture upon a seat such as a woolen blanket (*kambala*), and having sat down with the present Vidyā;
and having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of the present Vidyā or its constituent *Vāgbhava* seed-syllable (*bīja*);
and having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with the sixteen-syllable mantra; [one should worship] one’s own *Nātha* on one’s own head in due order with those very respective mantras.

Having worshipped the nine presiding deities, recited the hymn to the Guru, and requested his permission, one should contemplate the identity of one's own Lord, the present deity of the practice, and the deity of the mantra with one's own self. In the independent worship (*svatantra-pūjā*), [the mantra is] *hrīṃ vārāhī cakrāya namaḥ*; in the worship of the limbs of Lalitā (*lalitāṅga-pūjā*), [it is as follows].
Having fully worshipped the two deities of the seat with "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Ikṣusāḍapatīrāya" (p. 33b) and "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Vārāhī Cakra," [one worships] the lion-throne.
Having placed between oneself and the yantra the common arghya vessel— made of any one of the five materials such as gold, filled with water mixed with *gorocanā* and other substances,
and resting upon its base— one should [purify] the waters in that base vessel by means of the three seed-syllables of Kulasundarī, representing fire, sun, and moon.

Having meditated upon the pentad beginning with *ārocanā* as having the nature of form, and the five elements beginning with earth as consisting of the five *bhūtas*, one should contemplate the water as having the form of the worship-circle and the form of the deity in question; then, having consecrated it ten times with the present *vidyā* and worshipped the deities of the six limbs therein with the present six-limbed mantras.

With that consecrated water, having sprinkled oneself with the aforementioned mantra, one should sprinkle the fourfold set beginning with the *pādya* (water for washing the feet) situated in the northern part of the general *arghya* vessel, as well as the garments, ornaments, perfumes, and so forth, located in one's own southern part; or again, with the *vidyā*, or by means of the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable which is a constituent of the *vidyā*.

Having restrained the breath (prāṇāyāma) and taken the general water for the arghya offering, one should perform the mental resolve (saṅkalpa), specifying the place, time, lineage (gotra), zodiac sign (rāśi), and desire, saying: "I shall perform the worship of Vārāhī. Then one should pour out water from the hands. If the worship is as a preliminary part of the worship of Lalitā, the same wording of the resolve should be modified accordingly; however, some [teachers] [hold that it should be done] for Lalitā.

They say that because the entire collection of items to be performed from beginning to end has already been introduced into the *saṅkalpa* (resolution) statement by the word "according to rule" (*vidhinā*) within the very sentence of the vow for the performance of worship, there is no need to make the vow again.
On this occasion, even though it was not previously performed, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth are included by way of incidental context.

One must certainly perform it when that [rite] is the primary action. Even when it is a subsidiary (aṅga), having performed it at that very moment, one should perform it again there immediately after the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) regarding that primary action. And thus:

Having performed the six-limbed nyāsa of the Mātṛkās, one should first utter the present vidyā or its seed-syllable for each [limb] individually; then, having assigned each respective Mātṛkā to those respective locations: *aiṃ namo bhagavati hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *vāttāli vāttāli śirase svāhā*, *vārāhi vārāhi śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras— *varāhamukhi*, *varāhamukhika*, *vacāya huṃ*, *andhe andhinyai namaḥ*, *netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*,

*rundhe rundhinyai namaḥ*, and *astrāya phaṭ*— upon the thumbs and other fingers as well as the heart and other limbs, and having performed the three-fold pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the aforementioned mantra of one hundred and ten syllables;

One should follow the sequence beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*). That is as follows: having formed the *trisvarāḍā* mudrā, with both hands full of flowers, one should contemplate the radiance of the present vidyā pervading from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*.
By casting that handful of flowers through the path of the nostrils, it should be united with the *bindu* residing in the present *cakra*.
Visualizing that [deity] as having been transferred, one should pray at the end of the *hīṃ* and *māyā* seed-syllables: "O Vārāhī, be invoked here in this wheel!

Having thus performed the rite of invocation (*āvāhana*), one should visualize the masses of light-rays emanating from her on all sides as transforming into the forms of the Lord, the weapons, and the retinue; then, one should meditate upon the light situated in the center.

One should contemplate the form described in the words, and that should be meditated upon as follows: one should meditate on the goddess Kolāsyā, whose splendor is like molten gold; who is female in form up to her neck, with blazing tawny hair;
three-eyed, and possessing eight arms, [holding] a discus, a conch, and a goad.
One should meditate upon her seated upon the shoulders of Garuḍa, holding a noose, a mace, a plow, as well as the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. (Nityapūjā, p.

One should meditate on Śivā as "su-tac-chakti-sahāmānāḥ" (together with those powers that endure her splendor). Such is the meditation for the powers (śaktis) who constitute the enclosure of the Lord’s weapons.
Regarding the aspect of the weapons, they possess the additional feature of having their own specific forms as crest-jewels. Then, at the end of the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*), [one says]:
"O Vārāhī, be established here in this wheel. At the end of the seed-syllable of Māyā, [one says]: "O Vārāhī, be firmly restrained here in this wheel."

At the end of the *māyā*-seed syllable, [one should pray]: "O Vārāhī, be veiled here in this wheel. At the end of the *māyā*-seed syllable, [one should pray]: "O Vārāhī, be present here in this wheel. Having made this request preceded by the display of the respective mudrās, and having performed the fourfold ritual beginning with installation (*sthāpana*), one should perform the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) using the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra.

Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) of Vārāhī upon the present worship-circle using the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā* in the form "The vital breaths of such-and-such Vārāhī are here in this circle," one should worship her with the twelve services (*upacāras*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*). The mantras for that are as follows: [the complete vidyā] 110.

Saying, "I offer water for the feet to Tevārāhī," one should present the *pādya* with the water from the general *arghya* vessel; then, having offered it, one should announce, "The [offering] is complete" (sampūrṇa) by means of the *vidyā* mantra. In this very same manner, having offered the *arghya* and other items—beginning with the *pādya* and ending with the *arghya*—for each respective limb using their specific mantras, one should present them upon the head and other parts, and then arrange the ritual services (*upacāras*) ending with *tāmbūla*.

One should offer the thirteen services as follows: on the back of the Goddess, within the space between the triangle and the circle, [one worships] Vimarśa, Ānanda, Śrījñāna, Śrīsatya, and Śrīpūrṇā; and the various Nāthas known by the names Svabhāva, Pratibha, and Subhaga, together with the three words for Nātha and the three words for Śakti.

Having worshipped [them] with their respective mantras, one should invoke the Goddess and worship, in sequence, in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya), [saying]: "Kroṃ! I worship the sandals of Krodhinī.

"I worship the *staṃstamninī* sandal. Having worshipped thus with "I worship the *kṣoṃcaṇḍoccaṇḍā* sandal," [one worships] in the space between the triangle and the circle, on the southern and northern paths, starting from the northwest corner and proceeding counter-clockwise:
"Hrīṃ, obeisance to Abhayā; Hrīṃ, obeisance to Varā; Hrīṃ, obeisance to Muśala."

Having worshipped the eight weapons with: *hrīṃ sīrāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ aṅkuśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ pāśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ cakrāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śaṅkhāya namaḥ*, and so forth; and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) with: "I worship the sandals (*pādukā*) of Vārāhī," [one worships] *hrīṃ etāvārāhī*.

"May the deities of the first enclosure accept the worship"—thus, having offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) as an offering of that worship, [one worships] in the six corners, starting from the northeast and proceeding clockwise: "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals (pādukā) of Brāhmī;
Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Māheśvarī; Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Kaumārī; Hrīṃ..."

"I worship the sandal of Vaiṣṇavī; hrīṃ, I worship the sandal of Aindrī; hrīṃ, I worship the sandal of Cāmuṇḍā"—having thus worshipped the group of six Mothers (mātṛṣaṭka), one should worship the Goddess situated in the center, saying: "I worship the sandal of Vārāhī, the complete root-mantra. Hrīṃ.

"May these goddesses of the second enclosure, the Vārāhīs, accept the worship"—thus, having offered a handful of flowers as an offering for their worship; then, on the western side of the circular path, having worshipped Mahālakṣmī with "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Mahālakṣmī"; and at the end of the complete mantra, [one worships] with "I worship the sandals of Vārāhī."

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as the dedication of that worship with the words: *Hrīṃ! May this third enclosure deity, Vārāhī, accept the worship*. Then, having performed the thirteen services (*upacāra*), one should perform whatever recitation of hymns, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and prostrations are appropriate.

Having performed the threefold service according to Vasiṣṭha, and having completed the recitation of the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) interspersed with the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa), one should perform the offering at the conclusion of the daily recitation— either a thousand or a hundred times— as consisting of the contemplation of non-difference [between oneself and the deity].

Having offered sixteen oblations according to the prescribed method, as well as a tenth-part of the daily recitation (*japa*), and having re-united the fire— now manifested as the radiant essence of the deity under worship— with its very root in the *bindu*-station, one should worship the deity who has arrived there with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) and present a *bali* offering of food, condiments, and so forth, using the sixteen-syllable mantra.

Having performed the *nīrājana* with wicks containing camphor and the like, and having asked for forgiveness, one should dissolve the deities of the enclosure along with their rays into a mass of light by means of the *śaktyutthāpana-mudrā*. Then, having absorbed even that mass of light into oneself by means of the *khecarī-mudrā*,
one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the thumbs and other fingers, the placement on the heart and other limbs, and the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) as before.

Having performed the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) and recited the hymns to the Guru and the Goddess, one should remain as one who has become the very self of the Goddess and depart as desired. However, in the case of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the procedure consists of the "liberated" (*muktā*) form, which includes everything up to the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*) but is devoid of the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) and so forth. Having performed the worship of Kāmeśvarī according to this procedure, one should dispel the fatigue of the night with dance, song, and the like. Then, in the morning, at the conclusion of the daily rites, [one should worship] with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*).

Having worshipped the presiding goddess and performed the rites of dismissal (*udvāsana*) and so forth, the Guru— having satisfied the disciple who has internalized the *mātṛkā* mantra by consecrating him with the sprouts placed in the ritual jar using the present vidyā, and having honored him with the nine services beginning with perfumes (*gandha*), and having gratified him with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other gifts— performs the sacrament known as "piercing" (*vedha*) according to the rite of piercing, beneath the ritual jar.
The specific distinction is that, having seated the disciple in the Vārāhī-cakra, one should impart the previously mentioned vidyā three times.

Having completed the worship— which is preceded by the worship of Śrīsundarī and concludes with the recitation of the Devīstotra in the manner described on page 36a— and having thus propitiated [the Goddess]:
The distinction is that, having received the command of this Vārāhī who guards the shore of the Ocean of Sugarcane, one should strive for the sake of propitiating Kurukullā.

Having thus received initiation, one who is devoted daily to the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*), and who desires the collection of goals sought for oneself and others through practical application, should perform the means of attaining *vidyā*. The procedure for this has already been stated in the general introduction; however, there is a certain specific detail, such as [the practice of] eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) preceded by celibacy (*brahmacarya*).

Having undertaken the vow, one should perform the three daily prayers (sandhyā) at each of the three junctions of the day, preceded by the worship in the manner previously described; having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one must then practice these three: libation (tarpaṇa), worship, and fire-offering (havana) consisting of sesame seeds, rice, and so forth, each being one-tenth of the recitation count, continuously for the duration of a year.
Furthermore, the performance of worship according to the previously mentioned methods also brings about the accomplishment of the Vidyā.

Now, these are the optional ritual applications (*kāmyaprayoga*) for the Goddess. One should meditate upon Vārāhī as red in color, with red ornaments and red decorations, surrounded on all sides by her own Śaktis;
having first performed such meditation, one should recite the present vidyā, whereby the subjugation (*vaśyatva*) of men, women, kings, and others is achieved.

Success is attained. One should meditate upon the present Vidyā, who is yellow in color, wearing yellow garments and yellow ornaments, adorned with garlands and unguents, and surrounded by Śaktis who are likewise yellow and decorated with yellow clothing and ornaments; and one should recite her mantra.
By that means, in disputes concerning knowledge and the like, in legal cases regarding debts, land, and so forth, and in battle against an enemy, [success is achieved].

The accomplishment of immobilization (*stambhana*) through wrath and other [emotions] is as follows: for one desiring to travel on a difficult path, one should visualize the Goddess mounted upon a lion,
dark-complexioned, terrifying to others, and endowed with great prowess, seated upon a lion.

Meditating on the present Vidyā, which is enveloped by the power of the dark-colored [deity], and reciting it while visualizing oneself as situated in the midst of the powers of the present Goddess, one should proceed; thus being happy in every respect,
one should return again to one's own home, free from the difficulty of fear of lions, tigers, and the like, as well as thieves and so forth.

Due to fear of those bearing various weapons and other such dangers, and likewise due to the absence of finding a path and the inability to climb great mountains, one proceeds everywhere according to the manner described; thus, traveling to the intended destination with ease and returning again to one's own home is accomplished.

Even in battles, victory is obtained through meditation (*dhyāna*). For example, she is herself mounted upon an elephant, surrounded by attendants likewise mounted on elephants; she has sixteen arms: in her right hands, [she holds] an upward-pointing goad, a bell, a small knife (*churikā*), a sword, an arrow, a trident (*śūla*), a mace (*gadā*), a discus (*cakra*), and a wheel; in her left hands, [she holds] a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), a shield (*kheṭaka*), and a shield of hide (*carma*).

The Goddess Vārāhī herself, blue in color, bearing a bow, a hand-drum, a mace, a noose, and a conch, having struck down the entire hostile army upon the earth with her iron clubs, moves about suddenly with her powers— consumed by the pride arising from the excess of her own strength and valor— with a banner made of plantain trunks raised aloft.

Meditating thus— visualizing her as standing upon the sun's orb, impaled upon a trident with an enemy’s body, and her trident smeared with the blood dripping from that enemy’s body— if one stands in water such as a river up to the neck and recites the present vidyā a thousand times or more, then, having practiced in this very manner for even seven nights, [the result follows].

Through this practice, the death of enemies shall occur. While standing in water up to the neck, one should meditate upon the body of the enemy—reduced to pieces by the sixteen weapons of the Goddess together with her retinue, beginning with the *nasvara* (the nose) and ending with the conch shell—and being devoured by jackals, vultures, carnivorous beasts, and dogs. Thus meditating, [the enemy's death occurs]. p. 37a) [End of page 37]
Throughout the three days, if one should recite the present vidyā, then by those very three days the enemy will be heard to have been slain.

If, while meditating upon the present goddess— who is smoke-colored, two-armed, smoke-limbed, and who with one hand tears out the tongue of the enemy and with the second hand uproots the heart-lotus of the enemy— one recites the present vidyā...

Then his enemy shall go to the city of Yama. If he recites the present vidyā while meditating upon the Goddess mounted on Garuḍa, accompanied by Śaktis mounted on Garuḍas and surrounded by hosts of attendants, and likewise meditating upon the enemy army overcome by fainting due to the great wind produced by the flapping of various Garuḍa wings, then [the result follows].

At that very moment, the enemy army is destroyed. Having meditated upon the Goddess as she is presented—mounted upon Tārkṣya, surrounded by the Śaktis in the form of Tārkṣyas, holding eight swords with her own eight hands—one should recite the aforementioned Vidyā while reciting [the mantra] over the enemy army. [Likewise, one should meditate upon] the King, mounted on a horse, surrounded by horses, and red in color.
Having become the bearer of the conch and the arrow, with disheveled hair,

she was surrounded by multitudes of spears mounted upon hyenas, lions, monkeys, boars, bears, and Garuḍas— each standing upon chariots, infantry, horses, and elephants belonging to the enemy army, and each impaled upon the tips of their respective tridents.

Meditate upon the Goddess currently present, seated upon a lion standing within a pavilion made of rubies— a lion who provides diversion through various sports such as playing with dust, water-sports, and mounting and dismounting from various animals.
One should mutter [the mantra] for the sake of conquering the enemy's host with one's own army. Thus end the applications of meditation.
For the practitioner who,

throughout the time of the maṇḍala and other rites, worships the present goddess of yellow complexion with yellow garments, ornaments, perfumes, and so forth, the intellect, movement, and the effort of the tongue of his enemies [are destroyed].

The immobilization (*stambhana*) of all objects that are the targets of a practitioner’s desire for immobilization— such as urine, feces, and so forth— is accomplished. For a practitioner who worships within the mandala at midnight using flowers of an orange-red color,
even an enemy who has exerted effort to kill that practitioner will certainly and swiftly come under his control.

It happens as follows: if one worships the present goddess in her black form during the time of the poison-vein (*viṣanāḍī*) and so forth, or at the commencement of the [inauspicious] conjunctions of time, while pervading the mandala and other [ritual spaces], the enemy shall go to the city of Yama. Furthermore, if the practitioner worships the present goddess in her dark-blue form with fragrant black flowers, pervading the mandala and other [spaces] throughout the duration of the time, he shall attain Lakṣmī.

Or else, one becomes free from illness, possesses happiness, and attains long life. Thus are the applications of worship. At the time of midnight, in a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), [one should offer] rice mixed with pieces of turmeric, or sesame seeds mixed with pieces of turmeric, or māṣa beans mixed with pieces of turmeric, or grains of rice mixed with pieces of turmeric, or...

If a practitioner performs oblations throughout the ritual period using yellow flowers such as campaka mixed with turmeric, or yellow fruits mixed with turmeric, within the mandala and other settings, there will be the immobilization (*stambhana*) of the enemy's mind and so forth. On palm-leaf slips numbering one hundred or more, one should write [the mantra] such as: "Paralyze, paralyze the mind of so-and-so! and so on.
When oblations are offered— consisting of items written with turmeric in the colors of the person to be accomplished and combined with turmeric— in quantities of one hundred or more,
pervading the entire mandala, there occurs the paralysis of the enemies' minds and so forth.

One becomes subject [to one's will] through the offering (*homa*) of turmeric powder smeared with ghee; furthermore, by practicing at the proper time within a mandala and so forth, the aforementioned immobilization (*stambha*) shall occur. In a fire kindled with wood from a tree belonging to the enemy’s *nakṣatra*, [one should offer] the flesh of a creature born under the enemy’s *nakṣatra*.

By performing oblations numbering one hundred or more every day at the time of midnight for a period extending over a full cycle (maṇḍala), using fuel sticks smeared with the fat and oil of a relative, the death of the enemy will inevitably occur by some means.
One should meditate upon the Goddess as smoke-colored, mounted upon a heron, and bearing the previously mentioned weapons such as claws.

If, when the ascendant is in the sign of Virgo (Kanyā), one performs a fire oblation (*homa*) with goat’s ghee, mustard seeds, and black pepper, continuing for the duration of the ritual circle (*maṇḍala*), then the enemy— having been made unconscious, tormented by an extremely painful burning sensation, and possessing distorted hands, feet,
and limbs due to the influence of malevolent spirits— is slain. [This applies during] Bālārka.

Meditating upon the goddess Varāhī— who possesses a radiance of equal splendor, has sixteen arms, and bears the previously mentioned sixteen weapons beginning with the claw— one should avoid contact with faded offerings (nirmālya) that have fallen on the ground while still in their bud-like state, those defiled by living beings, those smelled, those touched by the feet and other limbs, or those that are stale due to having been kept overnight.

One who, using red flowers free from defects, red *vatsaka* fruits, and red-colored cow-ghee, performs the *mohanavāna* (the rite of enchantment) daily for the duration of the *maṇḍala* and other rites, shall become equal to a king— possessing elephants, horses, and the like, with various limitless riches, and with unimpeded courage and other virtues. [The goddess] is sixteen *raktavarṇā* (red-colored).

Meditating upon the goddess as she is presented—bearing the sixteen weapons beginning with the arms, claws, and conch—and facing the direction of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), he who [performs] the mandala and so forth at the time of midnight...
He who offers oblations of *marīca* daily for a period measured by a hundred or more [days] brings under his control men,
noble women, and kings; indeed, even upon the entire earth, he alone shall be preeminent through fame and prosperity.
Thus concludes the procedure for the fire offering (homa).

First, having made a square with a desired dimension, one should draw a circle outside it that touches its corners tangentially; then, having drawn another circle outside that with a six-finger interval between them,
one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus within the six-finger wide space between the circles, and also [proceed] outside the outermost circle.

Having drawn two other circles with an interval of six finger-breadths between them, and having fashioned a hexagonal wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*) within that space, one should draw another circle outside the inner circle of the hexagon with an interval of one finger-breadth; then, one should construct a square outside of that. Once the diagram consisting of these lines has been thus prepared, one should inscribe the letters [of the alphabet] as follows:

Having formed three rows within a square situated in the center of all, one should write the names of the practitioner along with the words of action in ascending order from the top down; then, outside of that, in the path formed by the square and the circle, starting from this [point] and proceeding clockwise.
Having written the ten earth-born syllables upon lotus petals,
one should write the letters of the root-vidyā on each petal in groups of six; having again written the ten earth-syllables in the outer path (vīthī),
one should write the present vidyā in each of the corners of the hexagonal wheel (ṣaṭkoṇacakra) outside that, in groups of six.

Without having written the forty-nine letters beginning with *ā* [in their respective places], one should place them within the interior of the hexagon, six by six in each interval, as before, starting from the northern interval of the eastern corner with the eighty-fifth letter and so forth.
Having written the syllables of the root-vidyā, one writes the two remaining vidyā-syllables that were left over in the fifth interval,

as well as the four preceding earth-element syllables. Then, having written the six remaining earth-element syllables in the sixth interval, one writes the Mātṛkā in reverse order along with the visarga on the path outside of that.
Between that circle and the square, one should write the Mātṛkā along with the bindu in direct order (anuloma).
One who is skilled in deliberation, worshipping this yantra with the present vidyā, can subjugate the entire world and paralyze enemy armies.

As for another method of the yantra: having drawn two circles according to the desired measurement and having fashioned a nine-yoni wheel in the very center of them; then, outside of that, having fashioned an eight-cornered wheel by means of two square enclosures (bhūpura) at the cardinal and intermediate directions;
and outside of that, one circle touching the eight corners and another [circle] with an interval of one finger-breadth (aṅgula).

Having drawn two circles and then a square outside of them with an interval of one finger-breadth (*ekāṅgula*), having fashioned the yantra within the lines, one should write six syllables of the mantra for each of the nine *yonis* in sequence— beginning with the *yoni* located in the very center, then the *yoni* at its tip, and then the *yoni* to its right— and so on; thereafter, [one writes] starting from the tip in the eight corners outside of that.

Having written the syllables of the sixfold Vidyā in a clockwise direction, one by one within the intervals of the eight squares, and having thus completed the writing of the entire Vidyā-syllables; then, having written the Mātṛkā in reverse order together with the Visarga within the path formed by two outer circles; and [having written] upon the path formed by the square and circle situated outside of that...

One should write the *mātṛkā* in the form of a *bindu* in the direction of the natural order (*anuloma*). This applies to all [mandalas] consisting of nine *yoni*s, eight triangles, eight intermediate spaces, and two paths (*vīthi*).
Having written the words of the practitioner's action and the words of the target in each of the twenty-seven prescribed locations for writing,
one should invoke the goddess of the present context there— possessing eight arms— and worship her according to the method described for the daily worship;
thus, the immobilization (*stambhana*) of the enemies' intellect, movement, and other aforementioned objects is accomplished.
As for another type of yantra: first, a circle in the very center; outside that, a triangle; outside of that, another circle; then another circle with an intervening space between them;

within that intervening space, a six-spoked wheel (ṣaṭkoṇacakra); outside of that, a circle; outside of that, an eight-sided figure (aṣṭāsra); outside its corners, another circle touching the tips of those corners; and outside of that, a circle with an interval of one finger-breadth (aṅgula).

Having prepared a line-drawn wheel (*rekhāmayacakra*), the practitioner should write in the very center the *Vāgbhava* syllable— which is the first letter of the present Vidyā— adorned with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within three concentric rows. Then,
having written the three letters of the Vidyā in a clockwise direction starting from the front of the triangles, one should likewise write them in the intermediate spaces between those corners.

Having written the syllables of the subsequent mantras one after another in groups of three according to the previously described sequence, and having likewise written three syllables each in each of the six corners starting from the outermost,

and having written three syllables each in the intermediate spaces between those corners starting from the outermost, and having likewise written three syllables each in each of the desired [outer] corners starting from the outermost—

Having written [the syllables] in the intermediate spaces between them according to a sequence of three by three, and having written the subsequent syllables outside of that, one should write the remaining seven syllables of the Vidyā and the ten syllables of the *bhauma*, making seventeen syllables in total within the space between the two outer circles; thus the yantra is completed.

Having worshipped the Goddess preceded by the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites, and having performed the recitation of the Vidyā enfolded by the syllable *Aṃ* along with the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and the pervasive assignment (vyāpakanyāsa) in numbers such as one hundred thousand, [one should place it] in a shallow bowl (*śarāva*).
Having placed that yantra inside a shallow bowl, covered it with another bowl, and set it in a location such as against a wall, the practitioner should worship it there,
offer an oblation (bali) with the sixteen-syllable mantra, and effect the paralyzing of the enemies' movements and so forth.

As for another yantra: in the very sequence mentioned in the introduction regarding Vārāhī, if the third yantra is extracted, one should draw tridents all around the tips of the lines; then, having written the three syllables "stambhaya" on the middle, right, and left sides of each of those tridents, and having placed it in a shallow earthen bowl (śarāva), [one should proceed].
Having covered it with another shallow bowl, one should place it within a wall, in a secluded spot, or on the ground.

Here, the materials for writing on birch bark, cloth, gold, silver, copper, crystal, or stone, as well as the tools for engraving, consist of red ochre, turmeric, or yellow orpiment; any of these may serve as the liquid for writing. Furthermore, the concealment of this [mantra] within a house or a city [is achieved] by means of iron.
The rule applies specifically to one of these materials— such as stone— but not to birch bark or cloth;

having established the Vedic diagram (yantra) upon it, preceded by invocation (āvāhana), the consecration of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and so forth, one should worship it daily with flowers and fragrant substances such as camphor at dawn, at twilight, and until the time of the fruit, whereby [the power over] enemies...
The paralyzing of intellect, movement, and so forth, necessarily occurs. As for the *śānti*-yantra:

first, having fashioned a great circle (*mahāvṛtta*), one fashions a great hexagon (*mahāṣaṭkoṇa*) in its pericarp (*karṇikā*). Having constructed a hexagon in each of the six corners of that [central] pericarp, one thus produces a group of seven hexagons. Outside of that, at the tips of the corners...

Having drawn another circle with an intervening space from the [first] touching circle, one should draw an eight-cornered wheel within that interval using two square enclosures for the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having fashioned that [mandala], one should draw another circle outside the first, touching its corners and tips, with an interval of one *aṅgula* between them;
then, upon the resulting wheel composed of lines, one should inscribe the letters of the Vidyā from the outside toward the center by way of entry.
Specifically, starting from the front corner of the eight-spoked wheel and proceeding clockwise, one should write the letters of the Mātṛkā together with the *visarga*.

Having written the eight syllables, one should write the syllables of the present *vidyā* within them according to the lost-number system (*naṣṭasaṃkhyā*). Thus, [the sequence is]: *aḥ*, *aiṃ*; *āḥ*, *na*; *iḥ*, *mo*; *īḥ*, *bha*; *uḥ*, *ga*; *ūḥ*, *vaṃ*; *ṛḥ*; *ṝ*, *vā*. In this way, two syllables are written in each corner; the same should be applied in the subsequent cases as well. And then:

Having written the letters of the Mātṛkā and the Vidyā, beginning with the ninth and ending with the sixteenth, in the corners and the intervening spaces as before; then, within that, starting from the front-facing hexagon among the seven hexagons and proceeding clockwise until the central hexagon, [one should place them] in each respective corner and in each respective interval between those corners.

Among the eighty-four locations, having written the thirty-four syllables of the *mātṛkā* and the *vidyā*, beginning with the seventeenth and ending with the fiftieth, according to the stated sequence, and having encircled them once and performed the *amāpau nattyā* [offering], one should rely upon the *amāpamata* in the center and [place] the fifty *mātṛkā*s.

Having completed [the first cycle] among the remaining fifty positions as before, he wrote one syllable of the Vidyā at the end of each letter of the Mātṛkā with its visarga; thus the second rotation of the Mātṛkā was also finished. As for the Vidyā, ten syllables remain, and those along with the ten elemental syllables (bhūtākṣaras) together amount to [twenty].
"One should write twenty syllables in the remaining row. Herein, whatever specific nakṣatra, lunar day (tithi),
or weekday is to be employed for a ritual application such as the pacification of disease, the names of those respective nakṣatras, lunar days, weekdays, and so forth [are to be written].
Having uttered the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) ending in the locative case, that too is placed solely in the very center of all [the diagrams].

However, in the central portions of all seven hexagonal wheels (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*), the sequence there proceeds from the front corner to the center and so forth, moving clockwise until the end of the very center. Thus, for Devadatta, it is on Aśvinī, the first lunar day (*pratipad*), and on Sunday.

In the manner of "pacify, pacify all diseases without harming this body," and so forth, one should repeat the name of the practitioner and others seven times within the centers of the six triangles; likewise, in other yantras,
starting from the first lunar day (pratipad) up to the fifteenth (pañcadaśī), according to the divisions of the fifteen lunar days, one should place [the mantra] on the second, third, and so on.

There are fifteen yantras associated with Sunday; likewise, there are fifteen yantras associated with each of the six days beginning with Monday. Thus, in total, one hundred and five yantras are produced.
Since these are composed of Aśvinī, they are the yantras of Aśvinī alone, [with one] in the place of Aśvinī.
In the entry of each of the twenty-six lunar mansions, beginning with Śravaṇa, Revatī, and Aśleṣā, there are one hundred and five instruments (*yantra*) for each;
thus, in total, two thousand eight hundred and thirty-five instruments are produced. And this refers to each individual instrument.
The seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ) should be written in the center. Then, by wearing the yantra— which has been consecrated through worship,

recitation, and other rites— on its respective lunar mansions, lunar days, and weekdays, there occurs the pacification of all diseases, the warding off of calamities such as malevolent spirits, and the elimination of ailments in elephants, horses, and other animals.
p.

41b) Therefore, here is a summary verse: This collection of yantras, numbering five hundred and forty-four, conjoined with their respective asterisms, lunar days, and days of the week, has been maintained here by men as a remover of fear and disease caused by all living beings.

Now, regarding the Vajrayantra which bestows all accomplishments (*sarvārthasiddhi*), its true nature has already been shown by the Goddess through the demonstration of the second type at the very commencement of this discourse. As for its application: having drawn it on a stone slab made of the three metals (*triloha*) and having consecrated it, this Yantra, when installed in houses, cities, and so forth, [protects against] thieves...

It pacifies disturbances caused by spirits, ghosts, and the like. Furthermore, even the pacification of disturbances arising from the propitiation of the local deities (*vāstudevatā*) residing in the house occurs through the installation of this yantra in the home. Moreover, there will be no fear for the practitioners dwelling in that house from thieves, or from acts such as incantations of hatred (*vidveṣaṇa*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*). [This is because] it is presided over by this yantra.

For those living in a household, there may also be an increase in prosperity every day. As for another yantra: the yantra named Vajravajra, which was first extracted at the very beginning of the section on Vārāhī, should be engraved upon a plate of gold, silver, or copper; then, having performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and other rites, in whichever house it is kept—

When it is installed, there shall be no suffering from disease, malevolent spirits (*bhūta*), planetary afflictions (*graha*), insanity, *piśācas*, epilepsy, and so forth for those residing therein. Furthermore, having constructed this diagram known as "Vajra-vajra" with red ochre on the ground, one should install within its center a jar filled with a decoction of milk-tree wood; then, in that water, according to the previously mentioned direction—

Having performed the concluding rites ending with the worship and dismissal of Sarvamaṅgalā, one should worship the presiding Goddess in that water, preceded by the invocation (āvāhana) and other rituals. Then, having recited the present vidyā three thousand times while touching that water, the consecrator—being satisfied by the fees and other offerings received—should consecrate the disciple and others who are facing east. By that [act]...
Freed from all diseases, he lives preceded by happiness.
p.

42a) As for another diagram that accomplishes all desires: having first drawn a circle with an interval of four finger-breadths, one should then fashion eleven successive circles outside of it, each with an interval of two finger-breadths; therein—

Starting from the circle of the pericarp (karṇikā) up to the outermost circle, one should draw lines at twelve marks on each successive circle; having thus produced one hundred and twenty-one squares,
one should extend the ends of all the outermost lines slightly outward and there fashion trident-shaped points.
Having written the name of the practitioner and others in the central square according to the prescribed method,

one should then write the letters of the mantra— numbering one hundred and ten— in the surrounding row, starting from the center of the eastern side and proceeding clockwise in an outward direction with single steps, until all those squares are filled; then, in the remaining squares...

One should write the ten earth-syllables, numbering ten, within the ten squares; thus prepared, this yantra accomplishes every purpose through wearing, worship, installation, consecration with a water-pot (kalaśa-abhiṣeka), and so forth.
Thus end the applications of the mechanical devices.

And by means of these methods— meditation, worship, fire-oblation, following the ritual diagrams (yantra), and so forth— this Vidyā, whether already mastered or not yet mastered, unfailingly bestows upon all her own worshippers the entire multitude of their desired objects throughout all worlds.
Thus concludes the introduction to Vārāhī.

Having thus instructed the Vārāhī-vidyā, which accomplishes various desired aims, [the teacher] should, in a place where the bathing water flows naturally toward either the eastern direction or the northeast intermediate direction, draw the Mātṛkā-cakra in a square area. There, having seated the disciple facing east, [he should perform the rite] within the power of aṇimā itself.
Having lifted the first power-vessel, which has become the site of battle, and having brought it to the place of consecration,
[the master places] the citron and the plow held in its mouth into the cupped hands of the disciple, and the sprouts held in its mouth upon the disciple’s head.

Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should consecrate him with the mantras of the deities worshipped in that water-pot (*kalaśa*). In the same manner, immediately after the consecration with the other fourteen water-pots, one should consecrate him with the water from the Maṇimāka pot using its specific mantra.
Following this same procedure, after the consecration with the eight water-pots of the eight weapons belonging to the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*),...

After the consecration with the fifteen jars situated around the principal jar (pradhānakalaśa) using their respective vidyās, one brings the principal jar located in the very center to the place of consecration. The disciples place the fruit held in its mouth into their own mouths and, using the sprouts held in its mouth, [perform the rite] with the fifteen Nityā-vidyās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā.

Having placed those sprouts upon the head of the disciple at the conclusion of each successive consecration, and being surrounded by yogis and yoginīs who have been gratified by the prior distribution of garments, ornaments, and other gifts, he— accompanied by his own wife—
commences the rite preceded by a festival of music from horns, conchs, bells, and the like, as well as dance and song.

One should consecrate the disciple with the *gust-pradhāna-vidyā* while contemplating that this water has entered through the pores of the skin and is washing away every single beginningless, worldly latent impression (*durvāsanā*) accumulated throughout *saṃsāra*. Having retained only as much water as is necessary for the ablution (*avāmana*), one should bathe with all the remaining water. This is his bath.

If the water goes toward the direction of fire (southeast), there is a burn; if it goes toward the southern direction, death; if toward the southwest, disease; if toward the west, poverty; and if toward the northwest, the loss of one's country—these occur for the person performing the bath. Thereafter, the disciple [should provide] a clean lower garment, an upper garment, perfumes, garlands, and so forth.

Having put on [the garment], one should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) three times with the water remaining from the principal flask while reciting the root-vidyā. Thereafter, one should worship one's own guru, who is the consecrator, with the nine offerings (*navopacāra*). The procedure for this is as follows: the general *arghya* for the guru...

Having established [the deity] with the *vidyā* and sprinkled the incense and other offerings with it, one should offer the incense by reciting at the end of one's own *guru-vidyā*: "I present this incense to Amukānandanātha," and then offer it upon the forehead with the *nātha-mantra*. [One should likewise offer] flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel, whatever else [is appropriate], the recitation of hymns, and prostrations.
Having likewise prepared the eight types of external offerings consisting of the surrender of one's own self, as well as all one's possessions, half of them, or a quarter of them,

ending with the dedication of total dependence at all times; and having satisfied [the deity] with these sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), recited the *Nāthastotra* three times, offered three handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali), and performed prostrations three times—

With palms joined in *añjali*, he should remain silent; and the Guru, having performed the piercing rite (*vedhakarma*) in the manner to be described, should sit in the appropriate place so that the *Śrīcakra* falls upon his own flowing nostril at the time of the disciple’s birth-lagna. Having placed the disciple at the location of the *bindu* within the *Śrīcakra*, [he should focus] upon his *brahmarandhra*.

Having visualized a Śrīcakra at each of the heart, the root, and the base (mūlādhāra), one should worship the principal Goddess there with mental offerings consisting of the five services— scent, flowers, incense, lamps, and food— preceded by invocation and the ritual installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). Then, placing the "living hand" upon the head of the disciple, [one should recite] three times into the disciple's ear.

One should teach the primary science: the state of being the life-force in the hands and ears, its presence in the portions of the nostril-paths as they flow, and [the state] when it flows in both, or neither.
Or, if that moment has passed during the flow [of the ritual], another time must be sought; however, instruction should not be given at that point.

Thereafter, the disciple, seated upon the Śrīcakra itself, should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), the placement of the letters (*varṇanyāsa*), and the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*).
Having recited the obtained mantra one hundred times, encapsulated by these, he should cultivate the realization of non-duality with it.

Having performed the *japa* and, by the command of the Guru, having risen from the *Śrīcakra*, he should remain right there for three days while performing service to the Guru. Thus ends the ritual for the sixteenth day.
Thus ends the primary section concerning the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*).
Now follows the middle method of the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), which is to be accomplished in five days.

On the day prior even to the fifth day preceding the day of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), the disciple— having performed the daily and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*) in the morning, having paid homage to the Guru and his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*),
having performed the worship of Vināyaka and the remembrance of Viṣṇu, and having received the Guru’s permission— takes water in his right hand [and recites] the place and time (*deśakāla*).

Having inscribed the name of the disciple, including his lineage (*gotra*), zodiac sign (*rāśi*), and name, ending with the word "desire" (*kāmanā*), and according to the application of his intellect, he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with water according to the ritual rule: "I shall perform the second initiation for [Name], of [Lineage] and [Sign], preceded by the procedure of the Madhupūrṇā consecration, through the venerable Guru."

One should cast [the flower] upon the ground. Then, having again traced the second square as before, one should form the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that, preceded by worship as a preliminary limb of initiation, one will perform the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) according to the availability of the chosen materials for the venerable Guru, the Yoginīs, and the Yogins; and then [proceed with] what has been taught for each of them.

Having worshipped the venerable Guru with the complete array of materials for the ninefold ritual service (*navopacāra*), [one should honor him] with these items: a ring, two garments, ear-ornaments, and so forth, [and request] that he act as the preceptor (*guru*) to perform the second initiation for [the disciple] who studies such-and-such Veda and belongs to such-and-such lineage (*gotra*).
Having stated,
"I choose you, named so-and-so," and having presented the materials for the formal choice (*varaṇa*) to the venerable Guru,
and after stating, "I also choose the Yoginīs and others for the purpose of assisting in the consecration performed by the venerable Guru," at the conclusion of that statement—
Having first performed worship with perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings,

one should choose [the preceptor] with rings, garments, and ornaments. Once chosen, the Guru, having donned the materials for the choice upon the respective limbs as appropriate, [should proceed] with the Maṇḍala of the Lord suited to that day and the Lord suited to the state of the disciple's life and so forth.
One should worship each of the Vanathas, beginning with their respective lords, with nine offerings. Then,

on the first day of the five-day period occurring on the following day, having drawn the Śrīcakra upon a very smooth and level ground measuring nine cubits in length and so forth, one should [draw] the central triangle-line in the center of each [section], with equal intervals between them.

Having drawn three lines by dropping horizontal lines from one mark to another, one should fashion the location for the *bindu* (dot) enclosed within three triangles; then, having divided sixty-six portions of water, medicinal herbs, decoctions, and so forth— measuring one *khārī* each— into sixty-six parts, [one should place] one part into each of those sixty-six locations.
Having filled all of them, one should place within them the nine jewels and other items, wrap them with two red cloths, and perform the ritual of the food offering (*naivedya*). Then,
having performed the rites beginning with the visualization of the *Sarvamaṅgalā* wheel and ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*),
one should, preceded by touching the water-pot (*kumbha*), effect the identity of the mantra-deity and the water through the recitation of the six-limbed deity-mantras.
One should visualize [this]; in this very same way, one should also consecrate the other ninety-five vases.

Thus ends the ritual for the first day. Then, on the second day, according to the previously mentioned method, one should [worship] the principal goddess in the central jar (madhyakalaśa) with all [elements] neither deficient nor excessive. (p.

Having worshipped with the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*), and having honored her with the five services (*pañcopacāra*) in the *Aṇimā* flask, one should worship the fifteen syllable-energies (*varṇaśakti*) surrounding it, starting from its front and proceeding clockwise, with such mantras as: "I worship the sandals of the energy of form (*rūpaśakti-pādukā*) of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ A Ā Ī," and so forth. Then...

Having worshipped her in the *laghimā* pitcher, one should worship the fifteen powers beginning with *aṇimā*. Then, having worshipped her in the center of the *mahimā* pitcher, one should worship the fifteen powers beginning with *aṇimā* all around it.
Then, having worshipped her in the center of the *īśitva* pitcher, one should worship the fifteen powers beginning with *ājñā* all around it.

Then, in the center of the Vaśitva jar, one should worship her, and around her, the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Ābhāī. In the center of the Prākāmya jar, one should worship her, and around her, the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Igāī. Then, in the center of the Vaśitva jar, one should worship her, and around her, the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Ābhāī.

One should perform worship. In the *prākāmya* jar, one should worship her in the center and the fifteen *śaktis* beginning with *igāī* around her. Then, in the *bhukti* jar, one should worship her in the center and the fifteen *śaktis* beginning with *idāī* around her. Then, in the *icchā* jar, having worshipped her by name with that mantra, one should worship the fifteen *śaktis* beginning with *ihāī* around it.

One should perform worship. Then, having worshipped those two [deities] with the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra*) using their respective mantras at the flask for the accomplishment of *rasa* (mercury/alchemy), one should worship the fifteen *śaktis*, beginning with *Īḍā* and others, by circumambulating it clockwise. Then, having worshipped those two with their respective mantras in the central part of the flask for the accomplishment of all desires (*sarvakāmasiddhi*), one should [worship] by circumambulating it clockwise.
From *Irāī* (p.
45a), one should worship the fifteen powers (*śakti*s). In all these cases, the *māyā*-seed-syllable comes first.

The conjunction of the two *śrīvīja*s is the seven-syllable formula (*saptākṣarī*) in the form "I worship the sandal [Pādukā] at the end" (*carame pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*). Likewise, the four-syllable formula (*caturakṣarī*) consists of the individual forms of the *Śakti*s. By means of these, the sixteen-syllable nature of all the *Vidyā*s is established.
Then, having worshipped [the deity] in the Brahma-pitcher with that *Vidyā*, [one should proceed] around it clockwise... 2 ...ucāī 11.

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis from "ityādi" (2) to "unāī" (11), one should worship Māheśvarī in the pitcher with her respective mantra. Having worshipped her, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis surrounding her from "upāī" (2) to "ukṣāī" (11). Then, having honored Kaumārī in her pitcher with her mantra, [one worships] surrounding her from "ū... (2).

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis beginning with *āī* (11) and ending with *ukāī* (11), and having worshipped them in the Vaiṣṇavī jar with their respective mantras; then, having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis surrounding that [jar], beginning with *ūṇāī* (11) and ending with *ūvāī* (11), one should worship them in the Vārāhī jar with their respective mantras.

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis surrounding that [Aindrī vessel], beginning with *Ūjhāī* (11) and ending with *Ṛjāī* (11); having worshipped those two with their respective Vidyās in the Aindrī vessel; and having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis surrounding that [Aindrī vessel], beginning with *Ṛjhāī* (11) and ending with *Ṛvāī* (11); [and] having worshipped those two with their respective Vidyās in the Cāmuṇḍā vessel; [then] surrounding that...

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis beginning with *2 ṛbhāī 11* and ending with *2 ṝkhāī 11*, one should worship [the deity] by name within the Mahālakṣmī jar using its respective Vidyā. Then, surrounding that, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with *2 ṛgāī 11* and ending with *2 ṝthāī 11*.
Then, having worshipped the Mistress of the First Wheel with the Root-Vidyā and having offered the worship of the first enclosure as before,
one should display the Kṣobhiṇī Mudrā. Then, [one worships] Kāmākarṣiṇī in the jar.

Having worshipped those two with their respective mantras, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with "2 ṛ dā ī 11" and ending with "2 ṝ sā ī 11" all around them. Having worshipped Buddhyākarṣiṇī in the pitcher with her mantra, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with "2 ṛ hā ī 11" and ending with "2 ḷ ṭā ī 11" all around her. [Then one worships] Ahaṅkārākarṣiṇī.
Having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the *kalaśa*, one should worship the śaktis beginning with "2 ḷṭhāī 11" and ending with "2 ḷpāī 11" all around it;

then, having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the *śabdākarṣi* *kalaśa*, one should worship the śaktis beginning with "2 ḷrāī 11" and ending with "2 ḷṅāī 11" all around it. Then, in the *sparśākarṣiṇī* *kalaśa*...
Having worshipped that [deity] with its respective mantra, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with *ḷcāī* (11) and ending with *ḷnāī* (11) around it;

then, having worshipped that [deity] with its respective mantra in the Rūpākarṣiṇī jar, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with *ḷpāī* (11) and ending with *ḷkṣāī* (11) around it; and then, having worshipped that [deity] with its respective mantra in the Rasākarṣiṇī jar—

Having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *e ā ī* (11) and ending with *e ṭhā ī* (11) around that [vessel], one should worship that [central deity] in the Gandhākarṣiṇī vessel with its respective Vidyā; then, having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *e ṇā ī* (11) and ending with *e vā ī* (11) around that [vessel], one should worship that [deity] in the Cittākarṣiṇī vessel with its respective Vidyā; then, [having worshipped those] beginning with *e śā ī* (11) around that... [and so on].
Having worshipped the powers ending with *ai-jā-ī*, and having worshipped that [power] in the jar of the attractor of fortitude (*dhairyākarṣiṇī*) with its respective mantra,
one should worship the fifteen powers surrounding it, beginning with *ai-jhā-ī* (11) and ending with *ai-vā-ī* (11).

Having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the Smṛtyākarṣiṇī jar, and having fully worshipped the śaktis beginning with "2 aibhāī 11" and ending with "2 okhāī 11" surrounding it; having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the Nāmākarṣiṇī jar, and having fully worshipped the śaktis beginning with "2 ogāī 11" and ending with "2 oghāī 11" surrounding it; [in] the Vījākarṣiṇī jar...

Having worshipped that [deity] with its respective mantra, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis surrounding it, beginning with "2 odāī 11" and ending with "2 osāī 11"; then, having worshipped that [deity] with its respective mantra in the Ātmākarṣiṇī jar, one should worship the Śaktis surrounding it, beginning with "2 ohāī 11" and ending with "2 auṭāī 1"; and then, having worshipped that [deity] with its respective mantra in the Śarīrākarṣiṇī jar...

Having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *auṭāī* (11) and ending with *auyāī*, surrounding that [vessel], and having worshipped those two [deities] in the Amṛtākarṣiṇī jar with their respective mantras; and having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *aurāī* (11) and ending with *aṃṅāī* (11), surrounding that [jar];
then, at the conclusion of the worship of the Second Cakreśvarī with the Root Mantra, according to the method described for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).
Having offered the worship of the second enclosure, one should display the Drāviṇī mudrā.

Then, having worshipped those two with their respective mantras in the Anaṅgakusuma jar, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with *aṃ cāī* (11) and ending with *aṃ nāī* (11) all around it; then, having worshipped those two with their respective mantras in the Anaṅgamekhalā jar, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with *aṃ pāī* (11) and ending with *aṃ kṣāī* (11) all around it.
Having worshipped Anaṅgamadanākalashā with her vidyā, and having fully honored the Śaktis beginning with "aḥ āī" (11 times) and ending with "aḥ ṭhāī" (11 times), [one worships] Anaṅgamadanāturā.

Having worshipped those two [deities] in the *kalaśa* with their respective mantras, and having fully worshipped the powers (*śaktis*) beginning with "2 aḥṇāī 11" and ending with "2 aḥvāī 11" around it; then, having worshipped those two in the *anaṅgarekhā-kalaśa* with their respective mantras, and having fully worshipped the fifteen powers beginning with "2 aḥśāī 11" and ending with "2 sajāī 11" around it; [then, in the] *anaṅgavegā-kalaśa*...
Having worshipped that [deity] with its respective vidyā, one should worship the śaktis surrounding it, beginning with "2 sajhāī 11" and ending with "2 savāī 11.

Then, having worshipped that [deity] in the Anaṅga-kalaśa with its respective vidyā, one should worship the śaktis surrounding it, beginning with "2 samāī 11" and ending with "2 sākhāī 11. Finally, having worshipped that [deity] in the Anaṅgamālinī-kalaśa with its respective vidyā...

Having worshipped the Śaktis surrounding that [central deity], beginning with *tatparitaḥ* (2) *sāgāī* (11), and so on, up to *sāthāī* (11); having worshipped the Mistress of the Cakra (*cakreśī*) in the form of Tripureśī by means of the root mantra (*mūla*); and having offered the worship of the third enclosure (*tṛtīyāvaraṇa*) as in the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), one should display the Sarvākarṣiṇī Mudrā.

Then, having worshipped those two with their respective mantras in the *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* jar, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis surrounding it, beginning with "2 sādāī 11" and ending with "2 sāsāī 11. Then, having worshipped those two with their respective mantras in the *sarvavidrāviṇī* jar, one should worship the Śaktis surrounding it, beginning with "2 sahāī 11" and ending with "2 siṭhāī 11."

Having performed worship, one should worship the [deity] named *Sarvākarṣiṇī* in the jar with her mantra; then, having worshipped the powers (śaktis) surrounding it, beginning with "2 siṭhāī" and ending with "2 siyāī" eleven times each. Having performed worship, one should worship the [deity] named *Sarvāhlādinī* in the jar with her mantra;
then, having worshipped the powers surrounding it, beginning with "2 siṭhāī" and ending with "2 sīṅāī" eleven times each.

Having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the *sarvasaṃmohinī* jar, and having fully worshipped the Śaktis beginning with "2 sīcāī 11" (p. 47a) and ending with "2 sīnāī 11," one should worship those two with their respective vidyās in the *sarvastambhinī* jar.

Having worshipped the powers beginning with *2 sīpāī 11* and ending with *2 sīkṣāī 11* all around that [vessel], and having worshipped those two with their respective mantras in the *Sarvajambhinī* jar, one should worship the fifteen powers beginning with *2 suāī 11* and ending with *2 suḍhāī 11* all around that [jar]; then, having worshipped those two with their respective mantras in the *Sarvaśaṅkarī* jar.

Having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *suṇāī* (2) and ending with *suvāī* (11) around that [vessel], one should worship that [deity] in the *sarvarañjinī* jar with its respective Vidyā, and having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *suśāī* (2) and ending with *sujāī* (11) around that [jar], one should worship that [deity] in the *sarvonmādinī* jar with its respective Vidyā, and [worship the Śaktis] beginning with *sūjhāī* (2) and ending with [11] around that [jar].

Having worshipped the powers (śaktis) ending with "2 sūvāī 11" [in the first jar], one should worship that [deity] in the *sarvārthasādhinī* jar with its respective vidyā-mantra, and having worshipped the powers surrounding it beginning with "2 sūbhāī 11" and ending with "2 sekhāī 11"; then, having worshipped that [deity] in the *sarvasampattipūraṇī* jar with its respective vidyā-mantra, [one should worship the powers surrounding it beginning with] "2 segāī 11," and so forth.

Having worshipped the powers (śaktis) beginning with *2 sethāī 11* and ending with *2 sesāī 11*, one should worship those two [deities] with their respective mantras in the *sarvamantramayī* pitcher; then, having worshipped the powers beginning with *2 sadāī 11* and ending with *2 sesāī 11* around that [pitcher], one should worship those two [deities] with their respective mantras in the *sarvadvandvakṣayaṅkarī* pitcher; then, [beginning] with *2 sehāī 11* and so forth... *2*.

Having worshipped the powers ending with Saiṭāī (number eleven), and having worshipped Tripuravāsinī, the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśī), with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) using the five offerings (pañcopacāra), one should present the worship of the fourth enclosure just as in the daily worship (nityapūjā) and display the Sarvāveṣakarī mudrā.

Then, having worshipped those two with their respective mantras in the *sarvasiddhiprada* (bestower of all accomplishments) flask, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with *saiṭhāī* 11 and ending with *saidyāī* 11 around it; then, having worshipped those two with their respective mantras in the *sarvasampatprada* (bestower of all wealth) flask.

Having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with "2 saihāī 11" and ending with "2 soṅāī 11" all around that [vessel], one should worship those two with their respective Vidyās in the Sarvapriyaṅkarī jar; then, having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with "2 socāī 11" and ending with "2 sonāī 11" all around that [vessel], one should worship those two with their respective Vidyās in the Sarvamaṅgalakāriṇī jar.

Having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *tatparitaḥ 2 sopāī 11* and ending with *2 sokṣāī 11*, one should worship those two [deities] in the vessel that grants all desires (*sarvakāmaprada-kalaśa*) by means of their respective mantras; then, having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *tatparitaḥ 2 sauāī 11* and ending with *2 sauḍhāī 11*, one should worship those two [deities] in the vessel that liberates from all suffering (*sarvaduḥkhavimocanī-kalaśa*) by means of their respective mantras.

Having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with "2 sauṇāī 11" and ending with "2 sauvāī 11" all around that [vessel], and having worshipped those two [deities] in the vessel that pacifies all death (sarvamṛtyupraśamanī) by means of their respective mantras; and having worshipped the Vidyās beginning with "2 sauśāī 11" and ending with "2 saṃjāī 11" all around that [vessel] in the vessel that destroys all obstacles (sarvavighnavināśinī).

Having worshipped their names with that vidyā, one should worship the Śaktis surrounding them from "2 saṃdāī 11" up to "2 saṃvāī 11"; then, having worshipped their names with that vidyā in the *sarvāṅgasundarī* pitcher, one should worship the Śaktis surrounding them from "2 saṃbhāī 11" up to "2 saḥkhāī 11"; [and likewise] in the *sarvasaubhāgyadāyinī* pitcher.

Having worshipped those [deities] with their respective vidyās, one should worship the fifteen śaktis surrounding that [central deity], beginning with "saḥ māī 11" and ending with "saḥ thāī 11" (p. 48a), and then worship the Mistress of the Cakra (cakreśī), who is the embodiment of Tripuraśrī, with the root-vidyā.
Having performed the worship according to the daily ritual and offered the worship of the fifth enclosure, one should display the Sarvonmādinī mudrā.

Then, having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the Sarvajña-kalaśa, one should worship the fifteen śaktis surrounding it, beginning with *saḥdāī 11* and ending with *saḥsāī 11*. Then, having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the Sarvaśakti-kalaśa,
one should worship the fifteen śaktis surrounding it in sequence, beginning with *saḥhāī 11* and ending with *haṭāī 11*.

Having worshipped [the deity] in the *sarvaiśvaryaprada* (bestower of all sovereignty) jar with its respective vidyā-mantra, one should worship the fifteen śaktis surrounding it in sequence, beginning with "2 haṭhāī 11" and ending with "2 hayāī 11. Then, having worshipped [the deity] in the *sarvajñā* jar with its respective vidyā-mantra, one should worship those [śaktis] surrounding it in sequence, beginning with "2 harāī 11" and ending with "2 hāṅāī 11."

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis, one should worship that [deity] with its respective Vidyā in the vessel that destroys all diseases; then, having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis surrounding it, beginning with "2 hā cā ī 11" and ending with "2 hā nā ī 11.
Thereafter, having worshipped that [deity] with its respective Vidyā in the vessel whose nature is the support of all, one should [worship] surrounding it with "2 hā pā ī 11" and so forth.

Having worshipped these fifteen Śaktis ending with *hākṣāī* 11, one should worship those two [deities] with their respective Vidyās in the *sarvapāpahara* (all-sin-removing) jar; then, having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis surrounding it, beginning with *hiāī* 11 and ending with *hiḍhāī* 11, one should worship those two [deities] with their respective Vidyās in the *sarvānandamayī* (all-blissful) jar, surrounding it.
Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis beginning with *hiṇāī* (11) and ending with *hivāī* (11), [one should worship] in the pitcher (*kalaśa*) which is the embodiment of all protection (p.
