Having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās, and having fully worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *hī śāī* (11) and ending with *hī jaiī* (11) around them; and having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the jar that bestows all desired fruits, and having fully worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *hī jhāī* (11) and ending with *hī vāī* (11) around them; [one should worship] her who has the form of Tripuramālinī with the root-vidyā.
Having worshipped Cakreśī just as in the daily worship (nityapūjā) and having offered the worship of the sixth enclosure,
one should display the Great Hook Mudrā (mahāṅkuśamudrā).
Then, having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the Vaśinī jar, one should worship the powers (śaktis) surrounding it, beginning with "Hī Bhāī" (x11) and ending with "Hukhāī" (x11).

Then, having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the Kāmeśvarī jar, one should worship the fifteen powers surrounding it, beginning with "Hugāī" (x11) and ending with "Huthāī" (x11). [Then] in the Modinī jar...

Having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with "Hudāī" (11) and ending with "Husāī" (11) around them; having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the Vimala-kalaśa, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with "Huhāī" (11) and ending with "Hūḍhāī" (11) around them; having worshipped those two with their respective vidyās in the Aruṇa-kalaśa, [one should worship] "Haṭhāī" (2) around them.
Having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with "2 hūyāī" and ending with "11," one should worship that [deity] in the Jayinī-kalaśa with its respective Vidyā;

then, having worshipped the Śaktis surrounding it, beginning with "2 hūrāī" and ending with "11 heṅāī," one should worship that [deity] in the Sarveśī-kalaśa with its respective Vidyā; then, [one worships] the Śaktis beginning with "2 hevāī" and ending with "11."
Having worshipped [her] in the *kaulinī* vessel with that mantra, and having worshipped those two [deities] with that same vidyā (p.
one should worship the Śaktis surrounding it— beginning with "2 he pā ī 11" and ending with "2 he sā ī 11"— using the root mantra.
Having worshipped the Mistress of the Cakra (Cakreśī), who is the embodiment of Tripurasiddhā, and having offered the worship of the seventh enclosure according to the procedure for daily worship,
one should display the Khecarī Mudrā.
Then, having worshipped that [Vāṇa] jar with its own mantra at the location learned from the mouth of the Guru,

one should worship the Śaktis beginning with "2 hai āī 11" and ending with "2 hai ḍhāī 11" all around it; likewise, having worshipped those same [Śaktis] in the Śaiva Vāṇa jar, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with "2 hai ṇāī 11" and ending with "2 hai vāī 11" all around it.

Having worshipped those [deities] in the Śaiva-bow pitcher, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with *haiṇāī* (11) and ending with *haivāī* (11) around it; then, having worshipped that [deity] in the Śākta-bow pitcher with its own mantra, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with *haiśāī* (11) and ending with *hojāī* (11) around it; [and finally] in the Śaiva-arrow pitcher, with its own mantra...

Having worshipped that [deity] and, surrounding it, having fully worshipped the Śaktis beginning with "2 hojbhāī 11" and ending with "2 hovāī 11," one should worship that [deity] in the Śākta-pāśa-kalaśa with its own mantra and, surrounding it, fully worship the Śaktis beginning with "2 hobhāī 11" and ending with "2 haukhāī 11"; then, having worshipped that [deity] in the Śaiva-pāśa-kalaśa with its own mantra and, surrounding it, [worship the Śaktis].

Having worshipped the Śakti powers from *haugāī* 11 and so forth up to *hauthāī* 11, one should worship that [deity] in the Śākta-aṅkuśa-kalaśa with that mantra; then, having worshipped the Śakti powers surrounding it from *haudāī* 11 and so forth up to *hausāī* 11, one should worship that [deity] in the Śaiva-aṅkuśa-kalaśa with that mantra, and [worship those] surrounding it.

Having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *haujhāī* (11) and ending with *hovāī* (11), one should worship that [deity] in the Śākta-pāśa-kalaśa with its respective mantra; then, having worshipped the Śaktis surrounding it, beginning with *hobhāī* (11) and ending with *houkhāī* (11), one should worship that [deity] in the Śaiva-pāśa-kalaśa with its respective mantra; then, surrounding that as well, [beginning with] *haugāī* (11) and so on... (2).

Having worshipped the Śaktis ending with *hauthāī* (11), one should worship that [deity] in the Śākta-aṅkuśa-kalaśa with its own mantra; then, having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *haudāī* (11) and ending with *hausāī* (11) surrounding it, one should worship that [deity] in the Śaiva-aṅkuśa-kalaśa with its own mantra; then, [having worshipped] the Śaktis beginning with *hauhāī* (11) and ending with *haṃṭāī* (11) surrounding it...

Having thus worshipped these powers, one should worship Kāmeśvarī in her jar with her mantra; then, having consecrated the jar [with the mantra] "haṃ ṭhāī" eleven times, [one should place] it around that [central jar]. (p.

One should perform the recitation of the thousand-rooted vidyā, followed by a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number, and the offering of sacrificial food (bali). One should then establish the nyāsas.
Thus concludes the ritual duties for the fourth day.

Then, on the fifth day, which is the disciple’s birthday, having first performed the consecration (*vedha*) by sprinkling him with the water from the jar that was infused during the preliminary rite (*adhivāsa*) on the fourth day— according to the previously mentioned method of the Vārāhī-vidyā— the teacher should thereafter place the disciple within the *mātṛkā-mantra* diagram drawn upon the ground in the eastern direction.

Having consecrated [the disciple] in sequence with the jars of *aṇimā* and so forth, preceded by the empowerments (*abhiṣeka*) performed by means of his own fifteen sets of fifteen *vidyās* of the Śaktis, the Guru— supported by the consort (*rūpatnī*)— should likewise consecrate the disciple with the principal jar (*pradhānakalaśa*) as before. And the disciple [should receive it].

Having first performed the purification, the disciple, having put on a clean, washed upper garment and adorned himself with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) three times with the principal water while reciting the *vidyā*. Then, having worshipped the Guru with the nine offerings (*navopacāra*), and having satisfied him with all his possessions, including the offering of one's own self and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he should recite the *Nātha-stotra* three times.

Having recited [the mantra] three times, offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) three times, and prostrated three times, he should remain silent with palms joined in reverence (*baddhāñjali*). Then the Guru, having performed the piercing rite (*vedhakarma*) in the manner to be described,
should sit in such a place that the *Śrīcakra* falls within his own nostril-passage as it flows, specifically at the location of the *bindu* situated within the *Śrīcakra*.
Having seated the disciple, and having first meditated upon each respective *cakra* in the three locations beginning with the *brahmarandhra*,

he should worship the principal deity there with the five mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*). Then, placing his hand upon the head of the disciple, he should impart the primary *vidyā* thirty times into the ear of the disciple, while the disciple remains seated upon the *śrīcakra*.

Having worshipped the Śaktis, beginning with the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*), the placement of the letters (*varṇa-nyāsa*), and the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) repeated one hundred times and so forth, ending with "haṃ yāī" (11), one should worship them with their respective mantras in the Vajreśī flask.

Having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with *haṃ rā ī* (11) and ending with *haḥ ṅa ī* (11) all around that [vessel], and having honored the [deity] in the Bhagamālinī jar with its specific mantra, one should worship the Śaktis beginning with *haḥ cā ī* (11) and ending with *haḥ nā ī* (11) surrounding that [jar], and then worship Tripurā, who is the form of Vāruṇī and the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśī*).
Having offered the worship of the eighth enclosure as prescribed for the daily worship, one should display the seed-syllable mudrā (*bījamudrā*).
Then, having worshipped Lalitā with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) in the principal jar situated within the triangle located at the center of the wheel (*binducakra*),
one should [worship] each of the fifteen powers (*śakti*) surrounding it, beginning with *2 haḥ pāī* (11) and ending with *2 haḥ sāī* (11).

Having worshipped with the sixteen-syllable vidyās, and having worshipped the Mistress of the Cakra (cakreśī) in the form of Tripurasundarī with the root-vidyā using the five services (pañcopacāra), one should offer the worship of the ninth enclosure as before, display the yoni-mudrā,
and perform the fourteenth service in the form of reciting hymns of praise.

Thus concludes the ritual for the second day. On the third day, at the conclusion of one’s daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), one should worship the principal Goddess with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). Then, having worshipped the ninety-six Śaktis who were worshipped on the previous day with their respective mantras (*vidyā*), one should worship a single couple consisting of one Yogin and one Yoginī with the root-mantras (*mūlavidyā*).

Having worshipped with the five types of offerings (pañcopacāra), preceded by the secret worship (rahasyapūjā), one should present to the Goddess, together with her retinue (sāvaraṇāya), the fifteenth offering known as *arpaṇa*.
Thus concludes the ritual duties for the third day.
Then, on the fourth day, having performed the recitation (*japa*) of the primary and secondary *vidyās* according to the *Kālanityā* rites,
and having offered the presentation consisting of the contemplation of non-duality with them, one should rise from the *śrīcakra* by the command of the Guru.
Performing service, you shall dwell in his very abode for three days.
Thus concludes the ritual duties for the fifth day.
The ritual for the middle full consecration is complete.
Now, the "younger" method of the Full Consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), which is to be accomplished in two days,
is being clearly demonstrated as it currently exists in practice due to the abundance of qualified candidates. Since that [consecration] depends upon its constituent materials, the materials for it,
the initiation (*dīkṣā*) consisting of the rites preceding and following it, and the entire collection of requisites are described first.
For the purpose of drawing the mandala of the Primordial Lord (Pūrvanātha), a space of one cubit for the palāśa-seat and other requirements is needed;
the liquid for the paste used in drawing consists of sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and musk;
and for the purpose of drawing the Śrīcakra, a level ground measuring three cubits in length and breadth is required.

Having mixed together white sandalwood and red sandalwood with any one of the substances— saffron, vermilion, red ochre, lac, or lead— orpa— a paste is prepared, and with that, the drawing is made. At every initiation,
a single *mātṛkā* wheel is extracted from the *palāśa* seat and so forth at each initiation.

Having extracted from the *palāśa* seat and so forth each individual *vedhacakra*, and having likewise [extracted] each individual *nityapūjācakra* from the *dīkṣaṇīyavidyā*, one should, according to the rule, produce four *cakras* for each initiation together with the *nāthacakra*. The materials for their manifestation are, just like those of the *śrīcakra*, gold, silver, and copper.

In the center of the five silver jars, which are the primary ones facing east, one jar is placed for each initiation (dīkṣā) as determined by the sequence of the disciple’s own power; and the number of initiations is twenty-one.
Therein, the first initiation, the *nityādīkṣā*, is prescribed for the purpose of examining the disciple;

the second is the *jvālāmālinīdīkṣā* for the sake of establishing fitness for the primary piercing (*prathamāvedha*); and the third initiation is for the purpose of removing the impurities (*mala*) from the principal Vidyā.

The third is the initiation of Vārāhī, which is to be received at a previous time following the instruction on the second principal *vidyā* subsequent to the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*). Then follow the sixteen initiations beginning with the sixteen *nityā*s in sequence; then the initiation of Kurukullā, numbering twenty-one. Furthermore, although there is also the initiation of the fourteen mantras later on, [the total is as stated].
Furthermore, although these [other vessels] cannot be specifically defined, since they do not depend on consecration (*abhiṣeka*), there is no requirement for the [standard] twenty-one marks;

thus, twenty-one jars (*kalaśa*) should be acquired, each capable of holding a *khārī* measure of water. In each jar, one should place gold, copper, the nine gems, grains such as rice, and sandalwood.
Sprouts of the *indravallī*, mango, jackfruit, and *aśvattha* trees; a *mātuluṅga* fruit; two red garments for placing beneath the jar;
rice measuring one *droṇa*;
rings, cloth, earrings, and so forth, for the purpose of choosing a preceptor at each initiation; and the initiation preceded by the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*.

Just as with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should follow the same principle regarding the abundance of requisites for the initiation (*varaṇa*) intended for that purpose. For practitioners (*yogins*), there should be an adornment of the initiands with rings, garments, and so forth; furthermore, when initiating others, a gradation should be made according to the value and other factors of the materials offered. This applies to the offering substances (*balidravya*), the individual worship (*pratipūjā*), and generally twice for each initiation (*dīkṣā*).

The ritual worship (*sāmayī-pūjā*) consists of two types of offerings: garments, ornaments, perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel leaves (*tāmbūla*), and so forth; for each individual offering, there is a general vessel for the *arghya* water and a primary vessel for the *arghya*. (p.

There should be five water-vessels for each ritual bath, each equipped with a spout; and five substances—namely gorocanā, camphor, saffron, agallochum, and musk—should be placed into each common arghya vessel.
For each worship, there should be sacrificial materials, wood from a sacrificial tree, forest grass, and kuśa grass.

A vessel for bringing the fire and for covering it; either a *pippala* or *palāśa* leaf for the purpose of the *homa*; either a *kūrca* (bundle of grass) or a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*); and one’s entire property, half of it, or a fourth part of it—likewise, an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, a cow, a bull, land, and the earth traversed by circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*): these seven items may be given either collectively or individually, according to one’s capacity to give.

Having abandoned stinginess regarding wealth, one should provide gold ornaments, clothing, a house, food, and so forth, as prepared offerings; the teacher’s fees (guru-dakṣiṇā) must be fulfilled without overstepping the will of the venerable Guru.

In the case of the Full Consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), the teacher’s fee should be increased due to the greater difficulty involved. The wife of the Guru and the Yoginī are also to be honored separately from the other Yogins.
Separately, a more abundant sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), a pair [of animals], and the complete assembly of materials for feeding the Brahmins should be prepared according to one's capacity.

When these materials are thus fully assembled, there is no need to perform this rite again; for this is not like the Sandhyā or Agnihotra rites, which must be performed by a fire-maintainer (agnisādhya) regardless of whether the full assembly of materials is present. Rather, [this rite] is to be honored only when the complete assembly of materials is available.

It is not the case that [the performance of this rite] is optional (*kāmya*) like the *tulāpuruṣa* gift or the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), for in the view of any [authoritative] teacher, the commencement of an optional rite must occur through the primary set of materials (*mukhya-sāmagrī*). However, regarding the commencement when the primary materials are unavailable: according to some teachers, one should employ substitute materials (*pratinidhi-dravya*); according to others, there is simply the omission (*lopa*) of such a rite. It is not [optional].

"Any hope for fruit [is found] elsewhere," as explained in detail in other sources. And therefore, according to the method described for the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*), she is colored with vermilion, lac, and so forth.
In one's own guru’s residence or similar location, which is adorned with canopies illuminated by rows of lamps and well-perfumed by incense from the guru and others,

for a disciple who has attained purity through the first initiation and instruction, [the ritual] is to be performed prior to the day of the specific solar reckoning (*sāvana-dina*) characterized by the disciple’s birth date, lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), or weekday, according to the procedure for the instructions to be practiced thereafter.
On the morning of the third day, after performing the preliminary rites (*prātaḥkṛtya*) and so forth, having performed the worship of Vināyaka and the remembrance of Viṣṇu,

and having paid homage to one’s preceptor (*guru*) and tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and received their permission; then, taking water in the hand, one should specify the place, time, lineage (*gotra*), zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), one’s own name, and the desired object (*kāmanā*), and perform the ritual injunction according to the rules as best as one can.

"I shall perform the second initiation (dvitīyadīkṣā), preceded by the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), through the venerable Guru [named] so-and-so, belonging to such-and-such Veda, such-and-such Gotra, such-and-such Rāśi, and such-and-such name, according to the younger branch (kaniṣṭhapakṣa). At the conclusion of this primary *saṅkalpa*, having inscribed "the second" as before, [one proceeds] as a preliminary limb (*pūrvāṅga*) to the initiation.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I shall perform the worship preceded by the offering of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*), having prepared the necessary materials according to my intelligence through the command of the venerable Guru, the Yoginīs, and the Yogins," one should perform [the worship] with the nine services (*navopacāra*)— namely, perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and betel— as well as whatever hymns may be recited and prostrations.
Having honored the Brāhmaṇa— who has been determined as the Guru through the act of self-surrender—

with these ornaments such as rings, garments, and so forth, one should state: "I choose you as my Guru to perform the second initiation preceded by the *kaniṣṭha-pakṣa-pūrṇābhiṣeka*," and then present the materials for the choice (*varaṅ-sāmagrī*) to the Guru.

Having made the offering, and having stated, "I choose you as well as the Yoginīs and others to act as assistants for the consecration performed by the venerable Guru," one should perform worship with the five offerings beginning with fragrance, followed by [presenting] a signet ring, garments, and so forth, with the Goddess as the second [participant].

The powers beginning with *ūpāī* are her [powers]; the third is Kaumārī, whose powers begin with *ūāī*; the fourth is Vaiṣṇavī, whose powers begin with *ūsāī*; the fifth is Vārāhī, whose powers begin with *ūśāī*;
and the sixth is Aindrī, whose powers begin with *ṛjhāī*.

Having worshipped the deities of the first enclosure— namely, Cāmuṇḍā on the seventh day with her powers beginning with Ṛbhāī, and Mahālakṣmī on the eighth day with her powers beginning with Ṛgāī— thus together with their respective fifteen powers each, as well as the eighteen [deities] beginning with Aṇimā up to Mahālakṣmī; [one should worship] the Root-Vidyā.

At the end of the third section, having worshipped the principal goddess with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) using the mantra "I worship the pādukā of Tripurā," one should offer the worship of the first enclosure to its deities while reciting: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these manifest yoginīs accept the worship of Trailokyamohana."
One should display the Kṣobhiṇī mudrā. Thus ends the first enclosure. Two hundred and eighty-eight (288) Śaktis, beginning with Aṇimā, have been worshipped.

Having worshipped the one associated with the sixteen-petaled lotus at the front petal of the Goddess, saying: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Aṅkāmākarṣiṇī Nityākalā," one should then worship its fifteen powers with the mantras beginning with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Dāī Rūpaśakti," and so forth.

Likewise, in the subsequent [sections] as well, following the sequence of the left, one should worship each respective [deity] with mantras endowed with the union of two seed-syllables, one after another, the vowels, their respective names, the *nityā* portions, and the seven-syllable phrase;
having worshipped each one individually at its respective end, [one places] *hrīṃ śrīṃ* in the place of *prākāmya*.

Having worshipped that [pādukā] with the mantra, "I worship the pādukā of the siddhi of *prākāmya*," and having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis around it with the mantras beginning with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the pādukā of the Śakti of Form (Rūpaśakti)," one should worship at the place of enjoyment (*bhukti*) with the mantra, "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the pādukā of the siddhi of enjoyment (*bhukti*"), and [worship] around that.

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis with the mantras beginning with *hrīṃ śrīṃ idāī rūpaśakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, one should worship that [sixteenth] at the station of Will (*icchā-sthāna*) with the mantra *hrīṃ śrīṃ icchāsiddhi-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. Then,
surrounding that, one worships with the mantras beginning with *hrīṃ śrīṃ i hāī rūpaśakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis, one should worship the *pādukā* at the place of *rasa* (taste) with the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the *pādukā* of Rasasiddhi-Śakti. Then, surrounding that, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis in number with the fifteen mantras beginning with: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the *pādukā* of Īṭhāī-Rūpa-Śakti," and so forth; and at the place of *sarvakāma* (all desires), [one should worship].

Having worshipped her with the mantra, "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandal of the accomplishment of all desires," one should then worship the fifteen Śaktis surrounding her with the mantras beginning with, "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandal of the Śakti of Form (Rūpa-Śakti)," and so forth; furthermore, in the subsequent [section], the names beginning with Brāhmī are to be inserted between the two seed-syllables and the seven-syllable mantra.
Having caused [them] to enter with the perfected mantras beginning with the eleven syllables and so forth,
[one should place] the eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, in their respective locations; for each, there are two seed-syllables numbering fifteen each,
and the final four-syllable form consisting of the nature of Rūpa-Śakti situated between them, which is named by the three syllables.

The worship of the powers (śaktis) who perform the rites of mantra and who are to be honored should be followed. Thus, because the mantra has been extracted, only its name is shown. One should choose as a preceptor (guru) Brāhmī as the first, along with her powers such as Ūrdhvā and others. And once chosen, the preceptor [should provide] the requisites for the selection as appropriate.

One should place [the offerings] upon those respective limbs. Then the Guru, having drawn the Maṇḍala of the Nāthas—whose distinct forms are determined by the specific joints, the Guru-pervasion (*guruvyāpti*), and the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—either on a seat made of *palāśa* wood or on smooth, level ground; there, preceded by the installation of the general *arghya* vessel...

Having performed the ritual offerings of fragrance and so forth for each [deity] through both dismissal (*utsarga*) and invitation (*nivedana*), having approached each of their respective lords and worshipped all nine lords, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Guru and ask for his forgiveness.

Then, on the day preceding the initiation (dīkṣā), after performing the morning rites, one should place a heap of grain measuring one *droṇa* in the center of the *bindu* of the *Śrīcakra*, using materials such as *śrīkhaṇḍa* (sandalwood) as prescribed; this heap should be three cubits in length and breadth. Upon that [heap], [one should place] gold, silver, copper, and...

A vessel made of one of the types of clay, each succeeding one being of superior quality, filled with water containing its own seeds, appropriate measurements, colors, and decoctions of medicinal herbs; with its base and neck each wrapped in a single red cloth;
containing the nine gems, gold, copper, grains such as rice, and sandalwood within; and with *indravallī* tied at the mouth.

Having placed a water-pot (kalaśa) there, filled with the sprouts of the *aśvattha* and *sahakāra* trees and joined with *mātuluṅga* fruits, one should perform the perpetual worship of Sarvamaṅgalā therein— including the meditation on the wheel (*cakra*) and so forth, along with the seven enclosures— within the midst of the Sarvamaṅgalā worship, ending with the dismissal (*udvāsana*), the recitation of the pair of hymns to the Guru and the Goddess.
At the conclusion of all rites, as previously described in the introduction to the *Sarvamaṅgalā*,

one should again contemplate the Śrīcakra— which exists in the form of a *bindu* at the primary deity’s location— situated within the vessel (*kalaśa*) that occupies the aforementioned space, and [visualize] the seat (*āsana*).

Having performed the sequence of rites beginning with entering [the pavilion], sipping water (ācamana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and so forth, up to the end as stated in the introduction to the section on the primary Full Consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka)—
thereby recalling the collection of items prescribed by the sūtra— one should offer the guest-water (pādya) and other offerings to the principal Goddess, ending with betel (tāmbūla).

Having worshipped with the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*), one should worship the ninety-six deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*), beginning with *Aṇimā*, together with their respective fifteen-fold enclosures, in the locations of the *Śrīcakra*’s enclosures starting from *Aṇimā* as established by direct perception; for instance, in the place of *Aṇimā*, [one worships] *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*.

Having worshipped the *aṇimā* siddhi with the five offerings, saying "I worship the sandal of the *aṇimā* siddhi," and having worshipped the fifteen powers surrounding it— which are of the nature of its rays— with the sixteen-syllable mantras beginning with "hrīṃ śrīṃ a ā ī, I worship the sandal of the power of form (rūpaśakti)," [and so on], [one should place] hrīṃ śrīṃ in the place of *laghimā*.

Having worshipped the sandal of the *laghimā-siddhi* with the mantra "I worship the sandal of the *laghimā-siddhi*" using the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), and having fully worshipped the fifteen Śaktis surrounding it with the mantras beginning with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṇāī, I worship the sandal of the Śakti of Form" (*rūpaśakti-pādukā*) and so forth,
one should then worship the sandal of the *mahimā-śakti* at the station of *mahimā* with the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandal of the *mahimā-śakti*."

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis around that [seat] with the mantras beginning with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the pādukā of Aśā," and having honored her at the place of Īśitva with the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the pādukā of the Siddhi of Īśitva," [one worships] around that [seat] with the mantras beginning with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the pādukā of the Śakti of Form (Ājñā)."

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis, one should worship that [Śakti] at the station of Vaśitva with the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ vaśitvasiddhipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. Then, surrounding that, one worships the fifteen Śaktis with the mantras beginning with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ābhāyai rūpaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth.

The two seed-syllables, together with their respective names and the term *rūpaśakti*, constitute sixteen-syllable mantras through the combination of four and seven syllables; by means of these, one should [worship] fifteen Śaktis for each [of the deities].
One should worship [them]. Since the mantras have been shown in this manner, only their distinct names are stated here.
The second is Buddhyākarṣiṇī; her fifteen powers begin with Ṛ, Hā, Ī, and so forth. The third is Ahaṅkārākarṣiṇī; her fifteen powers begin with Ḷ, Ṭhā, Ī, and so forth. [The fourth is] Śabdākarṣiṇī.

The fourth [vowels], beginning with *ḷrāī*, are the powers (*śakti*) that attract touch; the fifth, beginning with *ḷcāī*, are their powers that attract form; the sixth, beginning with *ḷpāī*, are their powers that attract taste; the seventh, beginning with *eāī*, are their powers that attract smell; and the eighth is *egāī*.

The powers beginning with *prabhṛti* are those that attract the mind; the ninth is *aiśāī*, and the powers beginning with it are those that attract fortitude (*dhairya*). The eleventh is *smṛtyākarṣiṇī*, and the powers beginning with *aibhāī* are those [that attract it]. The twelfth is *nāmākarṣiṇī*, and the powers beginning with *ogāī* are those [that attract it].

The thirteenth [power] is Vījākarṣiṇī; her powers begin with Odāī. The fourteenth is Ātmākarṣiṇī; her powers begin with Ohāī. The fifteenth is Amṛtākarṣiṇī; her powers begin with Auṭāī. The sixteenth is Śarīrākarṣiṇī; her fifteen powers begin with Aurāī. Thus.
Each of these sixteen Nityās, beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī and ending with Śarīrākarṣiṇī, is accompanied by its own fifteen respective Śaktis. (p.

Having worshipped the *kalās*, at the end of the *mūlavidyā* of the complete *trikūṭa*, one should worship the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra "I worship the sandals (*pādukā*) of Tripureśī" using five prostrations (*pañcoñcāra*). Then, by offering a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these Guptayoginīs accept this worship that fulfills all desires," one performs the worship of the second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*).
Uttering "Samarpya drīṃ," one should display the Rāviṇī mudrā.

Thus, in the second enclosure, one hundred and fifty-six (156) powers, numbering 256 including those beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī, have been worshipped. Then, in the eight-petalled lotus, on the petals of the cardinal directions starting from the east, and on the petals of the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, [one should worship] in clockwise order: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Anaṅgakusumāpādukāṃ...

Having worshipped her with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) using the mantra "I worship" (pūjayāmi), one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Ambāī by circling around her clockwise, using the sixteen-syllable mantras such as "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ambāī Rūpaśakti Pādukāṃ Pūjayāmi," and so forth. In the same manner, in subsequent instances as well, the two seed-syllables (bīja) should be joined at the beginning and in the middle.

The "Name-yoga" consists of the application of the seven-syllable mantra at the end; having worshipped her with those extracted mantras consisting of names, one should also worship the Śaktis surrounding her with the respective name-mantras, which take the form of the two seed-syllables and the seven-syllable mantra inserted in the middle, ending with the word "Śakti. Only the names differ; we shall demonstrate them: Anaṅga... [and so forth].
Mekhalā is the second; Ampāī and others are her Śaktis. Anaṅgamadanā is the third; Āḥ-Āī and others are her Śaktis. Anaṅgamadanāturā is the fourth; Āḥ-Ṇāī and others are her Śaktis.
Anaṅgarekhā is the fifth; Āḥ-Śāī and others are her Śaktis. Anaṅgavegā is the sixth.
Sajhāī and the others are her powers; Anaṅgāṅkuśā is the seventh, and Sabhāī and the others are her powers; Anaṅgamālinī is the eighth, and Sāgāī and the others are her powers.

Having worshipped fifteen times each the eight Śaktis, beginning with Anaṅgakusumā, together with their respective powers, and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete Mūlamantra of the three peaks (Trikūṭa) with the words "I worship the sandals of Tripurasundarī," [one recites]:
"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! These most secret Yoginīs [perform] the worship for the agitation of all."

One should offer the worship of the third enclosure by presenting a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) while saying, "May they accept. Then, uttering *klīm*, one should display the *ākarṣiṇī* mudrā. Thus, in the third enclosure, one hundred and twenty-eight (128) Śaktis have been worshipped.

Then, on the fourteen-spoked wheel, starting from the front corner and proceeding counter-clockwise, one should worship her with the five offerings using the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇīśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.
Surrounding that, one worships her with the mantras beginning with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ sādāī rūpaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth.

One should worship the fifteen Śaktis; likewise, in the following cases as well, one should worship each respective [Śakti] with the extracted mantras consisting of the two Bījas at the beginning, the seven-syllabled mantra at the end, and the specific name ending in "Śakti" in the middle. Then, surrounding those, one should also worship the respective Śaktis by adding the four-syllabled phrase "Rūpa-Śakti" after the name, which has been inserted between the two Bījas and the seven-syllabled mantra.
One should worship them with perfected mantras; we shall now demonstrate that they are distinct merely by their names:
the second is Sarvavidrāviṇī, beginning with Sāhāī and the others, who are her śaktis; the third is Sarvākarṣiṇī. (p. 56a)

Siṭhāī and the others are all her powers as the fourth, Sarvāhādinī; Sirāī and the others are her powers as the fifth, Sarvasaṃmohinī; Prabhṛti and the others, numbering fifteen, are her powers as the sixth, Sarvastambhinī; Sīpāī and the others are her powers as the seventh, Sarvajambhinī; and Suāī and the others are her powers...

The eighth [wheel], Sarvavaśaṅkarī, consists of Suṇāī and the others as its śaktis; the ninth, Sarvarañjinī, consists of Suśāī and the others as its śaktis; the tenth, Sarvonmādinī, consists of Sūjhāī and the others as its śaktis;
and the eleventh, Sarvārthasādhanī, consists of Sūbhāī and the others as its śaktis.

The twelfth [tithi], which fulfills all perfections, consists of the powers beginning with Segāī; the thirteenth, which consists of all mantras, consists of the powers beginning with Sedāī; and the fourteenth, which causes the destruction of all dualities, consists of the powers beginning with Sehāī—thus, there are fifteen [tithis] each accompanied by their own fifteen measured powers.

Having worshipped the fourteen powers beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, one should worship the central goddess with the mantra: "I worship the sandals of Tripuravāsinī," at the end of the complete root-vidyā of the Trikhaṇḍa. Then, [one should say]: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ!
May these Saṃpradāyayoginīs accept this worship which bestows all prosperity."
Having offered the fourth worship of the enclosure with a handful of flowers, one should utter "Klūm" and display the Āveśinī mudrā.
Thus, in the fourth enclosure, two hundred and twenty-four (224) Śaktis, numbering that same amount, have been worshipped.
Then, on the outer ten-spoked wheel, beginning from the front corner and proceeding counter-clockwise from the southwest to the northwest, [one places] *hrīṃ śrīṃ* for the goddess Sarvasiddhipradā.
Having worshipped the Goddess, the bestower of all accomplishments, with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra) using the mantra "I worship the sandal" (pādukāṃ pūjayāmi),

one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Saiṭhāī around her, using the mantras such as "Śrīṃ, I worship the sandal of the form-Śakti Saiṭhāī," and so forth. Likewise, in the subsequent [sections], there are two seed-syllables at the beginning and the seven-syllable mantra at the end.

In the center, having worshipped each respective goddess with the perfected mantras consisting of "the name of such-and-such" ending in "Devī," one should also worship their respective Śaktis by adding the four-syllable mantra "Upaśakti"— formed by inserting the name between the two seed-syllables and the seven-syllable mantra— and thus perform the worship with the resulting mantras. The only difference lies in the name.

We shall demonstrate that: the second [mudrā], which bestows all prosperity, is Sairāī, and its powers (śaktis) beginning with [Sairāī] are the Sarvapriyaṅkarī; the third is Socāī, and its powers beginning with [Socāī] are the Sarvamaṅgalakāriṇī; the fourth is Sopāī, and its powers beginning with [Sopāī] are the Sarvakāmapradā; the fifth is Sauāī.

The powers beginning with *Prabhṛtikā* are the sixth, Sarvaduḥkhavimocanī; those beginning with *Sauṇāī* are the seventh, Sarvamṛtyupramocanī; those beginning with *Sauśāī* are the eighth, Sarvavighnavināśinī; and those beginning with *Saṃjhāī* are the ninth, Sarvāṅgasundarī. *Saṃbhāī*... [is the tenth].

The powers beginning with *Sarvasaubhāgyadāyinī*— namely *Sangā*, *Prabhṛti*, and so forth— are its powers; having thus worshipped the ten powers beginning with *Sarvasiddhipradā*, each accompanied by their respective fifteen powers, at the end of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) of the complete three-sectioned [yantra].

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra, "I worship the *tripuraśrīpādukā*," one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these *Kulakaula-yoginīs* accept this worship for the accomplishment of all aims. (p. 57a)
Having offered the worship of the fifth enclosure, he should display the Sarvonmādinī mudrā while reciting the mantra "saḥ".

Thus, one hundred and sixty (160) powers (śaktis), equal in number to the fifth enclosure, have been worshipped. Then, in the fourteen-spoked [mandala], beginning from the front corner of the Goddess and ending at the northwest corner, one should worship that Goddess Sarvajñā with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra) using the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ sarvajñādevīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. *Hrīṃ śrīṃ*...

With the mantras beginning with "I worship Saḍāī, the Śakti of Form, and her sandals," and so forth, he should worship the fifteen Śaktis, starting with Saḍāī, surrounding her. Likewise, in the following [sections], having worshipped each respective Goddess with mantras complete with their own names ending in the word "Devī" inserted between the two seed-syllables and the seven-syllable [mantra], he should also worship those respective Śaktis.

Having worshipped each respective goddess with her own name-mantra preceded by the two seed-syllables and ending with the seven-syllable mantra, one should also worship their respective Śaktis with their own name-mantras preceded by the two seed-syllables and ending with the word "Śakti" inserted between the two seed-syllables and the seven-syllable mantra; we shall demonstrate these [mantras] according to the differences in their names. The second is Sarvaśakti.

Sahāī and the others are her powers that bestow all sovereignty; Haṭhāī and the others are her powers; Sarvajñā is the fourth, and Harāī and the others are her powers that destroy all diseases; Hācāī and the others are her powers.

The sixth [day] is the nature of the universal support; its powers begin with *hā-pā-ī*. The seventh is the remover of all sins; its powers begin with *hi-ā-ī*. The eighth is composed of universal bliss; its powers begin with *hiṇā-ī*. The ninth is the embodiment of universal protection; its powers begin with *hiśā-ī*.
The ten [deities] beginning with Hīṃ-Jhāī, who bestow all desired fruits, are their respective powers (*śakti*).
Thus, having worshipped the ten powers beginning with Sarvajñā, each accompanied by its own fifteen powers, (p. 57b) ...

At the end of the complete *trikhaṇḍamūla*, having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra "I worship the *pādukā* of Tripuramālinī," one performs the worship of the sixth enclosure with a handful of flowers using the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these Embryonic Yoginīs (*garbhayoginyas*) accept the worship that effects all protection."
Having offered [it], one should utter "KROM" and display the Great Hook Mudrā (Mahāṅkuśamudrā).
Thus, in the sixth enclosure as well, one hundred and sixty-six (160) powers are worshipped.

On the eight-spoked wheel, starting from the front of the goddess and proceeding clockwise as before, one should worship her with the mantra: "A Ā I Ī U Ū Ṛ Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ E AI O AU AṂ AḤ RA CA LA ŪṂ, I worship the sandals of Vaśinī, the goddess of speech. Then, surrounding that [wheel], one worships with the fifteen mantras beginning with: "HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ HĪBHĀĪ, I worship the sandals of Rūpaśakti," and so forth.

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Hīṃ Bhāī, one should worship Kāmeśvarī, the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā), with the mantra: *Kha Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ka La Hīṃ, I worship the pādukā of Kāmeśvarī Vāgdevatā*. Then, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Hugāī with the mantras: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hugāī, I worship the pādukā of Rūpaśakti*, and so forth.

Having worshipped with the mantra "Cha Ja Jha Ña Na Va La Ī, I worship the sandals of Modinī, the goddess of speech," and having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Hudāī around that [seat] with the mantras "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Rūpaśakti Hudāī," and so forth, [one worships] Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa Hūṃ Vimalā.

Having worshipped her with the mantra "I worship the sandals of Vāgdevatā," one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Huhāī around her with the mantras "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hu Hā Ī, I worship the sandals of Rūpaśakti," and so forth, and likewise with the mantra "Tha Dha Dha Na Ja Ma Ra Īṃ, I worship the sandals of Aruṇā Vāgdevatā."

Having worshipped her with the five *uccāras*, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis, beginning with Hūṭhāī, by proceeding clockwise around her in front with the mantras: "I worship the sandals of the Śakti Rūpa," and so forth, starting with Hūṭhāī.

Having worshipped [the deity] with the mantra "I worship the sandals of Vāgdevatā, who worships *pa pha ba bha ma ha sa la va*," and having honored her, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Hūrāī around her with the mantras: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Hūrāī Rūpaśakti," and so forth, ending with *ya ra la va śa ū*.

Having worshipped her with the mantra, "Maṃ ra yūṃ, I worship the sandals of Sarveśvarī Vāgdevatā," and having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis surrounding her with the mantras beginning with, "Hrīṃ śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Hevārī Rūpaśakti," [and so on], [he worships] "Ṣa sa ha la, Lakṣmī Kaulinī Vāgdevatā, the sandals..."

Having worshipped her with the mantra "I worship [her]," one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Hepāī around her using the mantras such as "hrīṃ śrīṃ hepāī rūpaśakti pādukāṃ pūjayāmi," and so forth; then,
having performed the worship of the eight goddesses of speech (Vāgdevatās) beginning with Vaśinī, each accompanied by their respective Śaktis, one completes the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*).

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra "At the end of the root-vidyā, I worship the pādukā of Tripurasiddhā," and having offered the seventh enclosure worship with a handful of flowers using the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, may these secret Yoginīs accept this worship that removes all diseases," [one recites] "Hasakhaphareṃ."
While reciting the mantra, one should display the khecarīmudrā.

Thus, in the seventh enclosure, one hundred and twenty-eight (128) Śaktis have been worshipped. In the two pathways situated on both sides of the central triangle, the four corners beginning with Vāyavya and Nairṛtya are divided twice each, serving as the locations for the arms of the Goddesses.

Having thus visualized [the arrows], one should worship the Śākta arrows with the five offerings using the mantra "Yāṃ Rāṃ Lāṃ Vāṃ Vāṇebhyo Namaḥ. Then, starting from the northeast (īśāna) and so forth around that, [one worships] "Hrīṃ Śrī Hai Āī Rūpaśaktipādukām."

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Hai and Āi using the mantras "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) and so forth, and having honored the Śiva-arrows (*śaivabāṇa*) with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) using the mantra "Oṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ vlūṃ saḥ, obeisance to the arrows" (*bāṇebhyo namaḥ*), one should worship the sandals of the Śaktis of form (*rūpaśaktipādukā*) surrounding them with the mantras "Oṃ hrīṃ ścī haiṇāī, I worship the sandals of the Śakti of form" (*rūpaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*) and so forth. O Haiṇāī!

Having worshipped the fifteen powers beginning with *Prabhṛti*, one should worship the Śākta bow (*śāktacāpa*) with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) using the mantra *thaṃ cāpāya namaḥ*. Then, surrounding it, one should worship the fifteen powers beginning with Haiśānī using the mantras such as *hrīṃ śrīṃ haiśāṇī-rūpa-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi* and so forth.

Having worshipped the bow of Śiva with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) while reciting "Oṃ Dhanuṣāya Namaḥ," and having fully worshipped the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Hojhāī— starting with the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hojhāī Rūpaśaktipādukāṃ Pūjayāmi" and so forth— one should [worship] with the five offerings while reciting "Hrīṃ Pāśāya Namaḥ."

Having worshipped the Śākta-pāśa, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Hobhāī around it with the mantras "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hobhāī Rūpaśakti Pādukāṃ Pūjayāmi" and so forth. Then, having worshipped the Śaiva-pāśa with the five services (pañcopacāra) using the mantra "Āṃ Pāśāya Namaḥ," one should [worship] Hrīṃ Śrīṃ around that as well.

Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Haugāī with the mantras "I worship the pādukā of the Śakti Haugāī," and so forth, one should worship the Śākta-aṅkuśa with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) using the mantra "Kroṃ,
obeisance to the goad," and then [worship] around it with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the pādukā of the Śakti Haudāī..."
Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis, beginning with Haudā, with the mantras "pūjayāmi" and so forth, [one should worship] with the five offerings using the mantra "kyeṃ aṅkuśāya namaḥ."

Having worshipped the Śiva-aṅkuśa, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with *Hauṃ Hāī*, using the mantras such as "I worship the pādukā of the Śakti Rūpa" (*hrīṃ śrīṃ hauṃ hāī rūpaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*), and so forth. Then,
[one worships] the eight weapons accompanied by their respective fifteen-fifteen Śaktis.

Because of the specific mention of the deities who are equal in rank to those for whom form is primary, one hundred and twenty-eight (128) Śaktis are worshipped by means of worship at this juncture. This concludes the worship of the weapons. Starting from the tip of the central triangle, proceeding counter-clockwise: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, in the Kāma-pīṭha, the goddess Kāmeśvarī.

Having worshipped with the five offerings using the mantra "I worship the pādukā," one should worship the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Haṭhāī using the fifteen mantras beginning with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the pādukā of the form-Śakti Haṭhāī," and so forth; then [worship] with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, at Pūrṇapīṭha, the pādukā of the goddess Vajreśī."

Having worshipped her with the five offerings (pañcopacāra), saying "I worship," and having fully worshipped the fifteen Śaktis around her with mantras such as "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Haṃ Rāī, I worship the pādukā of Rūpaśakti," and so forth, [one should worship] with the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, in the Jālaśvara-pīṭha, I worship the pādukā of the goddess Bhagamālinī."

Having worshipped [the deity] with its name using the mantra, one should worship the fifteen Śaktis, beginning with *Haḥ Dhāī*, by means of the fifteen mantras starting with "I worship the sandals of the Śakti of Form (*Rūpa-śakti-pādukā*)— *hrīṃ śrīṃ hācāī*," and so forth. Then,
having worshipped the triad of Śaktis together with their respective fifteen Śaktis, one worships the complete three-sectioned [mantra] at the end of the *mala-vidyā*.

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra) using the mantra "I worship the pādukā of Tripurā," and having offered the worship of the eighth enclosure with a handful of flowers using the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, may these Parāpara-Rahasya Yoginīs accept this worship that bestows all siddhis," [one should utter] "Hmauṃ."
While uttering the seed-syllable, one should display the seed-gesture (bījamudrā).
Thus, in the eighth enclosure (āvaraṇa), forty-eight (48) powers (śaktis) have been worshipped. Then, within the triangle,
in the center of the bindu, [one worships] with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the seat of consciousness (saṃvidāsana)," making the venerable Śiva himself the seat.

Having worshipped the conceptualized form, at the end of the *trikhaṇḍa-vidyā*, one should worship with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) using the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the goddess Śrī Mahātripurasundarī at the Udyāna-pīṭha. Then, surrounding that [central deity], one worships with [mantras] such as: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Haḥ Pāī, I worship the sandals of Rūpaśakti," and so forth.
Having worshipped the fifteen Śaktis with the fifteen mantras,
and having worshipped the single Śakti accompanied by one's own fifteen Śaktis, at the end of the complete Trikaṇḍa-vidyā,
one should worship the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra: "I worship the pādukā of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī," followed by *hrīṃ śrīṃ*.

Having offered the worship of the ninth enclosure with a handful of flowers while reciting the mantra, "May this most secret Yoginī accept the worship consisting of bliss," one should display the Yoni-mudrā while uttering the mantra *aiṃ*.
Thus, sixteen (16) powers have been worshipped in the ninth enclosure.
Thus, this is the summary: in the first [section], the power (*śakti*) is measured by two hundred and eighty-eight; in the second *rasa* (six), it is measured by twenty-five;
in the next, it is declared to be measured by one hundred and twenty-eight; in the fourth, the measure is remembered as four;
and when combined in the six seasons (*ṛtu*), it is said to be measured by one thousand five hundred and thirty-six. Thus ends the group of chapters (*vṛtti*). Then...
Having duly performed the remaining three services consisting of recitation of hymns, libations, and prostrations,

and having performed the daily japa along with the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), the placement of syllables (varṇanyāsa), and the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) encapsulated [by the mantra],
one should contemplate non-duality with that.

Having performed the offering consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and having offered oblations into the fire according to the ritual procedure, one should dissolve the visualized goddess into the radiance of the [central] deity.
Then, having worshipped the goddess who has returned with the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should present the *bali* offering with the *Kurukullā* mantra.

Having offered lamps filled with camphor and other substances, performed the *ārātrika* ceremony, and sought forgiveness, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) for the mantras of the Kālanityās preceded by meditation. While touching the jar during the "making of the living" (*jīvakaraṇa*), one should mutter all the mantras of the Kālanityās.
On that night, one should hold a great festival with dance, song, and so forth, according to one's capacity, such as the sixty-six-fold [offering] and others.
One should satisfy the couples here with garments, ornaments, and so forth, according to their number.
Thus concludes the ritual duties for the first day.

And on the second day, at a time connected with the student’s birthday, lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), or weekday, after performing the morning obligatory rites, one should worship the Goddess with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*). Having performed the recitation (*japa*) one thousand times interspersed with the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and other rituals, and having made the offering according to the prescribed method, one should perform one thousand oblations of ghee and so forth according to the rules for the daily fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*).

Then, having offered oblations, having brought the goddess Vindā herself, and having performed the *nīrājana* and the rite of seeking forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*), one should recite the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) for the principal goddess. Contemplating the unity of the water and the presiding deity, one should perform the *śaktyutthāpinī* mudrā.

Then, the powers of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-śaktis*) beginning with *aṇimā* are dissolved into their respective principal powers, which take the forms of *aṇimā* and the others; and those [principal powers] also...

Having visualized that the principal deities have dissolved into the Goddess who constitutes the primary essence, and having visualized the principal deity— united with the Goddess by means of the khecarīmudrā and entered into one's own self through the path of the nose by the scent of whatever flower [was offered]— the Guru should recite the Guru-stotra and the Devī-stotra on that very same day.

Having performed the ritual consecration (*samadhivāsana*) according to the rules on that day, and having completed the entire sequence of rites beginning with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacārapūjā*) and ending with the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) for the Vārāhī flask, [one should proceed] preceded by the water-consecration (*jalābhiṣeka*).
And having performed the piercing (*vedha*), one should impart the Vārāhī-vidyā. Then,

in that location of the ground where water flows naturally toward the east, northeast, and north according to the prescribed bathing rites, one should draw the diagram characterized by the Mātṛkā-cakra as shown, and upon it, facing the east...

Having seated the disciple and brought the principal pitcher to the place of consecration, he should place the fruit situated at its mouth into the joined palms of the disciple; then, using the sprouts situated at its mouth, he should perform the consecration once with each of the mantras of all the deities who constitute the primary enclosure in the form of the powers such as *aṇimā*, and likewise with the fifteen *Nityā* vidyās.
Having performed the consecration (abhiṣeka) repeatedly, and having placed those sprouts upon the head of the disciple,
[the preceptor], surrounded by yogis satisfied by the prior gift of garments,
ornaments, food, and drink, and joined by his own wife, [should perform the rite] preceded by the festival of music such as horns, conchs, and bells, and by dance and song.
The Guru should sprinkle [the disciple] three times with the primary vidyā. And the disciple,

while contemplating that this water, having entered the interior of his body through the openings of the pores of his skin, washes away all the impurities of the evil latent impressions (durvāsanā) inherited from his beginningless succession of births, should reflect thus.
One should bathe with the remaining water that has been left over from all the others; then, having put on a clean,

washed upper garment and being adorned with perfumes and garlands, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with the water remaining in the pitcher and worship the Guru, the consecrator, with the nine offerings (navopacāra) dedicated to the Guru-vidyā.

"Even now, because [the truth] has not been taught [to me], salutations to that illustrious Guru by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the probe of the ointment of knowledge. At the end of this, [one says]: "Salutations to Amukānandanātha."

Having worshipped with the mantra preceded by the general *arghya* offering, and having performed the nine-fold service (*navopacāra*) consisting of fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel, the recitation of hymns, prostration, and the surrender of one's own self, as well as the rites of renunciation (*utsarga*) and dedication (*nivedana*), [one should offer] the entirety, half of that, or a fourth part of that.

Having satisfied his own guru with lifelong, voluntary sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and having performed the recitation of the hymn three times, the offering of handfuls of flowers three times, and prostrations three times,
he should stand silently with palms joined in reverence. Then the guru shall perform for the disciple the sacrament known as *vedha*.

The method for that is as follows: having extracted one of the nine yantras— which yield superior results because they are composed of both the *mātṛkā* and the *vidyā*, and which are found among the ten *pūjācakra*s of the *Jvālāmālinī* or other tantras—
according to the procedure to be described, and having seated the disciple therein, [one should invoke] one's own *mūlādhāra-śakti*.
Having expelled [the consciousness] through the path of the flowing breath and brought it back inside by means of the internal breath,

one should contemplate it as having entered the self of the disciple; then, having joined it with the power of retention (*dhāraṇā-śakti*), one should again withdraw the six faculties of the disciple— the five organs of knowledge, such as hearing, and the mind— and [unite them] within one's own self.

Having meditated upon the *ādhāra-śakti* as bringing [the powers] together, one should perform the recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth of the present vidyā in the seven locations of the disciple, beginning from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*, namely the six cakras and the end of the cranial aperture. (p.

Having meditated in sequence upon the seven *repha* syllables— which serve as the constituent parts of the [mantra] accomplished by both the teacher and the disciple— and having visualized the disciple’s body as being pervaded by the garlands of flames arising therefrom,
one should contemplate that all the disciple's negative latent impressions (*durvāsanā*) have been burnt away by it, and then visualize the disciple as being rendered unconscious.

Having again placed water for the *arghya* offering in the disciple's mouth and visualized that consciousness has been restored, the Guru should look upon him with a compassionate gaze through the *upadeśyavidyā*. Having thus completed the consecration known as *vedha*, the Guru sits down in the place where the *śrīcakra* is located, according to its position within his own nostril-passage (*nāsāpuṭa*).

Having seated the disciple above the *bindu* within the *śrīcakra*, and having visualized a *śrīcakra* in each of his *brahmarandhra*, heart, and *mūlādhāra*, and having worshipped each of them with mental offerings (*pañcopacāra*) preceded by invocation (*āvāhana*) and the consecration of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and having placed the "living hand" upon the head of the disciple while [the mantras] resound in the disciple's ear—

When sounds such as those of a conch, a horn, or a camel occur, one should impart the principal vidyā three times. Then, while the disciple remains seated upon the Śrīcakra itself, having performed the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), the placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa), and the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa), he should recite the received mantra one hundred times while encapsulated [by these nyāsas]. Furthermore, [the teacher should ensure] the state of being alive and the presence [of the breath] within the nostrils. Then the disciple... [recites].

Having performed the offering consisting of the meditation on non-difference with that [deity], and having prostrated before and praised the venerable Guru, he should go outside the Śrīcakra by the Guru’s command; he should preserve the Śrīcakra until the time of the instruction in the entire Vidyā.
Performing service to the Guru step by step, the disciple should reside in the Guru’s very abode for three days.
Thus ends the ritual duties for the second day. Thus concludes the method for the Lesser Full Initiation (*kaniṣṭha-pūrṇābhiṣeka*).
Thus concludes the introduction to the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Śrī Tripurasundarī. Now, impelled by Śrī Ramānātha who resides within the heart—
In accordance with the *Śrītantrarāja* as understood by Gurumati,
we shall describe the daily, occasional, and other rites for the Tithinityās, which are performed according to the desires of all people, measured by the lunar days (*tithi*).

The rule regarding the constant and non-constant Tithinityās as derived from the *Tantrarāja* is presented here, having been understood both in its general and specific aspects. Worship of the Tithinityās is twofold: as an ancillary (*aṅga*) and as a primary (*pradhāna*) rite;
of these, the first type of worship is to be performed at the time to be described in the midst of the worship of Śrī Lalitā.

The nature of worship by means of one's own respective vidyās and the mantras of the nine Nāthas will become clear further on. However, we shall now demonstrate the second [topic] in detail. Since this practice depends upon initiation (dīkṣā), its procedure must first be explained.
Because the initiation of the Nityā Kāmeśvarī is prescribed for the first lunar day (pratipad), it should be performed on the day preceding that.

Having extracted the Maṇḍala of the Nāthas according to the method taught in the Tantra, and having worshipped the nine Nāthas with their own lineage of gurus using the nine offerings (navopacāra), one should recite their hymn of praise (stotra) and receive their permission. Then, having drawn the Cakra for the daily worship of Kāmeśvarī upon the ground with red sandalwood paste, vermilion, and other substances, [one should place] gold or silver upon it.

A copper vessel or one made of any other kind of clay, filled with colored medicinal herbs (varṇauṣadhi) corresponding to the respective vidyā-mantras, or with medicinal herbs of the visarga-syllable alone, or filled with water from any sacred ford such as the Gaṅgā, containing within it the nine gems,
gold, copper, grains such as rice, sandalwood, and a citron fruit (mātuluṅga).
Its mouth is covered with sprouts of *aśvattha*, *āmra*, and *panasa* tied with *indravallī*;
its base and neck are wrapped in two reddish garments; it is the size of a *svārī* and capable of being immersed in water.
And having placed [the substances] in the jar, one should contemplate within that water the entire cycle of worship of Sarvamaṅgalā; [one should contemplate] Bhagamālinī in the second [day],
Nityaklinnā in the third day of initiation, Bheruṇḍā in the fourth day of initiation,
and Vahnivāsinī in the fifth day of initiation, in the sixth.

On the seventh day is the initiation of Mahāvajreśvarī; on the eighth, the initiation of Śivadūtī; on the ninth, the initiation of Tvaritā; on the tenth, the initiation of Kulasundarī; on the eleventh, the initiation of Nityānityā;
on the twelfth, the initiation of Nīlapatākā; and on the thirteenth, the initiation of Vijayā.

Since the initiation for Sarvamaṅgalā takes place on the fourteenth day, the initiation for Jvālāmālinī on the fifteenth, and the initiation for Citrā on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), on the preceding day— whether it be the first, second, or other such day— one should perform the ritual for one’s own chosen Lord (svanātha), beginning with that Lord and concluding with all the Lords, using the respective mantras based upon the mandala of the Nine Lords (navanātha).

At the conclusion of the request for permission to perform the worship, one should extract the perpetual worship-circle (*nityapūjācakra*) there, place the previously described jar— characterized by all its specific attributes— upon the *bindu* thereof, and contemplate within it the perpetual worship-circle of the goddess Sarvamaṅgalā; this is the foundation for maintaining all instructions, and therein one should worship Sarvamaṅgalā.

Its specific mode, which is its particular form, must be revealed in that very context; having performed the ritual actions up to the dismissal (*udvāsana*) and the recitation of the hymns to the Guru and the Goddess, whatever *Nityā* initiation is desired,
that respective *Nityā* or non-*Nityā* worship-circle (*pūjācakra*), even if already drawn below the *kalaśa*, [should be prepared].

Having again contemplated the respective *nityās*—such as *Deśa*, *Kāla*, and so forth—in the manner to be described hereafter, for the purpose of worshipping those drops (*bindus*) which constitute the respective *nityās* and have been made primary, and which are pervaded by the *kalaśas*; (p. 63a) [one should proceed].
Beginning with the worship of the thirty-eight deities of the *pīṭhas*, the establishment of the general *arghya* and other offerings,
the sprinkling of the ritual materials for worship, the primary formal resolve (*pradhāna-saṅkalpa*), the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*) and so forth up to one’s own consecration,

followed by the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) preceded by the *mātṛkā* and the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) nyāsa, as well as the six-limbed nyāsa and the letter-nyāsa (*varṇanyāsa*) as prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpas*).

At the conclusion of the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*), having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, and up to the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should worship with the twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*).

Having also performed the worship of one's respective enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth, the yogis, together with other yogis, should perform on the preceding day the rites ending with the daily recitation (*nityajapa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), the removal of impurities (*āśuṣalāpana*), re-worship (*punar-pūjana*), the offering of oblations (*balidāna*), the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), and the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*).

Previously, it was stated that after the selection of the Guru, the Guru— surrounded by those provided with finger-rings, garments, and other offerings— should pass that night in activities such as dancing. Here, in order to dispel the doubt as to which specific Anityā resides in which particular place at which specific time, those respective places and times are now demonstrated.
In every yuga, during the first year, after fifty-seven hundred and sixty-six (576) civil days have elapsed,
Lalitā resides in the region of Meru at a time corresponding to the interval between the lunar orbit and the earth;
and in that same year, Kāmeśvarī-nityā resides in the region of Jambūdvīpa at a time corresponding to the lunar orbit.

Bhagamālinī resides between the oceans of Nīla and Candra and the orbits of Budha and Śukra; Nityaklinnā resides between Plakṣadvīpa and the orbit of Budha; and Bheruṇḍā resides between the oceans of Śākṣu and Budha and the orbits of Śukra and Tvaṣṭṛ.
In [the regions of] Vahnivāsinī and Śālmalidvīpa-Śukrakakṣa;
in [the regions of] Vajreśvarī and the Surā-ocean, between Śukra and Ravikakṣa; and in [the regions of] Śivādūtī and Kuśadvīpa-Ravikakṣa.

Tvaritā is between the orbits of the ocean of clarified butter (Ghṛtasamudra) and the Earth; Kulasundarī is between the orbit of Krauñcadvīpa and the Earth; Nityānityā is between the orbit of the ocean of wine (Ādhisamudra) and Jupiter; Nīlapatākā is between the orbit of Śākadvīpa and Jupiter; and Vijayā is between the orbit of the ocean of vinegar (Kṣārasamudra) and Mars.

She resides in the space between the Puṣkara-dvīpa and Śani-kakṣa of Sarvamaṅgalā; in the space between the Jala-samudra and Śani-nakṣatra-kakṣa of Jvālāmālinī; and in the space between Citrā-paravyoma and Nakṣatra-kakṣa of Citrā.
Therefore, in the first year of each respective Yuga, during the worship of that particular Nityā, the practitioner should first [place her] in the direction below him with the syllable *hrīṃ*.

"Śrīṃ, salutation to Jambūdvīpa; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the orbit of the moon in the upward direction"—with these two mantras, place and time are to be worshipped. In this same manner, even in other years ending with the sixteenth year, one should recognize one's own respective subsequent place and time as pertaining to oneself, and [worship them] with the name preceded by the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) and ending with the fourth case suffix and the word "namas."

By means of the two mantras, place and time are to be worshipped. Furthermore, from the sixteenth year until the end of the next sixteen years, place and time are to be contemplated in the same manner as previously stated. We shall explain later the method for determining the number of years up to the end of the Yuga; in certain tantras, [this refers to] Mathurā and Ayodhyā.

It has been taught that while external worship may be performed at the very place where one resides— by means of the power of the mantra— at locations presided over by one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) such as Māhiṣmatī and others; however, in the present case, one should personally go to the location of one’s own chosen deity within the mantra itself and perform the worship there.

In that regard, since going there is not possible without the permission of its guardians, their worship is necessary for the sake of obtaining that favor. Therefore, having mentally gone to the shore of the ocean of sugarcane juice, [one should worship] Vārāhī, the guardian of the shore.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed method, and having gone near the ocean of sugarcane juice by the command obtained through his grace,

one should worship the Guardian of the Ocean there with mental offerings and the fivefold offerings beginning with fragrance, preceded by meditation. Then, having ascended the boat by the command obtained through her grace, and having performed that worship there, [one remains] exceedingly...

Having attained a state of clarity through that [practice], one should worship the fourfold collection beginning with the Ocean of Sugarcane (Ikṣusāgara), which has been encountered midway on the journey while the ship was set in motion by the two powers of *drāvaṇī* and *bhrāmaṇī* residing in the eastern and western regions;

then, having reached Ratnadvīpa, one should descend onto the ground of ruby gems (*padmarāga*). From there, [one should worship] Ratnadvīpa and the others, which are the respective [abodes of] the sixteen *Nityās*.

One should propitiate with offerings everything that surrounds the location of the abode; for without such propitiation, how could the presentation of services such as water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth be carried out for the Goddess by those surrounded by the deities?
This applies even to all the sixteen regions, all the continents, and the entire secret [realm] such as the Jewel Island (*ratnadvīpa*).

The deities ending with the manifest Yoginīs reside [there], and because of the wonderful majesty of the meditation upon each individual deity, there is nothing here that cannot be logically established. Thus, it follows that these are the seat-deities (pīṭhadevatā) of all the Nityās; however, while they are present in one place such as Meru and so forth, in the second and subsequent years, their [presence] is [elsewhere].

How could you also be the presiding deity (pīṭhadevatā) of Lalitā? For it has not been stated that there is a difference in the presiding deities of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) according to differences in regions, as is the case with space and time; therefore, [the deity] is present everywhere in every region.

The entire [universe], beginning with the continents, is eternal; yet it is differentiated according to the various regions (*varṣa*). The worship-diagram (*pūjā-yantra*), however, is indeed distinct in each case upon the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*), because the worship of the Mother of the Wheel (*Cakrāmbā*) differs in those respective places. Therefore, having gone personally to those various locations, one should perform the worship along with its attendants for all sixteen *Nityās*.

The secret intended for the understanding of all wise ones is that, having completed whatever one desires to do, one should reflect upon returning once again to the very place of one’s own abiding. The mantras for their worship are as follows:
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kṣusāgarāya Namaḥ; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Irāsāgarāya; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ghṛtasāgarāya; Hrīṃ.

Śrīṃ, to the Milk Ocean; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, to the Island of Jewels (Ratnadvīpa)—A Ā I Ī U Ū Ṛ Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ E AI O AU AṂ AḤ KA KHA GA GHA ṄA CA CHA JA JHA ÑA ṬA ṬHA ḌA ḌHA ṆA TA THA DA DHA NA PA PHA BA BHA MA YA RA LA VA ŚA ṢA SA HA LA KṢA—Salutation! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, to the Kalpaka Garden—Salutation! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ to the blue gem; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ to the blue gem; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ to the lapis lazuli gem;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ to the bindu-gem; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ to the pearl gem; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ to the emerald gem;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ to the diamond gem; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ to the go-meda gem—thus are the eight gems [placed] in the eight directions, with Hrīṃ Śrīṃ in the center.
Obeisance to the ruby-jewel! Above and above the ruby-jewel:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Kālacakreśvarī. *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Mudrācakreśvarī.
*hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Mātṛkācakreśvarī. *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Ratnacakreśvarī. *hrīṃ śrīṃ*.

*Deśacakreśvarīpā*. *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of *Gurucakreśvarīpā*. *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, [I worship] *Tattvacakreśvarīpā*. *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, [I worship] *Tattvacakreśvarīpā*. *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, [I worship] *Graha cakreśvarīpā*.
*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of *Mūrticakreśvarīpā*.
Having worshipped the nine sovereign goddesses (*navacakreśvarī*), [one should worship] all around with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ karuṇātoyaparikhāyai namaḥ* (homage to the moat of the water of compassion).
In its central part: *hrīṃ śrīṃ māṇikyamaṇḍapāya namaḥ* (homage to the ruby pavilion). In its center: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*...

Having worshipped the quartet of Śaktis with: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the Śakti whose form is Ākāra," and "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the Śakti whose form is the syllable Śabda"; then in the front portion: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Saṅgītayoginī"; and all around: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the entire circle of Guptaprakaṭasiddhayoginīs."

By means of these two mantras, these Śaktis are to be worshipped collectively. From Deśa onwards, ending with Siddhayoginī, these thirty-eight deities of the *pīṭhas* are common to all the Nityās. Now follows the procedure for establishing the general *arghya* vessel common to all.

Having placed the general *arghya* vessel— constructed from gold, silver, copper, iron, or clay— between the respective worship diagram (*pūjāyantra*) and oneself; this vessel should have a base, be filled with water scented with the five fragrances consisting of yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), camphor (*karpūra*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), agallochum (*aguru*), and musk (*kastūrī*).
Having meditated that the water in the supporting vessel consists respectively of fire, sun, and moon by means of the three seed-syllables of Kulasundarī uttered [in sequence],
and having meditated that the five elements contained within that water consist respectively of earth, water, fire, air, and space;

and having meditated upon the identity between the waters of the respective daily and occasional worship-circles (*pūjācakra*) and [the water in the vessel], [one should contemplate] its non-difference from the present Goddess.
Having visualized the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in the water with the respective mantras associated with each *Nityā*, and having worshipped the deities of the six limbs in that water,
one should consecrate (*abhimantrayet*) or worship that water ten times with their respective *vidyās*. [This applies to] the general *arghya* vessel.
On the northern side, there is the common vessel for water for the feet (pādya); further north than that is the vessel for the respectful offering (arghya);
further north than that is the vessel for water for sipping (ācamanīya); and further north than that is the vessel for water for bathing (snānīya).

One should sprinkle the four items beginning with water for the feet, oneself, the materials on one's own right side— namely perfume, unbroken rice, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, betel, and so forth— as well as the materials for the worship of the enclosures and the materials for the fire sacrifice, each individually with the respective vidyā-mantra and with the general arghya-water held in the right hand of the Goddess.
Then, having restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of the *vidyā* to be worshipped at that time, or by the seed-syllable (*bīja*) such as *tadvighāghaṭaka*,

one should perform the primary formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for either the daily worship according to the rules of instruction or the optional worship, having clearly articulated [the details] ending with the specific place, time, lineage (*gotra*), zodiac sign (*rāśi*), name, and desired object.

"O Brāhmaṇa of such-and-such lineage, such-and-such constellation, and such-and-such name, according to my understanding and by command, I shall perform the instruction of the daily *nityā-vidyā* according to the prescribed rule. In this manner, the procedure should be carried out. Then, regarding the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth—if these have already been performed as part of the practice of another deity, yet the purification of the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*) must be performed daily—then [the following should be done].

Since that which was previously stated has already been accomplished, it need not be performed again now; however, if it has not been performed at all, then it must be performed on this occasion. For this very reason, as in the case where one says "with a pure body and face" and so forth, rather than separately mentioning acts such as washing the face, bathing, and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), which are common to other deities.

In what way was that mere performance authorized by the Blessed One? Its manner is as follows: one should visualize the earth mandala, extending from the feet to the knees, square in shape, marked with a vajra, yellow in color, adorned, and endowed with its seed-syllable;
from the knees to the navel, it resembles a half-moon and is marked with a lotus.
One should meditate on the region of water as white in color and joined with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, extending from the navel up to the throat;
and the mandala of fire as red in color, triangular in shape, marked with a svastika, and joined with its seed-syllable.
