One should meditate on the mandala of air as being black, extending from the throat to the center of the eyebrows, hexagonal and joined with six dots and its seed-syllable; and the sky-element (ākāśa) as being smoke-colored, circular, marked with a banner, extending from the center of the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and joined with the seed-syllable *haṃ*. Thus is the manner [of meditation].

Having meditated upon all five elements within one's own body, having raised Kuṇḍalinī from the *mūlādhāra*, and having taken the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—which is situated in the heart and shaped like the flame of a lamp—and having united it with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) located at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) by means of the present mantra; and having likewise contemplated oneself as being united [with that Self], [one dissolves] the elements: earth into water, water...
Having contemplated that fire is dissolved into fire, air into air, space into space, and space into the Supreme Self (Paramātman) according to this method;

and having contemplated that the letters *kṣaṃ*, *laṃ*, *le*, *he*, *sa*, *ka*, *haṃ*, *saṃ*, *ṣe*, *ṣaṃ*, *śe*, *ṣa*, and the letter *va* are dissolved into the letter *a* according to the sequence beginning with *vevaṃlerela ma*, one should contemplate that [the letter *a*] is dissolved into the Supreme Self (*Parātman*). Then:

In the region of his own left side [the practitioner visualizes] the Person of Sin (pāpapuruṣa), who has the murder of a Brahmin for his head, the theft of liquor for his two arms, the drinking of liquor joined to his heart, the violation of the Guru’s bed for his two hips,
association with such sinners for his pair of feet, major sins for his limbs and minor limbs, and minor offenses for his body hair.
Having thus visualized the Pāpapuruṣa (the personification of sin), who has blood-red eyebrows, beard, and eyes, who holds a sword and a shield, and has the luster of lampblack;
and having meditated upon both the Pāpapuruṣa and one's own body as dried up by the wind produced by the present Vidyā; [one should then act] with the fire produced by the present Vidyā.
Having contemplated that both have been burnt, one should expel the sinful person (pāpapuruṣa) along with its ashes by means of the wind produced from the present vidyā. [End of page 66b]

Having drenched the ashes of the body with the nectar produced by the Vidyā, one should contemplate that another body has arisen, resembling pure crystal; and even the elements have attained purity through union with the Supreme Brahman— from the Supreme Self arises space, and from space, air.

Having generated fire from air, water from fire, and earth from water in this sequence, and having visualized them established in their respective locations, one should—by means of the present vidyā—place the Kuṇḍalinī herself, who is pure, and the individual soul (jīvātman), which has likewise attained purity, within the heart; then, one should contemplate them as united at the Mūlādhāra. Thereafter:

One should perform the self-consecration (*svaprāṇapratiṣṭhā*). The procedure for that is as follows: having applied the mantras—*parahṛdayāya namaḥ*, *ralaśirase svāhā*, *lavaśikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *vaśakavacāya huṃ*, *śaṣanetrāya vauṣaṭ*, *ṣa sa astrāya phaṭ*—to one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as to the heart and other limbs, and then placing the hand upon the heart while reciting *hrīṃ yaṃ*.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) by encasing each of the seven syllables from *ya* to *sa*— namely, *hrīṃ hrīṃ raṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ vaṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śaṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ ṣaṃ hrīṃ saṃ hrīṃ*— within the *māyā-bīja* (*hrīṃ*), and having performed the three-fold pervasive placement (*tridhā-vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the complete *pratiṣṭhā-mantra* that is about to be described;
For the purpose of restoring life to the heart: "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of this Devadatta are here in Devadatta;

the life-force (*jīva*) of this Devadatta is established here in Devadatta; all the sense-faculties (*sarvendriyāṇi*) of this Devadatta, as well as the speech, mind, and breath (*vāṅmanaḥprāṇāḥ*) of this Devadatta, let them come here to Devadatta, svāhā!"—one should then recite this mantra three times.

Having recited [the mantra], and having recited each of the mantras pertaining to the respective vidyās once, one should contemplate that each individual sacrament (saṃskāra), beginning with conception (garbhādhāna), has been accomplished. Then, the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) of the Mātṛkās. (p.

One should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* preceded by the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*). The method for this is as follows: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ śirase svāhā*;
*uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; *eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ*.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-limbed mantras— *aiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *oṃ paṃ phaṃ vaṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ*,
and *aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ astrāya phaṭ*— upon the thumb and other fingers, as well as upon the heart and other limbs, at the conclusion of the aforementioned entire vidyā:

In the context of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*), one should pronounce each letter of the Mātṛkā alphabet individually at the beginning of each constituent seed-syllable (*bīja*) and place them in their respective locations. Specifically: *a* on the forehead; *ā* on the perimeter of the mouth; *i* and *ī* on the two eyes; *u* and *ū* on the two ears; *ṛ* and *ṝ* on the nostrils; *ḷ* and *ḹ* on the two cheeks; *e* and *ai* on the two lips; *o* and *au* on the upper and lower rows of teeth; and *aṃ* on the head.
Aḥ on the tongue; ka at the base of the right hand; sva at the first joint; ga at the second joint;
gha at the third joint; ṅa at the tip of the right hand; ca at the base of the left hand; cha at the first joint;
ja at the second joint; ña at the third joint; ña at the tip of the left hand; ṭa at the base of the right foot; ṭha...

*Ḍa* at the first joint; *ḍha* at the second joint; *ṇa* on the tip of the right foot; *ta* at the base of the left foot; *tha* at the first joint; *da* at the second joint; *dha* at the third joint; *na* on the tip of the left foot;
*pa* on the right side; *pha* on the left side; *ba* on the back; *bha* at the navel; *ma* at the heart.
Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) and having placed the hand upon the heart while recollecting "ca," one should recollect "ya" while remembering blood; "ra" while remembering flesh;
"la" while remembering fat; "va" while remembering bones; "śa" while remembering marrow; and "ṣa" while remembering semen. (p. 67b)

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) while recollecting *sa* as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), *ha* as power (*śakti*), *la* as the self (*ātman*), and *kṣa*. There is also another method for the placement of the letters beginning with *ya*: *ya* in the heart, *ra* on the right shoulder, *la* on the left shoulder, *va* on the crown of the head, *śa* in the right side of the abdomen, *ṣa* in the left side of the abdomen, and *sa* from the heart down to the tips of the fingers of the right hand.

Having encircled [the body] ending at the left hand; having encircled from the heart and so forth, ending at the right foot or ending at the tip of the left foot; one should place *la* in the belly and *kṣa* in the mouth. Here, there is neither the use of those accompanied by the visarga, nor those accompanied by the bindu, nor especially those accompanied by both; nor those beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, nor those enclosed by *praṇava*.

The placement (nyāsa) of the letters of the Mātṛkā, however, is to be performed only for those [letters] as they have been described. Furthermore, in that context, locative endings such as "on the forehead" (lalāṭe) or "on the circumference of the face" (mukhavṛtte) serve merely to indicate the location; they are not to be included within the actual formula of the rite.

In the second alternative, even when both the letter *ma* and the letter *pa* are assigned to the heart (*hṛdaya*), there should be no confusion due to the authority of the scriptures. In that regard, although in the internal correspondence the word *hṛt* (heart), which assigns the location for the letter *ma*, refers to the belly (*udara*), the word *jaṭhara* (belly), which assigns the location for the letter *la* as the referent of the word *ilā*, shares the same location.

Just as in the *Śrīrājarājeśvara-kavaca*, in the passage beginning with "in the heart, in the belly, in the navel," a distinction in the referents of the words *udara* (belly) and *jaṭhara* (stomach) is observed based on their falling within the upper and lower portions relative to the navel; likewise here too, the word *hṛt* refers to the upper portion of the navel, while the word *jaṭhara* refers to the *udara*.

Furthermore, establishing a distinction between the locations according to the method of "limitation of the lower part" (tadadhobhāga-parimiti) appears to contradict the natural sense of the root text; for even in a single limb, there is the placement of three entities according to the division of right, left, and middle.

Thus, by means of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the two syllables according to the distinction between the right and left limbs, there arises a ninefold conceptualization preceded by desire, which lacks the natural flavor (*saurasya*) of the root word. Having thus performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* according to one or another established position based on the instructions of one's own respective lineage of gurus, [one should perform] the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) as prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*).

One should perform the *varṇanyāsa*, the *vyāpakanyāsa*, and so forth. Here, in the *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment), because it is based on the root mantra, the application is not "aṃ to the two thumbs, svāhā to the two index fingers," and so on; rather, it is simply "namas to the heart (*hṛdaya*), svāhā to the head (*śiras*)," and so forth. For in this context, the terms "heart" and so on refer specifically to the presiding deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatā*), and not to the [principal] deity itself.

This refers specifically to the particular limbs of the practitioner. Therefore, regarding the placement [of mantras] on the thumb and so forth, any suspicion of impropriety and the like should be examined in detail in our work, the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī*.
As for the two applications—*netrāya vauṣaṭ* and *netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*—we have no insistence on either one.

Then, by joining the tips of the thumb and forefinger and making the sound of snapping fingers (*choṭikā*) in the eight directions of oneself— above and below— he should dispel the three kinds of obstacles, distinguished as terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial. Then, with hands joined in the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā and filled with red flowers, [he should proceed] from the *mūlādhāra*...

Having visualized that light, which had pervaded up to the *brahmarandhra* and was carried along the path of the breath through the nose, as having entered [the disciple] by means of the casting of that handful of flowers;

and having visualized its rays, having issued forth from there, as having transformed into the form of the enclosures consisting of the Lord’s weapons; and having meditated upon that light situated in the center, as understood from the verse anointed with meditation.

Having meditated upon one's own essential form (*svarūpaka*), one should likewise visualize the Lord, the weapons, and the deities of the enclosure; these should be identical in appearance to the principal deity, with the exception that regarding their weapons, they possess crowns marked by their respective individual forms.
Having meditated and performed the fourfold ritual beginning with *sthāpanā* (establishment), preceded by the display of the respective mudrās;

and having performed, as before, the placement (*nyāsa*) on the thumbs and so forth, the placement on the heart and so forth, the seven-syllable placement, and the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*); then, at the end [of these], touching each respective *Nityā*-cakra with the *jīva*-mantra: "Of this [Name] Nityā..."

"O vital breaths, come here to this *amuka-nityānitya-pūjācakra*; may the speech, mind, and vital breaths of this [deity] *amukī-nityā* come here to this *amuka-nityānitya-pūjācakra*, svāhā!"—this is the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra*.
One should recite it ten times, corresponding to the number of the *mātṛkā-cakra*, or finally three times. However, where...

The *cakra* has been consecrated according to the procedure for the installation of the *Śrīcakra*; therefore, there is no further installation required, nor is there any ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*). [This is performed] with five jars made of gold, silver, copper, or any other metal, filled with the five substances: honey, ghee, milk, coconut water, and the decoction of medicinal herbs and pigments.

Having bathed each respective *cakra*, and having established the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) recited one thousand times while touching each respective *cakra*— preceded by the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites— and having worshipped each respective *Nityā* with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should consecrate and worship them with all the mantras of the *Kālanityā*.
He should feed ninety-six couples, or else a single married woman (*suvāsinī*) and one Brahmin,

or ninety-six married women, or that same number of virgins (*kumārī*). In this very manner, all the rites— from the consecration with water from the jar (*kalaśa*) up to the feeding of the couples and others— should be performed on the preceding day.
Having meditated upon it for three days,

one should perform [the rite], but not on a single day alone. Then, once the *cakra* has been received from the venerable Guru, [one performs] the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and the dismissal (*udvāsana*).

One should perform the daily obligatory worship (nityapūjā) every day after being liberated from [worldly] karma. Regarding the consecration (abhimantraṇa) and worship of the Nityās of the Wheel of Purification (āpavanityācakra), those who have established the treasury [of tradition] teach that it should not be done with the Kālanityā-vidyās; rather, it should be performed with the respective vidyās of each individual Nityā in a number such as one thousand times. To this, the following must be said:

What is the authority for the installation (*pratiṣṭhāpana*) of these various wheels (*cakras*) in such a manner? Is it not this very Tantra? No, because the installation of other eternal wheels (*nityācakras*) is not mentioned here. Nor is it another Tantra, because that would entail a contradiction with the statement regarding the independence from other Tantras. Now, the worship of the Guru-maṇḍala and so forth, which is common to all [the Nityās], has been declared.

If it is argued that— since it is stated, "The means for the Nityās are likewise [those] beginning with the primordial vibration and the stone, and the fire-sacrifice (havana) is their limb," and by such a statement of extension (atideśa), the procedure for the installation of the Nityā-cakra is exactly the same as the procedure for the installation of the Lalitā-cakra, and this is understood from the present Tantra itself— then, [the answer is: the installation is [to be performed] at the conclusion of that installation procedure.

Having worshipped those [Nityās] in sequence with the Vidyās arising at the time of attaining the Nityā-tattva, one should recite [the mantra] while touching the Śrīcakra with the tips of the fingers; thus, one should worship it.

Therefore, why do you harbor such animosity toward the consecration (abhimantraṇa) and other rites performed with the Vidyās of the Nityās at the times prescribed by this Tantra? Furthermore, the procedure for the installation of the Nityā-cakra is even more clearly evident therein; [this is] the installation of the Śrīcakra.
The introduction should be connected as follows: then, at the end of each respective *nityā-vidyā* for worship,
having written the name of the deity ending in the dative case,
one should append the word "kalpayāmi" (I offer) after the name mentioned in the relevant tantra, which ends in the accusative case and serves to present the ritual offerings (*upacāra*).

Having worshipped with the twelve services (*upacāra*), beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) and ending with betel (*tāmbūla*), by means of perfected mantras; and having arranged three rows behind that worshipped *Nityā*, starting from the row nearest the Goddess and proceeding from the northeast (*īśāna*)—

Gradually, gradually, having emerged from the divine Prakāśa, Vimarśa, and Ānandanātha; from the Siddhas Śrījñānanātha, Śrīsatyanātha, and Śrīpūrṇanātha; and from the human Mānavasubhaganātha—who is like his own essential nature—these nine in number: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ.
One should worship with the sixteen-syllable mantras, beginning with "I worship the sandal of the power of light-bliss" (prakāśānandaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi), and so forth.

At the conclusion of each individual enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), at the end of its respective primary *vidyā*, one should worship the Goddess situated in the center with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) using the mantra: "I worship [Name] Nityā along with her attendants. Then, according to the specific procedure of the relevant *kalpa*, having placed either two or one seed-syllable (*bīja*) at the beginning, [one identifies: "[Name] Nityā is the deity of the first enclosure."
"Such-and-such Nityā, deity of the second enclosure; such-and-such Nityā, deity of the third enclosure," and so forth.

Having uttered the names of the respective deities of each enclosure according to their number, and having recited the remainder of the mantra beginning with "may they accept the worship," one should offer the worship with a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, having recited whatever hymn (*stotra*) one wishes, [one should conclude].
Having performed the fourteen services (upacāra), one should proceed with the fifteenth service, known as libation (tarpaṇa).

The method for that procedure has already been revealed in the introduction to the Śrīvidyā; however, for the purpose of reflecting upon the specific categories contained therein, a mnemonic summary is now written.
Having properly prepared two seats in front of oneself, in the very space attached to one's own seat, one should arrange those two.
Having worshipped [them], one should contemplate light (*prakāśa*) in the form of Śiva and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of Śakti above those two. Then,
upon the limbs of that light in its masculine form, starting from the big toe of the right foot on the first day of the bright fortnight (*pratipad*), [one should perform the placement].

Having placed the sixteen Kāmakalās—preceded by the third seed-syllable and joined with the sixteen vowels ending in that [third seed]—one should perform the placement as follows: on the second lunar day, from the back of the feet up to the heart; on the third, from the right ankle up to the end of that [heart]. In this manner, having performed the placement on each successive lunar day from the first of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) starting from the respective limbs up to the heart. On the first day of the dark fortnight:

Having first deposited the Kāmakalā, starting from the left side of the head and ending at the heart, according to the previously stated seed-syllables; then on the second [tithi], starting from the left ear; on the third, starting from the left eyebrow and ending at the heart;
and likewise on each subsequent lunar day (tithi), depositing the respective limbs starting from the next part, therein depositing the teeth upon the limb of Vimarśa, which is of the nature of Śakti.

On the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the digits of the moon (*candrakalā*), beginning from the big toe of the left foot, conjoined with the third seed-syllable (*tṛtīyabīja*) and accompanied by the sixteen vowels, starting from *pūṣā* and so forth. On the second day, [the placement] begins from the back of the left foot. On the third day, it begins from the left ankle and extends to its respective end. Thus...

Having performed the placement starting from each successive limb up to its own end on the fourth day and so forth; on the first day of the dark fortnight, one places [the mantras] from the right side of the head to the end of the self, on the second day from the right conch-shell [ear], and on the third day starting from the right brow; thus, on the fourth day and so forth, having performed the placement starting from each successive limb up to its own end.

In the male limbs, which serve as the abodes of nectar according to the specific lunar days of the bright and dark fortnights, reside the sixteen Kāmakalās, conjoined with the seed-syllables of the sixteen Amṛteśvarīs. Likewise, in the female limbs, which serve as the abodes of nectar according to the specific lunar days of the bright and dark fortnights, reside the lunar digits (candrakalās), beginning with Pūṣā.

Having determined the essential meaning of the root text as "one should install the third seed-syllable together with Amṛteśvarī, who is connected with the sixteen vowels" (p. 70b), [one should proceed] regarding the two, *prakāśa* and *vimarśa*.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five arrows, each joined with its own seed-syllable, upon the forehead, face, heart, root, and base (*mūlādhāra*), as well as upon the base, navel, heart, face, and forehead of the two ends of the five objects of desire;
and having assigned six parts to each of those two garlands; [one should place] the six deities beginning with Mahāśakti upon them.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*): having placed Vasantamada on the two breasts and Candra on the mouth, and having placed [them] upon each of those; and having touched that nectar-body of Vimarśa on that day with one's own mind—preceded by the recitation of the mantra and preceded by the unfolding of the *drāviṇī-mudrā*—[one perceives] the light of both.

In the two *vimarśas* (reflections), one should place the nine lords in the nine locations: the right and left ears, the mouth, the right and left eyes, the secret organ, the right and left nostrils, and the location called the anus. [Furthermore,] in the front and back parts of the body of this non-woman (*asrī*), one places *Drāviṇī* and *Bhrāmaṇī* in the right foot, the buttock, the side, the hand, the left hand, the side, the buttock, the foot, and the back.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the nine Śaktis—beginning with Sūryā and ending with Pakṣiṇī, excluding the [central] Tārā—into the nine locations known as the *vaṃśas*;

having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*); and having placed the Space-form (*vyomarūpiṇī*) and the powers of sound (*śabdaśakti*) and so forth upon the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose; one should place the Prāṇa-Śakti on each of the two hips.

Having placed the *buddhi-śakti* in the heart and the *śakti-śakti* in the secret place, and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the root mantra, [one places them] in the western part of the secret place, the left side of the navel, the left side of the heart, and the left side of the throat. (p. 71a)

Having performed the mental placement of the eight deities of speech preceded by tactile contact on the chin, the right side of the neck, the right side of the heart, and the right side of the navel; having placed the four weapons on the eyes, eyebrows, ears, and nostrils; and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the root mantra.

Having projected the triad of powers beginning with Will (icchā) into the front corner, left corner, and right corner of the triangle situated at the *mūlādhāra* of Light (*prakāśa*) and Self-awareness (*vimarśa*), and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the root mantra, one should project the seat of consciousness (*samvidāsana*). Upon that, preceded by the display of the *drāviṇī* mudrā with the mantra "drāṃ," [one should worship] Madakalā.
Having meditated [upon the deity] again, and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) by means of the root mantra,

one should contemplate the identity of the seat consisting of the nature of consciousness (*samvidrūpa*) and the drop (*bindu*). Then, having recited sixteen times each the mantras interspersed with the colors of the three fires, one should [offer] the substances for libation appropriate to their respective colors.

Having brought the Goddess before oneself by means of the Tārā-vidyā as an offering, one should place her in the general arghya-vessel. With that [water], at the end of each respective root-vidyā, one should satisfy each respective Nityā three times with the mantra "I satisfy [Name] with this vidyā" (amukavidyāṃ tarpayāmi), and having offered it to the Guru, one should satisfy even one's own prāṇas by the command of the Guru.
Then, having recited the mantra "I offer salutation to [Name] Nityā" at the end of the *Nityā-vidyā*,

and having performed the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) by prostrating like a staff, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), the phoneme placement (*varṇanyāsa*), and the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*), combined with the specific number of repetitions prescribed for each respective ritual manual; in the absence of such a manual, [the standard number is used].

Having recited the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*) one hundred times, plus twenty-one times, or any other such number, one should perform the offering (*nivedana*) consisting of the meditation on non-difference from that [mantra]. Then, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*). Regarding what is to be performed therein: [p.

Having prepared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one cubit with sand as a thread for recollecting the collection of ritual objects, and having sprinkled it with the water of the general *arghya* offering while reciting the respective *nityā-vidyā*,
one should leave a space of one finger-breadth on all sides and fashion a nine-cornered wheel in the center.

Having brought from the house of a Śrotriya fire that is covered by another vessel using a ladle, and having cast one piece of charcoal toward the southwest with the mantra "Obeisance to the flesh-eaters" (*kravyādebhyo namaḥ*),
and having sprinkled the remaining fire and the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) three times with water, [he should cover it] with *kuśa* grass whose tips point either eastward or northward.

Having first strewn [the sacrificial grass] from the beginning, one should join either two seed-syllables or a single seed-syllable— uttered in the respective ritual manual (*kalpa*) during the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*)— to the initial portion of the fire, having meditated upon the fire as non-different from each respective *Nityā*. Then,
with the mantra consisting of the name of the fire in the dative case followed by *namaḥ*, such as *hrīṃ śrīṃ vahnaye namaḥ* or *aiṃ vahnaye namaḥ*.
Having worshipped with either the form *hrīṃ vahnaye namaḥ* or *hrīṃḥ vahnaye namaḥ*,
and having bypassed the western square which takes the place of one's own front square,
[one worships] the seven tongues named Bahurūpā, Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, and Asiraktā, in sequence within the seven squares starting from the east.

Having performed worship with mantras consecrated according to the method of fire-mantra purification (*vahnimantrapariṣkāra*), using such forms as *hrīṃ śrīṃ hiraṇyāyai namaḥ*, *aiṃ hiraṇyāyai namaḥ*, *hrīṃ hiraṇyāyai namaḥ*, and *hrīḥ hiraṇyāyai namaḥ*, one should perform the oblation of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*) with either a leaf of the *palāśa* or the *aśvattha* tree; for other oblations such as cooked rice (*caru*), one should use the hand itself.

Having performed the worship of the seven tongues of the fire in their proper sequence using the nine worship-mantras ending in *svāhā* for each, and having likewise performed the fire-oblation (*homa*), [one should proceed with] those [deities] obtained through the order of worship. (p.

Having offered one oblation each with the respective Vidyās ending in *svāhā* for the Lord, the weapons, and the deities of the various enclosures; having offered oblations according to the number of ten parts of the daily recitation (*nityajapa*);
and having also offered once each with the *bhūta-mantras* and *ātma-mantras* sixteen times.

One should offer oblations with each of those respective *nityā-vidyās* ending in *svāhā*. Even in a mantra that already ends in *svāhā*, another word for *svāhā* should be inserted. Then, having united the Goddess—who has been meditated upon as non-different from Fire—within the *bindu* of the wheel during one's own worship, and having cast the *paristaraṇa* *darbha* grasses into the fire, [one should proceed] as before with the *nityā-vidyā* under discussion.

Having sprinkled [water] around, and having again worshipped the fire with the mantra stated previously, beginning with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vahnaye Namaḥ," one should apply a *tilaka* mark with that ash using the respective *Nityā-vidyā*. Then, having performed the recitation (*japa*) of the present *vidyā* as many times as the number of oblations (*homa*), interspersed with the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*,
*varṇa-nyāsa*, and *vyāpaka-nyāsa*, [one attains] non-duality with that.

Having performed the offering consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one should come to the place of sacrifice. Then, having performed the worship of each respective *Nityā* with the five services (*pañcopacāra*), at the conclusion thereof—with no specific mantra mentioned, the mantra prescribed in her particular *kalpa* is used—one should worship Kurukullā with the seven-syllable mantra: *oṃ kurukulle svāhā*, or *oṃ kurukulle hrīṃ svāhā*.

One should offer the sacrificial substance (*bali*)—consisting of food, condiments, flowers, and water—placed at the three locations, using the thirteen-syllable mantra of Kurukullā, *oṃ kukulle hrīḥ mama sarvajanaṃ vaśamānaya ho svāhā*, and the twenty-five-syllable mantra as well. Then, having performed the *nīrājana* ceremony with wicks containing camphor and other substances, one should ask for forgiveness (*kṣamāpayet*). [Then] her...
Having passed the night with dancing, singing, and other such activities, at dawn, after completing the daily and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*) and so forth,
[one should perform the worship] for each of the deities of the various enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), beginning with the Lord’s weapons.
Having offered one oblation for each with those respective Vidyās ending in *svāhā*, and having offered oblations according to the number of ten parts of the daily recitation (*nityajapa*),

and having also offered once each with the Bhūta-mantras and Ātma-mantras, one should offer oblations sixteen times with those respective Nityā-vidyās ending in *svāhā*. Even in a mantra that already ends in *svāhā*, the word *svāhā* should be added again at the end.

It should be cast [into the fire]. Then, having united the Goddess—who has been meditated upon as non-different from Fire—within the *bindu* situated in one’s own worship-circle (*pūjā-cakra*), and having thrown the *darbha* grass used for strewing into the fire, one should sprinkle [the offerings] as before with the present Nityā-vidyā, using the mantra stated previously: *hrīṃ śrīṃ vahnaye namaḥ*, etc.

Having again worshipped the fire, and having applied a *tilaka* mark with its ashes using the respective *nityā-vidyā*, one should perform the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*, *varṇa-nyāsa*, and *vyāpaka-nyāsa* conjoined with the number of oblations (*homasaṃkhyā*). Then, having recited the present *vidyā* once more and performed the offering characterized by the contemplation of non-duality (*tadabheda-bhāvanā*), one should proceed to the place of sacrifice (*yāgasthāna*).

Then, having performed the worship of each respective Nityā with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), at the conclusion of that, one should perform the worship of Kurukullā with the seven-syllable mantra *oṃ kurukulle svāhā*— as no specific mantra is mentioned for her— or with the thirteen-syllable mantra *oṃ kurukulle hrīṃ svāhā*, or [with the mantra] *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ mama sarvajanaṃ*.

With the mantra "vaśamānaya ho svāhā," which consists of twenty-five syllables, one should offer the sacrificial substance (*bali*)—consisting of food, condiments, flowers, and water—which has been placed at the three locations. Then, having performed the *nīrājana* ceremony with wicks containing camphor and other ingredients, and having asked for forgiveness, one should spend that night with dance, song, and other such activities. At the time of dawn:
Having again performed the constant and occasional rites and other rituals up to the end (p.
and having worshipped the eternal Vidyā with the five offerings using the Śaktyutthāpinī mudrā;
Visualize that all the deities of the enclosure situated upon the wheel have dissolved into the principal deity being invoked.
Then, visualize that the splendor of the principal Nityā being invoked merges with one's own body along with whatever flower [was offered].
By means of the *khecarīmudrā*, through the inhalation of breath via the nostrils, [draw] that flower into one's own heart.

Having meditated on [the deity] as having entered [himself], he should contemplate his own self as being the very nature of each respective Nityā. Then, he should recite the hymns to the Guru and the hymns to the Goddess. Having thus completed the worship of each respective Nityā, which constitutes a limb of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), he should draw the *mātṛkā-cakra* in the northeast direction—east, north, or north-east—on the specific lunar day (*tithi*) corresponding to each respective Nityā, such as the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*).
Having seated the disciple facing east upon the seed-syllable at the center of its pericarp,
and having placed a citron fruit from atop the mouth of the water-pot into the cupped hands of the disciple,
and having placed some leaves upon the head of the disciple positioned at the mouth of that [pot], [he should act] with the remaining leaves from the pot.
Having consecrated [the disciple] once each with the mantras of the primary respective Nityās, as well as the deities of their weapons and armor,

the Guru— accompanied by his consort, surrounded by Yoginīs and Yogis— and the disciple, having put on washed, white garments along with waistbands, should be consecrated three times with the Vidyā of the primary respective Nityā. The remainder...

Having sipped water from the *kalaśa* vessel and worshipped the feet of the Guru with the ninefold offerings (*navopacāra*), one should satisfy him with a gift consisting of all one’s possessions—such as elephants, horses, and buffalo-cows—or with gold and other valuables as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Then, praising him three times with five verses and bowing down three times, one should rise and stand with palms joined in reverence. The Guru, having summoned the disciple to the *vedhacakra*, [proceeds].
Having performed the purificatory rite of *vedha* and established [the disciple], and having seated him again and again upon the wheel of the daily worship of the Vidyā-Nityās,
one should contemplate oneself as the form of the deity, [and then initiate] the disciple on the lunar days beginning with the first day (*pratipad*).

Having meditated upon [the deity] in the *brahmarandhra*, the heart, and the *mūlādhāra*— which are the respective *nityāpūjācakra*s— and having worshipped with the five mental offerings (*pañcopacāra*) preceded by invocation (*āvāhana*), the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and so forth, one should, accompanied by song and instrumental music,
impart the respective *nityā-vidyā* into the ear of the living being (the disciple) thirty times. Then the disciple:

Having attained the vidyā, while seated right there in that very cakra, one should recite that vidyā one hundred times and perform the offering consisting of the meditation on non-difference from it. Then, having received the guru’s permission, rising from that cakra, one should worship the guru with flowers and, while reciting the hymn of praise to the guru, [recite] three more times.

Having prostrated for three days and spent them in the teacher's house, with palms joined over his head, from that time forward he should always serve the teacher—who has obtained the knowledge through those various instructions—and [serve] that which is eternally present; such is the procedure for the general initiation (sāmānyadīkṣā).

Thus, the practitioner who has received initiation and mastered the methods of worship and so forth, should perform the practice for the attainment of the *vidyā* (mantra) in order to accomplish his own or another’s desired goal through specific modes such as recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), worship (*pūjana*), meditative identification (*abhedabhāvanā*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and the use of diagrams (*yantra*) or effigies (*puttalika*). Generally, its procedure is as follows:
For example: one should begin [the vow] on the full moon day during either the spring or summer season.
In this regard, subsisting solely on milk until the time of completion of the performance is the primary (mukhya) option;
subsisting on fruits and roots is the intermediate (madhyama) option; and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) is the secondary (gauṇa) option. Herein—

In all these positions, *ekabhakta* (eating once a day) is determined to consist in the absence of a second meal; and [the vow consists in] the absence of sexual intercourse with one's own wives other than during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*), beyond the act of approaching them for worship.
In every way, while the Guru is still alive, one must carry out his commands even by traveling to a very distant foreign land;
doing so without entertaining even a dream-like suspicion as to how one’s own life would be sustained for such a large family once this much wealth has been bestowed,
and having satisfied the Guru with wealth, clothing, ornaments, and the like— free from stinginess regarding money— one should act according to his command.

During the period when the Guru is in a state of pervasive presence (*vyāptatva*), one should likewise satisfy his wife, sons, and others; then, by his command, from the previous full moon until the subsequent full moon, there are thirty-two solar days (*sāvana-dina*) according to the increase of lunar days (*tithi*). At that time, preceded by an anointing with fragrant oil, [one should bathe] with fragrant waters using the aforementioned mantra.

Having bathed preceded by the *mārjana* and *aghamarṣaṇa* rites, having put on two garments— one red and one pure, new, and washed as an upper cloth— and having applied unguents of sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and so forth, and being smeared with red sandalwood,
one should meditate upon the Vidyā to be worshipped, which is red in color, within the *mūlādhāra*, the heart, and the *brahmarandhra*.
And by means of that radiance, the practitioner, contemplating his own self as red, with eyes adorned with collyrium,
his face having become naturally flushed from the chewing of betel, and his mouth made fragrant by the offering of camphor and excellent incense,
[should worship] with a canopy and other ornaments dyed with lac and the like, and with camphor, agallochum, and so forth.
In a room well-perfumed with incense and illuminated by rows of lamps, in a place purified by the *kūrma-cakra* diagram, one should perform worship at the three junctions of the day—

morning, midday, and evening— at each respective time. At the conclusion of all rites, including worship, constant recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), offering of oblations (*bali-dāna*), waving of lamps (*nīrājana*), and the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*), [the procedure is repeated] individually during both the morning and midday periods.
p.
74a) Having recited [the mantra] one thousand forty-three times at evening time while maintaining silence, [this is to be done] every day.

One should complete the count of one hundred thousand, starting from the full moon and ending with the full moon, by means of a number equal to three thousand one hundred and twenty-five forms. At the conclusion of the daily practice and recitation, one should offer oblations according to that same numerical proportion, using clarified butter smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu) and flowers appropriate to each respective ritual manual (*kalpa*).

In the absence of special substances, having offered oblations, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with pure water scented with camphor, saffron, musk, and sandalwood, in a number equal to one-tenth of the total count of recitations (*japa*). This should be done from the day of commencement until the day of completion,
according to one's capacity, in a large quantity whenever possible.

One should feed those who are constant worshippers of that [deity] and endowed with qualities such as being perpetual performers of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, or, in their absence, others who are not censured or divided, using food consisting mostly of sweet items. Having fed them with devotion and preceded by worship, one should bow down and dismiss them. One should personally honor the Guru or one who occupies the position of a Guru every day, especially so.

When the eighth part of the day remains, one should eat the aforementioned substances, as well as that which was offered to the deity after worship and the remnants of what was sacrificed. Having thus completed the rite on the final day, setting aside any concern for wealth, one should satisfy the Guru with riches, garments, and ornaments, and recite a hymn of praise to the Guru.

For the sake of ensuring the successful completion of the ritual procedures (*sādhana-karma-sāṅgatā*), one should feed Brāhmaṇas, satisfy the poor, the destitute, and others to their heart's content, and at the conclusion of the remembrance of Acyuta, one should personally partake of the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*). Regarding the number of recitations for the *sādhana*, specifically in the case of silent recitation (*mukti-sthala*), there are three types: up to nine syllables, for each syllable repeated, and three hundred thousand (*lakṣa-traya*) for each syllable.

Up to twenty syllables, each individual syllable constitutes one hundred thousand [recitations]. Beyond that, for all mantras, it is merely one hundred thousand. Furthermore, this number is multiplied fourfold in the Kali Yuga. Thus...

Since it is impossible for one who has already become [an initiate] to perform the means [of initiation] by oneself, the Blessed One— teaching the performance of the *homa* ritual through a Brāhmaṇa, which is to be carried out after satisfying [the officiant] by means of choosing him, providing food, giving materials, and offering sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) either through a preceptor, a disciple, or a brother of the respective Vidyā-practitioner— has also established the means [of initiation] through another.
This is the general procedure for accomplishing the vidyā, because it indicates that the performance of recitation (japa) brings about its fruit.

Primarily, the morning ritual for those who constantly worship that [deity] is as follows: having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should meditate upon the Lord (Nātha) in the form of light within the *brahmarandhra*, possessing the form of one's own Guru; having worshipped Him mentally with nine offerings (*navopacāra*), one should recite the five hymns beginning with *Gurustotra*, *Namastenaatha*, and *Maganityā*.

Having recited the verses consisting of the *śloka*s, while meditating on the respective *nityā*’s six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), the placement of syllables (*varṇanyāsa*), and the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) mantras upon the various limbs; and having meditated upon oneself as the form of the threefold radiance and as the essential nature of that respective *nityā*; one should regard the sacrificial offering (*balidravya*)—consisting of rice, condiments, flowers, and water—as being present.

Having prayed, "O women who possess various colors, weapons, forms, vehicles, and ornaments; who are omnipresent and granters of all perfections— at the conclusion of the offering of oblations," [one recites] the Kālanityā-vidyā numbering 20,736, the Pūrṇamaṇḍala numbering 576, and the Sandhyā-devatās numbering 6, corresponding to the twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths arising from one's own *āhuti*.

Having contemplated the forms of the sixty *ghaṭikās*, the twelve signs beginning with Aries, the nine planets beginning with the Sun, the five elements beginning with space, and the fifty *mātṛkās* (pp.

One should meditate on the ninety-one breaths (*śvāsa*) of Vasiṣṭha according to their respective natures as the forms of their own presiding deities, and that all these breaths are also the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of their respective Nityās. Then, with the *vidyā* of one's own chosen Nityā, one should perform the rites of rinsing the mouth, sipping water, bathing, and so forth, using the appropriate mantras even if they have not been explicitly mentioned.

Having performed the *manuṣṭhāya*, one should perform the three *sandhyās*—consisting of morning, midday, and evening—in the manner already described. The recitation of the *nāmapārāyaṇa*, the sixty-fold *japa*, and the *japa* of the *pūrṇamaṇḍala-mantra*: these constituent elements constitute this daily obligatory rite (*nitya*).
These [rites] must necessarily be performed even by those who are merely lay disciples (*upāsaka*). Likewise, the worship of the *ghaṭikā-cakra* is also mandatory;

for since even the sixteen *Nityās* are to be worshipped there as objects of inscription, the scriptural injunctions regarding the sin of failing to worship them encompass every single practitioner (*sādhaka*), even one who worships only a single *Nityā*.
The primary course is the daily worship of that deity; the intermediate course is worship on every festival day (parva);

and the lowest course is worship within a month consisting of thirty-six solar days (sāvana). Even upon the omission of that [lowest course], one should perform the expiation for the lapse in the sequence of obligatory rites (nityakarman).

Furthermore, that [daily practice] must be commenced; it is not otherwise. Although the primary focus is on a single daily worship (*nityopāsana*), all daily worships are indeed necessary as auxiliary components (*aṅga*), because this very point has been made known through the ritual of the evening twilight (*sāyaṃ-sandhyā-vidhi*), which consists of sixteen daily recitations (*japa*). Nor is [the scripture] intended to refer to the primary worship alone.

It should not be suspected that this refers to the *sandhyā-vidhi* (the ritual of the twilight prayers), because [if it did], everything other than the *yantra* would apply to all [deities], which would result in a contradiction of the established tenets of the *Mūlasiddha*. Furthermore, there would be a contradiction of the statement that when one *Nityā* is worshipped as the principal (*aṅgin*), the others are worshipped as its subordinate members (*aṅga*).
Nor can it be argued that this [text] concerns only worship based on a *yantra* common to all the *Nityās*.

Since the relationship of these [meditations] as parts and whole is established, their status as such follows without hindrance from the very force of the scriptural enumeration of those meditations occurring within the scope of that [system]. Thus, the meditation on the deities as couples is also necessarily required for each individual [part].

This is the summary even for those who worship daily. In that regard, since the worship of the couple (*mithunārcā*) must be performed upon the head of the *yantra* of the Wish-Fulfilling Lotus (*kāmyakamalā*), the dial of hours (*ghaṭikācakra*), which has not been extracted anywhere else, is now shown by means of honey. Having arranged the rotation of the crank (*karkāṭaka*) all around the desired measurement and having produced a circle, [one draws] a line extending from east to west.

Having laid the Brahma-thread, and having fixed it at its center, one should lay a thread extending from south to north up to the limit of the circular line. Then, starting from both ends of that [thread], one should stretch two threads from the Brahma-thread to the point of the western junction of the circle. Having thus produced a downward-pointing triangle, [the area] to its left is the *yoni*.

Having produced an upward-pointing triangle by drawing two lines from the right-side line— whose two tips meet at the center— to the end of the junction of the circle and the Brahma-line (the vertical axis),
[one should draw] the north-south line from the middle of those two lines located in the upper portion.

Having drawn two other lines from the points where the two diagonal lines located at both sides meet the westernmost point, up to the junction of the two Brahma-lines; and having fashioned the lower triangle known as the "womb-base" (yonipada), which is fierce and has three corners; then, having erased the Brahma-line and the circular line, [one obtains] the wheel of the hour-glass (ghaṭikācakra).

Having completed the drawing of the lines, one should write the three syllables of the *paryāya-nityā*— whose form consists of three letters— beginning from the tip and proceeding counter-clockwise within the three external *yoni*s. Then, within the upward-pointing triangle,
beginning from the eastern triangle and proceeding counter-clockwise, one should write the three syllables of the *taddinanityā*, whose form consists of three letters.

Having written the three letters, one should [place] the five vowels starting from the lower region on the left side of the *yoni* located in the center of all, proceeding in order; and the five vowels starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) on the upper line on the right side.

One should write the five vowels in order from top to bottom. In the central portion, having written the sixty-four syllables of the present Yuga, one should write within that the vowel *a* and the others as the *ghaṭikā*-syllables in the form of dots (*bindu*), and not in their conventional forms; and outside of them are the long vowels (*dīrgha*) beginning with *ā*.

It is by way of the fifteen well-known forms (*prasiddhākāra*) alone, and not by way of the form of the *bindu*, that the letter *ā* constitutes a *ghaṭikā*-syllable. Having written the letter *i* and so forth, the short *ā* should be written at the end; in the same manner, it should be inferred for what follows. Regarding the consonants beginning with *ka* as *ghaṭikā*-syllables: having joined the *yuga*-syllable and the *ghaṭikā*-syllable, they should be written in the middle; therefore—
Having written [the name] in the midst of the *kāminīs*, the fifteen syllables beginning with *kākikīkukū* are to be written on the outside.

When the syllable *kha* is the *ghaṭikā*-syllable, the fifteen letters beginning with *kha*, *khā*, *khī*, *khū*, and so forth, are to be written externally in the center as "kham. In this context, for both vowels and consonants, there is only the state of having the nasal dot (*bindu*), not their naked state. Thus, by means of the various arrangements of the fifty *ghaṭikā*-syllables starting from the center, [this occurs] within a single day.

There are fifty-six sixty-day cycles (*ṣaṣṭikā-cakras*). In each cycle, during the rotation of the daily *Nityās* whose forms correspond to their respective days, there are 1,036,800 instruments (*yantras*) as the measure.
However, in that final cycle, it is stated that for certain final days, they are governed by the two-fold daily *Nityās*.
The reduction should be calculated by subtraction. Here,
having worshipped with the primary vidyā that which is intended as the principal— the eternal form consisting of the letters situated in the center of all— one should [proceed].

Having worshipped the fifteen Nityās in the fifteen syllables surrounding that [central one]: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the power I (I-śakti). Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the power Ḍā (Ḍā-śakti). Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the power Ī (Ī-śakti). Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the power Ṭhā (Ṭhā-śakti). Hrīṃ...

One should worship the respective *paryāya-nityā* phoneme-śaktis and the *dinanityā* phoneme-śaktis of that day in the following manner: "Śrīṃ, I worship the *pādukā* of Ā-śakti; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the *pādukā* of Ī-śakti," and so forth.
This was stated with reference to the case where *Īḍāī* is the *paryāya-nityā* and *Īṭhāī* is the *dinanityā*.

At other times, one should infer for oneself according to the specific occasion. Furthermore, the primary daily worship (*nityapūjā*) in the center is also performed with the *vidyā* composed of the syllables written in the middle, such as: *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth;
or in the form of *hrīṃ śrīṃ kaṃ śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth—namely, with the *vidyā* of the primary *Nityā*.

The worship should be performed as follows: for all fifteen Nityās surrounding [the central deity], the worship must be done using the Vidyā composed of their respective syllables alone, in the form "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Āṃ Śaktipādukāṃ Pūjayāmi" and so forth; that is, the worship should be performed in the form "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kāṃ Śaktipādukāṃ Pūjayāmi" and so on. Even though this is the case for the Vidyā consisting of a single Ghaṭikā-syllable...
Thus, it becomes a worship of only the syllable of one *ghaṭikā*, not a worship of the syllables of sixty *ghaṭikās*. Nevertheless,
by writing whichever rising syllable occurs on whichever day in the center, and then writing the remaining syllables starting from that one as before,
and performing worship with the *vidyā* composed of those [syllables], the daily worship of all *ghaṭikās* is accomplished.

"The meaning is established by tradition" (p. 77a), says the author of the *Nidhi*; [this refers to] "the letter of the *yuga* [period] by means of the letter of the *ghaṭikā*" because of the designation "*ghaṭikācakra*."
The meaning of the scripture is not merely the recording of the measures (*mātrā*) and syllables (*akṣara*) of the *Mūlasaura*;

rather, one should worship the deities of the sixty *ghaṭikās* at a single time by means of the fifty mantras associated with the syllables of those respective *ghaṭikās* within the fifty *cakras* of the *ṛṭhikās*. And thus:

The writing of all the syllables becomes consistent with what was previously stated. Alternatively, it appears that there is no possibility of the omission of other rites, because the rite of worshipping the wheel of the sixty ghaṭikās has already been undertaken.
If a matter, though already stated during a general discussion, is seen again during a specific discussion, then for the sake of firmer recollection, that is not redundant. Furthermore,
what was not stated there [in the first instance] but is stated here— being left unstated due to fear of increasing the bulk of the work— is not a cause of deficiency.
The general introduction is presented separately solely for the sake of brevity in the text. Thus ends the general introduction.

Now, the ritual applications preceded by the method of instruction for the goddess Kāmeśvarī Nityā are being written. Having constructed the Bhūpura (the outer square enclosure) with nine lines like the Śrīcakra, one should draw within it a hexagon; inside that, another sixteen-petaled lotus;
further inside that, again a sixteen-petaled lotus; inside that, an eight-petaled lotus; and inside that as well, a five-petaled lotus.

One should perform [the drawing]. Here, in all cases, although every lotus may consist of the forms of the pericarp-circle (*karṇikā-vṛtta*), the filament-circle (*kesara-vṛtta*), and the petal-tip-circle (*dalāgra-vṛtta*), because of the instruction to erase the filament-circle, it should be made with double circles (*viddhi-vṛtta*). And thus, following that continuously, they should be made within the outer square (*bhūpura*). Therein, situated at the very center...
Between two circles with an interval of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*), there is a five-petaled lotus;
outside of those two, between two circles with an interval of four finger-breadths, there is an eight-petaled lotus.

Between the two circles outside those [inner ones], which have an interval of four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula) between them, there is a sixteen-petalled lotus; again, between the two circles outside those [sixteen-petalled lotuses], which likewise have an interval of four finger-breadths, there is another sixteen-petalled lotus;
and between the circle at the tip of each preceding lotus and the circle at the root of each succeeding lotus, there is one [lotus] for each.

The interval [between the lines] is merely the width of a hair (*kālamātra*). Outside of that, between two circles separated by an interval of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*), there is a hexagon;

thus is this *pūjācakra* completed. Having drawn it on some pure, level ground, and having placed the *kalaśa* there according to the prescribed method, one should contemplate within the water of the *kalaśa* the entire *maṅgalā-pūjācakra*.

Having worshipped Sarvamaṅgalā along with her enclosure using the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra) and then dismissed her, one should again worship the Nityā Kāmeśvarī within that very worship-circle (pūjā-cakra) previously contemplated. However, the daily worship (nityapūjā) is performed in the circle alone. The procedure for that is as follows: having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) with the aforementioned mantra and offered the oblation (bali) with the sixteen-syllable mantra.

Having worshipped the lineage of Gurus upon one's own head with their respective mantras— or alternatively, having worshipped Nāthanātha— having recited the Hymn to the Nātha and received his command, one should begin the worship. Having meditated upon one's own self as the present, eternal, and stainless embodiment of the Guru, [one should perform] all the secret and manifest [rites], regulated by the specific country, time, and other factors determined for each particular year.
Having worshipped the Siddhayoginīs, the deities of the thirty-eight pīṭhas ending with Cakrāntā, with their respective mantras,

one should place a common arghya vessel together with its base between the yantra and oneself, filled with water scented with gorocanā, camphor, saffron, agallochum, and musk; [then] that base vessel...

Having sequentially meditated upon the waters as having the forms of fire, sun, and moon by means of the seed-syllables of Kulasundarī, and having visualized the five substances beginning with gorocanā as the five elements beginning with earth, one should [use] that water.
Having meditated upon the identity between the present Nityā-pūjā and the Cakra, one should consecrate water— meditated upon as non-different from the present Nityā—
by reciting the present Vidyā ten times; then,
having worshipped it and likewise worshipped the deities of the six limbs with the mantras of its six limbs, one should [sprinkle] oneself with that water using the present Vidyā.

Having consecrated each item of the twelve-fold service (*dvādaśopacāra*) materials— consisting of water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), water for bathing (*snāna*), water, clothing, ornaments, fragrance, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and betel leaf (*tāmbūla*)—
and having again performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *vidyā*, one should take water along with flowers and unbroken rice grains in the hand, [mentioning] the place, time, and lineage...

Having written the end of the name of the zodiac sign [of the disciple], one should form the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "For the pleasure of the eternal goddess Śrī Kāmeśvarī, I shall perform the daily worship of the eternal goddess Śrī Kāmeśvarī according to the prescribed rule and to the best of my ability.
However, in the case of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and worship, this resolve is to be made by the preceptor (*guru*), and it pertains to Sarvamaṅgalā, who is a constituent part of that [rite].

Since the commencement of worship has already been performed, it need not be done again now; for by this very injunction, the entire collection of purposes such as worship and so forth is subsumed. [One should perform] the *mātṛkā-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ śirase svāhā*; *uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ*... [and so on].

Ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (śikhā). Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ, *huṃ* to the armor (kavaca). Oṃ paṃ phaṃ vaṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ, *vauṣaṭ* to the eyes (netra). Aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ la. kṣaṃ aḥ, *phaṭ* to the weapon (astra). Thus, [one should assign] these mantras to one's own thumbs and other fingers.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart and other parts, one should manifest the perfected form endowed with the specific *mātṛkā* letters beginning with 'A' belonging to the vidyā under discussion.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the respective locations of the *mātṛkās*, one should place the mantras on one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other limbs, as follows: "Aiṃ, salutation to the Heart; sakalahrīṃ, svāhā to the Head; nitya, vaṣaṭ to the Crest-lock (*śikhā*); klinne, huṃ to the Armor (*kavaca*); madadrave, vauṣaṭ svāhā to the Eye; phaṭ to the Weapon (*astra*). In all these instances, regarding the mantra for the eye:

Even in the application of the mantra "netratrayāya vaṣaṭ," there is no loss of the scriptural meaning; thus, the establishment of these two positions follows from the respective traditions of one's own gurus. As for the application in *karanyāsa* (hand-consecration) such as "to both thumbs, namaḥ" and so forth, that is indeed outside the scope of the present scripture. Therefore, with the snapping of fingers accompanied by sound, [one should ward off] obstacles in the ten directions.

One should perform the clearing away (*utsāraṇa*) of the terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial [obstacles]. Then, one should place: *aiṃ* on the right eye; *sakala hrīṃ* on the left eye; *ni* on the right ear; *ittha* on the left ear; *ikti* on the right nostril; *nte* on the left nostril;
*ma* on the tongue; *dṛ* on the heart; *edi* on the navel; *ve* on the secret place; and *sauḥ*.

Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) from the crown of the head down to the feet, one should again perform the threefold pervasive placement with the complete mantra: *aiṃ sakala hrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave*.
This is to be done within the drop (*bindu*) visualized inside the pitcher during the worship that is an ancillary of initiation (*dīkṣāṅga-pūjā*), or elsewhere.
Precisely in the center of the *bindu* within the filaments of the lotus of fifteen parts,

having first displayed the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā* and taken flowers with joined palms (*añjali*), one should offer the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) along the path of the central channel (*vaha-nāḍī*), which is the radiance of the present *vidyā* visualized from the *mūlādhāra* up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Having visualized that [the deity] has been transferred, and having visualized the transfer by the one who casts it, as before, at the end of the vidyā—
[reciting] "O Nityā, Mistress of Desire, you have been invoked here into this wheel"— one should pray thus, while [visualizing] the rays of that splendor radiating here and there.

One should meditate, visualizing [the goddess] as having spread out to the locations to be described hereafter, transformed into the forms of the deities who are the lords of those respective enclosures and their weapons. Alternatively, after meditation, one performs the invocation by scattering handfuls of flowers; as for the visualization, she is like ten million rising suns.

Resplendent with a crown of rubies, adorned with necklaces, waist-bands, girdles, rings, anklets, and other ornaments, wearing crimson garments and decorated with red jewels; six-armed and three-eyed, her head crowned by the crescent moon; she who dwells within the pentagon, the octagon, the sixteen-petaled lotus, the pair [of triangles], the hexagon, and the square.

She has a face radiant with a gentle smile and glances languid with compassion; she holds in her hands a noose, a goad, an unerring sugarcane bow, flower-arrows, a jewel-vessel filled with wine, and the gesture of granting boons.
The Śaktis, identical in form to her in dress, ornaments, and weapons, [are likewise visualized]. This is the meditation on the Śaktis, which applies everywhere in these [sections].

Then, [reciting] "O Mokāmeśvarī-nityā, be established here in this cakra, marked with your own respective insignia," at the end of the mantra; "O Mokāmeśvarī-nityā, be firmly restrained here in this cakra," at the end of the mantra;
"O Mokāmeśvarī-nityā, be veiled here in this cakra," at the end of the mantra; "O Mokāmeśvarī-nityā, [be present] here in this cakra," at the end of the mantra.

Having requested, "May they be present," preceded by the display of their respective mudrās, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) using the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*), carry out the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs, and perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā* in the form:
"The vital breaths of this Nityā Kāmeśvarī are here in the yantra; [the vital breaths... and so forth.

Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should perform the worship with the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*). The mantras for this are as follows: at the end of the root-vidyā, saying "O Kāmeśvarī, I prepare the water for the feet (*pādya*) for Nityā," one offers the water for the feet using the water from the general *arghya* vessel.
One should offer [the substances] at the feet with the root-vidyā. In this very manner, by substituting the word "pādya" (water for the feet) with the words "arghya," "manasnāna" (mental bath),

"vastra" (clothing), "bhūṣaṇa" (ornaments), "gandha" (scent), "puṣpa" (flower), "dhūpa" (incense), "dīpa" (lamp), "ācamana" (water for sipping), "naivedya" (food offering), and "tāmbūla" (betel leaf) one by one,
and having offered each respective article with the resulting mantras, one should perform the repetition of the vidyā for each individual object.

One should offer [the oblation] appropriately upon the head, face, and all limbs; upon the primary and secondary limbs; and as is fitting, upon the forehead, feet, chest, shoulders, navel region, eyes, and mouth.

Then follows the thirteen-fold service (*trayodaśopacāra*). Its procedure is as follows: on the back part of the Goddess, in three rows arranged from top to bottom, beginning with the row closest to the Goddess and proceeding in groups of three, one worships:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of the power of Light-Bliss (*prakāśānandaśakti*); *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of the power of Reflection-Bliss (*vimarśānandaśakti*).
Pū0 Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ānandaśaktipāda Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Jñānānandaśaktipāda Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Satyānandaśaktipāda Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Śrīpūrṇānandaśaktipāda Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Svabhāvānandaśaktipāda Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Pratibhānandaśaktipāda Hrīṃ Śrīṃ.

Having performed worship with the mantras, "I worship the *pādukā* of Subhagānandaśakti," one should worship [the goddess] starting from the region near the left lower hand of the Goddess and ending at the region near the right lower hand of the Goddess, reciting:
"Aiṃ, obeisance to the Giver of Boons; Aiṃ, obeisance to the bow of many sugarcanes; Aiṃ, obeisance to the noose; Aiṃ."

Having worshipped the principal deities of equal status with the mantras: "Oṃ Aṅkuśāya namaḥ," "Aiṃ Puṣpaśilīmukhebhyaḥ namaḥ," and "Aiṃ Sīdhupūrṇaratnapātrāya namaḥ," one should worship [the arrows] on the five-petaled lotus, beginning from the eastern petal:
"Aiṃ Drāṃ Unmādanabāṇāya namaḥ" and "Aiṃ Drīṃ Unmādanabāṇāya namaḥ."

Having worshipped the five arrows with: *aiṃ klīṃ namaḥ to the arrow of illumination*, *aiṃ vlūṃ namaḥ to the arrow of enchantment*, and *aiṃ saḥ namaḥ to the arrow of piercing*, at the conclusion of the complete ritual procedure, [one worships] Kāmeśvarī.

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra, "I worship the sandals of Nityā," one should offer that worship with: "Aiṃ! May these deities of the first enclosure of Kāmeśvarī-Nityā accept this worship. Then, on the eight petals, beginning from the petal in front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise: "Aiṃ! I worship the sandals of Anaṅgakusumā. Aiṃ.

Having worshipped the eight Śaktis with: "Aiṃ, I worship the sandals of Anaṅgamekhalā; Aiṃ, [I worship] Anaṅgamadanā; Aiṃ, [I worship] Anaṅgamadanāturā; Aiṃ, [I worship] Madaveginī; Aiṃ, [I worship] Bhuvanapālā; Aiṃ, [I worship] Śaśirekhā; Aiṃ, I worship the sandals of Gaganarekhā," and at the end of the Vidyā, [one says]: "I worship the sandals of the Nityā Kāmeśvarī."

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center, one should offer [the oblation] with the words: "Aiṃ! May these deities of the second enclosure, the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī, accept this worship. Then, in the sixteen-petaled lotus, beginning from the eastern petal and proceeding clockwise:
"Aiṃ! Aṃ! I worship the sandals of the Śraddhā-kalā. Aiṃ! Āṃ! [I worship] the Prīti-kalā. Aiṃ! Iṃ! [I worship] the Rati-kalā..."

Aiṃ Īṃ, the goddess Dhṛtikalāpā; Aiṃ Uṃ, Kīrtikalāpā; Aiṃ Ūṃ, Manoramākalāpā; Aiṃ Ṛṃ, Manoharākalāmā; Aiṃ Ṝṃ, Manoharākalāmā; Aiṃ ṝṃ, Manorathākalāpā; Aiṃ Ḷṃ, Madanonmādinīkalāpā; Aiṃ Ḹṃ, Mohinīkalāpā; Aiṃ Eṃ, Śaṅkhinīkalāpā; Aiṃ Aiṃ.

Having worshipped the digits of passion (*madanakalāḥ*) with: "I worship the sandals of Śoṣiṇīkalāpā; Aiṃ Oṃ Vaśakārīkalāpā; Aiṃ Auṃ Siñjinīkalāpā; Aiṃ Aṃ Subhagākalāpā; Aiṃ Aḥ Priyadarśanikākalāpā," [one worships] Kāmeśvarī at the end of the Vidyā.

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra, "I worship Nityāpādukā," one should offer that worship with the words, "Aiṃ! May these deities of the third enclosure, Kāmeśvarī and Nityā, accept this worship. Then, on the sixteen-petaled lotus outside [the previous circle]:
Beginning from the front and proceeding clockwise: *Aiṃ Aṃ*, I worship the sandals of the *Pūṣā* digit;

*Aiṃ Āṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of the *Icchā* digit; *Aiṃ Īṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of the *Sumanasā* digit; *Aiṃ Īṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of the *Rati* digit; *Aiṃ Uṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of the *Prīti* digit;
*Aiṃ Ūṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of the *Dhṛti* digit; *Aiṃ Ṛṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of the *Ṛddhi* digit; *Aiṃ Ṝṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of the *Saumyā* digit; *Aiṃ Ḷṃ*.

Having worshipped the digits of the moon (candrakalāḥ) with the following: "I worship the sandals of the digit Marīcikalā, Aiṃ Ḷṃ; the digit Aṃśumālinīkalā, Aiṃ Eṃ; the digit Śaśinīkalā, Aiṃ Aiṃ; the digit Aṅgirākalā, Aiṃ Oṃ; the digit Chāyākalā, Aiṃ Auṃ; the digit Sampūrṇamaṇḍalākalā, Aiṃ Aṃ; and the digit Tuṣṭikalā, Aiṃ AḤ; [and] the digit Amṛtākalā. Thus, having performed the worship of the lunar digits.

At the end of the *vidyā*, having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with the mantra, "I worship the sandals of the eternal Kāmeśvarī," one should offer that worship with: "Aiṃ! May these deities of the fourth enclosure, the eternal Kāmeśvarī, accept this worship.
Then, in the southwest corner of the hexagonal wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*), [one worships]: "Aiṃ! I worship the sandals of Ḍākinī. In the northwest corner, "Aiṃ! Rākinī..."

Having worshipped with "I worship the *pādukā*," one worships the *pādukā* of Aiṃ Lākinī in the eastern corner, the *pādukā* of Aiṃ Kākinī in the southeast corner, the *pādukā* of Aiṃ Sākinī in the northeast corner, and the *pādukā* of Aiṃ Hākinī in the western corner.
Then, at the end of the complete Vidyā, one worships the central [deity] with "I worship the *pādukā* of Nityā Kāmeśvarī."

Having worshipped the Goddess: "Aiṃ! May these deities of the fifth enclosure, Kāmeśvarī and Nityā, accept this worship. Thus one should offer that worship. Then, in the square, on the southern path of the east (p.
Aiṃ Iṃ, I worship the Sandal of Śakti. In the southeast corner: Aiṃ, [I worship] the Sandal of Agni-Śakti. On the southern path:
Aiṃ, [I worship] the Sandal of Yama-Śakti. In the southwest corner: Aiṃ, [I worship] the Sandal of Nirṛti-Śakti. On the northern path of the west:
Aiṃ, [I worship] the Sandal of Varuṇa-Śakti. In the northwest corner: Aiṃ, [I worship] the Sandal of Vāyu-Śakti. On the northern path: Aiṃ, [I worship] the Sandal of Soma-Śakti.

Having worshipped the powers (śaktis) who are the essence of the world-protectors (lokapālas)—saying "aiṃ, I worship the sandals of the power of Īśāna" in the northeast corner; "aiṃ, I worship the power of Ananta" on the southern path of the west; and "aiṃ, I worship the sandals of the power of Brahmā" on the northern path of the east—one should then worship the central goddess, saying at the end of the complete vidyā: "I worship Kāmeśvarī Nityā."

Having worshipped [them], one should offer that worship with: *Aiṃ*, "May these goddesses of the sixth enclosure, Kāmeśvarī and Nityā, accept this worship. Then, in the inner path between the square and the outer circle of the hexagon, in the four corners starting from the southeast, moving counter-clockwise: *Aiṃ*, "I worship the sandals of Vaṭuka-Śakti. *Aiṃ*.

Having worshipped with "Gaṇapa-śaktipāta aiṃ, Durgā-śaktipāta aiṃ, I worship the sandals of Kṣetrapāla-śakti," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with "At the end of the Vidyā, I worship the sandals of Nityā Kāmeśvarī," [one should say]: "Aiṃ! These deities of the seventh enclosure of Nityā Kāmeśvarī [accept] the worship..."

One should offer worship by presenting a handful of flowers with the words, "May [they] accept. Then, having performed the remaining three services consisting of the recitation of hymns (*stotra*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), and prostration (*praṇāma*),

one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the thumbs and other fingers belonging to the hands and limbs, as well as the placement of the heart and other parts, in such a manner that they are encapsulated by the placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*).

Having performed the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) with a number of repetitions equal to one thousand, twenty-one hundred, one hundred, or one hundred and eight, and having offered it, [one should perform] its tenth part with ghee.

Having offered oblations with red flowers smeared on one of the poles, or with pure ghee alone, using the Kurukullā-vidyā, and having presented the bali offering and performed the lustration (nīrājana), one should complete the remainder according to the procedure for the worship of the principal vidyā.
However, in the case of initiation (dīkṣā), one should perform the remaining rites as described in the general introduction.

Thus, the disciple who has acquired the knowledge and obtained the means for its accomplishment through the grace of the guru should practice that vidyā. The method for doing so shall be demonstrated immediately hereafter: having performed the worship according to the previously mentioned directions—preceded by the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites—in one of the eight desire-yanttras (kāmayantras), at its conclusion...

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times so that the count is equal. Until the completion of the hundred-thousand recitations, one should subsist solely on milk. By this, there shall be the destruction of all sins; what need is there to mention the destruction of the sins that obstruct the success of the ritual application?

In the absence of the perfection of the vidyā, one should likewise perform forty lakhs of recitations; having thus accomplished the vidyā, one should carry out the ritual applications (prayoga). Among these, first is the application of the Kāmapañcayantra as follows: *hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ huṃ strīṃ*—these are the five mantras of desire (*pañcakāma*). In this context, the letters *ha*, *ra*, *ka*, *la*, and the diphthong *ai* [are to be combined with the vowel *va*].

If the letters *sa*, *ka*, *ta*, and *ra* are repeated as the sixth [letter], then when each of these is joined with the sixteen vowels, they result in forms such as *ha-hā-hi-hī* and so forth. However, when joined with the sixteen vowels beginning with *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū* and so on, they result in those very same vowel forms. Having first constructed a hexagon, one should draw a pathway (*vīthī*) outside of it by means of three circles.
Having prepared the two [circles] there, one should write the seed-syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) in the pericarp; having arranged three rows in its central portion,
one should write in the first row the name of the person, such as "Devadatta’s," ending in the genitive case.

The name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) [is written] in the bottom row. In the middle row, having written the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—such as "Yajñadanta"—ending in the accusative case, followed by the intended word of action (*karmapada*) in the form "subjugate" (*vaśaṃkuru*), "make do" (*kurviti*), and so forth; one should write that very same [mantra] in the three lower corners of the hexagon, joined with the *bindu*, situated within the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Having written that same seed-syllable (*bīja*) again, omitting the *bindu* and making it joined with the *visarga*, one should write the three corners situated in the upper portion. Then, [one writes] *haḥ*, *hāḥ*, *hiḥ*, *hīḥ*, *huḥ*, *hūḥ*, *hṛḥ*, *hṝḥ*, *hḷḥ*, *hḹḥ*, *heḥ*, *haiḥ*, *hoḥ*, *hauḥ*, *haḥ*, *haḥ*, and so forth; these are the modifications of the previously mentioned group of four syllables, joined with the *visarga*.
Having written the sixty-four syllables on the inner path—namely, the fourfold group beginning with *ai* (the modified vowels), such as *aḥ*, *āḥ*, *iḥ*, *īḥ*, and so forth;
*paḥ*, *pāḥ*, *viḥ*, *vīḥ*; *sruḥ*, *vuḥ*, *ḷḥ*, *ḹḥ*;
*ceḥ*, *caiḥ*, *coḥ*, *cauḥ*, *caṃḥ*, *caḥ*, and so forth; *saḥ*, *sāḥ*, and so forth; *taḥ*, *tāḥ*, *tiḥ*, *tīḥ*, and so forth—one should then [place] the *visarga*.

One should write sixty-four syllables on the outer path; this is the first yantra. In this very same [yantra], if one writes the *kāmabīja* in the place of the *māyāvīja* and performs all the aforementioned rites, then it is the second.
