Now, if the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable is written in the place of the *māyā* seed-syllable, while the subsequent procedure remains exactly as previously stated, then that is the third yantra. Now, if "blūm" is written in the place of the *māyā*, and everything else remains as before, then that is the fourth yantra. Now, if the *vadhū* seed-syllable is inscribed in the place of the *māyā*, and all the rest [remains as before]...

As before, that is the fifth yantra. These five yantras are, in sequence, formed by the Kāma-mantras named Kāmarāja, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makaraketana, and Manobhava, consisting of six-angled figures with pericarps. (p. 82b)
These are called the various *kāmayantṛ* (desire-machines).

Having performed their placement (*nyāsa*) in sequence upon the forehead, mouth, heart, navel, and *mūlādhāra*, one should [worship] those known as Madana, Unmādana, Uddīpana, Mohana, Śoṣaṇa, and so forth, together with their respective previously mentioned mantras, in the five locations beginning with the *mūlādhāra* and ending with the forehead.
By the mere placement of the five arrows, one becomes the deluder and the satisfier of all women.

The sixth yantra is as follows: having written the *kāmabīja* in the large pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the same aforementioned hexagon, and having written the *māyābīja* within that, and within that again the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth; then, in the very pericarp, on the outer side of those two seed-syllables, having enclosed those two seed-syllables within [the next layer], [one proceeds] from the northeast (*īśāna*) to the southeast (*āgneya*).

Having formed another hexagon by joining the western corner with the lower part of the west [triangle] as its tail, and the southwest, northwest, eastern corner, and lower part of the east [triangles] as the tails of the two *vāgbhava* syllables; then, having written the fourth *kāma-bīja*, "plūm," in a circular sequence within the six corners of this [hexagon], using the second seed-syllable in the form of the *kāma-bīja*.

Then, having filled the hexagon by means of six repetitions with the *bindu* and *visarga* joined respectively to the upper and lower regions, one should surround the two previously mentioned paths with the fifth *kāma-bīja* in the form "strīm," but not with the aforementioned letters. This is the seventh yantra, as before, from the two paths already described.
Furthermore, having drawn two outer circles and, with the assistance of the previously drawn circle, having fashioned two pathways (vīthī),

one should fill both of them with the sixty-four aforementioned distorted letters (vikṛtākṣara) and perform the remainder exactly as in the sixth yantra. As for the eighth yantra, it is as previously described.

Having performed all the duties according to the seventh method, one should draw a single circle on the outside of everything; then, with the assistance of the previous circle, another path (vīthī) should be produced by means of the pure *mātṛkā*.
"One should envelop" means that by means of all these yantras individually, through methods such as wearing them and worshipping them,

the accomplishment of all goals occurs. One should meditate on the person to be subjugated as being situated within any one of these yantras and pervaded by the threefold light proceeding from one's own *mūlādhāra*, heart, and head.

One application is as follows: for the practitioner who recites the previously mentioned one hundred and twenty-eight modified syllables (*vikṛtākṣara*) along with the five modified syllables, that person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) shall remain under his control for as long as he lives.

Visualizing one's own goal as being situated within the center of the aforementioned eight-spoked yantra— reddish like a hibiscus flower, pervaded by the rays of the luster of the mantra-syllables, and also pervaded by its own radiance— one who recites all the unaltered syllables along with the five seed-mantras of desire brings even kings under their control.

The second [alternative] is that all the wealth of women and the like would protect one's life-breaths. Having placed the *kalaśa* in the eighth *yantra*, one should perform there—as before—all the rites beginning with the visualization of the *Sarvamaṅgalā-cakra* and ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*).
Then, having again performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites for the Goddess in that *kalaśa*, and having worshipped the presiding Goddess therein, [one should take] that water.
Having consecrated [the water] with the present vidyā a thousand times or more, one should sprinkle it upon the person to whom a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) has been given;
he shall become free from misfortune, disease, and poverty—this is the third [method].

Having written one of the aforementioned eight yantras using any of the substances—red sandalwood, vermilion, red ochre, or realgar—on any of the following surfaces: the ground, a wooden board, or a stone; and having written that all the seed-syllables situated in the center are to be encircled by the present mantra, thus it is for the purpose of writing.

Having followed the specific [instructions], once the yantra is perfected, one should worship it preceded by the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the ritual installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).
For the practitioner who recites [the mantra] before it, there is the destruction of sins accumulated in previous births, and in this life, [one becomes] irreproachable.

The fourth [method] is that there shall be an increase in happiness preceded by the attainment of prosperity desired by all people. For one whose objective is subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), the name of that person should be written between the central seed-syllables. The incense should consist of saffron, the flowers should be red, and the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of plantain fruit, milk, sugar, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and jaggery.

The duration should be established by considering whether the task is very heavy, heavy, or light, for a period of up to twenty-five days, fifteen days, or seven days. In the sixth yantra, there is a hexagon;
the *māyābīja* written in the pericarp and the two seeds consisting of the *kāmabīja*, which are to be visualized as being both internal and external.
Having clothed the person to be subdued with the aforementioned Nityā-vidyā and having fashioned the remainder as before, one should visualize the target situated within this yantra,
performing the acts of going and coming through the path of the *suṣumṇā* from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*; by this, the target becomes subjugated— this is the fifth [method].

The ritual application (*prayoga*). Thus concludes the ritual application of the *kāmayantra*. Now follows the ritual application of the *kāmeśvarīyantra*. In this vidyā, there are nineteen syllables in total; therein, twelve syllables—consisting of the twelve vowels, the letters *sa*, *ka*, *la*, *ha*, *na*, *ta*, *pa*, *ma*, *da*, and *va*—are not repeated.
The seven syllables— *pa*, *re*, *ka*, *ka*, *la*, *ta*, *ta*, *ma*, *ka*, *da*, *da*, and *ra*— are repeated. Therein,
when each of the twelve non-repeated syllables is joined with the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and so forth, the first group of sixteen is *sa*, *ptā*, *si*, *sī*, and so on.
The second group of sixteen begins with *ka kā ki kī* and so forth; the third group of sixteen begins with *la lā li lī* and so forth;
the fourth group of sixteen begins with *ha hā hi hī* and so forth; the fifth group of sixteen begins with *anayārī*.

Sixteen becomes twelve in number; thus, all the phonemes (varṇas) associated with the mantra amount to one hundred and ninety-two (192). By means of those phonemes, thirty-two yantras are accomplished. The method for this is as follows: first, a hexagon, and outside of that, with an intervening space.

Having drawn two circles, one should write the *māyā-bīja* (the syllable *hīṃ*) in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and within that, the names of the practitioner and the person to be acted upon (*sādhya-sādhaka*). Then, having written one letter at a time in each of the six corners— beginning with the first letters associated with the modified vowels in the sequence *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū*— one should fill the path (*vīthī*) with the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*).

One should fill this first yantra; then, if the subsequent group of six syllables is written in the six corners in place of the previous syllables and the remainder is done as before, that is the second. Or, if the group of six syllables—o, au, aṃ, aḥ, sa, sā—is written in place of the aforementioned syllables, that is the third.

By writing the six-syllable mantra in this successive manner, all the modified syllables become complete, and thirty-two yantras are perfected. Among them, from the first yantra comes the acquisition of gold;
from the second, the attainment of ornaments; from the third, the acquisition of a maiden; and from the fourth yantra, [the mastery] of kings.
From the second house comes success in enmity, eradication, and so forth; from the fifth, the acquisition of mounts such as horses; from the sixth, the subjugation of women;
from the seventh, the acquisition of a house; from the eighth, the acquisition of cows; from the ninth, the subjugation of kings;
and from the tenth house, the mastery over elephants and horses.
From the eleventh [lagna], there is victory in battles; from the twelfth, in disputes concerning debts, land, and so forth,
whether they have been initiated without a wager or with one— thus, in both types of gambling, there is the attainment of wealth in the form of victory.

By the thirteenth machine, there is the destruction of enemies; by the fourteenth machine, there is the destruction of the hosts of elephants, horses, donkeys, camels, men, cows, deer, birds, serpents, rams, buffaloes, cattle, dwellings, places, and groups of spirits numbering twelve; and by the fifteenth [machine], rain.

By means of this yantra, there occurs the immobilization of the anger, enemies, efforts toward slaughter, speech, and the discharge of urine and feces belonging to one's foes. Furthermore, for whatever animals— such as tigers, serpents, elephants, buffaloes, and so forth— one intends to immobilize, [one should use] the oil extracted from the skin of a creature of that same species, [consecrated] with the six-syllable mantra consisting of the forms *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*.

Having drawn the interconnected six-cornered yantra and placed it on its respective path—whether within a mandala, at a distance of one *mātrā*, or extending for several days—it shall effect the desired immobilization (*stambhana*) of things such as tigers; this is the fifteenth application of the yantra. With the sixteenth yantra, [the sequence is]: *ari-rair-orairaḥ*.

By means of the hexagon joined with six syllables, there is the cessation of afflictions caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and the like. By means of the seventeenth yantra, when it is placed upon the ground, protection is afforded to all living beings situated therein. Having written the eighteenth and nineteenth yantras on two wooden boards made of *palāśa* or similar wood, [one should place them] upon the ground.

By burying [the image], there is the destruction of crops situated in that ground; by burying it in the place of a tree, there is the destruction of those trees. With the aim of destroying that region, by burying it there, the destruction of that region shall occur due to a conflict between two kings.

By means of the twentieth yantra, when buried at the site of a treaty between two kings, mutual hostility among rulers will arise after a very short time. By means of the twenty-first yantra, there will be an alliance with enemies; by the twenty-second—
By the twenty-third [mantra], there is disease for cows; by the twenty-fourth, for elephants; by the twenty-fifth, for horses;

by the twenty-sixth, for kings; and by the twenty-seventh, for royal ministers. Through the worship of the twenty-seventh yantra, there is the destruction of the six diseases beginning with fainting (dairya).
By means of the twenty-eighth yantra, when it is worn on one's own body, or dug into one's own dwelling place, or planted like a tree near oneself, or deposited in ponds, wells, tanks, and the like,
there is the destruction of the obstacles created by the Vāśaras. By means of the twenty-ninth yantra:
Even a mute becomes eloquent. By the thirtieth yantra, there is the paralysis of the speech of enemies;

by the thirty-first yantra, the movement of elephants and horses [is controlled]; by the thirty-second yantra, ships traveling upon the ocean shall reach the opposite shore after being protected from calamities such as winds. In small [quantities]...

However, there is no need for the doubt as to how a greater arising of fruit could possibly occur through hardship alone, because gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth possess inconceivable power; this is the summary. Thus end the ritual applications of Kāmeśvarī Nityā. Now, Bhagamālinī Nityā is introduced. The procedure for initiation is essentially as already described.

The subject matter to be explained first consists of the ritual procedures beginning with the daily worship and ending with the concluding rites. Having sat upon the seat by means of the fourfold seats and the Vidyās, having sipped water for purification with the Vidyā, having prostrated before the Guru and received his permission, one should perform the worship, preceded by the drawing of the mandala, and worship the eternal Bhagamālinī.
The procedure for that is as follows: having first made a square on a level, smooth surface the size of a hand,
one should then make another square inside it with an interval of four finger-breadths between them, and then, at its western part—

Having fashioned a single door provided with two side-panels, one should draw a circle that touches the inner lines within it; then, having constructed another circle with an interval of two finger-breadths between them,
one should fashion a five-petalled lotus in the pathway between those two circles, and [proceed] within its pericarp.

Having made one circle with an interval of one finger-breadth and another [concentric] circle, one should draw a triangle facing oneself within the space between those two circles— that is, in the path between the two circles— such that its tip touches the circle of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Then, each of these three lines forming the mouth of this triangle should be divided into twenty-four parts.

Having marked twenty-three points at the terminal ends of those divisions, and having excluded a measurement equal to one part on both sides within [the circle], one should form another triangle facing oneself.
Then, having divided each of those three lines into twenty-two parts, and having excluded a measurement equal to one part on both sides...
One should make twenty-one marks. Then,
having drawn the first horizontal line from the first mark of the outer triangle to the tip of the line of the inner triangle,
one should again start from that same first outer mark.

Having laid down the second [line] from the inner first mark to the end of the [second] mark, then the third from the inner first mark to the outer second mark, and so on in sequence from the outer mark back to the inner mark—
having thus laid down forty-two lines ending at the twenty-first lower mark; then...
From the twenty-first mark on the base, extending outward to the twenty-second mark, one [line] goes to the tip of the inner triangle, and another [line] from that same point extends forward. (p.

Having drawn another line from the end of the corner-point to the very edge of the front [corner], or from the front to the end of the outermost mark, and having thus produced forty-five lines, one should form forty-four triangles.
When such a procedure is performed on both sides, there will be a total of one hundred and thirty-two [triangles].

The outer and inner tips form triangles; including each individual triangle situated at the three corners, there result one hundred and thirty-five triangles in total. Then, having constructed another circle that touches and does not touch the lines of the inner triangles, [one proceeds] within that as well.
Having drawn another circle within the space between the previously drawn circle and the fifth circle of Vyāsa,

one should mark ten points at equal intervals on the outer circle. Likewise, having marked ten points in the same manner on the inner circle, such that horizontal lines are formed by the meeting of the outer and inner points, [one proceeds].

From the outer mark to the inner mark, or from the inner mark to the outer mark, one should form twenty triangles in the manner of a cow’s urine (gomūtraka) by means of twenty horizontal lines. Having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with either the *vāgbhava* syllable or the sixteen-syllable mantra according to the present daily rite, and having offered the preliminary oblation (*vali*) for worship upon one's own head;

Having worshipped the nine Nāthas and one's own Guru in sequence with their respective mantras, and having recited the *Nātha-stotra* and received their permission, one should begin the worship after meditating upon one’s own Self as one's own Nātha in its manifest, eternal form, non-different from one's chosen deity (*svanātha*). [One should then perform it] according to the place, time, and other factors regulated by the specific rules for each year.
Having worshipped all the deities of the thirty-eight sacred seats (pīṭhas), ending with the entire circle of the secret and manifest Siddhayoginīs,
[one should place] the arghya vessel together with its base between the yantra and one's own self.

Having placed [the vessel] filled with water mixed with the five substances beginning with *gorocanā*, and having meditated upon the triad of supports and so forth as being of the nature of fire, sun, and moon—manifesting as radiant light—by means of the three seed-syllables of *Kulasundarī*; and having meditated upon the five substances beginning with *gorocanā* as consisting of the five elements beginning with earth; [one should contemplate] that water.
Having contemplated the identity of the present *nityācakra* with the [deity], and having meditated upon the water as non-different from the present *nityā*,

one should consecrate it ten times with the mantra of the present *nityā* and worship it. Then, having worshipped the six limbs and the deities of those limbs there with the six-limbed mantras of that same vidyā which are to be described hereafter, one should [sprinkle] oneself with that water.

Having sprinkled with water the water for the feet (pādya), the guest-offering (arghya), the sipping-water (ācamana), and the bathing-water (snānīya)— each placed in separate vessels and arranged one after another to the north of the primary vessel— and having also sprinkled the perfumes, flowers, and other offerings placed on one's right side.

Again, having restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable of the *vidyā-ghaṭaka*, and taking in his hand water mixed with sesame seeds, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), he should recite [the details] ending with the deity, time, lineage, zodiacal sign, name, and desire,
and [perform the rite] according to the rule and as far as his intellect permits, for the sake of pleasing the eternal goddess Śrī Bhagamālinī.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with the words, "I shall perform the worship of the eternal goddess Śrī Bhagamālinī," one should then perform the placement of the *mātṛkās* and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).

Following that, having performed the placement of each respective letter of the *mātṛkā* in its corresponding location using the constituent letters of the present vidyā preceded by the *vāgbhava* syllable, one recites: *aiṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.

"Bhaga-bhug-īśirase svāhā! Bhaginī-śikhāyai vaṣaṭ! Bhagodarika-vacāya huṃ! Bhagāvaha-netrāya vauṣaṭ! Bhagamāle-astrāya phaṭ!"—with these mantras, [one should assign them] to one's own thumbs and other fingers. (p. 87a)

And having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart and other parts [of the body]: Aiṃ bhagabhuge | bhagini | bhagodari | bhagamāle | bhagāvahe | bhagaguhye | bhagayoni | bhaganipātī | sarvabhagavaśaṃkari | bhagarūpe | nityaklinne | bhagasvarūpe | sarvāṇi bhagāni mehyānaya | varade rete surete | bhagaklinne | klinnadrave |
Moisten! Melt! O Amoghe! O Bhagavicce! Agitate! Shake all sentient beings, O Bhageśvarī!

Aiṃ blūṃ aṃblūṃ bheṃblūṃ heṃ blūṃ heṃ klinne! Bring all female organs (bhagas) under my control! Strīṃ hre hrīṃ. Thus, with this complete root mantra consisting of one hundred and thirty-five syllables, [one should recite] three times.

Having performed the Vyāpakanyāsa, and having first displayed the Trikhaṇḍā mudrā, one should visualize that the splendor of the present Vidyā— manifested within the flowers held in the añjali from the Mūlādhāra up to the Brahmarandhra— transfers through the path of the nostrils. Then, [one offers] that flower-añjali...

Having visualized [the deity] transferred into the center of the drop (bindu) within the pericarp during the rite of projection (*prakṣepaṇa*), one should invoke her as before with the mantra "O Bhagamālinī, come here into this wheel" at the end of all the vidyās. One should then contemplate her rays of light radiating here and there into the locations to be described.

Having visualized [the seed-syllables] as having transformed into the forms of the presiding deities of those respective obstructions and their weapon-deities, one should meditate upon that light as it has transformed according to the manner described in the upcoming meditation. The method of meditation is as follows:
[one should meditate on her] who is ruddy, resembling the dawn, beautiful with a smiling face, three-eyed, and endowed with six arms.
Seated upon a lotus, she holds in her left arms a white lotus, a noose, a city, and a sugarcane bow;
and in her right hands, she bears a lotus, a goad, and arrows tipped with lotuses.

Likewise, she is surrounded on all sides by the Vidyās, by the praised hosts of Śaktis, by others arising from the syllables, and by those whose nature is the intoxication of the madness of Smara. Then, at the end of the Vidyā: "O Bhagamālinī Nityā, be established here in this Cakra.
At the end of the complete Vidyā: "O Bhagamālinī Nityā, be firmly bound here in this Cakra."
At the conclusion of the complete mantra: "O Bhagamālinī Nityā, be veiled here in this wheel! O Bhagamālinī Nityā, be made present here in this wheel!
Having thus prayed while displaying the respective mudrās, [one performs] the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) mantra.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs, one should establish the vital breaths by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra in the form "The vital breaths of this [deity] Bhagamālinī Nityā are here in this wheel," and so forth. One should then perform worship with the twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*). The mantras for that are as follows: at the end of the solitary *vāgbhava* seed-syllable, [one adds] "to Bhagamālinī Nityā."

Saying "I offer the water for the feet (pādya)," one should set aside the water for the general arghya; then, with the Vāgbhava-bīja alone—which has been consecrated by the full vidyā at its locus—one should present it at the two feet. In the same manner, having offered each respective article of worship placed in the position of the word "pādya," one should do so with the mantra stated in the section on the arghya and other words.

Having offered the twelve services ending with betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*), one should present them in their appropriate places. Then follows the thirteenth service; its procedure is as follows: behind the Goddess, in the area near the back of the Goddess and so forth, [one offers] *hrīṃ śrīṃ* to the sandals of the power of manifestation-bliss (*prakāśānandaśakti*).

Having worshipped the nine Nāthas— known as Prakāśa, Vimarśa, Ānanda, Śrījñāna, Śrīsatya, Pūrṇasvabhāva, Pratibha, Subhaga, and [the ninth]— with their respective mantras beginning with "I worship" (pūjayāmi), etc.
On the right side of the door: "Aiṃ, I worship the sandals of Rāgaśakti. On the left side of the door:
"Aiṃ, I worship the sandals of Dveṣaśakti. Having thus worshipped that pair, [one worships] the complete Vidyā.

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with the mantra: "I worship the sandals of the Nityā Bhagamālinī, who consists of one hundred and thirty-five syllables," he should offer her worship with: "Aiṃ! O deities of the first enclosure of the Nityā Bhagamālinī, accept this worship. Then, beginning from the eastern petal among the five petals, [he recites]: "Aiṃ Aiṃ..."

*aiṃ pāśāya namaḥ*, *aiṃ kahlārāya namaḥ*, *aiṃ padmāya namaḥ*, *aiṃ aṅkuśāya namaḥ*,

Having thus worshipped the six weapons, and at the end of the complete vidyā, having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra: "I worship the pādukā of the eternal Bhagamālinī," [one recites]: *Aiṃ*, these are the eternal Bhagamālinīs.
Having offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) with the words, "May the deities of the fourth enclosure accept the worship," and having presented that worship,

one should perform the remaining three services consisting of the recitation of hymns, libations (tarpaṇa), and prostrations. Then, having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should offer oblations into the fire— previously consecrated as before— with clarified butter and other substances in a quantity equal to one-tenth of that recitation.

Having performed the *karāṅganyāsa* (hand and limb assignment) in its encapsulated form (*sampuṭita*), one should contemplate the radiant energy (*tejas*) within the fire; having united that with the *bindu* which is the form of the Goddess’s wheel from the fire, and having worshipped the Goddess residing in the wheel with the complete root mantra and the *vāgbhava* mantra as before using the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should present the *āvali* offering with the Kurukullā mantra.
Having performed the *nīrājana* with wicks containing camphor and other substances, and having asked for forgiveness, one should dissolve [the deity] into oneself as before;

at the conclusion of the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), the Guru should recite the hymn to the Goddess consisting of twelve verses. For the practitioner who performs the daily rites in this manner, men, women, and even kings come under his power without further effort. Of this...

In the Kali age, the recitation (*japa*) of a mantra consists of four hundred thousand repetitions; for each of these, one hundred and ten oblations (*homa*) and libations (*tarpaṇa*) constitute the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*). Having thus mastered the knowledge [of the mantra] by the command of the Guru, one should perform rites for desired ends (*kāmyakarman*). Among those, the oblation for desired ends is as follows: by means of *puṇḍarīka* lotuses smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), Brahmins become submissive through the performance of the *homa*.

Through oblations of *āragvadha* flowers smeared with the three sweets, Kṣatriyas are brought under control. Through oblations of *karavīra* flowers smeared with the three sweets, Vaiśyas are brought under control. Through oblations of blue lotuses smeared with the three sweets, Śūdras are brought under control.
Through oblations of *japā* flowers smeared with the three sweets, women are brought under control.
Through oblations of bilva fruits smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), there is the attainment of Mahālakṣmī;
through oblations of lotuses smeared with the three sweets, there is the attainment of land; and through oblations of kairava flowers smeared with the three sweets, [the same result follows].

Through an oblation of *śaṅkhapuṣpa* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one obtains vehicles; through an oblation of *campaka* flowers smeared with the three sweets, one obtains great fame; through an oblation of red *saugandhika* flowers smeared with the three sweets, one obtains good fortune; and through an oblation of red *saugandhika* flowers smeared with the three sweets, there is especially the accomplishment of all desired objects not otherwise mentioned.

Likewise, by offering red lotuses soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhu*), or by the sequential offering of *tagara*, *punnāga*, *madhuka*, *palāśa*, *kiṃśuka*, and *pāṭala* flowers soaked in the three sweets,
one obtains clothing, ornaments, a bride, gold bands, garments, and cattle. [The three sweets are] honey, clarified butter, and milk.

One should perform the primary fire-offering (*pradhānahoma*) with honey, sugar, and ghee, or with honey, curd, and milk—these being the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*)—offered in single rounds for all the Lords and their surrounding deities; this may be performed one thousand or one hundred times.
As for the duration, it may last until the end of the mandala, half of that, seven days, or until the food is exhausted at the conclusion of the offering.
The recitation of the *ekakaraṇa-vidyā* is performed according to the number of oblations; the remainder is as in the case of the oblation of the principal *vidyā*.

Now, the applications of these eternal yantras: here, on any one of the following materials— gold, silver, copper, cloth, or birch bark— and using the five substances combined together known as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron, all the yantras described in this section should be prepared on all [of these materials].

One should draw the *kāmanā* (the desired object) well. Having drawn it, should it be worn on the head—distinguishing between male and female—or on the right or left arm, or perhaps on the neck, or on the waist, or on the forearm?
Or else, having placed it in some pure location, one should perform worship of it constantly; by that, the fruit of the *yantra* which is about to be described [shall be attained].
It is accomplished.
The nature of the yantra is as follows: first, a downward-pointing triangle; outside of that, a hexagon;
and further outside, two paths separated by an interval, each consisting of three circles. Therein, in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), is the seed-syllable of Māyā (*māyāvīja*).

Having written the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable within that [triangle], and within that [seed-syllable] having inscribed the words for the goal (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the ritual action (*karmakriyā*);
then, having inscribed the letters *bha*, *ga*, and *bhu* in the three corners starting from the front in a counter-clockwise direction;
and likewise in the six corners starting from the front in a counter-clockwise order, [the syllables] *ge*, *bhagini*, and *bhagorūpāt* from the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
Having extracted the six syllables from the fifth to the tenth [cells],

one should surround the first row with the remaining syllables, numbering one hundred and twenty-five, which are related to the mantra; then, one should encircle the outer row with the letters of the Mātṛkā along with the *bindu*— this is the first yantra.
Having inserted the ten syllables beginning with *vāgbhava*— namely "yadi daribhagāvahe bhagamāle"— into the ten places occupied by the syllables from *go* onwards,
one should fill the first enclosure (*vīthī*) with the remaining one hundred and twenty-five syllables from the self-written *daśākṣara*.

Having filled [the first row] as before with the *mātṛkā* letters, the second row is filled; then, that is the second yantra. Now, if instead of the ten syllables mentioned previously, the *parāpara* syllables are introduced and the remaining procedure is followed exactly as before, then the fourth, fifth, and subsequent yantras arise. Thus, by means of thirteen yantras, there are one hundred and thirty.

The mantra-syllables are written. With the five remaining syllables of five colors, one should fill the pericarp of the fourteen-spoked yantra, the three corners [of the triangle], the first corner in the form of the front corner of the hexagon,
and the remaining five corners with *jaṃḥ*, *jhaṃḥ*, *ṭhaṃḥ*, *vaṃḥ*, and *saṃḥ*.
One should fill the outer path (vīthī) with the syllables ja, jha, ta, and sa, one by one in succession, using forms that are oceans of nectar.

One should encircle [the diagram] with the sixty immortal syllables (*amṛtavarṇa*), which are produced by the combination of the twelve vowels—excluding the neuter ones—and the unmodified consonants, all accompanied by the *bindu*. Furthermore, the outermost path should be encircled, as before, with the letters of the *mātṛkā* accompanied by the *bindu*.
When each of these very immortal syllables is joined with the sixteen vowels, there are eighty variations.

In that regard, by the conjunction of the *bindu* with each individual [letter] while omitting the *bindu*, or by the conjunction of the *visarga*, there are two sets of eighty—that is, one hundred and sixty varieties.

The application (*viniyoga*) of these, however, will occur in other diagrams (*yantra*). [They are used] for subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), immobilization (*stambhana*), health (*ārogya*), victory (*vijaya*), the acquisition of fortune (*lakṣmīlābha*), the protection of elephants, the protection of horses, the protection of cattle, and the protection of sheep and buffaloes.

For kings who have become excessively bitter toward men, the protection of women is for the protection of the kings; thus is the sequential application of these fourteen yantras. Now, the thirty-three yantras:
therein, the one hundred and sixty varieties of the *amṛtārṇa* (the ocean of nectar), which are the phonemes of the present *Nityā-vidyā*, were previously extracted.

One hundred and thirty-five letters have been finalized; their application should be made within the diagrams (yantras) to be described hereafter. To that end, first draw a triangle, then outside that an eight-petalled lotus, and further outside that a single circle.
By means of that circle, using the tips of the petals as an aid, one should create a path (vīthī). Within the pericarp (karṇikā) of the triangle...
In the center of that is the seed-syllable *māyā* (hīṃ), as before, with the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth.
Starting from the tip of each of the three corners of the triangle...
Having written the three syllables *jaṃ jaṃ jaṃ* in clockwise order,
one should then write the three syllables *jīṃ juṃ jūṃ* starting from the innermost interval among those three intermediate spaces; then,
beginning from the foremost petal and proceeding clockwise, one writes *jṛṃ jṝṃ jḷṃ jṛṃ jeṃ jraiṃ joṃ jauṃ*.

Having written the eight syllables, one should fill the pathways with the *mātṛkā* letters. Thus is established the first yantra. However, if one writes the three syllables *jaṃ jaḥ jhaṃ* in the three corners of the triangle, and having written the triad of syllables *jhāṃ jhiṃ jhīṃ* in the space between them, one writes *jhuṃ jhūṃ* clockwise on the eight petals starting from the front.

Having written the eight syllables *jhṛṃ jhṛṃ jḷṃ jhe jha i miti*, the completion of the verse should be performed with the *mātṛkā* letters; that is the second yantra. According to this method, [the process continues] with fourteen amṛta-syllables and fourteen modified syllables written in succession, each subsequent one following the previous.

By means of fourteen sets of fourteen modified syllables, thirty-two yantras are accomplished. There are four hundred and forty-eight unassigned phonemes, of which eight remain; by writing these, one should fill the triangle up to the end of the two petals within its interior, and the remainder—

One should fill the six petals with the five syllables of *amṛta* and the seed-syllables of *māyā*; thus one should extract the thirty-third yantra. It [removes] general fever, cold-fever, quartan fever, boils, smallpox, eye diseases, abdominal diseases, consumption, affliction by *rākṣasas*, and affliction by *gandharvas*.
Affliction by *piśācas*, affliction by serpents, affliction by infant-seizing spirits (*bālagraha*), misfortune, barrenness, affliction by fate,
inability in debate, insanity, attachment to royal wrath,
fear of thieves, fear of *kākinīs*, fear of *sākinīs*, fear of *hākinīs*, fear of *lākinīs*, fear of *kākinīs*, and fear of *rākinīs*.
Affliction by *brahmarākṣasa* (p.
92a), urinary disorders (*prameha*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), vomiting, and afflictions consisting of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*).

Furthermore, these yantras should be applied in sequence for the desire to pacify the thirty [types of] karma. Now, one optional yantra for the fifteen Nityās is described: twenty lines extending east-west and twenty lines extending north-south, intersecting one another with equal intervals.
Having constructed three hundred and sixty-one square-shaped compartments,

one should set aside six compartments on each side; then, within the forty-nine central compartments situated in the middle row, by erasing the six lines that divide the compartments in each row, they are reduced to single units, and within those [units], along with the intervening spaces...

Having fashioned a fourteen-petalled lotus, one should construct an upward-facing triangle by means of four squares—consisting of three squares from the sixth row and one square from the fifth row—located in the four directions starting from the east. Thus, having employed sixty-five squares in total, [the remaining squares are used as follows: in the remaining [squares].

Having written the syllables of the fifteen Nityā-mantras beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā, starting from the northeast (īśāna) compartment and proceeding around the outer path consisting of sixty-two compartments; then, starting again from the northeast, one proceeds according to the mantra.
Having filled the row consisting of sixty-four squares starting from the reached square and proceeding all around;
then again, having filled the path consisting of fifty-six squares starting from the previously commenced square and proceeding all around; then again, from the commenced square...
Having filled the path consisting of forty-eight squares, starting from the square reached by the movement of the mantra,
one proceeds again from the initial square, starting from the square reached by the movement of the practitioner.

Having filled the remaining squares by assigning them to the triangles of every tenth square in each of the four directions within a surrounding path of forty squares, one should then proceed again from the starting square,
beginning with the square situated below the one reached by the movement of the minister, and continue around the thirty-two-square path.

By assigning three triangles to each of the three directions, one should write the letters of the Vidyā in the remaining twenty-five squares; thus, the two hundred and ninety-six letters of the Vidyā are written. Then, having drawn a triangle facing oneself within the pericarp of the fourteen-petaled lotus, therein—

Having written the *māyā*-seed syllable (*hrīṃ*), one should worship Bhagamālinī. Furthermore, having written the *māyā*-seed syllable enclosed within a triangle on each of the fourteen petals, one should worship the fourteen Nityās in sequence there, beginning with Nityaklinnā and ending with Kāmeśvarī-Nityā. However, in the four triangles, having written the *māyā*-seed syllable on each one, [one should worship].

Within that [mandala], one should inscribe the rites of the goal and the means of attainment. Here, there is no fixed rule that worship must be performed for Bhagamālinī alone; rather, having worshipped whichever Nityā one desires in the center, one should worship the other Nityās from the west, proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction in the order of the quarters starting with Vāyu (the northwest).
Outside the previously mentioned yantra, one should construct a *bhūpura* (earth-fortress) with two gates in each of the four directions using two parallel lines;
therein, following the sequence from east to west, one should place Brāhmī and Māheśvarī as a pair, and Kaumārī and Vaiṣṇavī as a pair, while Vārāhī is placed in the north.

Having worshipped the pair Māhendrī and Cāmuṇḍā-Mahālakṣmī at each door on the east and south, [one should worship] the syllable *va* in the northwestern corner, *ī* in the northeastern corner, *ā* in the southeastern corner, and [the syllable *na*] in the southwestern corner.

Having worshipped the sound with the aforementioned mantras, and then having performed worship there of the written syllables of the mantra with such mantras as "I worship the sandals of Aiṃ Rūpiṇī Varṇaśakti," [one worships] the Nityā intended as primary in each of the Māyās containing the directions, starting from the east among the four cardinal directions.

Having worshipped [the central deity] fourfold, one should worship the other Nityās on the fourteen petals. Some say that one should again worship the principal deity in the center. According to the stated method, having worshipped the one intended as the principal with the central Śakti, one should worship the other Nityās starting from the west and ending at the northwest on the petals.
The fundamental established meaning is that one should worship the twelve deities, beginning with Brāhmī, within the square [mandala]. Furthermore,

this worship of the fifteen Nityās— whether concise or extensive— should be preceded by offerings of food (naivedya) such as milk-rice, cakes, plantains, and jackfruit, as well as flowers such as *campaka*, *aśoka*, and *mallikā*, performed with the square as the locus of action.

It was performed with devotion for a period of one night, three nights, five nights, seven nights, a fortnight, a month consisting of thirty-six days beginning from the dark fortnight and ending on the full moon,
or a month beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight and ending on the new moon, or a year such as Caitra through Phālguna,
or any other time comprising a year of five hundred and seventy-six solar days (sāvana).

It brings about an absence of adversity regarding terrestrial, celestial, and atmospheric portents; it prevents the occurrence of calamities such as the displacement of deities or the breaking of the sky;
and it acts to pacify poverty while bringing to an end the afflictions of famine and enemies.

As for the construction of the wheel (*cakra*), it should be made upon pedestals (*pīṭha*) using *palāśa* wood and so forth, or on a level ground-circle using the previously mentioned red sandalwood and other materials. Although in this root-text the nature of the "accomplished substance" (*siddhadravya*) for the worship to be performed by *śūdras* blinded by passion is not explicitly stated, its essential form is as follows:

Although the method for its emanation was taught and a combination with the aforementioned ritual materials (*pūjā-dravya*) was mentioned, it has not been shown here because it does not provide benefit to Vedic Brahmins and others. Now follows the mantra for attracting women; it measures twenty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Having fashioned a triangle facing oneself on a level and smooth surface with three equal lines, one should mark thirteen points:
two at each end of the northern and southern lines, and eleven points along both sides of those lines at intervals of two finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
using marks placed at the two ends of the lines as reference points.
Without counting the mark at the end of the line, having made thirteen marks starting from the first mark to the north of the north-south line, including the two marks placed at the ends of the line—
without counting the mark at the end of the line— the first mark to the north of the north-south line...
Having joined the two marks— namely, the first mark situated near Īśāna on the eastward line with the first mark situated near Nirṛti on the southward line—
one should likewise join the second [mark] with the second pair, and the third with the third pair, until the end.
One should join the eleventh mark on the horizontal line with the two eleventh marks located on the two side lines.

Then, one should join the marks on the two side lines in the following manner: the first with the first, the second with the second, and so forth. By this, one hundred and forty-four triangles are produced. Therein, [the mark at] its own apex...

Starting from the triangle and proceeding clockwise in the order of entry, one should write the one hundred and thirty-five syllables of the present vidyā all around; this is calculated starting from the front portion.
From the fourth line extending south to north, below it are five triangles; below those, three triangles;

and below those, one triangle. Having thus written the mantras of the nine lords associated with their respective groups within the remaining nine triangles combined, [one should place] each [mantra] in every single square of the wheel.

One should write the name of the practitioner as the agent (*sādhaka-karman*) and the name of the target (*sādhya*) in the form "I am drawing Devadatta before Yajñadatta," and so forth. Having thus accomplished the wheel and meditated upon the naked Goddess, at the time of midnight, one should [worship] with pomegranate, bandhūka, and other fragrant flowers.

One should worship [the deity]. And while performing the ritual until its conclusion, the practitioner should meditate upon the woman to be won over as being consumed by the fire of passion, her body and mind aflame, devoid of discernment, and free from pride, shame, and fear; her body trembling and her hands joined in *añjali* upon her head—as if she were a mere shadow following the practitioner.
One should draw her into one's own following by name, but not merely as something dependent upon oneself, like a maidservant or even a wife;
this is the summary. Thus end the applications of the goddess Bhramamālinī Nityā. Now, the goddess Nityaklinnā Nityā is introduced.

Since the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*) for this [practice] has already been largely explained, the ritual components beginning with the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) and ending with the practical application (*prayoga*) are now described.

First, the practitioner, having occupied either a *svastika* or *padma* seat upon a seat made of woolen cloth (*kambala*) or similar material that has been worshipped with the fourfold knowledge of the seat (*āsana-vidyā*), [proceeds].
Having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the present *Nityā-vidyā*,
and having offered the oblation (*bali*) with the sixteen-syllable mantra, one should worship the nine *Āpīnāthas* upon one's own head with their respective mantras.

Having recited the *Nāthastotra* and received his permission, one should begin the worship. Therein, first, one should draw the wheel of worship (*pūjācakra*). That is to say: having first fashioned a triangle with a central dot, its apex facing oneself; and having drawn a circle outside that [triangle] so as to be neither touching nor separated from the three sides of the triangle.

Then, having drawn another circle with a four-finger interval outside that, one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus within the resulting path (*vīthī*). Furthermore, outside of that, one should construct two squares in the eastern and western directions, provided with door-frames (*dvāraśākhā*). Then, having meditated upon one's own Lord—the present *Nityā*—as one's own self non-different from the Lord (*nātha*).

Having worshipped all the deities of the thirty-eight *pīṭhas*, ending with the circle of the secret and manifest *siddha-yoginīs* whose locations, times, and so forth are determined by the distinctions of their respective years; and having extracted the *nityapūjā-yantra* from between oneself and the vessel, [one should apply] *gorocanā*...

Having placed the ordinary *arghya* vessel filled with water scented with camphor, saffron, agallochum, and musk; one should then sequentially contemplate the waters in its supporting vessel as consisting of fire, sun, and moon by means of the three *kulasaundarī* seed-syllables, and as consisting of the five elements beginning with earth, such as yellow orpiment and so forth. Then, that water...
Having contemplated the identity between the present worship and the wheel [of deities], and having contemplated non-difference from the present *Nityā* within that water;

having consecrated it ten times with the present *vidyā* and worshipped it— or else, having worshipped the six limb-deities (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*) with the six limb-mantras of that *vidyā* which will be described hereafter— with that water and the present *vidyā*.

Having consecrated oneself and the materials for worship—consisting of water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), clothing, ornaments, perfumes, incense, flowers, and so forth.

Again, having restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) through the *vidyā*, and taking water, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth with his hand, he should announce the place, time, lineage, and name, and form the resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the goddess Śrī Nityaklinnānityā, I shall perform the worship of the goddess Nityaklinnānityā according to the prescribed rite and as far as my intellect permits. Then, [he should perform] the *mātṛkā* in the manner previously described.

Having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should perform the placement of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*) beginning with *a*, each accompanied by the present mantra, individually upon the forehead and other respective locations. Then follows the placement of the present mantra (*prastutavidyānyāsa*), which is as follows: *hrīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *nitya* to the head, *svāhā*; *klinne* to the tuft (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *mada* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras of the deities of the six limbs—*dve netrāya traya-va-uṣaṭ svāhā* for the eyes and *astrāya phaṭ* for the weapon—upon one’s own thumbs and other fingers, as well as upon the heart and other parts of the body: *hrīṃ* at the heart;
*ni* at the right ear and *da* at the left ear; *kli* at the right eye and *ne* at the left eye; and *ma* at the right nostril.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra-syllables on the two nostrils, the skin, the sense organs, the forehead, the private parts,

and the two feet, and having again performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) three times with the complete mantra in the form *hrīṃ nityaklinne madadve svāhā*, one should take flowers in the hollowed palms preceded by the formation of the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā.

Having visualized that the splendor of the present Vidyā, which has been manifested from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*, has transferred into the handful of flowers by way of the central channel (*vaha-nāsā-mārga*), and having further visualized that it has transferred into the *bindu* within the triangle (*trikoṇa*) by means of its projection; then, having made this prayer at the end of the complete Vidyā: "O Nityaklinnā, O Eternal One, be invoked here into this *cakra*."
Those rays of light from that fire,
having spread out in various directions to the locations to be described, have transformed into the lords, weapons, and protective deities of those respective places.
Having thus dissolved that radiance, one should meditate upon the Bindu situated therein as follows:
she is ruddy, resembling the dawn, wearing ruddy garments, adorned with ruddy garlands and unguents,
her lotus-face graced with a beautiful smile, her countenance radiant with three eyes, and the pearls from the perspiration on her forehead.

Having meditated upon her as she shines resplendent, with a crown adorned by a shimmering crescent moon, seated upon a lotus, languid with intoxication, and bearing in her four arms a noose, a goad, a drinking vessel, and the gesture of fearlessness— having likewise meditated upon the Śaktis, who are identical in form to her in their garments, ornaments, weapons, and so forth.

Among the weapons, one should especially meditate upon the fact that each bears its respective crest-mark (*lāñchana*). In all these cases, even for the Lords (*nātha*s), their form is identical to that of the respective *Nityā* goddesses. Therefore, at the end of the *vidyā*: "O Nityaklinnā, be established here in this wheel! O Nityaklinnā, be firmly restrained here in this wheel! At the end of the *vidyā*: "O..."

Having made the request preceded by the display of the respective mudrās: "O Nityaklinnānitye, become veiled here in this cakra! O Nityaklinnānitye, at the end of the Vidyā, be present here in this cakra!"—and having performed the Kara-nyāsa and Aṅga-nyāsa for the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā Vidyā according to the stated method.

Having performed the ritual installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) for this [deity] Nityaklinnā-nityā by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā* in the form "The vital breaths of such-and-such Nityaklinnā-nityā are here in this wheel; the vital breaths," and so forth, one should worship her with the twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*). The mantras for that are as follows:
at the end of the complete *vidyā*, with the mantra "I offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to Nityaklinnā-nityā."

Having offered the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) with the general *arghya* water, one should present the water for the feet at the two feet using the currently recited *nityā-vidyā*. In this very same manner, [one should do so] in place of the word "water for the feet" (*pādya*).

Having inserted the words designating each offering, such as *arghya* and so forth, and having performed those respective offerings with the perfected mantras, one should present them at the locations of the head, face, and other parts by means of the root-vidyā.
Then follows the thirteen-fold service (*trayodaśopacāra*); its procedure is as follows: [at] the rear of the present Nityā, *hrīṃ*.

I worship the sandal of the Śrī Prakāśānanda-śakti. 2. The sandal of the Vimarśānanda-śakti. 2. The sandal of the Ānandānanda-śakti. 2. The sandal of the Śrī Jñānānanda-śakti. 2. The sandal of the Śrī Satyānanda-śakti. 2.
The sandal of the Śrī Pūrṇānanda-śakti. 2. The sandal of the Svabhāvānanda-śakti. 2. The sandal of the Pratibhānanda-śakti.

Having worshipped the nine Nāthas with the mantras, "I worship the pādukā of Subhagānandaśakti," and so forth; then, in the square, on the southern path of the western door: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, "I worship the pādukā of Śrīmadovilā.
On its northern path: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, "I worship the pādukā of Maṅgalā. In the northwest corner [2].

To Manmathārtā on the northern path of the northeast corner (2), to Manasvinī (7); in the northeast corner (2), to Mohā (7); on the northern path of the eastern gate (2), to Āmodā (7); on its southern path (2), to Mānamayī (7);
in the southeast corner, to Māyā (7); on the southern path (2), to Mandā; in the southwest corner, to Mitāvatī’s sandals (2).

Having worshipped the respective powers (*vaśa-śakti*) with the mantras "I worship [them]," and at the end of the complete *vidyā* having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with "I worship the *pādukā* of the eternal *Klinnā-nityā*," one performs the offering of the worship with: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the first enclosure of the eternal *Klinnā-nityā* accept this worship."

One should perform the offering of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, on the eight-petaled lotus, starting from the petal in front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise, [one should worship] *hrīṃ śrīṃ* and the sandals of Nityā (*nityāpādukā*).

Having worshipped those respective eight Śaktis with the mantras: "I worship [the Pādukā] of Nirañjanā" (x2), "of Klinnā" (x7), "of Kledinī" (x7), "of Madanāturā" (x7), "of Madadravā" (x7), "of Drāviṇī" (x7), and "I worship the Pādukā of Draviṇī"; then, starting from the portion adjacent to the right hand of the Goddess, [recite] "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ".

Having worshipped the weapons with the mantras: "Obeisance to Abhayā," "Obeisance to Pānapātra," "Obeisance to Pāśa," and "Obeisance to Aṅkuśa"; and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the conclusion of the complete Vidyā with the mantra: "I worship the pādukā of the eternal Nityaklinnā Nityā"; [one worships] Hrīṃ Śrīṃ these [deities] of Nityaklinnā Nityā.
One should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering for that worship with the mantra: "May the deities of the second enclosure accept the worship.

Then, on the two sides of the triangle, in the northwest (*vāyavya*), [one says]: *hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, "I worship the sandals (*pādukā*) of the Heart-Śakti. In the northeast (*īśāna*), [one says]: *hrīṃ śrīṃ nityaśirase svāhā*, [the Head...].

I worship Śaktipādukā. In the southeast: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klinne, Vaṣaṭ to the Śikhā; I worship the descent of the power of the Śikhā-Śakti. In the southwest: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Madaka, Huṃ to the Kavaca; I worship the descent of the power of the Kavaca-Śakti. In front of the Goddess: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Drave, Vaiṣaṭ to the Netra; I worship the descent of the power of the Netra-Śakti. In the four directions starting from the east: Hrīṃ...
Having worshipped the deities of the limbs with the mantras: *Śrīṃ svāhā astrāya phaṭ; I worship the sandals of the weapon-power (astra-śakti-pādukā)*;
and having worshipped the principal deity of the rite with: *Hrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā; I worship the sandals of the goddess Nityaklinnā*, [one recites]: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*.

Having offered a handful of flowers as an offering of worship with the words, "May these ever-moist deities of the third enclosure accept this worship," one worships in a clockwise direction within the triangle, beginning from the corner facing the Goddess: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Kṣobhiṇī; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Lolā."
Having worshipped the triad of Śaktis with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Mohinī," [one should then,
at the end of the previously mentioned essential-form Vidyā, recite] "I worship the sandals of the Nityaklinnā-nityā."

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center, and having offered the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for the dedication of the worship with the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, "May these deities of the fourth enclosure, the Nityaklinnā-nityās, accept this worship," one should perform the remaining services consisting of whatever hymns of praise, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and prostrations there may be, [and recite] a thousand [times].

Having performed the constant recitation (*nityajapa*) one hundred times, or sixteen times, or ten times that number, one should offer oblations (*homa*) with milk-mixed water, or with clarified butter, or with fragrant flowers. One should then dissolve the Goddess’s radiant energy (*tejas*), which has been meditated upon in the fire, into the *bindu* located within the circle of the Goddess (*devīcakra*). Having again worshipped the Goddess residing in the circle with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), [one should proceed].

Having offered a garland with the Kurukullā-vidyā, performed the *nīrājana* with wicks filled with camphor, and sought forgiveness, one should visualize the subordinate powers (*paraśakti*) residing in the wheel as dissolved into the principal goddess by means of the Śaktyutthāpana-mudrā.
Then, by means of the Khecarī-mudrā, one should dismiss (*udvāsya*) the present principal Nityā from her own self and into the wheel. [As previously stated...]

At the conclusion of the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and the phoneme placement (*varṇanyāsa*), one should recite the Guru-stotra and the twelve-verse Devī-stotra; this specific detail regarding the worship as an ancillary of initiation (*dīkṣāṅga-pūjā*) should be noted from the general context. Thus, having acquired the knowledge that brings about its own fruit...
To achieve the accomplishment of the application of the *vidyā*, one should perform the means for attaining that *vidyā*. The method for this is as follows:

as before, adorned with red garments and so forth in a red chamber, at each junction of the day (*pratisandhya*), after completing one's regular daily worship, one should perform the regular recitation (*nityajapa*) numbering one thousand; then, by a count of three thousand one hundred and twenty-five [recitations].

Performing the *puraścaraṇa* recitation, having completed one hundred thousand repetitions during a specific period of thirty-two solar days (*sāvana-dina*)— increasing from the full moon day (*pūrṇimā*) until the full moon day, covering the middle portion.

In the same manner, even elsewhere, after an interval of one hundred thousand such periods of thirty-two days, there occurs again an interval of one hundred thousand such periods of thirty-two days; according to this sequence...
In the Kali age, the perfection of the vidyā is attained through forty-eight lakh recitations; at the conclusion of the complete number of recitations,

or at the end of each daily session of one hundred thousand recitations, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with a tenth part of the total recitations using either madhūka or vakula flowers smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu).

One should perform the *tarpaṇa* (libation) with water scented with sandalwood, camphor, and musk, using a number equal to one-tenth of the *japa* (recitation), or one-tenth of the number of *homa* (fire-offerings). Having fed the Brahmins and satisfied the Guru with fees and other offerings, the Vidyā shall become perfected. One who has thus accomplished the Vidyā should then perform the ritual applications (*prayoga*), which are as follows:

There are four types [of practice], distinguished by the application of *homa* (fire-oblation), the application of *puttalī* (effigy), the application of *tarpaṇa* (libation), and the application of *yantra* (diagram). Among these, the *homa* is as follows:
from the *homa* of lotuses smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one attains prosperity (*lakṣmī*);
from the *homa* of red water-lilies (*raktakairava*), women become submissive; and for that cow whose calf is white, [the same applies].

By performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) with any one of the *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jātī*, or *śatapatra* flowers soaked in milk, one attains success in fame, knowledge, wealth, health, good fortune, victory, immobilization (*stambhana*), and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).
From the oblation of *āragvadha* fuel-sticks smeared with honey, there is the acquisition of gold, as well as the paralyzing of the anger of enemies, kings, or disputants.
From the offering of red *karavīra* flowers smeared with ghee, or of red garments smeared with ghee, [the same results follow].
From this fire-oblation (homa), the practitioner shall attain mastery over women, kings, and their ministers;
there shall be the acquisition of ornaments, the acquisition of mounts such as horses, and success in trade.
By performing a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with either white, yellow, or black mustard seeds smeared with mustard oil, the desired woman is summoned.
By performing a fire sacrifice at midnight with black *śaṅkhapuṣpī* flowers smeared with oil, [the result is achieved] within one month.
By employing fever against an enemy, suffering will certainly arise.

(2) By anointing with *arūṣkara* oil and performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) with *arūṣkara* seeds, an enemy suffers from wounds that cannot be remedied even by physicians; through that very suffering, his death also occurs.
By anointing one's limbs with *aṅkola* oil and performing a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with *aṅkola* seeds, death preceded by the suffering of wounds occurs.
By anointing black pepper with mustard oil and performing a fire sacrifice at midnight for the duration of a month,
the desired woman is summoned.
By performing oblations for seven nights with mustard seeds and black pepper smeared with sesame oil,

one obtains a woman who is difficult to attain— whether she be a girl whose marriage is the desired fruit— or one who is superior even to those families possessing wealth, stability, and honor. At the end, it should be performed in this manner, mixed with clarified butter.

Through a fire-oblation (*homa*) performed one hundred and eight times, or one hundred and one time, the state of being filled with food and the capacity to consume it arise respectively through slight delay or speed. From an oblation of *śāli* rice mixed with ghee comes fullness of *śāli* grain; from an oblation of mung beans comes fullness of mung beans; and from an oblation of ghee comes fullness of ghee.

From the oblation (*homa*) of sweet substances such as sugar and the like, there is the attainment of sweet substances such as sugar and the like. Now, regarding the applications of the effigy (*puttalī*):
for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*) and other rites, [the effigy] may be made from the wood of a tree corresponding to the birth-star (*nakṣatra*) of the person to be acted upon;
or it may be made from rice flour mixed with the dust from the feet of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*); or it may be made from black pepper and salt.

At midnight, one should offer oblations twelve times with the aforementioned vidyā into a doll made from ground royal rice-flour (*rājīpiṣṭha*) into which the vital breath has been infused (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Therein, beginning from the region of the joint of the heel...

Two oblations with the two severed tips of the feet; two oblations with the two severed shanks below the knees; two oblations with the two severed knees starting from the knee-joints; and two oblations with the two severed thighs below the hips.
Having combined these, there are eight oblations (*āhuti*). One oblation is offered with the portion cut from the navel down to the thighs;

one oblation with the portion cut from the heart to the navel; one oblation with the portion cut extending from the heart to the throat; and one with the remaining portion up to the head. Thus, in total, twelve oblations are completed.

In this way, through the fire-oblation (homa), the subjugation of the object to be accomplished occurs. If one desires to cause affliction such as fever, within seven days there shall be suffering from fever and the like. If one desires death, that too shall occur after the aforementioned number of oblations performed with the previous power. Another application: having fashioned an effigy out of rice-flour mixed with black pepper, cumin, and molasses; of that—

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in such forms as "O Devadatta, bring [him] under control! O Yajñadatta, do so! and so forth; and having offered oblations with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) one hundred or one thousand times using the aforementioned *nityā-vidyā* following that name of the person to be accomplished; and having placed the resulting residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*) in some vessel—

Having cooked that doll, and having consecrated it one thousand times with the tip of the *jīvaka* grass while touching it, and having performed the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣ�ṭhā*) of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) and worshipped it,
he should again smear it with ghee while mentally contemplating, "This doll is indeed the very form of the person to be acted upon."
When one consumes [the substance] of the present Nityā-vidyā (p. 99a), kings and others become subject to one's will for as long as one lives. Another application follows.

Having fashioned a round cake (*apūpa*) from the aforementioned substances, one should write the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*)— expressed in its true form— in the center of it, which serves as its heart; then, having cooked it with the *sampāta* clarified butter as before,
by eating that cake while contemplating the specific nature of the person to be acted upon and reciting the present mantra for the duration of one year, [the desired result is achieved].

Men become submissive. Another application: having written the previously mentioned name of the flour-cake (*piṣṭa-jāpūpa*) in its previously described form, and having baked that flour-cake with *saṃpāta* ghee, the practitioner, while eating it, shall subjugate men for a period of six months. Due to the absence of a thousand-fold consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), this is the middling [method] compared to the former.

There is a diminution of the fruit. In the state of being ground into flour, because there is no writing of the name, there is a scriptural diminution of the fruit compared to the middle stage; thus, in the final case, there is a diminution of the fruit.

However, the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of the object to be accomplished, the meditation on identity with it, and the consumption performed by means of the mantra (*vidyā*) under discussion apply in all cases.
These are equal [in effect]. Now, the practical applications of *tarpaṇa* (libation): by performing *tarpaṇa* with coconut water, women come under one's control.

By performing *tarpaṇa* with water scented with camphor, men come under one's control. By performing *tarpaṇa* with the water of the salt ocean, both men and women come under one's control. By performing *tarpaṇa* with water mixed with salt, women come under one's control for a month.
Having performed libations with pure water for either a fortnight or seven nights at the conclusion of the recitation of the present Vidyā,
using the mantra-formula "Subdue [Name], subdue Yajñadatta," all those whose names are written in the accusative case therein come under one's control.

By means of coconut water scented with ketakī flowers and camphor, as if through a libation, women become submissive and offer their lives and wealth; what then need be said of their surrendering their hearts and other such things?

By performing libations with water scented with *rudrākṣa* seeds, kings become submissive. By performing libations with water scented with *campaka* flowers, one gains the power to delight all people.
One should perform daily libations with water scented with *pāṭalī* flowers and *śatapatra*.
It bestows the power to cause wonder in all the worlds. Offering libations with water scented with musk brings about the attainment of all perfections (*siddhis*).

For one who offers libations while pervading the entire circle (*maṇḍala*) with water scented with camphor and sandalwood, there is the complete accomplishment of all undertakings in every way. Through offering libations with water mixed with parched grain flour (*saktu*), [the result] endures for a long time.

There shall be abundance of wealth, grain, elephants, horses, and so forth. A libation (tarpaṇa) performed at night with water mixed with jaggery destroys obstacles. A libation made with water mixed with tamarind causes mutual hatred among those who were previously affectionate toward one another. A libation with hot water mixed with black pepper brings about the death of enemies.

By performing *tarpaṇa* (libation) with exclusively warm water, there shall be the destruction of enemies through the affliction of abdominal diseases such as diarrhea and dysentery. As for the number of oblations (*homa*) and libations, it should consist of either one thousand or one hundred; the duration of time, however, may be one night, three nights, five nights, seven nights, a fortnight, or a month.
Now, regarding one of the mandalas, the application of the yantras: first, having drawn a circle,

then outside of that a hexagon, and further outside of that, having fashioned two walkways (vīthī) by means of three circles, one should write in the very center the first syllable of the mantra in the form of the *māyāvīja*, joined with the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the object of the rite (*sādhya*), and so forth.

Having written the six syllables, beginning with the second and ending with the seventh, one by one in the six corners; and having written the four syllables of the Vidyā in the four directions within the space between the outer circle; [one writes] the first [syllable] in the four corners of that [circle].

In the southeast corner, the form of the element air consists of two syllables: *a* and *ā*. In the southwest, the form of fire consists of three syllables: *e*, *i*, and *ca*. In the northwest, the form of water consists of two syllables: *u* and *ū*. In the northeast, the form of earth consists of three syllables: *ṛ*, *ṝ*, and *ḷ*. Having thus written these ten syllables, [one should draw] a circle on the outside.

It is established that one should encircle [the seed-syllable] with the *mātṛkā*; this is the first yantra. Now, if the second syllable is placed in the central form at the position of *māyā*, while *māyā* itself is written in the northern direction of the inner path at the very end, then it is the second yantra. By placing the third and subsequent letters in the center, [one proceeds] with the letters previously omitted.
By arranging nine new [yantras] in the eleven positions [of the body], eleven yantras are accomplished.

All of these are made of leaves and are suitable for the practice of subjugation (*vaśya*). However, if they are drawn with the letters of the elements, such as earth and so forth, for use in recitation (*japa*) and other rites for the pacification of calamities (*śānti*), then it is as stated regarding the eleven.

By combining each of the yantras with the colors of the five elements according to their respective desires and powers, fifty-five yantras are produced. Among them, for the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*) regarding men, women, and kings, there are first three yantras obtained in sequence. Regarding attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), they are categorized by the objects being women or men.

The fourth and fifth yantras of two types [are used for] the pacification of diseases and the like; the sixth and seventh yantras are for the pacification of the three types of portents, and for the two types of pacification, they are respectively employed for subduing,
deluding, creating enmity, expulsion, killing, inducing disease, destroying families of afflictions, protecting elephants, and protecting horses.
Protection for camels, protection for horses, protection for buffaloes, protection for sheep, protection for cattle, protection for men, protection for women;
victory over enemies encountered in battle, victory in duels, victory in legal disputes, and victory at dice.
Regarding the twenty-four activities— namely, the protection of the capital city (*jayanagara*), the protection of the village (*grāma*), and the protection of the district (*maṇḍala*)—
there is a twofold division based on the distinction between male and female, the distinction between the king and his queens, and the distinction between having a male or female owner.
When this results in a total of forty-eight [activities] beginning with *māyā*, it is stated that upon adding the number seven, [the total becomes fifty-five].

Fifty-five fruits are to be applied respectively to fifty-five yantras. This is the secret of the mantras: for the twenty-four yantras pertaining to the twelve protections beginning with the elephant—which are divided into two categories based on whether they concern women or men—the letters of the earth (the vowels) [are used] for the pacification of disease.
In the three types of pacification (*śānti*) for portents, there are the colors of water in the four *patra* (leaves/sections) which possess the distinctions of male and female;

in the five [karmas]—namely, subjugation (*vaśya*) which is threefold through the distinction of man, woman, and king, and delusion (*mohana*) which is twofold through the distinction of female and male—the colors are gold and copper; and [the results are] victory over enemies encountered in battle, victory in duels, victory in debate, and victory in legal proceedings such as debts.

In the victories of gambling, which are of ten types when combined—being each twofold according to the distinction between women and men—the letters of fire (ra) are to be written; and in the twelve types [of rites]—namely *stambhana*, *vidveṣaṇa*, *uccāṭana*, *māraṇa*, causing disease, causing affliction, and the destruction of hostile families—which are likewise twofold as before, the letters of space (ha) are to be written. Thus it is said.

From the sequence of the *yantras*, there follows the sequence of the elemental letters (*bhūtavarṇa*): the rule is that one elemental letter is to be written in each of the nine, eleven, and eleven *yantras*. Now, regarding the *vikṛtākṣara* *yantras*, whether in the ritual procedure for the preparatory service (*pauraścaraṇika-vidhi*) or independently, even when counting the vowels and consonants...

In the chapter on the construction of the machine, such sounds are [produced] from the city of the vowels: the letter *ha*, the letter *ra*, the letter *na*, the letter *ta*, the letter *ya*, the letter *ka*, and the letter *la*.

By joining each of the eleven letters— consisting of *ma*, *da*, *va*, and *sa*— which belong to the present vidyā and lead to non-return, with the sixteen vowels, one hundred and seventy-six modified syllables (*vikṛtākṣara*) are established. Among these, one letter is *ha*.

Having written [the mantra] containing the names of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth, within the pericarp of the aforementioned specific-lined diagram; having written the six syllables *hā*, *hi*, *hī*, *hu*, *hū*, and *hṛ* once each in the six hexagons;
and having written the four syllables *hṛ*, *hḷ*, *hḹ*, and *he* in sequence in the four directions of the outer path surrounding that.
Having applied the eleven modified mantra-syllables, one should fill the outermost path with the *mātṛkā* letters;

this is the primary yantra. If, however, within the letter *e*, there are the six syllables *ho hau haṃ haḥ rarā* in the six corners, and *ri rī ru rū* in the four directions of the first path, [and] in the outer path...
Then the second yantra is written as the "mātṛkā" (matrix).

In this very manner, having written each of the eleven successive phonemes one by one in each yantra, the remaining fourteen yantras are to be produced; thus, in total, sixteen yantras are perfected therein.

Regarding the fruit of the first ritual manual (*yantra*): having performed in the ritual vessel (*yantra*) all the rites according to the prescribed method—including the installation of the pitcher (*kalaśa*), the worship of Sarvamaṅgalā, and the concluding rite of its dismissal (*udvāsana*)—one should then invoke the presiding deity (*prastutanityā*) therein and worship her according to the stated directions. Having consecrated that water with the recitation of the presiding mantra (*prastutadvayā*) one hundred or one thousand times, [one should proceed].
