By means of that water-consecration (*tajjalābhiṣeka*), preceded by such a consecration, and through the wearing of that yantra, the maidens previously mentioned come under one’s control; furthermore, the afflictions such as diseases pertaining to maidens are destroyed by both the aforementioned type of consecration and the wearing of that yantra.
Furthermore, having drawn this yantra on the ground and reciting the vidyā mentally, the practitioner,
while meditating upon a certain maiden as being possessed by the disease under discussion, [should apply] it with lac-resin (*sarjarasa*).

While offering incense and performing the dismissal (*visarjana*), one should invoke the Nityā introduced in the Tantra, perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths), and carry out worship with the sixteen services beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*). Then, one should inquire about one's desired task in such a manner as: "O Nityaklinnā, when and how will this work of mine be accomplished? and so forth.

When questioned, she should give an answer according to the facts. Once the answer has been obtained, one should again worship the Nityā (the Eternal Goddess) present there with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), and then dissolve her into one's own self. Furthermore, when girls are possessed by spirits such as *bhūtas* or *pretas*, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with a jar empowered by a yantra according to the stated method, and [instruct them] to wear that yantra.
By this means, their well-being shall be secured. As for the result of the second yantra:

having drawn the second yantra with *karṣaṭaga* and red ochre (*gairika*) juice, with the seed-syllable of the *karṇikā* containing the name of the person to be accomplished and so forth, one should place it in the middle space between the proponent and the opponent. By that, even a very eminent proponent will, at that moment, become tongue-tied.

With a dry mouth and restless eyes, looking toward the ten directions and speaking incoherently, he would say, "Have I been defeated by you? and thus become renowned. This is the result of the third yantra. Having written the third yantra—containing the seed-syllable in the center and surrounded by the name of the desired object—with a paste of turmeric on a piece of cloth or a shard;

One should dig beneath a hearth (*cullyāḥ*)— which serves as a place of cooking and whose surface has become exceedingly hot from being heated by fire— and by that means, within two or three days, [one may affect] the enemy's firm anger, movement, intellect, tongue,
military exertion, and coming and going.

One may also paralyze actions and so forth. Furthermore, having heard that an enemy is approaching with an army directed toward one's own position, one should dig the previously mentioned yantra into the middle of the path of his arrival at night.

One should offer an oblation to the *nāman*, *nakṣatra*, and *yoni* of the enemy. By that means, the army of the general will flee and become devoid of any effort to return; furthermore, the army shall suffer afflictions such as vomiting and dysentery.
The result of the fourth machine (*yantra*) is as follows: on a surface made from the wood of the tree belonging to one's own *nakṣatra* or that of the enemy, [one places] the fourth...
One should bury the yantra in the city center. By that means, there shall be no end to the enemies' afflictions caused by mutual strife among their subjects, enmity, fever, and so forth.
The results of the five yantras from the fifth to the ninth are as follows:
having engraved the yantras for the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth [houses] twice each upon copper plates in sequence—

Having fashioned eight [yantras] in number and having engraved the ninth yantra upon a single copper plate, one should consecrate it through the ritual of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and worship according to the prescribed rules; then, for whichever [place] among the kingdom, city, village, or house is to be protected, [one should place them] in the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate corners of its perimeter.

Having dug eight yantras in the [surrounding] directions and the ninth yantra in the center, one should perform worship there. By means of these yantras, the magical rites (*kṛtyā*) performed by enemies against one’s own intended victim are neutralized; for they are rendered ineffective by the protection of these yantras, and because the consumption [of the victim] produced by the power of the mantras is rendered impossible, the consumption is treated as that of a bystander, being devoid of fault.

By their very nature, they devour the user himself, who has committed the offense of producing them, just like the fruit of the tenth machine. For example, by drawing the tenth machine on a silver plate and placing it within one's own armor, a hero entering the battlefield would conquer the enemy and put the army to flight.
p.

102b) The fruit of the eleventh yantra is as follows: Having written the eleventh yantra on a cloth with red ochre rubbed with the juice of turmeric, one should bury it in the path by which the enemy’s army approaches. By that means, the enemy’s preparations for battle are pacified.

It occurs. As for the result of the twelfth yantra: this yantra, written with saffron and camphor on birch bark or cloth, and consecrated through the ritual of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and other rites, provides protection in every respect for the practitioner who wears it. As for the result of the thirteenth yantra: [on] palm leaf...

Having drawn this yantra with saffron and camphor, and having coated the exterior with yellow orpiment, one should place it inside a wall. By that means, protection for the house associated with that wall is secured against various kinds of diseases, thieves, planetary spirits (grahas), serpents, kings, enemies, tigers, and wild beasts. This is the fruit of the fourteenth yantra.

For example: by writing [this mantra] on birch bark with saffron and camphor, consecrating it through rituals such as *pratiṣṭhā* and worship, and wearing it, women attain incomparable good fortune. As for the fruit of the fifteen-fold yantra:
by engraving and wearing this yantra inscribed upon a golden plate, even a barren woman attains long life.

She gives birth to a son endowed with all praiseworthy qualities. Just as is the fruit of the sixteen-fold yantra: having worshipped this yantra—which is engraved upon a gold plate and well-established—placed according to rule in a pitcher set upon a drawing of that same yantra on the ground, and having again worshipped the Nityā currently under discussion, [one should worship] Sarvamaṅgalānityā along with her retinue and attendants.
A woman who wears [this] after first performing an ablution with water prepared as previously described shall, through her abundance of love for her husband, attain supremacy over all her co-wives.
Furthermore, by wearing that yantra written on birch bark, preceded by the aforementioned consecration, one obtains protection from kings, thieves, spirits, ghosts, and the like.
Thus concludes the introduction to the Nityaklinnā-vidyā.
Now, the Nityā Bheruṇḍā is introduced.
Having constructed the *bhūpura* (earth-city) with two lines, each provided with door-panels (*dvāraśākhā*) in the four directions;
having then drawn one circle within that [space] such that it touches and does not touch the inner line of the *bhūpura*;
and having drawn another circle within that with an interval of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*), [one should mark] the path between them with two squares.
Having fashioned an eight-sided figure with its corners aligned to the cardinal and intermediate directions; having fashioned two circles within that with a space between them;

having made a six-cornered wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*) in the space between those; and having again made two circles within that with a space between them, and having made a triangle facing oneself in the space between those, one should then fashion an eight-petalled lotus within that as well.
Having drawn two circles with a four-finger space between them, one should place dots within the triangles on that path.

Having prepared this worship-circle (pūjācakra) by drawing it upon some pure, level ground, and having performed therein— during the initiation— the additional rites beginning with the placement of the jar (kalaśasthāpana), the worship of Sarvamaṅgalā, and ending with the dismissal (udvāsana), [one should worship] the present Nityā.
Furthermore, the worship (*pūjā*) is performed there in the water-pot (*kalaśa*), but at other times it is performed in the maṇḍala (*cakra*); such is the worship. Its procedure is as follows:

first, one performs the worship of the seat (*āsana-pūjā*) with the seat-mantras (*āsana-vidyā*); finally, having sat down there with the *vidyā*, and having performed the sipping of water (*ācamana*) and breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of the *vidyā*, one offers the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with the sixteen-syllable mantra.

Having worshipped the nine lords according to the lineage of one's own guru with their respective mantras upon one's own head, having recited their hymn of praise and obtained their permission, one should begin the worship; and having meditated upon one's own lord— the present Nityā— as one's own self in the form of the Lord.

Having worshipped all the deities of the thirty-eight sacred seats (*pīṭha*), including the secret and manifest *siddha-yoginīs* whose locations, times, and so forth are regulated by their respective class-distinctions (*varṇabheda*), one should [apply] *gorocanā* between the yantra and oneself.

The general *arghya* vessel, made of gold or another such material, along with its supporting base, is filled with water scented with camphor, saffron, agallochum, and musk. The waters in that supporting vessel are, in sequence, of the nature of fire, sun, and moon by means of the three *kulasaundarī* seed-syllables; and the five substances therein, such as *rocanā*, are of the nature of the five elements beginning with earth.

And having meditated [on this], one should contemplate the identity between that water and the wheel of the present Nityā-pūjā. Having meditated on the water as being the very nature of the present Nityā, one should consecrate it ten times with the present Vidyā and worship it.
Then, having worshipped the deities of its six limbs with their respective mantras, one should [sprinkle] oneself with that water using the present Vidyā.

The water for the feet (pādya), the guest-offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the bathing water (snānajala)— placed in vessels situated one after another starting from the vessel for the general guest-offering (sāmānyārghya)—

are contained in separate vessels. Likewise, the garments, ornaments, perfumes, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), and betel leaves (tāmbūla), placed in their respective vessels on one's own right side, should each be consecrated by sprinkling (saṃprokṣya).

Again, having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) with the Vidyā, and having recited the place, time, lineage, zodiacal sign, name, and intention, ending with the word "intention" (kāmanā), one should form the resolve: "I shall perform the worship of Bheruṇḍā Nityā according to the injunctions and as ordained by the Buddha. Taking water with flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata) in one's hand, one should proceed.

Having first performed the nyāsa of the six limbs of the Mātṛkā, and having applied each respective Mātṛkā—conjoined with the present Vidyā—to its corresponding Mātṛkā-locations: "Oṃ kroṃ svāhā, obeisance to the heart; Oṃ mroṃ svāhā, svāhā to the head."
*Oṃ krauṃ svāhā śikhāyai vaṣaṭ; oṃ hroṃ svāhā kavacāya huṃ; oṃ chrauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ;
oṃ jrauṃ svāhā astrāya phaṭ.* With these mantras, [one should perform the nyāsa] on one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other [limbs].

Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*): *oṃ* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), *kroṃ* between the eyebrows, *bhrīṃ* on the face, *krauṃ* at the throat, *hrauṃ* at the heart, *chrauṃ* at the navel, *jrauṃ* at the root-base (*mūlādhāra*), *svā* on the right foot, and *hā* on the left foot—having thus placed these mantra-syllables; again, in this form: *oṃ kroṃ krauṃ hrauṃ chvauṃ jrauṃ svāhā*.

Having performed the threefold pervasive nyāsa of the complete Vidyā, and having first displayed the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā, one should visualize the present Nityā from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra* within the cluster of red *karavīra* and other flowers held in the joined palms; she is then transferred via the path of the *vaha* channel along with her radiant splendor.
Having visualized this, and having visualized her arrival there by casting that handful of flowers into the *bindu* situated within the pericarp of the triangle;
at the end of the complete mantra as previously stated, one should pray: "O Bheruṇḍā-nityā, be invoked here in this wheel (*cakra*).
Then, [one should visualize] the rays of that splendor reaching the respective locations to be described.

Having visualized that [the offerings] have been transformed into the forms of the deities who are the protectors of the food, weapons, and armor, one should visualize that mass of light situated in the center as having been transformed into its essential nature through meditation. As for the meditation: [one should contemplate her] with a body resembling molten gold, adorned with three eyes, and a face graced by a beautiful smile.
Adorned with divine ornaments— decorated with earrings, necklaces, armlets, and clusters of jewels;

beautified by ornaments such as waves fashioned from gems and other materials— the beautiful one, holding in her hands a noose, a goad, a shield, a sword, a mace, fire, a bow, and arrows, is seated during worship, or otherwise situated [in her natural state].
One should always worship the Śaktis surrounding [the central deity], endowed with splendor and weapons identical in form to his, their faces ever smiling and gentle; likewise,
the visualization of the various weapons and so forth is exactly the same as in the visualization of the weapons themselves.
It must not be forgotten that in all instances, one’s head should be slightly bowed. Therefore, at the conclusion of the present vidyā, [one should recite]:
"O Bheruṇḍānityā, be established here in this cakra! At the end of the previously mentioned nineteen syllables, [recite]:
"be firmly restrained (sanniruddhā bhava)! Again, at the end of that many syllables, [recite]: "be veiled (avaguṇṭhitā bhava)! Again, at the end of that many syllables...

Having made the request, "May you be present," preceded by the display of the respective mudrās, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs for the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, one should perform the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) using the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra in the form: "The vital breaths of this Bheruṇḍā-nityā are here in this wheel; the vital breaths... and so forth.

One should perform worship with the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*). The mantras for this are as follows: at the end of the *vidyā* stated in the nine-syllable [mantra], one offers the water for the feet (*pādya*) using the twenty-one syllable mantra, "Bheruṇḍā-nityāyai pādyaṃ kalpayāmi," with the water from the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*). Having thus offered the water for the feet, one should present the water for the feet at the two feet using the aforementioned nine-syllable *vidyā*. In the same manner...

Having inserted the words for each of the services beginning with *arghya* and ending with *tāmbūla* in place of the word *pādya*, and having offered those respective *arghya* and other items with the perfected mantras, one should present them upon the head, face, and other parts [of the deity] using the root-vidyā.
Then follows the thirteen-fold service; its procedure is as follows: on the back part of the Goddess, [one offers] *prakāśa*, *vimarśa*, and *ānanda*.

Having worshipped with their respective mantras the nine Nāthas— Śrījñāna, Śrīsatya, Śrīpūrṇa, Svabhāva, Pratibha, Subhaga, and the others— along with the Śakti-padas inserted into the positions of the Nātha-padas;
On the eight paths situated at the sides of the four gates, beginning with the western gate, proceeding clockwise:
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Brāhmī twice; Māheśvarī seven times; Kaumārī seven times; Vaiṣṇavī seven times.

Having worshipped the twelve Śaktis with the mantras: "I worship the sandals of Vārāhī (7) 2, Aindrī (7) 2, Cāmuṇḍā (7) 2, Mahālakṣmī (7), the Kṛtayuga-Śakti (7) 2, the Tretāyuga-Śakti (7) 2, the Dvāparayuga-Śakti (7) 2, and the Kaliyuga-Śakti," in the corners starting from the northwest (Vāyavya) and proceeding clockwise; and at the end of the Vidyā, [worshipping] the Bheruṇḍā-Nityā-pādukā.

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with "I worship," one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for the dedication of that worship, saying: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these first enclosure deities, the Nityās beginning with Aghorā and Beruṇḍā, accept the worship. Then, on the eight petals, starting from the petal in front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! I worship Vijayā-pādukā... [twice]."
Having worshipped the eight Śaktis named Vikārā and the others with the mantras: "I worship the sandals of Vimalā," "Vibhā," "Viśvā," "Vibhūti," "Vinatā," "Viṭavidhā," "Vimatā," and "Pādukā";
and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete Vidyā with the mantra: "I worship the sandals of Bheruṇḍā-Nityā."
*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, may these goddesses of the second enclosure, the Nityās beginning with Bheruṇḍā, accept this worship;
thus, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering of that worship. In the eight corners, starting from the corner in front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise:
*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship Kamalāpādukā; [2] Kāminīpādukā; [7] Kirātīpādukā; [7] Kīrtisahitāpādukā.
Having worshipped the eight Śaktis whose names begin with the letter *ka*—namely, *Kuṇḍinīpā*, *Kulasundarīpā*, *Kalyāṇīpā*, and "I worship the sandals of Kālakālā"—[one proceeds].

In the intermediate spaces of the eight corners, beginning from the area near the lower left hand of the Goddess and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction, one should worship the eight weapons with the following: *hrīṃ śrīṃ dhanuṣe namaḥ*, *2 gadāyai namaḥ*, *2 carmaṇe*, *2 pāśāyaṃ*, *2 aṅkuśāya*, *2 khaḍgāya*, *2 vahnaye*, *2 śarebhyo namaḥ*. [This concludes] at the end of the Vidyā.

Having worshipped the central Nityā with the mantra "I worship Bheruṇḍānityā," one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an oblation for that worship, saying: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the third enclosure, Bheruṇḍānityā, accept this worship. Then, in the southwest corner of the hexagonal wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*), [one should worship] Hrīṃ Śrīṃ...
I worship the power (śakti) Ḍākinī, whose vehicle is the sandalwood shoe. In the northwest corner: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the power Rākinī. In the eastern corner:
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the power Lākinī. In the southeast corner: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the power Kākinī. In the northeast corner:
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the power Sākinī. In the western corner: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] Hākinī.

Having worshipped each of those Śaktis with the mantras "I worship the sandals of [Name] Śakti," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the Vidyā with "I worship the sandals of Bheruṇḍā Nityā," one performs the offering of that worship with: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the fourth enclosure of Bheruṇḍā Nityā accept this worship."

One should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, having performed the remaining three services consisting of the recitation of hymns, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and prostrations, one should perform the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) with a number of either one thousand, one hundred and twenty, or another [specified] count, and contemplate its essence.

Having performed the offering (nivedana) according to the prescribed rite, one should offer oblations into the fire— conceived as non-different from the Goddess— using ghee and other substances according to the sixteen-fold procedure mentioned in the context of Lalitā, in both the number ten and its fractional parts (daśāṃśa).
This is to be done specifically within the *bindu*, which is the very locus of the Goddess.
Having withdrawn that fire and once again worshipped the Goddess residing within the wheel of the *bindu* with the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra*),
one should now likewise offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) using the sixteen-syllable mantra as before.

Having performed the *nīrājana* with wicks scented with camphor and other substances and having offered prayers, one should dismiss the subordinate deities residing in the *cakra* by means of the *śaktyutthāpana-mudrā*.
Then, having dismissed the principal deity into one's own self by means of the *khecarī-mudrā*,
one should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) and the placement of the syllables (*varṇa-nyāsa*) as before, followed by the recitation of the hymn of praise to the Guru.

One should perform the recitation of the hymn consisting of twelve verses. Regarding the specific details for the worship that forms part of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should pay attention to them from the general introduction. Thus, having acquired the knowledge, one should perform the means of realizing the mantra (*vidyāsādhana*) in order to establish oneself as a practitioner of the application of the knowledge that bestows the *halopadhā* [power]. The method for this is as follows: [using] fragrant...

Having first performed a bath in water and subsisted solely on milk as before, the practitioner, remaining seated upon a *svastika* or similar posture in a place purified by the *kūrma-cakra* and adorned with various items such as red charcoal,
should perform the practice three times daily— at dawn, noon, and sunset— during the thirty-two days beginning from the first day of the waxing moon until the full moon.

At the conclusion of the worship, performing an additional recitation of three thousand two hundred and twenty-five—beyond the daily recitation—one should complete the count of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) in thirty-two days. By practicing in this ninefold manner, the completion of nine hundred thousand is achieved; however, in the Kali Yuga, it is as follows:

Having performed thirty-six hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) in this manner, the success of the preparatory rite (*pauraścaraṇika-japa*) is achieved. If one lacks the capacity for this oneself, it should be accomplished through a preceptor, a disciple, or another Brahmin who worships that deity.

At the conclusion of the *japa*, an offering (*bali*) consisting of lotuses smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), equal to a tenth part of the *japa*, should be made with the sixteen-syllable mantra.
One should offer the first [oblation] as previously described; the fire sacrifice (homa) is performed with exactly one-tenth of the number of recitations (japa).
An offering of water scented with camphor and sandalwood must be made. This applies to the worship at the three junctions of the day (trisandhya) in the event of incapacity.

One should perform only one daily worship at a specific time of the twilight (saṃdhyā). Regarding the practice of a single daily worship, on the days of the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa), the obligatory recitation (nityajapa) must be performed with a count of exactly one thousand, not with any other number mentioned.
Likewise, even after the accomplishment of the mantra (vidyāsādhana), one should perform only those ritual applications (prayoga) taught by the Guru, and not those taught by others.

Since one might not only fail to achieve the intended result but even incur something undesirable by performing applications differently than those seen in new books, instruction from a guru is absolutely necessary regarding the subject matter of application.

Now follow the applications for constant practice (*nityaprayoga*). First, regarding the binding diagrams (*yantra*): having constructed a hexagon surrounded by two circles with an intervening path (*vīthī*) between them, one should draw this line-diagram twice—once with the juice of *mārjāra* and *mūṣaka* plants ground with the resin of *uśīra*, and once with the liquid of charcoal from a cremation ground.

In the pericarp (*karṇikā*), in both cases, having written the second seed-syllable containing the names of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth— such as "cause enmity between Caitra and Maitra"— and having written the third, fourth,
and sixth seed-syllables with the *bindu* in the upper [petals], namely those in the northeast, east, and southeast corners, [one should write them] in the lower [petals].

Having written the third, fourth, and sixth seed-syllables (*bīja*) by placing a *bindu* in the western and southwestern corners and adding a *visarga* in their respective positions, one should surround the path with the letters of the wind element (*pavana-bhūta-varṇa*) joined at the end with the previously mentioned letters of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), etc.; thus the yantra is perfected and endowed with the rite of vitalization (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).

Having performed [the rite], and having recited two thousand times the seed-syllables of the mantra— namely the second, third, fourth, and sixth seeds related to the present mantra— one should write [them] in a cremation ground at the time when the enemy’s eighth zodiacal sign is the ascendant.

There will necessarily be mutual enmity between the two enemies whose names have been written by him. Here, although the act of inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*) is performed through mantras such as *japa* and so forth, and involves obtaining the letters of space (*ākāśa*), fire (*vahni*), and so on, it is nonetheless composed exclusively of the letters of air (*pavana*) due to the specific injunction "by the letters of air. Thus, all the suppressive yantras (*nigrahayantra*) mentioned in this section are indeed constructed from the letters of air.
The rites are to be performed; we understand that the act of worship is to take place within the circle of wind itself. Thus ends the diagram for inciting hatred.

Having written one's own name in the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhyanta) using a solution of yellow orpiment rubbed with turmeric juice upon a tiger-skin, and having inscribed the enemy's name and so forth upon a cow-hide in such forms as "O Cow-hide, bring victory to Yajñadatta! Do it! Do it!"—and having placed the cow-hide yantra beneath and the tiger-skin yantra above, one should deposit it somewhere in a secluded place.

Having covered it with a very large stone and sitting upon that stone, one should recite the four seed-syllables a thousand times during the morning twilight and a thousand times during the evening twilight. By this, victory will certainly be achieved;
what more need be said? On that day, [the enemy] will either flee from that place or say, "I have been defeated by you."

This is the mantra for victory in debate. Having written the aforementioned yantra on the skin of a specific deer named *ruru* using the blood of that very deer, and having performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and worshipped it, one should recite the four aforementioned seed-syllables two thousand times and bury it in the house of an enemy located in the eighth astrological sign from the enemy's birth star. By this, within a month—

Thus, by the specific power of the yantra, the enemy becomes utterly uprooted in every way; this is the uccāṭana-yantra (the uprooting yantra). Having written the yantra on the skin of any man whatsoever and with the blood of any man whatsoever, one should perform the ritual installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and worship it.

Having consecrated the four seed-syllables two thousand times, one should bury them in a cemetery at the time when the victim’s eighth zodiacal sign is rising. By this means, within a month, the victim shall meet death through the affliction of a burning fever. Thus it is said.
The ritual application for the destruction of one who intends to kill oneself:

having written the third seed-syllable— containing the name of the target (*sādhya*) and other details— in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), which is the location of the second seed-syllable, within the previously described line-diagram yantra using the blood of a person born under a specific lunar mansion (*nakṣatra-yoni*), [one should then place] the second, fourth, and sixth seed-syllables.

Having written it out by revolving as before, and having encircled it with the letters of the wind-mantra (*pavana-arṇa*) joined with the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) at the end, this yantra is perfected. Having encircled it properly so that there is no connection with water from the outside to the inside— just as with the inner yantra— and having smeared the exterior with ashes from a cremation ground, [it serves for] the fetching of lost water and other such purposes.

One should cast the enemy's natal ascendant into the water-well of the judicial officer; by that immersion in water, the death of the enemy shall occur. This is the "Water-Door" method for causing death. Furthermore, having written the previously mentioned yantra on a cow-hide with *citraka* ground with human blood, one should place it beneath a hearth and [keep it] upon it for one month.

One should also cause it to blaze continuously. By that means, the enemy's crossing [of obstacles] shall be rooted out by fire. This is the application for destruction through the medium of fire. Having written the aforementioned diagram with the powder of *citraka* root rubbed with human blood on the skin of a donkey, using the wings of a crow and an owl, one should bury it within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Then, having filled that [pit] with earth and ignited a fire upon it with *araṇī* wood of the tree belonging to the victim's birth constellation (*nakṣatra*), the enemy— who has attained madness through the oblation (*homa*) of *dhattūra* seeds smeared with pungent oil— shall meet his death.
Thus, this is the ritual for causing death by means of inducing madness. Having fashioned a stake from the wood of the *nakṣatra* tree of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*),
one should place upon it the diagram (*yantra*) written on the skin of a donkey as previously described.

Having wrapped it with the ashes of a donkey and the fat of a goat, one should bury it at night in the eighth house or the ascendant (lagna) within that city. By this means, that city will, within a month, become like a cremation ground—unapproachable and terrifying due to such conditions.
This is the application of the *sakīlayantra* for causing the evacuation of a city. Having drawn the very same *yantra* described in the *Pretacāra*:

Having bound [the effigy] by both feet with any one of the following—crow, owl, heron, hawk, crane, or partridge—one should bury it at a crossroads on a Tuesday during the rising of the eighth house from the enemy’s sign. By this means, within twenty-one days, the enemy will wander through the ten directions becoming insane; he shall not remain steady in even a single place.
Thus ends the application of the machine for expulsion (*uccāṭana*). Among the machines previously mentioned,

if one writes a certain machine on the skin or with the blood of any among elephants, horses, humans, cows, donkeys, camels, rams, or buffaloes, and buries it at that person's dwelling site, then within seven days, that person will certainly [be expelled].

Destruction may occur at any one of the months presided over by the Yakṣas. In this context, within the previously mentioned yantras, the letters of the name to be protected (sādhya-varṇa), joined with the letters of the wind (pavana-arṇa), are to be written everywhere; such is the yantra for destruction. Now, for the peace yantra (śānti-yantra):
having fashioned an eight-petalled [lotus] and having created a single path outside of it by means of two circles, [one should place] in the pericarp (karṇikā)...
Having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) containing the name of the person to be treated— such as "Oṃ, pacify such-and-such a disease without harming this body of Devadatta"—
starting from the front petal and writing the fifth, seventh, eighth, and ninth syllables twice over the eight yantras, [one should write] the *mātṛkā* in the surrounding path (*vīthī*).
"One should encircle" means that this *yantra* should be drawn with white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron on birch bark for the purpose of wearing it;
or, having drawn it on the ground for the purpose of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should perform the previously established ritual presiding over it.
Through the consecration with the water from the ritual jar (kalaśa), there occurs the pacification of all previously mentioned sufferings.
Now, the Vijaya-yantro (the Victorious Machine).

Having drawn thirteen lines each extending from east to west and from south to north, intersecting one another, one should produce one hundred and forty-four squares. Outside of that, having formed an eight-sided figure with two concentric square enclosures (*bhūpura*), and outside of that, with two parallel lines separated by an interval...
Having completed one row, having written the modified syllables starting from the northeast (Īśāna) square up to the southeast (Agni) square,

and then writing them again below that in the manner described, all the modified syllables will have been written. For indeed, by joining each of the nine mantra-syllables with the sixteen vowels, there are exactly that many [syllables].
The modified syllables (*vikṛtākṣara*) are produced as follows: the conjunction with the sixteen vowels, beginning with *ca* and connected with *ka* and so forth, is intended;
not merely by *ka* and so forth alone. Thus, *kra, krā, kri, kro, kru, krū*, and so on;
and *bhra, bhrā, bhri, bhrī, bhru, bhrū*, and so on. The modified syllables of *kro* and *krau* are identical in both ways.

The writings [are as follows]: through the union with the form of the vowels according to the *praṇava*, it results precisely in the form of the vowels. Here, in whichever place a syllable of the mantra is written in its altered form—such as *oṃ*, *krodhaḥ*, *krau*, *hau*, *chau*, *jau*, *svāhā*—and falls [into the sequence], therein [is placed] the end of that respective mantra-syllable, provided it is devoid of the *bindu*.
The diagram of the object to be accomplished (sādhya), the means of accomplishment (sādhaka), and so forth, is drawn in a square of thirteen (13),
twenty-nine (29), forty-five (45), sixty-two (62), or seventy-eight (78) cells.

The letters of the *sādhya* (the name to be accomplished) are established as follows: having caused them to enter the heart of the mantra-syllables located in the 94th cell (*śrutinanda*), the 110th cell (*svakṣmāku*), the 114th cell (*vidhibhūku*), and also the 130th cell (*khāgnīndu*).
Outside of that, on the eight-spoked [wheel], the fifth, seventh, eighth, and ninth letters are placed in the corners starting from the southeast (*āgneya*).

Having written [the mantra] by repeating it twice; one should write the first syllable in its prostrate form eight times within the intermediate spaces of the eight corners. On the outer path, the letters of the Mātṛkā and the letters of the *sādhya* are interlaced (*vidarbhitāni*). [The sequence is]: a ā uṃ u ī kroṃ u ū bhroṃ ṛ ṝṃ krauṃ ḷ ḷ hau aiṃ aiṃ chauṃ ū auṃ jrauṃ aṃ aḥ svākakhahāgadya.

Having completed the letters of the Mātṛkā in pairs according to the sequence beginning with "Oṃ" and so forth, one should write the letters of the *sādhya* (the name to be accomplished) in the same pair-by-pair sequence in the middle, following the manner of the mantra, one by one. And if this is done in such a way, there will be an excess of the mantra's letters even though they have been repeated again and again.

Therefore, syllables exceeding that [number] should not be taken for the purpose of *avidarbhaṇa*, because since *avidarbhaṇa* has already been completed, further addition would be purposeless. Thus, having drawn the perfected yantra upon a cloth, one should make that cloth-yantra a banner at the time of battle and display it facing the enemy army; by means of that, the enemies—

The enemy soldiers would flee to various different locations and not remain together; furthermore, it is the enemies who are intended here by the term "enemy," not merely the city itself as the enemy. Alternatively, the enemies who have turned away from the side of flight might offer their own fortune as a gift and perform a prostration—this is one application of this machine. Or else:
At the time of the heart [period] of the zodiac sign presided over by Saturn (p.
or during the rising of the elements water, ether, and earth, this yantra should be placed in the enemy's camp at the time of the rising and setting of Saturn.

The second application is that if it is buried during a mutual quarrel, there will be the immediate destruction of the enemy. If this very same yantra is buried in one's own city at the time of the rising of Jupiter, or in the heart of the zodiac sign presided over by Jupiter, or at the time of the rising or setting of Jupiter, or in the element of space or earth, then [it neutralizes] the malevolent rites performed by others; what need is there to say more? It destroys all roots of suffering.

The third application is that even sins do not remain there. Having engraved this very *yantra* on a copper plate, a king or other authority should install it at the eight directions and the center of the boundaries of his city. Alternatively, he should bury it in his own temple, treasury, elephant stable, or horse stable, at the time of the eleventh zodiac sign (*rāśi*), and perform daily worship at that location.

One should perform those respective rites for prosperity; this is the fourth application. Now, regarding the nine diagrams (*yantra*) formed with the nine-syllable mantra: having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should create a path (*vīthī*) outside of it, between two circles. Therein, the first seed-syllable (*bīja*) is placed in the pericarp.

Having written [the central syllable], one should write the eight syllables beginning with the second and ending with the ninth, one by one, in sequence in front [of the center]; then, one should perform an encirclement with the pure *mātṛkā* on the outer path. This is the first yantra. Having written the second seed-syllable in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and having filled the eight petals with those beginning with the third and ending with the first, this is the second yantra.

Having written the third seed-syllable in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), the third yantra is formed by filling the eight petals with the seed-syllables beginning with the fourth and ending with the first and second. For each of the seed-syllables beginning with the fourth,
[the syllables] starting from the fifth element corresponding to each respective one are placed in the center.
By filling the eight petals with the seed-syllables ending in the first, second, and third [vowels], six other yantras are also accomplished.
Their fruit is as follows: here, one's own birth-stars (svanakṣatras) are [to be placed] in one's own birth-star.
The tenth, eleventh, and nineteenth asterisms are intended here as synonyms for the "birth asterism" (*janmatārā*).

Furthermore, the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth asterisms following each respective [birth] asterism are what are intended by the terms "second," "third," and so forth. Thus, whichever asterism causes affliction by planets for the practitioner—

If there is suffering from the king, suffering from disease, or suffering from enemies, and that asterism occurs as the first, second, third, or up to the ninth from one's own asterism, then— according to what is taught for the first through the ninth— one should perform the wearing of the yantra and the consecration with the jar presided over by it.

The second application is as follows: having reduced to ashes the letters and medicinal herbs that constitute the specific vidyā under consideration, one should place the aforementioned yantra upon them. Then, by drinking the water containing those ashes and performing ritual ablutions (abhiṣeka) with it, there will be supreme protection for all people and deliverance from all calamities; such is the second application. These are the yantras.

There are nine yantras for the nine planets in sequence; by means of wearing, consecration, drinking, placing them above [the head], wearing the earth from beneath those yantras, worship, burying, and so forth, applied respectively to each of the first and subsequent yantras, the afflictions caused by the nine planets beginning with the Sun shall be pacified— this is the third [section].
The ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: having written some kind of yantra in the midst of water, having installed and worshipped it, [the result follows] from drinking that water.

The fourth application is that there shall be the pacification of all afflictions caused by poison. When, having first buried the primary yantra in the center of a region, city, village, or the like, one buries the eight secondary yantras in the eight directions starting from the east, then prosperity and the increase of dharma and wealth shall occur in that region. This is the second [application].

If, having dug from the center, the yantras beginning with the third and ending with the first are buried in the directions starting from the east, then all the people in that region will become unrighteous; however, the deities of those [yantras] will quickly become pleased toward the people of that region through worship and other means. In the case of digging in the middle of the third [yantra], it is as stated for the others.
By digging in the east and other directions, there is an increase in longevity; by digging in the center of the fourth, there is an increase in health;
by digging in the fifth, there is an increase in fame; by digging in the sixth, there is an increase in strength;
by digging in the seventh, there is an increase in sons; by digging in the eighth, there is an increase in knowledge; and [the same applies] in the center of the ninth.
The fourth application of digging is as follows: by digging in the directions starting from the east (pūrva) corresponding to the first [asterism] and so forth, there shall be an increase of wealth.

If a person suffers affliction due to the occupation of a particular asterism by malefic planets and so on, then in that specific asterism—whether it falls within the group of nine beginning with Aśvinī, the group of nine beginning with Maghā, or the group of nine beginning with Mūla—one should proceed accordingly.

Having sequentially drawn one of the nine yantras, beginning with the first and ending with the ninth, one should worship the relevant Nityā therein with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), preceded by her invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites.
This much is the specific distinction here: that the visualization (*dhyāna*) is not performed now according to the manner of visualization previously described for the daily practice (*nitya*).

However, in this context, that which is to be meditated upon is precisely the form identical to the respective deity of each lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Whether she be a woman, a girl, an old woman, or a brahmin woman,
if one wishes to perform the worship of the present *Nityā* together with her enclosures (*sāvaraṇā*), [one should meditate on her in that manner].

Even with the worship of Anirāvaraṇaka, those who are not patient [with the affliction] do not obtain the aforementioned result— the pacification of suffering— associated with each respective constellation, even if they possess devotion. Thus ends the fifth application for the pacification of suffering from the constellations (*nakṣatrapīḍopaśāmaka*).
Thus end the applications of the yantras.

Even for one afflicted by poison, through the recitation of the Bheruṇḍā-vidyā twice over a grain of mustard, the torment of the poison— which at that moment would be incurable even by physicians— is pacified.
Thus concludes the procedure for the recitation.
Having written one of the nine aforementioned yantras— using red sandalwood, red ochre, realgar, sandalwood, vermilion, rice, mung beans, black sesame, or white sesame, respectively—
with whatever materials have been prescribed for its acquisition, and having placed a water-pot there according to the stated procedure as before;

Having first performed the visualization of the wheel of Sarvamaṅgalā, and having completed the rites beginning with her worship along with the enclosures (sāvaraṇa), followed by recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and dismissal (visarjana), and then having performed the ritual procedure starting from the present daily invocation (nityāvāhana) up to the worship of the enclosures;

and having attained perfection through the Trailokyamohana-vidyā by means of one hundred thousand recitations, ten thousand fire-oblations, ten thousand libations (tarpaṇa), and worship— with that [vidyā], O Caitra...

The first day of the bright fortnight; the sun’s transit into Aries, Libra, Capricorn, and Cancer; one’s own birth asterism; its tenth asterism; its nineteenth asterism; the day of Jupiter’s birth; the day of attaining learning; one’s own birth day; the day of Jupiter’s conjunction with one’s natal asterism; a day when three syllables coincide; and any festival such as the full moon or the new moon.
One should perform the consecration at any one of the nine specified times.
p.
111b) For everyone who possesses devotion, including the consecrated officiant (*abhiṣekakarmatārāja*), his wife, her co-wife, the commander-in-chief (*senāpati*), and so forth.

The fee for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and the practitioner’s sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*), however, should be followed according to one's financial capacity without transgression; yet, when financial capacity exists, the very rite of consecration would consume the consecrated person along with his sons, wife, and fortune. Once the offering of all available wealth has been made, there remains only the power to alleviate the hunger and suffering of the donor together with his family.

The absence of giving material wealth constitutes the obstacle of poverty (*vitta-śāṭyam*). Furthermore, there is the non-giving of what is prescribed for giving, such as "one part to the Guru" and so forth. Regarding the nature of the conjunction of the three syllables on the *parvan* day:
the first syllable of the daily *nityā* for that day is the syllable of the rising of that day; [this is determined] within the total count of days (*ahargaṇa*) of that specific day.

When the number of days is divided by thirty-six, the remainder is the number of syllables; thus, the day on which there is only one syllable is called a "parvan" (sacred festival) of that kind. The first syllable of the Kālanityā-vidyā consists solely of the *tattva* (principle).
The day on which those three— the second syllable, the syllable of the *ghaṭikā*, and [the first syllable]— become one,
is considered by others to be such a festival (*parva*); that is, on whichever day the three syllables that constitute the mantra of Śrī Tripurasundarī become one.

Another opinion holds that the meaning is derived from the consonantal coincidence (*akṣara-saṃnipāta*) of the syllables of the year, the month, and the hour, such that the conjunction with those deities constitutes a *parvan*; this is the meaning of the word "conjunction" (*sampāta*) consisting of three syllables. An example of the Trailokyamohana-vidyā is as follows:
*aṃ oṃ kroṃ bhroṃ krauṃ jhauṃ chauṃ jrauṃ svāhā aṃ āṃ oṃ-mādi da āṃ*.

Paṃ phaṃ 9, phaṃ vaṃ 9, vaṃ bhaṃ 9, bhaṃ maṃ 9, maṃ yaṃ 9, yaṃ raṃ 9, raṃ laṃ 9, laṃ vaṃ 9, vaṃ śaṃ 9, śaṃ ṣaṃ 9, ṣaṃ saṃ 9, saṃ haṃ 9, haṃ laṃ 9, kṣaṃ 9, kṣam—this consists of five hundred and sixty-one syllables. Alternatively: oṃ kroṃ dhoṃ krau jhauṃ chrauṃ.

*jrauṃ svāhā*. By means of such methods—enclosing all the phonemes of the Mātṛkā with mantras according to the sequence *aṃ oṃ kroṃ bhrauṃ jhauṃ chrauṃ jrauṃ svāhā* and so forth—one forms the reality (tatva) of them; thus there are nine hundred and sixty-nine syllables. The arrangement of these [syllables] depends on the abundance or scarcity of results, speed, and so forth. Likewise, [this applies] to other mantras and vidyās as well.

Through the combination with the letters of the *mātṛkā*, those [results] become manifold. Thus, the fruit of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) consists of the removal of the fruits of evil yogas such as *kemadruma* and others, the attainment of sons endowed with the qualities of living beings,
and the removal of the connection to the adverse fruits produced by ill-omened marks and wicked karma, as previously described.
Through initiation at all nine auspicious parvas, one attains liberation while living (jīvanmukti), and in the end, at Śiva, there shall be the attainment of union (sāyujya).
Thus concludes the introductory section on the eternal Bheruṇḍā.
Now, the Nityā Vahnivāsinī is introduced.

Having constructed two square enclosures (*bhūpura*) on a clean, level ground, each equipped with door-frames in the eastern and western directions, and having drawn two circles with a four-finger interval between them outside of all [the squares],
one should fashion a twelve-petaled lotus in the path between those two.
In the space between those two, having drawn two circles with an interval of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*),
one should extract the wheel of nine sources (*navayonicakra*) together with its central point (*bindu*) within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that circle. Herein:

The intervening space between the circle at the tip of the petals and the circle at the tip of the *yoni* is exactly one *aṅgula*. The method for drawing the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*) is as follows: having constructed a triangle within the previously mentioned circles, with its three corners touching the circle and facing toward oneself; then, from the line in the eastern portion, moving outward...
Having drawn another north-south line in the eastern portion, touching the circle and equal in measure [to the first],
one should then construct two other triangles, each having its apex at the midpoint of the previous triangle.
Extending the lines from those two apices until they meet the circle-line in the western portion, from those two points...
Having constructed a triangle whose upper line touches the tips of the lines forming the eastern portion [of the diagram],
one should place a *bindu* within the triangle of the completed nine-yoni wheel (*navayonikacakra*). Therein,

during initiation (*dīkṣā*), preceded by the visualization of the wheel based upon the water contained in the jar (*kalaśa*) established in the sky, [one performs the rite] together with its enclosures (*sāvaraṇa*).

Having performed the additional rites beginning with the worship of Sarvamaṅgalā and ending with her dismissal (*udvāsana*), the practitioner, whose body has been purified by bathing in fragrant water and other such means, enters the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) for the sake of the present daily worship (*nityapūjā*). Furthermore, that procedure—whether in that very same jar (*kalaśa*) or elsewhere in the *cakra*—is as follows: [the practitioner] having arrived at the sacrificial pavilion...

Having performed the worship of the seat with the aforementioned *āsana-vidyās*, and having sat there while praising with the previously mentioned *vidyā*, one should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of that very *vidyā* and then begin; therein, having first worshipped the Lord and meditated upon oneself as the nature of the deity, non-different from the Lord.

Having worshipped the thirty-eight deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), ending with the circle of *siddhayoginīs* whose locations, times, and so forth are determined by the distinctions of their respective years.

Having offered the *bali* with the seven-syllable mantra "Kurukulle svāhā," one should worship the nine lords according to the lineage of one's own guru using their respective mantras; having recited their hymn of praise and received their permission, one should place the *rocanā* together with its support between the worship and one's own head, within the *yantra* of one's self.

Having placed a common vessel made of any one of the five materials such as gold and filled with water scented with camphor, saffron, agallochum, and musk, and having visualized the waters in its supporting vessel as being of the nature of fire, sun, and moon by means of the three *bījas* of Kulasundarī in their respective order, [one should visualize] the five substances such as *rocanā* as earth and so forth in sequence.

Having contemplated [the water] as consisting of the five elements, and having contemplated the identity between that water and the *nityāpūjācakra* currently under discussion, one should consecrate the water— contemplated as being of the very nature of the present *nityā*— ten times with the present *vidyā*, and then worship it.

Having worshipped the six limbs and the deities of those six limbs with the six-limbed mantras, one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the water for bathing (*snāna*)— each contained in its respective vessel— with that water and the present vidyā. [One should also offer] the garments, ornaments, perfumes, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*) placed in one's own right-hand portion.

Having consecrated each of the betel leaves contained in their respective vessels, and having again performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the Vidyā-mantra, one should take flowers, unbroken rice (akṣata), and water in the right hand; then, having articulated the place, time, lineage (gotra), zodiac sign (rāśi), name, and desire, and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "I shall perform the daily worship of the Nityā Vahnivāsinī according to the prescribed rite as best as my intellect permits," [one proceeds]. Mātṛkā...

Having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) preceded by the aforementioned daily mantra (*nityavidyā*), one should pronounce each letter of the *mātṛkā* alphabet one by one at its respective location as prescribed, and [place them] with: *hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śirase svāhā*, *hrūṃ*...

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras— *śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *hariṃ kavacāya huṃ hrauṃ*, *netrāya vauṣaṭ*, and *astrāya phaṭ*— upon one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as upon the heart and other parts of the body; [and having placed] *oṃ* on the right eye, *hrīṃ* on the left eye,
*vaṃ* on the right ear, *hiṃ* on the left ear, *vāṃ* on the right nostril, *siṃ* on the left nostril, *nyaiṃ* on the mouth, and *naṃ* on the anus.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the nine syllables— *maḥ guhye* and so forth— upon the nine apertures, and having performed the threefold pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the complete mantra of nine syllables, *oṃ hrīṃ vahnivāsinyai namaḥ*, preceded by the display of the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā.

Having visualized the mass of flowers held in the joined palms (*añjali*) as having been transferred via the path of the central channel (*vaha-nāsā-mārga*)—having first been manifested from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*—into the central *bindu*, one should imagine that it is transferred by the casting of those flower-offerings (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, at the end of the complete recitation of the mantra, [one says]: "O Nityā Vahnavāsinī, here in this wheel (*cakra*)."

Having prayed, "Be invoked," one should contemplate some rays of that light as having issued forth from the locations to be described below, transformed into the form of the Lord's weapons, retinue, and powers,
[and then dissolve them] into the mass of light situated in the center.
One should meditate on her as transformed by the essential nature understood through the verses on meditation. That meditation is as follows:
[one should meditate on her] resembling molten gold, beautiful in the bloom of fresh youth, with a lotus-face graced by a lovely smile, and possessing three shimmering eyes.
She is endowed with eight arms, radiant with rubymine ornaments,
and she dyes the sky crimson with the intermingling rays of her ruby crown.
Clad in yellow silk garments, with red anklets and a girdle,
radiant with ornaments consisting of clusters interspersed with jewels and pearls,
she holds in her left arms a red lotus, a beautiful *puṇḍra* flower, a bow of sugarcane, and the orb of the full moon.

She holds a white water-lily (*kahlāra*), a golden horn, and a citron (*mātuluṅga*) in her right hands, and is surrounded on all sides by *Śaktis* who resemble herself; such is the visualization of the Lord’s weapons and all the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*). Furthermore, each [deity] possesses a crown marked with their respective insignia, and this is the only difference regarding the weapons. Thereafter—

"O Vahnavāsinī, who resides at the end of the present vidyā, be established here in this cakra! Again, at the end of twenty-one syllables, be firmly restrained (sanniruddhā)! Again, at the end of twenty-one syllables, be veiled (avaguṇṭhitā)!
Again, at the end of twenty-one syllables, be made present (sannidhāpitā)!"—having thus spoken, preceded by the display of the mudrās.

Having offered prayers, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs upon the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, one should perform the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra in the form "The vital breaths of this Vahnivāsinī Nityā are here in this wheel," etc.,
while touching the instrument that contains the life-force.
One should worship with the twelve services using that mantra as follows: "Oṃ hrīṃ vahnivāsinyai namaḥ;
vahnivāsinīnityāyai pādyaṃ kalpayāmi.
Having offered the water for the feet (*pādya*) with the general *arghya* water using this twenty-three-syllable mantra, one should proceed.
Having spoken thus, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the two words of the nine-syllable mantra. In the same manner, omitting the word *pādya*,

one should sequentially assign the words for the ritual services beginning with the water for respectful offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and ending with betel (*tāmbūla*), to those respective positions.

Having offered the various *arghya*, *ācamana*, and other services with perfected mantras, one should present [the offerings] at the head, face, and other parts using the primary *vidyā*. Then follows the thirteen-fold service (*trayodaśopacāra*); its procedure is as follows: on the back of the Goddess are *prakāśa*, *vimarśa*, and *ānanda*.

Having worshipped the nine lords (Navanātha) by name— Śrījñānaśrī, Satyaśrī, Pūrṇasvabhāva, Pratibha, Subhaga, and so on— with their respective mantras, placing the words for power (*śakti*) at each step of the word "lord" (*nātha*),
one should [worship] in the pathways on both sides, in the vicinity of the left lower hand and other areas, with: *hrīṃ pūrṇendumaṇḍalāya namaḥ*.

Having worshipped the eight weapons with: *hrīṃ puṇḍrekṣucāpāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ kaṃvave namaḥ*, *hrīṃ raktāñjāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ kahlārāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ hemaśṛṅgāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ puṣpeṣubhyaḥ namaḥ*, *hrīṃ mātuluṅgāya namaḥ*, [one worships] in the eight corners.

In relation to the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*), starting from the front and proceeding clockwise, one worships the aforementioned Śaktis with the following mantras: *hrīṃ jvālinīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ visphuliṅginīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ maṅgalāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ sumanoharāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ kanakāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*,
*hrīṃ kitavāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ viśvāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and *hrīṃ vividhāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having performed the worship, at the conclusion of the complete mantra, one should worship the Goddess situated in the center with the words: "I worship the *pādukā* of the eternal Vahnivāsinī. Then: *Hrīṃ*. These are the deities of the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*) of the eternal Vahnivāsinī; [this concludes] the worship.
Saying "May they accept," one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering. Then, on the twelve petals, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise, one should worship:
*hrīṃ* I worship Meṣāpādukā; *hrīṃ* Vṛṣāpādukā; *hrīṃ* Mithunāpādukā; *hrīṃ* Karkaṭāpādukā; *hrīṃ* Siṃhāpādukā; *hrīṃ* Kanyāpādukā; *hrīṃ* Tulāpādukā; *hrīṃ* Vṛścikāpādukā; *hrīṃ* Dhanurāpādukā.
Having worshipped the powers of the directions with the mantras: "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Makarāpā," "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Kumbhāpā," and "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Mīnāpādukā";

and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the conclusion of the complete Vidyā with the mantra: "I worship the sandals of the Nityā Vahnivāsinī"; [one worships] these Vahnivāsinyas with "Hrīṃ."

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering of worship with the words, "May the deities of the eternal, non-dual enclosure accept this worship," one worships *hrīṃ dyasmarāpādukāṃ* on the northern path of the western gate of the square;
*hrīṃ sarvabhakṣyapādukaṃ* in the northwest (*vāyavya*); *hrīṃ viśvāśāpādukāṃ* on the northern path; and [worships] in the northeast (*īśāna*).
Hrīṃ Hrīṃ! I worship the goddess Vividhodbhavāpādukā. On the southern path of the eastern gate:
Hrīṃ Citrarūpāpādukā; in the southeast: Hrīṃ Sapatnāpādukā; on the southern path: Hrīṃ Nirātaṅkāpādukā;
in the southwest: Hrīṃ Pāvinīpādukā; on the southern path of the western gate, in the downward direction: Hrīṃ...

Having worshipped those respective Śaktis with the mantras: "Hrīṃ! I worship the sandals of Raktāpādukā in the northern lane of the eastern gate in the upper direction," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the Mūlavidyā with the mantra: "I worship the sandals of the Nityā Vahnivāsinī," [one recites]: "Hrīṃ! These..."
"May the deities of the third enclosure, the Vahnivāsins, accept the offering"—with these words, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an oblation for that worship.
Then, having offered the three-fold service (*upacāra*) to Vasiṣṭha consisting of whatever hymns, recitations, libations, and prostrations [are appropriate],

and having performed the daily recitation (*japa*) with a count of either one hundred or one thousand, one should perform the offering (*nivedana*) characterized by the contemplation of non-difference from him,
according to the prescribed method as being non-distinct from the Goddess at hand.

Having offered sixteen oblations— consisting of the cultivated brilliance of fire and so forth— and ten additional oblations in accordance with the ten-part proportion, one should withdraw that splendor from the fire back into the *bindu* (drop) within the *cakra* (wheel) where the Goddess resides. Then,
having worshipped the Goddess situated in the *bindu-cakra* again with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should [proceed] as before even now with the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā.

Having offered the *bali* and performed the *nīrājana* with camphor-filled wicks and other offerings, and having asked for forgiveness (*kṣamāpya*), one should dissolve all the powers (*śakti*) residing in the wheel into the principal goddess by means of the *śaktyutthāpana-mudrā*. Then, dissolving her into one's own self by means of the *khecarī-mudrā*, one should perform the placement of the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) and the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*) as before, and [recite] the hymn of praise.

The specific procedure for initiation and worship is precisely as previously stated: one should recite the *Devīstotra* consisting of twelve verses. Thus, a practitioner (*sādhaka*) who has received initiation and has mastered the methods of worship and so forth, and who possesses the mantra that brings about the fruits of ritual application, should perform this means of accomplishment once that [mantra] has been established within himself. The method for that is as follows:
Having first performed anointment with fragrant water and partaken of sacrificial food (*haviṣyāhāra*) and other such items, during either the spring or summer season,

one should sit upon a red seat— either a *svastika* or a *padma* posture— on a red throne in a place adorned with consciousness and other [elements], situated within a red chamber as previously described, and prepared with a ritual grass mat (*kūrca*) and a mandala (*cakra*).
At the end of the full moon of the thirty-second *sāvana* day, calculated from the beginning of the practitioner's [practice] period,

at the conclusion of one's daily obligatory worship (*svanityapūjā*) and daily recitation (*nityajapa*) during the three junctions of the day (*trisandhya*), [one should perform] three hundred and twenty-five [recitations] every day.

By reciting thirty-two thousand times over the course of thirty-two days, one should complete the count of one hundred thousand. Since this vidyā consists of eight syllables, if one performs three hundred thousand recitations for each syllable, the success of the *puraścaraṇa* recitation in the Satya Yuga is achieved at a total of ninety-six million recitations.

In the present age, the recitation (*japa*) is accomplished by way of a hundred thousand repetitions; and if that cannot be performed by oneself, it must be carried out through a preceptor, a disciple, or a Brahmin.

At the conclusion of the recitation, one should master the *vidyā* by performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth of that number, followed by an equal number of water-libations (*tarpaṇa*), feeding Brahmins, and giving a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor, and so forth. Then, from that point on—
Having obtained permission, one should perform the ritual applications (*prayoga*). Now follow these daily ritual applications. Among them, the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) is as follows:

in a fire consecrated according to the prescribed rules for oblations, one should [offer] sixteen *palas* (the measure of a *prastha*) of rice grains into a *prastha* measure of milk from a cow that has a red calf and is herself red in color.

Having cooked it, once it has become fully cooked, one should soak it in clarified butter, mix it with sugar, take it in hand, and after reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should offer it as an oblation on the first lunar day (pratipad) for the duration of a year;
by that, the attainment of Mahālakṣmī shall occur. Likewise, if performed every Friday for a year using that same sacrificial offering (havis), [the same result is achieved].

The *homa* of the practitioner shall bring about equality with a king in terms of sovereignty. By performing *homa* on the fifth lunar day with white jasmine and other flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), and by performing *homa* with food and ghee, one becomes abundant in food.

Through the oblation of pure ghee, sesame seeds, and rice, there may be the accomplishment of all desired goals; by performing worship with white flowers on the fifth lunar day (pañcamī), by observing a fast or a milk-vow on the fifth lunar day, and by making one’s resolve true, there shall be the accomplishment of the desired goal. Now follow the applications of this Nityā Yantra: having constructed two circles with an intervening space between them...

Having constructed an eight-spoked wheel with two square enclosures within that intermediate space, and having further produced two paths outside of that by means of two circles assisted by the tips of the eight corners, one should write the *māyā-bīja* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) containing the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the object of practice (*sādhya*), and so forth in the center; then, one should encircle the *māyā* with the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) on the outside.

Having written the eight vowels beginning with *a*—which are forms derived from the *praṇava* (oṃ) and constitute the letters of the present mantra—starting from the front corner in the eight auspicious corners;
and having written the ten elemental letters corresponding to one's desire in the first enclosure; [and] in the outer enclosure...

One should write the letters of the alphabet beginning with *ma* and ending with *kṣa*; this is the first yantra. In the very same yantra previously described, one should write the eight letters beginning with *ḷ* in the place where *a* and the others were located; this is the second yantra. For in this vidyā, the letters *ū*, *ha*, *ra*, *va*, *na*, *sa*, *pa*, and *ma* are the non-repeated letters.

There are eight [syllables] for each of these; when joined with the sixteen vowels, there are one hundred and twenty-eight modified syllables (*vikṛtavarṇa*). In that regard, by means of the sixteen modified syllables associated with each individual mantra-syllable, two yantras are accomplished for each. Among those, the modified syllable of the vowel *u*—
The two completed diagrams have been shown. By this same method,
[the diagrams] should also be formed for each individual letter of the mantra syllables, from *ha* to *ma*, arranged in pairs according to their sequence.

Having combined them, fourteen machines (yantras) are to be produced; thus, together with the two previously mentioned machines, sixteen machines are completed. Among them, the result of the first machine, along with its procedure, is as follows: the root of red *citraka* and *sinūra*—these two [are to be processed] with the juice of the root of red *citraka* and the juice of the leaves of *dhattūra*.

Having ground [the ingredients] with that liquid, one should write the first yantra on a shallow pan (kharpara) and, while reciting the established Nityā-vidyā at night, heat it with charcoal from Khadira wood. By this, the attraction of men, women, kings, and others who are worthy of being drawn occurs. Or else, if...

Having written this very same yantra on either a copper plate or a bell-metal plate according to the aforementioned method, if it is heated at night with charcoal from the *khadira* tree, then there occurs the attraction of all those whose names are inscribed within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that yantra. As for the result of the second yantra: on a broken earthenware shard (*kharpara*).

Having drawn a second "liberated" yantra with a substance prepared by rubbing vermilion with the juice of the root of red citra and the juice of the leaves of dhattūra, if one heats it at night with charcoal from the khadira tree, then all the women whose names are inscribed within the pericarp of that yantra— along with their family duties, customs, and so forth— [will be revealed].
Having even abandoned [worldly attachments], one becomes self-controlled. For a practitioner of inferior birth, the fruit of the third yantra is as follows:

having written the third [yantra] composed of distorted syllables such as *ha*, *hā*, *hi*, *hī*, etc., using the juice of *dhattūra* rubbed with the root of *citraka* and red-colored [pigment] in a skull-cup (*kharpara*), and having released one's hair at night—

If one should heat it in a funeral pyre fire, then at that very moment the enemy— whose name has been written upon the pericarp of the aforementioned yantra— will be afflicted by fever. [One should do this] with charcoal from a funeral pyre, having ground it with the juice of *nimba* until it has become a liquid paste.

Having drawn the third yantra on a shard of pottery and heated it with charcoal from the *khadira* tree, one should—with a mind full of wrath—chant the aforementioned vidyā while the enemy is in the eighth house or the ascendant at the time of birth, and bury it in a cremation ground. Then, at that very moment, the enemy will become agitated and possessed by a *piśāca*. As for the result of the fourth yantra:

On a cloth or garment that is black in color, or on a black cotton rag, having drawn the fourth yantra with the aforementioned substance and heated it with charcoal from *khadira* wood, one should bury it at night in a cremation ground during the rising of the eighth house of the enemy’s zodiacal sign.
By this means, the enemy will go to the abode of Yama within seven days due to the affliction of fever. This is the result of the fifth yantra.

For example: having written [the enemy's name] once each on two shards with a stylus made from the feathers of a crow and an owl using the aforementioned liquid, one should bury them at a cremation ground, at the junction of two rivers, or in a river full of water, when the enemy’s eighth zodiac sign is rising; by that means—

Enmity is accomplished between two enemies whose names are inscribed upon the [respective] yantras. The sixth yantra also functions in this same way by means of such a procedure. Alternatively, having taken two shards of pottery and having inscribed the fifth and sixth yantras separately upon them for the sake of the crow and the owl, [one should proceed].

By burying [the yantra] in the previously mentioned location, the attainment of the stated results occurs. As for the fruit of the seventh yantra: having rubbed a lead leaf with the juice of neem leaves, one should write the name of the person to be affected (sādhya) and so forth within a pericarp using charcoal from a funeral pyre;
then, having written this seventh yantra, one should place it inside a human skull.
At night, one should bury [the enemy's image] in a cremation ground under the ascendant of the eighth house from the enemy; by this, the enemy becomes possessed by a piśāca.

The result of the eighth yantra is as follows: having drawn the eighth yantra using the very substances prescribed by Kharpara, one should bury it at the door of the house of the enemy of the fire belonging to the eighth zodiac sign; by that means, the enemy is expelled from every region within seven days, remaining only in his own home. The result of the ninth yantra is as follows: on a Sunday...

During a Siddhi-yoga, at an auspicious lagna, under the presiding deity of Jupiter, or during the rising of either Sagittarius or Pisces, or at the time of the aforementioned Jupiter's heliacal rising, one should write the ninth yantra on a gold plate with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron; having engraved it and placed it upon one's own ring, one should perform the rite of Prāṇapratiṣṭhā (the invocation of life-force).

Worship and the offering of a guru’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā) constitute the entire [rite]. For the practitioner who maintains [the mantra] preceded by consecration with a jar presided over by that yantra, there shall be no touch of suffering such as sorcery (kṛtyā), untimely death, disease, poverty, and so forth. As for the tenth fruit of the yantra: having inscribed it on a silver plate with sandalwood, camphor, and other substances prescribed for the yantra of grace (anugraha-yantra).

For the practitioner who places it in some secluded spot within his own home and worships it daily, no suffering such as the stroke of Saturn (śanipāta) shall occur, even if it has already arrived at his hands or body. Furthermore, for one who wears this very yantra around the neck, on the hand, or elsewhere, there is protection from the afflictions of spirits, ghosts, and the like. The fruit of the eleventh yantra is as follows: [on] birch bark.

Having drawn, as before, a yantra with eleven petals and eight corners filled with the eight letters *sa*, *sā*, *si*, *sī*, *su*, *sū*, *sṛ*, and *sṝ*, with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and others placed within the pericarp, and having ground it into a paste, one should place it inside a lump shaped like a *śivamaya* liṅga.

Having performed the ritual worship of the deity at hand, preceded by the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (invocation of the life-force) and other rites, and having placed the bowl of honey and other offerings therein, one should worship it daily with fragrant white flowers and whatever fruits are available during the three junctions of the day.

Within seven days, fifteen days, or at the latest within a month, the practitioner’s enemies will certainly be brought under control. If one desires to cause illness, even healthy enemies will become ill; conversely, even those who are ill will attain health through various methods such as dhāraṇā, consecration (abhiṣeka), drinking water from a vessel empowered by that [mantra], and so forth.

It yields results that are very difficult to obtain; it shall come to pass through the power and majesty of the *yantra*. Those afflicted by fever shall, in an instant and without effort—even without following the procedures such as ritual ablution (*abhiṣeka*)—become happy. These are the four applications of this *yantra*, which require no further ritual manual (*kartavyatā*); they have been declared [to be performed] in fermented gruel (*bhūtakāñjika*).

If a lotus-liṅga distinguished by this yantra is placed [therein] and worshipped as before, then enmity between two mutual enemies is accomplished. Furthermore, if this yantra is boiled in *sovīra* (sour gruel), then there is a destruction of their mutual enmity;
and if there is a desire for it, there shall also be the destruction of the diseases of those two enemies.

Then, having placed this very yantra into finely ground ginger, black pepper, and long pepper mixed with the juice of *lakucha* fruit, the practitioner, facing the direction of the enemy’s eighth house at the three junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*) during the enemy’s eighth lunar mansion,
heats it over charcoal from the *khadira* tree; at that time, [the enemy] becomes possessed by heat and thirst.
The enemy shall be afflicted by fever. As for the result of the twelve-fold yantra: having drawn the twelve-fold yantra on a piece of cloth with a solution of turmeric...
Having joined two bricks together so that they are firmly embraced,

one should place that embraced mechanical device and the pair of bricks either in a temple of Caṇḍikā, in the house of a master, in their respective places of rest, or within the wall of one's own house; then, the enemy’s anger, preparations for battle and the like, and the intent to perform other harmful acts [will be neutralized].

One should paralyze transactions such as the giving of wealth, as well as eating, sleeping, speaking, and conversing.
