The result of the thirteenth yantra is as follows: having inscribed the thirteenth yantra on birch bark with camphor and sandalwood, and having performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and offered the oblation (*argha*), a woman who wears it—even if she is barren—shall obtain a son. Fourteen.

The result of the yantra is as follows: Having written the yantra fourteen times with camphor and sandalwood on a leaf of the *bhūrja* tree and placed it inside a ball of dough, if the practitioner heats it at midnight with charcoal from the *khadira* tree, then within seven days men, women, and kings will certainly become submissive. What need is there to say more? Even elephants and horses [will be subdued].
Even serpents, tigers, and other [beasts] will remain submissive and stay [there]. This is the result of the fifteenth yantra. For example:

on a board made of *palāśa* wood or similar, one should draw a lotus with its pericarp enriched by the *māyā-bīja* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) containing the name of the person to be acted upon—such as "Devadatta"—and the words "perform, perform the easy delivery for this woman Devadatta," using sandalwood and camphor.

Having drawn the fifteen-fold yantra consisting of eight corners joined by the verse beginning with "mamāmimi," the easy delivery of women shall occur through its worship, observation, wearing, and the consecration with water from a jar empowered by it.
As for the fruit of the sixteen-fold yantra: on birch bark, [draw] the sixteenth [yantra] with sandalwood and camphor.
For one who draws this yantra and wears it, there is protection from the fear of malevolent planets, diseases, and other such dangers.
This very same yantra, when engraved upon a gold plate, [is to be used for] recitation (japa) and worship (pūjā).
The practitioner, having first performed the consecration with the jar presided over by that [deity], and having placed [the mantra] upon necklaces, armlets, neck-chains, and so forth, wears them;

thus liberated from mental and physical ailments, free from enemies, having conquered sin and the fickleness of the senses, he experiences various pleasures such as those derived from women and the groves of Mount Kailāsa.
Performing meritorious deeds such as sacrifices, Vedic study, and charity, one may remain on earth for a lifespan of one hundred years.
Thus ends the introduction to the Nityā Vahnivāsinī.
Now, the Nityā Mahāvajreśvarī is introduced.

Having constructed two square enclosures (*bhūpura*) on a pure ground, each provided with door-frames on the four sides, extending entirely outward; and having fashioned three such squares within them with an interval of four finger-breadths between each;
[one should draw] a sixteen-petaled lotus on the outer path and a twelve-petaled lotus on the inner path.
Having fashioned that [mandala], having constructed a hexagon within its pericarp, having drawn two circles inside it,

and having drawn a triangle within those two circles with its apex facing oneself, one should place a bindu in its pericarp; thus, having fashioned the mandala for daily worship (*nityapūjācakra*), one should place the water-pot (*kalaśa*) therein, and within its water—
After performing the ritual sequence beginning with the visualization of the *sarvamaṅgalā* worship-circle along with its enclosures (*sāvaraṇa*),

including its worship and concluding with its dismissal (*udvāsana*), one performs the worship of the present *nityā* preceded by the visualization of the present *nityā*-circle; this involves visualizing the circle as the drop (*bindu*) constituting that location, which is presided over by the water-pot (*kalaśa*).
However, because the locations of the enclosures (*āvṛti*) have not been occupied by anyone else, their worship is performed precisely in their respective places.
This same method applies to all fifteen *Nityās* in the daily worship that is distinct from the initiation rites (*dīkṣāṅga*). [End of page 120a] It has been stated.

The worship is indeed performed upon the *cakra*. Its procedure is as follows: having first anointed himself with fragrant oil and bathed with perfumed waters, the practitioner—adorned with red garments, sandalwood paste, garlands, and ornaments, and with a mind free from distraction—having entered the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), sits upon a seat such as a red woolen rug that has been consecrated with the previously mentioned mantras for the seat.
Having assumed either the *svastika* or *padma* posture by means of this very rite, and having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this same mantra,
one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with the seven-syllable mantra "Oṃ Kurukulle Svāhā," and [worship] upon one's own head according to the lineage of one's gurus.

Having worshipped the nine lords with their respective mantras, recited their hymn of praise, and requested permission for the worship, one who has received that authorization should begin the rite. Having contemplated oneself as the embodiment of the daily practice (nityā) presented by one’s own lord, and as non-different from that lord, [one should proceed] according to the specific place, time, and other factors determined by the rules for each particular year.
One should worship all the thirty-eight deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), ending with the circle of the *yoginīs* who possess both secret and manifest accomplishments.
The specific distinction here is that, having worshipped as far as the Ocean of Milk with the aforementioned mantras, one should worship with:
*hrīṃ oṇāṣvaye namaḥ* and *hrīṃ hemapotāya namaḥ*.
Again, having worshipped the previously mentioned deities of the *pīṭhas*, beginning with the continents (*dvīpa*) and ending with the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*),

and having worshipped with "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Jewel Lion-Throne" (*hrīṃ ratnasiṃhāsanāya namaḥ*), one should contemplate the present circle of worship (*pūjācakra*) situated upon that. Then, between one's own self and the *yantra*, [one should place] the *gorocanā* together with its support.

Having placed the general *arghya* vessel filled with water scented with camphor, saffron, agallochum, and musk, [the practitioner] [should purify] the waters in its supporting vessel with the three *kula-sundarī* seed-syllables.

Having sequentially meditated upon the forms of fire, sun, and moon, as well as the five substances such as *gorocanā* contained therein— which consist of the five elements beginning with earth— and having meditated on the identity between that water and the present *nityā*-wheel, one should consecrate the water— visualized as being of the nature of the present *nityā*— ten times with the present *vidyā*, and then worship it.

Having worshipped the deities of the six limbs with the mantras of the six limbs, one should, with that water and the present vidyā, [purify] oneself and the waters for the feet (pādya), the guest-offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the bathing water (snāna)— each contained in its respective vessel— which have been placed in successive positions starting from the general arghya-vessel.

Having sprinkled with water the garments, ornaments, perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel leaves placed on one's own right side, as well as the respective vessels containing them; and having again performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *vidyā* mantra, taking the water for the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) in the hand, one should recite the place, time, lineage, zodiacal sign, name, and purpose.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) according to the rule, in accordance with the application of my intellect, for the eternal Mahāvajreśvarī," and having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā*, one should place each letter of the *mātṛkā* in its respective location at the end of the present eternal mantra (*nityavidyā*) in due order. [Then recite: *hrīṃ klinne hrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-limbed mantras upon one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as the heart and other body parts—namely: *hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śirase svāhā*; *hrīṃ krauṃ hrīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; *hrīṃ nityā hrīṃ kavacāya huṃ*;
*hrīṃ madahrīṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ*; *hrīṃ draghe hrīṃ astrāya phaṭ*—[one should then place them] on the right eye with *hrīṃ kliṃ hrīṃ*.

*Hrīṃ* *Nne*, *hrīṃ* *Vyamanetre*; *hrīṃ* *Aiṃ* *hrīṃ* on the right ear; *hrīṃ* *Kroṃ* *hrīṃ* on the left ear; *hrīṃ* *Hrīṃ* on the right nostril; *hrīṃ* *Tya* *hrīṃ* on the left nostril; *hrīṃ* *Mahrīṃ* on the speech; *hrīṃ* *Da* *hrīṃ* on the chest.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) by enveloping the syllables of the mantra—*hrīṃ drahrīṃ* at the two names (the heart), and *hrīṃ vehrīṃ* at the secret place—one should perform the three-fold pervasive placement (*tridhā-vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with this twelve-syllable present vidyā: *hrīṃ klinne aiṃ kro nityamadadrave hrīṃ*. Then, preceded by the display of the Tri-khaṇḍā mudrā...

Visualizing that the mass of red flowers held in one's own joined palms has been transferred via the path of the central channel— the radiance of the present *nityā-vidyā* which pervades from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*— one should contemplate it as having arrived at the circle (*cakra*) of the present [deity] through the casting of that handful of flowers, thereby becoming complete.

At the end of the *vidyā*, having performed the invocation with the prayer, "O Bhīmamahāvajreśvarī Nityā, be invoked here in this wheel," one [visualizes] some rays of that splendor issuing forth from the various locations to be described hereafter, in the form of the Lords (*nātha*), weapons, retinues (*āvaraṇa*), and powers (*śakti*).
Having meditated upon [the seed-syllables] transformed, one should meditate on a mass of one's own light in the center,
with some rays emanating toward the various aforementioned locations in the form of the Lord, his weapons, the protective enclosure, and the Śaktis.
Having meditated upon [the seed-syllables] transformed, one should meditate on a mass of one's own light in the center.
One should meditate upon [the deity] as not transformed from the nature understood through the verses on meditation. As for the meditation:

[She is] red, dressed in red garments, adorned with red perfumes and garlands, four-armed, three-eyed, and radiant with a crown of rubies; likewise holding a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and an arrow made of *tāḍimī* wood.
She holds [the weapon] in her arms and gazes with eyes that are exceedingly cool with compassion at the practitioner within the six-cornered lotus of the weapon;
she is seated in the center of the wheel, her lotus-face smiling,
surrounded by powers who are her own forms, situated in the middle of a boat.
Surrounded by Śaktis who have emerged from the lion-throne and from the swaying seats, she is ever engaged in diversions such as coming and going.

One should meditate on the Mistress of Mantras as being in a crimson ocean; this same visualization applies to the weapons of the Lord as well as to the powers of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-śakti*). However, regarding the aspect of the weapons, there is the additional feature that each bears its own respective crest-mark upon its head. Then, at the conclusion of the present Vidyā: "O Mahāvajreśvarī, here in this wheel..."

"Be established! Again, at the end of twenty-three syllables, "be firmly restrained. Again, at the end of that many syllables, "be veiled. Again, at the end of that many syllables, "be made present"—having thus prayed while displaying the respective mudrās. [Then follows] the mantra for the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhāvidyā*).

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs, one should establish the vital breaths by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra in the form: "The vital breaths of this Mahāvajreśvarī Nityā are here in this wheel," and so forth; then one should worship her with the twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*). The mantras for these are as follows: at the end of the complete mantra, [one offers] water for the feet (*pādya*) to Mahāvajreśvarī Nityā.
Having offered the water for the feet (*pādya*) with the twenty-seven-syllable mantra "I offer" (*kalpayāmi*) using the general *arghya* water,
one should present it at the feet with the current root-vidyā. In the same manner,

omitting the word "feet" (*pādya*) and substituting it with the words "arghya," "water for sipping" (*ācamana*), and so forth, one should offer the *arghya*, *ācamana*, and other services individually with the mantras thus produced.

One should offer [the offerings] individually at the head, face, and other parts with the present mantra. Having thus worshipped with twelve services ending with *tāmbūla*, one should perform the thirteenth service. The procedure for that is as follows:
on the back part of the Goddess, [one offers] *prakāśa*, *vimarśa*, *ānanda*, *śrījñānaśrī*, and *satya*.

Having worshipped with their own respective mantras— containing the word *śakti* within the words "Obeisance to the Lord who bestows lords" (*nāthapradanātha*)— the illustrious Lord named Śrīpūrṇasvabhāvapratibhasubhaga, [one should worship] in front of the triangle in a counter-clockwise direction: *hrīṃ*.

I worship the Sandal of the Power of Will (icchā-śakti-pādukā). Hrīṃ, [I worship] the Sandal of the Power of Knowledge (jñāna-śakti-pādukā). Hrīṃ, [I worship] the Sandal of the Power of Action (kriyā-śakti-pādukā). On the two sides of the triangle, starting from the northwest and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction: Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Pomegranate-Arrow (dāḍimī-sāyaka); Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Sugarcane-Bow (ikṣu-cāpa); Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Noose (pāśa); Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Goad (aṅkuśa). Thus.

Having worshipped the powers such as Icchā and the weapons, and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the conclusion of the complete recitation of the present Vidyā with the mantra: "I worship the pādukā of the eternal Mahāvajreśvarī," [one says]: "Hrīṃ!
May these deities of the first enclosure of the eternal Mahāvajreśvarī accept this worship."

Having offered a handful of flowers as an oblation for that worship: in the southwest corner of the hexagonal wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*), *hrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Ḍākinī; in the northwest corner, *hrīṃ*, the sandals of Rākinī; in the eastern corner, *hrīṃ*, the sandals of Lākinī; in the southeast corner, *hrīṃ*, the sandals of Kākinī; in the northeast corner, *hrīṃ*, the sandals of Śākinī; in the western corner, [the sandals of Yākinī].

Having worshipped the respective Śaktis with the mantras "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Hākinī," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the root-vidyā with "Mahāvajreśvarī, I worship the sandals of Nityā," one performs the offering of that worship with: "Hrīṃ,
may these deities of the second enclosure of Mahāvajreśvarī accept this worship."

Having offered a handful of flowers, [one worships] on the twelve petals, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise: *Hrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Hṛllekhā; *Hrīṃ*, the sandals of Kledinī; *Hrīṃ*, the sandals of Klinnā; *Hrīṃ*, the sandals of Kṣobhiṇī.

Having worshipped those respective Śaktis with the mantras: *hrīṃ madanāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ āturāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ nirañjanāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ rāgavatīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ madanāvatīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ mekhalāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ drāviṇīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ vegavatīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; and having [worshipped] at the end of the root-vidyā [with]: *mahāvajreśvarī nityāpādukāṃ*.

Having worshipped with the words "I worship," and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering of that worship while saying: "Hrīṃ! May these deities of the third enclosure, headed by Vajreśvarī, accept the worship," one worships starting from the tip of the sixteen petals and proceeding clockwise: "Hrīṃ! I worship Kamalāpādukā."

hrīṃ Kāminī-pāda, hrīṃ Kalpā-pāda, hrīṃ Kalāpā-pāda, hrīṃ Kalitā-pāda, hrīṃ Kautukā-pāda, hrīṃ Kirātā-pāda, hrīṃ Kālā-pāda, hrīṃ Kadana-pāda, hrīṃ Kauśikī-pāda, hrīṃ Kambu-vāhinī-pāda, hrīṃ Kātarā-pāda, hrīṃ Kapaṭā-pāda, hrīṃ Kīrti-pāda, hrīṃ Kumārī-pāda, hrīṃ Kuṅkumā-pādukām.

Having worshipped the respective Śaktis with the mantras "I worship," and having honored the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the Mūlavidyā with "I worship the sandals of Mahāvajreśvarī," [one should say]:
"Hrīṃ! May these deities of the fourth enclosure of the Nityā Mahāvajreśvarī accept this worship."

Having offered a handful of flowers as an oblation for that worship: in the square, on the southern path of the western gate, *hrīṃ* I worship the sandals of Bhaṇḍinī; on the northern path, *hrīṃ* the sandals of Veginī; in the northwest (*vāyavya*), *hrīṃ* the sandals of Nāgā; on the western path of the northern gate, *hrīṃ* the sandals of Capalā; [on the eastern path] of the northern gate...

In the eastern path: Hrīṃ, I worship Peśalāpāda. In the northeast (Īśāna): Hrīṃ, I worship Satīpāda. In the northern path of the eastern gate: Hrīṃ, I worship Ratīpāda. In the southern path of the eastern gate: Hrīṃ, I worship Śraddhāpādukā. In the southeast (Āgneya): Hrīṃ, I worship Bhogalolāpāda.
On the eastern path of the southern gate: *hrīṃ madāpā* (I worship Madāpā). On the western path of the southern gate:
*hrīṃ unmattāpā* (I worship Unmattāpā). In the southwest (*naiṛtya*): *hrīṃ manasvinīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi* (I worship the sandals of Manasvinī).

Having worshipped the twelve Śaktis of the square with their respective mantras, and having honored the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete root mantra with "I worship the sandals of Mahāvajreśvarī," [one should say]:
"Hrīṃ! May these deities of the fifth enclosure of Mahāvajreśvarī accept this worship."
One should offer a handful of flowers as an act of worship (*pujārpaṇa*). Then, having performed the three-fold service (*upacāratraya*) for the disciple according to the rules,
and having recited [the mantra] one thousand or one hundred times, at the conclusion of the offering consisting of the meditation on non-difference from that [deity],
one should meditate on the non-difference of the Goddess in the fire according to the prescribed method, using only red flowers smeared with ghee.

Having offered oblations with clarified butter either sixteen times or in a number equal to one-tenth [of the total], one should withdraw the fire-located radiance into the *bindu* at the site of the Goddess; then, having worshipped the Goddess residing in the *bindu* again with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*),
one should offer the bali-oblation once more with the seven-syllable Kurukullā mantra.

Having performed the *nīrājana* with camphor-filled wicks and other offerings and having asked for forgiveness, one should dissolve the powers (*śaktis*) residing in the wheel into the principal goddess by means of the *śaktyutthāpana-mudrā*.

Then, dissolving the principal goddess by means of the *khecarī-mudrā*, and having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) and the phoneme-placement (*varṇa-nyāsa*) as before, one should conclude by reciting the hymn to the Guru and the hymn to the Goddess. Thus ends the procedure.

Thus, the practitioner who has acquired the knowledge and practiced the previously described modes of worship, desiring the success of the ritual application (*prayoga*), should accomplish the *vidyā*. The procedure for this is as follows: during the spring or summer—whether in their primary or secondary seasons—beginning from one full moon until the next, over a period of thirty-two days with an increase of one day [each month], while subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
Subsisting on milk alone or on fruits and roots, having bathed with fragrant waters,
wearing red garments, and anointed with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron paste.
Anointed with red sandalwood paste, having visualized the Vidyā in a crimson hue at the *mūlādhāra*, the heart, and the *brahmarandhra*,
and contemplating one’s own self as red through contact with its radiance;
with a pair of eyes smeared with collyrium and a face whose ruddiness has arisen from the habitual chewing of betel.

Having placed a piece of camphor in his own mouth, and with a mind satisfied by the certainty that he would attain even that accomplishment which is difficult to obtain within a few days from now, the practitioner— free from all fickleness, mental agitation, and the like—
having prepared every requisite for the practice of the Vidyā, [proceeds] as before.
While the guru is alive, one should go to him even from a distant land as often as possible and prostrate repeatedly;

having abandoned the evil thought of how one’s livelihood or freedom from public reproach might be maintained by giving such-and-such wealth, one should satisfy him with riches, grain, clothing, ornaments, vehicles, and the like, and then, with his permission—

During the three junctions of dawn, midday, and evening, one should perform the recitation silently at each session one thousand forty-one times; at the time of sunset, one should recite it one thousand forty-three times. This should be done every day.

Having completed one hundred thousand recitations by performing three thousand one hundred and twenty-five repetitions [of the mantra] in equal numbers, one should again complete another two hundred thousand recitations for the current *nityā* in the same manner. As for the tenth part of the recitation,
it may be performed with pure ghee, or else—
Having offered oblations continuously until the completion of the prescribed number, using flowers of *āragvadha*, *vakula*, *madhuka*, or *myaka* anointed with the three sweets (*trimadhura*),
one should [continue] until the completion of the number with pure water mixed with camphor, musk, saffron, and sandalwood.
One should satisfy [the deities] according to the number of oblations in the sequence of the rite;
from the day of commencement until the day of completion, one may perform them in a large number according to one's own capacity.

Having bowed down with devotion and honored with food consisting mostly of sweet items those Brahmins who are distinguished practitioners of that knowledge and so forth, one should feed them and then dismiss them. One should perform the worship of the Guru or one who stands in his place with devotion;
and oneself, during the *nakta* period—the eighth part of the day—one should eat the food remaining from the oblation and that which has been offered.

And before concluding, one should complete this rite after satisfying the Guru with wealth without stinginess, and having praised him with devotion through hymns of praise. Thus, although the procedure for the practice of the Vidyā is common to all the Nityās, it has been stated here specifically according to one’s own preference; however, it should be understood as applicable everywhere. As for the recitation of three hundred thousand [mantras], that pertains to the specific subject of that particular Nityā.

That [rule] also pertains specifically to the Kṛtayuga; in the present age, it is fourfold. It should be understood that even the substances for the *homa* and libations (*tarpaṇa*) pertain only to the practice of the vidyā-sādhana currently under discussion. Thus, one who has completed the practice of the vidyā, being devoted to the guru and intent on the performance of daily worship, should make the recitation (*japa*) of a thousand times every day his primary practice.

One should practice the applications of the *vidyā*. If one— whether out of attachment to wife, children, and so forth, for the sake of displaying wonders in the world, or out of a desire for wealth— should undertake the optional (*kāmya*) applications, being other than the [proper] qualified person described above, such a person will not only fail to obtain the desired objects, but will moreover suffer the loss of wealth, children, wife, and so on, as well as diseases such as fever.
One will suffer excessive affliction from kings, thieves, and the like; this [result] also applies commonly to all the *nityā* goddesses.
Now, these are the constant applications.

Beginning from the full moon day until the next full moon, one should daily perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with a thousand red lotuses soaked in the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*), or with a thousand naturally blooming white water-lilies (*kahlāra*) soaked in honey alone; at the conclusion of the sacrifice,
one should likewise perform a recitation (*japa*) of a thousand times on each of those sacrificial days with devotion.

For the practitioner who performs this in conjunction with feeding a large number of Brahmins with food consisting mostly of sweets, there shall arise within his circle great and magnificent prosperity, praised by all people. Furthermore, for one who offers oblations day after day for the duration of a month, numbering one thousand times, using *campaka* flowers soaked in honey:
There shall be the acquisition of gold weighing one hundred *niṣkas*.

By performing three thousand oblations of *pāṭalī* flowers soaked in clarified butter, extending over the months beginning with the new moon (*darśa*), there shall be the acquisition of variegated garments.
By performing *homa* for one month with fragrant substances such as camphor and sandalwood, one obtains the object of one’s heart’s desire.
By performing *homa* on every seventh day for one month with *śāli* rice smeared with milk,
one will undoubtedly obtain *śāli* rice within six months.

By performing *atilā-homa* (oblations of sesame seeds) for seven years inclusive, one attains health; by performing *dūrvā-homa* (oblations of *dūrvā* grass) for a hundred times over the course of three years during the three *janmatārās* (birth-constellations), one becomes free from affliction, attains various kinds of enjoyments, and lives for a hundred years. Alternatively, one may perform oblations with *guḍūcī*, sesame, and *dūrvā* respectively during the three *janmatārās*.
For those who offer oblations for a period of one hundred years, there shall be longevity, prosperity, fame, enjoyment, merit, learning, the quality of pleasing the world, and so forth.

By performing one hundred oblations for each of the three birth-constellations (*janmarkṣa*) respectively— using clarified butter, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and milk— for the duration of a year, there shall be long life, health, prosperity, and royal honor.
By performing one hundred oblations on the seventh lunar day for the duration of a year, women shall attain good fortune (*saubhāgya*).

Success is attained. By offering into the fire daily for six months—or for a year if the gravity of the task requires it—one hundred oblations of three-bladed *dūrvā* grass and *samidh* fuel sticks, each the size of a span (*prādeśa*) and soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhura*), even an incurable fever caused by the simultaneous disturbance of all three humors (*sānnipātika-jvara*) shall be pacified. This applies as well to great diseases such as consumption (*kṣaya*).

If one performs oblations for a period of six months or more with *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, or *guḍūcī*, preceded by immersion in honey and clarified butter— or if, due to the gravity of the task, one performs oblations three hundred times with each of these three substances— one will become healthy after being freed from disease. Thus concludes the application of the fire-offerings (*homaprayoga*).

On the days of illness, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times while merely touching water. For the practitioner who daily performs bathing, drinking, cooking, sipping water (ācamana), and other rites with that water, there shall be liberation from disease.
Thus concludes the application of the recitation (japa-prayoga).
Now follow the applications of the effigy (puttalī).

Having taken six substances—powdered wood from the tree of the lunar mansion of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), ginger, black pepper, long pepper, mustard seeds, and sesame seeds—mixed with the dust from the feet of that person to be accomplished, one should then fashion a doll according to the method to be described, and [perform the rite] upon that tree with the mantra: "Devadatta! Make [him] subject to Yajñadatta! Kuru kuru! and so forth.

Having written down the names of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth, and having first performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the rite of infusing life), one should [use] this twelve-fold *chinnāmā* on that same night.

For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*): by performing oblations for three nights or seven nights while fashioning an internal effigy (*puttalī*), kings and others shall remain under the control of the practitioner for a long time. Having fashioned an effigy with the seven previously mentioned substances and having buried it within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should then fill the earth back into the pit from its northern direction as performed previously.

In that regard, having established the fire according to the prescribed rule, if one offers oblations at night with mustard seeds smeared with mustard oil, reciting the aforementioned vidyā three thousand times, even a beloved woman situated in a distant land will be drawn by the power of the ritual application. This is for the purpose of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). [Furthermore,] one should prepare a doll (*puttalī*) out of the seven previously mentioned substances.

Having smeared half the body down to the waist with beeswax, having performed the *prāṇapratiṣ�ṭhā* (infusion of life-force) for the person to be targeted (*sādhya*), and having buried it at night in a cremation ground under the eighth astrological house (*aṣṭamala*) of the enemy, one should perform the severing of the victim's birth-constellation (*nakṣatra-yoni*) and offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) using this very mantra. As previously stated...

Preceded by an ablution with the water from a jar empowered by the yantra of the daily worship, one should recite the present *nityā-vidyā* three hundred times; by that, within a month, the enemy will certainly succumb to various diseases such as fevers, or to afflictions caused by spirits and the like. Thus [it is] for destruction. Having fashioned an effigy (*puttalī*) from the wood of the tree belonging to the victim’s lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*),...

Having written her name preceded by [the syllable] *hrīṃ* upon its heart as before, and having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-breath) for the victim there, one should immerse it in mustard oil and boil it in water. By that, after seven nights, three nights, or even a single night, the enemy shall be afflicted with a violent fever. Thus ends the section on affliction by voice. If [the victim] departs from that particular place...

Having extracted each of those figurines from their respective forms—the cremation ground, the place of decoction, and the reservoir—one should cast them into the midst of water; then, for the two aforementioned afflictions of fever and pain, there is peace. Thus ends the section on pacification (*śama*). As previously stated...

Having fashioned an effigy (puttalī) composed of the asterism of the person to be subdued (sādhya), and having performed the ritual installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) therein—if the subject is a man, one should bury it in the temple of Caṇḍikā; if the subject is a woman, in a temple for female spirits (śāvāstu); and having dug up the earth at that location where the asterism of the subject resides, one should then offer an oblation (bali) with the present mantra. By this means, [one subdues] either a man or a woman.
"Through the union with the state of being accomplished, one enters into madness. Thus, regarding madness.
Now, the applications of the mechanical devices (yantras).

In that regard, the Great Vajra Machine (*mahāvajrayantra*) is as follows: having drawn twenty lines extending east-west and twenty lines extending north-south with equal intervals, three hundred and sixty-one (361) squares are produced. Therein, one should erase forty-five squares in each of the four corners in such a manner that—

In the center, with one hundred and sixty-five squares, the form of a vajra for the yantra may arise. The method for this is as follows: in the outermost path consisting of seventy-two squares, having omitted every tenth square starting from the east in the four directions, there are seventeen [squares] located in the middle of each of those tenth squares.

Having cleared seventeen squares, in the second row—which consists of sixty-four squares—one should omit three squares in each of the four directions: namely, the single square below the remaining square of the first row, and one square on each of its two sides, making three in total;
[and then] the thirteen squares situated in the middle of those [remaining squares].
Having wiped it clean; in the third path, which consists of fifty-six squares (p.
126b), [one should place] the three squares situated below the three squares abandoned by the second path.
One square on each of its two sides, making five in total; having set aside five squares in each of the four directions;
having erased the group of four squares located in the center of that [area];
and within the fourth path, which consists of forty-eight squares—

Having discarded the seven squares in total— consisting of everything below the previously abandoned group of five squares and one square each on both sides— and having erased the four groups of five squares situated in the center thereof, [one proceeds] within the fifth row,
which consists of forty squares.

Having abandoned the seven squares of the eastern row, and having abandoned one square each located on both sides of that [row], making nine squares in total; and having abandoned nine squares in each of the four directions,
having erased one square each from the central group of four, [one should proceed] at every corner.
By erasing forty-five squares, one hundred and eighty squares have been erased in total,

and thus the first yantra consisting of eighty-one [squares] is completed. Therein also, each single square situated on the outermost row in the four directions, together with the single square directly below it and the single square on each of its two sides, amounting to—

The three squares located in the second row— meaning the four squares situated across the two rows— should be unified by erasing the three lines that divide those squares; thus, when sixteen squares have been erased in this manner,
one hundred and sixty-five squares remain.

Therein, having first written [the letters] in the thirty-six squares reached by circling from the center of the fifth square in the eastern direction to the end of that same eastern square, beginning from the central square;

Then, starting from the very center square in the second inner row as well, one should write the letters situated above the previously written letters in the thirty-two squares reached there; thereafter,
starting from the very center square in the third inner row, [one proceeds] all around.
Having written those same final letters above the last letters previously written in the twenty-eight squares reached [thereby],
one should then begin from the very middle square in the inner fourth row and proceed around it.
Having written those same final letters above the previously written letters in the twenty-four squares already reached,
one should then write four groups of three letters each, starting from the central square within the sixth row from that point.
For here, in this present Nityā, the five letters are *ha*, *ra*, *ka*, *la*, and *na*, with *e* as the sixth and *ta*.

The five syllables *pa*, *ma*, *da*, *va*, and *ka* together constitute eleven distinct phonemes (*anāvṛtta-varṇa*). When each of these is joined with the sixteen vowels, they become one hundred and seventy-six modified mantra-phonemes (*mantravikṛta-varṇa*). Among those, one hundred and forty-four phonemes are written in as many squares, beginning with *ha*, *hā*, *hi*.
In the passage beginning with *hī* and ending with *somaumaṃmaḥ*,
thirty-two letters remain, written in the sequence of the syllables: sixteen instances of the letter *da* and sixteen instances of the letter *va*.

And twenty-one squares remain. Within those twenty-one squares, having written the five letters beginning with *da*, *dā*, *di*, *dī*, *du*, *dū*, and so on— ending with sixteen instances of the letter *da* followed by sixteen instances of the letter *ca* in their respective forms (*va*, *vā*, *vi*, *vī*, *vu*)— one should again [place them] within these very twenty-one squares connected to the modified syllables (*vikṛtākṣara*).

Having written the six vowels beginning with *paryāyanityā* (i.e., *ī*, *ai*, *au*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ṅ*) in the sequence of each individual letter, and having written the two letters representing the *ghaṭikā* of the four ages (*yuga*) combined together in the seventh square presided over by the letter *ha*, [one proceeds] in the eighth and subsequent squares,
which are composed of both natural and modified syllables such as *hva*, *hlaṃ*, *hḹ*, *de*, *dai*, *do*, *dau*, *daṃ*, *daḥ*, *va*, *vā*, *vi*. Thus the present [arrangement] is established.

Having written the twelve unchanging syllables of the *nityā*, one should place the three— the name of the practitioner in the dative case, the word for the action [in the accusative], and the verb— in the order of top to bottom within the two remaining squares located on the seventh and eighth rows, which are distinguished by the letters *vī* and *vu* and have mutually attained the status of mantras.

Having written the two [items], namely the name of the object of proof (sādhya) ending in the accusative case, one places the three modified phonemes *vū*, *vṛ*, and *vṝ* on the upper exterior of the eastern triangle; the three phonemes *vḷ*, *vḹ*, and *ve* on the upper exterior of the southern triangle; and the three phonemes *vai*, *vo*, and *vau* on the upper exterior of the western triangle.
Having written the two syllables "vaṃ" and "vaḥ" on the upper outer portion of the northern triangle,
and having constructed an upward-facing triangle within each of the four combined squares in the four directions,
[one should place therein] according to one's own intended desires for the elements.

Having written out the ten true colors by dividing them in the sequence of two and three, one establishes the accomplished Great Vajra Mantra through the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* vidyā. Therein, having worshipped the present Nityā with the hand—

Having first performed the ritual touch (*sparśa*) and recited the aforementioned mantra three thousand times, one should properly employ it for the rites of victory, immobilization (*stambhana*), inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and subjugation (*vaśya*). Likewise, one should apply this *yantra* for protection, nourishment, pacification, and the suppression of enemies; however, regarding protection at a crossroads (*catuṣka*), this is the specific distinction.
Having drawn this yantra with red earth upon the ground and having invoked the Goddess therein,

one should worship her at each of the three junctions of the day for three nights, six nights, or nine nights— according to whether one’s desire is slight, moderate, or very great— and perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) every day.
This is the specific procedure for a king whose kingdom remains only as a mere village after a great defeat:
having inscribed this yantra within the king's palace with the name of the target (sādhya) and other details inside it,
one should perform worship there during the nine nights of the Goddess and other such occasions, preceded by festivals of dance, song, and the like, especially at the three junctions of the day.

One should worship with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). For the practitioner who worships in this manner, even if the patron is destitute, he shall become victorious through the power of the king’s inner circle, or by the outbreak of diseases and the like, or through mutual strife, or by the force of even powerful enemies. And when victory has been achieved, having cleansed the Great Vajra Machine (*mahāvajrayantra*) and applied a mark (*tilaka*) with it upon the rosary, [he should honor] the practitioner.
And having placed him upon an elephant and escorted him forward, he should proceed to the city accompanied by his own forces.

As before, having laid down ten lines each extending east-west and ten lines each extending north-south, with equal intervals and intersecting one another, one should produce eighty-one squares; this is the *vajrayantra*.

In the four corners starting from the southeast (āgneya), one should erase ten squares in each so that the central wheel takes on the form of a vajra; the method for this is as follows: having omitted the fifth square in each of the four directions along the outermost path, there remains a group of four sets of seven squares.
Having cleared away everything, in the second row— starting from the square below the one left out in the first row—
one should discard three squares in each of the four directions (one directly below,
and one on each of its two sides), and then the two squares situated in the center of that [remaining area].

Having cleared two squares, one should likewise clear five squares in the third row— namely, the square directly below the one already cleared in the second row, and one square each on both its sides— and then clear one square in the center of those. When this has been done:

When forty-one squares remain, as before, in all four directions, one should take the fifth square from the first row on every side; from the second row, the one immediately below that [fifth square], and the one situated on each of its two sides— thus, three squares for each direction, totaling twelve.

Having unified the four compartments by erasing three of the lines that divide the grid, one should form upward-pointing triangles within them. Therein, as before, one should write the ten syllables associated with the elements according to the desired purpose, dividing them in the sequence of two, three, two, and three; [then] in the remaining [spaces].
In the twenty-five corners, beginning from the central square of the third path and proceeding around it,
one should fill twenty-four squares by writing the twelve syllables of the present Nityā-vidyā twice.

In the remaining central square of the *māyā* [grid], one should write the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth. This *yantra* as well should be employed for all the aforementioned purposes; there is no excess or deficiency whatsoever.

The difference in degree produced by the excellence of the internal receptacle (*koṣṭhaka*) is such that, nevertheless, the fruit of a divine [seed] is long-lasting and arises quickly; whereas from a diamond (*vajra*), the fruit is inferior, lasts for a shorter time, and arises more slowly—this is the fundamental meaning. Furthermore, this...

Having placed the *yantra*— upon which his own name is inscribed— in his armor, at his heart, or on his head, a king or other nobleman entering the battlefield shall conquer even an army consisting of a multitude of elephants, chariots, horses, and foot soldiers; remaining himself unharmed and radiant, he shall become enriched with fame, fortune, and the lands of his enemies.

May he who grants all enjoyments according to one's own desire live long! Having engraved this on a copper plate according to the prescribed method, one should place it in the dwelling place of the elephant, horse, person, or other object to be protected; by that means, its protection shall be secured.
Now, regarding another yantra: first, having drawn two circles with an intervening space between them, one should draw a hexagon in their center;

then, having fashioned another circle within that as well, one should place the mantra and so forth—containing the object of the rite (*sādhya*) such as "O Goddess, bestow upon Devadatta an excess of love for his husband Yajñadatta, do, do!"—in the very center of all.

Having written the *māyābīja* (the seed-syllable of Māyā), one should write it in such a manner upon the path situated outside and inside the hexagon that the entire path becomes connected by means of that single *māyābīja*, specifically using the final portion of the mantra; [then] in the front corner of the hexagon and in the rear corner.
Having written the third mantra-syllable,
one should [place] the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh seed-syllables respectively on the right and left sides of the front corner.

Having written [the mantra], one should inscribe the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh seed-syllables (bījas) respectively on the right and left sides of the rear corner. One should then fill the outer path with the Mātṛkās accompanied by the nasal bindu.
Thus the yantra is perfected; having performed the consecration of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and other rites, one should worship it and wear it on the neck or the arm.
A woman who wears this [amulet] shall immediately become most beloved by her husband; thus ends the "Amulet that Delights the Husband."

Now, for the yantra that accomplishes all desires: having drawn five lines extending east-west and north-south, equally spaced and intersecting one another, one should produce a wheel consisting of sixteen squares.
Within those squares, one by one, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus provided with a pericarp-circle and a circle at the tips of the petals.
Therein, having first written the first modified syllable upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*), having written the second modified syllable within that,

and having also written the third modified syllable within that, one should then divide the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the subject of the rite (*sādhya*), as well as the sixty *ghaṭikā*-syllables, into sixteen parts.

Having written three or four [syllables] in accordance with the measure of the *ghaṭikās* of day and night, and having written one distorted syllable (*vikṛtākṣara*) on each petal, the first yantra is produced by eleven initial distorted syllables,
along with eleven subsequent distorted syllables for each, corresponding to the number of syllables obtained for their respective *ghaṭikās*.

The second and subsequent lotuses are also to be filled in. In this manner, within this yantra of sixteen compartments, all the modified letters of the mantra and all the letters of the ghaṭikās are written.
In this regard, the performance of the rites for these yantras must be carried out in connection with their respective times of worship, the ghaṭikās, and the [corresponding] colors.

Through the consecration with the water from a jar presided over by these yantras, through the worship of these yantras at its conclusion, through the recitation (japa) of these mantras, and through the wearing of these yantras, every desired goal is accomplished. Furthermore:

This yantra, engraved or written upon gold, silver, or copper, should be worshipped during the eight watches of the day according to their respective hour-measures; when buried in the ground, it shall bring about the accomplishment of all one's desires.
Thus concludes the introduction to Mahāvajreśvarīnityā.
Now, the Nityā Śivādūtī is introduced.

Having fashioned two square enclosures (*bhūpura*), each measuring one cubit (*hasta*) in size, provided with door-panels in the eastern and western directions and having an interval of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) between them;
and within those, having made an inner circle with an interval of one finger-breadth, followed by another circle with an interval of four finger-breadths.
In the space between those [two circles], there is an eight-petalled lotus. At a distance of one finger-breadth from the circle at the tips of its petals, another circle is drawn;

then, having fashioned yet another circle at a distance of four finger-breadths, and having constructed a six-pointed wheel within that completed path, one leaves a space of one finger-breadth inside it and draws a single circle.
Leaving a space of four finger-breadths within that [circle],
one should fashion a six-petaled lotus within the path formed by those two circles; then,
having made another circle inside its pericarp with an interval of one finger-breadth, one should draw a triangle inside that circle with its apex facing oneself.

Having performed that [preliminary rite], one should establish the daily worship-circle (*nityapūjācakra*) which constitutes the ritual procedure; having constructed it on some level and pure ground using substances such as vermilion (*darada*), one should perform the installation of the jar (*kalaśasthāpana*) there,
preceded by the contemplation of the wheel of all-auspicious Nityās (*sarvamaṅgalānityācakracintana*) together with its enclosures (*sāvaraṇa*).

At the conclusion of the ritual sequence beginning with its worship and ending with its dismissal, because the central drop at the primary place of worship has been pervaded by the water from that [same] jar, one should again perform the worship within another jar.

Having visualized the present Nityāpūjācakra, even though it has been drawn below, one should perform the worship there; the manner for that [worship] when it is not an auxiliary to the initiation (dīkṣā) but is performed solely upon the cakra is as follows: having first anointed oneself with fragrant oil, one performs the ritual bath with fragrant waters.

Having performed the morning rites and other duties, and having already carried out the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth as an incidental part of the worship of another deity,
the practitioner— possessing a purified body and face,
adorned with ornaments such as red sandalwood paste and garlands, and with an undistracted mind— arrives at the place of sacrifice.

Having sat upon a seat such as a red woolen blanket worshipped with the four previously mentioned vidyās, and having assumed either a *svastika* or *padma* posture while seated, one should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the present vidyā; then,
having offered the oblation (*bali*) with the sixteen-syllable mantra and worshipped the nine Nāthas upon one’s own head according to the sequence of one’s own lineage, [one should proceed].

Having recited that hymn consisting of five verses and requested permission for the worship, one should begin it after visualizing one's own Lord as the present Nityā and oneself as identical with that Lord,
[taking into account] the place, time, and other factors regulated by the specific rules of each respective year.

Having worshipped all the thirty-eight deities of the sacred seats (pīṭhas), including the entire circle of secret and manifest Siddhas and Yoginīs, upon the lion-throne and other supports that constitute the basis for the present wheel of daily worship—
between one's own self and the wheel of worship— one should [place] the *gorocanā* along with its vessel.
Having placed a general *arghya* vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or any one of these, or even of clay, filled with water scented with camphor, saffron, agallochum, and musk; (p. 131a)

Having meditated upon the waters that serve as its support—respectively taking the form of the external sun and moon through the three seed-syllables of the Kula-sundarī—and having visualized therein the five substances such as *gorocanā* as being the nature of the five elements beginning with earth;

and having meditated upon the identity of those waters with the present worship-circle (*pūjā-cakra*) and with the nature of the present Nityā; [one should contemplate] the water thus manifested as the very essence of the present Nityā.

Having consecrated the water ten times with the present vidyā and having worshipped it, one should worship the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*) with the mantras of the six limbs. Then, with that water, one should take from the general arghya vessel the water for washing the feet (*pādya*),
the arghya, the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the bathing water (*snānajala*) located in the progressively higher sections, and place them in one's own vessels in the right-hand portion.

Having consecrated the garments, ornaments, perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel leaves with the recited mantra; then, having again restrained the breath with the mantra,
one should take the water for the general *arghya* offering of the Goddess in the right hand, together with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, flowers, and unbroken rice grains.

Having specified the place, time, lineage, heap, name, and desire, and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) of the eternal goddess Śivādūtī according to the prescribed rule and as my intellect dictates," [one should proceed];

and in case there is no manifestation due to the context of another deity, [one should perform] the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and everything up to one's own consecration (*svasaṃskāra*).
Having performed the ritual application (*viniyoga*) by employing the present *vidyā* itself in place of all other mantras assigned to their respective locations;

and having performed the placement of the *mātṛkā* letters (*mātṛkā-nyāsa*) up to the end of the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*), one should then place each individual letter of the *mātṛkā* at its corresponding location at the end of each part of the present *vidyā*, as follows: *hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śirase svāhā*.
Hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock;
Hariṃ, huṃ to the armor; Hrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the eyes; Hraḥ, phaṭ to the weapon.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra syllables on one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other body parts: *hrīṃ śi hrīṃ* on the two ears; *hrīṃ vā hrīṃ* on the skin; *hrīṃ dū hrīṃ* on the two eyes; *hrīṃ tyai hrīṃ* on the tongue; *hrīṃ na hrīṃ* on the nose; and *hrīṃ maḥ hrīṃ* on the mind. Then, [recite] the seven-syllable mantra: *hrīṃ śivādūtyai namaḥ*.
Having performed the three-fold pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the complete mantra, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the subsequent rites. This is as follows:

preceded by the display of the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā, while holding a handful of red flowers in the hollowed palms (*añjali*), the light of the present *Nityā*—which pervades from the *mūlādhāra* to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)—is transferred via the path of the central breath (*nāsā*).
While visualizing that [deity] as having arrived at the circle (cakravindu) currently under discussion through the scattering of that handful of flowers,
one should pray at the end of the complete root mantra: "O Śivādūtī, O Nityā, be invoked here in this wheel," and having performed the invocation, that splendor...

Having visualized some rays, which have emanated from the locations to be described, as having transformed into the forms of the Lord’s weapons and ornaments; one should meditate upon the mass of light situated in the center as having likewise transformed into that form—
some rays, which have emanated from the locations to be described, [appearing] in the form of the Lord’s weapons and ornaments.

Having visualized them as thus transformed, one should meditate upon the mass of light situated in the center as having been transformed into this very form. And that form is as understood from the verses of meditation:
"Possessing a radiance equal to the sun at dawn, midday, or noon, and wearing a crown of nine jewels..."
She has three eyes and wears crimson garments; her body is resplendent with the luster of various ornaments adorning it.
She possesses a pure smile and eight arms, and is being praised by great sages.
With her left hands she holds a noose, a lotus, a mace, and a jeweled goblet; with her right hands she holds a goad, a sword, an axe, and a lotus.
Likewise: "bearing [the weapons], endowed with the effort to grant the desired objects of the practitioner"—
such is my meditation upon the powers (*śaktis*) who constitute the various weapons and retinues.

[Bestow] upon the weapons the state of having their respective crests marked; then, at the end of the present mantra: "O Śivādūtī, O Nityā, be established here in this cakra. Again, at the end of the eighteen-syllable [mantra]: "Be firmly restrained.
Again, at the end of the eighteen-syllable [mantra]: "Be veiled. Again, at the end of the eighteen-syllable [mantra]: "Be made present."

Having thus made the request preceded by the display of the respective mudrās, and having performed the *karanyāsa* and *aṅganyāsa* of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā*, one should establish the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā* in the form "The vital breaths of this Śivādūtī Nityā are here in this wheel," and so forth; [then one should worship] with the twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*).

One should worship. Their mantras are as follows: at the end of the complete vidyā, having offered the water for the feet (pādya) with the general arghya-water using the mantra "I offer the wine to Nityā Śivādūtī," one should present the water for the feet at her two feet with the root-vidyā. In the same manner, omitting the word "pādya" and substituting it with "arghya," "ācamana," and so forth.

Having performed the offering of water for honor (*arghya*) and the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) with mantras perfected by the placement of steps (*padaprakṣepa*), one should present [the offerings] beginning with the head and face using the principal root-vidyā as prescribed. Having thus worshipped with the twelve services (*upacāra*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) and ending with betel (*tāmbūla*), one should proceed to the thirteenth service. Its method is as follows:

The Goddess is at the rear. Having worshipped Prakāśānandanātha in the northern part of the first row located near the Goddess, using the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Prakāśānanda-śakti," one should [proceed] by substituting the syllable "prakāśa" with "vimarśa," "ānanda" with "śrījñāna," and "śrīsatya" with "śrīpūrṇa."
Regarding "svabhāva":
having inserted the eight-word phrase consisting of the three syllables *pratibhā*, *subhagā*, and *iti*.

Having worshipped the nine Āpināthas in their respective locations with the perfected sixteen-syllable mantras, [one worships] on the path to the south of the western door: *hrīṃ śrīṃ vihvalāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. On the path to the north: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ākarṣiṇīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. In the northwest (*vāyavya*): *hrīṃ śrīṃ lolāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

In the northern street: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Nityāpādukāyai, in the northeast (Īśāna). Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Madanāpādukāyai, in the northern street of the eastern gate. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Mālinīpādukāyai, in its southern street. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vinodāpādukāyai, in the southeast (Āgneya). Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kautukāpādukāyai, in the southern street. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Purāpādukāyai, in the southwest (Nairṛtya).

Having worshipped those respective Śaktis with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Purāṇā," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Śivādūtī; I worship the eternal sandals of Śivādūtī," [he says]: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, may these deities of the first enclosure, the eternal Śivādūtīs, accept this worship."
Having offered a handful of flowers as an oblation for that worship, [one worships] on the eight petals, proceeding clockwise starting from the front of the Goddess:

*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vāgīśī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Varadā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Viśvā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vibhavā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vighnakāriṇī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vīrā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having worshipped those respective Śaktis with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vighnaharāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi" and "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vidyāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete Mūlavidyā with "Śivādūtīnityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi," [one should say]: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, these are the deities of the second enclosure of Śivādūtīnityā."

"Accepting the worship" means having offered the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for that worship. On the eight-sided [mandala], starting from the front corner of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals (*pādukā*) of Sumukhī.

*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Sundarī-pāda*, *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Sārā-pāda*, *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Sumanā-pāda*, *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Sarasvatī-pāda*, *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Samayā-pāda*, *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Sarvagā-pāda*, *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Siddhā-pāda*. Thus, at the end of each respective mantra, one worships these powers with the formula: "I worship the sandals of Śivādūtī Nityā."

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center, and having offered a handful of flowers for the dedication of that worship with the words: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the third enclosure, namely Śivādūtī and Nityā, accept this worship*, [one proceeds] clockwise from the front corner of the Goddess in the hexagon: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! I worship the sandals of Hākinī. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! [I worship] the sandals of Rākinī.*

Having worshipped those respective Śaktis with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ lākinīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ kākinīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ sākinīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ ḍākinīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ* at the end of the complete Vidyā, followed by *śivādūtīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; [one should worship] these: *hrīṃ śrīṃ etāḥ*.

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an oblation for that worship with the words, "May the deities of the fourth enclosure, the messengers of Śiva (*śivadūtī*), accept this worship," one should worship those powers (*śakti*) on the six petals, starting from the petal in front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise, saying: "I worship the sandals of Manonmanī" (*hrīṃ śrīṃ manonmanīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*). Then, at the end of the complete mantra (*vidyā*), [one worships] the sandals of Śivādūtī.

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with "I worship," and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for the dedication of that worship with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the fifth enclosure, the Śivādūtīs and Nityās, accept the worship," [one proceeds] from the region near the left supporting hand on both sides of the triangle.
In the eight locations up to the region near the right lower hand: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ratnacaṣakāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ gadāyai namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ kheṭāya namaḥ*.
Having worshipped the weapons as follows: *hrīṃ śrīṃ pāśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṅkuśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ khaḍgāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ kuṭhārāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ kamalāya namaḥ*;
then, proceeding clockwise from the front corner of the triangle: *hrīṃ śrīṃ icchāśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center, one should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) as an offering of worship with the words: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the sixth enclosure, the Śivadūtīs, accept this worship. Having thus completed the thirteen types of ritual services (upacāra), the remaining three services—consisting of whatever hymn-recitation, libation (tarpaṇa), and prostration (namaskāra)—should be performed.

Having performed the placement of the source (ākaranyāsa), the placement of the heart and other limbs (hṛdayādinyāsa), the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa), and the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) with a number such as one hundred and twenty-one thousand, and having performed the offering consisting of the contemplation of non-difference from that [deity] at the end of the daily recitation in such a way that it is encapsulated (sampuṭita), it is said:

Having performed oblations with the previously mentioned general substances such as clarified butter (*ājya*)—numbering sixteen times or according to the tenth part of one's daily recitation (*nityajapa*)—using the root-vidyā at hand;
and having united the fire-born radiance within the *bindu* which serves as the site for the worship of the Goddess; [one should worship] the Goddess who has arrived at that *bindu*.

Having again worshipped with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) and offered the bali with the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā, one should perform the lustration (nīrājana) with a wick containing camphor and so forth, and having asked for forgiveness (kṣamāpana), [one should contemplate] the rays— transformed into the form of those respective Śaktis— by means of the Śaktyutthāpana-mudrā, as being the form of the central Goddess herself.

Having meditated upon the mass of radiant energy as having dissolved away, one should withdraw that mass of energy in the form of the Goddess into one's own self by means of the *khecarīmudrā*. Then, having performed the placement of the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) and the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*) as before, one should conclude by reciting hymns to the Goddess and hymns to the Guru. However, the specific procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*) has already been stated.
p.

134a) Thus, the practitioner who has received initiation and has practiced the aforementioned modes of worship should follow the method for accomplishing the *vidyā* out of a desire for the success of the ritual application (*prayoga*). It is exactly as previously stated.

The procedure for its accomplishment is neither deficient nor excessive; it consists of forty lakhs (4 million) repetitions, since it has been stated that the number of repetitions is one lakh for each syllable of the mantra without repetition. In the Kali Yuga, that [number] is quadrupled, resulting in forty lakhs;
furthermore, the materials such as the *homa* offerings are not specifically prescribed here.

This is indeed obtained from the general scriptures. Having thus accomplished the knowledge, one should perform ritual applications solely for the sake of benefiting others by the command of the guru;
one must not perform them out of greed for wealth or other such motives. One should not act toward those who have already attained perfection through the performance of rituals.

Now, regarding the applications for this daily rite: by the principle that "that which is not found elsewhere should be equal," through the oblation of guggulu mixed with honey in equal parts, women come under one's control.
From the oblation of coconut fruit and jaggery mixed together, there is the attainment of prosperity (lakṣmī). [Likewise] from [the oblation of] kahlāra flower soaked in clarified butter...

Through the oblation of red lotuses soaked in milk, or of campaka flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), or of bakula flowers smeared with the three sweets, there is the attainment of great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*). Through the offering of madhūka flowers smeared with the three sweets, for the purpose of one's own marriage, there is the attainment of a maiden. Through oblations with buffalo ghee, there is the attainment of a queen (*mahiṣī*); through oblations with goat ghee, there is the attainment of a goat.
Through the oblation of cow's ghee, there is the attainment of cows; through the oblation of food, the attainment of food.
By offering red *karavīra* flowers—or in their absence, white *karavīra* flowers—dipped in the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one shall attain great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*) within twenty-one days.
By performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) of goat meat saturated with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), one gains gold;
by performing it with goat meat smeared with milk, one obtains [gold] in a number equal to the thousands of morsels consumed while covering the entire sacrificial circle (*maṇḍala*).

From daily burnt offerings (homa), there shall be the acquisition of land filled with grain. From the offering of lotus seeds smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), practiced for three days, there is the attainment of fortune (lakṣmī).
Thus concludes the procedure for the fire offering (homa).

Having fashioned an effigy from the flour of *śāli* rice mixed with sugar according to the procedure to be described, and having cooked it at night in a mixture of ghee and oil, one should consume that effigy— which has been consecrated by recitation [of mantras] a hundred or more times— while fasting entirely during the day. This should be done for a period extending over seven nights.

For the practitioner who performs the ritual application beginning with the construction of a doll and ending with its consumption, men, women, and kings become submissive like servants, being brought under his control through wealth and life; thus, intent on doing him service, they remain so.
This is the application of the doll in this rite.
Now follow the applications of this perpetual yantra.

In this context, the unobscured syllables of the Vidyā consist of ten elements: the letter *ha*, *ra*, the fourth vowel (*ī*), *śa*, *ca*, *da*, *ta*, *ya*, *na*, and *ma*. When each of these is joined with the sixteen vowels, there are one hundred and ninety (160) phonemes; by means of these, the yantras to be described [are formed].
The procedure is as follows: first, having fashioned two equal squares with an interval of two finger-breadths between them, and having made two circles with intervals within those two squares,
[one should then fashion] two square enclosures (*bhūpura*) within those two, such that they touch and do not touch the inner lines.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus by means of diagonal lines from corner to corner, one should [place] within the pericarp of that eight-spoked wheel, along with the intervening spaces...

Having established that one should draw two circles within the line-drawn mandala, one should first write the *māyābīja*, which is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) at the beginning of the mantra, together with the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the object of practice (*sādhya*), and so forth, in the very center. Then, having written the remaining six syllables of the *vidyā* on the path of the circle outside of that;
Having written the sixteen distorted phonemes (vikṛtavarṇa) in the eight corners starting from the northeast in the sequence of the eight vowels— beginning with *ha, hā, hi, hī* and ending with *he,
hai, ho, hau, haṃ, haḥ*— and having written the phonemes of the elements corresponding to one's specific desire upon the outer path formed by the two circles;
In the space between two squares, having written the twelve vowels beginning with *a* along with their nasal dots (*bindu*) in the eastern direction;

having written the group of four syllables *o*, *au*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ* together with their nasal dots in the southern direction; and having written the eight consonants from *ka* to *ja* together with the visarga in the western direction; [one should proceed].

Having written the twelve consonants from *ū* to *na* along with the *visarga*, and having written the twelve consonants from *pa* to *sa* in the northern direction, one should write the syllable *kṣa* in the four corners starting from the southeast;
thus is established the first yantra. If, in place of the sixteen [syllables] such as *ha, hā, hi, hī*, etc., there are *ra, rā, ri*...

The sixteen [vowels] beginning with *ṛ* are written [in the first square]. Then, the second [square] is filled by the sixteen beginning with *a, ā, i, ī*, and so on; the third by the [next] sixteen; the fourth by the sixteen beginning with *va, vā, vi, vī*, and so on; the fifth by the sixteen beginning with *da, dā, di, dī*, and so on;
the sixth by the sixteen beginning with *ta, tā, ti, tī*, and so on; and the seventh by the sixteen beginning with *pa, pā, pi, pī*, and so on.

The eighth [yantra] is by means of sixteen [syllables]; the ninth is by means of sixteen [syllables] beginning with *na nā ni nī*; the tenth yantra occurs by means of sixteen [syllables] beginning with *ma mā mi mī*. Among them, the fruit of the first yantra is as follows:

In a suitable location, having first drawn the yantra with red ochre (gairika), one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) and the consecration of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and so forth; then, every seventh day— or for twenty-five days— during the morning twilight, an offering (naivedya) consisting of milk along with sugar and cakes should be presented.

At the midday *sandhyā*, one should offer cooked rice mixed with curd as the *naivedya*; at the evening *sandhyā*, having offered plantain fruit and milk as the *naivedya*, the practitioner who worships during the three *sandhyās* shall, by the grace of the Goddess, achieve all his desires. This is the result of the second yantra, as follows: with vermilion...

Having drawn the second yantra, for the practitioner who worships it daily— beginning from every seventh day until the time of the maṇḍala ceremony and so forth— preceded by the offering of food consisting of well-cooked goat meat and honey as a naivedya, [the results] occur for both the king and his queen starting from the very moment the application of the yantra is completed, and not otherwise.

They shall remain under control for as long as one lives, and not merely for a short time; such is the fruit of the third yantra. Having drawn the third yantra with vermilion on a level piece of ground, and having performed the invocation (āvāhana) and other preliminary rites, one should offer an oblation (naivedya) consisting of goat meat and honey along with food.

For the practitioner who worships constantly throughout the time of the mandala and so forth, all enemies of various kinds become submissive. As for the fourth result: having drawn the fourth yantra on the ground in some place with saffron, and [having performed the practice] there for a period of seven days...
Having first offered goat meat and food mixed with honey, and having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and so forth, (p.

For the practitioner who worships the present Nityā every day in the manner described, there occurs the cessation of all calamities. The fruit of the fifth yantra is as follows: on a certain pure ground, one should draw the fifth yantra, composed of sixteen *ṣa*-syllables, using *śrīkhaṇḍa* (sandalwood) paste on a surface [made] with *amṛtā* (immortality).
Having written [the mantra] there, preceded by the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites,

and having offered oblations (*naivedya*) consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), plantain fruit, sugar, and ghee, for the practitioner who worships it during the three junctions of the day for the duration of one month, all diseases are destroyed and [he attains] happiness.

And she shall be long-lived. Having placed the ritual jar (kalaśa) upon this fifth yantra according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the entire sequence of rites beginning with the visualization of the maṅgalā-pūjā-cakra and ending with its dismissal; then, at the conclusion of that, one should again perform the visualization of the present *nityā*-lac-cakra along with its enclosures, and the worship ending with its dismissal.

The practitioner, consecrated with the water of the *kalaśa*, shall likewise be freed from disease, become happy, and live for a long time. As for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it may consist of one’s entire possessions and so forth; furthermore, the concluding consecration (*anta-nobhiṣeka*) must necessarily extend until the point of complete satisfaction. The fruit of the sixty-fold yantra is as follows:
on a smooth surface of stone, upon a seat made of *palāśa* leaves or similar materials, [one should apply] sandalwood paste mixed with camphor.
Having drawn this sixth yantra upon a ground consecrated with lime (sudhā), preceded by the invocation (āvāhana) and the ritual installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā),

and preceded by the offering of cooked rice, side-dishes, ghee, milk-rice (pāyasa), and cakes, one should perform the mandala and other rites at the three junctions of the day (sandhyās) until the appointed time.

Having worshipped each [deity] individually at the three aforementioned places of worship, and remaining in one of them rather than standing in a place separate from those sites of worship, one should recite the present vidyā either one hundred or one thousand times.

For the practitioner performing the recitation (*japa*), immediately upon the completion of the ritual application (*prayoga*), liberation from even the most terrifying malevolent fever (*abhicāra-jvara*) occurs within twenty-one days. As for the fruit of the seventh *yantra*: having engraved the seventh *yantra* on a copper plate and worshipped the Goddess there, preceded by the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), etc.
In whichever temple that yantra is installed, there dwells exceedingly stable Lakṣmī. As for the fruit of the eighth yantra:

for the man who, having engraved it upon a royal umbrella and worshipped it following the rites of invocation and the consecration of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), wears that yantra, all prosperities come to pass. As for the fruit of the ninth yantra:

Having engraved the ninth yantra upon a golden plate and performed its consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and worship (*pūjā*), one who wears it either as an ornament or as armor attains all prosperity; such is the fruit of the tenth yantra. Regarding the tenth yantra, according to one's desire, it may be placed upon any one of the following: birch bark, copper plate, silver plate, or golden plate.
Having drawn this yantra and having inscribed one's own desired object within it,

while keeping that purpose in mind, for the practitioner who performs the worship of the present Nityā therein— preceded by the invocation and the ritual installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā)— everything desired is accomplished in its entirety within the mandala.
Just as the fruit of ten yantras is produced by a single yantra,
one should write all ten aforementioned yantras in sequence upon a broad birch-bark leaf using the respective substances specified for each.
Having placed a birch-bark leaf— which serves as the support for all the diagrams rolled into balls— into a vessel made of *sikya* filled with honey,

one should perform worship with red flowers and other offerings at all three junctions (*sandhyā*) for a period of twenty-one days. Then, facing the direction where the target resides, one should bind [the target] by the neck with a noose at one's own feet.

While meditating upon one's own objective—a person brought before the presiding deity who says, "I am your servant," and stands with palms joined in reverence at the crown of the head—the practitioner should recite the prescribed mantra either one hundred or one thousand times; by doing so, all intended persons come under one's control. However, if [the mantra] written on birch bark as previously described...
