At twilight, one should slightly warm ten yantras written with substances for scratching one's own body using charcoal from *khadira* wood,

and then cast them into a previously mentioned wax vessel filled with honey. At that time, [the woman's] shame— attained through her feminine nature— which consists of observing the dharma of her own family and the absence of going to or coming from another's house, [is removed].

Having cast far away such discernment as that "it is not fitting to endure the supreme sufferings of falling into the animal realm, the hells, and so forth— which must be experienced for a long time— even if one's own happiness lasts but a very short time," a young woman should remain as a servant to the practitioner.
Thus concludes the introduction to the Nityā Śivādūtī.
Now, the "Not-Hurried" (Athatvaritā) is introduced.

On a level ground measuring one cubit in extent, having constructed a square enclosure (*bhūpura*) with two squares each separated by an interval of two finger-breadths using vermilion or other pigments, and provided with a door and side-panels in the western direction; (p. 137b)

Having drawn two circles within that [space] with an interval of four finger-breadths between them, and having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus in the pathway between them, one should fashion a *bindu* in its pericarp; thus, having constructed the mandala for daily worship (*nityapūjācakra*) according to this procedure,
one should perform the installation of the jar (*kalaśasthāpana*) there according to the prescribed rite.

After the completion of the ritual procedure— which begins with the visualization of the wheel (*cakra*) for the worship of Sarvamaṅgalā, including the worship of her enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) and concludes with her dismissal (*udvāsana*)—

one should again visualize within the water of that very pitcher the wheel (even though it was drawn below), as the Bindu which constitutes the locus of the primary Nityā under discussion, by means of the pitcher’s descent [upon it]. Therein lies the initiation (*dīkṣā*), beginning with the worship that is an ancillary to initiation and ending with initiation itself.

It should be performed on the first day. Then, one should pass that night with festivities such as dance and song. The daily worship, which is an ancillary part of that, is of two kinds: [the first] is performed upon a yantra engraved on materials such as gold, silver, copper, or crystal, in the form prescribed and according to the method described for the Śrīcakra.

"Once the single ground with the living beings has been drawn," it means: all those various modes of worship, such as anointing with fragrant oil and bathing in fragrant water; and since the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth have already been performed at the beginning and end of the morning rites and other rituals due to the context of other deities, for that very reason—

Having purified his body and face, and having adorned himself with red garments, sandalwood paste, and ornaments, the practitioner enters the sacrificial pavilion. Upon a seat— such as a red *kavala* and so forth— which has been purified according to the *kūrma-cakra* and worshipped with the four aforementioned *vidyās*, he [should draw] a *svastika* with the *vidyā* under discussion.
Seated upon one of the lotus-thrones, having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) through knowledge,
and having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with the sixteen-syllable mantra, [one should worship] the nine Nāthas upon one's own head according to the lineage of one's own gurus.

Having worshipped with their respective mantras, which have been described as being of a single form, and having recited that hymn, one should begin the worship by his command, [realizing] one's own Lord (svanātha) as one's own object of worship (svopāsya), one's own Self (svātman) as eternally free from disease (nityāmaya), one's own Self as consisting of one's Lord (svanāthamaya), and one's own Nityā-vidyā as consisting of one's object of worship (svopāsyamayī)— thus [perceiving] the non-difference of one's own Self from one's own Vidyā, Nityā, and Nātha.

Having meditated upon one's own impermanent and permanent worship-circle (*pūjācakra*) above the lion-throne and other supports of the foundation, and having fully worshipped all the deities of the thirty-eight sacred seats (*pīṭha*), from the various *siddhayoginīs* of the specific locations, times, and so forth belonging to that particular year, up to the end of the circle; [one should place] the worship-circle between oneself and one's own self.

Having placed the common *arghya* vessel— made of any one of the five materials such as gold and filled with water scented with *gorocanā*, camphor, saffron, agallochum, and musk— one should [visualize] the nature of fire, sun, and moon respectively for the base, the vessel, the water, and the five substances beginning with *rocanā* by means of the three *kulasaundarī* seed-syllables.

Having contemplated that [the water] consists of the five elements beginning with earth, and having contemplated the identity between that water and the worship-circle currently under discussion, and finally having contemplated the identity between that water and the mantra currently under discussion; having consecrated it ten times with the mantra currently under discussion, and having worshipped the deities of the six limbs with the six limb-mantras.

With the general *arghya* water, one [purifies] oneself; and from the general *arghya* vessel, the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), the *arghya*, the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the water for bathing (*snāna*)—each situated in its own respective vessel—are likewise [offered]. And in this manner, the perfumes (*gandha*), unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers (*puṣpa*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), food offerings (*naivedya*), and betel leaves (*tāmbūla*) situated in the southern portion [are offered].
Having sprinkled each [item] with the recitation of the present vidyā,

one should again perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the vidyā and place the water for the general offering (sāmānyārghya) in the hand, which is equipped with a ladle (darvī) and flowers and so forth.

Having taken [the water], and having inscribed [the mantra] ending with the place, time, lineage, heap (rāśi), name, and desire; having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) according to one's intelligence, "I shall perform the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) according to the rule and without haste," one should pour the water from the hand onto the ground. Furthermore, even in the worship of another deity, if the rites beginning with the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and ending with one's own consecration (*svasaṃskāra*) have not been performed, then in each respective case—
In the place where another mantra was previously enjoined, one should employ the present vidyā itself;

having performed that ritual action at this very opportunity, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) of the Mātṛkā, and then, at the end of the present vidyā, place each individual letter of the Mātṛkā in its respective locations: *khe ca hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *cha ce śirase*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras—*svāhā*, *chekṣaḥ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *kṣaḥ strī kavacāya huṃ*, *strī&huṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ*, and *hū& kṣe astrāya phaṭ*—upon one’s own thumbs and other fingers, as well as upon the heart and other body parts; [one should then place: *hrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ* on the head;
*hrīṃ huṃ hrīṃ* on the forehead; *hrīṃ khe& hrīṃ* on the throat; *hrīṃ ca hrīṃ* on the heart; *hrīṃ che hrīṃ*...

At the navel: *hrīṃ kṣaḥ hrīṃ*. At the *mūlādhāra*: *hrīṃ strī hrīṃ*. With the repetition [of *hrīṃ*], at the thighs: *hrīṃ hrīṃ*. With the repetition, at the knees: *hrīṃ kṣeṃ hrīṃ*. With the repetition, at the shanks: *hrīṃ phaṭ hrīṃ*. With the repetition, at the feet: thus having infused the syllables. Then: *oṃ hrīṃ khecachekṣaḥ strī hūṃ kṣe hrīṃ phaṭ*. Thus [it is done].
Having performed the threefold pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the complete form of the root-mantra, one should proceed with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and subsequent rites.

That is to say: having followed the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā and placed water and red flowers therein, the light pervading from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra* flows through the path of the nose and comes to rest; by the casting [of the flowers] into that [water], [the deity is invoked].
While clearly visualizing [the goddess] ending at the wheel of circles marked by the *cakravindu* of the present [deity],
one should say:
"O Nityā, come quickly here to this wheel at the end of the complete root-mantra and remain!"
Having performed the invocation after making the formal request,
one should contemplate that light as having issued forth from certain hands in the form of the Lord’s weapons, retinues, and powers, which will be described below;
then, one should meditate upon the mass of light situated in the center as having been transformed into the form perceived through meditation.
The nature [of the goddess] as realized through meditation is as follows: she is dark-complexioned, of auspicious form, and endowed with beauty and youth;
she is seated upon a blazing pedestal fashioned by eight serpents arranged in two rows of four;
and she is adorned with earrings, armlets, a girdle, and anklets corresponding to those [serpents].

Her arms were adorned with beautiful bracelets fashioned from the feathers of peacocks and wrapped in garments of young leaves by those of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, who had assumed terrifying forms;
she was radiant with a crown of rubies, her hair bound with a crest of peacock plumes, and she held a parasol above her.

She possesses a banner; her chest is adorned with a string of *guñjā* berries, and the circles of saffron on her breasts are radiant. She has three eyes, a beautiful face, and a lotus-like countenance with a gentle smile.
Her four arms shine as they hold a noose, a goad, the gesture of granting boons (*vara*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for the weapons, armor, and powers is exactly like this;
however, they additionally possess crowns marked with their respective forms.
Then, at the end of the present mantra: "O you who are swift, remain eternally established here in this wheel. Again, at the end of the twenty-two syllables:
"Be veiled. Again, at the end of the twenty-two syllables,
having requested the fourfold rite beginning with installation (*sthāpana*) preceded by the display of the respective mudrās,
saying "be made present," one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra.

Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) using the *vidyā* for *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* in the form beginning with "The vital breaths of that eternal one who has descended here are the vital breaths in this wheel," one should worship [the deity] with the twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*). The mantra for that is as follows:

At the end of the complete twelve-syllable mantra, having offered the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) with the general *arghya* water using the mantra "I offer the *pādya* to Tvaritā Nityā," one should present the *pādya* at her feet with the mantra currently in use. In the same manner, by substituting the word "feet" (*pāda*) with "water for the *arghya*" (*arghya*), "water for sipping" (*ācamana*), and so forth, one should perform the respective offerings.

Having offered the *arghya*, water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), and so forth with the perfected mantras, one should present [these offerings] to the head, face, and other parts using the primary *vidyā*.

Having worshipped with these twelve services (*upacāra*) beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and ending with betel (*tāmbūla*), one should follow the thirteenth service. The method for that is as follows: on the area behind the Goddess, in those respective locations, using their own specific mantras...

Having worshipped the nine Nāthas— Prakāśa, Vimarśa, Ānanda, Śrījñānaśrī, Satyaśrī, Pūrṇasvabhāva, Pratibha, Sumaga, and Nāmaka— by means of the inserted verses, and having meditated upon Jayā and Vijayā as possessing hands like golden cane-stalks and lotuses, [one should place them] on the southern and northern sides of the western door.

Having worshipped with "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Jayā; Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Vijayā," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete vidyā with "I worship the sandals of Tvaritā Nityā," one performs the offering of worship with:
"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, O deities of the first enclosure of Tvaritā Nityā, accept this worship."

Having offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), and having meditated upon the servant (kiṅkara) before the Goddess— dark-complexioned, holding a mace (gadā) in hand, with matted hair standing erect on his head— one should worship him with "Oṃ kiṅkarāya namaḥ. Then, at the end of the root mantra, having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with "I worship the sandals (pādukā) of the eternal Tvaritā," one should proceed.

"HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ! May this second enclosure deity accept the offering. Having thus offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an act of worship, [one visualizes] the Goddess at the fierce portion of the eight-petaled lotus connected to the front petal of the Goddess.

Having meditated upon Phaṭkārīśakti—who possesses the same form, garments, and ornaments [as the principal deity], who holds weapons such as the arrow and bow, and who is therefore distinctively characterized by being two-armed—one should worship her with the eleven-syllable mantra: "Phaṭ phaṭkārīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi. At the end of the root mantra, [one worships] Tvaritā.

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra, "I worship the ever-present *pādukā*," and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering for that worship with the words, "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May this [Goddess] accept the worship of the deities of the third enclosure," one should worship the *pādukā* of Huṃhuṃkarī on the eight petals, beginning from the front and proceeding clockwise.
I worship the sandal of Kheṃ Khencarī. I worship the sandal of Caṃ Caṇḍā. I worship the sandal of Cheṃ Chedanī. I worship the sandal of Kṣaḥ Kṣapaṇī.
I worship the sandal of Strīṃ Strīkārī. I worship the sandal of Hūṃ Hūṃkārī.

Having worshipped the sandals with the mantra, "I worship the sandals that grant security (*kṣema-karī-pādukā*"), and having worshipped their powers (*śakti*), one should worship upon the pericarp itself, on both sides of the Goddess, in the counter-clockwise direction starting from the northwest (*vāyavya*) with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ amītaye namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ varāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ pāśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṅkuśāya namaḥ*. Then, at the end of the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*):

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra "I worship Tvaritā Nityāpādukā," and having offered the handful of flowers for the dedication of the worship with the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the fourth enclosure of Tvaritā Nityā accept this worship," one should perform the thirteen-fold ritual service (upacāra).

Having performed the remaining three services—whatever they may be—in the form of reciting hymns, waving lamps, and prostrations; and having performed the daily *japa* (repetition) either one hundred or one thousand times, enclosed by the *aṅguṣṭhādinyāsa*, *hṛdayādinyāsa*, *varṇanyāsa*, and *vyāpakanyāsa*; [one should perform] the offering consisting of the contemplation of non-difference from that [deity].

Having performed ten parts of that [number of oblations] with ghee and other substances, preceded by sixteen oblations and following the previously mentioned rules for the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), one should unite the splendor manifested as fire with the drop (*bindu*) which constitutes the place of the Goddess's worship. Having worshipped her with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), [one should worship] with the mantra: *Oṃ kiṅkarāya namaḥ*.

Having offered the aforementioned oblation (*bali*) consisting of actual substances to the servant (*kiṅkara*) stationed within the maṇḍala crowded with his own peers, and having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) with camphor-filled water and asked for forgiveness, one should— by means of the *śaktyutthāpana-mudrā*—
at the time of concluding the rite, [withdraw] the rays that have been transformed into the form of those respective powers, just as the sun withdraws its rays at the end of the day.

Having caused [the deity] to dissolve into the principal Goddess who is present before her, and having gathered all the rays back into that principal Goddess, one should dismiss her into one's own self by means of the *khecarīmudrā*. Then, having performed the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) and the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), as well as the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*) as before, and having recited the hymn to the Goddess and the hymn to the Guru, one may conclude. This is the specific procedure regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*).
It has been for the most part already stated.

Thus, one who has received initiation should follow the method for accomplishing the means of confidence when there is a desire for ritual application; and that [method] has already been stated. Here, since it has been established through the previously mentioned procedure that the twelve-syllable mantra possesses eleven non-repeated syllables, its accomplishment consists in performing one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣa*) according to the number of those non-repeated syllables.
In the present context, while eleven lakhs of recitations were prescribed for the Kṛta Yuga, the number of recitations for this current age is forty-four lakhs using bilva leaves. (p.

The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with one-tenth of the number of recitations (japa) using any one of the sacrificial fuels (samidhā) appropriate for the specific fruit sought; the substance for the libation (tarpaṇa) is the same as that used generally.

Even when a substance has been thus prepared, one should employ it only by the command of the Guru and not out of one's own desire, for it is only then truly beneficial; nor should one perform a practice even if it is not prohibited, out of greed for wealth and the like.
Now, these are the applications for the obligatory rites.

One should strike the face of one bitten by a serpent with handfuls of water consecrated by the aforementioned mantra, recited either a hundred or a thousand times; by this, even one who is nearly dead from the serpent's bite shall be restored to life. Alternatively, for one bitten by a serpent, one should mutter the present mantra into both ears a hundred or other such number of times; by that, even one who is nearly dead shall rise up.

Alternatively, one should strike the head of a person bitten by a snake with sixty [stalks] consecrated by recitation [of the mantra] up to a hundred times; by that means, even one who is as if dead shall rise up.
Thus concludes the application of the recitation.
Having constructed a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the prescribed method, having fashioned a vulva (*yoni*) in the form of a triangle facing oneself in its center,

and having established the fire within it, one should perform oblations with the substances to be mentioned below— sesame, mustard, wheat, rice, grain, and barley— anointed with the three sweets; this is the general procedure common to all the homas under discussion.

Through oblations performed with these combined or mutually unmixed, one shall attain all prosperity. By offering oblations of *vakula* flowers, *campaka* flowers, lotuses, *kahlāra*, red lotuses, white water-lilies, jasmine, *kṛndama*, and *madhūka* flowers—
each smeared with the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar)— whether combined or unmixed with one another, the attainment of *lakṣmī* (prosperity) shall occur.
Of flowers— Aśoka, Pāṭala, Bilva, Jātī, Vicikila, Nīlotpala, Karavīra, and Karṇikāra—
that have blossomed spontaneously, and which are smeared with the three sweets, whether they are joined together or not.

From this oblation, there shall be the attainment of prosperity, good fortune, long life, and the acquisition of a treasury of fame; furthermore, one’s own desired fruit shall be realized. [This is achieved] with three blades of *dūrvā*, *guḍūcī*, *pippala*, *vaṭa*, *āragvadha*, white *arkapla* (white sunflower), and *plakṣa* fuel-sticks.
From the offering of each individual oblation or from the collective offering of items smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), there shall be the destruction of disease.

From the offering of sugarcane joints, *jambīra* fruit, coconut fruit, plantain fruit, jaggery, and sugar—whether combined or not—with them smeared by the three sweets, there shall be unshakable prosperity (*lakṣmī*) and one shall become a partaker thereof. However, if it is sesame seeds and so forth...

If the oblation (homa) is performed by abandoning the practice of anointing substances ending with sugar with the three sweets (trimadhu) and instead resorting to anointing them with ghee, honey, and milk, then for as long as one lives, one remains under the control of women through wealth and life-force. Now, [if it is] performed with substances anointed with ghee alone—

If the oblation is performed with [the aforementioned substances], then kings become submissive. Furthermore, if the oblation is performed with offerings smeared solely with milk, then deities other than those mentioned become submissive. Through an oblation in a fire kindled by *kāraskara* wood using mustard oil, the death of an enemy occurs; likewise, the death of an enemy occurs from an oblation of the flesh of the animal corresponding to the enemy's birth-nakṣatra, smeared with mustard oil.

Having prepared a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) cooked in blood from the birth-star of an enemy, anointed with *aruṣkara* oil and clarified butter, over a fire kindled with *vibhītaka* wood; wearing black garments and a turban, holding a sword in hand, with a mind overcome by wrath, the practitioner, appearing like the head of a serpent, [should perform this] one hundred times or more at midnight.

If one were to perform the oblation according to a specific number, then even when there is an obstacle to the death of the enemy, one would kill the enemy solely by the power of the efficacy of one's own mantra.

By performing *homa* with a fire kindled by *kāraskara* wood, using either the fruits or the leaves of the *kāraskara* plant— each practiced separately for seven nights with a recitation of a thousand or more mantras— the enemy's elephants and horses will contract disease. Likewise, [the same result follows] from the fruits and leaves of the *caturaṅgula*, also known as *āragvadha*, each used separately.

By performing oblations practiced for seven nights, the fourfold army of enemies— consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry— will certainly become afflicted by disease and brought under one's control.
Thus end the procedures for the fire-oblation (homa).
Now, the applications of the mechanical devices (yantras).
Having drawn twelve lines each extending east-west and twelve lines each extending north-south, with equal intervals and intersecting one another, thus forming one hundred and twenty-one squares;
and having placed a trident at each of the tips of all those lines; [one should place it] in the very center square.

Having set aside five squares in each of the directions and having written the *praṇava* in the sixth form, and having written the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the object of practice (*sādhya*), and so forth within that [central space], and having written the *māyāvīja* once in all the squares starting from the northeast (*īśāna*), one should write the twelve syllables of the mantra— beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with the weapon (*astra*)— in sequence in twelve rounds.

This yantra is perfected; for the practitioner who, after performing worship preceded by the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), empowers it with the present vidyā a thousand times or more and wears it, there shall be prosperity, fame, the power to bring all women under the control of their own husbands,
and the pacification of poisons.
There is pacification of planetary afflictions, pacification of those ending with insanity, victory in battles,
and the subjugation of men, women, kings, ministers, and others. Another yantra is as follows:
Having drawn nine lines each extending from east to west and from south to north, with equal intervals and intersecting one another,
one should prepare a diagram consisting of sixty-four squares. Then,
starting from the northeast square, one should write the Mahālakṣmī mantra facing westward across four rows within those squares.
Furthermore, beginning from the southeast corner and facing east, one should write that same *anuṣṭubh* Lakṣmī mantra.

Considering the central group of four squares as the middle cell, the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the person for whom the rite is performed (*sādhya*), and so forth, should be written there.
The present Vidyā should be written in such a way that its tips touch the lines of the outer square.

This yantra, which has attained the state of fourteen syllables through the addition of the syllable *vaṣaṭ* to the twelve-syllabled [mantra], having been smeared [with substances] and perfected by means of the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), worship, consecration with mantras, and so forth— [is now complete].

Worn on the left arm and other limbs, it brings about great prosperity and confers auspiciousness in every respect. In whatever house, village, or city this Yantra is installed, there shall not even be a mention of inauspiciousness; how much less, then, any connection with ill fortune? The Lakṣmī-mantra is as follows: *Śrī-sāmāmāyāmāsā*.
Śrī-sā-no-yāj-ña-jñeyā-no-sāmā-yā-līlā-līlī-yā-mā-yāj-ñe-lālī-līlā-jñe-ā.

As for another yantra: having drawn ten lines—one extending east-west and the others north-south—equidistant from one another and intersecting each other, one produces a wheel of eighty-one squares (*ekāśīti-koṣṭhaka*).

Having written the letter *ṭa* in the central square, which is the fifth from all sides, and having inscribed within it the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the object of practice (*sādhya*), and so forth;

In each of the four directions beginning with the east, one should write the syllables *juṃ*, *saḥ*, *va*, and *ṣaḍ* by entering downward in sequence, starting from the fifth square of the outermost row.

In this manner, seventeen squares have been assigned. In the remaining sixty-four squares, one should write the *Sarvatobhadra* mantra of Mahālakṣmī starting from the northeast (Īśāna) in a single circuit as before;
then, starting from the southwest (Nairṛtya), one should write it in a second circuit. Outside of that, as before, [one should write] the mantra of the present Nityā.

Having written [the mantra] devoid of *phaṭ* but accompanied by *vaṣaṭ*, thereby attaining the state of having thirteen syllables, one should encircle it in sequence; then, having encircled that with the letter *va* so as to form a garland-shape, one should fashion two circles outside of that in the shape of a water-pot (*kumbha*),
facing upwards and upwards, and in the surrounding portion of their openings—
One should fashion an eight-petalled lotus facing downwards at the base of the pitcher (*kumbha*) starting from the *mūlādhāra*,
and another eight-petalled lotus facing upwards, in such a way that the pitcher, once the mechanical device has been inserted within it, becomes enclosed between the two lotuses. Thus...

This yantra is perfected. Having engraved it upon plates of gold, silver, or other metals, and having worshipped the yantra after performing the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force) and other rites;
and furthermore, having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, and so forth there, one should worship the present Nityā [goddess] a thousand times or more.
Having consecrated it with the prescribed number of recitations, wherever it is buried—in houses, villages, cities, or the like—there shall be an increase in prosperity;

the people residing there shall enjoy freedom from disease, and there shall be an increase in cattle, elephants, horses, and other livestock. Furthermore, by wearing it on the hand or other limbs, affliction caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and the like shall cease.

The *nigrahayantra* is as follows: having constructed a wheel of eighty-one squares as before, one should place the syllable *svāra* in the middle square among all those containing the fifth form, and in the center of that—

Without writing down the names of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth, one should write the four seed-syllables *bhrūṃ*, *kṣūṃ*, *chrūṃ*, and *hrūṃ* in order, each in the fifth square of the four paths leading to every direction on the exterior. Then, in the remaining sixty-four squares, starting from the northeast square (*īśāna*)...

Having written the Kālī-mantra in the Anuṣṭubh meter according to its sequential order, one should inscribe that Anuṣṭubh mantra starting from the southwest corner (nirṛtikoṇa) upon a black cloth or similar surface. Then, having encircled this entire yantra with the letter *ya* on the outside, one should again encircle it on the outside with the letter *ra*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of fire. Thus.
This yantra is perfected when it is smeared on the outside with *brahmadaṇḍī*, the eight types of poison, *kāmpā*, and the root of *markaṭī*; then,
having performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), the practitioner— wearing black garments, sword in hand, and his mind overcome by wrath—
should recite the present *nityā* mantra while [the enemy] is in the eighth zodiacal sign at the time of birth, within a hollow of a *vibhītaka* tree.

Or rather, one should cast it into an anthill, or into a temple of the Mothers such as Brāhmī, or into a temple of the Teacher (the Buddha), or even into a cemetery. By that means, misfortune, all diseases, and pestilence shall dwell perpetually in that place.
The mantra of Kālī is as follows:
The mantra of Yama is as follows: *kālīmāraramālīnamokṣakṣamonalīmāmodetadatademomārakṣatatvatvatakṣaro*.
Just as the mantra of Yama is:
*yamāvāṭaṭavāmāyamāṭamoṭaṭhamoṭhamāvāmobhūriribhūmovāṭaṭarītvatva-*.
Regarding "rīṭaṭa": another yantra is also to be fashioned as before, having constructed a yantra consisting of sixty-four squares with ever-new lines. (p.

There, having written the names of the practitioner, the object of practice, and so forth within the central four squares, and having written the Kālī mantra starting from the northeast (Īśāna) cell, and again having written the Kālī mantra starting from the southwest (Nairṛtya) corner,
one performs the encirclement with the previously mentioned Yama mantra and with the letters *ya* and *ra*.

One should further follow two other enclosures. However, in the case of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) directed against women, one should write the *Yama-mantra* twice within the squares and then perform the writing with the *Kālī-mantra*. This very *yantra*, according to the previously mentioned method, effects the subjugation of enemies as described before.

The *anugraha* (favor-bestowing) *yantra* is as follows: having drawn an eight-petalled lotus and having written the *māyā-bīja* (*hrīṃ*) in its pericarp, one writes the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), which is the form of the first letter of the mantra to be employed, within that; then, having written the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object of the rite (*sādhya*) therein, one places the eight syllables beginning with *huṃ* and ending with *kṣa* starting from the tip [of the petals].
Having written this upon wooden leaves, one should encircle that lotus with the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīḥ). Outside of that,

having formed a jar (*kumbha*) with two circles serving as the support for the yantra, and having enclosed that jar between two *kasalā* vessels— one facing upward and one facing downward— this is the first yantra.

The second yantra consists of the placement of the syllable *huṃ* in the position of the *praṇava*. By the placement of eight other supreme syllables beginning with *khe* and ending with *phaṭ*, there arise the eight subsequent yantras from the third to the tenth; thus, in total, ten yantras are perfected. Among them, from the first yantra comes all-protection (*sarvarakṣā*), and from the second comes victory (*vijaya*).
From the third [recitation], there is the subjugation of men; from the fourth, the attainment of the state of being a determiner of the subjugation of women;
and from the fifth, the subjugation of kings, their wives, sons, and ministers.
The immobilization of enemy armies occurs from the sixth [house]; the acquisition of fortune from the seventh; the attainment of fame from the eighth;
and the gain of gold from the ninth.
The gain of clothing results from the tenth house through means such as its retention, worship, and consecration with jars filled with that [water].
I.
Now, the yantras with modified syllables.
In this *vidyā*, there are eleven unmodified syllables: the syllable *oṃ*, the letters *ha*, *ra*, and *ka*; *kha*, *ca*, *cha*, and *kṣa*;
and *sa*, *la*, and the two *pha*s. When each of these is joined with the sixteen vowels, there are one hundred and seventy-six modified syllables (*vikṛtākṣara*).
By joining sixteen modified syllables (*vikṛtākṣara*) to each one of these [diagrams], eleven yantras are produced.

To illustrate: having fashioned two circles with an interval of four finger-breadths between them, and having fashioned a sixteen-petalled lotus within that space, one places the *māyābīja* in its pericarp, and inside that—

Having inscribed the sixteen modified syllables of the *praṇava*— in the form of *a, ā, i, ī*, and so forth— in a clockwise direction starting from the tip upon the petals named after the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*), following the sequence beginning with the first; then, having drawn one outer circle and created a single path (*vīthī*) by means of the "planet-circle" (*grahavṛtta*), one should encircle that path with the *māyā-bīja*.

Having surrounded that with a garland of vowels (a-kāra) so that it may be as described, one should fashion a jar encased within two lotuses by means of two circles, as before; thus the first yantra is accomplished. In this same manner, there are ten other [yantras] for the ten mantra-syllables beginning with *ha* and ending with *ṭha*, using sixteen modified letters (*vikṛtārṇa*).
Together, eleven types of machines were completed. Among them, first were the elephant-protections; second, the horse-protections; third, the king-protections.

From the fourth [yantra] comes the protection of the authority over the royal insignia; from the fifth, the protection of the army; from the sixth, the protection of the royal palace; from the seventh, the protection of the city; from the eighth, the protection of all dwellings; from the ninth, the pacification of all diseases and afflictions; and from the tenth and eleventh yantras—

The fruit is characterized by a specific duty to be performed (*setikartavyatā-viśeṣaka*). For example, having written the tenth yantra on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*), having inserted that yantra into a lump of beeswax (*siktha*) in the shape of a linga, and having placed it into a jar filled with cool water, one should station the patient near it. Then, having worshipped the present-day *Nityā* in that jar, [one should perform the rite] with the *Jīvakara* [mantra].

While touching the patient, one should mutter eighteen syllables— namely the sixteen syllables beginning with *pha*, *phā*, *phi*, *phī*, and so forth, along with the *māyā-bīja* (*hrīṃ*) and the letter *va*— either a thousand or a hundred times. When this is done, even a fever caused by malevolent rites such as *abhicāra* that is otherwise incurable will quickly [leave] the patient.

Having liberated [the obstacle], one should cast it upon the practitioner himself. This very procedure is the duty; this indeed is the fruit. Even for the eleven-fold yantra, when reciting, in place of *pha pha* and so forth, *ṭa ṭā ṭi ṭī* and so forth should be inserted—this is the distinction that must be understood. Thus ends the introduction to Tvaritā Nityā. Alternatively:
The Nityā Aparaparyāyakulasundarī is now introduced.

On a certain pure patch of ground measuring one cubit in size, having constructed two square enclosures (*bhūpura*) with a slight interval between them, each provided with door-frames on the eastern and western sides; and having constructed two circles within those, with an interval of four finger-breadths between them.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus within the intermediate path, touching the inner circle at its base and touching the outer circle at its tip;
Within the circular area of that pericarp, one should draw the *yonicakra*.
Having drawn the Brahma-sūtra extending from east to west, touching both tips of that circle at its central point,
and having divided that sūtra into sixteen parts— one should [mark] there at the fourth part, then at the third part, and then at the fifth part.
Starting from each of those marks, one should draw three lines running north-south; then,

from the two points where the middle line intersects the northern and southern circles, one should strike two horizontal lines reaching as far as the junctions at the ends of the Brahma-line and the respective circular segments.

Then, starting from the two points where the line situated at the western end of one's own front row of *bhūtas* meets the southern and northern circles, and drawing two lines reaching as far as the junction point between the *brahmasūtra* and the eastern portion of the circle,
[one proceeds] from the third line located in the eastern direction.

As before, starting from the junctions of the circular sections at the southern and northern tips, and having first broken the junction points of the two upward-pointing triangles on the central axis, one should draw two lines reaching as far as the junction point of the western line and the Brahma-line, and then erase the portion of the Brahma-line.

A nine-yoni wheel is thus established, consisting of a circle touching eight triangular fields, with one additional square on each side and at the rear of the yoni situated above its own apex. Having thus prepared the wheel of the elements, one should place a *bindu* in the central portion of the triangle in the very middle; then, having extracted the wheel for the daily worship once it is complete.

Therein, at the conclusion of the ritual actions beginning with the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśa*), the performance of all auspicious rites (*sarvamaṅgala*), the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), the visualization of the maṇḍala (*cakracintana*), and the worship of the deity along with the surrounding retinue (*sāvaraṇa*), and ending with the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*)— on page 146a:

Again, having visualized the aforementioned wheel of daily worship (*nityāpūjācakra*) within that very vessel (*kalaśa*), the worship that constitutes a limb of initiation (*dīkṣā*) should be performed there. However, worship that does not constitute a limb of initiation is performed in the wheel alone, and not even the installation of the vessel; the procedure for that is as follows: preceded by anointing with fragrant oil and so forth.

Having bathed with fragrant waters and performed the other morning duties, as well as the daily rites for the deities and ancestors, he— having already practiced the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*),
and the concluding rites of his own personal purificatory ceremonies— possesses a body and face that are completely purified.

The practitioner, having adorned himself with red garments, sandalwood paste, forehead marks, and so forth, and having arrived at the sacrificial pavilion, should sit upon a red seat worshipped with the previously mentioned fourfold seat-mantras; then, assuming either a svastika or lotus posture upon that seat while reciting the present mantra, he should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth and breath control (prāṇāyāma) using the mantra.

Having offered the *bali* with the sixteen-syllable mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-limbed mantras upon one’s own thumbs and other fingers, as well as upon the heart and other parts of the body, reciting: *Āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *Ī śirase svāhā*, *Oṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *Aiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *Auṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ*, *Aḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Then, [recite] *Aiṃ Āṃ ūrdhvavaktrāya*.
*Namaḥ* to one's own head in the Īśāna portion. *Aiṃ īṃ*, obeisance to the eastern face in the eastern part;
*aiṃ ūṃ*, obeisance to the southern face in the southern part; *aiṃ aiṃ*, obeisance to the northern face in the northern part;
*aiṃ oṃ*, obeisance to the western face in the western part; *aiṃ aḥ*, obeisance to the downward face.

In the western, southwestern, and central sections— having thus performed the placement of the six faces (*ṣaḍvakranyāsa*)— one should worship the nine lords upon one’s own head according to the sequence of one’s own lord and with their respective mantras. Having recited that hymn consisting of five verses and having requested permission for the worship, one should begin it [focusing on] one's own self, one's own lord, one's own universe, and one's own object of worship.
Having meditated upon the identity of the deities,
[one should consider] the place, time, and so forth, as determined by the specific rules for each respective year.

Having worshipped all the thirty-eight deities of the *pīṭhas*, ending with the entire circle of the secret and manifest *siddha-yoginīs*, upon the lion-throne which serves as the support for the wheel of the present daily worship;
[one should place] between one's own self and the *yantra* a vessel containing water mixed with the five substances beginning with yellow pigment (*gorocanā*).

Having placed a common *arghya* vessel made of gold or any other suitable material, one should meditate on the waters in its supporting vessel as being, in sequence, composed of the present *nityā*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*), fire, the sun, and the moon. One should then contemplate the *rocanā* and other substances contained therein as consisting of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*). Finally, one should contemplate the unity of those waters with the present *nityā-cakra*.
Having meditated upon the water as having the nature of the present *nityā*, and having consecrated and worshipped it ten times with the present *vidyā*;

or else, having fully worshipped the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*) by means of the six-limbed mantras located in the middle portion of the worship; [he should then] with that water and the present *vidyā, [sprinkle] himself from the general offering vessel (*sāmānyārghyapātra*).

The water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the water for bathing (*snāna*) located in their respective vessels on the northern side; and likewise, having individually sprinkled the garments, ornaments, perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and betel leaves located on the southern side— then, having again restrained the breaths (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *vidyā*, [he takes] the water from the common respectful offering (*sāmānyārghya*) with a ladle (*darvī*).

Holding rice, sesame seeds, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) in his hand, he should state: "Having specified the place, time, lineage, *rāśi*, name, and desire, I shall perform the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) of the goddess Kulasundarīnityā according to the prescribed rule and as far as my intelligence permits. Having thus stated this, he should pour the water held in his hand onto the ground. Then, even if [the worship] has not been performed due to the intervention of another deity—
In rites such as the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*),

at this juncture, by means of the very *vidyā* under discussion— which has been employed in place of other mantras prescribed for various specific instances— one should perform [the rite] in that manner.

Having performed the ritual actions, at the conclusion of the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā*, one should perform the individual placement (*pratyekanyāsa*) in each respective location using each letter of the *mātṛkā* together with the present vidyā: *klāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*,
*klīṃ śirase svāhā*, *hūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *klaiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *klauṃ netrābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ*, *klaḥ*.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limb-mantras on one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other body parts, [recite]:
*aiṃ klāṃ* to the upper face, *namaḥ*; *aiṃ klīṃ* to the eastern face, *namaḥ*;
*aiṃ klūṃ* to the southern face, *namaḥ*; *aiṃ klaiṃ* to the northern face, *namaḥ*; *aiṃ klauṃ* to the western face, *namaḥ*.

"Oṃ namaḥ aiṃ klīṃ adhara-vaktrāya namaḥ"—thus one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the aforementioned locations on one's own head. Then: *aiṃ* at the *mūlādhāra*; *klīṃ* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*); *sauḥ* at the heart. This is the first *yoninyāsa*. *Aiṃ* at the left eye; *klīṃ* on the forehead; *sauḥ* at the right eye. This is the second *yoninyāsa*. *Aiṃ* at the left ear; *klīṃ* at the right ear; *sauḥ* at the chin. Thus [the third].

The third [placement]: *aiṃ* in the left nostril; *klīṃ* in the right nostril; *sauḥ* at the base of the palate. This is the fourth *yoninyāsa*: *aiṃ* in the left ear; *klīṃ* in the right ear; *sauḥ* on the chin. This is the third [placement]. *Aiṃ* in the left nostril; *klīṃ* in the right nostril; *sauḥ* at the base of the palate. This is the fourth *yoninyāsa*.
Aiṃ on the left shoulder; Klīṃ at the navel; Sauḥ on the right shoulder—this is the fifth [set]. Aiṃ at the base of the right hand; Klīṃ in the middle of the right hand;
Sauḥ at the tip of the right hand—this is the sixth. Aiṃ at the base of the left hand; Klīṃ in the middle of the left hand;
Sauḥ at the tip of the left hand—this is the seventh. Aiṃ at the base of the right foot.
*Klīṃ* in the middle of the right foot; *Sauḥ* at the tip of the right foot. Thus is the eighth [set]. *Aiṃ* at the root of the left foot;
*Klīṃ* in the middle of the left foot; *Sauḥ* at the tip of the left foot. (p. 147b)

Thus ends the ninth placement (nyāsa) of the womb. Having thus performed the ninefold placement of the syllables, one should perform the threefold pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) with the root mantra complete with its three syllables—*aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*—and then follow the sequence beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*). It is as follows:

While visualizing that the mass of red flowers held in cupped hands— preceded by the recitation of the *trikhaṇḍā* mantra— has been transferred via the path of the central channel (*vaha-nāsādhvan*) from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*, where it was pervaded by the splendor of the present vidyā,
and has now arrived at the present *cakravindu* through the casting of that handful of flowers;

Having made the prayer, "O Nityā Bhogakulasundarī, at the conclusion of the complete Vidyā, be invoked here in this cakra," and having performed the invocation, [one should contemplate] some rays of that splendor issuing forth toward the locations to be described, in the form of the Lord, the weapons, and the retinue.

Having visualized [the seed-syllable] as having undergone transformation, one should meditate upon the mass of light situated in the center as transformed by its essential nature realized through meditation. As for the meditation: she is red, attended by a multitude of powers of red form, wearing red garments, ornaments, garlands, and unguents; she has six lotus-faces, each with three eyes.
Likewise, she was endowed with a beautiful smile; radiant with a crown of rubies set in priceless gems;
her auspicious chest was adorned with clusters of jewels;
she was the supreme bliss of compassion, seated upon a red lotus; and she was possessed of twelve arms for the sake of all.
She who embodies all systems of speech, holding in her right hands a coral rosary, a lotus, a water-pot fashioned of jewels,
a jar filled with gems, a citron, and the gesture of exposition; and in her left hands, a book, a blue lotus, a golden pen, a jewel garland, and a fine silken garment.
And he was praised by the *abhijñās*, as well as by gods, *gandharvas*, *kinnaras*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, celestial sages (*devarṣis*), *siddhas*, *vidyādharas*, and others. (p. 148a)

This same meditation applies to the weapons, armor, and powers (*śakti*) of the Lord as well. However, regarding the aspect of the weapons, there is the additional feature of having a crest marked with their respective forms. Then, at the end of the complete mantra:
"O Bhukulasundarī, O Nityā, be established here in this wheel. Again, at the end of the fifteen syllables:
"Be completely restrained" (*sanniruddhābhava*). Again, at the end of the fifteen syllables, [pray]: "Be veiled" (*avaguṇṭhitābhava*).

Again, at the end of the fifteen syllables, [pray]: "Be made present" (*sannidhāpitā bhava*), having first displayed the respective mudrās. Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs for the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra of this [deity]...

Having established the vital breaths by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra in the form "The vital breaths of Kulasundarīnityā are here in this wheel," one should worship her with the twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*). Her mantras are as follows:
at the end of the complete mantra, with the mantra "I offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to Kulasundarīnityā."
Having offered the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) with the general *arghya* water, one should present the *pādya* at the feet using the mantra of the deity being invoked.
In the same manner, by substituting the word "arghya" or "ācamana" and so forth in place of the word "pādya," and having offered the *arghya*,
*ācamana*, and other services using the *saṃpanna* mantra, one should [offer them] at the head, face, and other parts using the mantra of the deity being invoked.

Having thus offered [the oblation] and worshipped with the twelve services (*upacāra*), one should proceed to the thirteenth service. Its manner is as follows: on the rear part of the Goddess, [one worships] those named Prakāśa, Vimarśa, Ānanda, Śrījñāna, Satya, Pūrṇasvabhāva, Pratibha, and Subhaga.

Having worshipped with their respective mantras, which incorporate the word *śakti* in place of the word *kānnātha*, one begins from the front corner of the triangle and proceeds counter-clockwise: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Bhāṣā;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Ānandā; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Kautukā."

On the two side-paths of the triangle, starting from the region near the Goddess’s left lower hand and ending at the region near her right lower hand, [one should perform the ritual] counter-clockwise in twelve places.

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Varāya; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Kavaca; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Ratnamālā; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Hemamekhalā; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Aruṇotpalā; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Pustaka;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Pravālākṣasraj; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Padma; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Ratnakuṇḍikā.

Having worshipped with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ratnapūrṇacaṣakāyai namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ luṅgyai namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ vyākhyānamudrāyai namaḥ*; and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete Vidyā with: *sampūrṇavidyānte kulasundarīnityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; [worship] *hrīṃ śrīṃ etāḥ*.

Having offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) as the dedication of the worship with the words, "May the deities of the first enclosure of Kulasundarīnityā accept this worship," one proceeds clockwise through the eight triangles of the ninefold wheel (navayonicakra), beginning from the foremost triangle:
"I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Sarasvatī; I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vāṇī."

Having worshipped those respective Śaktis with the mantras: *hrīṃ śrīṃ saṃskṛtāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ prākṛtāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ parāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ bahurūpāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ citrāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ ābhyāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*;
and at the end of the complete Vidyā, [worshipping] the one situated in the center with: *kulasaundarīnityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having worshipped the Goddess: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the second enclosure, the Kulasundarīs and Nityās, accept this worship. Having thus offered a handful of flowers for the dedication of that worship, [one worships] on the eight petals, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise:
"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! I worship the sandals of Brāhmī. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! [I worship] the sandals of Māheśvarī. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! [I worship] the sandals of Kaumārī."
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vaiṣṇavī-pāda; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vārāhī-pāda; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aindrī-pāda; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Cāmuṇḍā-pāda.

Having worshipped each of those eight Mothers with the mantras "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Mahālakṣmī," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete Vidyā with "I worship the sandals of Kulasundarī Nityā," [one should say]: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, may these deities of the third enclosure of Kulasundarī Nityā accept this worship."
Having offered a handful of flowers as an act of worship for that, [one should worship] in the square on the southern path of the eastern gate:

*hrīṃ śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Indra-Śakti; in the southeast (*āgneya*): *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Agni-Śakti; on the southern path: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Yama-Śakti; in the southwest (*nairṛtya*): *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Rakṣas-Śakti.

On the northern path of the western gate: *hrīṃ śrīṃ* Varuṇa-śaktipāda; in the northwest (*vāyavya*): *hrīṃ śrīṃ* Anila-śaktipāda; on the northern path: *hrīṃ śrīṃ* Soma-śaktipāda; in the northeast (*īśāna*): *hrīṃ śrīṃ* Īśa-śaktipāda;
on the southern path of the western gate: *hrīṃ śrīṃ* Ananta-śaktipāda.
On the northern path of the eastern gate, having worshipped those respective Śaktis with the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ vidiśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*;

and at the end of the complete Vidyā, having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra: *kulasundarīnityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; [one should know: *hrīṃ śrīṃ etāḥ kulasundarīnityācaturthāvaraṇadevatāḥ* (these are the deities of the fourth enclosure of Kulasundarīnityā).

One should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for the presentation of that worship with the words, "May [the deity] accept the worship. Thus, at the conclusion of performing the thirteen services (*upacāra*), one should perform the constant recitation (*japa*) after completing the three remaining services consisting of the recitation of whatever hymns are appropriate, the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and prostration (*praṇāma*). Regarding that, the specific procedure is as follows: *Āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *Īṃ śirase svāhā*, and so forth, as previously stated.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs upon the faces according to the six-limbed mantras in the manner previously described,
and having completed half the number of recitations to be performed— whether one thousand or one hundred— in the form of five hundred and fifty;
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the hands, limbs, and mouth with the mantras stated as "klāṃ to the heart, namaḥ; klīṃ to the head, svāhā," and so forth,
one should complete the recitation according to the number prescribed for oneself.

Having performed the placement of the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) on one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other parts of the body, with the following: *sāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *sīṃ śirase svāhā*, *sūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *saiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *sauṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ*, *saḥ astrāya phaṭ*;
[one should then recite]: *aiṃ sāṃ ūrdhvavaktrāya namaḥ*, *aiṃ sīṃ prāgvaktrāya namaḥ*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the appropriate locations of one's own head with the mantras: *aiṃ sūṃ dakṣiṇavaktrāya namaḥ*, *aiṃ saiṃ udīcyavaktrāya namaḥ*, *aiṃ sauṃ paścimavaktrāya namaḥ*, *aiṃ saḥ adharavaktrāya namaḥ*;
[one should perform] the contemplation of the essential identity between oneself and the deity of the mantra being recited.

One should perform the offering to the fire (*agninivedana*). Then, having offered sixteen oblations of clarified butter according to the prescribed rite, as well as a tenth part of the total number of recitations (*japa*), one should unite the radiant energy (*tejas*) of the present *Nityā*—which has been manifested by the fire—with the *bindu* that serves as the locus for the worship of the Goddess. One should then again worship the Goddess, who has arrived at the *bindu*, with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*).

Having worshipped with the seven-syllabled mantra of Kurukullā and offered the bali-oblation, having performed the lustration (ārati) with a wick containing camphor and other substances, and having asked for forgiveness; one should contemplate that the deities who constitute the Goddess's retinue have been absorbed back into the mass of the Goddess's splendor by means of the mudrā of the rising power (śaktyutthāpana).

Having dissolved even the mass of radiant energy that has become the Goddess by means of the *khecarīmudrā* into one's own self, and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs with "Soṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ,

Sīṃ śirase svāhā," and so forth, as well as the placement of the faces in the form of "Aiṃ sāṃ ūrdhvavaktrāya namaḥ, Aiṃ sīṃ prāgvaktrāya namaḥ," and so on, [one should recite] the hymn to the Goddess and the hymn to the Guru.
Having recited [the mantra], one should cease.
The specific procedure to be performed immediately after the worship that is an ancillary of initiation (*dīkṣāṅga-pūjā*) has already been shown; it should be followed here as well.

Thus, immediately after attaining the *vidyā*, the practitioner (*sādhaka*), intent upon daily worship and desiring to accomplish his own cherished goals through ritual applications (*prayoga*), should perform the means for their attainment. The method for this is as follows:

here, there are four non-repeated syllables; according to the principle that for each non-repeated syllable there are three hundred thousand repetitions (*lakṣa-traya*), [the total is calculated accordingly].

In the Kṛta Yuga, the recitation (japa) for this vidyā was twelve lakhs; since that has become fourfold in the present yuga, forty-eight lakh recitations are required. A fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with one-tenth of that number, using unbroken palāśa flowers that have blossomed naturally, free from defects such as hair or insects, and soaked in the "three sweets" (trimadhura).

The libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be performed with water scented by camphor, saffron, and other substances, equal in number to the oblations (*homa*); the remainder is entirely as previously stated in the section concerning Vahnivāsinī in all cases.
Now follow the perpetual applications (nityaprayoga) of this.

Having anointed his body with a paste composed of ten fragrant substances— namely sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, musk, gorocana, saffron, kālāguru, mṛgasveda, and mṛgamada— and wearing variegated garments and adorned with garlands of flowers and other ornaments,
he should worship the Goddess at the time of dusk with the perfumes and other offerings made from the aforementioned group of ten substances beginning with sandalwood.

In the manner previously described, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands, limbs, and heart preceded by reciting each seed-syllable— obtained in sequence during the middle and final periods— conjoined with the six long vowels, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) a thousand times or more; then, having risen in the morning and completed the morning rites up to the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vandana*), one should take water in the right palm (*culuka*) and [place it] therein.

Having visualized the *mātṛkā* yantra as it will be described hereafter, one should recite the *mātṛkā*— from *a* to *kṣa*, accompanied by the *bindu*— three times. Then, having likewise recited the principal mantra (*prastutavidyā*) three times,
[one should proceed].

Having meditated upon that consecrated water as being of the nature of nectar (*amṛta*), and having visualized the channel named Sarasvatī— which is to be meditated upon— extending from the *mūlādhāra* up to the tip of the tongue, one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) while conceiving it as a form of oblation (*homa*). By this, one shall attain the very nature of all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Regarding the attainment of the Kākathā-vidyā, the maximum duration for its practice here is one year.
Thus concludes the ritual application for attaining the vidyā through drinking water.

Having cooked this quartet of substances— four parts of ghee taken according to one's own desire, a fourth part of *brāhmī* juice relative to the ghee, a quantity of *vacā* powder equal to the ghee, and milk equal in measure to the ghee—
for three days over a very gentle fire, and having removed it once cooled, [one should apply] the *mātṛkāyantra* to the ghee.
Having written [the mantra] there and performed the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the deity of the present vidyā, having worshipped it, touched that ghee,

and recited the *mātṛkā-mantra* a number of times equal to its syllables, and having also recited the vidyā of the present Kulasundarī ten thousand times, one should, in a secluded place, [perform the rite] daily according to the sequence of the nine nights (*navarata*) for the duration of a year.
For the practitioner who consumes it every morning, even if he has become mute, the power of poetic composition arises.
Thus ends the application of poetic power brought about by the consumption of clarified butter.

Having written the *mātṛkā* yantra upon the ashes of the colored medicinal herbs, one should worship the present *Nityā* therein after performing the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*. Then, having consecrated those ashes ten thousand times each with the *mātṛkā* and the specific *vidyā* under discussion, one should apply that ash to the head, forehead, and other respective locations corresponding to the syllables, [reciting] the respective *vidyās*.
Accompanied by the utterance of each respective letter of the Mātṛkā, one should touch the body of the person to be protected.
By this means, protection is afforded to all who suffer from afflictions such as fever, and especially to kings. Thus it is said.
The application of protection using the ashes of annual medicinal herbs.

If a practitioner, repeatedly meditating upon these three syllables of the present Nityā-vidyā on his own tongue, should enter an assembly of learned scholars, then he would be honored by the wise present in that assembly.
Thus is the ritual application that bestows equality with the assembly. Having meditated upon the present vidyā as residing within the lunar disc,
and then, becoming one-pointed in mind, meditating upon a shower of nectar flowing from it onto one’s own head, one should recite the present vidyā a thousand times or more.

The practitioner, reciting while pervading the maṇḍala, shall obtain poetry encompassing all languages and shall be victorious in all scholarly debates concerning knowledge. Thus ends the application for poetic skill. Having drawn two verses with an intervening space between them, one should draw a six-pointed wheel (ṣaṭkoṇacakra) in its pericarp (karṇikā), and within the pericarp of that wheel, the seed-syllable of Kāma (kāmabīja).

Having written the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable within that [triangle], and having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—such as "Devadatta, kurukuru, bestower of all assemblies"—within that as well; and having written the three seed-syllables of the present vidyā joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) in the three downward-pointing compartments of the hexagon; [then] in the upward-pointing ones...
Having written the three seed-syllables joined with the *visarga*, and then having written the *mātṛkā* along with the *bindu* upon the path starting from the foremost point,

and having worshipped it preceded by the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, for the practitioner who wears the yantra— written on birch bark or similar material— rolled into a ball and held in the mouth while meditating upon it at the tip of the tongue, [success occurs] in the assembly.
One would attain the status of being the foremost among all learned persons.
Thus ends the application [of the term] that brings about preeminence in the assemblies of the learned.

These six applications are, like those of Kulasundarī, indistinguishable from the seventy-eight Vidyās and the Sampatkarī Vidyā. Therefore, one who desires such a goal should worship any one of these Vidyās rather than being restricted to only one; thus, we shall now analyze the essential nature of that Vidyā and the method of its worship. Aiṃ Īṃ.

The first division is *auḥ aiṃ īṃ srauḥ*. This very division has two names here: *Traipurakanda* and *Saṃketā*. In this very [division], through the addition of the letter *ka* to the second seed-syllable and the letter *la* to the third, and the letter *sa* to the third, it is expressed by the two terms *Kulasundarī* and *Yadavālā*: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*; this is the second division.

Due to the optional inclusion of the *bindu* (anusvāra) and *visarga*, there is a twofold division here. Within this very second division, by joining the letter *ha* to all three seeds, one obtains the forms *haiṃ*, *klīṃ*, and *hlauḥ*; this is the third division, named Vijayā.
By joining the letter *sa* in place of the letter *ha*, one obtains the forms *saiṃ*, *klīṃ*, and *sauḥ*; this is the fourth division, named Jīvā. [This applies] to the aforementioned seed-syllables.

If the letters *sa* and *ha* are inserted as additions in sequence, then there is the fifth division, consisting of Śakti, Śakti, and Vidyā, in the form: *śaiṃ śaklīṃ śatsauḥ*. If the letters *ha* and *sa* are instead inserted in sequence into those very same seed-syllables (*bījas*), then there is the sixth division, which consists of Śiva, in the form: *hsaiṃ hṛśīṃ hṛsauḥ*.
If the letter *ra* is also added to each of the three seed-syllables already joined with *ha* and *sa*, then—
provided that this addition occurs immediately after the *ha* and *sa* in the first and third seeds, and after the fourth consonant in the second— the result is: *hasarai haṃsakalarī hasasauḥ*.
Thus, this seventh division, named Viśvābhidhāna, consists of the three seed-syllables of Kulasundarī,
each encased by Māyā (HRĪM): HRĪM AIṂ HRĪM KLĪṂ HRĪM HRĪM SAUḤ HRĪM.
Having accepted the unity of those [syllables] encapsulated by the nine-syllable [mantra],

there is the eightfold division known as the "Deluder of the Universe" (*viśvamohanī*), consisting of three syllables, which takes the form: *valai hrīṃ aiṃ vale hrīṃ vale hrīṃ klīṃ vale hrīṃ vale hrīṃ sauḥ vale hrīṃ*.

The ninth division, named Tripurāmṛtā, consists of three syllables formed by applying the water-seed (va), the earth-syllable (la), the eleventh vowel (au), and the bindu to each of the three seed-syllables of Kulasundarī, which are encased by the Māyā-bīja (hrīṃ) according to the previously described method for Avidyā; this is accomplished by removing the first seed-syllable and replacing it with [the aforementioned elements].

Having added the *māyā* seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*), the resulting form is *hrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ*; this is the Vidyā known as Mohinī, the tenth division. By removing the second seed-syllable and substituting the *māyā* seed-syllable in its place, the resulting form is *aiṃ hrīṃ sauḥ*; this is the Vidyā known as Akṣobhiṇī, the eleventh division. [By] discarding the third seed-syllable and [substituting] in its place...
In the insertion of *māyā*, the form *aiṃ klīṃ* is the *kledinī* (moistening) *saṃjñā-vidyā*, the twelfth division.
Having first set aside the *vāgbhava* [syllable], by introducing the first vowel (*a*) in its place, the form *aklīṃ sauḥ* is the *vidyā* named *mahodayā*, the thirteenth division. And of these...

There are seventy-eight distinct varieties of the *vidyās*. To explain: for each individual *vidyā*, there are three syllables. Among them, by relying on the primacy of the first syllable, the second and third syllables may occupy the positions of the second and third, or the third and second.
The twofold nature is based on the wheel (*cakra*).
Based on the primacy of the second seed-syllable, the first and third [positions] are designated as the second and third.

The twofold nature [of the first two] is based on their being the third and the second respectively; and for the first and second, their twofold nature is based on their being the second and third, and the third and second respectively, while the third's twofold nature is based on its being the first. Thus, there are six varieties in total for a single vidyā; and since each of the thirteen vidyās possesses these six varieties...
The total number of these distinct Vidyās is clearly established by their combination. For example, the Sampatkarī-vidyā is as follows:
*kala ā ī a eṃ hasa auḥ*. The method of worship for this Vidyā and the methods of worship for the previously mentioned Vidyās are stated together as being identical. This is the Sampatkarī-vidyā.

Having included within this the sixfold divisions arising from the aforementioned method for the *tryarṇā* [three-syllable mantra], and not including those [divisions] because the ritual procedure for the *kulasundarī-vidyā* along with its divisions was previously stated, there is the description of the ritual procedure consisting of seventy-eight completed divisions.

One should not entertain the confusion as to what the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) for the *sampatkarī-vidyā*— which is included within the seventy-eight *vidyās*— is, on the grounds that it has already been performed by the Blessed One. Nor should one entertain the confusion as to why the ritual procedure for the *navākulasundarī-vidyā* is stated again, given that its procedure has already been explained previously.
This must be accepted. For instance, having constructed two equal squares with an interval between them— one situated in the eastern direction and the other in the western—
each possessing twenty-two branches, and having drawn two circles within that space with an interval of four finger-breadths between them;

Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus within that intermediate space, one should draw a triangle with its apex facing oneself in the pericarp of that lotus; then, upon its lines, starting from the northeast (Īśāna), one should place the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* in sequence.

Having written the sixteen letters beginning with *ka* in the southeast and the sixteen letters beginning with *tha* in the west, and having written the three remaining letters consisting of *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa* in the center— it follows that among the seventy-eight aforementioned vidyās,
whichever vidyā is to be worshipped as the primary one, that too should be written in the very center; thus it is established.

At the conclusion of the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), having first performed the visualization of the wheel of the eternal worship of Sarvamaṅgalā along with its enclosures (*sāvaraṇa*), including the rites beginning with the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśasthāpana*) and ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*); one should again visualize within that very pot the wheel of the specific worship (*bhedapūjā*) whose nature was described immediately above. Therein, [one performs] that which constitutes a limb of initiation (*dīkṣāṅga*).
Having performed the worship until the ritual dismissal (*anudvāsana*), and having spent that night preceded by festivities such as dance and song,

one should, at the conclusion of the daily rites in the morning, worship the presiding deity of the specific division (*bheda*) whose name was previously indicated with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). At the end of the consecration with the water-jar (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), the worship of the Guru follows, beginning with the offering of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

Having received the instruction preceded by the piercing (*vedha*) from a satisfied Guru, one should follow the worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), and other rites according to the path taught by the Guru. However, the worship that is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to initiation is performed solely upon the *cakra*, and not upon the *kalaśa* visualized above the *cakra*. The method for both types of worship is as follows:

After performing the morning rites, such as bathing with fragrant oils and similar waters, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*). Having sat upon a seat of red wool or other materials, which has been worshipped with the previously mentioned four seats and vidyās, one should sit using the vidyā of one’s own chosen deity (*svopāsyavidyā*). Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with that same vidyā, [one recites]: *oṃ hrīṃ*.

Having offered the bali with the sixteen-syllable mantra, *sarvavighnakṛdbhyaḥ sarvabhūtebhyo hūṃ svāhā*, one should worship the nine Nāthas upon the head in their proper sequence using their respective mantras, and then recite the Guru-stotra.

Having bowed again and again and requested permission for the worship, one should begin it. Having meditated upon the identity of one's own master, one's own vidyā, one's own deity, and one's own self,
[one proceeds] from the seven oceans beginning with the ocean of sugarcane, up to the circle of the manifest and hidden Siddha-yoginīs.

Having worshipped the thirty-six deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) upon the lion-throne that serves as the support for the present maṇḍala, one should place the vessel of general offering (*sāmānyārghyapātra*)— made of gold or some other material, containing water mixed with the five substances such as *gorocanā* and provided with its base— between oneself and the yantra. Then, [one should take] the waters from its supporting vessel...

Gradually, having visualized Kulasundarī as consisting of fire, sun, and moon by means of the three seed-syllables; having visualized the yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and so forth contained therein as being composed of the five elements beginning with earth; and having visualized the oneness of that water with the present wheel—[the practitioner] consecrates the water, which has been meditated upon as the very nature of the deity of the present *vidyā*, ten times with the present *nityā*.

Having worshipped with the mantras of the present *Nityāṣaḍaṅga*, one should sprinkle the materials for the ritual services beginning with the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and ending with the betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), as well as all other items required for the fire sacrifice (*homa*) and so forth, using that water and the present *vidyā*. Then,
having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) again with the present *vidyā*, [one should offer] the ten times [the oblation] with the water of the general *arghya*.

Having inscribed [the mantra] up to the *gotrarāśi* and *kāmanā*, and having made the sixth leaf contain the inscription of the specific Vidyā-deity to be worshipped—such as *Traipurakadāsampatkarī* and so forth—one should form the *saṃkalpa*: "I shall perform the worship according to the prescribed rule, in accordance with my intellectual capacity," and then pour out the water held in the hand. Thereafter, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the Mātṛkās.

At the end of the specific vidyā of one's chosen deity, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the respective locations of the Mātṛkā; at the end of the specific vidyā of one's chosen deity, having uttered the corresponding Mātṛkā [syllable].

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the respective locations of the *mātṛkā*, one should perform the ritual placement of the specific *vidyā* of one’s own deity using the third seed-syllable (*vīja*) conjoined with the six long vowels: *ĀṂ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ*, *ĪṂ Śirase Svāhā*, *OṂ Śikhāyai Vaṣaṭ*, *AIṂ Kavacāya Huṃ*, *AUṂ Netrāya Vauṣaṭ*, *AḤ Astrāya Phaṭ*. Then: *Hasaṃ Āṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ Ha Sa...*

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon one’s own thumbs and other fingers, as well as upon the heart and other body parts, by means of the forms ending with: *īṃ śirase svāhā*, *hasa ūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *hasa aiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *hasa auṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ*, *hasa aḥ astrāya phaṭ*, and so forth;
[one should then recite] the complete vidyā: *aiṃ īṃ auḥ kala-āīṃ a aiṃ hasa auḥ*.
Having thus performed the threefold pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) in this manner and other such ways, one should proceed with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and subsequent rites as follows:

having followed the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā, [the deity] is transferred via the path of the vital breath (*vaha-nāsādhvan*) from the present vidyā’s splendor— which pervades [the body] from the *mūlādhāra* up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)— into a heap of red flowers held in a handful of blossoms.

Then, while visualizing that [the deity] has been transferred onto the specific syllables of the respective vidyās inscribed upon the wheel presented through the offering of handfuls of flowers and prostration, one should address each vidyā with its respective name ending in a vocative case— such as "Bhaute," "Puraka," "Indrabhīṣaṃpatkari," or another— and say: "Be invoked here in this wheel."

Having performed the invocation after making the formal supplication, one should contemplate the mass of light situated in the center— whose essential nature is known from the verse of meditation— as having transformed into the forms of the Lord’s surrounding powers (āvaraṇa-śaktis), which are certain rays of that light radiating here and there. The meditation is as follows:
Her body, garments, and ornaments are radiant with the filaments of the pomegranate flower; she has four arms and three eyes,
her face is bright and smiling, and she is endowed with the consecration of jewels while seated in the center of an eight-petaled lotus.

Seated upon a svastika within a triangle, she is the gentle temple of compassion. Holding in her hands a coral rosary, a jeweled cup filled with gems, a book, and the gesture of granting boons—she is Sarvamaṅgalā. She is seated upon the Kula-seat fashioned from the sixteen vowels from 'A' to 'Sa', in the midst of which is the syllable 'Ha', conjoined with this Vidyā.
