In that regard, for those who are without a lord, weapon, armor, or name, [the mantra] is likewise: then, at the end of the complete *vidyā*, [one says] "O Bhautre Purakanda, O Bhos Sampatkari," or with the end of any other such name, "be established here in this *cakra*.
Again, preceded by the *vidyā*, at the end of each respective name, [one says] "be firmly restrained here in this *cakra*."

Again, after first reciting the *vidyā* and at the end of the name, pray as follows while displaying the respective mudrās: "O Goddess, be veiled (*avaguṇṭhitā*) in this wheel! Again, after first reciting the *vidyā* and at the end of the name, pray: "O Goddess, be made present (*sannidhāpitā*) in this wheel! Then, [perform] the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs, one should establish the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra in the form "The vital breaths of this Traipurakandā are here, the vital breaths," and so forth; then one should worship her with the twelve services (*upacāra*), beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*). The mantras for these are as follows: at the end of the complete Vidyā, [one says] "I offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to Traipurakandā."

Having offered the water for the feet (*pādya*), one should present it at the [deity's] feet with the corresponding mantra. Having also offered the other services, such as betel, food, and so forth, using other mantras containing the words "other services" (*apara-upacāra*) placed where the *pādya* was set down, one should present them. Then, one should follow the thirteen services (*upacāra*). For example, on the rear part of the Goddess, beginning with *prakāśa*...
Having worshipped the fortunate lords of the nine [Navanātha] with their respective mantras as presented in the introduction to the Nityā [Tantra], [one offers]:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the coral rosary*; *hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the jeweled goblet filled with gems*;
*hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the book*.
Having worshipped with "hrīṃ śrīṃ varāya namaḥ" in the regions near the right lower, left lower, left upper, and right upper hands;

In the three triangles, starting from the front and proceeding counter-clockwise, one should worship the triad of Śaktis with the mantras: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Rati; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Prīti; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Manobhavā. Then, at the end of the complete Vidyā, [one should worship] with: "I worship the sandals of Traipurakanda."

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantras beginning with "At the conclusion of the complete Vidyā, I worship the *sampatkarī* *pādukā*," and so forth; and [having worshipped] with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the first enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) of the *traipurakaṇḍa* accept the worship," and so forth; [one worships] Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! Sampatkarī, the deity of the first enclosure, [with the worship].

Having offered the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering for that worship with the appropriate mantra beginning with "gṛhṇantu" (may they accept), one worships on the eight petals, starting from the front petal and proceeding counter-clockwise: *hrīṃ śrīṃ brāhmīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*;
*hrīṃ śrīṃ māheśvarīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; *hrīṃ śrīṃ kaumārīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; *hrīṃ śrīṃ vaiṣṇavīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having worshipped the eight Mothers with: "I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vārāhī," "I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aindrī," "I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Cāmuṇḍā," and "I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Mahālakṣmī";
then, at the end of the complete mantra, [one says]: "I worship the sandals of Tripurakanda. At the end of the complete mantra...

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with any appropriate mantra such as "I worship the *sampatkarī* sandals," and having offered the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for the presentation of the worship with any appropriate mantra such as "O deities of the second enclosure, [emerging] from this triple-city root (*traipurakanda*), may you accept the worship," beginning with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ."
In the square, on the southern path of the eastern gate, I worship Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Indraśaktipādukāṃ.
In the southeast, on the southern path, [I worship] Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Agniśaktipādukāṃ.

*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Aśakti at Nairṛtya; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, [I worship] Rakṣaḥśakti at Paścima; on the path leaning toward the northern part of the western door, *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, [I worship] Varuṇaśakti; at Vāyavya, *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, [I worship] Anilaśakti; and on the northern path, *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship Vidhiśakti.

Having worshipped the powers (śaktis) of the world-protectors (lokapālas), one should worship the Goddess situated in the center with appropriate mantras such as "At the end of the complete vidyā, I worship the pādukā of Traipurakanda" or "At the end of the complete vidyā, I worship the pādukā of Sampatkarī," and so forth.

*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, may these deities of the third enclosure (*tṛtīyāvaraṇa*) from the *Astrapurakanda* accept this worship! *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, may these deities of the third enclosure, the *Saṃpatkarīs*, accept this worship! Having offered the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for the presentation of worship using any of these or similar mantras as appropriate, and having performed the thirteen types of service (*upacāra*), [one should offer] what remains as well.

Having prepared the three-fold service consisting of a brief recitation of hymns, libations, and prostrations, and having performed the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) in a number such as one thousand, one should perform the offering (*nivedana*) in the form of contemplating the identity of oneself with the deity of the mantra being recited; then, according to the prescribed rule, [one should offer] with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Having offered sixteen oblations along with a tenth-part of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the fire’s radiant energy within the *bhūtacakra* at the site of worship. Then, having worshipped the goddess who has returned with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*),
one should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) with the seven-syllable *Kuru-kullā* mantra and perform the *nīrājana* ceremony using a wick soaked in camphor and other substances.

Having asked for forgiveness, one should unite the rays forming the enclosure of the Goddess with the mass of splendor that constitutes the body of the Goddess by means of the *śaktyutthāpana* mudrā; then, by means of the *khecarī* mudrā, one should dissolve even that splendor of the Goddess into one's own self. Then, according to the previously mentioned method, using the third seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels—
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*), and having recited the hymn to the Goddess (*devīstotra*) and the hymn to the Guru (*gurustotra*).
For the practitioner who performs the daily worship of the seventy-eight sciences according to this method,
there arise longevity, prosperity, fame, enjoyment, beauty, health, knowledge of the past, future, and present, knowledge for achieving the next world,
and the realization of the sciences. Through these sciences, [all goals are attained].

A practitioner desiring the perfection of the ritual application (*prayoga*) should perform the means of accomplishing that mantra. Regarding the number of recitations (*japa*) for the accomplishment of that mantra, it is three hundred thousand per syllable;
however, for the *tripurakandā* [mantra], it is accomplished in the Satya Yuga by fifteen hundred thousand recitations, because [the syllables] are twelve.
In the Kali age, for the four unchanging vowels— the fourth, fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth—
the recitation (*japa*) should be fourfold, amounting to six million; for these six unchanging syllables,
since there are four consonants in the sequence of two pairs at the beginning and end, with two vowels situated in the middle, they are [derived] from the *bindu*.

Because the sound connected with another [deity] is repeated according to its own nature; thus, it should be understood that while the number of recitations (*japa*) in the Satya Yuga is eighteen lakhs, in the Kali Yuga the number for the practice of means (*sādhana-japa*) is seventy-two lakhs.
In this same manner, other variations should be inferred by oneself. Everything else besides this follows the direction already stated. [The] applications (*prayoga*).

These have indeed been mentioned. Since the meditation on the *mātṛkā*-yantra and so forth has already been explained previously in connection with these applications, the *mātṛkā*-yantra and other such diagrams, which must necessarily be described, are now set forth.
Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus provided with a pericarp and filaments...

By means of an outer circle encompassing the tips of the petals, one should create a single path (vīthī); having drawn another inner circle with an intervening space, one should fashion the *bhūpura* (earth-fortress) outside with two square lines, devoid of doors and the like. Therein, in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*)...
Having written the seed-syllable *hasauḥ*, which is produced from the letter *ha* and the fourteenth vowel (*au*) with the *visarga*,
and which is expressed by the terms "the seed of life," "power" (*śakti*), and "the temple" (*prāsāda*), [one should place it] on the filaments in pairs.
Having written the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* at the tips of the filaments and so forth;

having written the five letters beginning with *ka* on each petal starting from the tip; and having written the thirty-five letters from *ka* to *kṣa* on the seven petals; [one writes] *a*, *i*, *u*, *aṃ*, *aḥ* on the eighth petal.

Having written the forms of the repeated syllables, one should write the *ṭha* and *va* characters combined eight times in rotation within the cardinal and intermediate directions. Some, however, say that one should write the *ṭha* character four times in each of the cardinal directions and the *va* character four times in each of the intermediate directions; this [should be done] in the center of the seed-syllable written in the middle of the pericarp of this *yantra*.
Having written the names of the practitioner and others,

through the water-consecration of the jar presided over by that [deity]— the jar of Nityā, which is adorned with all auspiciousness (*sarvamaṅgalā*) and her retinue, and is worshipped— all accomplishments (*siddhis*) come to pass. Furthermore, having drawn this wheel upon a pedestal or similar surface, therein...

Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) and worshipped [the yantra], one should sit down. If one were to sprinkle it with water—whether consecrated or unconsecrated—the desired success will accrue to the one thus sprinkled. Furthermore, by wearing this yantra after it has been consecrated through worship, recitation (*japa*), and other rites preceded by *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, everything that is wished for is attained.
It is accomplished. Thus, by worshipping this yantra every day, even through such worship, the accomplishments of one's desires are attained.

For the practitioner who carves this yantra onto a leaf made of gold, silver, or copper, and installs it in his house, region, city, or elsewhere after performing the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and other rites, all goals are accomplished. [Upon] the head...
In that [mandala] is this *mātṛkā*-yantra; for those who remember it every morning, all prosperities come to pass.
Having established the wheel of the daily worship of one’s own deity within the pericarp of this yantra,
for the practitioner who worships their respective chosen deity there, that very chosen deity becomes present; thus, it bestows all desired objects.

Under the guise of revealing this ignorance (*avidyā*), the Blessed One has taught that it must necessarily be worshipped by seekers of knowledge (*vidyārthin*). For instance, the syllable *a* is the first syllable of the *Ṛgveda*, beginning with "agnim īḷe" and so forth; and by means of indirect indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*)—whereby the word does not abandon its primary meaning—it refers to the entire collection of syllables of the *Ṛgveda* beginning with *a*, as they are subordinate to their respective subsequent syllables.

The syllable *ikāra* is the first syllable of the Yajurveda, beginning with "iṣe tvorje tvā" and so forth; like the previous case, it too encompasses all the syllables contained within the Yajurveda. Through the euphonic combination (*guṇasandhi*) of the vowels *a* and *i*, the syllable *e* is produced, and the syllable *akāra* itself is the beginning of the Sāmaveda.

The first syllable of the mantra beginning with "āyāhi" is also the collector of all the syllables contained within that Veda; furthermore, through the formation of the diphthong *ai* by the rule of *vṛddhi* sandhi with the eleventh vowel produced from the junction of the two Vedic syllables, the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda are represented by the sound *ai*.

The nature of the present Goddess as the essence of the Sāmaveda has been stated. Furthermore, the letter *ka*, which constitutes the middle seed-syllable (*madhyamabīja*), represents all the *mātṛkās* by virtue of its relationship as the effect of the letters preceding it, such as *a*, and its relationship as the cause of the letters following it, such as *kha*; indeed, the letter *la* is the designator of that which transcends all.
He is the supreme one who, by virtue of his authority over all the tantras of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and so forth, sustains the bodies of superior humans and others,
and is the ultimate designator of all elements (*bhūta*), beginning with the earth element.

And thus, the nature of the Goddess as both the signifier and the signified has been stated: for the universe is threefold, by way of the distinction between the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the means of knowledge (*jñāna*), and the knower (*jñātṛ*). Among these, the letter *sa* denotes the object of knowledge, being of the nature of power (*śakti*). The letter *au*, because it is a syllable of nectar (*amṛta*), denotes the means of knowledge, which is of that same nature. The *visarga*...
It designates the one who does not know [the Self] as being of the nature of Śiva.

And thus, through the distinction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the means of knowledge (*jñāna*), and the knower (*jñātṛ*), the state of being the soul of the universe (*viśvātmakatva*) of the Goddess has been proclaimed by the third seed-syllable. By means of this contemplation (*anusandhāna*), preceded by daily worship, recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth—

A practitioner who serves the present Nityā—even if he is guilty of great sins, or is a fool, dull-witted, or mute—will in the course of time attain equality with Śiva; what then need be said regarding the attainment of other desired goals? However, this must be understood: the visualization of her as "red, with red garments, ornaments, garlands, and unguents" is not for all cases, but rather...

For the accomplishment of speech (*vāk-siddhi*), one should meditate on her as having a measured form. There is an option: she may have the singular radiance of Lakṣmī’s attainment, or she may be reddish.

For the subjugation of enemies and for their restraint, she is smoke-colored. For silencing [opponents], she is blue-colored. For pacification (*śānti*), she is white-colored; such are the specific meditations for desired ends (*kāmya-dhyāna-viśeṣa*). She is the Kamalā of desire; of that... [the rest is illegible].

The Introduction to Kulasundarī. Now, the Nityānityā is introduced. Here, the circle of worship (*pūjācakra*) is threefold, according to the division of superior, middling, and inferior. Among these, the superior Nityā-pūjā-cakra is as follows:
it measures one cubit (*hasta*) and consists of two sets of four-lined squares, each with door-frames (*dvāraśākhā*) in the four directions.
Having fashioned [the mandala], one should draw a single circle that touches and does not touch the internal lines of the square;
then, within that [circle], one should likewise draw thirty-six intermediate circles with equal intervals between them.

Having combined and produced thirty-seven internal sections, and having completed thirty-six rows (vīthīs), one should fashion sixteen-petaled lotuses in each [row]. In the central pericarp of all, one should draw a six-pointed star with a bindu; or otherwise, within the previously mentioned square enclosure (bhūpura).

One should construct eighteen paths using nineteen circles and place thirty-two-petaled lotuses in each of them; however, in reality, one should construct twelve paths using thirteen circles and place fifty petals in each of the eleven paths.

The meaning of the root text is as follows: having fashioned a twenty-six-petaled lotus in the outermost enclosure (*caramavīthī*), one should worship there the five hundred and seventy-six powers of the phonemes (*varṇaśakti*). As for the middle worship-circle (*madhyamapūjācakra*): as previously stated, having drawn two circles with an interval of four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) within the square enclosure (*bhūpura*), [one proceeds].

Having drawn a lotus with fifty-one petals within that intermediate space, one should construct a six-pointed wheel (ṣaṭkoṇacakra) in its pericarp. This is the wheel for those of lower birth (*adhamajācakra*). As it has been taught: having drawn seven circles with intervening spaces in the middle of the previously described square enclosure (*bhūpura*), and having thus prepared the six-fold path (*vīthī-ṣaṭka*); there, beginning from the outermost path—
Having fashioned lotuses with two, four, six, ten, twelve, and sixteen petals according to the sequence of entry,
one should construct a hexagonal wheel within the pericarp located at the very center.

Having removed one of the wheels and placed the *kalaśa* there, one performs the rites beginning with the visualization of the wheel of the eternal worship of Sarvamaṅgalā along with its enclosures and their worship, and ending with her dismissal; then, once again within that very *kalaśa*, preceded by the visualization of the wheel of the present eternal goddess (*nityā*), [one proceeds].
The worship as an auxiliary to initiation (*dīkṣāṅgapūjā*), however, pertains solely to the *cakra*. The method for both types of worship is as follows:
having performed a bath with fragrant waters preceded by an anointing with fragrant oil, and having also completed the other morning duties;
p.

158b) Precisely because of the consequence of having to perform the daily rites for other deities, the practitioner— whose body and face are purified by the performance of the preliminary rites ending with the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*)— [should wear] red garments...

Having adorned himself with two sandalwood garlands and other ornaments, he entered the sacrificial pavilion; there, having worshipped the four seats according to the prescribed ritual, he sat down upon a red seat, assuming either a svastika or lotus posture by means of the mantra currently in use.
Having performed the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the present ritual, and having offered the oblation (*bali*) with the sixteen-syllable mantra,
one should worship the nine Ādināthas upon one's own head in the lineage of one's own master (*svanāthakrama*), each with their respective mantra. Then,
having recited the five-verse hymn to the Guru and requested permission for the worship, one should commence it.
Having meditated upon the identity of one's own lord, the eternal [goddesses], the chosen deity, and one's own self,

[one should worship] all the deities of the thirty-eight sacred seats (pīṭhas), ending with the wheel of the secret and manifest Siddhayoginīs, as regulated by the specific place, time, and other factors determined for each respective year.
Having performed worship upon the lion-throne and other supports that constitute the basis for the currently presented *nityāpūjā* mandala,

one should place the vessel for general offerings (*sāmānyārghyapātra*)— made of any one of the five materials such as gold and containing water mixed with the five substances beginning with yellow orpiment (*gorocanā*)— supported by its stand between one's own self and the *yantra*.
Having visualized the waters in the vessel used for that [libation] as being of the nature of fire, sun, and moon by means of the three seed-syllables of the Kula-sundarī,
and having visualized the *rocanā* and other substances as consisting of the five elements beginning with earth, as well as the identity between those waters and the present *nityā*-worship circle;
then, having consecrated the water— visualized as the very form of the present *nityā*— ten times with the present *vidyā*.
There, having worshipped the deities of the six limbs with the mantras of the six limbs, one should [sprinkle] oneself with that consecrated water using the present vidyā. (p.

The water for the feet (pādya), the guest-offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the bathing water (snāna)— each placed in its respective vessel starting from the general arghya-vessel and proceeding to the subsequent ones— as well as the items such as clothing, ornaments, and everything ending with betel-leaf (tāmbūla) placed on one's own right side,
and furthermore, whatever is required for the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites, having consecrated these all, one should again perform breath-control (prāṇāyāma) with the Vidyā-mantra.

Taking the general *arghya* water in the right hand along with a ladle, *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should specify the place, time, lineage, zodiac sign, name, and desired object; then,

having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)— "I shall perform the daily worship according to the rule of the application of the eternal, the non-eternal, and the illusory intellect"— one should pour out the water.

At this juncture, even if the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites have not been performed, one should perform the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* of the Mātṛkā using the Vidyā. Having first recited the specific Nityā-Vidyā for each [letter], one should place the respective letters of the Mātṛkā in their corresponding locations: *hsāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hlīṃ śirase svāhā*.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) on the fingers beginning with the thumb and on the body parts beginning with the heart—namely: *hlūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *hlaiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *hlauṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ*, *laḥ astrāya phaṭ*—one should then place the consonant-syllables of the mantra as follows: *haṃ* between the eyebrows, *ḍaṃ* at the throat, *raṃ* at the heart, *laṃ* at the navel, *kaṃ* at the secret place, and *saṃ* at the root-support (*mūlādhāra*).

Having performed the triple placement (*vāpaka-nyāsa*) with the complete root mantra in the form *hasakalaraḍaiḥ*, *hasakalaraḍīṃ*, and *hasakalaraḍauḥ*, one should proceed with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and subsequent rites. For example,
while forming the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā* and holding a cupped hand (*añjali*) filled with red flowers, [one proceeds] from the *mūlādhāra*...

Meditating that the aforementioned flower-offering, having been transferred via the path of the nose which carries the light of the present Vidyā pervading as far as the *brahmarandhra*, has arrived at the *bindu* situated in the center of the present wheel—
[recite] the complete Vidyā ending with "O Nityānityā, here in this wheel."
Having made the formal request, "Be present," and having thus accomplished the invocation (*āvāhana*),

one should contemplate those masses of rays of light as having issued forth from that very [deity] into their respective locations in the form of the retinue and the protective enclosures (*āvaraṇa*).
Having meditated upon the transformed [elements], one should meditate on the mass of light situated in the center, whose true nature has been realized through meditation.
As for the meditation: she shines with a crown of rubies possessing the luster of the rising sun’s orb;
her ornaments are made of ruby, and she wears garments of scarlet hue.

She is resplendent with six lotus-like faces graced by beautiful smiles, each face possessing three eyes, and endowed with twelve arms. With her left hands, she holds a noose, a rosary, a lotus, a sugarcane bow, a shield, and a trident; likewise, she holds a boon-granting gesture (*vara-mudrā*), a goad, a book, a flower-arrow, and a dagger.
One should meditate with undistracted mind upon the Goddess holding a human skull in her right hands.
Such is the visualization for the weapons and protective powers of the Lord;
however, regarding the weapons, there is the additional feature that their crests are marked with the shapes of those respective weapons. Thereafter—

Having made the following prayer while displaying the respective mudrās: "O Nityā, at the end of the complete Vidyā, be established here in this wheel; again, at the end of the twelve syllables, be firmly restrained; again, at the end of the twelve syllables, be veiled; again, at the end of the twelve syllables, be made present."

Having performed the placement of the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) with the *Prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā*—in the form "The vital breaths of this Nityānityā are here in this wheel," and so forth—and having thus established the vital breaths, one should worship her with the twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*). The mantras for that are as follows: at the end of the present *Vidyā* consisting of three complete syllables...

Thinking, "I offer water for washing the feet to the eternal and the non-eternal," one should offer the *pādya* with the general *arghya* water and present it at the two feet using the currently recited vidyā.

In this very manner, having offered the *arghya* and other offerings with the mantras recited using the words for *pādya*, *padābhiṣeka*, *arghya*, and so forth, one should present them upon the head and other parts [of the deity] with the *vidyā* currently under discussion. Thus, after the worship with these twelve services (*upacāras*), one should follow the thirteenth service. Its procedure is as follows: on the back part of the Goddess—
Having worshipped the nine divine Siddha-Mānavas known as Prakāśa, Vimarśa, Ānanda, Śrījñāna, Śrīsatya, Śīla, Pūrṇasvabhāva, Pratibha, and Subhaga—
their feet having been consecrated by the Lord— with their respective mantras and the words "Obeisance to the feet of the Lord."
Beginning from the region near the left lower hand of the Goddess and ending at the region near the right lower hand,

one should worship in twelve places in counter-clockwise order: *hrīṃ śrīṃ varadāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ triśūlāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ kheṭāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ puṇḍreṣucāpāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ akṣaguṇāya namaḥ*.

Having worshipped the weapons with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ pāśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṅkuśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ pustakāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ puṣpeṣubhyo namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ maṇḍalāgrāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ nṛkapālāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ abhayāya namaḥ*, [one worships] in the six corners, starting from the southwest (nairṛtya).

Having worshipped those respective Śaktis with the mantras: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Ḍākinī" in the northwest; "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Rākinī" in the east; "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Lākinī" in the southeast; "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Kākinī" in the northeast; "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Śākinī" in the west; and "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Hākinī," at the conclusion of the complete Vidyā:

Having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra, "I worship Nityānityā," one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering of worship with the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the first enclosure of Nityānityā accept this worship. [One should then worship] on the petals reached by proceeding clockwise, beginning from the petal in front of the Goddess.

160b)* I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aśakti. I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Āśakti. Thus begins the first group of sixteen principles (*tattva*). In the first [group]: I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kaśakti.

"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the power (Śakti) Kā," and so forth— this is the sixteenfold second principle. In the second [section], by this same method, on the petals of the twenty-sixth lotus, one worships those respective powers with mantras beginning with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the power Kṣa" and ending with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the power Kṣaḥ," at the conclusion of each complete Vidyā.
Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with the mantra, "I worship Nityānityā," one should offer a handful of flowers as an oblation for that worship, saying:
"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the second enclosure of Nityānityā accept this worship. This is according to the middle view.
Having worshipped with these mantras, which consist for the most part of fifty-one syllables, and having honored the Goddess situated in the center,

one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an oblation of that worship. Even in the shorter alternative, having combined [the letters] in the six lotuses upon the fifty petals, one should exclude either the *visarga* or the letter *kṣa*, according to the tradition of one’s own Guru.
One should worship with the very mantras mentioned for the fifty Mātṛkās. This constitutes the second enclosure (āvaraṇa) in all systems.
Then, in the square (caturasra), in the area near the inner line on the southern path from the western door:
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Brāhmī.

In the location near the inner line of the northern path of the western gate: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Māheśvarī-pādukāṃ. In the location near the inner line of the western path of the northern gate: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kaumārī-pādukāṃ.
In the location near the inner line of the eastern path of the northern gate: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vaiṣṇavī-pādukāṃ.
In the region near the inner line of the northern path of the eastern gate: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vārāhī-pādukāṃ.
In the region near the inner line of the southern path of the eastern gate: [Vārāhī-pādukāṃ].

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aindrī-pādukāṃ: in the region near the inner line of the eastern path of the southern gate. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Cāmuṇḍā-pādukāṃ: in the region near the inner line of the western path of the southern gate. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Mahālakṣmī-pādukāṃ: in the region near the outer line of the southern path of the eastern gate.

*Hrīṃ śrīṃ indraśaktipātaḥ* at the location near the outer line of the eastern path of the southern gate. *Hrīṃ śrīṃ agniśaktipātaḥ* at the location near the outer line of the western path of the southern gate. *Hrīṃ śrīṃ yamaśaktipātaḥ* at the location near the outer line of the southern path of the western gate.

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Rakṣaḥ-Śaktipāta near the outer line of the northern path of the western door. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Varuṇa-Śaktipāta near the outer line of the western path of the northern door. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Anila-Śaktipāta in the region near the outer line of the eastern path of the northern door.

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Somaśaktipāda, near the outer line on the northern path of the eastern gate. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Iśānaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi, in the northwest corner. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Anantaśaktipāda, in the northeast. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Brahmaśaktipāda, in the southeast. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Niyatiśaktipāda, in the southwest.
Having worshipped the twenty Śaktis mentioned with the mantras beginning with *hrīṃ śrīṃ kālī-kālī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*,
and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete Vidyā with the mantra *nityānityā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, [one should say]:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ etā nityānityā-tṛtīyāvaraṇa-devatāḥ pūjāṃ gṛhṇantu*.
Having offered a handful of flowers as an act of worship, having performed the thirteen services (*upacāra*),
one should perform whatever hymns, recitations, libations, and prostrations constitute the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth services.

Having completed the ritual according to the rules, at the conclusion of the sixteen-fold worship (ṣoḍaśopacāra-pūjā), there is no inference of a redundant intention regarding the injunction for the ritual placement (nyāsa) to be performed at the end of the worship— extending up to the dismissal (udvāsana)— which consists of specific activities conducive to generating delight.

Since the Lord’s [ritual] is intended to extend up to the dismissal (udvāsana), and because the offering of oblations (balidāna) and so forth— as well as the recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa)— are already encompassed by the very resolve for worship (pūjā-saṅkalpa), one need not now perform a separate resolve.
[One should perform] the placement of the thumbs and other fingers (aṅguṣṭhādi-nyāsa), the placement on the heart and other limbs (hṛdayādi-nyāsa), and the placement of the phonemes (varṇa-nyāsa).

Having performed the recitation one thousand or one hundred times, preceded by the ritual application (*nyāsa*), at the beginning and end of the pervasive applications (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*); and having offered the oblation consisting of the contemplation of non-difference from that [deity];
and having sacrificed with the sixteen oblations as prescribed, and with a portion equal to one-tenth of the daily recitation (*japa*).
Having again joined the *bindu* that constitutes the abode of the goddess Tejas, which has been meditated upon as fire,

one should worship the goddess who has arrived there with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), offer the *bali* with the *Kurukullā* mantra, perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) with a wick containing camphor and other substances, and ask for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*).

Having visualized the multitude of veils that have become rays as being absorbed into the mass of light situated in the center, which has itself become the Goddess, by means of the Śakti-utthāpana-mudrā; and having dissolved even that central light into one's own self by means of the Khecarī-mudrā;

one should perform, as before, the placement upon the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa), the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), the placement of the colors (varṇanyāsa), and the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa).

Having recited the *Devīstotra* and the *Gurustotra*, one should conclude [the ritual]. However, in the case of initiation (*dīkṣā*), having performed the worship—excluding the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) and following the procedure for liberation—one should dispel the fatigue of the night with dance, song, and so forth; then, on the morning of the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*), having performed the daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), [one should worship] with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*).

In the morning, having worshipped the Goddess and performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*), and having recited the hymn to that Goddess and the hymn to the Guru at the conclusion of the aforementioned ritual placement (*nyāsa*), [he should place] the disciple upon the *mātṛkā*-yantra. (p.

Having consecrated [the disciple] with the prescribed vidyā using sprouts placed at the mouth of the *kalaśa*, and having worshipped him with the nine offerings beginning with perfumes (*gandha*), the Guru— having abandoned all stinginess regarding wealth and being satisfied by the offered sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)— should instruct [the disciple] according to the previously stated procedure for piercing (*vedha*).

In the initial instruction of this [mantra], intended for the purpose of testing the disciple’s devotion and other qualities, the procedure of piercing (*vedha*) should not be followed, because the science of piercing has not yet been acquired. Nor is it proper to grant even that [science] without prior testing. However, since this is a specific form of eternal knowledge (*nityā-vidyā*), it should be imparted only after being tested by means other than [piercing], as stated in the specific injunctions. Thus...

One who has received initiation and is devoted to the daily performance of worship as prescribed should practice the means for attaining the *vidyā* when there is a desire for its application. Regarding the specific details of that practice, it should be performed according to the direction shown in the general introduction, as there is some distinction therein. And here, the recitation (*japa*) is as follows:

Since the seven syllables do not repeat, each individual syllable amounts to three hundred thousand [recitations]; thus, in the Satya Yuga, it is twenty-one hundred thousand, and in the present Yuga, it is eighty-four hundred thousand, just as in the case of Lalitā—so says the author of the Nidhi. Because of the specific observation that "there are one hundred thousand for each syllable," it is precisely seven hundred thousand in the Satya Yuga and [eighty-four hundred thousand] in the present Yuga.
The actual state of affairs is that the recitation (*japa*) for the purpose of accomplishment consists of twenty-eight hundred thousand [repetitions];

the fire-oblation (*homa*) is to be performed at one-tenth of the number of recitations using red lotuses smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*); and furthermore, the practitioner’s subsistence on milk alone is prescribed here—this is the specific detail. In the manner thus shown, [one performs] the recitation, the fire-oblation, and the libation (*tarpaṇa*).

Having performed the worship in the manner described and having invoked one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) upon one’s own head, one should perform an ablution there with the mantra “I consecrate Nityānityā,” using water from the vessel presiding over this perpetual worship-circle (*nityapūjācakra*), at a tenth part of the number of libations (*tarpaṇa*) offered. Furthermore, this refers to the ablution performed by means of the water from the jar presiding over this perpetual worship-circle.
And having performed [this],
one should carry out the applications to be described by means of this vidyā that has been accomplished.
However, for those who engage in the practice without having mastered the vidyā,
there is not merely a failure to achieve the intended goal; rather, the deities, becoming enraged, [seize] the practitioner's skin, blood, flesh, and so forth, as well as his very life-force.

"Even if [these] were removed, what other undesirable consequence could there be? Now, regarding the constant applications (*nityāprayoga*): when each of the letters constituting this Vidyā—namely the phonemes *ai*, *ha*, *sa*, *ka*, *la*, *ra*, and *u*—is joined with the sixteen vowels, there arise one hundred and twelve modified syllables (*vikṛtākṣara*) related to the mantra.
It has already been largely explained that through the application of accents, the diphthong *ai* exists precisely in the form of those respective accents.

Furthermore, since each individual yantra is produced by these seven modified syllables taken seven at a time, sixteen yantras are produced in total. The method for this is as follows: first, having drawn two circles with an interval between them, inside of that—

Having drawn a hexagonal wheel and within it two circles with an intervening space, one should write the primary syllable *he*— the present modified letter— within the seed-syllable *mati* in the very center of all that; then,

having written the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object of attainment (*sādhya*) and so forth within that as well, one should write *hā hi hī* in the six corners, beginning from the front corner.

Having written the six syllables *hu hū hṛ* which constitute its essential form (*svarūpa*), having encircled it with ten letters corresponding to the desired qualities of the inner path (*ābhyantaravīthī*), and having surrounded that path with the *mātṛkā* letters, the first yantra is completed according to the prescribed ritual.

For the practitioner who wears it, there is the destruction of abdominal disease. By wearing the second yantra— which is distinguished solely by the writing of the seven syllables beginning with *ha* (i.e., *hr*) in place of the previously mentioned seven syllables beginning with *ha*— there is the destruction of head diseases.

By wearing the third yantra— which is distinguished solely by the writing of the seven syllables beginning with *haṃ* and ending with *su* in place of the previously mentioned seven [syllables] beginning with *hrīḥ*—
there is the destruction of eye diseases; [and by wearing it] in the aforementioned locations of the letters, [the syllables] beginning with *sū*.

From the fourth yantra, produced by writing the seven syllables beginning with *sa* at the aforementioned locations, ear diseases are destroyed. From the fifth yantra, accomplished by writing the seven syllables beginning with *so* at those same locations, hand diseases are destroyed. From the sixth yantra, perfected by writing the seven syllables beginning with *kī* at those very same locations, foot diseases are destroyed.

In that regard, from the seventh yantra produced by writing the seven letters beginning with *e* (*ekāra*) and so forth, diseases located in the region of the body above the waist, from the throat down to the two hands— that is, the lower part of the body designated as the "inner lord" (*antarādhipa*)— are destroyed. From the eighth yantra, produced by writing the seven letters beginning with *la* (*lākāra*) and so forth in those very same locations...

The diseases residing in the five sense organs, beginning with the eyes, are destroyed by means of the ninth yantra, which is accomplished by writing the seven syllables beginning with *ḷ*. The diseases residing in the hands, feet, speech, anus, and genitals— which constitute the nature of the organs of action— are destroyed by means of the tenth yantra, which is accomplished by writing the seven syllables beginning with *ḷa*.

Diseases arising from the provocation of the wind (*vāyu*) attain pacification through the eleventh yantra, which is perfected by the writing of the seven syllables beginning with the seventh vowel joined with the letter *ra*. Diseases arising from bile (*pitta*) are pacified through the twelfth yantra, produced by the writing of the seven syllables beginning with the letter *rau*. Diseases produced by phlegm (*kapha*) are pacified through the [thirteenth] yantra, produced by the writing of the seven syllables beginning with the letter *rau*.
Through the yantra consisting of thirteen syllables, perfected by the writing of the seven syllables beginning with *du* (*du-kā-rā-di-sap-ta-ka*),
there is the pacification of diseases arising from the provocation of wind, bile, and phlegm.

From the yantra produced by writing the seven syllables beginning with *ḍai*, numbering fourteen, there is the pacification of afflictions caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and so forth; from the yantra produced by writing the seven syllables beginning with *i*, numbering fifteen, [there is the cure for] wind-related disorders, urinary diseases (*prameha*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇḍara*).
Stone in the bladder, obstructed fetus, and likewise abdominal enlargement as the eighth—

these eight are by their very nature great diseases that are difficult to treat. Consumption, dysentery, blindness, asthma, choleraic vomiting, rheumatism (āmavāta), cough, and cold-limbedness as the eighth— these are the [other] diseases.
Known as *kālajvara*, it consists of seventeen great diseases. Thus, there is the pacification of these enumerated seventeen diseases.

By means of this sixteenth yantra, which is accomplished by writing the seven syllables beginning with *ḷ* in those very locations in the form of a hexagon in the center of everything, freedom from disease and the increase of longevity occur. As stated in the aforementioned [texts]:
Even regarding other diseases not mentioned by name, by wearing any one of these sixteen yantras,
the disease of every living being— both the practitioner and others— is pacified; this applies to all the yantras already described and those yet to be described,
wherein [the rite of] consecration is performed.

The cakras that are worn—being based upon the offering of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the sixteen-fold service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), the ritual application of the yantra (*yantrādhikaraṇaka*), and the worship of the deity of the yantra preceded by firm conviction—bestow their fruit;
however, if even one of these four is deficient in the interim, they do not do so. Among those, the cakra currently under discussion is to be worn as one's own.

Having lifted [the vessel] from the ground and placed the *kalaśa* upon it according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the worship of Sarvamaṅgalā there— preceded by meditation— along with her attendants (*āvaraṇas*), and at the conclusion of the ritual ending with her dismissal (*udvāsana*),
[one should again focus on] the yantra to be worn on oneself.
Having first performed the visualization, one should worship the deity of the yantra along with its enclosures, then perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*).
Only after performing the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with that water should the yantra be worn; one must not fail to give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's means.

And it is essential for the one who performs the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Thus, the yantra should be worn only after first performing the invocation (*āvāhana*), the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and so forth, followed by worship with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) and ending with prostration (*praṇāma*). By wearing this yantra in this manner, [the desired result] will certainly be attained.

It should be understood that even the conviction in the form of a certainty—that "all obstacles will be warded off and the fruit will be attained"—is an auxiliary factor (*sahakārī*) for the production of the fruit through its maintenance. Now, regarding the six consonants constituting the present Vidyā, there are seven hundred and twenty variations produced by the transposition of their sequence; from these, sixty yantras arise. These [are as follows]: [The sixty yantras follow]... [The text continues with the description of the yantras] ...[End of yantra descriptions]... Thus, having described the yantras, the author now states the method for the worship of the yantras: *athaitadyantrapūjāvidhiḥ |* *atha prathamamasyā vidyāyāḥ ṣaḍvarṇānāmekaikavarṇasyaikaikakoṣṭhe vilikhya tadupari tattadvarṇasvarūpiṇīṃ devatāṃ dhyātvā tatraiva gandhapuṣpādibhirabhyarcya tadanantaraṃ sarvakoṣṭhagata-ṣaḍvarṇātmaka-mūlavidyāṃ samastāṃ yathākramaṃ vilikhya tasyā upari mūladevatāṃ dhyātvā pūjayet |* *iti yantrapūjāvidhiḥ |* Now, the procedure for the worship of this yantra: First, having written each of the six syllables of this Vidyā in a separate square and meditated upon the deity in the form of each respective syllable therein, one should worship them with scents, flowers, and so forth. Thereafter, having written the entire root Vidyā consisting of the six syllables located in all the squares according to the sequence, and having meditated upon the principal deity above it, one should perform the worship. Thus ends the procedure for the worship of the yantra.
We shall now demonstrate [the procedure].

Having drawn eighteen lines each extending east-west and north-south, with equal intervals between them and intersecting one another, and having thus produced squares numbering two hundred and eighty-nine (289), which is the measure of Nanda’s elephants (nandakuñjarabhuja), one should [arrange] the outermost rows there in all four directions.
The ninth [square] is the ninth cell; below it is one, and on each of its two sides is one— thus,
in total, there are four cells formed by the two vertical lines (east-west) and the single horizontal line (south-north) that divide the cells.
Having unified [the grid] through cleansing, there are fifteen squares in each of the four corners situated within the four directions for the first row; eleven for each corner of the second row;
seven for each corner of the third row; and three for each corner of the fourth row, making a total of [fifty-two].
In each corner there are thirty-six squares; the four corners combined thus comprise one hundred and forty-four squares, along with the sixteen squares situated in the four cardinal directions.
When the sixty-first [square] is subtracted from the total count of one hundred and sixty squares (160),
one hundred and twenty-nine squares (129) remain. Therein, starting from the beginning,
one begins from the middle square among the five squares situated in the third row.

Having written the *bhedavidyās* associated with the first *kūṭa*, which are connected to the final syllables of the *vāgbhava* seed-mantra, in the thirty-two squares surrounding those first squares in a clockwise direction; then, starting from the square immediately below that very one,
one should write the *bhedavidyās* in twenty-eight squares, as before, ending at their respective preceding squares.
Having written those [syllables] connected with the first peak (kūṭa), then, starting again from that very same lower square and continuing up to its own preceding square,
having written the Bhedavidyās connected with the first peak in the twenty-four squares, then, starting again from that very same lowest square...

Having written the variant mantras (bhedavidyās) associated with the first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) in twenty squares, starting from that [central] square and ending with the square immediately preceding it; and again, having written the variant mantras associated with the first peak-syllable in sixteen squares, starting from the square below that and ending with the square immediately preceding it— there are one hundred and twenty variant mantras in total.

And the remaining nine squares, situated in the very center, are as follows: in the three squares on the left side, arranged from top to bottom, one should place the six consonants read in reverse order, formed respectively as *duralakasaha aiṃ*, *ḍaralakasaha īṃ*, and *ḍaralakasaha auṃḥ*.
The three seed-syllables are in the first [square]. The second, first, and third seed-syllables are in the second. The third, second, and first seed-syllables are in the third.
"In the lower square" means in the one situated on the right side.
In the first [square], one should write the triad beginning with Vāgbhava, distinguished by the six consonants in direct order (*anuloma*).

In the second [square], they are written according to the sequence of the second, first, and third seed-syllables. In the third square, having written them in the sequence of third, second, and first, from top to bottom; then, in the square adjacent to the eastern direction, designated as the "upper position" (*ūrdhvapada*).

In the middle square directly below that, one should write the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in the genitive case, such as "of [Name]," followed by the ritual action (*karma*) in its appropriate form, such as "subjugate" (*vaśaṃ kuru*).
Below that, one should write the word for the object to be acted upon (*sādhya*), such as "Devadatta," in the accusative case. Then, one should draw a triangle extending to the four directions.

One should bring about the state of nine squares for each [triangle] by means of two pairs of lines—one extending east-west and the other extending north-south—placed in the middle. To do so: having made two marks on each and every line of the triangle, one should mark the two north-south lines such that the first [mark on the first line] corresponds to the first [mark on the second], and the second [on the first] to the second [on the second].
Having joined them face-to-face: having joined the first mark on the left side of the line from the south-north axis with the second [mark],
and the first mark on the right-side line with its own corresponding [mark].
Having joined the second mark on the north-south line with the point where it meets the second mark on the left (west) side;
[and] having joined the second mark on the right (east) side with the first mark on the north-south line, which faces it and is the point where it meets the second mark on the left (west) side.
"One should combine them together" means that on the left and right sides,
there are three squares each in the sequence of up, middle, and down, and likewise in the center.
The "three compartments" refers to the wheel consisting of nine triangular compartments; therein,
the three *pratiloma* vidyās are in the three compartments on the left side,
and the three *anuloma* vidyās are in the three compartments on the right side.
In the middle triad as well, one should not write [the letters] starting from the top for the sake of the practitioner's ritual goals;
thus, by means of the various divisions of the *vidyā* beginning with the letter *ha* found in the first section, the primary yantra is established.
For in the expansion of the *vidyā*, there are as many expansions of the syllables of the *vidyā* as one intends to perform.
The sections are divided. The number of each individual section's cell corresponds to the number of variations for its respective first syllable.

It has been established that within those sections, the specific vidyās of those various variations, composed of the first, second, and subsequent syllables, are to be arranged. This is the case here.

The six sections of the grid for the first five-syllable variety of the six-syllable Vidyā consist of one hundred and twenty squares; in those sections, [the letters] beginning with *ha* appear in sequence.
The six groups of mantras beginning with consonants and ending in the vowel *u* are each three-syllabled;

they should be written such that the consonants occupy the first seed-syllable (*bīja*) in forward and reverse order, while the second and third seed-syllables are joined with the consonants according to the traditional transmission (*āmnāya*).
Thus, in the six sections combined, there are seven hundred and twenty mantras that have been written down.
Even in the present yantra, the number of squares is likewise that of a single section; thus, all varieties of vidyās are inscribed by means of these six vajra-yantras, in sequence,
on page 166a.

Sixty yantras have been established for the seventy-two hundred and twenty-one variations associated with the first seed-syllable of the present Nityā, beginning with the letters *ha*, *sa*, *ka*, *la*, *ra*, and *ḍa*. And these yantras...

The four initial yantras should be inscribed, respectively, on plates of gold, silver, copper, and on stones such as crystal or gaṇḍakī; alternatively, the four initial yantras may be inscribed on the four materials beginning with gold in any desired order, without regard for sequence. However, the final [yantra]...

The two diagrams, beginning with the letters *ra* and *ḍa*, are composed of mantras (*vidyā*) and are not made of gold or other such materials; rather, they should be drawn on cloth or on a pedestal made of *palāśa* wood and the like. Alternatively, all six diagrams may be drawn at will in the six aforementioned locations; there is no fixed rule here. However, there is a certain distinction: it has been stated that they may be written on a wooden board or a cloth.

If worship is performed for either of these *yantras* in one's own home due to the gravity of the task—even if they have been brought from another country—then within one month or even within the *maṇḍala*, it grants everything desired.

However, as for those inscribed on gold and other materials, one should bring them there, carry them back from there, and worship them; but in some cases, they must be installed with stability in that very place.
The procedure for that is as follows: in the vicinity of the place where the yantra is to be installed,
one should construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa) measuring nine cubits in length and breadth, adorned with banners, arches, canopies, flower garlands, and other ornaments.

In that regard, according to the method of installing a single machine, one should construct an altar (*vedi*) measuring one cubit in height and width in the central portion; however, according to the method of installing all six machines,
[on page 166b]:

Having prepared six altars in the northeast, east, southeast, southwest, west, and northwest, as well as one altar in the center according to the described characteristics; [one should place] upon the central altar the eternal wheel of worship for the Nityās,
the first yantra composed of the mantra beginning with the letter *ha* in the southwest, and [the yantra] composed of the mantra beginning with the letter *sa* in the northeast.

The second yantra is composed of the Vidyā beginning with *ka* in the east; the third yantra is composed of the Vidyā beginning with *la* in the southeast; the fourth yantra is composed of the Vidyā beginning with *ra* in the west;
and having placed the sixth yantra, composed of the Vidyā beginning with *ḍa*, in the northwest, one performs the invocation (*āvāhana*).

Having performed the ritual installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and so forth, and having worshipped [the deity] with the five offerings consisting of perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, water for libation, and food offerings, preceded by dance and song;
and having likewise worshipped the *ḍākinīs* and others in their respective diagrams (*yantras*) in the sequence of wind, fire, northeast, and west.

Having worshipped Rākiṇī, Lākiṇī, Kākiṇī, Śākiṇī, and Hākiṇī together with their respective six syllabic powers (akṣara-śakti) which will be described hereafter, one should perform the recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa) in numbers such as a thousand or a hundred according to the method prescribed for the daily practice (nitya). In this manner—

Having performed worship, recitation, and fire-offerings for three days, at the time when Jupiter is in its exaltation, or when the Sun is in its exaltation, or during a fixed *lagna*, at the time of the exit of breath through the left nostril, or at the time of the rising of the earth-element (*bhūtodaya*), one should—somewhere on pure ground where the seven [elements] are present— [The remainder of the verse follows: ...draw a circle with a radius of twelve finger-breadths, having first worshipped the deity of the site (*vāstudeva*) and the guardian deities of the directions. Then, having offered oblations to the *kūṣmāṇḍas* and the *piśācas*, one should perform the ritual of piercing (*vedha*) by means of the *śakti*. Having drawn a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp, one should place the seed-syllables (*bīja*) upon it. Having meditated upon the *nāḍīs* as being like the fibers of a lotus stalk, one should contemplate the *kuṇḍalinī* as being like a coiled serpent. Then, having drawn the *prāṇa* upward from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra* by means of the *yoni-mudrā*, one should pierce the seven centers (*cakras*) starting from the *mūlādhāra*. Having thus pierced the body, one attains the state of a *siddha*. This is the secret method for piercing the body taught by the Lord. One who performs this according to the rules becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). There is no doubt about this. Thus ends the chapter on the piercing of the body.
