Having dug an interior pit in the sequence of center, southwest, northeast, east, southeast, west, and northwest, and having established it, one should firmly fix it with stones upon its upper part; then, on the upper part of the binding stones—(p.

Having fashioned the seventh [image] out of gold or other materials as the form of Nityānityā, surrounded by the six forms beginning with Ḍākinī, one should perform daily worship and recitation of the present Nityā together with Ḍākinī and the others. By that means, even if one has not constructed the seven buried yantras, there shall be neither famine nor misfortune; rather, in that [place],...

Prosperity (*lakṣmī*) itself always arrives; there is no affliction from malevolent planets (*duṣṭagraha*), nor any harassment by *piśācas*. The people who go there become exclusively righteous (*dhārmika*). In that place, auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) prevails in every way at all times. Now, [follow] the ritual applications for the independent worship of the powers (*śakti*), such as the *Ḍākinīs* and others, who reside within the six faces.

In the region of the throat there is a sixteen-petaled wheel (*cakra*). It is smoke-colored, and there resides the Ḍākinī, who has assumed the nature of the power (*śakti*) of the enclosure of Nityānityā and is distinguished by her specific form, name, and weapons. The Ḍākinī is at the pericarp (*karṇikā*), while on the petals, starting from the foremost petal, are the sixteen vowels. Therein—

Having worshipped Ḍākinī with the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Śrī Ḍākinī," using perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel; and having worshipped the sixteen Śaktis with the mantras beginning with: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Aśakti," and "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Aśakti."

Having performed the remaining three services (*upacāra*), one should perform the *nīrājana* and the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*) at the conclusion of the daily recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*). Thus,

for the practitioner who worships with mental services in the inner wheel (*ābhyantara-cakra*) and with the sixteen services beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*) in the manifest wheel drawn upon the ground, [the result follows].

Knowledge of past, present, and future objects is accomplished. In the region of the heart, there exists a twelve-petaled lotus known as the *anāhata* (unstruck) wheel; it is as red as vermilion, and within its pericarp—
Parāṅgarākinī stands as the letter Āhākinī, identical in form [to the others]. On the petals are the twelve syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*;
these are the Śaktis. Therein, one performs the worship with the twelve services (*upacāra*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*). [The mantra is: *hrīṃ śrīṃ rākinī-pādukāṃ*.

Having performed [the preliminary rite] with the mantra "I worship," and having fully worshipped the twelve syllable-śaktis with mantras such as "hrīṃ śrīṃ kaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi" (I worship the sandals of the śakti Ka) and "hrīṃ śrīṃ śūśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi" (I worship the sandals of the śakti Śū),
one should perform the remainder as before; this is the worship for both the internal wheel-ground and the extracted wheel.

For the practitioner who performs [the rites] gradually with both mental and external offerings, there arises fame, long life, wealth, and prosperity such as elephants, horses, and so forth. In the region of the navel is a ten-petaled wheel named Maṇipūra; it is blue in appearance, and in its pericarp resides Parāṅgabūtalākinī.
Lākinī of identical form resides upon the petals; there, the ten syllable-energies beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha* are present.
Having performed the worship with the twelve offerings, beginning with the first (*mālya*), by means of the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Lākinī*;
[one worships] *hrīṃ śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the energy of Ḍa*; *hrīṃ śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the energy of Ḍha*.
Having worshipped the ten syllable-energies (*varṇaśakti*) with the mantras beginning with *pūjayāmi*, and having performed the remainder as previously described,
for one who performs the worship of the internal ground and the extracted wheel (*cakra*) respectively with mental and external offerings,
there arises victory over enemies and the increase of prosperity. [This applies to] the *liṅga*, which manifests masculinity, femininity, and so forth.

At the root region, there is a six-petalled wheel named Svādhiṣṭhāna. It has the luster of the rising sun, and in its pericarp resides the goddess Kākinī, whose form is identical to that of Parāṅga-Kākinī. On the petals reside the six energy-deities (varṇa-śaktis) beginning with the letter *va* from the labial class (*pa-varga*) and ending with *la*. Therein [one worships] *hrīṃ śrīṃ kākinīpādukāṃ*.
Having worshipped with the twelve types of offerings using the mantra "I worship," [one recites]:
"I worship the sandals of the power *Va* (hrīṃ śrīṃ va-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi); I worship the sandals of the power *Bha* (hrīṃ śrīṃ bha-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi)," and so forth.
Having worshipped the powers of the six syllables with mantras, one should perform the remainder as before; thus,
for the practitioner who performs the worship of both the internal wheel-ground and the extracted wheel respectively with mental and external offerings.
There occurs the cessation of afflictions such as disease, thieves, and kings, as well as the attainment of desired goals in the form of gains of wealth, land, and so forth.
In the region between the anus and the genitals, at the *mūlādhāra*, there is a four-petaled wheel known as the *ādhāra-cakra*.
It has the luster of gold, and in its center is a triangular wheel; it is joined with the fire-element (*tejas*) that resides within it, or else it is joined with the energy in the form of Kuṇḍalinī.

The Sākinī, whose form is identical to that of Parāṅgasākinī, resides upon the petals starting from the front; there are four energy-letters (varṇaśakti) beginning with *va* and ending with *sa*. Therein, with the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Sākinī," one performs worship with the twelve services (upacāra) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*). At the conclusion of the worship, [one says]: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Vaśakti."

Having worshipped the powers of the four syllables with mantras such as "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Śaśakti," one should perform the remainder as before. For the practitioner who performs the worship of the inner circle-ground and the extracted circle respectively with mental and external offerings, [there arises] knowledge of the events of the three periods of time.
Knowledge of the mental states and activities residing in the minds of all people arises;
and the power to perform the acts of creation, maintenance, and destruction arises from the practice of extraordinary effort in worship.

Between the eyebrows is the wheel named Ājñā, which has two petals and is white in color. At its pericarp resides Hākinī, who is identical in form to Parāṅgahākinī. On its two petals reside two Śaktis in the form of the syllables *Ha* and *Kṣa*.
There, at the conclusion of the worship with the twelve services beginning with water for the feet (pādya) using the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ,

I worship the sandals of Hākinī," one should worship the powers of the letters (varṇa-śaktis) with the two mantras "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Ha-śakti" and "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Kṣa-śakti," and then perform the remainder as before.

For the practitioner who performs worship of the two wheels raised from the inner ground in sequence, by means of both mental and external offerings, the very same result as previously described occurs without interval. Even in the case of the previously mentioned [worship], that which is performed within their respective wheels, beginning with Hākinī and ending with Ḍākinī, is twofold according to the distinction between internal and external.
It brings about the subjugation of enemies of the practitioner through rites such as hatred and eradication, which are to be performed.

Worship resulting in grace (*anugraha*) or restraint (*nigraha*) by another method is as follows: having fashioned a circle on ground measuring one cubit (*hastamātra*), and having constructed a hexagonal wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*) such that its lines touch or do not touch the perimeter of that circle;
then, having fashioned a single hexagonal wheel in each of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and the corners (*koṇa*), there are six hexagons in total.

Having prepared the sevenfold wheel (*saptakacakra*), one should worship, according to the previously stated method, the twelve-fold offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*) neither less nor more, preceded by the offering of the *bali* and so forth, at the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the six-pointed wheel situated there. Then,

having worshipped the group of six beginning with Ḍākinī in their respective locations within the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) using their respective mantras, [one should perform] recitation (*japa*) and fire-offering (*homa*).

One should perform the ritual actions ending with the offering of the *nīrājana* lamp and the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpanā*). Then, in the southwest intermediate direction, upon the pericarp of a six-spoked wheel, one should worship her with the twelve offerings using the mantra: "I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ḍākinī. Then, in the corners starting from the front, proceeding clockwise—
I worship Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aśaktipādukā. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Īśaktipādukā. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ūśaktipādukā. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṃśaktipādukā. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aḥśaktipādukā.

Having worshipped the six syllable-śaktis who are identical in form to the Ḍākinīs with the mantras "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Kaśakti," and having again worshipped Ḍākinī with the aforementioned *svavidyā*, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an oblation for that worship, saying: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, may these deities of the first enclosure of Ḍākinī accept this worship."

One should complete the remainder of the worship (*pūjā*). Then, within the six-cornered [diagram] in the northwest (*vāyavya*), having cast Rākinī into the place of Ḍākinī, one should worship the deity as before with the mantra stated in the verse concerning the word *rākinī*. In the corners are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the powers (*śakti*)—the letters *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, and *cha*—situated in the midst of the seven-syllable mantra.

Having worshipped with the three-syllable name-mantras of the respective varṇa-śaktis, and having worshipped Rākinī again with the previously mentioned *svavidyā*, one should offer the flower-oblation (*puṣpāñjali*) as the conclusion of worship using the mantra stated for the substitution of the word "Rākinī" in the place of "Ḍākinī," and thus complete the remainder. [In the center] of the six-cornered [yantra] previously [drawn], within the pericarp (*karṇikā*)—
Having worshipped Lākinī with the twelve offerings using the mantra stated in the *Lākinīpada* section of the *Ḍākinīsthāna*,

one should worship the six Śaktis— Jaśakti, Ūśakti, Traśakti, Ṭaśakti, Uśakti, and Ḍaśakti— who are identical in form to Lākinī and reside in the corners, by means of mantras consisting of their names placed between two seed-syllables and seven syllables.

Having again worshipped Lākinī with the previously mentioned mantra, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as before for the presentation of worship using the mantra composed of the deities of the first enclosure, beginning with *hrīṃ śrīṃ* and so forth;
then one should conclude the remainder [of the rite]. In the southeast, within the pericarp of the six-pointed star (*ṣaṭkoṇa*),...
Having worshipped Kākinī with the twelve offerings using the mantra spoken by another, Kākinī, which was cast into the station of the Ḍākinīs;
In the corners are the six Kākinīs of identical form: Cha-śakti, Ṇa-śakti, Ta-śakti, Tha-śakti, Da-śakti, and Dha-śakti.

Having worshipped these six syllable-forms of Śakti with the two seed-syllables as before, and with the mantras containing the names inserted into the midst of the seven-syllable mantra, one should worship Kākinī with the aforementioned mantra.
Having worshipped again with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ" and so forth, using the mantra composed of the deities of the first enclosure beginning with Kākinī,

one should offer a handful of flowers for the presentation of worship as before and complete the remainder. In the northeast, upon the pericarp of the six-cornered [mandala], one should worship Śākinī with the mantra stated in the section concerning the placement of Śākinī at the station of Ḍākinī.

Having worshipped with the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*), one should worship the six energy-deities (*śakti*) in the corners— namely Na-śakti, Pa-śakti, Pha-śakti, Va-śakti, Bha-śakti, and Ma-śakti— with their respective forms, using the mantras consisting of two seed-syllables and seven syllables as before, with the name inserted in the middle. Then, one should again worship Śākinī with the aforementioned mantra.

Having offered a handful of flowers as before with the mantra containing the words "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ" and so forth, which includes the name of the deity of the first enclosure, Śākinī, one should complete the remainder of the ritual. Then, in the west, upon the pericarp of the hexagon, one should perform the twelve services beginning with water for the feet (pādya) using the mantra stated with the word Hākinī inserted in the place of Ḍākinī.

Having performed worship, one should worship the six energy-deities (śaktis) in the corners— Hākinī and those identical in form to her: Raśakti, Laśakti, Śaśakti, Ṣaśakti, Saśakti, and Haśakti— using mantras consisting of their names inserted between two seed-syllables and the seven-syllable mantra, as previously described, together with the aforementioned mantra.

Again, having worshipped Hākinī with the mantra beginning with *hrīṃ śrīṃ* and so forth— which incorporates the name of the deity of the first enclosure— one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an oblation for her worship and conclude the remainder of the ritual.

In this way, for the worshipper, there occurs the destruction of all suffering and the full attainment of all prosperity. If the worship is performed in the manner described, beginning with Hākinī and ending with Ḍākinī, then—
The incantations for the hatred, eradication, and so forth of enemies are accomplished. As for the worship for the purpose of grace (*anugraha*) by another method:

having prepared a seven-pointed hexagonal wheel as before, one should likewise [place] the six powers, such as Ḍākinī and the rest, each joined with their respective power, within that [wheel]. Ḍākinī and the others...

After performing the worship of the Nityās endowed with their respective powers (*svaśakti*), one should perform the worship here. Regarding the food offerings (*naivedya*) in this worship, there is no fixed rule;
however, for Ḍākinī it is milk-rice (*pāyasa*); for Rākinī, rice mixed with jaggery; for Lākinī, rice cooked with mung beans; and for Kākinī, turmeric rice.

For Śākinī, rice mixed with sesame; for Hākinī, pure rice (*śuddhodana*). For Nityānityā, who stands in the center, the food offering (*naivedya*) consists of the six items beginning with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), accompanied by fish and other meats.
Thus, the worship of the Goddess is performed according to the method of daily worship, wherein the portion of the powers of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-śakti-aṃśa*) has reached a state of reduction.

It is without fabrication. Furthermore, having fashioned another seven-six-cornered wheel (*saptasatkoṇacakra*) and stationed therein women endowed with beauty and youth, whose forms are identical to those of the Nityās and Anityās;

and having worshipped them—beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*)—together with the Nityā-Anityā and the Ḍākinīs and others manifested within the six corners, as well as the Ḍākinīs and their retinue.
Having worshipped the young women stationed at each respective *cakra* with the twelve types of offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*), beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*),
and having worshipped the energy-deities (*varṇa-śakti*) of their respective colors— characterized as previously described— in their respective corners;
[one should worship] the young women presided over by one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) with gifts of various garments, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, food, and so forth.
One should satisfy them. When they are satisfied, the Nityā who is the subject at hand, together with her powers (śakti), becomes thoroughly pleased.
When she is pleased, everything desired by the practitioner is accomplished. Now, the applications for suppression (nigraha) are as follows:
Having extracted the six hexagonal wheels (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*) in the directions starting from the southwest as prescribed for the six powers (*ṣaṭśakti*) beginning with the *Ḍākinī*,
and having placed jars upon those wheels,
one should fill them with the water associated with the tree of the enemy’s birth-constellation (*nakṣatra*) as previously described, each individually.

Having wrapped [the vessels] with two black-colored cloths, one should worship the group of six, beginning with Ḍākinī, along with their respective retinue-shaktis, within those jars at the hour of midnight according to the ritual rules and in accordance with their respective directions;
then, at the conclusion of the entire worship, one should offer a bali-oblation to the *nakṣatra* and *yoni* of one's own enemy.

Having offered as an oblation to Varuṇa blood cooked from the blood of one related to his own enemy’s asterism and birth-sign, he should then perform oblations with each of the six mantras beginning with Ḍākinī, using a sacrificial ladle (sruva) shaped like a serpent’s head, preceded by the assumption of a wrathful demeanor, black garments, and so forth, with a number of one hundred or one thousand offerings for each mantra.
At the time of worship and fire-offerings (*pūjā-homa*), they are overcome with wrath; thus, with their lips bitten by their own fangs,
they strike their enemies with their twelve hands and scatter the mangled limbs of the slain foes to the *piśācas*, while their necks are adorned with *japā* flower buds.

The practitioner should meditate upon the *ḍākinīs* and other *śaktis* uttering terrifying cries; by this, the *ḍākinīs* and other *śaktis* in the form of *kṛtyās*, produced from the skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow of the enemies, bring about the destruction of those enemies in that very instant. As for the wheel of suppression (*nigrahacakra*): [it is as follows].

Having drawn ten lines each extending east-west and north-south, with equal intervals and intersecting one another, one should produce a wheel consisting of eighty-one squares, [marking] the fifth [square] in each direction.
Having omitted the fifth square,

and having erased the seven squares situated in the middle, starting from the fifth square at one end of the row and ending at the fifth square at the other end of the row; [this is done] in the second path.
Having set aside three squares each— in one square directly below the remaining square of the first row and one square on each side of it—
and having erased the three remaining squares in each corner,
a total of ten squares are erased in each corner within both rows.

Forty squares are wiped clean, and forty-one squares remain. Therein, having fashioned a central, prominent triangle within each of the single squares at the four cardinal directions, and having divided each into three rows, one should write the name of the practitioner and the name of the object of the rite respectively from top to bottom; then, all around—

Having transcended everything, one should write the name of the practitioner and the name of the object to be accomplished in three rows within the central square of the fifth form, following the sequence from top to bottom; then, starting from the square directly below the square containing the first syllable of the practitioner’s name, one should fill the eight squares surrounding and connected to it.

Again, having gone outside that [square], one should fill the cells surrounding it, starting precisely from the cell below it. Again, having gone outside that, one should fill the cells connected to that row, surrounding it, starting from the cell below that. Again, starting precisely from the cell below that, one should fill the cells surrounding that row. Here, among the thirty-six cells—

The other [mantras] should be written as follows: *ḍa-ra-la-ka-sa-ha-ḍa-ra-la-ka-sa-hīṃ*; *ḍa-ra-la-ka-sa-hauḥ*; *ḍa-ra-la-ka-sa-hauḥ*; *ḍa-ra-la-ka-sa-hīṃ*; *ḍa-ra-la-ka-sa-haiṃ*; *ra-ḍa-ca-ka-sa-haiḥ*. (p. 171b)

raḍaralakasahīṃ raḍalakasahauṃ raḍalakasahauḥ raḍalakasahīṃ raḍalakasahaiḥ laḍarakasahaiḥ laḍarakasahīṃ laḍarakasahauḥ laḍarakasahauḥ laḍarakasahīṃ laḍarakasahaiḥ kaḍaralasahaiṃ kaḍaralasahīṃ kaḍaralasahauḥ kaḍaralasahauḥ
kaḍaralasahīṃ, kaḍaralasahaiḥ, saḍaralakahaiṃ, saḍaralakahīṃ, saḍaralakahauḥ, saḍaralakahīṃ, saḍaralakahaiṃ, saḍaralakasahau, ḍaralakahau,
sahaḍaralakahasau, haḍaralakasauḥ, haḍaralakasīṃ, haḍaralakasaiṃ— thus.

There are thirty-six varieties of the present vidyā in reverse order; likewise, having written each of those respective reverse varieties in each individual square, the yantra for suppression is accomplished. Having inscribed it in a vessel of bell-metal or a vessel of lead, using the blood of the enemy’s birth-constellation mixed with the powder of that same enemy’s birth-constellation.

Having inscribed that [mantra] upon the base of the yantra, if a practitioner installs it in the house, city, field, or other locations of an enemy—at the ascendant of the eighth house from the enemy’s birth chart—preceded by the ritual of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the life-force) and worship, the very lineage of that enemy shall be destroyed;
what need is there to mention the destruction of the individual? This is so even in this very case.
Having inscribed the reverse-order *vidyā* in the form of a *kūṭa* within the *Vajrayantra*, followed by the various forward-order *vidyās*,

and having performed the consecration of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and worship, if this [yantra]— engraved on a plate of gold or other materials— is installed in one's own house, city, or elsewhere during one’s own eleventh or other astrological ascendant (*lagna*), then there will be an increase in longevity, health, prosperity, victory, and so forth; thus it is a single [method].

By means of the presentation of the various types of *kāmanās* (desires) in the center and the triangles, and by means of the presentation of the various types of *vidyās* (mantras) in both reverse (*pratiloma*) and direct (*anuloma*) order, this wheel successively brings about various kinds of calamities for enemies and accomplishes various kinds of desired goals for oneself.

All these very same applications [of ritual] apply also to the eternal *pañcakūṭā*, which consists of five consonants excluding the letter *ḍa*; there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), whereas the assignment of the letters (*varṇanyāsa*) is as follows:

Precisely because that color is absent, it is not a subject of doubt; for since the author of the root-text has established in the passage beginning with "other than the yantra" that this applies in common to other mantras as well, the possibility of identity regarding the non-yantra portion is present, and thus all the ritual applications of worship (pūjāprayoga) are stated to be exactly the same, resulting in the accomplishment of all desired objects on the leaf.

The fruit has been stated there; however, the distinction is that from the *pañcakūṭavidyā*, a fruit indeed superior to the accomplishment of speech (*vāksiddhi*) arises. Thus ends the introduction to the *Nityānityā*.
Now, the Nīlapatākānityā is introduced.
Having constructed a triangle facing oneself with a bindu placed in its center, then outside that a hexagon,

then outside that an eight-petaled lotus joined by circles at its base and apex, and then outside that an eight-spoked wheel formed by two intersecting squares whose sides touch and do not touch the outer circle; having thus constructed [the mandala].

Outside of that, one should construct two concentric circles including the intervening space, and beyond those, two square enclosures (bhūpura) in the four directions provided with door-frames; having thus prepared the yantra for daily worship according to the prescribed procedure,
one should perform the placement of the nine jars (navakalaśa), the worship of Sarvamaṅgalā, the visualization of the wheel (cakra), and the worship of that [deity] along with its attendants.

At the conclusion of the ritual sequence ending with the dismissal (*udvāsana*) of that [deity], one should again contemplate the current *nityā*-wheel—even though it was already drawn below—within the very water of that same ritual jar (*kalaśa*). Therein, as an ancillary part of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), the rites to be performed on the preceding day are to be carried out. Then, having passed that night with dance, song, and other such festivities, [The text continues...]

In the morning, at the conclusion of the necessary rites, one should again worship the Imperishable [Goddess] with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), then perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*), and finally, at the conclusion of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and other rites, one should impart her mantra according to the method previously described.

Now, as for the worship of the Bodiless One (Anaṅga), the method of worship based on all those aforementioned substrates— whether on a wheel engraved upon gold or other materials, or drawn on the ground with red minerals— is as follows: it begins and ends with the essential morning rites, such as anointing with fragrant oil and bathing in scented water.
In the course of worshipping another deity, the practitioner— having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites,
and having adorned himself with red sandalwood paste, garments, and ornaments— arrives at the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*).
At the site purified by the *kūrma-cakra*, he [recites] the aforementioned Vidyā.
Having sat down upon a svastika seat or similar seat placed over a red woolen rug and other articles honored with the fourfold offerings,
having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of the Vidyā-mantra, and having offered the oblation (*bali*) with the sixteen-syllable mantra,

one should worship the nine Nāthas on one’s own head according to the lineage of one’s own gurus using their respective mantras; then, having recited their hymn of praise, [one should proceed] by their command.

One should commence the worship. Having meditated upon the identity of one’s own self with the Lord who is to be worshipped, and having fully worshipped the thirty-eight deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), beginning from the pedestal and lion-throne of the wheel of worship up to the entire circle of the secret and manifest *siddhayoginīs* distinguished by their respective years, places, times, and so forth; [one should proceed].

Between the wheel of worship (*pūjācakra*) and oneself, one should place the common *arghya* vessel— made of gold or other materials, provided with a base, and filled with water consecrated by the five substances such as *gorocana*. Then, by means of the three seed-syllables of Kulasundarī,
one should sequentially visualize the base, the vessel, and the water as having the nature of fire, sun, and moon.

Having contemplated the fivefold nature of earth and the other elements within the five substances—such as yellow orpiment—that have been cast therein, and having contemplated the single nature of those waters and the present wheel; and contemplating the non-duality of the present Nityā and the water, one should consecrate [the substance] ten times with the present Vidyā and worship it. The present Vidyā...
Having worshipped the deities of the limbs there with the six-limbed mantras,
one should [purify] oneself with the consecrated general *arghya* water using the present vidyā.

Having sprinkled with water the general *arghya* vessel and the water for the *pādya* and other rites placed in the successive vessels to its right, as well as the garments, ornaments, perfumes, and so forth placed on one's own right side;
and having again performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *vidyā*, [one takes] the general *arghya* water with a ladle.
Holding kuśa grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth in his hand,

he should state the place and time, the month, fortnight, lunar day, lineage, zodiac sign, name, and the specific desire; then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) according to the prescribed rule and according to his intellectual capacity— thinking, "I shall perform the daily worship of Nīlapatākā"— he should pour water upon the ground.

Even in the event of the involvement of another deity, one who has not yet performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth should perform those rites ending with one's own consecration (*svasaṃskāra*) at this very juncture; having employed the present Vidyā in place of the other mantras used therein and having completed that ritual, [one proceeds] after the installation of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the Mātṛkā.
Having recited the complete *Prastuta-nityā-vidyā* at the beginning of each [syllable],
and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the respective letters of the Mātṛkā upon their corresponding locations, one should utter: *hrīṃ preṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *srūṃ kroṃ śirase svāhā*,
*āṃ hrīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *aiṃ klūṃ kavacāya huṃ*, and *nityamadadrave netrāya vauṣaṭ*.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras *huṃ phreṃ hrīṃ astrāya phaṭ* on one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other limbs;

[then] *hrīṃ* on the right ear; *phreṃ* on the left ear; *srūṃ* on the right eye; *kroṃ* on the left eye; *āṃ* on the right nostril; *klīṃ* on the left nostril; *aiṃ* on the palate; *klūṃ* on the throat; *ni* at the heart; *ha* at the navel; and *mam* at the *mūlādhāra*.

Having performed the placement of the syllables as follows: *da* on the right thigh, *dra* on the right knee, *ve* on the right ankle, *huṃ* on the left thigh, *phreṃ* on the left knee, and *hrīṃ* on the left ankle; [then recite] *hrīṃ phreṃ*.
Having performed the three-fold pervasive nyāsa with the complete mantra of seventeen syllables— *srū kroṃ ā klīṃ aiṃ klūṃ nityamadadrave huphreṃ hrīṃ*—
one should proceed with the invocation and subsequent rites as follows: having followed the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā and placed flowers within the hollowed palms (*añjali*).

There, while contemplating that [deity] resting there—having pervaded the path from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra* through the fire-carrying *nāḍī* (suṣumṇā)—and having been transferred to the present wheel (*cakra*) by the scattering of that handful of flowers, one should utter the complete root mantra: "O Nīlapatākā-nityā, be invoked here in this wheel! (*iha cakre āvāhitā bhava*).

Having performed the invocation after making the formal request, one should contemplate some of the clusters of rays of that splendor which have radiated out to their respective locations as having transformed into the form of the weapons and the protective armor. One should then meditate upon the mass of splendor situated in the center as having transformed into the form perceived through meditation. As for the meditation:

She shone with a crown of radiant jewels resembling sapphire; she had five faces and three eyes, wore crimson garments, and was adorned with ten arms graced by trembling pearls and ornaments. Her body was inlaid with clusters of gems, and her face was brightened by a beautiful smile.

She holds in her left hands, which are adorned with all ornaments and placed at her left side, a noose, a banner, armor, a bow, and a blue jay; and she holds in her right hands a lotus, a spear, a sword, arrows, and the gesture of fearlessness, while seated upon a lotus throne.

"In the sequence of the daily worship of the Goddess, one should meditate on her as surrounded by hosts of Śaktis, [each] with their own specific forms, colors, dress, faces, hands, weapons, and ornaments. Thus, the meditation for the weapons is also exactly like this;
however, regarding the aspect of the weapons, they possess the additional quality of being marked by their respective individual forms. Thereafter—
At the end of the aforementioned vidyā, [say] "O Nīlapatākā, be eternally present here in this cakra.
Again, at the end of twenty-nine syllables, [say] "be firmly restrained. Again, at the end of twenty-nine syllables...
Become veiled. Then, at the end of the twenty-nine syllables, she should be made present.

Having requested the fourfold ritual beginning with *sthāpana* (establishment) preceded by the display of the respective mudrās, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the fingers starting with the thumb and the placement of the heart and other limbs upon the *Prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā*.

Having established the vital breaths by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra in the form "The vital breaths of this Nīlapatākā-nityā are here in the wheel, the vital breaths," and so forth, one should worship her with the twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*).
Her mantras are as follows: at the end of the complete seventeen-syllable vidyā, [one offers] water for the feet (*pādya*) to Nīlapatākā-nityā.

With the mantra "kalpayāmi," having offered the *pādya* (water for washing the feet) using the water from the general *arghya* vessel held in the right hand by means of a ladle, one should offer it at the two feet of the deity with the *nityā-vidyā* currently being recited. In this very same manner,
omitting the word "pādya" and substituting it with the words "arghya," "ācamana," and so forth, [the offerings are completed].

Having offered the arghya, ācamana, and other services with their respective mantras, one should present those same offerings to the head, face, and other parts using the vidyā under discussion. Having thus completed the worship with the twelve services, including betel and food, one should proceed to the thirteenth service. Its procedure is as follows: on the rear part of the Goddess—

Having worshipped the nine divine Siddha-Mānava-Nāthas— named Prakāśa, Vimarśa, Ānanda, Śrījñāna, Śrīsatya, Śrīpūrṇasvabhāva, Pratibha, Subhaga, and Abhidhāna— who are the very embodiments of the power (śakti) cast into the feet of the Lord by means of their own respective mantras; starting from the tip of the triangle and proceeding clockwise.

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Icchā-śakti. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Jñāna-śakti. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Kriyā-śakti. On both sides of the triangle, beginning from the area near the goddess’s left lower hand...
(page 174b)
In the ten well-placed locations at the edge of the area near the right lower hand, proceeding clockwise: *hrīṃ śrīṃ varāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ śārṅgacāpāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ carmaṇe namaḥ*,
*hrīṃ śrīṃ patākāyai namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ pāśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ abhayāya namaḥ*.

Having worshipped the weapons with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ vāṇebhyo namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ khaḍgāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ śaktyai namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṅkuśāya namaḥ*, and so forth; and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete Vidyā with: "I worship the sandals of the eternal Nīlapatākā," [one worships] these: *hrīṃ śrīṃ etāḥ*.

Having offered a handful of flowers for the presentation of worship with the words, "May the deities of the first enclosure, Nīlapatākā and Anityā, accept this worship," one worships in the six corners, beginning from the front and proceeding clockwise:
*Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, I worship the sandals of Hādinī; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, [I worship] the sandals of Rākinī; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, [I worship] the sandals of Śākinī.*

Having worshipped those respective Śaktis with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Lākinī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi," "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kākinī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi," and "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ḍākinī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi," and having worshipped the central Goddess at the end of the complete mantra with "Nīlapatākā-nityā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi," [one worships] "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ these deities of the second enclosure of Nīlapatākā-nityā."

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering of worship with the words, "May [the deities] accept the worship," one worships starting from the eastern petal of the eight-petaled lotus: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Brāhmī; *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the sandals of Māheśvarī; *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the sandals of Kaumārī; *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the sandals of Vaiṣṇavī; *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the sandals of Vārāhī; *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the sandals of Aindrī; *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the sandals of Cāmuṇḍā.

Having worshipped each of those Mothers with "I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Mahālakṣmī," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete Vidyā with "I worship the sandals of the Nityā Nīlapatākā."

Having offered a handful of flowers as an act of worship with the words, "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the third enclosure, Nīlapatākā and Nityā, accept this offering," one should place the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aśā at the first corner of the eight-cornered wheel.
I worship. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ā-śaktipāta, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ I-śaktipāta, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ī-śaktipāta, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ U-śaktipāta, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ū-śaktipāta, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṛ-śaktipāta, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṝ-śaktipāta,
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ḷ-śaktipāta, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ḹ-śaktipāta, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ E-śaktipāta, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ai-śaktipāta.

Having fully worshipped the sixteen Śaktis of the *a*-group with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ auḥ śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ auḥ śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and *hrīṃ śrīṃ aḥ śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*;
[one worships] the Śaktis of the *ka*-group in the second corner: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ka śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having worshipped with the mantras: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kha-śaktipāda, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ga-śaktipāda, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Gha-śaktipāda, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṅa-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi," one should worship the group-energies (varga-śaktis) in the third corner: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ca-śaktipāda, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Cha-śaktipāda, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ja-śaktipāda."
Having worshipped with the mantras: *hrīṃ śrīṃ jha-śaktipāda*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ tra-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth;

then in the fourth corner, one worships the powers of the *ṭa*-group with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ṭa-śaktipāda*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ ṭha-śaktipāda*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ ḍa-śaktipāda*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ ḍha-śaktipāda*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ ṇa-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.
Having worshipped with the mantras, one worships the powers of the *tavarga* (t-class) in the fifth corner with the mantras:

*hrīṃ śrīṃ ta-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ tha-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ da-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ dha-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ na-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. Then, in the sixth corner, [one worships] the powers of the *pavarga* (p-class).

Having worshipped with the mantras: *hrīṃ śrīṃ pa-śaktipāta*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ pha-śaktipāta*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ va-śaktipāta*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ bha-śaktipāta*, and "I worship the *pādukā* of *hrīṃ śrīṃ ma-śakti*. (p. 175b)

In the seventh corner, having worshipped with the mantras: "I worship the sandals of the power Ya," "I worship the sandals of the power Ra," "I worship the sandals of the power La," "I worship the sandals of the power Va," and "I worship the sandals of the power Śa"—namely the powers of the *y*-group;
then, in the eighth corner, [worship] the powers of the *ṣa*-group: "I worship the sandals of the power Ṣa" and "I worship the sandals of the power Sa."

Having worshipped with the mantras: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ha-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ la-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and *hrīṃ śrīṃ kṣa-śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; and having worshipped the goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete Vidyā with the mantra: *sampūrṇavidyānte nīlapatākānityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; [one should know]: *hrīṃ śrīṃ etā nīlapatākānityā-caturthāvaraṇa-devatāḥ* (these are the deities of the fourth enclosure of Nīlapatākānityā).

Having offered the handful of flowers for the presentation of worship with the mantra "May they accept the worship," [one worships as follows]: at the eastern gate of the square, *hrīṃ śrīṃ indraśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; in the southeast, *hrīṃ śrīṃ agniśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; at the southern gate, *hrīṃ śrīṃ yamaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; in the southwest, *hrīṃ śrīṃ rakṣaḥśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; at the western gate...

*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, the descent of the power of Varuṇa in the northwest; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, the descent of the power of Anila at the northern gate; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, the descent of the power of Soma in the northeast; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, the descent of the power of Īśa in the southwest-northwest intermediate region; *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of the power of Vidīśā between the east and the northeast.

Having worshipped the ten divine weapon-powers (*divyāstra-śakti*), and having honored the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra "At the conclusion of the complete vidyā, I worship the pādukā of Nīlapatākā-nityā," [one should worship] with the mantra:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ etā nīlapatākā-nityā-pañcamāvaraṇa-devatāḥ pūjāṃ gṛhṇantu*.
Having offered a handful of flowers as an act of worship and performed the thirteen modes of service (*trayodaśopacāra*), one should also complete the remaining three modes of service.

At the conclusion of the worship consisting of the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra), since the daily recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa) have already been encompassed by the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) for that worship, one should now perform [the recitation] a thousand times or more— without making a new resolve for the recitation— ensuring it is integrated with the previously shown finger-assignments (aṅguṣṭha-nyāsa), heart-assignments (hṛdaya-nyāsa), phoneme-assignments (varṇa-nyāsa), and pervasive assignments (vyāpaka-nyāsa).

Having performed an indefinite number of recitations (*japa*) and having made an offering (*nivedana*) while contemplating non-difference from that [deity], one should offer oblations according to the prescribed rule— either with rice smeared with clarified butter or with sesame and rice— preceded by sixteen oblations,
and then offer ten parts of the recitation using the present *vidyā*. Finally, one should unite [the deity] with the drop of the Goddess’s splendor, which has been meditated upon within the fire.

Having again worshipped the goddess who has arrived there with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), and having offered a *bali* once more with the *Kurukullā* mantra, one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) with a wick containing camphor and other substances, and seek forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*). Then, by means of the mudrā for raising the power (*śaktyutthāpanamudrā*),
one should visualize the deities of the surrounding retinue as rays of light, which have become absorbed into the principal deity being propitiated.

Having dissolved even the light situated in the center—which is the form of the principal deity—into one's own self by means of the *khecarīmudrā*, and having recited the hymns to the Goddess and the Guru as before at the conclusion of the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*), and the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*), one should cease.
However, the specific procedure regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*) has already been introduced in the general discussion. Thus...
The practitioner (*sādhaka*), having received initiation and being one who performs the daily and occasional rites of worship, recitation, and so forth,

should perform the practice for the realization of the mantra (*vidyāsādhana*) in order to attain the fitness for performing ritual applications (*prayoga*) when there is a desire for specific desired fruits. The method for this is as follows:

In all cases, including daily worship as well as the recitation for the purpose of accomplishing a *vidyā*, the practitioner facing east shall subsist on milk alone for as long as the performance of the recitation lasts; in the *Satya-yuga*, this consists of fifty-three *lakṣas*,
but in the *Kali-yuga*, it is twelve *lakṣas* more.
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) twenty-one million two hundred thousand times (21,200,000), according to the count of two crores.

The fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed with one-tenth of that number. All else has already been explained. Having thus mastered the mantra, one should carry out the ritual applications (*prayoga*).

For when this vidyā is accomplished, the ten siddhis arise. Even though there are other mantras that possess the ten siddhis, whenever a particular siddhi is desired by someone, then that person should accomplish that specific mantra; once it has been accomplished—

It is stated that by means of any one of the ten *siddhi-vidyās*—which are included within the present *nityā-vidyā*—once they have been accomplished, every desired goal is attained; therefore, all of that is now set forth. First, the names of the ten *siddhis* are as follows:
*vijayasiddhi*, *kāmarūpasiddhi*, *pādukāsiddhi*, and *rañjanasiddhi*.

The accomplishment of the sword (*khaḍgasiddhi*), the accomplishment of the vetāla (*vetālasiddhi*), the accomplishment of the piśāca (*piśācasiddhi*), the accomplishment of the yakṣiṇī (*yakṣiṇīsiddhi*), the accomplishment of the servant (*ceṭakāsiddhi*), and the accomplishment of illusion (*māyāsiddhi*).
Now, we shall demonstrate in order their mantras, the methods of their respective practice, and their fruits.
The mantra for the accomplishment of victory (*vijayasiddhi*) is fourfold: *hrīṃ phreṃ*, "O pair, grant victory in battle! *hrīṃ phreṃ*.
The first is fifteen syllables: *hrīṃ phreṃ*, "O Nityā, grant victory in the fourfold battle!

The second is eighteen syllables: *hrīṃ phreṃ*, "O Nityā, grant victory in the battle of the peak-syllable (*kūṭa-yuddha*)! The third is sixteen syllables: *hrīṃ phreṃ*, "O Nityā, grant victory in the difficult battle (*durga-yuddha*)!"

"Hrīṃ Phreṃ" is the fourth mantra, consisting of exactly sixteen syllables. Among these, when there is no specific desire for a particular mantra, one should worship [this one]. Since desires are manifold, the accomplishment of various aims requires diverse forms of worship. In this regard, having stayed in any auspicious place whatsoever, the recitation of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) of the syllables should be performed, and its tenth part (*daśāṃśa*)...

The *homatarpaṇa* (libation with oblations) should be performed. Furthermore, in the diagram (*yantra*) to be described on page 177a, according to the sevenfold division by day (*vāra*), one should worship on those respective days with the previously mentioned mantra using the five services (*pañcopacāra*) beginning with fragrance (*gandha*).

Worship should be performed by him; thereby, the success of victory mentioned in the mantra comes to pass. *Hrīṃ phreṃ made kāmarūpaṃ bhedehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—this thirteen-syllable mantra for the attainment of Kāmarūpa is indeed one alone. Here too, the recitation (*japa*) consists of one hundred thousand syllables as the preparatory rite (*pauraścaraṇika*). The fire-oblation (*homa*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) are to be performed at one-tenth of that amount, and worship is to be done in the yantra which will be described later. Thus...
The practitioner who accomplishes [the rite] gains, by virtue of his own will, the power to assume various forms.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ ity adyapādukām*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this twelve-syllable mantra is indeed a single *pādukā-mantra*. Here too, the recitation (*japa*) consists of one hundred thousand syllables; the offering of libations (*tarpaṇa*) is one-tenth of that. Worship is to be performed according to the specific hands depicted in each of the seven diagrams (*yantra*) which will be described. For the practitioner who performs it in this manner, this *siddhividya-pādukā* becomes gracious.

Having mounted it, he should bestow [the power] upon you; the practitioner may go to any desired region, even a difficult one, with extreme speed, and return again at his own will. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityaprade dehy añjanaṃ* (O Ever-Giving One, grant the ointment). *Hrīṃ preṃ*—this twelve-syllable mantra is the sole mantra for the accomplishment of the ointment (*añjana*). Here too, the recitation of one hundred thousand syllables constitutes the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), and its tenth part [is the homa].
In the *homatarpaṇa*, worship is performed upon the yantra itself—which will be described later and is divided into seven types according to the planets and so forth.

When the mantra has thus been mastered and this Vidyā has become propitious, she bestows a collyrium for the purpose of accomplishment. With eyes anointed by that, the practitioner perceives treasures buried in the earth, as well as gods, Gandharvas, and others dwelling in the intermediate space.

He beholds [the sword]. *Hrīṃ phreṃ drava nitye dehi khaḍgaṃ hrīṃ phreṃ*. This twelve-syllable mantra is one for the attainment of the sword (*khaḍgasiddhi*). Here too, the recitation (*japa*) consists of one hundred thousand syllables. (p.

One-tenth of that [number] is for the fire-oblation (*homa*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*), as will be described; worship is performed through each of the seven diagrams (*yantra*) according to their respective gates. Thus, by means of the perfected mantra (*siddhavidyā*), this divine sword is obtained;
grasping it in battle, one slays all enemies. One's enemies shall either flee or fall at one's feet.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadrave vetālān dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the thirteen-syllable mantra for the accomplishment of the Vetāla.

Here too, the recitation (*japa*) consists of one hundred thousand syllables; the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) are one-tenth of that amount. The yantra, which will also be described below, should be employed for the purpose of worship according to the specific differences of its gates. When one [mantra] has been thus perfected...
In the science of the accomplishment of the *vetāla*, all *vetālas* without exception, though innumerable, become individually perceptible.
Among them, some have deformed limbs, some have deformed faces, some have animal-like faces, and some have terrifying voices;
yet all, having come under control, mount the practitioner upon their shoulders and roam throughout every region observed by him.

At the word of the practitioner, they devour the enemies of the practitioner; what more need be said? Until death, they become like servants, performing everything commanded by him. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityamadadrave piśācān preṣaya* (Send forth the Piśācas).
This seventeen-syllable mantra, *hrīṃ phreṃ*, is for the attainment of the Piśāca-siddhi. Here too, one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣa*) constitute the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).

The recitation (*japa*) is ten times that [number], and the fire-oblation (*homa*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) are likewise; the *yantra* is the same, though it may differ for each occasion. Even Piśācas and Vetālas, who are otherwise innumerable and possess extremely emaciated bodies, become subject to the practitioner after the attainment of the *vidyā*.
They fulfill all the desires of the practitioner. Having previously fled from him...

Having made the adversary—who is the object of one's enmity—directly perceptible through mantras, medicinal herbs, and other such means, one should indeed seek to slay him by means of *piśācas*; for there is no one, even among them, who is imperceptible.

The mantras for the accomplishment of the yakṣiṇīs are thirty-six. Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāvicitrā. Hrīṃ phreṃ—this thirteen-syllable mantra is the first yakṣiṇī-vidyā. Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāvibhramā.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the second [mantra], consisting of thirteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāhaṃsī*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the third [mantra], consisting of twelve syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadābhīṣaṇī*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the fourth [mantra], consisting of thirteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadājanarañjikā*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*.

The fifth [mantra] consists of fifteen syllables: *hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāviśālā*. The sixth consists of thirteen syllables: *hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāmadanā*. The seventh consists of thirteen syllables: *hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadātuṣṭā*.

The eighth [mantra] consists of eight syllables: *hrīṃ phreṃ nitya*. The ninth consists of fourteen syllables: *hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadākālakaṇṭhī*. The tenth consists of fourteen syllables as well: *hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadābhayāṃ hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*... [and so on].

The *Aindri* [is] *Nityadravamadā*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the eleventh, consisting of thirteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ Nityadravamadā Śaṅkhinī*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the twelfth, consisting of twelve syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ Nityadravamadā Aindrī*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the thirteenth, consisting of twelve syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*.

The fourteenth [syllable] consists of thirteen phonemes: *hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāmaṅgalā*. The fifteenth consists of fifteen phonemes: *hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāvaṭavāsinī*. The sixteenth consists of thirteen phonemes: *hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāmekhalā*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* [is the seventeenth].

*Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāsakalā*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the seventeenth [mantra], consisting of thirteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadālakṣmī*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the eighteenth [mantra], consisting of twelve syllables.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāmālinī*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the nineteenth [mantra], consisting of thirteen syllables.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāviśvanāyikā*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* consists of fifteen syllables and twenty [syllables].
*Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāsulocanā*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* consists of twenty-one and fourteen syllables.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāsuśobhā*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this [mantra] consists of twenty-two syllables and thirteen phonemes. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadākāmadā*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this [mantra] consists of twenty-three syllables and thirteen phonemes. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāvilāsinī*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this [mantra] consists of twenty-four [syllables].

*Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadākāmeśvarī*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the twenty-five-syllable [mantra] consisting of fourteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadānandinī*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the thirty-six-syllable [mantra] consisting of thirteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāsvarṇarekhā*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the twenty-seven-syllable [mantra].
*Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāmanoharā*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* consists of twenty-eight and fourteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāpramodā*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadārāgiṇī*.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ* consists of thirty-one and thirty syllables; these are the *yakṣiṇī* vidyās, each consisting of thirteen syllables.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ*—the *Nityadravamadāsiddhā* consists of thirty-one syllables.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ*—the *Yakṣiṇīvidyā* consists of twelve syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—the *Nityadravamadāpadminī* consists of thirty-two syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—this [mantra] consists of thirteen syllables.

*Hrīḥ phreṃ nityadravamadāratipriyā*. *Hrīḥ phreṃ*—this is the fourteen-syllable vidyā of the Yakṣiṇī named Trayastriṃśatmitā. *Hrīḥ phreṃ nityadravamadākalyāṇadā*. *Hrīḥ phreṃ*—this is the fourteen-syllable vidyā of the Yakṣiṇī named Catustriṃśatmitā.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadākalādakṣā*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* is the Yakṣiṇī consisting of thirty-five [syllables] and fourteen phonemes.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ nityadravamadāsurasundarī*.
The *vidyā* of the Yakṣiṇī consists of thirty-six syllables, beginning with *hrīṃ phreṃ*, and comprises fifteen letters.
All these Yakṣiṇīs are individually two-armed, beautiful young women, adorned with various colors, garments, and ornaments; each one [is thus]. Not, however, [multiple arms for each].
The places where the deities to be meditated upon have the habit of coming simultaneously to the vicinity of the practitioner are as follows: the foot of a banyan tree in a forest;
a cave on a mountain peak; and a grove situated in the midst of gardens, such as the foot of a *śleṣmāntaka* tree, the foot of a *karañja* tree, or the foot of a *vibhītaka* tree.
The roots of the *nimba* tree, the roots of the *pippala* tree, the roots of the *kadamba* tree, the roots of the *vilva* tree,

the roots of the *vaṭa* tree, and a forest on a riverbank— these are the twelve locations. The vidyās of the Yakṣiṇīs, obtained through the sequence beginning with Vicitrā and numbering thirty-six, are to be accomplished by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times according to their respective colors.

The fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed with one of the following flowers—*kadamba*, *bandhūka*, *japā*, or red *karavīra*—in a number ten thousand times the tenth part of the recitation (*japa*). The libation (*tarpaṇa*) and worship (*pūjā*), equal in number to the oblations, must likewise be performed using the yantra common to all accomplishments. That yantra is as follows: two circles with an intervening space between them.
Having drawn that [outer circle], one should fashion a nine-yoni *cakra* within the inner circular pericarp according to the method stated in the introduction;

then, having fashioned a square with its corners at the cardinal and intermediate directions from the two circles, and having fashioned an octagon by connecting the two [corners] with lines mutually joined; and then, having drawn two more circles with an intervening space outside of that.
Having fashioned a sixteen-petalled lotus whose root and tip are aligned with the circle [of the previous figure],
and having likewise drawn a second circle outside of that by counting the tips of the petals, and having constructed two outer square enclosures (bhūpura),
one should inscribe the syllables once the yantra is perfected; in the very center is the *māyābīja*, and within that, the word "aravau."

Having written the name of that door ending in the seventh case (locative) once on each machine, one should write the name of the person [suffering] in the genitive case— such as "of Yajñadatta"— above the portion containing the vowel *ī* across three lines; in the middle, the verb phrase "kurukuru-kuru" (do, do, do), and below that—

Having written the name of the object to be accomplished— such as "the pacification of disease" (*rogaśāntim*) or "the summoning of Devadatta" (*devadattākarṣaṇam*)— using specific words ending in the accusative case,
one should then write the thirty-two unaltered syllables of the *vidyā* in the thirty-two petals combined, namely, in the eight outer *yonis*, the eight triangles, and the sixteen petals.

Having written the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* on the innermost circular path, the sixteen consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ta* on the middle path, and the sixteen consonants beginning with *tha* and ending with *sa* on the outermost path, the remainder consists of the *ha* and *kṣa*.
One should write the three syllables in the four corners of the square, starting from the southeast (āgneya) and proceeding in four rotations;

thus the first yantra is established. In this very same yantra, if one writes the thirty-two syllables beginning with the thirty-third letter and ending with the sixty-fourth letter in place of the word *ravi* (sun), [it becomes the second yantra].

If, in the place where the thirty-two syllables were previously stated to be written, [the syllable] *vidīyate* appears, then it is the second [type]. In this very same yantra, if in the place of *ravāvi* there is *bhaume*, then the thirty-two syllables beginning with the sixty-fifth and ending with the ninety-sixth are in the place of the aforementioned syllables;
then it is the third. In this very same yantra, in the word *ravāvi*, [if there is] *vudhe*...
In the previously mentioned thirty-two syllable positions, one writes the one hundred twenty-eighth syllable starting from ninety-seven;

this is the fourth [arrangement] when writing those thirty-two syllables. In this very same yantra, where "ravau" (in the sun) was stated, one substitutes "gurau" (in Jupiter); in the previously mentioned thirty-two syllable positions, one writes the one hundred sixty-first syllable starting from one hundred twenty-nine.
Regarding the writing of those thirty-two syllables, this is the fifth [point].
On page 180a, it says "in the white place within the *yantra* at the location of the sun"; that is, in the aforementioned location for the thirty-two syllables.
The sixth [yantra] is established by writing one hundred and sixty-one, up to one hundred and ninety-two, and from one hundred and thirty-two syllables.

In this very yantra, in the place where "ravau" (in the sun) occurs, [one writes] "saure" (in Saturn); and in the place of the aforementioned thirty-two syllables, by writing the syllables starting from one hundred and ninety-three up to one hundred and twenty-four, the seventh yantra is accomplished. Among these...

Regarding the yantras, it is as if already stated that the worship of the Siddhavidyās should be performed on a yantra composed with the name of the specific day (vāra) upon which the accomplishment is desired; thus, within the span of seven days, the worship is effectively completed in every case.
In this way, the accomplished Yakṣiṇīs [bestow] divine garlands, ointments, fragrant substances, gold, and garments.

They also bestow various ornaments; likewise, they provide food, drink, and edible things for as long as one lives. Even though I made a prayer to the yakṣiṇī—who had appeared in person through the power of my service to her father—saying, "Grant me your constant presence," it was not granted.

One should not think, "Now that success has been attained, what further need is there for worship? Rather, even after that, one should perform worship upon the eternally liberated yantra and recite the mantra one thousand and eight times. Now, regarding the nature of the written syllables:
in this Vidyā, when counting the *kūṭas* (composite syllables), there are seventeen.

By stating that there are fifty-three when counting separately and fourteen when counting the unobstructed vowels (*anāvṛttākṣara*), the Blessed One has indicated that even the two vowels taken independently should be counted separately just like the consonants; however, in such a context, even a single [vowel] joined with a consonant is not to be counted. And thus, in this case:
In sequence: the letters *ha* and *ra*, the letter *pha*, the letter *sa*, the letter *ka*, the letter *ā*, the letter *la*, the letter *ai*, and both the letters *va* and *e*. (p. 180b)

Although they are of a single form due to the conjunction with the sixteen vowels, there is a scriptural injunction that in the third and fourth yantras—those not composed of the names Maṅgala and Budha—one should write the sixteen vowels upon the sixteen petals;
this is the method for attaining the Yakṣiṇī. Now, the method for attaining the Vetāla.
Since there are sixty-four female attendants (*ceṭakā*), their vidyās are likewise exactly that many. For instance:
*hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave vibhramaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* consists of fifteen syllables.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave vāhakaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* also consists of fifteen syllables.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadravā, give me a hero! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this consists of fourteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadravā, give me a mutilated one! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this consists of fifteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadravā, give me a bud! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this consists of fifteen syllables.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, grant me the *ekavinda*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the fourteen-syllable mantra.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrava*, grant me the *siṃhanāda*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the sixteen-syllable mantra.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrava*, grant me the *mahānāda*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this also is the sixteen-syllable mantra.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, grant me Sugrīva! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is a fifteen-syllable mantra.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, grant me Markaṭa! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—this also is a fifteen-syllable mantra.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, grant me Śaṭha! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, grant me Kumāra!
*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, give me that which is impermanent and moves in the sky; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this consists of fifteen syllables.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, give me that which has arisen from the impermanent flow; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this consists of fourteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, give me the peacock of the impermanent flow; *hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Hrīṃ preṃ*, [give me] the impermanent goddess of the flow.
Grant auspiciousness!
Hrīṃ phreṃ is the fifteen-syllable mantra; hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave dvīpivaktraṃ dei.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, "O Madanityadrava, grant me a beautiful face. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—each [of these] consists of sixteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave mātaṅga dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—this consists of fifteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave niśācāraṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave viṣayāhaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* is the sixteen-syllable mantra. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave paśuvaktraṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Hrīṃ preṃ madanityadrave viṣayāhaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* is the sixteen-syllable mantra.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, *madanityadrave*, give me the face of a dog! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave*, give me the face of a deer! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*. And these are the sixteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave*, give me the agitator! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*; this consists of fifteen syllables.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave māṇibhadraṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the sixteen-syllable mantra. *Hrīṃ kreṃ madanityadrave krīḍakaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the fifteen-syllable mantra. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave siṃhavaktrakaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the seventeen-syllable mantra.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, grant me a face! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the fifteen-syllable mantra. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, grant me a face like that of a crow! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the seventeen-syllable mantra. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, grant me a face like that of a crow! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the fifteen-syllable mantra.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, give me Hayavaktra! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—this is the seventeen-syllable mantra. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, give me Mahodara! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, give me Mahāśiras! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, O Madanityadrava, give me Vikṛtāsya! *Hrīṃ phreṃ*.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave varānanam dehi*—*hrīṃ phreṃ* consists of sixteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave capalam dehi*—*hrīṃ phreṃ* consists of fifteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave kukkuṭāsyam dehi*—*hrīṃ phreṃ* consists of sixteen syllables.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave māyāvidehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* is the fifteen-syllable [mantra].
*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave madanālasaṃ dehi*.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ*: this is the seventeen-syllable mantra. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave manoharaṃ dehi* (O Madanityadrava, grant me what is charming). *Hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave dīrghajaṅghaṃ dehi* (O Madanityadrava, grant me long shanks). *Hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave sthūladannaṃ dehi* (O Madanityadrava, grant me thick teeth). *Hrīṃ phreṃ*.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrava daśānanaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—each of these consists of sixteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrava sumukhaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrava paṇḍitaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*—this consists of fifteen syllables.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave kruddhaṃ dehi*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—this consists of fourteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave varāhāsyaṃ dehi hrīṃ phreṃ*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave saṭāmukhaṃ dehi*; *hrīṃ phreṃ*—and this consists of sixteen syllables.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ*, give me the garment of eternal flow, *hrīṃ phreṃ*. *Rīṃ phreṃ*, give me the curiosity of eternal flow, *hrīṃ phreṃ*; this consists of fifteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, give me the time of eternal flow, *hrīṃ phreṃ*;
this consists of fourteen syllables. *Hrīṃ phreṃ*, give me the servant of eternal flow, *hrīṃ phreṃ*.

The fifteen-syllable [mantra] is: *hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave khalaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* is fourteen syllables. [The mantra] is: *hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave bhakṣakaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* [is fourteen syllables]. [The mantra] is: *hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave bhayadaṃ dehi*. And *hrīṃ phreṃ* is fifteen syllables.

*Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave siddhaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* is the fourteen-syllable mantra. *Hrīṃ phreṃ madanityadrave sarvagaṃ dehi*. *Hrīṃ phreṃ* is the fifteen-syllable mantra, which is the final *dheṭaka* (vessel) *siddhi-mantra*. Of these...

Having stayed in each of the twelve locations mentioned in the introduction to the *Yakṣiṇī*— beginning with the forest at the foot of a banyan tree and ending with the bank of a river— from among the five sets of five servant-mantras,
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times according to its color.
The remaining final group of four vidyās should also be accomplished at Sindhutīravana alone.

Furthermore, the fire-oblation (homa) and worship should be performed with the previously mentioned red karavīra flowers and other materials, according to a tenth part of that [number], as described before.

Having fashioned a nine-petaled lotus in the place of the *yantra* consisting of the nine sources (*navayoni*), one should perform all the practices for the attainment of the *siddhi-vidyā*; one must observe silence during the day and not engage in conversation with anyone. The fire-oblation (*homa*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be performed only at midnight, while the recitation (*japa*) should be performed both by day and by night—this is the method for attaining all accomplishments.

This is common to all the means of accomplishing the *vidyās*. At the time of accomplishing their own *vidyā*, the *ceṭakas* manifest in their own nature as extremely terrifying bodies; at midnight, they [assail] the practitioner in various ways, such as by the dancing and singing of young women, the casting of sidelong glances, the displaying of breasts, hips, and so forth, the rising of rivers to their highest levels, and the falling of thunderbolts and other weapons.

Great rain; the sight of one's father, mother, son, and others being severed; the humiliation of one's wife and others by being stripped naked—by such means they adorn [the rite]. However, when the practitioner remains unperturbed, [the deity] appears before him in person and becomes his servant, saying, "What desired goal shall I accomplish for you? In this way, whatever vidyā has been accomplished, he alone shall know it all.

Nor is it the case that one who has not accomplished the vidyā [is not entitled], for there is no rule that everyone must perform the sādhana; nor is there a rule that when everyone else has accomplished it, one alone becomes accomplished. Furthermore, the practitioner, having said "this must be done as I desire," might even say "release me. [This may be done] through various means by way of Brahmins and others.

If [the deity] is pleased with various servants (*ceṭaka*), one should pray using the plural form: "Perform what is desired by me; do not abandon me! Even after this response, worship and so forth must be performed daily. When the servant has been thus propitiated, even a single one will approach the practitioner immediately upon being summoned and accomplish every desired goal.

One may effect the striking down of enemies, the attraction of desired young women, and the immobilization of intoxicated elephants, tigers, horses, and so forth; as well as [the acquisition of] food, drink, things to be licked, things to be sucked, and the like, along with garlands, ornaments, and such.
Having brought [it] from afar, he gives it; thus is the *ceṭhaka* accomplishment. Now, the *māyā* accomplishment:

"Hrīṃ Phreṃ, O Madanityā, grant me the power of Māyā! "Hrīṃ Phreṃ"—this is the sole mantra for the attainment of Māyā. Here too, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of one hundred thousand syllables; the fire-oblation (*homa*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be one-tenth of that amount. Worship should be performed upon that very same yantra. One should observe silence during the day, while the oblations and libations are performed at night. One may also recite either by day or by night; in such a manner [the practice is completed].

The ten *siddhividya*s have been described as bestowing the power to perform various kinds of magical illusions (*māyā*). Thus concludes the section on the Nityā Nīlapatākā. Now, the Nityā Vijayā is introduced.
On a level and smooth ground measuring one cubit,

having constructed two square enclosures (*bhūpura*) each with four doors provided with two-fold side-branches and with intervals of one finger-breadth between them, and having made two circles within that area with an interval of four finger-breadths, on that path—

Having fashioned an eight-spoked wheel by means of two square enclosures (bhūpura) intersecting at the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should then leave a space of one *aṅgula* inside that as well and draw two circles with an interval of four *aṅgulas*. Upon that path, one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus; and within its pericarp—

Having clearly extracted the *vijayānityā* worship-circle of the *nityā*s by means of vermilion (*darada*) and other substances, one should place the *bindu*. Therein, one should perform the installation of the jar (*kalaśa*), the visualization of the *sarvamaṅgalānityā* worship-circle along with its enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), the worship thereof, and so forth;
then, at the conclusion of the rite of dismissal (*udvāsana*), [one should again take] that jar.

Having first performed the meditation on the wheel of the present Nityā, one should perform the worship of that present Nityā as a constituent part of the initiation (*dīkṣā*). As for the specific details to be performed following the worship, they have already been explained in the general introduction.

However, the worship that is not an ancillary to initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth is performed solely upon the *cakra* itself; that too is of two kinds: first, the installation of one engraved on gold, silver, copper, or other materials according to the ritual for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the Śrīcakra, and its application in the daily and other forms of worship; second, the application of one drawn upon the ground. In all these cases— [The rest of the text follows: ...the procedure for worship is as previously described. Thus, having understood the various types of *cakras*, one should perform the worship of the Goddess with devotion. The manner of worship is as follows: Having performed the morning rites, including anointing with fragrant oil and bathing in scented water, and having completed the acts of purification and so forth incidental to the worship of other deities,

the practitioner— adorned with a red washed upper garment, sandalwood paste, garlands, and the like— having arrived at the sacrificial pavilion, [should sit] upon a seat consecrated by the *āsana-vidyā*.
Having sat down upon a seat such as a red woolen blanket, employing a posture like the *svastika*,
and having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the present mantra; having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with the sixteen-syllable mantra,
and having worshipped the nine Nāthas upon one's own head according to the lineage of one's own Master, one should recite their hymn of praise.

Having honored that command for worship, one should begin it. Having meditated upon one's own master as consisting of the present daily rite (*nityā*) and oneself as consisting of the master, [one should worship] all the deities of the thirty-eight sacred seats (*pīṭha*), ending with the circle of the secret and manifest *Siddhayoginīs*, which are regulated by the specific place, time, and other factors determined for each respective year.

Having performed worship upon the lion-throne and other elements of the currently presented *cakra*-support, one should place the common *arghya* vessel— made of gold or another suitable material, provided with its support (*ādhāra*), filled with water mixed with the five substances such as *gorocanā*, and situated in the space between one’s own self and the *cakra*. Then, [one should pour] the waters from that support in sequence...
Having first uttered the seed-syllable of Kulasundarī and contemplated [the three centers] as consisting of fire, sun, and moon,
one should contemplate the yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and other substances therein as composed of the five elements, and then visualize the unification of that water with the present wheel.
Having meditated upon the water as non-different from the deity under worship, one should consecrate it ten times with the relevant vidyā and perform worship; then,
having worshipped the deities of the six limbs with the mantras of the six limbs, one should [sprinkle] oneself with the consecrated arghya-water,
and likewise the water of the fourfold set beginning with pādya— which was placed in vessels situated progressively to the north— from the general arghya-vessel.
Having consecrated with the present vidyā each of the substances for worship, oblation, and so forth, which have been placed on one's own right side;

and having again performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the vidyā; taking the water of the general arghya with the hand along with the wooden ladle (darvī), together with rice grains, flowers, and other items; [one should state] the specific place and time, consisting of the month, fortnight, lunar day, and so on.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), saying: "Having inscribed [the names] ending with the day, the lunar mansion, the zodiac sign, and my own name, I shall perform the worship of Vijayānityā according to my understanding and as prescribed," one should pour out the water held in the hand. Then, even if the rites such as the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) have not been performed due to circumstances, at this juncture, the respective mantras should be applied to their proper places.

Having performed this rite by means of the very vidyā under discussion: at the end of the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) of the Mātṛkā, one should place the vidyā under discussion at the beginning of each [letter], and then assign the respective letters of the Mātṛkā to their own respective locations.
[The mantras are: *Bhauṃ* *hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *Mūṃ* *śirase svāhā*, *Rauṃ* *śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *Pūṃ* *kavacāya huṃ*.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*)—namely, *Bhauṃ* for the eyes with *vauṣaṭ*, and *Bhūṃ* for the weapon (*astra*) with *phaṭ*—upon the thumbs and other fingers as well as the heart and other limbs; and having placed *Bhaṃ* on the two ears, *Maṃ* on the skin, *Yaṃ* on the two eyes, *Nyaṃ* on the tongue, *Auṃ* on the nose, and *Ūṃ* on the mind; [one should recite] *Bhaṃ Ma Ra Ya Au Ūṃ*.
