Having performed the threefold pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the *nityākūṭa* mantra consisting of the complete single syllable, one should proceed with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and subsequent rites. It is as follows:

By following the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā*, one visualizes within the handful of red flowers held therein the confluence of the splendors of fire, sun, and moon, extending from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*; this greatly intensified light then enters through the path of the nostrils and comes to rest there.

Visualizing that [deity] having been transferred into the *bindu* within the mandala currently under discussion by the casting of a handful of those flowers, one should perform the invocation after making this prayer:

"O Vijayānityā, may you be invoked into this mandala at the conclusion of the complete mantra. Then, from some of the rays of that radiance, [one should project her] into the locations to be described hereafter.

Having visualized [the deities] as having emerged from the Lord’s weapons and armor, one should contemplate the mass of light situated in their midst, whose true nature has been understood through meditation. And that meditation is as follows:
[one should meditate on the Goddess] who has five faces, ten arms, and three eyes in each face.

Adorned with a crescent moon set upon her radiant crown, endowed with all ornaments, and resplendent in yellow garments; possessing the bodily luster of the rising solar disc and a pure smile; [holding] in her left arms a conch, a noose, a shield, a bow, and a white lotus; and likewise a discus, a goad, and a sword.
Holding arrows and a mātuluṅga fruit in her right hands, she possesses a terrifying form during the ritual application (*prayoga*).

For the propitiation (*upāsana*), she is gentle, seated upon a lion; she is surrounded on all sides by countless spear-wielding goddesses mounted on tigers. In battles and other ritual applications, she is easy to approach; and the spears (*śaktis*) are also to be worshipped in the rite of worship.
All the goddesses are seated upon comfortable thrones, and they all possess identical forms, faces, hands, and weapons.
Even for the lords (nātha), their weapons, their retinues, and the śaktis, there is indeed identity of form with the principal goddess under discussion;
however, regarding the weapons, they additionally possess crowns marked by their respective individual forms.
And you, O Anityā, who are victorious over the ends of the present vidyā, remain stationed here in this wheel. Again, at the end of thirteen syllables, become firmly restrained.
Again, at the end of that many syllables, become veiled. Again, at the end of that many syllables...

Having requested the fourfold ritual beginning with *svāpana* (the act of inducing sleep) preceded by the display of the respective mudrās, saying "Be present," and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra for the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) upon the hands and limbs, one should install the vital breaths by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā*, reciting: "The vital breaths of this eternal Vijayā are here in this wheel; the vital breaths... and so forth.

One should worship with the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*). Their mantras are as follows: at the end of the complete *vidyā*, having offered the water for the feet (*pādya*) using the general *arghya* water with the mantra, "I offer the *pādya* to Vijayānityā," one should present it at her two feet using the current *vidyā*. In the same manner, [one should proceed] by substituting the word "feet" (*pāda*) for the following items.

Having offered each of the services beginning with *arghya* and ending with *tāmbūla*, accompanied by the respective mantras for their presentation, one should offer those [services] to the head and other parts of the body using the primary *vidyā*. Thereafter, one should follow the thirteen services (*upacāra*). The procedure for this is as follows: having arranged three rows behind the Goddess, [one should place] the one situated near the Goddess along with half [of the offerings].
Having worshipped the Divine Lords (divyanātha) named Īśāna, Prakāśa, Vimarśa, and Ānanda in the first row;
then the Siddha Lords (siddhanātha) named Śrījñāna, Śrīsatya, and Śrīpūrṇa in the row above that;
and then the Mānava Lords (mānavanātha) named Svabhāva, Pratibha, and Subhaga in the row above that; [one should worship] at the eastern door of the square.
Beginning from the southern path and extending to the northern path of that very door, in the regions near the outer lines, [I worship]:
Hrīṃ, I worship the sandal of Indra’s Śakti; Hrīṃ, [I worship] Agni’s Śakti-sandal; Hrīṃ, [I worship] Yama’s Śakti-sandal.

Having worshipped the eight Śaktis with these mantras: "Hrīṃ, I worship the Śaktipāda of Rakṣas; Hrīṃ, I worship the Śaktipāda of Varuṇa; Hrīṃ, I worship the Śaktipāda of Anila; Hrīṃ, I worship the Śaktipāda of Soma; Hrīṃ, I worship the Śaktipādukā of Īśāna," [one proceeds] from the southern path of the western door to the southern door.

In the western row, at the end of the eight rows, in the regions near the inner lines: "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Brāhmī; Hrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Māheśvarī; Hrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Kaumārī; Hrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Vaiṣṇavī; Hrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Vārāhī; Hrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Aindrī; Hrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Cāmuṇḍā; Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Mahālakṣmī."

Having worshipped the eight Śaktis, beginning with Brāhmī, by means of their respective mantras, one should worship the twenty Śaktis collectively as follows: in the northwest corner, *hrīṃ anantaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*;

in the northeast corner, *hrīṃ brahmaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; in the southeast, *hrīṃ niyatiśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; and in the southwest, *hrīṃ kālaśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. Thus, having worshipped all twenty Śaktis.

At the conclusion of the complete *vidyā*, having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with the mantra "I worship the *pādukā* of Vijayānityā," and having offered the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering of worship with the mantra "Hrīṃ! May these deities of the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*) of Vijayānityā accept this worship," [one worships] in the eight corners, starting from the corner in front of the goddess and proceeding clockwise: "Hrīṃ! The *pādukā* of Jayā..."

"I worship. Having thus worshipped those respective Śaktis with: "Hrīṃ, I worship Vijayā-pādukā; Hrīṃ, I worship Durgā-pādukā; Hrīṃ, I worship Bhadrā-pādukā; Hrīṃ, I worship Bhadrakarī-pādukā; Hrīṃ, I worship Kṣemā-pādukā; Hrīṃ, I worship Kṣemakarī-pādukā; Hrīṃ, I worship Nityā-pādukā," at the end of the complete mantra, [one says]: "I worship Vijayā-nityā-pādukā."

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering for that worship, saying: "O Hrīṃ, these deities of the second enclosure of the Nityā Vijayā, may you accept this worship. Then, in the sixteen-petaled lotus, starting from the petal in front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise: "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals (*pādukā*) of Vidārikā."
Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Viśvamayī-pā, Hrīṃ Viśvā-pā, Hrīṃ Viśvavibhañjinī-pā, Hrīṃ Vīrā-pā, Hrīṃ Vikṣobhiṇī-pā, Hrīṃ Vidyā-pā, Hrīṃ Vinodā-pā, and Hrīṃ Vittavigrahā-pādukā.

Having worshipped the sixteen Śaktis named Vikārā and the others with these mantras: "Hrīṃ, I worship Vītaśokāpā; Hrīṃ, I worship Viṣayīvāpā; Hrīṃ, I worship Vipulāpā; Hrīṃ, I worship Vijayapradāpā; Hrīṃ, I worship Vividhāpā; Hrīṃ, I worship Vibhavāpā; Hrīṃ, I worship Viprāpādukā."

At the conclusion of the complete vidyā, having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with the mantra "I worship the pādukā of Vijayānityā," and having offered a handful of flowers as an oblation for that worship with the mantra "Hrīṃ! May these deities of the third enclosure accept this worship," [one proceeds] clockwise, beginning from the eastern petal of the eight-petaled lotus: "Hrīṃ! I worship the pādukā of Manoharā."

Having worshipped the eight Śaktis whose names begin with the letter *ma*, using the mantras: "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Maṅgalā," "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Madotsiktā," "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Manasvinī," "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Māninī," "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Madhurā," "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Māyā," and "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Mohinī."
On the pericarp itself, having prepared ten locations starting from the area near the left lower hand and ending at the area near the right lower hand, [one should offer] *hrīṃ kahlārāya namaḥ*,
*hrīṃ cāpāya*, *hrīṃ kheṭāya*, *hrīṃ pāśāya*, *hrīṃ śaṅkhāya*, *hrīṃ cakrāya*, *hrīṃ aṅkuśāya*.

Having worshipped the weapons with "Hrīṃ! To the sword," "Hrīṃ! To the arrow," and "Hrīṃ! Salutation to the mātuluṅga fruit," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the conclusion of the complete vidyā with "I worship the pādukā of Vijayānityā," one performs the offering of that worship with: "Hrīṃ!
May these deities of the fourth enclosure of Vijayānityā accept this worship."

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and having performed the thirteen-fold ritual service (*upacāra*), the remaining three services— which consist of whatever [recitation of] hymns (*stotra-pāṭha*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), and prostrations (*namaskāra*)— should also be performed according to the prescribed rule.

Having performed [the ritual], having completed— according to the previously mentioned method— the daily recitation (nityajapa) in a number of one thousand twenty-one, one hundred and twenty-one, or one hundred, enclosed by the *aṅguṣṭhādi-nyāsa*, *hṛdayādi-nyāsa*, *varṇanyāsa*, and *vyāpakanyāsa*,
and having performed the offering (*nivedana*) consisting of the contemplation of non-difference from that [deity]; [one should offer] with rice and clarified butter according to the prescribed rule.

Having performed the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) sixteen times with sesame seeds or rice, and having offered oblations in a number equal to one-tenth of that daily oblation, one should again unite the deity under discussion with the Fire from within the *bindu* of the wheel of the worship of the elements at the Goddess’s abode. Having worshipped the Goddess who has arrived at the *bindu* once more with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), [one should perform the rite] with the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā.

Having offered the oblation (*bali*), performed the *nīrājana* with wicks containing camphor and other substances, and asked for forgiveness, one should contemplate that the masses of rays— which have emanated here and there in the form of the powers (*śakti*) of the Lord’s weapons and retinue— have been absorbed into the mass of light situated in the center, which has become the principal deity currently being worshipped, by means of the *śaktyutthāpana-mudrā*.

Having dissolved even that mass of light into one's own self by means of the *khecarīmudrā*, and having performed, as before, the *aṅguṣṭhādi-nyāsa*, the *hṛdayādi-nyāsa*, the *varṇa-nyāsa*, and the *vyāpaka-nyāsa*, one should conclude by reciting the hymn to the Guru and the Goddess. As for the specific details regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), they are exactly as stated in the general introduction. Thus...

The practitioner (*sādhaka*), having received initiation and mastered the methods for daily and occasional worship and so forth, should perform the practice for attaining the *vidyā* when there is a desire to accomplish a specific means for himself or others through ritual application (*prayoga*). The procedure for this is exactly as described in the section concerning Vajreśvarī. As for the recitation (*japa*) here, it consists of five hundred thousand repetitions as prescribed for the Satya Yuga.

By following the fourfold procedure (*cāturguṇyānusaraṇena*), there is a fire offering (*homa*) with twenty lakhs of red lotuses at one-tenth the number of recitations; such is the specific distinction. Thus:

Having accomplished the vidyā, one who has received the permission of the guru should perform the ritual applications out of compassion for the worlds, and not out of greed, delusion, or other such motives.

Now, these are the daily applications (*nityāprayoga*). Having performed the worship of the respective lords of the days within the circle of the planets (*grahamaṇḍala*), on the days of the sun and the other [planets] in sequence,
one should [offer] red lotuses, red *kairavas*, white *kairavas*, *saugandhika* lilies, blue lotuses, fragrant flowers, jasmine (*jāti*), *mālatī*, and so forth.

Having offered oblations by the hundreds or thousands with any of the flowers known as *puṣpa* or *śephālikā* smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), [one should perform] the two types of gambling and combat: that which is conducted by staking one's own body and that which is conducted by staking mere wealth; and furthermore, in horse-riding combat, dueling, wrestling, or scholarly debate.

In disputes concerning debts, land, and so forth, one shall obtain victory in every case. Through *homa* with *āragvadha* flowers, there shall be the immobilization (*stambhana*) of an enemy’s arrival and other such matters. On Sunday, through *homa* with *karṇikāra* flowers; on Monday, with *punnāga* flowers; on Tuesday, with *nameru* flowers; on Wednesday, with *campaka* flowers; and on Thursday, with *ketaka* flowers.

By means of an oblation (*homa*) performed in the respective planetary mandala on the day of each specific planet, preceded by the worship of the presiding deity of that day— using *rājavṛkṣa* flowers for Venus and *śanī-mādhava* flowers for Saturn—
the destruction of enemies occurs. Even in the absence of scriptural contradiction, through the assistance of a powerful mantra, [the planets] act against one another.

In the context of battle, the enemy's defeat will certainly occur. By performing a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with a number of one thousand or more oblations of mustard seeds soaked in oil, using fuel-sticks of the wood of the very tree associated with the enemy’s birth-star ignited in a fire, the enemies will become submissive and fall at one's feet; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding the performance of the enjoined rite (p.

when the fire has been kindled by means of wood that produces the sounds *kāra* and *rakāra*, one should perform any one of the oblations using the leaves, flowers, fruits, or sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) of the *kāraskara* tree.

By first performing the worship of the presiding deity of that door, victory will certainly be achieved over the enemy, disease, fire, or death. On a Sunday, having kindled a fire with wood from the *arka* tree, one should offer all five limbs of the *arka* tree—
namely, leaf, flower, fruit, branch, and root— either collectively or individually.

If the practitioner, facing the house of the enemy, performs a fire sacrifice according to the prescribed ritual in a triangular hearth for eight days on Sundays, using red cow’s ghee smeared with the blood of a red calf and a red bull,
then— even one who is enriched by a fourfold army consisting of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry— [shall be overcome].

Even if an enemy is endowed with solar and lunar power, he may flee, or be afflicted by disease; being stricken by fear, he shall not fall before the two [feet], but shall bow down with the eight limbs of the body, and never otherwise. On a Monday, one should offer leaves of the *palāśa* tree into a fire kindled with *palāśa* wood.
By performing a fire sacrifice (homa) every Monday, using fuel-sticks made of flowers, fruits, and branches, extending as far as the mandala,
preceded by the offering of red cow-ghee soaked with the blood of a red calf, the aforementioned result of the form of freedom from old age is attained.
[One should also perform it] with the five products of the *khadira* tree in a fire kindled with *khadira* wood.

By offering oblations on every Tuesday until the completion of the maṇḍala, using red *vatsaka* and red cow’s ghee soaked [in the liquid], the aforementioned fruit is attained. Furthermore, by offering oblations on every Wednesday until the completion of the maṇḍala, using *apāmārga* fuel-sticks ignited in a fire lit with *apāmārga* wood and smeared with white *vatsaka* and white cow’s ghee.
The aforementioned fruit is obtained even by offering oblations in a triangular sacrificial pit (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*).

When fire is kindled with fuel-sticks of *pippala* wood, the aforementioned fruit is obtained even by offering oblations in a triangular sacrificial pit every Thursday until the completion of the mandala, using the five limbs of the *pippala* tree soaked in white ghee.

By performing oblations every Friday until the completion of the mandala in a triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), using five parts of an *audumbara* tree along with the fat of a white cow and a white calf, soaked in clarified butter over a fire kindled with *udumbara* wood, one obtains the aforementioned fruit.

By performing oblations every Saturday until the completion of the mandala— facing the direction of the person for whom the rite is intended— in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) where fire is kindled with *śamī* wood and offerings are made using the five parts (*pañcāṅga*) of the *śamī* tree soaked in the ghee of a black cow—
the aforementioned fruit of victory is attained. This applies everywhere in this context.

Just as the worship of the respective lords of the days (dhāreśas) is necessary, so too is the worship of the respective lords of the lunar days (tithīśas) essential there; for without the worship of those respective lords of the days and lunar days, even if performed, all rites such as recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), the application of yantras, effigies (puttalī), and other practices would be entirely fruitless. Thus end the applications of Vāravijaya. On the first lunar day (pratipad), [one should perform the rite] with śāli rice grains; on the second, with chickpeas (caṇakas).

On the third day, [one should offer] mung beans; on the fourth, barley; on the fifth, black gram soaked in buffalo ghee. By performing the oblation in a triangular sacrificial pit while facing the house of the enemy, the practitioner shall obtain the aforementioned fruit of victory. Alternatively, on the sixth day, [one should offer] husked rice; on the seventh—

On the eighth day, [one should offer] dehusked chickpeas; on the ninth, dehusked mung beans; and on the tenth, dehusked barley. On the eleventh day, by performing oblations in a triangular sacrificial pit (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*) while facing the abode of the deity to be propitiated, using dehusked black gram soaked in goat’s ghee, the aforementioned fruit in the form of victory is accomplished.

Likewise, on the eleventh day [one should offer] a mixture of śāli rice, chickpeas, mung beans, barley, and black gram; on the twelfth day, white sesame seeds; on the thirteenth day, black sesame seeds; on the fourteenth day, cooked rice made from white rice grains; and on the fifteenth day, milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in goat-ghee.

By performing the oblation in a triangular *kuṇḍa* while facing the house of the one to be conquered (*sādhya*), even from what has been prescribed, the aforementioned fruit of victory is attained. Thus end the ritual applications for victory on the lunar days (*tithi-vijaya-prayogāḥ*).

In a triangular sacrificial pit (*tri-koṇa-kuṇḍa*), one should offer oblations into a fire kindled with wood from the trees corresponding to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) beginning with Aśvinī, using the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) of those respective trees soaked in honey.

By performing oblations while facing the direction of the location to be conquered, even from the mandala onwards, the aforementioned fruit of victory is attained. Thus end the applications for victory by means of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). Now follow the applications for the *Nityā* yantra.
In this context, there are five unchanging syllables (*anāvṛttākṣara*);

through their respective conjunction with the sixteen vowels, eighty modified mantra-syllables (*mantravikṛtākṣara*) are produced, which are to be accomplished by drawing them into the diagrams (*yantra*) to be described hereafter. For instance, [the lines] extending from east to west...

Having drawn ten lines each extending from south to north and intersecting one another at equal intervals, one should produce eighty-one squares. Therein, in the very center square— specifically in the upper portion of the fifth form from all the surrounding paths— one should place the name of the practitioner in the nominative case (ṣaṣṭhyanta), with the word "madhya" (middle) in between, and below it.
Having written the name of the objective to be accomplished— such as "the victory over such-and-such an enemy"— in the accusative case,

one should write the eighty *vikṛtākṣara* syllables either starting from the central square of the bottom row and proceeding clockwise, or starting from the central square of the row immediately above and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction.

One should also fashion tridents upon each of the forty lines at their extremities. Having thus prepared the yantra, one should perform worship with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), preceded by the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, and then perform the recitation (*japa*). For the practitioner who acts in this manner, the desired goal in the form of victory is accomplished. [Now follows] another yantra:
For example: having produced a wheel of squares by drawing four lines each of equal measure, extending east-west and north-south, intersecting one another.
Therein, having fashioned eight-petalled lotuses with pericarp in each of the nine squares, one should construct outside of that three quadrangles measuring two cubits each, devoid of door-frames.
By virtue of the width of these quadrangles, the wheel of nine squares will also become spacious; and because of that spaciousness—

The lotuses shall become fully blossomed. Therein, upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the central lotus, one should write the present vidyā consisting of seven syllables: *bhaṃ ma ra ya au ūm*. In its center, within three rows, one should write the name of the practitioner, the words of the rite, and the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Outside of that, on the petals starting from the tip, [one should write] *bhaṃ bhāṃ bhiṃ*...

Having written the eight distorted syllables *bhiṃ bhuṃ bhūṃ bṛṃ mi* and filled the central lotus [of the yantra] with them, one should write *bhḷṃ*— containing the name of the practitioner and others— in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the lotus at its tip;
then, on its petals and so forth, [one writes] *bhḷṃ bheṃ bhaiṃ bhoṃ bhauṃ bhaṃ bhaḥ*.
Having written "ma" with the nasal bindu (m̐) in the eight syllable positions, and having filled the lotus of the western direction,
one should write "mā" containing the name of the practitioner and so forth within the pericarp of the northwest lotus;
then, by writing the eight syllables mi, mī, mu, mū, mu, mṛ, mṝ, ml, and ml̥ starting from the petal at its tip.
Having filled the lotus in the northwest,

one fills the northern lotus by writing "meṃ" containing the name of the practitioner and others within its pericarp, and then writing the eight syllables "maiṃ moṃ mauṃ maṃ maḥ raṃ ṇam" starting from the petal at its tip; then, in the pericarp of the northeastern lotus...

Having written "rīṃ" containing the name of the practitioner and others within it, one fills the lotus of Īśāna by writing the eight syllables "hlūṃ hlūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ re raiṃ" on its front petals and so forth.
Having written "rom" containing the name of the practitioner and others within the pericarp of the eastern lotus;

and having filled the eastern lotus with the eight syllables "raḥ raṃ riṃ rīṃ ruṃ" at its tips and petals; and having written "yūṃ" containing the name of the practitioner and others within the pericarp of the southeastern lotus.

Having filled the fire-lotus with the eight syllables *pṛ*, *ṛṃ*, *ṝṃ*, *ḷṃ*, *ḹṃ*, *yeṃ*, *yaiṃ*, *yoṃ*, *yaum* starting from its front petal; and having written the syllable *yam*—containing the name of the practitioner and others—within the pericarp of the southern lotus starting from its direction; [and] *yaṃ*, *ḥ*, *aṃ*, *āṃ*, *iṃ*, *īṃ*, *uṃ*, *ūṃ*, *ṛm* starting from its front petal...

Having written the eight vowels and filled the southern lotus, one should write the eighth vowel *ṝ* together with the bindu (*ṝm*)— containing the name of the practitioner and others— in the pericarp of the southwestern lotus; then, having written the remaining eight vowels on the petals starting from the tip of that [pericarp], one fills the southwestern lotus.

Having written the fifty-one letters of the Mātṛkā, from *kṣa* to *ka*, each accompanied by the *visarga*, on the first outer square of the path; and having written the fifty-one letters of the Mātṛkā, from *a* with the *bindu* (*ā*) to *kṣa*, on the second outer path;
Regarding the phrase "outside the square," one should simply inscribe [the mantra] devoid of both the two syllables and the *bindu* and *visarga*.

Once this yantra has been perfected, having placed a water-pot (*kalaśa*) in the pericarp of the central lotus and filled it with the decoction of the medicinal herbs of the present vidyā, [one should place] all the materials such as the nine gems and so forth, as previously described.
Having cast [the object] by means of the present vidyā, having enveloped it with two red cloths,

and having completed the entire cycle of ritual actions according to the previously described method— beginning with the visualization of the Sarvamaṅgalā-cakra and ending with its dismissal— [one should proceed].

Furthermore, having performed the rites there itself— beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, worshipping the present Nityā, and concluding with her dismissal (udvāsana)— one should consecrate that water by reciting the present Vidyā ten thousand times (ayuta), and [purify oneself] through the sprinkling of that water.
When there is a desire to attain all afflictions, a desire for a son, or a desire for happiness, the Aparā-śakti becomes active;

the previously mentioned Sakala-vijaya state arises. In the pacification of the affliction of the nine planets, in the destruction of the aforementioned afflictions caused by one's own enemies, in the success of military endeavors, in the attainment of fame and prosperity, and in the desire for a son or other purposes, [this state prevails].

This procedure for consecration (*abhiṣeka*) should be performed according to one’s own desire during the three auspicious lunar mansions (*tārās*), preceded by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) that is not lacking in wealth. By means of that, the accomplishment of each respective desired object will surely occur. Having drawn this very *yantra* with red ochre (*gairika*) upon a pedestal made of *palāśa* wood or similar materials;

There, having worshipped with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) preceded by the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites, one should recite the present vidyā ten thousand times (ayuta). For the practitioner who performs this for either twenty days or seven days, men, women, and kings become submissive. This very yantra should be written on birch bark with turmeric...
Having written [the mantra] and placed it either inside a water-pot or between two shallow bowls, and having deposited it either in the middle of a wall or at the place of one's bed,

one should worship the present Nityā there with the present Vidyā during all three junctions of the day. Reciting [the mantra] one thousand times at each junction for twenty-one days— or for seven days if the task is to be accomplished— [one attains success].
The intellect, movement, anger, and all other faculties of the practitioner's enemy become completely paralyzed.
Having drawn this very yantra with fragrant substances such as camphor, saffron, and musk upon a seat made of *palāśa* wood or in the aforementioned locations,
[one should worship it] during all three junctions of the day.

For one who recites [the mantra] a thousand times each day, preceded by worship according to the previously mentioned procedure, for a period of twenty-one nights or up to thirty nights, there occurs an increase in great fortune (*lakṣmī*) through such thorough practice. Another *yantra* is as follows:

Having drawn fourteen lines each extending east-west and fourteen lines extending north-south, with equal intervals and intersecting one another, one should produce a wheel consisting of one hundred and fifty-nine (159) squares; then, in the first outer row, in the four directions, [place] the seventh...

Having bypassed the seventh square, and having erased the eleven squares situated in the middle— extending from the square at the end of one direction to the square at the end of the opposite direction— one should [mark] each successive square below the previously remaining square in that inner second row, as well as one square on each of its two sides.
Having set aside three squares in the four directions and cleared the seven central squares;

and in the third row as well, having set aside five squares in total— namely, the three squares situated below the previously set-aside squares in the four directions, plus one square on each side— [one should proceed].
Having erased three by three middle squares, a total of eighty-four squares were erased,
leaving eighty-five squares remaining. Having drawn a triangle in each of the four corner squares and in each of the central squares, one should write the present vidyā in its entirety within them.

Within its belly, one should write the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the words of the ritual action (*kriyāpada*), and the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). In this manner, the fivefold writing of the names of the practitioner and others for the present *Nityā* mantra within this yantra is established. Thereafter, starting from the middle square among the three squares located in the bottommost row and ending at its first square—
Having first written twenty-four modified syllables (*vikṛtākṣara*) in the twenty-four compartments,
[one proceeds] from the compartment directly below the previously commenced syllable-compartment, ending at its first compartment.
Having marked twenty syllables, starting from the twenty-syllable [square] up to the forty-four-syllable limit,
one should again begin from the square immediately below the previously commenced square.
Having written the sixteen syllables from the forty-fifth to the sixty-second in the sixteen squares surrounding that preceding square, one should again proceed,
starting from the square below the square where the previous sequence began, moving around until reaching that same preceding square.
Having written the twelve modified syllables, beginning from the sixty-first letter and ending with the seventy-second letter, within the twelve squares; then again,
starting from the square directly below the square where the previous sequence began, [place them] in the eight surrounding squares.
Having written the eight transformed syllables starting from the seventy-third letter up to the end of the eighty squares,

one should fill in the number of squares and the number of letters. Then, having consecrated that very perfected yantra— prepared with gold, silver, copper, crystal, or other materials— through worship, recitation, and fire-offerings, [one should place it] where there is emptiness.

Whether in a country or a house, where this is established, there shall be steady and daily increase in prosperity; and there shall be no affliction from spirits, ghosts, piśācas, yakṣas, kṛtyās, and the like. By inscribing it on a palāśa board and installing it according to the prescribed rite in a vacant place or similar location, that site becomes a dwelling place for Brāhmaṇas.

It may be so. This yantra, written on a slab of rājavṛkṣa wood and consecrated by means of worship, recitation, burnt offerings, and other rites, should be buried in a place devoid of any other yantra; there a royal capital shall arise.
If one writes that [mantra] on a board made from a banyan tree and, having consecrated it as before, buries it in the ground,

then a city shall arise in that empty place. If one writes that [mantra] on a board made from an udumbara tree and, having consecrated it as before, buries it in the ground, then that place will become a source of food.

It would serve as the support for many kinds [of rites]. Having fashioned tridents within the triangular spaces at the four corners of this vajra-yantra, and having written *ram*, *yam*, and *cam* in the two central positions thereof, one should place upon it the patient,
whose forehead has already been adorned with ashes consecrated a thousand times as previously described.

Having established [the deity], one should again empower the ashes applied to the forehead one thousand times with the aforementioned vidyā. By that means, that very [demon] who has departed in the form of fever, dysentery, and so forth, will himself go away of his own accord, returning to his own abode; this applies even to *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and the like.
People go far away from the path of the means for attaining their own respective goals due to their own lack of understanding.

Furthermore, by drawing this aforementioned diagram with its spikes upon a board made of *rājavṛkṣa* wood and placing it in some secluded spot within the royal palace, the king’s entire lineage will also [be protected] as he worships the present *Nityā* there.

How much less so for its sons and others? Having divided the dwelling place of elephants and horses into nine parts, one should carve this yantra—made of copper or other materials—into nine sections upon a leaf. One should bury it in the center and in the eight directions, and every day worship the deity of the yantra above it, who is the present *nityā*. By that means, that region...
Enemies, sorcery, and other such things, as well as diseases, will not even be able to look upon [the practitioner], let alone enter.

Having written this yantra on a new cloth with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, one should worship it after performing the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and other preliminary rites.
Having consecrated [the medicine] with the aforementioned vidyā one hundred or one thousand times, if one lies down in milk,
then even others will be cured of burning fever and other diseases. This yantra should be drawn with cinnabar on a drum, a kettledrum, or similar musical instruments.

Having written [the mantra], one should there worship the present Nityā with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), preceded by the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the ritual installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Simultaneously, one should cause the sounding of musical instruments and the display of the enemy army; terrified by that sound, the adversary flees in all ten directions and does not remain.

Should he ever come face-to-face with him, having staked one's very self in a game of dice or battle that has commenced, one should write this yantra in vermilion on birch bark, consecrate it through the rites of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, worship, and recitation (*japa*), roll it into a pill, and wear it around the neck;
then one should engage in such a battle. One who wears such a yantra—

Merely by the sight of the practitioner, such gamblers would flee; what need is there to mention victory? Even in a gambling battle where one's life is the stake, victory is certain from this yantra held at the throat.
By meditating on this yantra or this deity-vidyā as having a red form upon the face of the enemy, the enemies are surely brought under control.

What need is there for much? In brief, there is no task whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by this Vajra-mechanism. Thus concludes the introduction to Vijayānityā. Now, the introduction to Sarvamaṅgalānityā is set forth.

Having constructed two square enclosures (*bhūpura*) one within the other, each measuring one cubit (*hasta*) in dimension, with a gap of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) between them, provided with door-panels on the four sides;
and having drawn a single circle that touches and does not touch the inner enclosure.
Having drawn another three circles with a five-finger space between them at their ends,
and having fashioned three paths (vīthī) by means of these four circles together with the previous circle, [one should place] there, in the outermost path—
Then, having fashioned a thirty-two-petaled lotus, and within that path a sixteen-petaled one,

and further within that path an eight-petaled lotus, one should fashion a *bindu* in its inner pericarp. Having established the ritual procedure for the daily worship mandala (*nityapūjācakra*) according to the previously described method, one should install the water-jar (*kalaśa*).

One should contemplate the vessel situated below the wheel—even though it is already depicted there—as being occupied by the vessel that serves as the primary place of worship for Vindu; then, one should worship Sarvamaṅgalā therein. This applies to the worship that is an ancillary to initiation from all [deities], whereas in the worship that is an ancillary to that [specific] rite, [she is worshipped] alone.
The ritual circle (cakra) itself must be raised, and the placement of the vase (kalaśa) [is performed] there. In both cases, the method of worship is as follows:

the morning rites and so forth, including anointing with fragrant oil and bathing in fragrant water; and furthermore, the purification of the ground and other preliminary rites already performed in connection with other deities.
The practitioner, having donned a red-washed upper garment and being adorned with garlands, perfumes, and ointments, enters the sacrificial pavilion.

Having purified the site according to the *kūrma-cakra*, he sits upon a seat such as a red woolen blanket that has been worshipped with the fourfold seat-mantras (*āsana-vidyā*), assuming either a *svastika* or *padma* posture while reciting the present mantra.
Having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the present vidyā, and having offered the bali-oblation with the sixteen-syllable mantra;

having worshipped the nine Āpināthas on one's own head, beginning with one's own Nātha, using their respective mantras; and having recited their hymn and prayed for their permission, one should perform the worship of one's own vidyā, one's own nityā, and one's own nāthas.

Having meditated on the identity of [the deity] with one's own self, [one should contemplate] all the secret and manifest *siddhayoginīs*, distinguished by their respective years, locations, times, and so forth, upon the lion-thrones and other supports of the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*) which constitute her eternal nature (p. 192b).
Having worshipped the thirty-eight deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha) located at the ends of the wheels, one should perform the self-worship. In the central space between the two wheels,
one should place a common arghya vessel made of gold, silver, copper, glass, or clay, along with its stand, filled with water mixed with yellow orpiment, camphor, saffron, agallochum, and musk.

Then, having meditated upon the water in the vessel that supports it as being composed of fire, sun, and moon by means of the three *kulasundarī* seed-syllables in sequence; and having contemplated the five substances, such as yellow pigment (*rocanā*), as being composed of earth, water, fire, air, and space;
and having first cultivated the realization of the identity between that water and the *pūjācakra*, one should contemplate the identity between that water and the present *nityā*.
Having consecrated and worshipped [the deity] ten times with the present vidyā,

and having fully worshipped the deities of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅgadevatā) with the mantras of the six limbs, one should [purify] oneself and the vessel for the general arghya water with the present vidyā using the consecrated general arghya water.

Having sprinkled once each the water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and the water for sipping and bathing located in their respective vessels situated in the area to one's right, as well as the perfumes and other items, the ghee used for the fire-oblation, the rice-grains, the jar, the wealth, and so forth,
one should again perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the Vidyā-mantra.

Taking the general *arghya* water with the *darvī* ladle using the right hand, and having mentioned the general place and time, followed by the specific place and time, and further mentioning one’s own lineage (*gotra*), zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), name, and desired object (*kāmanā*) according to one’s understanding, one should state according to the ritual: "I shall perform the perpetual worship of Sarvamangalā," ending with the word "water" (*jala*).

One should cast [it] upon the ground. At this very juncture, even for one who has not performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other preliminary rites, one should employ the present Vidyā itself in place of any other mantra assigned to the ritual action (*kṛtya*).

Having completed all those rites, at the conclusion of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should write each respective letter of the *mātṛkā* at the end of each [limb] of the present *vidyā*. Then, having performed the placement of each respective *mātṛkā* in its corresponding locations:
*svāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *svīṃ śirase svāhā*, *svūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras— *khāṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *svauṃ netrāya vaṣaṭ*,
and *svaḥ astrāya phaṭ*— upon one’s own thumbs and other fingers, as well as upon the heart and other limbs; [one should place them] with *svāṃ* on the skin,
*svīṃ* on the two eyes, *svūṃ* on the nose, *svaiṃ* on the two ears, and *svauṃ* on the tongue.

Having placed [the syllable] *svaḥ* upon the mind, and having placed the complete Vidyā—*svauṃ*—by means of its threefold pervasion, one should follow the procedure beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*). That is as follows: following the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā, one should place red flowers there; therein, [the deity] is pervading from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*.

While burning away the mass of radiant energy produced by the blending of the three fires, and contemplating that [energy] which has been transferred to the *bindu-cakra* through the unceasing scattering of handfuls of flowers along the wrong path, one should pray at the conclusion of the complete root-mantra: "O Bhagavatī Sarvamaṅgalā, Nitye, be invoked here in this cakra!"
Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*),

one should contemplate that certain rays of light from that splendor have issued forth into the positions of the weapons and the retinue of the Lord to be described hereafter, and have transformed themselves into the respective deities of those various retinues and so forth, within the mass of splendor situated in the center.

One should meditate on her as being unchanging, having realized her true nature through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). As for the meditation: she is golden-hued and beautiful, adorned with pearls and rubies, wearing a ruby crown, and filled with compassion as she gazes with her two eyes; she has two arms and is seated upon her own throne.
On a lotus with thirty-two petals arranged in eight, sixteen, and two [rings], together with a pair of four-gated palaces on the ground,
she holds a citron fruit in her right lotus-hand and, with her left, bestows [it] upon her own devotees.
[She is surrounded] by wealth and so forth; [she is] encircled on all sides by powers equal to herself;
she is endowed with seventy-six other and yet other powers arising from the syllables.
This same visualization applies to the powers of the Lord’s weapons and retinues as well; however, regarding the aspect of the weapons:

[The mantra] is further distinguished by its respective insignia (*lāñchana*). Then, at the end of the present vidyā: "O Sarvamaṅgalā, O Eternal One, be established here in this cakra. Again, at the end of thirteen syllables: "Be firmly restrained (*sanniruddhā*).
Again, at the end of that many syllables: "Be veiled (*avaguṇṭhitā*). Again, at the end of that many syllables: "Be made present (*sannidhāpitā*). Thus [he says].

Having made the request preceded by the display of the respective mudrās, and having performed the placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, one should establish the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of this very Nityā Sarvamaṅgalā within this wheel by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra in the form beginning with "The vital breaths of [Name] are here in this wheel. Thus, one establishes the vital breaths of the present Nityā.

One should worship with the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*). Their mantras are as follows: saying "SVAUṂ, I offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to the eternal Sarvamaṅgalā," one takes the ladle and, having offered the first service called *pādya* with the general water of oblation (*sāmānyārghya*), one should present it at her two feet while reciting "SVAUṂ. In the same manner...

Having offered the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and having set aside the second and subsequent offerings such as the water for respectful reception (*arghya*) and the water for sipping—which were already indicated by the mantras recited with those respective words—one should offer [the remaining items] beginning with the face using the current Vidyā-mantra while uttering "Svauṃ. Thus, having worshipped with the twelve offerings ending with betel (*tāmbūla*), one should proceed to the thirteenth offering. The method for that is as follows:

Having arranged three rows behind the Goddess, one should proceed from the row nearest the Goddess in a sequence of three by three starting from the northeast (Īśāna), according to the divisions of the divine (divya), the accomplished (siddha), and the human (mānava).

Having first worshipped one's own Lord (Svanātha) and then the nine Lords— named Prakāśa, Vimarśa, Ānanda, Śrījñāna, Śrīsatya, Śrīpūrṇasvabhāva, Pratibha, Subhaga, and [the ninth]— by means of their respective mantras, [one should worship] near the right arm with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ mātuluṅgāya namaḥ*.
Having worshipped the two weapons with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Varāya Namaḥ" near the left arm, one should worship on the eight petals,

beginning from the petal in front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Bhadrāpādukāṃ Pūjayāmi," "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Bhavānīpādukāṃ Pūjayāmi," "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Bhavyāpādukāṃ Pūjayāmi," and "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Viśālākṣīpādukāṃ Pūjayāmi."

Having worshipped the eight Śaktis with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ śucismitā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ kuṅkumā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ kamalā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ kalpāṇī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; and having again worshipped her in the very center with: *svauṃ sarvamaṅgalā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; [one worships] these: *hrīṃ śrīṃ etāḥ*.

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering while saying, "May the deities of the first enclosure of Sarvamaṅgalā accept this worship," [one worships] in clockwise order starting from the front petal of the sixteen-petaled lotus: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Kamalā; *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the sandals of Pūriṇī; *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the sandals of Nityā; *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the sandals of Amṛtā; *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the sandals of Jīvitā.

Having worshipped the sixteen Śaktis with: *hrīṃ śrīṃ dayāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ dayāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ aśokāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ viśvāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and *hrīṃ śrīṃ vinatāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; and having worshipped her again in the center with: *svauṃ sarvamaṅgalānityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the second enclosure, all of whom are Maṅgalānityās, accept this worship. Having thus offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering for that worship, [one proceeds] to the thirty-two petals.

Moving clockwise from the foremost petal of the Goddess [to the others], I worship: Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Kāminīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Khecarīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Garvāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Purāṇāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Parameśvarīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi;
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Gaurīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Śivāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Ameyāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Vimalāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi.

hrīṃ śrīṃ pāpāpahāriṇyai namaḥ | hrīṃ śrīṃ pavitrāyai namaḥ | hrīṃ śrīṃ padminyai namaḥ | hrīṃ śrīṃ vidyāyai namaḥ | hrīṃ śrīṃ viśveśyai namaḥ | hrīṃ śrīṃ aśeṣarūpāyai namaḥ | hrīṃ śrīṃ nandāyai namaḥ | hrīṃ śrīṃ ambujākṣyai namaḥ | hrīṃ śrīṃ aninditāyai namaḥ | hrīṃ śrīṃ varadāyai namaḥ |

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Vākpradā; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Vāṇī; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Vividhā; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Vedavigraha; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Vindhyā; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Vāgīśvarī; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Sandhyā; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Saṃyatā;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Sarasvatī; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Nirmalā.

Having worshipped the thirty-two Śaktis with these mantras: *hrīṃ śrīṃ nādarūpāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and having worshipped her situated in the center with *svauṃ sarvamaṅgalānityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, [one should say]: *hrīṃ śrīṃ etāḥ sarvamaṅgalānityā tṛtīyāvaraṇadevatāḥ pūjāṃ gṛhṇantu*.

Having offered a handful of flowers as an act of worship, [one should place] Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Brāhmī-pādaḥ, Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Māheśvarī-pādaḥ, and Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Kaumāry-pādaḥ in the eight locations starting from the southern path of the western gate and ending at the western path of the southern gate, in the vicinity of one's own seat within the inner sanctum.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Vaiṣṇavī; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Vārāhī; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Aindrī; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Cāmuṇḍā;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the sandals of Mahālakṣmī.
In the regions near the outer lines, starting from the southern path of the eastern gate and ending at the northern path,
[one should place]: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Indraśaktipāda, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Agniśaktipāda, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Yamaśaktipāda,
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Rakṣaḥśaktipāda, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Varuṇaśaktipāda, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Anilaśaktipāda.

Having worshipped the twenty Śaktis, [one says]: "I worship Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Somaśaktipāda in the west; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Īśānaśaktipāda in the north; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Anantaśaktipāda in the east; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Nidhiśaktipāda in the north; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Niyatiśaktipāda in the east; and Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kālaśaktipādukā in the south. Thus, having fully honored them.

Having worshipped the present Nityā in the center with the mantra *svauṃ sarvamaṅgalānityā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an oblation for that worship, saying: *hrīṃ śrīṃ etāḥ sarvamaṅgalānityā-caturthāvaraṇa-devatāḥ pūjāṃ gṛhṇantu*. Thus, there are exactly four deities in the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) within the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).
The thirteen-fold ritual service (*trayodaśopacāra-pūjā*) is completed in the practical applications consisting of consecrations;
however, in those cases, there is an additional triad of enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) in the form of the deities of the pairs of fire, sun, and moon.

Furthermore, in the installation of the wheel (*cakrapratiṣṭhā*), the installation of the image (*mūrtipratiṣṭhā*), and the first initiation (*prathamadīkṣā*), [this applies] to the ritual jars (*kalaśa*).

In rites for the purpose of removing the defects of weapons, fire, and students, as well as the defects of the intellect, the deities of the couples (mithuna-devatās) are to be worshipped according to the sequence of Fire, Sun, and Moon; however, in the Full Consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) and others, their worship is performed according to the sequence of Moon, Sun, and Fire. It is the same in consecrations for the desire of prosperity and so forth.

The sequence of emanation for the moon and so forth is for the purpose of averting what is undesirable, whereas the sequence of emanation for Brahmā and so forth pertains to the consecration (*abhiṣeka*); this is the distinction.
Therefore, in this context, as the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is being introduced, the ritual application (*prayoga*) is set forth beginning with the digit of the moon (p.

Beginning from a portion of the fire, one should oneself infer the application for each respective place, as we have already shown in the context of the first consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Since the eight-petaled, sixteen-petaled, and thirty-two-petaled lotuses are occupied by the *Bhadrā* and other Śaktis, one should worship at the tips of those petals with the formula: "I worship Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṃ Amṛtapādukā."
Each pair of deities is to be worshipped in each of the two petals, since from each [pair] there arises a dual manifestation. Likewise, in all subsequent cases:

*hrīṃ śrīṃ āṃ mānada-pādukābhyāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ iṃ pūṣa-pādukābhyāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ īṃ tuṣṭa-pādukābhyāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ uṃ puṣṭa-pādukābhyāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ ūṃ rata-pādukābhyāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ ṝṃ dhṛta-pādukābhyāṃ pūjayāmi*.

*Hrīṃ śrīṃ ṛṃ*, sandals of the Moon; *hrīṃ śrīṃ ḷṃ*, sandals of Kāntā; *hrīṃ śrīṃ ḷṃ*, sandals of [the third vowel]; *hrīṃ śrīṃ eṃ*, sandals of Jyotsnā; *hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ śrīṃ*, sandals of Vṛā; *hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ*, sandals of Prītā; *hrīṃ śrīṃ auṃ*, sandals of Aṅgada; *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ*, sandals of Pūrṇā.
Having worshipped the deities of the couple Candrakalā with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṃ Pūrṇāmṛtapāduke,
I worship," and having honored her in the center with "Sauṃ Sarvamaṅgalānityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi," one performs the offering of that worship with: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ,
may these deities of the fifth enclosure of Sarvamaṅgalānityā accept this worship."

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and because the worship of the pairs of lunar-digit deities (*candrakalā-mithuna-devatā*) is properly assigned to the thirty-two-petaled lotus from the tip of the eight petals inward, one should worship from the tip of the *nama* petal to the end of the *racama* petal with the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ kaṃ maṃ dhātṛtāpinīpāduke pūjayāmi*.
*Hrīṃ śrīṃ khaṃ vaṃ*—the sandals of Aryamatāpinī; *hrīṃ śrīṃ gaṃ phaṃ*—the sandals of Mitradhūmrā;
*hrīṃ śrīṃ ghaṃ paṃ*—the sandals of Varuṇamarīcī; *hrīṃ śrīṃ ṅeṃ naṃ*—the sandals of Aṃśujvālinī.

Having worshipped the deities of the solar *kalā*-couples with: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Caṃ Dhaṃ, I worship the sandals of Bhagaruci; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṭhaṃ Thaṃ, I worship the sandals of Tvaṣṭṛdhāriṇī; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṭhaṃ Daṃ, I worship the sandals of Viṣṇukṣamā," one should then honor her in the center with: "Svauṃ, I worship the sandals of the eternal Nityā Sarvamaṅgalā."
"O Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the sixth enclosure, the eternal Sarvamaṅgalās, accept this offering.

Having thus offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an oblation for that worship, [one proceeds] in due order, right within the square, to the locations adjacent to the twenty deities beginning with Brāhmī, as previously described. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Yaṃ...

I worship the sandals of Agni-dhūmrārcis. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Raṃ, I worship the sandals of Vaṣmā. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Laṃ, I worship the sandals of Śuci-jvālinī. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vaṃ, I worship the sandals of Tejo-jvālinī. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Śaṃ, I worship the sandals of Prabhā-visphuliṅginī. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṣaṃ, I worship the sandals of Dāvasuśrī.

Having worshipped the deities of the pairs of fire-energies (*vahnikalā*) with the mantra: "I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Saṃ Śikhisurūpā; I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Haṃ Dyutikapilā; I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Laṃ Dāhahavyavaha; I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kṣaṃ Grāsakavyavaha."

Having worshipped her in the center with the mantra, "Svauṃ, I worship the sandals of the eternal Sarvamaṅgalā," one should offer a handful of flowers as an oblation for that worship, saying: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, may these deities of the seventh enclosure, the eternal Sarvamaṅgalās, accept this worship. Thus is the daily worship of the eternal Sarvamaṅgalā.

The worship of the limbs of initiation (*abhiṣeka*) consists of exactly four enclosures (*āvaraṇa*). However, for the consecration of a mandala (*cakrapratiṣṭhā*), the consecration of an image (*mūrtipratiṣṭhā*), the first initiation (*prathamadīkṣā*), and the initiations that pacify suffering (*duḥkhopaśamakābhiṣeka*), the sequence of worship for the digits of Fire, Sun, and Moon is of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); but in the case of the initiation for the attainment of knowledge (*vidyāprāptyabhiṣeka*) and so forth, [it is otherwise].
The sequence of worship for the digits of the moon, sun, and fire is of two kinds, namely the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and [the form of withdrawal].
Therefore, having performed whatever remains— consisting of the recitation of the three syllables, as well as the forms of libation (*tarpaṇa*) and prostration— [one should proceed].

Having performed the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) a fixed number of one thousand times— enveloped by the *aṅguṣṭhādinyāsa*, *hṛdayādinyāsa*, *varṇanyāsa*, and *vyāpakanyāsa*— and having carried out the offering (*nivedana*) consisting of the contemplation of non-difference from that [mantra], [one should perform the oblation] with food, clarified butter, and so forth, sixteen times, which is the tenth part of the number of recitations.

And having offered oblations according to the prescribed rite, one should once again unite the splendor of the goddess’s form— conceived as fire— with the *bindu* which constitutes the station of the goddess; then,

having worshipped her again with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should present the *bali* offering with the Kurukullā mantra, perform the *nīrājana* ceremony with a wick containing camphor and other substances, and seek forgiveness with the Śakti-utthāpana mudrā.

Having visualized that [light] as having transformed into the form of the various Lords, weapons, armor, and powers, with masses of rays emanating from it all around yet contained within the mass of light at its own root location, one should then,
by means of the khecarī-mudrā, dissolve even that mass of light into the union [of the supreme reality].
Having caused [the deity] to depart into one's own self through the path of the nose by smelling the flower,

and having performed— as before— the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), the placement of the letters (*varṇanyāsa*), and the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*), one should recite the hymn to the Guru and the hymn to the Goddess whose nature has been described, and then conclude while contemplating one's own self as being of that very form. However, in the case of initiation (*dīkṣā*):
Having performed the worship up to the concluding ritual of the inspection (*kṣamāpanā*) over the water-pot as before, and without performing the rites such as the dismissal (*udvāsana*),

one should pass that night with dancing, singing, staying awake, and so forth. Then, at dawn, having performed the necessary daily duties, one should worship the present *Nityā* with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*).

At the conclusion of the dismissal (*udvāsana*), the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the recitation of the Guru-stotra, and the recitation of the Devī-stotra, one should consecrate the disciple—who is positioned upon the *mātṛkā*-yantra—with the present vidyā.
One should instruct the disciple—who honors and respects their guru—preceded by following the method of piercing (*vedha*).
The remainder has been stated in its entirety regarding what is to be adopted.
Thus, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) who has received initiation, having practiced the modes of daily and occasional worship, [proceeds] with his own applications.
Desiring the multitude of goals sought by oneself and others, one should practice the means for attaining knowledge (*vidyā*). Its method has indeed been stated:

in this Kali age, the recitation (*japa*) should consist of one hundred and twenty-eight lakhs (one crore and twenty-eight lakhs), and it should be understood as being of the nature of the syllables *vyoma-vyomara-vyomahasti*. This should be performed with food and water, or with clarified butter alone.

The specific rule is that the fire-oblation (*homa*) is to be performed at one-tenth the number of recitations (*japa*). Thus, only one who has mastered the *vidyā* and possesses devotion to the Guru and the deity has the authority (*adhikāra*) for these practical applications (*prayoga*). Otherwise, even if one performs the application, the result is merely the expenditure of wealth, grain, and so forth; no attainment of the fruit whatsoever occurs, and death may even ensue.
Since one necessarily attains [the goal], one must certainly apply oneself to the means of knowledge when there is a desire for practice.

The applications of the *yantras* for this [goddess] should be demonstrated in the *Kāmyakamalā*; however, the applications such as libations (*tarpaṇa*) and fire-oblations (*homa*), which are obtained through these general statements, are to be inferred from the context of the respective daily rites (*nityā*).
Thus concludes the introduction to Sarvamaṅgalānityā.
Now the eternal goddess Jvālāmālinī is introduced.

On a level, smooth, and pure ground measuring one cubit (hasta) in size, having constructed two square enclosures (*bhūpura*) each equipped with door-panels in the four cardinal directions starting from the east,
and having drawn a single circle within them that neither touches nor leaves a gap between its lines, [one should proceed] in the space of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) inside that.
Having made another circle within that, having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus on its path,

having constructed an eight-spoked wheel within its pericarp using two square enclosures (*bhūpura*), and having made one circle inside that [wheel] such that it touches and does not touch the lines thereof;
Having fashioned a six-spoked wheel within that,
one should then draw a single circle inside it as well, such that its circumference touches and yet does not touch the tips of those spokes.

Having formed a triangle within that [square] with its apex facing inward, one should place a *bindu* within it; such is the procedure for the installation of the jar related to the Nityā currently under discussion in the *nityapūjācakra*,
followed by the contemplation of the *sarvamaṅgalānityānityapūjācakra* and the seven-fold enclosure (*saptāvaraṇa*) along with its worship.

At the conclusion of the ritual acts ending with the dismissal (*udvāsana*) of that [deity], one should again perform the worship that constitutes a limb of initiation (*dīkṣāṅga*), preceded by the contemplation of the present *nitya* and *anitya* worship-mandala (*cakra*) drawn upon the ground within that very same water-pot (*kalaśa*).
However, for that which is not a limb of it, the worship is performed on the mandala alone; there is no requirement for a water-pot in that case either. Regarding that [latter]:

On a single level, having performed the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) according to the method prescribed for the *Śrīcakra* on a wheel engraved with gold and other materials, one should perform the "extracting" (*uddhṛti*) and the "consecration of the vital breath" (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). The second [part] is as follows: the manner of all its worship is such that, in the morning, one should perform the bathing with fragrant waters, preceded by an anointing with fragrant oil.

Having also performed other rites, and because of the necessity of performing the daily rituals for another deity, the practitioner— having already performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*),
and all the concluding rites of his own purificatory ceremonies— possesses a body and face that are purified.

Having adorned oneself with two red garments, sandalwood paste, garlands, and so forth; having entered the sacrificial pavilion— which has been perfumed with red canopies, flower garlands, and aloeswood incense, and illuminated by lamps and colored with vermilion and other pigments—

one should take one’s place upon a seat of red wool or similar material, which has been consecrated with the previously mentioned mantras for the seat, and assume either a *svastika* or *padma* posture.

Having sat down with the root-vidyā and performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) and breath-control (prāṇāyāma) with that very same present vidyā; having offered the bali-oblation of food, condiments, and so forth with the sixteen-syllable mantra; and having worshipped the nine Nāthas upon one's own head according to their respective sequence and with their individual mantras.

Having recited the *Gurustotra* and requested his permission, one should begin the worship. Having meditated upon the identity (*aikya*) of one’s own master, one’s own vidyā, one’s chosen deity, and oneself, [one should proceed] according to the place, time, and other factors regulated by the specific requirements of each respective year.

Having worshipped all the hidden and manifest *siddha-yoginīs* and the thirty-eight deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) ending with [the goddess] Cakrāntā, upon the lion-throne and other supports that serve as the foundation for the circle of the present daily worship;
[one should place] between one's own self and the *yantra*, a vessel containing water mixed with the five substances such as *gorocanā* and so forth, made of gold or other materials.

Having placed a general *arghya* vessel made from any one of the five [substances], one should contemplate the waters in its supporting vessel as being of the nature of fire, sun, and moon by means of the three *bījas* of Kulasundarī; and one should contemplate the *gorocana* and other substances therein as consisting of the five elements, earth and so forth; and within those waters, the present *nityā* worship-circle.
Having visualized [the deity], one should empower the water—which has been conceived as having the form of the present *nityā*—by reciting the present *nityā*-mantra ten times.

With that water, using the present *vidyā*, one should perform the mental bath for oneself; likewise, one should purify the water for the *pādya* and *arghya* placed in vessels positioned one after another starting from the general *arghya* vessel, as well as the water for the garments, ornaments, perfumes, and so forth, which have been placed by oneself on the right side.

And having sprinkled each [item] with water, one should again perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of the *vidyā*. Then, with the common *arghya* water held in the right hand by means of a ladle (*darvī*), one should inscribe the place, time, lineage (*gotra*), zodiac sign (*rāśi*), name, and intention.
[One should then resolve: "I shall perform the worship of the eternal Jvālāmālinī according to the rule and application as prescribed."

One should form the general primary resolve (*saṅkalpa*). At this juncture, even if the rites such as the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) have not been performed due to incidental circumstances, one should accomplish them by means of the *vidyā* itself, employing it in place of the mantras required for those rites.
This continues up to the end of the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā*.

Having first performed the present vidyā, or at least the *praṇava* that constitutes it, one should install the entire *mātṛkā* in its respective locations. This is done by means of the *vāgbhava* syllable alone, as in the exposition of Bhagamālinī.

By teaching this worship, the Blessed One indicated that even with the first seed-syllable (*bīja*) of a *mālā-mantra*, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the installation of the alphabet (*mātṛkā-nyāsa*), and so forth. Thereafter, the six-limbed installation (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) and other rites should be performed as follows: *Oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ; Namaḥ śirase svāhā*.
"Bhagavati śikhāyai vaṣaṭ; Jvālāmālini kavacāya huṃ; Devadevinetrāya vauṣaṭ;

Sarvabhūtasaṃhārakārike astrāya phaṭ. Having thus applied the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) to one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as to the heart and other body parts, [one recites]: "Oṃ namo bhagavati jvālāmālini devadevi..."

Having performed the all-pervading placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) three times with the root mantra— *sarvabhūtasaṃhārakārike jātavedasi jvalanti jvalajvala hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ raṃ raṃ raṃ raṃ raṃ raṃ raṃ raṃ jvālāmālini hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, which consists of sixty-three syllables in its entirety— one should proceed with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the subsequent rites.

Namely, having followed the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā with both hands and placed red flowers there if available, one visualizes a mass of radiant light— abundant from the confluence of the three channels (*nāḍī*)— pervading from the *mūlādhāra* up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
and entering there by way of the nostril.

While visualizing that [light] transferred into the present wheel of drops (*binducakra*) by means of its projection, one should perform the invocation after making this request: "O Jvālāmālinī Nityā, be invoked here in this wheel at the end of the present root mantra, once it is complete. Having thus performed the invocation, that radiance—

Having visualized some of the masses of rays, which have spread out to the locations of the weapons and armor of the Lord to be described hereafter, as having transformed into the forms of their respective deities, one should likewise [visualize] the mass of light situated in the center.
One should meditate on her as transformed into the form described in the verse on meditation. And that meditation is as follows:

[one should meditate on her] resembling a blazing fire, radiant with a crown of rubies, six-faced, twelve-armed, adorned with all ornaments, [holding] a noose, a goad, a sword, a shield, a bow, an arrow, a mace, and a discus.
[One should meditate on her] holding a trident, fire, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness with her lotus-like hands, surrounded on all sides by Śaktis equal to herself,
possessing a lotus-face shining with a beautiful smile and endowed with three eyes;
thus, in the meditation on the Śaktis who are the weapons and retinue of the Lord, it is exactly the same regarding the portion of the weapons.

[The mantra] is further distinguished by having its own respective insignia (*lāñchana*) upon the crown. Then, at the end of the complete sixty-three syllables of the root [mantra], one should recite:

"O Jvālāmālinī, O Nitye, be established here in this *cakra*. Again, having uttered seventy-five syllables ending with the locative case-word "in the *cakra*" (*cakre*), one should recite: "be firmly restrained" (*sanniruddhā bhava*).

Again, at the end of the seventy-five syllables, pray as follows, preceded by the display of the respective mudrās: "Be veiled (avaguṇṭhitā bhava)"; again, at the end of the seventy-five syllables, "Be made present (sannidhāpitā bhava). Then, having performed the placement of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa) for the vidyā of the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), [one should proceed] for this Jvālāmālinī Nityā.

Having established the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the present *Nityā* within the present yantra by means of the *Prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā* beginning with "The vital breaths are here in the wheel" (*prāṇā iha cakre prāṇā*), one should worship her with the twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*). The mantras for this are as follows:
at the end of the complete mantra, [one says] "I offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to Jvālāmālinī Nityā."

Having offered the first of the ritual services (upacāra), known as *pādya* (water for the feet), with the seventy-seven-syllable mantra using the ordinary *arghya* water, and having set aside that ordinary *arghya* water, one should present it at the two feet with the sixty-three-syllable root mantra (*mūlamantra*). In this very same manner, the *arghya* water is poured in the place designated for the *pādya*.

Having offered the water for the guest (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and so forth, using the very mantra stated with words that present the second and subsequent ritual services (upacāra), such as the water for sipping.

One should offer [the oblation] on the head, face, and other parts with the root mantra currently under discussion. Having thus completed the worship with the twelve services (*upacāra*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) and ending with betel (*tāmbūla*), one should proceed to the thirteenth service. Its method is as follows: having prepared three rows to the west of the Goddess, [one should place] the Goddess there.

Beginning from the row of lamps situated nearby, in a sequence of three starting from Īśāna and so forth, one should contemplate the nine Nāthas— divided into the categories of divine (*divya*), accomplished (*siddha*), and human (*mānava*)— who reside in the abodes of the Nāthas and are named Prakāśa, Vimarśa, Ānanda, Śrījñānaśrī, Satyaśrī, Pūrṇasvabhāva, Pratibha, and Subhaga.

Having consecrated [the deities] with their respective empowered mantras (śaktipadaka) and worshipped them with their own specific mantras, one should worship the triad of powers (śaktitraya), beginning from the tip of the triangle in a counter-clockwise direction, with: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Icchā-śakti; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Jñāna-śakti; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Kriyā-śakti. Thus, having worshipped the three powers.
On both sides of the triangle, starting from near the Goddess’s left lower hand and ending at the region near her right lower hand, in twelve locations: *hrīṃ śrīṃ abhītaye namaḥ*,
*hrīṃ śrīṃ śūlāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ dūrāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ kheṭāya namaḥ*.
*Hrīṃ śrīṃ pāśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṅkuśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ khaḍgāya namaḥ*,
*hrīṃ śrīṃ vāṇāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ gadāyai namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ vahnaye namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ varāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped the weapons, at the end of the complete vidyā, [worship] Jvālāmālinī.

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with the mantra, "I worship Nityāpādukā," and having offered the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering of worship with the words, "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the first enclosure of Jvālāmālinī-Nityā accept this worship," [one worships] in the six corners, starting from the southwest (*nairṛtya*).

*Hrīṃ śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Ḍākinī in the northwest. *Hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Rākinī in the east. *Hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Lākinī in the southeast. *Hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Kākinī in the northeast. *Hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Śākinī in the west.

Having worshipped with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Hākinī," and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete mantra with "I worship the sandals of Jvālāmālinī Nityā," [one should say]: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ,
may these deities of the second enclosure of Jvālāmālinī Nityā accept the worship."
Having offered the handful of flowers for the presentation of worship, [one worships] in the eight corners, starting from the corner in front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise:

*hrīṃ śrīṃ ghasmarāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ viśvakavalāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ lolākṣīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ lolajihvikāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ sarvabhakṣāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ sahasrākṣīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having worshipped the eight *ghasmarā* powers with the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ niḥsaṅgāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ saṅgatipriyāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center at the end of the complete *vidyā* with the mantra: *jvālāmālinī nityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having offered a handful of flowers as a gesture of worship with the words: "Hrīḥ Śrīḥ! May these deities of the third enclosure, Jvālāmālinī and Nityā, accept this worship," one proceeds clockwise from the petal in front of the Goddess on the eight petals: "Hrīḥ Śrīḥ! I worship Acintyāpādukā; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ! I worship Aprameyāpādukā; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ! I worship Pūrṇarūpāpādukā."

Having worshipped the eight inconceivable powers (acintya-śakti) and others with: "I worship the sandals of Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Durāsadāpā," "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Sarvāpā," "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Saṃsiddhirūpāpā," "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Pāvanāpā," and "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ekarūpiṇīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi," [one should then, at the end of the complete vidyā, recite]: "I worship the sandals of the eternal Jvālāmālinī."

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center, offer the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for the dedication of the worship, saying: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the fourth enclosure, Jvālāmālinī Nityā, accept the worship.
In the square, in the location near the inner line of the southern path of the western gate:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Brāhmī. In the location near the inner line of the northern path of that same western gate: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Māheśvarī.
In the region near the inner line of the western aisle of the northern gate: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kaumārī-pādukāṃ.

In the region near the inner line of the eastern aisle of that same northern gate: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vaiṣṇavī-pādukāṃ. In the region near the inner line of the northern aisle of the eastern gate: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vārāhī-pādukāṃ.
In the region near the inner line of the southern path of the eastern gate: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aindrī-pādukāṃ.

In the region near the inner line of the eastern path of the southern gate: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Cāmuṇḍā-pādukāṃ. In the region near the inner line of the western path of the southern gate: [Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Cāmuṇḍā-pādukāṃ].

*Hrīṃ śrīṃ mahālakṣmī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*—in the region near the outer line of the western path of the southern gate. *Hrīṃ śrīṃ yamaśakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*—in the region near the outer line of the path in the direction south of the western gate. *Hrīṃ śrīṃ rakṣaḥśakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

In the region near the outer line of the northern path of the western gate: *hrīṃ śrīṃ varuṇa-śaktipāta*. In the region near the outer line of the western path of the northern gate: *hrīṃ śrīṃ anila-śaktipāta*.
In the region near the outer line of the eastern path of the northern gate itself: *hrīṃ śrīṃ soma-śaktipāta*.
In the area near the outer line of the northern path of the eastern gate: *hrīṃ śrīṃ* [to] Īśāna-śakti-pāda in the northwest corner;
*hrīṃ śrīṃ* [to] Ananta-śakti-pāda in the northeast corner; *hrīṃ śrīṃ* [to] Brahma-śakti-pāda in the southeast corner.

*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Niyati-Śakti in the southwest corner (*nirṛtikoṇa*). Having worshipped thus with *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Kāla-Śakti; and at the end of the complete *vidyā*, having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with "I worship the sandals of Jvālāmālinī Nityā," [one worships] these deities of the fifth enclosure (*pañcamāvaraṇa*) of Jvālāmālinī Nityā: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*.
Saying, "May you accept this worship," one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering for that worship. Then, having performed the remaining three services—
