which consist of the recitation of whatever hymns are appropriate, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and measurement— since the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) has already been encompassed by the very resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the worship at the conclusion of the sixteen-fold service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) worship, now...

Without forming another intention, having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*), and having performed the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) one hundred times or more, and again, at the conclusion of the six-limbed and pervasive placements, having performed the offering consisting of the contemplation of non-difference with that [deity], according to the prescribed rule, sixteen times or by the number representing a tenth part of the daily recitation.

And having offered [the oblation], one should again join the fire-born radiant energy (tejas) with the drop (bindu) at the location of the Goddess. Having worshipped the Goddess who has arrived there once more with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), and having presented the bali-offering with the Kurukullā mantra, one should perform the lustration (nīrājana) with a wick containing camphor and other substances, and seek forgiveness (kṣamāpana). Then, with the mudrā for raising the power (śakti-utthāpana-mudrā), [one should move] here and there.

Having visualized that the rays have spread out and transformed into the form of the Lord’s weapons and armor, and that [the deity] has entered into a mass of light within the body of the Goddess; then, by means of the khecarī-mudrā, having withdrawn even that mass of light situated in the center into one's own self, as before, at the conclusion of the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) and the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa), [one recites] the hymn to the Guru and the hymn to the Goddess.
Having recited [the mantra], one should dwell in happiness, having become abundant through the Goddess. Regarding the specific procedure for initiation (dīkṣā):
on the preceding day, having performed the worship ending with the request for forgiveness (kṣamāpanā), excluding the ritual dismissal (udvāsana), one should spend the night.
Having conducted [the rite] preceded by festivals such as dancing, and having performed his daily obligatory duties (*nityakriyā*) and so forth at dawn on the fourteenth day,

the Guru— having again worshipped the present *Nityā* with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) and then performed the ritual dismissal (*samudvāsana*)— at the conclusion of the recitation of the Guru-stava and Devī-stava, [places] the disciple together with the *mātṛkā*-yantra.

Having consecrated [the disciple] with the aforementioned mantra while fresh sprouts are placed upon the mouth of a water-pot, and having worshipped him with the ninefold offerings beginning with perfumes, the Guru— having abandoned all stinginess regarding wealth and having provided a suitable sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)—

should impart the aforementioned mantra according to the prescribed rite of piercing (vedha), provided that the first instruction has been given for the purpose of determining his fitness for piercing.
Regarding the examination of what is eternal and what is non-eternal in the initial instruction, only the method of examination should be followed here;
the rest concerning initiation (dīkṣā) is to be understood from the general discussion.

Thus, the practitioner who has received initiation and is proficient in the methods of the regular and occasional worship, desiring his own cherished goal through the present vidyā, should accomplish that vidyā. The procedure for this is exactly as stated in the general introduction: the recitation (*japa*) consists of thirty-two lakhs for three yugas.

The fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed with cow’s ghee for one-tenth of the number of recitations (*japa*), and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed with fragrant water for exactly one-tenth of the recitations. Thus, only one whose mantra has been perfected is fit for the practical application (*prayoga*); it is not otherwise. Furthermore, since the performance of oblations, libations, and so forth mentioned in the context of other *Nityās* also applies here—as indicated by the passage beginning with "other than the yantra, as previously described"—[the procedure is established].
Since it has been indicated that the instruments dedicated to the Blessed One (bhagavat) belong to the category of "other" (para),

and because it was stated in the introduction to another section that only the mere instrument is to be understood here, we shall now provide examples in due order of those very instruments mentioned as specific to this context.

Having fashioned two square enclosures (bhūpura), one inside and one outside, with the door-frames (dvāraśākhā) not being empty, on that day— as before— one should draw an eight-petalled lotus, and within that as well, an eight-cornered [figure].
Within that [triangle], one should draw a hexagon; within that, a triangle; having fashioned a *bindu* in its center, one should place the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the middle of the *bindu*;

within its belly, the *māyābīja* (hrīṃ), which constitutes the forty-sixth syllable of the present *Nityā-vidyā*; and within that as well, having written the words of the ritual action and the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Having written the second and following three syllables of the mantra under discussion in a clockwise direction starting from the front corner of the triangle; then, having written the six subsequent syllables in the six corners of the hexagon starting from the front corner as previously described; and finally, having written one syllable in each of the eight corners situated outside that—thus having written the eight syllables.
Having written [the syllables] upon the eight petals outside of that, one should produce a single yantra with all the syllables of the vidyā;
from among the five hundred and seventy-six syllables produced by the combination of each of the thirty-six tattva-syllables with the sixteen vowels, [one should take] sixty-three syllables.
If these [syllables] are written together with those very syllables of the previously written *vidyā* in their respective positions,
and if the sixty-fourth syllable is written within the central line of all [the diagrams],
then nine yantras are established by means of four groups of four *tattvas* each.

The first [yantra] consists of a single complete arrangement of syllables forming the vidyā; thus, taken together, ten yantras are produced. Among these, those produced by the combined use of both the letters of the mātṛkā and the letters of the vidyā constitute the second and subsequent [yantras].
p.
202b) According to the sequence of the nine yantras ending with the tenth, they belong to the nine planets beginning with the Sun and ending with Ketu.
Thus, on a pure ground or a wooden board, one should place the second Sun-yantra in the center and the third in the eastern direction.
The lunar yantra; in the southeast direction, the fourth, the Mars yantra;

in the southern direction, the fifth, the Mercury yantra; in the southwest direction, the sixth, the Saturn yantra; in the western direction, the seventh, the Jupiter yantra; in the northwest direction, the eighth, the Rāhu yantra.
Having established the ninth Venus-instrument in the northern direction and the tenth Ketu-instrument in the northeast direction,
one should worship the present Nityā, together with her enclosures, above the Māyā-bīja inscribed in the very center. Then,
whenever a solar eclipse occurs for a particular practitioner, by him—

In the fourteen intervals between the two hexagonal wheels, one should write the names of each respective planet fourteen times in fourteen rounds according to the method "I thoroughly propitiate [the planet] with solar oblations. Then, at those very locations where the names stand,
the Sun (Ravi) should be worshipped with his own mantras fourteen times in fourteen rounds during the period of the Moon's (Candra’s) adversity.

Having written "I fully satisfy with moon-vessels" fourteen times within the fourteen intermediate spaces of the moon-diagram, and having worshipped the deity under discussion in the center as before, as well as the Śaktis mentioned for the triangles and so forth,
one should worship the Moon in turn at the locations marked with the Moon’s name. The same applies to Mars and the other planets.

This should be applied to the first yantra, which is connected either with the letters of the *mātṛkā* or solely with the syllables of the present vidyā; for whichever planet is in distress, its name alone must be used. Having written the sentence "I fully propitiate [the planet] with solar oblations" fourteen times within the fourteen intermediate spaces, one should worship it during the period of that respective planet's prosperity.
However, this worship of each respective planet should be performed only on its specific day, and not at any random time.
203a) In the case of Rāhu and Ketu, the worship should be carried out specifically on the day of the week ruled by the planet that presides over the sign currently occupied by their own [nodes].
Through such worship, all malevolent planets, having abandoned their wicked disposition, bestow only the fruit of their presence in auspicious positions.
Having drawn one of the ten previously mentioned yantras upon the ground,
one should place upon it a girl who has entered into the state of *anusanna-kāmā* (one whose desire is not yet satiated), who has bathed herself, is dressed in clean garments, is well-formed,
and possesses all her limbs in their full perfection; or likewise, a young boy endowed with such specific characteristics.

Having established [the deity] and worshipped with the *vidyā*, one should recite the present *vidyā* one hundred times while touching the head of either [the disciple or the image]. Then, having worshipped again with fragrant flowers that are reddish or white,

[one should perform the ritual] starting from the time of installing the *kanyā* (maiden) and others upon the *yantra*, up until the time of the "Kāma-samaya" (the occasion of the desired question) regarding one's own inquiry.

The practitioner, while continuously offering incense of *guggulu*, should again worship the presented vidyā with the sixteen services beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*). While mentally reciting the presented vidyā, he should ask about the object of his doubt for the sake of his own desire; she (the vidyā) and he (the practitioner) shall both give the answer according to the purpose.

And after obtaining the answer to the question, one should again worship the present Nityā along with her veil (sāvaraṇā) with offerings such as water for the feet (pādya), and having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsya) within one's own self, one should recite the present Vidyā one thousand times.
Having drawn one of the ten previously mentioned yantras on the ground,
having written the syllables *ra*, *ra*, *pa*, *ta*, *ka* one by one in the pericarp and the six corners,
and having placed the patient there, one should worship the present Nityā with red flowers and other offerings using the present Vidyā at her head.

Having first touched [the patient] and empowered [the substance] one hundred times with mantras, the disease becomes possessed therein; then the disease itself, having entered the sufferer, shall declare the reason for its own arrival and the reason for its departure. Thereafter, that which was spoken by it—
Having performed [this], one shall become free from disease.
Now, we shall illustrate the results of the first and subsequent diagrams, which are to be performed when the conditions are met.

Having first inscribed upon the skull of some deceased non-human woman a yantra adorned solely with the basic letters, one should, while recollecting a young woman to be summoned and muttering the present vidyā, heat it at night with charcoal from the khadira wood.

Having cast aside all fear of her husband and others, as well as the modesty natural to women, shame, and pride in her own beauty, she, being tormented by desire, should immediately unite with him even if he is already married. This very yantra, written on a human skull at night with charcoal from *khadira* wood while recollecting the target person and reciting the present vidyā—

If one performs the heating at night in Japannevara, then even kings and others will cast aside their pride and remain under one's control for as long as they live. Having drawn the aforementioned yantra with red sandalwood paste upon a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, or on a seat of palāśa wood, on a stone slab, or on level, smooth ground;

Therein, preceded by the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, one should contemplate the present Goddess together with her retinue, and having considered whether the task is easily accomplished, accomplished with difficulty, or impossible to accomplish, [one should perform it] within the limits of one day, three days, seven days, a fortnight, or a month.
For the practitioner who worships daily throughout the entire duration, all desired effects— attraction, immobilization,
inciting hatred, eradication, killing, acquisition, delusion, and so forth— are accomplished. Furthermore, there shall be the destruction of all the aforementioned diseases.

Having inscribed the second yantra on a surface such as gold or another suitable material with red lead when the Sun has reached its highest exaltation during the rising of Aries, one who worships it for one day or more— having examined whether the task to be accomplished is achievable as before— [will succeed].

The practitioner shall attain a connection with all the aforementioned fruits. However, if during the exalted period (*uccakāla*) of the Guru, one writes a second yantra on a silver plate using vermilion while the Sun is in Cancer, and then, until the time of the ritual application, recites the previously mentioned mantra a thousand times or more every day while touching the yantra; therein—

Having placed a water vessel upon the yantra, if one performs bathing, drinking, cooking, and other such activities with that water, then all diseases of the practitioner, such as urinary disorders (prameha), will perish and he will attain well-being. Furthermore, having written the third yantra with red ochre on a wooden plank made from the wood of a tree belonging to an inimical asterism (nakṣatra)...

Because it is well-established on the ground, one should fill the enemy’s eighth house or ascendant with earth, and upon that, kindle a fire with *mṛtyu*-wood until the previously mentioned time limit; by this, the enemy shall suffer from a burning fever, or another burning disease, or from a secret conflagration and the like, and thus incur great loss. However, if...

When anger arises due to the enemy's repeated entreaties or out of fear of the hells produced by one's own nature, one should then uproot that [enemy] from his land and cast him into a pond or similar body of water; by this, the enemy becomes well-disposed. Having written the fourth yantra with *gorocanā* on a leaf of gold or other material, one should worship the present Nityā along with her retinue therein.
One shall achieve victory in all debates. Having written the fifth yantra with saffron upon a leaf made of the three metals previously mentioned, one who worships the present Nityā therein—(p.
All men, women, elephants, and horses become submissive to the practitioner. Having drawn the sixth yantra with turmeric on a piece of cloth when Saturn is in its exaltation or in the sign of Libra,
and having placed it between two bricks, one should ensure that these two bricks containing the yantra do not move.

One should bind it in some secluded place. By that, the tongue and the intellect of the enemy become paralyzed; for kings, there occurs a paralysis of the impulse toward battle and of anger and the like. Having written the seventh yantra with camphor and sandalwood paste upon a leaf made of the three metals (triloha) and so forth, one should [recite it] daily at the junctions of the day (sandhyās), extending over a period of one, three, or more days, in one's own [place].

For the practitioner worshipping in his home, after the completion of the ritual with its ancillaries— whether at a time of one month, one fortnight, seven days, three days, or a single day— the most excellent prosperity shall arise from every quarter. When the Guru is in his exaltation, or when Cancer, the sign of the Guru’s exaltation, is rising, [the rite should be performed] in a vessel made of leaves such as *vaṭa* or *palāśa*, or upon its pedestal.

For the practitioner who draws [the yantra] with *aguru* paste and worships the present *Nityā* there with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) consisting of fragrant flowers, there shall be the acquisition of variegated garments. One should draw the ninth yantra in any one of the aforementioned locations, such as those made of the three metals (*triloha*), using musk and the secretions of a deer. Therein, [one should worship] the present *Nityā*.

Having worshipped [the deity] along with the enclosure and performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsya*), one should smear everything with the sweat of that deer until it is reduced to its own essence. Wherever the practitioner goes in public assembly, all those present will become submissive to him like a teacher and shall perform worship in various ways. Furthermore, women shall remain under his control for as long as he lives. [This is accomplished by using] red sandalwood and other such substances.

Or else, having written the tenth yantra on a leaf of any one of the metals such as iron, using all substances ending with deer-sweat— or rather, using those specific substances mentioned as being favorable for each respective desire— one should [proceed].
There, within the maṇḍala, one should constantly worship the present Nityā together with her retinue, extending beyond the previously mentioned time.
For the practitioner, all the aforementioned fruits are indeed attained. This concerns the ritual of drawing the central portion.
They exist in accordance with the respective substances that serve as the locus for the act of writing and the act of not writing.

The seventh [yantra] for the affliction of Venus, the eighth for the affliction of Saturn, the ninth for the affliction of Rāhu,

and the tenth for the affliction of Ketu; having written these respective yantras on their respective days using the appropriate materials and placing them in their respective directions during the rising sign (lagna) of each planet's exaltation,
one should duly place the wife upon the respective yantra and perform the consecration with the water-pot (kalaśābhiṣeka).

At the conclusion of the ritual actions ending with the dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the general worship of Sarvamaṅgalā along with her retinue, one should worship the current daily deity together with her retinue there, preceded by the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites;
then, having consecrated that water with either a thousand or a hundred recitations, [one should proceed].

Through the sprinkling of that water, the malevolence of those planets departs, and the planet becomes favorable. Regarding another method for planetary malevolence: having performed the worship of each respective planet daily at the time of the rising of its exaltation sign (ucca-rāśi-lagna), preceded by offerings of ghee and milk-porridge (ājya-pāyasa) as a food offering (naivedya), and preceded by the presentation of the respectful water-offering (arghya) and prostrations.

One should perform a fire oblation (homa) with clarified butter and milk-rice (pāyasa). Furthermore, this worship must be preceded by the worship of the present Nityā, just as before. For one who acts in this manner, even the planets situated in malefic positions become auspicious and bestow only the fruits of their favorable states.
The application of giving during planetary affliction is as follows: [one should perform it] with a measure of sixteen, twelve,
nine, six, or three *niṣkas*, placing [the offerings] in the respective positions within the intervals of the various planetary diagrams (*yantra*).

Having composed the aforementioned mantras incorporating the names of each respective planet, one should worship the current *nityā* together with her enclosures (*sāvaraṇa*) therein; then, having worshipped each of those planets— represented by the forms drawn in the fourteen locations— with fourteen rounds of offerings,
one should summon a Brāhmaṇa who is either a practitioner of the current *nityā* or a practitioner of another *nityā*, and seat him facing westward.

Having personally worshipped [the deity] facing east with the five offerings beginning with incense (*gandha*), and having meditated upon [the deity] as possessing the physical form of that respective planet and prostrated, one should give this yantra to him preceded by a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). By that, the malevolence of that respective planet is pacified; it is proclaimed here that four or even five *niṣka* of gold [should be given]. Thus it is said.
According to one's own capacity, there is a system of rites ranging from light to heavy; likewise, this applies to the five fortnights beginning with the sixteen-day period.

The application for increasing the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) is as follows: Having placed a water-pot (*kumbha*) in one of the aforementioned yantras and consecrated its water with a count of one thousand or more recitations, the digestive fire will increase by drinking that water. Immediately after eating, having become pure through sipping water (*ācamana*) and other rites, and having first touched the abdomen, [one should worship] the present *Nityā*.
If one should recite it by the count of a thousand or more, then there will be an increase in the digestive fire.

The application for the prosperity of wealth, grain, houses, and so forth is as follows: when the Sun is in the sign of Aries (Meṣa), for three days at a time, one should worship the present Nityā daily with a covering upon each of ten machines. In this same manner, even when the Sun has entered the signs beginning with Taurus (Vṛṣa) and ending with Pisces (Mīna), the worship should be performed for three days at a time. In this way, according to this method—

For one who constantly worships the eternal [goddess] throughout the entire duration of the Sun's course, there shall be an abundance of wealth, grain, and so forth, as well as long life and freedom from disease; this applies even for three days during the period of the Sun.

The worship is to be performed. In this manner, by worshipping the present Nityā daily throughout the solar year, the practitioner shall attain abundance of wealth, grain, and so forth, as well as long life and freedom from disease. This should be done previously when the Sun is situated in the sign of Aries (Meṣa) or when there is an Aries ascendant on a Sunday; or when the Moon is situated in the sign of Taurus (Vṛṣabha) or when there is a Taurus ascendant.

On Monday; on Tuesday when Mars is situated in the sign of Capricorn or when there is a Capricorn ascendant; on Wednesday when Mercury is situated in the sign of Virgo or when there is a Virgo ascendant; on Thursday, the day of Jupiter (Daityaguru), when Jupiter is situated in the sign of Cancer or when there is a Pisces ascendant;
on Saturday when Saturn is situated in the sign of Libra or when there is a Libra ascendant; [and so on] for the planets beginning with the Sun.

The procedures for worship, fire-offerings (homa), charity, and so forth have been explained in sequence. Now, when many, three, or even two planets— such as the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Venus, and others— are situated in a single sign beginning with Aries, then for all of them, [the results depend] on the lord of the sign they occupy, such as Mars and others, being in their exaltation sign, Capricorn, or in the ascendant (lagna).

It is stated that on the days of the planets, such as Mars and the rest, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, the application of yantras, charity, and so forth, cause the malevolence of those respective planets to depart.
Thus concludes another ritual application for removing the malefic influence of the planets.
Now follows another ritual application for crushing enemies.

At the time of an eclipse of the moon or the sun, having drawn the respective planetary yantras on level ground according to the number of planets favorable to the enemy— wherever it is prescribed that a sentence containing the name of a planet be written,
there one should write "ādityo devadattasya kṣobham" (the Sun [causes] the agitation of Devadatta) in fourteen repetitions within the intervening space.

Having written the mantra in such a manner as "May Candra accomplish [the goal]; may he accomplish the agitation of Devadatta," victory shall belong to the practitioner who performs worship daily once the yantra has been perfected.
Now follows the application of colored medicinal herbs and ashes.

Having taken one *karṣa* portion each of the medicinal herbs associated with the letters of the present mantra according to the procedure prescribed for the *homa*, and having further taken equal quantities of the repeated letters— taking all these together and combining them into a single mass measuring one *khārī*.

Having cooked it together with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), when the fire manifests within the interior of that cooking vessel due to the intensity of the heating, then one should offer oblations of ghee into that fire with the aforementioned mantra, recited either a hundred or a thousand times. Having taken all the ash produced from the burning of that [mixture], which consists of the medicinal herbs of excellent color, one should use that ash.
Having drawn the diagrams even with a mere glance, and having worshipped the present Nityā along with Sāvarṇī within each of those diagrams,

one should take all the ashes— including that used for the dismissal [of the deity]— which constitute the written means of accomplishment, and place them in some vessel. In those ashes, the worship of the present Nityā performed daily according to the prescribed rite [is contained].

One should perform protection on all sides. In whichever house this ash is placed, there shall be no misfortune caused by disease, thieves, planetary influences, kings, spirits, ghosts, and the like. By wearing that ash on the forehead and other limbs, by anointing oneself with it when combined with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, and by consuming it, [one attains these benefits].

The pacification of suffering caused by all types of malevolent rites, sorcery, sins, and the like occurs. Likewise, the application of the syllables of the mantra, medicinal herbs, and ashes of any other Nityā also yields such results. Through one Vidyā, there is the consecration with fire;
through other Vidyās, there is the oblation (homa); and the drawing of yantras composed of the syllables of those other Vidyās belongs to that specific Nityā.
Thus, it should be contemplated that the fruit of the worship is indeed equal.
The twenty-one yantras for the purpose of increasing the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) are as follows:

From the seven consonants *kha*, *cha*, *ṭha*, *tha*, *pha*, *ra*, and *kṣa*—which are associated with Fire—each being joined with the third, fourth, and twelfth vowels associated with Fire, twenty-one syllables arise.
By means of these, twenty-one yantras are produced; for instance, by way of internal and external arrangement.

Having drawn two upward-pointing triangles, one inside the other, and having drawn a single circle that touches and does not touch the lines of those triangles, one should draw a hexagon within it. This is the procedure for the line-drawn wheel (*rekhāmayacakra*); therein, the first syllable is of the form "khi," incorporating the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Having drawn [the diagram], one should write the six syllables *khī*, *khīṃ*, *kheṃ*, *chiṃ*, *chīṃ*, and *ṭi* in the six corners of the hexagon, beginning from the top. Then, on the path between the two outer triangles,
on the left side, one should write the five syllables *ṭhīṃ*, *ṭhaiṃ*, *tiṃ*, *tīṃ*, and *taiṃ* in an upward sequence.

Having written [the main mantra], one should write the five syllables *pi-pī-pe-pai-riṃ* in order from top to bottom on the right side; then, on the left side of that same upper portion, write *rau-kṣi-m*;
and on the right side, write the two syllables *kṣī-kṣai-m*. At the front portion—

One should write the name of the practitioner and the names of those to be accomplished; this is established as the first yantra. However, if twenty syllables each are written in the six corners starting from the second and third [syllables], then there are another twenty yantras;
thus, together with the previous one, twenty-one yantras are produced. Of these, one...

Having engraved the yantra in the shape of an upward-pointing triangle upon a copper plate, one should recite the present Nityā-vidyā one hundred thousand times while touching that yantra, with each syllable of the mantra encased by the twenty fire-syllables as prescribed.

In this manner, one should consecrate the prepared [substance] daily with the number of one hundred thousand recitations of the present vidyā, worship it with the five offerings, and place it in a water vessel.

Then, by means of this [practice] such as bathing and so forth, the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) increases, and the sin that obstructs digestion shall be diminished. This application pertains specifically to *Nityā* when she is recited while being encased (*puṭita*) by the syllables of *Vidyā* as prescribed; it is not restricted to any single *Nityā* alone. Thus concludes the introduction to *Jvālāmālinī Nityā*. Now, [The text continues: ...the *Śrīcakranavātmaka*... [and so on]. (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "atha".)

The *Citrānityā* is now introduced. Having constructed two squares with sides measuring one cubit (*hasta*), with an interval of four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) between them and each provided with door-frames on all four sides;

having then drawn a single circle within that [inner square] such that it touches and does not touch the lines thereof; and having [divided] the interior of that [circle] into sections each separated by four finger-breadths.

Having performed three rotations of the [mandala] lines, one should fashion a lotus with thirty-two petals on the outer path connected to those three paths, sixteen petals on the middle path, and eight petals on the inner path; then,
having fashioned a nine-yoni wheel within its pericarp, one should arrange the *bindu* within that— such is the procedure.

Having extracted the diagram for the daily worship (*nityapūjācakra*) from the ground according to the prescribed procedure, and having placed a water-pot (*kalaśa*) upon a heap of grain situated there, one should contemplate within the water that pot the entire *Sarvamaṅgalā* daily worship diagram along with its enclosures (*sāvaraṇa*), performing the ritual actions up to the conclusion of its dismissal (*udvāsana*).

The performance of worship and other rites preceded by drawing this [mandala] on the ground is to be practiced as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of initiation (*dīkṣā*); however, when it is not an auxiliary, it is performed in the *sāka* [tradition].

Both of these modes of worship are centered on the wheel (*cakra*), as follows: having bathed with fragrant waters following an anointing with scented oil, and having also completed the morning duties (*prātaḥkṛtya*), one [proceeds] toward the deity...
Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other general rites as an incidental consequence of the performance of the daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*),

the practitioner (*sādhaka*), having entered the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) characterized by the features described therein, [proceeds] to the place for the purification of the *kūrma-cakra*.

Having sat down facing east upon either the *svastika* or *padma* seat on top of the aforementioned *āsana-vidyā-āsana*, and having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the present mantra, [one should recite] the sixteen-syllable mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ sarvavighnakṛdbhyaḥ sarvabhūtebhyo huṃ svāhā*.

Having offered the *bali* consisting of food, condiments, and so forth; having worshipped one’s own *nātha* and, in due order, the nine *nāthas* on the head with their respective mantras; having recited the hymn to the Guru and requested permission for the worship, one should commence it. One should contemplate the identity of one’s own *nātha*, one’s own *nityā*, one’s own *vidyā*, and one’s own self.

Having worshipped the thirty-eight deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), beginning from the lion throne that serves as the support for the wheel of one’s own eternal daily worship, and extending up to the entire circle of secret and manifest *siddha*-yogins [specified] by their respective locations, times, and so forth according to the distinctions of those various years;
[one should place] between one’s own self and the *yantra* a vessel containing water mixed with the five substances such as *gorocanā*.

Having placed the general *arghya* vessel, one should sequentially visualize the waters in its supporting vessel as having the forms of fire, sun, and moon by means of the three *kula-sundarī* seed-syllables; then, visualize the five substances therein, such as *rocanā*, as consisting of the five elements beginning with earth. This is preceded by the contemplation of the identity between that water and the *nityā-cakra*.
Having consecrated the water— which has been visualized as having the nature of the present vidyā— by reciting the present vidyā ten times,

one should [sprinkle] oneself with that water using the present vidyā; likewise, the water for the feet (pādya), the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the water for bathing, which have been placed in vessels arranged in successive order starting from the general arghya vessel.

Having sprinkled with the general *arghya* water the garments, ornaments, perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, and so forth, which have been placed on one's own right side, and having again performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of the *vidyā*, [one should proceed] with the ladle held in the right hand.

Having recited [the details] ending with the place, time, lineage, heap, name, and desire, and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in such a manner as, "I shall perform the worship of Citrānityā according to the rule and according to my intellectual capacity," one should pour that water onto the ground. At this juncture, if the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites have not been performed incidentally, one should perform them by means of the relevant *vidyā*. [Then follows] the Mātṛkā...

At the conclusion of the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): having first performed the placement of the present *vidyā* syllable—namely *cakauṃ āṃ cakau iṃ cakau īṃ ckau uṃ ckau ūṃ*—along with the entire *mātṛkā* one by one at each respective location, the six-limbed placement of the present *vidyā* should then be performed. In that regard, *cā* is for the heart (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*) and *cā* is for the head (*śirase*).

The other [mantra] beginning with "svāhā" should be performed in that manner. According to the view of the authors of the *Manoramā* and the *Nidhi*, one should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by joining them with the wind-syllable (*vāyu*) and the long vowels in sequence, as seen in the text. However, others do not accept this; for it is impossible for the stated meaning to arise from the phrase "by the wind-syllable joined with the long vowels" alone.

It is not [the case that] "vidyādyā" (beginning with knowledge) [is the meaning], because it would result in an absurdity regarding the root meaning. Some rely on the *bahuvrīhi* compound, interpreting it as "that whose beginning is knowledge," and claim that "cakauṃ" is appropriate for the heart and "cakauṃcī" for the head. However, even this is not correct, because a *bahuvrīhi* is to be disregarded in favor of a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* due to its greater complexity.

Because it is agreed upon by all scriptures: some desire the application [of mantras] such as *cākauṃ hṁ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *cīkauṃ śirase svāhā*, and *cūkauṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, based on the root meaning that the wind (*vāyu*), which is the primordial constituent of *vidyā*, possesses the union of the six long vowels, while the subsequent portion remains just as before.

This [interpretation] is not superior either, because it would result in the word *vāyu* being redundant; for by [interpreting] "the beginning of knowledge" (*vidyādyena*) as "by that which is eternal" (*nityena*), the intended meaning is obtained. Furthermore, the meaning of the phrase "the sixth part," and so forth, is not obtained even when the word *vāyu* is supplied. And as for "knowledge" (*vidyā*)...

Regarding the phrase "the air uttered in the first part" (*ādyabhāgoccaritavāyuḥ*), there is no possibility of a dual number because it relies on a compound meaning "the initial air together with the *vidyā* of the six-limbed placement" (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa-vidyā*). Furthermore, the word "initial" (*ādya*) is used to dispel the doubt that the air— consisting of the six long [vowels] and the guru [syllable]— should be employed either in the first part of the *vidyā* or in its latter part.

In the absence of the word *vāyu* (wind), there would be the application of the six long vowels to only one [syllable]; therefore, the word *vāyu* is used. In the absence of the word *vidyā* (knowledge), how could the precedence of *vāyu* be attained? Therefore, that word [is used]. Thus: *cācakauṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *cīcakauṃ śirase svāhā*, *cūcakauṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *caiṃcakauṃ*.

"Kavacāya huṃ," "Cocakauṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ," and "Caḥcakauṃ astrāya phaṭ"—one should thus perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of these mantras on the thumbs and other fingers; such is the meaning of the root mantra. Then, having performed the threefold pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the two-syllable root mantra "Cavakaum,"...

One should follow the sequence beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*). That is to say: having formed the *trikhaṇḍa* mudrā, while the joined palms are filled with red flowers, the radiant energy (*tejas*) of the present Vidyā—which pervades from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*—is transferred via the path of the central channel (*nāḍī*).
By casting those handfuls of flowers, [the deity] enters the station of the drop (*bindu*) located within the mouth of the present [deity].

Meditating on [the deity] as having arrived, one should perform the invocation by praying, "O Bhocitrā, O Imperishable One, please be present here," and thus complete the invocation. Then, visualizing some of the masses of rays from that splendor as they spread to their respective locations,
transformed into the forms of the Lord, the weapons, and the retinue, one should contemplate the mass of splendor situated in the center.
One should meditate upon [the deity] whose essential nature is realized through dhyāna. In that regard, dhyāna is as follows:
[one should visualize her] possessing the radiance of the rising sun and the universe, adorned with ornaments of nine precious gems, and wearing a crown of nine precious gems.
Resplendent with a garment of variegated silk, four-armed, three-eyed, with a face shining upon a pure surface,

consisting of all bliss, thus described as the bestower of all desired objects; holding in her four arms the noose, the goad, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness— she is Maṅgalā, seated upon the pericarp of a lotus, and not in the womb.
The visualization for the weapons and armor of the Protectors is likewise;
however, they differ in that their crowns are marked with their respective insignia. Then: "O Cakrī-mocitrā-nitye, be established here in this wheel!
O Cakrī-mocitrā-nitye, be firmly restrained here in this wheel! O Cakrī-mocitrā-nitye..."

Having made the request while displaying the respective mudrās: "O Cakauṃbho-citrānitye, be veiled in this wheel! O Cakauṃbho-citrānitye, be present in this wheel!"—and having performed the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), one should worship with the twelve offerings (dvādaśopacāra).
Their mantras are as follows: "Cakauṃbho-citrānitye, [this is] the water for the feet (pādya)."

Having offered the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) with the general *arghya* water while reciting "I offer" (*kalpayāmi*), one should present it at the [deity's] feet with the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*) while reciting "I give" (*cakaumi*). In this very same way,
having offered the *arghya* and so forth by means of the mantras prescribed for the *arghya* and other stages— beginning with the offering of the *pādya*— one should [proceed] with the root mantra.

One should offer [the offerings] beginning with the head. Having thus worshipped with the twelve services ending with betel, one should proceed to the thirteenth service. Its method is as follows: on the back part of the Goddess, [one should worship] those named Prakāśa, Vimarśa, Ānanda, Śrījñāna, Śrīsatya, Pūrṇasvabhāva, and Pratisubhaga.

Having worshipped, in due order, the lords of the sacrificial substances, the perfected ones, and the lords of men, by means of their respective mantras with words inserted at the positions of the lord’s station;
In the middle [of the triangle], in the corners starting from the southeast (Agni) and proceeding clockwise, having worshipped the triad of powers with:
"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Icchā-śakti; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Jñāna-śakti;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Kriyā-śakti," [one worships] in the Goddess herself.
In the primary worship, from the lower right arm up to the area near the lower left arm, one should worship the four weapons with:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ varadāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṅkuśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ pāśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ abhayāya namaḥ*. Then, [worship] the sandals of the goddess Kauñcitrānityā.

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with "I worship," and having offered a handful of flowers for the dedication of the worship with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these deities of the first enclosure of Citrānityā accept the worship," [one places] outside, in the eight triangles, starting from the front: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au.

Aṃ Aḥ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Brāhmī. Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Māheśvarī. Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Kaumārī. Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Vaiṣṇavī. Ta Tha Da Dha Na Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Vārāhī. Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Aindrī.

Having worshipped the eight Mothers with the mantras: *ya ra la va śa hrīṃ śrīṃ cāmuṇḍāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi* and *ṣa sa ha la kṣa hrīṃ śrīṃ mahālakṣmīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and having honored the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra *cakauṃ citrānityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, [one should worship] these Citrānityās, the deities of the second enclosure, with *hrīṃ śrīṃ*.

Saying "May you accept [this]," and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an act of worship, one should worship the eight Śaktis— Bhadrā and the others— as described in the *Sarvamaṅgalā-paṭala* upon the eight petals. Having worshipped the Goddess residing in the center as before, and having presented the offering (*naivedya*) for the worship of the third enclosure, [one proceeds] to the sixteen petals.
Having worshipped the sixteen powers beginning with Kalā, and having offered the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for the fourth enclosure at the end of the worship of the central deity as before;
Having worshipped the thirty-two Śaktis, beginning with Kāminī, upon the thirty-two petals,

and having offered the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) for the worship of the fourth enclosure at the conclusion of the central worship as before— and at the end of the fifth enclosure worship— in the sequence starting from the east of the square, [one worships] Indra and the others.
Having worshipped the powers of the directions, beginning with Indra and the others, in their respective order;
having honored Ananta, Vichi, Pati, and Kāla in the northwest, northeast, southeast, and southwest corners;
and having worshipped the Goddess situated in the center with the mantra "I worship the sandals of the goddess Cakauṃcitrānityā."
"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May these various Nityās, the deities of the sixth enclosure, accept the worship.

Thus one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for the presentation of that worship. Then, having also performed the remaining three services (*upacāra*), one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the thumbs and other fingers, the placement on the heart and other limbs, and the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*), encapsulated by the mantra repeated a thousand times or other such numbers.

Having performed the recitation (*japa*) consisting of the meditation on non-difference from that [deity] and having made the offering (*nivedana*), one should offer oblations according to the prescribed rule—

sixteen times the portion of the recitation— with the sixteen-fold oblations. Then, having visualized the Goddess as having returned once more to the very place of the drop (*bindu*) of the deity’s splendor (*tejas*) which was previously meditated upon within the fire, one should again worship the Goddess who has arrived there with the five services (*pañcopacāra*).
Having offered the bali-oblation with the Kurukullā-vidyā, having performed the lustration (nīrājana) with a wick filled with camphor and other substances, and having asked for forgiveness,

one should contemplate the multitude of rays belonging to the retinue as being absorbed into the mass of splendor constituting the Goddess situated in the center by means of the Śaktyutthāpana-mudrā; then, having dissolved even that central splendor into one's own self by means of the Khecarī-mudrā.

At the conclusion of the previously mentioned *ṣaḍaṅganyāsa* and *vyāpakanyāsa*, having recited the hymn to the Guru and the hymn to the Goddess, one should move about as oneself being of the nature of the Goddess. However, in the case of an initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should perform the rites of dismissal (*udvāsana*)— excepted— the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*), and the worship with food (*annapūjā*), exactly as before, neither less nor more.
Having spent that night as before with festivities such as dance and song,
and having performed the morning obligatory rites and worshipped the current daily deity with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*).

At the conclusion of the recited nyāsa, having chanted the hymn to the Guru and the Goddess, he should sprinkle the disciple— who is positioned within the *mātṛkā* yantra— with sprouts offered at the mouth of the water-pot while reciting the present mantra. Then, the Guru, being fully satisfied by the ninefold offerings made without stinginess regarding wealth and by the presentation of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth, shall perform the piercing (*vedha*) according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
The specific instruction is that one should teach the present science on the full moon day.

Thus, one who has received initiation and performs the daily and occasional rites such as worship and so forth, desiring to accomplish his own and others' goals through practical application, should practice the means for attaining the Vidyā. The method for that is indeed as stated in the general introduction; however, regarding the recitation (*japa*) of this Vidyā in the Kali age, it consists of thirty-six hundred thousand repetitions.
All that is to be done is charming, as already stated in the introduction; thus, one who has accomplished the knowledge is indeed fit for the practical application.
Now follow the daily applications of this [mantra].

By performing the fire-sacrifice (homa) every day with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets (madhuratraya), numbering a thousand or more, even an unfortunate person becomes illustrious and possesses the enjoyment of prosperity and happiness;
by using white lotuses anointed with the three sweets, one attains great fame.
From the performance of the *maṇḍala* ritual involving oblations of red lotuses mixed with pure honey, one gains the acquisition of much gold,
or perhaps the discovery of a treasure, or even the acquisition of the earth;
and from the performance of the *maṇḍala* ritual involving oblations of white water-lilies mixed with milk, there is the acquisition of food and good fortune.

From the repeated performance of oblations of blue lotuses mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*), one shall obtain all desired things one by one, but not simultaneously. This same principle applies here as well, just as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice where [results are obtained] from all [the constituent parts]. From the repeated performance of oblations of white lotuses (*kahlāra*) smeared with clarified butter, one attains the favor of kings.

By performing the prescribed fire-oblation (*homa*) every day for as long as it takes to complete the mandala, using a thousand or more *palāśa* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), one attains all four forms of eloquence: that of a speaker, an expounder, a debater, and so forth.

There would be scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*). In this context, the singularity of scholarship means that from a single application of the fire-element portion alone, the fourfold fruit is accomplished; just as from a single application for the acquisition of a great kingdom, there arise various objects such as elephants, horses, chariots, people, gold, silver, copper, and so forth.

There is the acquisition of wealth through the practice of health; furthermore, there is the destruction of various diseases by means of various [remedies], for a single destruction does not have multiple counter-correlates. From the oblation of parched grains (*lāja*) soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhura*), and from the practiced *maṇḍala* [ritual], there is the attainment of a woman endowed with all excellent qualities. Coconut fruit powder... it.

Or, having smeared jaggery with honey, he who offers it daily, starting from a count of one thousand up to the number of the *maṇḍala*, becomes equal to Kubera; what then need be said of his mastery over the wealth of the earth? [This occurs] from the offering of ghee and goat’s milk combined, from the offering of sesame and rice, and from the offering of red flowers or certain other substances.
By performing oblations with *bandhūka* flowers daily and without interruption until the end of the maṇḍala, one will attain great wealth;
by offering oblations with white flowers, one will attain great wealth.

Through oblation with white flowers, one attains mastery over speech; through oblation performed day after day with a count of one thousand or more using both white and red flowers mixed together, pervading the mandala, there shall be an increase in lifespan preceded by good health. [Likewise] for three blades of dūrvā grass smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu).

By performing the fire-oblation (*homa*) every day for a thousand times or more until the completion of the mandala, all diseases are destroyed; likewise [is the result] for one who has anointed *guḍūcī* with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) and consumes it with food mixed with the three sweets.
An oblation of sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets is equal in power to three blades of *dūrvā* grass;
and from the daily offering of a hundred lotuses smeared with sandalwood paste and camphor, extending as far as the mandala,
there shall arise for the practitioner a fortune that pervades the entire lineage of adepts.

By performing daily oblations of blossoming *kahlāra* flowers ground with camphor, saffron, and *himatoya* (snow-water) in numbers such as a thousand and so forth, until the completion of the mandala, one will attain a status equal to a king through an abundance of elephants, horses, chariots, and wealth; becoming endowed with qualities such as the absence of rivals, he shall live for a hundred years.
From the homa of pieces of sugarcane stalks, one obtains clothing; from the homa of *karavīra* flowers, one also obtains clothing.

From the homa of *pāṭala* flowers mixed with honey, women become submissive. From the homa of *campaka* flowers, cane-workers become submissive. Daily, from the homa of white sugar smeared with the milk of a white cow and a white calf, [the desired result is attained].

From practicing this even as many as a thousand times or more up to the limit of a maṇḍala, the Goddess Lakṣmī shall become inexhaustible for the practitioner, even if he is a great sinner or suffers great expenditure. Thus are the *anugraha-homas*;
by offering white sugar smeared with *sauvīra* (sour gruel) in numbers such as a thousand every day, [the same result is attained].

Spreading throughout the entire circle, if one performs this daily for a number such as a thousand, the enemies will become mutually hostile; by which, due to the lack of mutual support, all of them can be conquered one by one.
Furthermore, [this applies] even to the seeds of one's desired [plants], such as the *ariṣṭa* leaf and so forth, when [the enemy] is anointed with *ariṣṭa* oil.

Even from performing the previously described fire sacrifice (homa) within the limits of the mandala, mutual hatred arises among enemies. From the fire sacrifice performed within the mandala using seeds of death (mṛtyubīja) smeared with neem oil, [the same effect occurs] for elephants.

By performing daily oblations numbering a thousand or more—up to the limit of one hundred thousand—for each of the leaves, flowers, fruits, branches, and roots of the *mṛtyu* tree, horses will become diseased; thereby, because an army becomes impossible [to mobilize], one shall be easily conquered by the enemy. [Likewise, by offering] *vibhītaka* seeds smeared with *vibhītaka* oil...

From performing oblations with *maṇḍala* seeds, there shall be the destruction of men, wealth, weapons, and all else. By this, even in foot-soldier combat, the enemies will become ineffective. From performing oblations with *karañja* seeds smeared with *karañja* oil, the enemy, having followed one as far as the boundary of the *maṇḍala*, becomes possessed by a *piśāca*.

By performing a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with the five parts— leaves, flowers, fruit, branches, and root— of the *vibhītaka* tree smeared with *vibhītaka* oil, or with *vibhītaka* fruit smeared with *nimba* oil, or by following [the ritual] for a span (*tāla*) [of time], the enemy becomes afflicted with a specific disease known as epilepsy (*apasmāra*).

When fire is kindled with fuel from the tree corresponding to the enemy's birth asterism (*nakṣatra*), the death of that enemy will occur through the performance of oblations (*havana*) using the flesh born of that very asterism, once the mandala has been practiced;
likewise, it occurs even by offering the five limbs of that same tree into the fire kindled with fuel from the tree of the enemy’s birth asterism.

Death occurs for enemies through the practice of the *maṇḍala* rite performed at the [appropriate] time. By offering oblations of *pakṣākṣa* seeds smeared with mustard oil during the practice of the *maṇḍala*, leprosy—a disease that destroys the body—shall arise for those enemies.
[This is done] with black pepper and mustard combined, smeared with mustard oil.

By performing oblations into the maṇḍala practiced for this purpose, the enemy shall become afflicted with a fever of burning heat. In all these cases, the number of oblations must not be forgotten; it is stated to be equal to the number of recitations (japa). Regarding the aforementioned applications for the nine cruel rites, any specific details such as the performance of self-protection (ātmarakṣā) that have been mentioned should be elaborated upon.

Thus end the applications for the performance of fierce *homa* rites. As for the applications for libations (*tarpaṇa*), all those mentioned in the context of *Nityaklinnā* should be performed with this *vidyā*; by means of that, the respective results as stated shall be attained.
Now, the applications of the yantras.

In that regard, as to how there might be two syllables of the *vidyā* in each of the various compartments (*koṣṭha*), the plurality of the *vidyā*-syllables must be accomplished. And since this is achieved by following the fact that the *vidyā* contains the phonemes of the full mandala (*pūrṇamaṇḍala-varṇagarbhatva*), it should be done so;
for some say that in the root [text], those phonemes are to be inserted before the letter *ca*, according to which [the sequence] would be *aca āca ica īca* and so forth.

Others maintain that *kaca* and *khaca*, and so forth, are to be inserted after those [letters]. According to their view, *cacāci* and *cīci*, and so forth, as well as *cakacakheca*, are joined at the end of the complete Vidyā; some say that in their system, *kacakācaki* and so forth, and *cakaukaṃ cakausvacakaugeti* and so forth, are the mantras to be written, and that the conjunction occurs between two letters of the Vidyā. However, [the correct view is] that the conjunction occurs between the two letters of the Vidyā.

Following the root syllables, here is a summary verse of these four views: Some say that there is first the conjunction with *vāyu* (the wind), while others say that there is the conjunction with *lipi* (the script). Yet others say this is the end of the *vidyā*, whereas we declare it to be the conjunction with another *vidyā*. According to this view, they are: *cakauṃ*, *cākauṃ*, *cikauṃ*, *cīkauṃ*, *cukauṃ*.
By the sequence beginning with *cūkauṃ*, *cṛkauṃ*, *cṝkauṃ*, *cḹkauṃ*, *cekauṃ*, *caikauṃ*, *cokauṃ*, *caukauṃ*, *caṃkauṃ*,

*caḥkauṃ*, *cakakauṃ*, *cakākauṃ*, *cakikauṃ*, *cakīkauṃ*, and so forth, the conjunction of twenty-six groups (*varga*) is accomplished. This indeed constitutes the "embodiment of the script" (*lipigarbhatva*) of the Vidyā, because the letters of the script are placed one by one within the Vidyā.
Thus, having indicated this, five hundred and sixty-six syllables of the *vidyā* are produced; by means of these, the yantras are to be constructed.

For instance: having first drawn one circle by rotating a compass with its desired radius, and then having drawn two further circles within it, each separated from the others by an interval of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
Having drawn another circle inside that with an interval of four finger-breadths,
and having fashioned a six-petalled lotus whose base is attached to that [circle], one should draw a circle with an interval of one finger-breadth from its pericarp.
Furthermore, having made another circle with an interval of four finger-breadths, and having drawn a hexagon within that space;
then, having fashioned another circle within that with an interval of one finger-breadth, one should draw a triangle there.
Thus, in the first lotus-center (*karṇikā*) of the line-drawn wheel, having written "kauṃ," therein—

Having written the account of the half-vowel *ka* in three lines in vertical order—first the word denoting the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in the nominative case, then the verb repeated twice, and finally the word denoting the goal (*sādhya*) in the accusative case—and having written the three peaks beginning with *cā* (namely *cākauṃ*, *cikauṃ*, and *cīkauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top; ... [the rest of the text follows] ... The procedure for the *kha*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *chā* (namely *chāchauṃ*, *chichauṃ*, and *chīchauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ga*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *jā* (namely *jājauṃ*, *jijauṃ*, and *jījauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *gha*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *jhā* (namely *jhājauṃ*, *jihauṃ*, and *jhījauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ṅa*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *ñā* (namely *ñāñauṃ*, *ñiñauṃ*, and *ñīñauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ca*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *ṭā* (namely *ṭāṭauṃ*, *ṭiṭauṃ*, and *ṭīṭauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *cha*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *ṭhā* (namely *ṭhāṭhauṃ*, *ṭhiṭhauṃ*, and *ṭhīṭhauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ja*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *ḍā* (namely *ḍāḍauṃ*, *ḍiḍauṃ*, and *ḍīḍauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *jha*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *ḍhā* (namely *ḍhāḍhauṃ*, *ḍhiḍhauṃ*, and *ḍhīḍhauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ña*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *ṇā* (namely *ṇāṇauṃ*, *ṇiṇauṃ*, and *ṇīṇauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ṭa*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *tā* (namely *tātāuṃ*, *titāuṃ*, and *tītāuṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ṭha*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *thā* (namely *thāthauṃ*, *thithauṃ*, and *thīthauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ḍa*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *dā* (namely *dādauṃ*, *didauṃ*, and *dīdauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ḍha*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *dhā* (namely *dhādhauṃ*, *dhidhauṃ*, and *dhīdhauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ṇa*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *nā* (namely *nānauṃ*, *ninauṃ*, and *nīnauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *ta*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *pā* (namely *pāpauṃ*, *pipauṃ*, and *pīpauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *tha*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *phā* (namely *phāphauṃ*, *phiphauṃ*, and *phīphauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *da*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *bā* (namely *bābauṃ*, *bibauṃ*, and *bībauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *dha*-syllable is as follows: having written the word denoting the practitioner in the nominative case, the verb in the imperative mood, and the word denoting the goal in the accusative case, one should write the three peaks beginning with *bhā* (namely *bhābhauṃ*, *bhibhauṃ*, and *bhībhauṃ*) clockwise in the three corners starting from the top. The procedure for the *na*-sy

Having written the form *rūpārā*, one should write the six peaks (*ṣaṭkūṭa*) in the form of *cūk-auṃ*, *cūk-auṃ*, *cṛk-auṃ*, *cṝk-auṃ*, *cḷk-auṃ*, and *cḷk-auṃ* clockwise starting from the front in the six corners outside of that. Then, outside of that, in the six petals, one should write clockwise starting from the front: *cek-auṃ*, *caik-auṃ*, *cok-auṃ*, *cauk-auṃ*, *caṃk-auṃ*, and *cak-auṃ*.

Having drawn the six peaks (*ṣaṭkūṭa*) of the forms, the first group of principles (*tatvavarga*), consisting of sixteen syllables, is completed. Then, having written the syllables of the ten elements (*bhūta*) according to one's respective desire within the path formed by the two circles outside the triangle, [one writes them] in the path between the two circles outside the hexagon.

Having written the name of the practitioner and the name of the object to be accomplished around [the center], one should write the *mātṛkā* with the *visarga* in the inner circle and the *mātṛkā* with the *bindu* in reverse order in the outer circle— these two paths being formed by three surrounding circles on a six-petaled lotus; this is the first yantra, provided that...
In the locations of the syllables of the first reality (prathamatattva),
within the three central corners of the hexagon consisting of six petals, one should place the sixteen [syllables] of the second reality (dvitīyatattva).
When it is written in the form *cakākauṃ*, *cakīkauṃ*, *cakukauṃ*, *cakūkauṃ*, *cakṛkauṃ*,

*cakṝkauṃ*, *cakḷkauṃ*, *cakḹkauṃ*, *cakekauṃ*, *cakaikauṃ*, *cakokauṃ*, *cakaukauṃ*, *cakaṃkauṃ*, and *cakaḥ kaum*, then that is the second yantra. In this manner, there are twenty-four [yantras] ending with the letter *ka*.

By writing out each of the sixteen principles (*tattvas*) individually, twenty-four additional yantras are formed; thus, twenty-six yantras have been extracted in total. Furthermore, with the remaining sixteen groups of ten principles beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa*, one Vajra-yantra is produced. This makes twenty-seven in number.
For example: having produced two hundred and eighty-nine (289) squares by means of eighteen lines— extending east-west and north-south, with equal intervals between them and intersecting one another—
and having omitted every ninth square in each of the four directions along the outermost perimeter;

Having erased fifteen squares each within that intervening space, and having drawn downward-pointing triangles in those four corner squares, [one should place] in the second row inside them one square from below the previously discarded square and one on each of its two sides, making a total of...
Having set aside five squares and having cleared the nine-by-nine squares situated within them,
one should likewise set aside seven squares in each corner of the inner path— consisting of the previously set-aside group of five squares plus one square on each of its two sides.
Having cleared away the five squares situated within that interval— that is, the group of five squares—
and having likewise discarded the seven squares located beneath the squares omitted from the previous row within that same path,
one should clear away three squares each at every corner situated within that interval.
Since thirty-two squares have been cleared away in each corner,
a total of one hundred and twenty-eight squares have been cleared away. This being the case:

In the row below the triangle, there are five squares in each direction. Then, in the next inner row, and further in the innermost row, seven squares remain in each direction. In the final [row], one square remains in each corner. Within that, situated in a regular square formation, are forty-nine squares.

"Remaining" means taken together; one hundred and sixty-one squares remain. Therein, having written the pure *nityā-vidyā* under discussion in the very center square, and having written therein the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the action (*kriyā*), and the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within the half-moon located at the beginning of the *kakārī*.

In the outermost set of four triangles, starting from the apex in sequence, is the first [syllable], which contains within its belly the letter *ka* along with the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the object of practice (*sādhya*), and so forth;
it takes the forms *cayakauṃ*, *cayākauṃ*, *cayikauṃ*, and *cayīkauṃ*, and is produced by the conjunction of the twenty-seventh *tattva* and the sixteenth vowel. It is situated within that.
Having drawn four peaks (*kūṭa*), there are one hundred and fifty-six peak-syllables situated above them.

Starting from the middle cell of the five cells located below the front triangle, proceeding clockwise in the manner of entry, [one recites] *cayukauṃ*, beginning with the peak of its own form (*svarūpakūṭa*), up to *cakṣaḥ*.

One should write the peak-syllables (*kūṭākṣara*), numbering the same as the squares up to the end of the *Kauṃ* [square], one by one. These twenty-seven yantras arise respectively through their conjunction with the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī; therefore, one should write the first and subsequent [yantras] for each respective mansion one by one.

Having combined in equal proportions these twelve substances— sandalwood, red sandalwood, vermilion, camphor, gorocana, saffron, agallochum, kuṣṭha, cardamom, kaṅkola, nutmeg, and the powders of the trees belonging to one’s own birth constellation (p. 215a)— one should mix them together.

Having finely ground [the ingredients] with the juice of the tree belonging to its own asterism and with snow-water, one should draw the respective yantra for each asterism, beginning with Aśvinī, during that specific asterism and not at any other time or for any purpose whatsoever. Thus, having drawn the Aśvinī-asterism yantra under the Aśvinī asterism, all diseases are destroyed through worship. The procedure for this is as follows:

In one's own house, upon a Palāśa or similar seat, or on a perfectly level ground, during the Aśvinī nakṣatra, one should draw the first yantra— consisting of a central square containing the full syllables of the vidyā interspersed with the name of the person to be protected (sādhya) in such forms as "May the disease of Devadatta be pacified"— and therein [place the mantra].

Having observed the relative lightness or heaviness of the task at hand, one should worship the present *nityā* together with her retinue for a period of either three nights or twenty-seven nights. Having placed a water-pot (*kalaśa*) there, one should fill it with a decoction of the medicinal herbs corresponding to the letters of the present *vidyā*. Within that pot, the general [rites] are to be performed.

After performing the rites beginning with the meditation on the *Sarvamaṅgalā* wheel and ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*), one should again worship the principal *Nityā* together with her attendants (*sāvaraṇa*). Having dismissed her and brought forth the water-pot (*kalaśa*), one should place the patient upon the yantra there and sprinkle him with the water. Then the patient, freed from his ailments, shall become happy; such is the first yantra.
Thus, it has been stated that [this practice] possesses both the duty to be performed and its fruit.

The second diagram is also written in the *Bharaṇī* asterism, containing within it the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and other details such as "the victory of Devadatta over Kurukuru," with the *kūṭaka* (cipher) situated in the center of the wheel.
By following the series of ritual procedures beginning with worship as previously described and ending with consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one shall attain victory.
There are nine yantras, starting from the third and ending with the eleventh, which consist of the nine lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Pūrvaphālgunī.

Among those [nakṣatras], one should write the *kūṭayantra*—which takes the form of a *cakhakauṃ* with the syllables situated in the middle and contains the *sādhya* (the person for whom the rite is performed) and other elements—in the form "O Devadatta, pacify, pacify the intense affliction of the sun," etc., within the asterism Kṛttikā. Therein, through the worship of the Sun preceded by the worship of the present *Nityā*, the affliction of the sun is pacified; likewise in the subsequent cases as well.

This is to be employed in the worship of the planets (*graha-pūjana*). However, here there is this addition: in the yantras of the nine planets beginning with the third [day], one should worship each respective planet in its corresponding location according to the sequence, using fifteen-fold repetitions of solar hymns in the intervals between the triangles, hexagons, and six-petaled lotuses, with such mantras as "I thoroughly propitiate [the Sun]," and so forth.

When various planets are worshipped at once, one should worship the respective planetary yantras at their corresponding gates and under their respective asterisms (nakṣatras), following the stated sequence of directions such as center, east, southeast, and so forth. Even when the day falls on an asterism other than those [specifically mentioned], it is logical to follow the requirement of the asterism itself; for the writing of the asterisms upon the yantras is the final step.
Because its power is understood [to be great], these eleven yantras are employed for their respective results.
Due to its circularity, the yantra numbered sixteen is joined with the previously mentioned rites such as worship and consecration;
it [brings about] the enemy's withdrawal from military exertion, the subduing of Yakṣas, and rain.

One should counteract [the obstacle]. Thus, following the movement of the *pratimitra* and others, the remaining spokes (*arā*) of the five-fold machine from that point onward—whose nature is described as the hands, the *Citrā* asterism, and so forth—are likewise the spokes whose nature consists of the fifteen lunar days (*tithis*) beginning with *pratipad*, as they have been traditionally taught. Among those [spokes] in the month of Caitra...

Immediately following [the phrase] "in Hastacitrā," etc., one should also write the words beginning with "the first lunar day" (*pratipad*) and "the second" (*dvitīyā*), ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*). Likewise, the traditional injunctions state: "Perform [the rite] for Devadatta on the first lunar day," and so forth.

One should write the name of the person to be acted upon—such as "Destruction of Disease" (roga-nāśam) and so forth—in the *kūṭa* (syllabic square) that arrives according to its respective sequence. By means of these yantras individually, through worship, consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and other rites, there is the accomplishment of all tasks, including the destruction of every disease, victory, and immobilization (*stambhana*). In all of these yantras...

One should worship the two lords of the weekday in the southeast and southwest corners, the lord of the lunar mansion in the northwest, and also the lords of the lunar day and the lord of the direction in the northeast;
otherwise, the attainment of the stated results will not occur.
Thus end the applications of the yantras.

Having meditated upon the twenty-seven yantras that have come down through tradition, located respectively in the six chakras named Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Anāhata, Viśuddha, Maṇipūra, and Ājñā— numbering five, four, four, five, four, and five [respectively]— therein resides Citrānityā, together with the Ḍākinīs and others who are joined with their respective powers within those chakras.

One should meditate upon the Śaktis. For one incapable of such meditation, having drawn five yantras preceded by the [deity's] form, one should draw a single Mūlādhāra-cakra outside of them. Having drawn six to nine cakras on the outside, one should draw a single Svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra consisting of six spokes outside of those. One should proceed in this same manner for the cakras drawn subsequently as well.

Having worshipped Citrā along with her enclosure (sāvaraṇā), one should again worship the Śākinī and other powers residing in the cakras beginning with the Mūlādhāra, each joined with their respective powers consisting of two, four, or more syllables. This practice of worship should be performed for three fortnights, seven nights, or twenty-seven nights according to one's purpose; by this, everything desired is attained.
The practitioner attains [this]. Thus are the applications of meditative cultivation.
Thus concludes the introduction to the manifold impermanence.
