In this manner, the various types of ritual applications (*prayoga*) and means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) have been demonstrated for the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*), beginning with the first day (*pratipad*) and ending with the full moon (*pūrṇimā*).

Having instructed [the disciple] regarding each respective *nityā* after performing the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the day prior to the guest-offering, one should instruct the mantra of the deity of the *bali* offering for that specific *nityā*, named Kurukullā. We shall now demonstrate the method of that instruction as well as the practical application (*prayoga*) of the worship of those *nityās*. On a certain level and smooth ground...
Having fashioned two squares joined by gates on the eastern and western sides,

and having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp within them, one should arrange a wheel of nine triangles (navayonicakra) upon that pericarp and a bindu within that as well; thus, having drawn out the mandala for daily worship according to this procedure using vermilion and other substances.

Above that, in the midst of a heap of rice, one should place a jar made of gold or any other material, filled with water from sacred fords and the like, gold, copper, grain, the nine gems, and sandalwood; it should be adorned with *indravallī*, *panasa*, *aśvattha*, and other plants, as well as with *mūyaka* and *mātuluṅga* fruits. Inside of that—

Having performed the entire cycle of rites beginning with the visualization of the Sarvamaṅgalā-cakra and ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*), one should again visualize the circle of the deities of the present rite according to the form described immediately above. Therein, one should worship Kurukullā together with her retinue (*sāvaraṇā*). However, the worship that is not part of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is performed in the circle alone; there is no requirement for a ritual jar (*kalaśa*) therein.

The method for the worship of both wheels is as follows: after completing the morning rites, such as anointing with fragrant oil and bathing in scented water, one whose body is adorned with sandalwood paste, garlands, and other ornaments enters the sacrificial hall.
Having sat upon a seat of red wool or similar material consecrated by the previously mentioned *āsana-vidyā*, one assumes either the *svastika* or *padma* posture.
Having sat down with the complete root-vidyā as presented, and having performed the rites up to the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) using the seed-syllable of the *māyā* of emanation [***],
one should worship the nine Nāthas upon one’s own head according to the lineage of one’s own gurus with their respective mantras; then, having recited the hymn to the Nāthas.

Having requested her permission, one should begin the worship according to the method to be described: having meditated upon the goddess at hand, one should worship Kurullā together with her retinue using the five mental offerings; then, having obtained her permission—

The practitioner should then ascend the jewel-boat (*ratnapota*). Thereafter, having meditated upon the identity of one's own self with the mantra of the deity presided over by one's own Lord, one should worship the three deities of the seat (*pīṭha*) situated above the lion-throne and other supports of the wheel, using the following: *hrīṃ ikṣusāgarāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ ratnapotāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ valicakrāya namaḥ*.

Having placed the general *arghya* vessel— made of any one of the five materials such as gold, possessing a base, filled with water scented by the five substances beginning with *gorocana*, and situated between the self-worship wheel and the jewel boat within the sugarcane ocean— one should [purify] the waters in that base vessel sequentially with the three *vāla* seed-syllables.

Having contemplated [the elements] consisting of fire, sun, and moon; the five [substances] such as *rocanā* contained therein; the five [elements] beginning with earth; the water contained therein; and the circle of goddesses (*devīcakra*) under discussion, one should—preceded by the meditation on the identity of that water and the goddess under discussion—proceed according to the method to be described.
Having meditated upon the goddess at hand and worshipped Kurullā together with her retinue using the five mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*),
the practitioner should receive her command and board the jewel-ship. Then,
having consecrated it ten times with the present mantra and worshipped it, he should also fully worship the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*) with the mantras of the six limbs.
With the consecrated *arghya* water, one should [sprinkle] oneself,
the water contained in the four vessels for washing the feet (*pādya*) and so forth placed on the northern side of the general *arghya* vessel,
and the perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, and other materials required for worship and the fire-oblation (*homa*) placed on one's own right side.

Having sprinkled [the materials] with the present vidyā, and having again performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the vidyā, one should take the water for the general arghya offering in the hand with a ladle. (p.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in this manner— specifying the place, time, one’s own lineage, zodiac sign, and intention, and saying, "I shall perform the worship of the goddess Kurukullā according to the prescribed rite and as my intellect dictates"— one should pour out the water held in the hand. Then,
even if one has not performed the preliminary rites such as the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) due to being occupied with another deity, at this point [they must be performed].
Having substituted the present vidyā itself in place of each respective other mantra assigned to those various rites and having performed those respective rites;

and at the conclusion of the nyāsa of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of the Mātṛkā, having joined the present vidyā—or the seed-syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ) together with the visarga or the nasal bindu—to each [letter] individually at the beginning [of each group]; and having performed the nyāsa of the letters of the Mātṛkā in their respective locations.

*Aiṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *klīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *sauḥ* to the tuft of hair, *vaṣaṭ*; *aiṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*; *klīṃ* to the eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *sauḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*. Having thus performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) by assigning [the mantras] to the thumbs and other fingers, as well as to the heart and other body parts, one should perform the complete root-mantra of Kurukullā: *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ*.

Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) three times with this twenty-five-syllable mantra: *mama sarvajanavaśamānaya hoṃ svāhā*, one should proceed with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and subsequent rites. This is as follows:
having first fashioned the triple-sectioned mudrā (*trikhaṇḍā*) and placed red flowers in the joined palms, [one should contemplate] from the *mūlādhāra* upwards.

While visualizing that mass of radiant light— abounding with the rays of fire, sun, and moon— pervading as far as the *brahmarandhra*, flowing unceasingly through the path of the nose, and being transferred into the *bindu* within the *cakra* by the casting of that handful of flowers; [one should recite] "Kurukullā svāhā," followed by seven syllables.
Having made the prayer, "O Bhoktruru-kulle-draha-cakra, please be invoked," and having thus accomplished the invocation,

one should visualize that some rays of its splendor have radiated out to their respective locations and have transformed into the forms of the Lords (nātha), weapons, and the protective enclosure (āvaraṇa).
One should meditate upon a mass of light situated in the center, having a form understood through meditation. And that meditation is as follows:
[one should visualize her] with disheveled hair, naked, red, with the body of an elephant, and bearing...

One should meditate on [the goddesses] holding a bow, arrows, a noose, and a goad in their hands; these goddesses, whose weapons, forms, and colors correspond to those [of the lords], reside in the musical instruments; they have performed the ritual bath after menstruation, possess throbbing yonis, and always have eyes reddened with bliss.
Thus, the meditation for the weapons and śaktis of the lords is of this single uniform kind.

Furthermore, one should perform the installation (*sthāpana*) and subsequent rites by first uttering the *māyābīja* (hrīṃ) together with the *visarga* (ḥ) and *bindu* (ṃ), preceded by its respective insignia, in place of the mantra-text. For example:
*hrīṃḥ bhokurukulle iha cakre sthāpitā bhava*; *hrīṃḥ bhokurukulle iha cakre sanniruddhā bhava*.

Having made the request while displaying the respective mudrās: "Hrīḥ Bhok Kurukulle, you are veiled here in this maṇḍala; Hrīḥ Bhok Kurukulle, may you become present here in this maṇḍala. Then, having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs for the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra: "The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of this Kurukullā are here in this maṇḍala," and so forth.
Having established the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) by means of the *rūpā-prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā*, one should worship with the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*).

The mantras for these are as follows: having offered the water from the general *arghya* vessel as the foot-water (*pādya*) with the mantra "Hrīḥ, I prepare the foot-water for Kurullāya," one should present it at the two feet with the seed-syllable of Māyā (the Visarga) preceded by "Hrīḥ. In this same manner...

Having offered the *arghya* and other items using the mantras prescribed for the respective places such as the *pādya*, one should offer the *arghya* and so forth while reciting the seed-syllable *Māyā* (Hrīṃ) together with the *visarga* and *bindu*. In this manner, having worshipped with twelve services (*upacāras*), one should proceed to the thirteenth service. The method for that is as follows:

In the middle portion between the two abodes of the goddesses of speech named Vimalā and Jayinī, within three rows, [he worshipped] the divine lords (divyanātha) named Īśāna, Prakāśa, Vimarsa, and Ānanda.
Above that row are the Siddhanāthas named Śrījñānaśrī and Satyaśrīpūrṇa;

further above that row are the Mānavanāthas named Svabhāva, Pratibha, and Subhaga, [accompanied] by the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) and so forth, with their powers (*śakti*) projected into the station of the Nātha.

Having worshipped [the deities] with their respective mantras, one should worship the mantra-gem power (mantramaṇī-śakti) situated at the rear—that is, the western part—of the ship, who is intent on going to her desired destination and is appointed for the task of moving the ship. Having worshipped her with the mantra: "Hrīṃḥ, I worship the sandals of the Bhrāmaṇī power," [one worships] of the ship...

Having worshipped the power Drāviṇī—residing in the foremost part of the eastern section, appointed specifically for the task of moving the boat—with the mantra: *hrīṃḥ, I worship the sandals of the power Drāviṇī*, one should perform the worship of the four enclosures (*caturāvaraṇa*). Therein, the practitioner, seated facing east within the square, [should worship] the one situated in the position directly in front.
Beginning from the northern branch of the western door situated on the right side of the Goddess and proceeding to the southern branch of the western door situated on her left side—

one should worship the ten powers, beginning with Sūryā, in sequence upon these ten faces. Specifically, on the path connected to the northern branch of the western door, one worships Hrīṃ Sūryarūpiṇī.

I worship the sandals of Śakti. In the square on the northern path of the northwest corner, I worship the sandals of Somarūpiṇī (OṂ HRĪṂ). On the northern path, I worship the sandals of Tithirūpiṇī Śakti (HRĪṂ). In the northeast square, I worship the sandals of Vārarūpiṇī Śakti (HRĪṂḤ).
On the northern branch of the eastern door, I worship the sandal of the power (śakti) in the form of Yakṣiṇī, Oṃ Hrīṃḥ. On the southern branch of that very same eastern door:

Hrīṃ, I worship the sandal of the power (śakti) whose form is Tārā. In the southeast corner: Hrīṃ, I worship the sandal of the power whose form is Vega. On the southern path: Hrīṃ, [I worship] the sandal of the power whose form is Nakṣatra.

I worship. In the southwest (nairṛtya), I worship the sandals of the power (śakti) Hrīṃḥ Rāśirūpiṇī. On the southern branch of the western door, I worship the sandals of the power Hrīṃḥ Karaṇarūpiṇī. Having thus worshipped these ten powers, at the end of the complete twenty-five-syllable mantra:

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with the mantra, "I worship the sandals of Kurukullā," and having offered a handful of flowers for the presentation of that worship with the mantra, "Hrīṃ! May these deities of the first enclosure of Kurukullā accept this worship," [one should worship] on the eight petals, starting from the petal in front of the goddess and proceeding clockwise: "Hrīṃ! The sandals of the power (śakti) Vyomarūpiṇī..."

I worship. Hrīṃḥ! I worship the sandals of the power of touch, whose form is that of wind. Hrīṃḥ! I worship the sandals of the power of form, whose form is that of fire. Hrīṃḥ! I worship the sandals of the power of taste, whose form is that of water. Hrīṃḥ! I worship the sandals of the power of smell, whose form is that of earth.
" Hrīṃḥ, I worship the sandal of the power of life-force (prāṇa-śakti-pādukā). Hrīṃḥ, I worship the sandal of the power of intellect (buddhi-śakti-pādukā).

Hrīṃḥ, I worship the sandal of the power of energy (śakti-śakti-pādukā). Having worshipped the eight powers with these mantras, one should worship the sandal of Kurukullā situated in the center at the end of the complete twenty-five-syllable vidyā, saying: "I worship the sandal of Kurukullā."

Having worshipped the Goddess, and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as the dedication of that worship with the words, "May the deities of the second enclosure of Kurukullā accept the worship," one should worship the eight goddesses of speech, beginning with Vaśinī, in the eight *yoni*s starting from the front and proceeding clockwise, using the very mantras mentioned in the introduction to the Lalitā [chapter]. [This completes the worship.]
At the end of the twenty-five syllable mantra, having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with the words "I worship Kurukullā-pādukā," [one should proceed].

"Hrīṃ! May these deities of the third enclosure of Kurukullā accept the worship. Having thus offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as an offering of that worship, [one places them] in the two side-paths of the triangle in the order of Vāyu, Nairṛti, Agni, and Īśāna:
"Hrīṃ! Salutation to the arrow (*vāṇa*); Hrīṃ! Salutation to the bow (*cāpa*); Hrīṃ! Salutation to the noose (*pāśa*); Hrīṃ!"

After the worship of the four weapons beginning with "Oṃ namaḥ to Aṅkuśa," [one worships] starting from the triangle in counter-clockwise order: "Hrīṃḥ, I worship the sandals of Icchā-śakti; Hrīṃḥ, I worship the sandals of Jñāna-śakti; Hrīṃḥ, I worship the sandals of Kriyā-śakti. Having thus worshipped the triad of powers, at the end of the complete mantra:

Having worshipped the goddess situated in the center with the words, "I worship Kurukullāpādukā," and having offered a handful of flowers for the dedication of that worship with the words, "Hrīḥ! May these deities of the fourth enclosure of Kurukullā accept this worship," one should perform the thirteen types of service (trayodaśopacāra). The remainder—

Having performed even some form of service consisting of the recitation of hymns, libations, and prostrations, one should then recite the present root mantra— either one hundred or one thousand times— preceded by the *aṅguṣṭhādinyāsa*, *hṛdayādinyāsa*, and *vyāpakanyāsa*; and again, having performed the *aṅguṣṭhādinyāsa* and *hṛdayādinyāsa*.
Having performed the pervasive nyāsa (vyāpaka-nyāsa) and having made the offering consisting of the meditation on non-difference from that [deity],
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the prescribed rule, using either red flowers smeared with ghee, or fragrant white flowers,
or a mixture of food and clarified butter, or simply clarified butter alone, sixteen times.

Having offered oblations one-tenth the number of the daily recitation (*japa*), and having again united that Goddess from the fire with the *bindu* within the worship circle (*pūjācakra*), one should worship Śrī Śiva, who is the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*) conceived as the Goddess’s own seat with the mantra: *hrīḥ saṃvidāsanāya namaḥ*. Above that [is] Kurukullā: *oṃ*...
With the twenty-five-syllable mantra: *kurukulle hrīḥ mama sarvajanaṃ vaśamānaya hūṃ svāhā*, one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and libations.

Having worshipped with the five services consisting of the food offering (*naivedya*), one should present the *bali* at the conclusion of the worship to Kurukullā with the ten-syllable Tārā mantra: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā*, using rice, condiments, and so forth. This presentation of the *bali* is to be performed immediately after the visualization (*dhyāna*), as follows: [one should visualize her] as dark-complexioned and two-eyed...

One should meditate upon her who has two arms, who holds a lotus, who is surrounded by many forms of Śaktis, whose face is smiling, who is adorned with jewels and pearls, and whose pair of lotus-feet rest upon jeweled sandals. This meditation, though intended for specific desires, is likewise [prescribed] when there is the imminent danger of being swept away by water.

Through meditation on Kurukullā, the danger of water is pacified. Some maintain that this very meditation belongs to Tārā. Having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) with a wick containing camphor and other substances, one should visualize the rays of light being withdrawn back into the mass of radiance by means of the mudrā for raising power (*śaktyutthāpana-mudrā*). Then, by means of the space-moving mudrā (*khacarī-mudrā*), one should [withdraw] even that radiance.

One should cause [the deity] to depart into one's own self. Then, having performed the nyāsa of the thumbs and other fingers, the nyāsa of the heart and other limbs, and the pervasive nyāsa (vyāpaka-nyāsa), and having recited the hymn to the Guru and the hymn to the Goddess, one should dismiss [the deity] as being of that very nature and enjoy the worship at ease.
However, in the worship that is an ancillary part of initiation (dīkṣā), the worship—ending with the request for forgiveness—is performed without the ritual of dismissal (udvāsana).
Having performed the rites on the previous day and spent that night in festivities such as dance and song, on the morning of the second day,

after completing the necessary daily duties beginning with the morning rituals, one should worship again with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) using the complete present root mantra. Then, at the end of the dismissal (udvāsana) and other concluding rites, one should [recite] the root-vidyā three times.

After first performing the consecration with the water from the *kalaśa* and satisfying the Guru with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other offerings, the Guru should instruct [the disciple] three times.

As for the remainder, that which was mentioned in the general discussion of initiation applies here as well; however, in the worship that constitutes a limb of the primary daily worship of the Nityā, one should complete the worship by means of the sixteen types of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).
Having performed the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) and the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*),
and even without performing the worship by means of the twenty-five-leaf mantra that occurs after the worship of the seat of consciousness (*saṃvidāsana-pūjā*);

Having performed the ritual acts ending with the offering of oblations (*validāna*), the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), and the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*), and having propitiated that [deity], while the ship is wandering upon the oceans,
one should worship the ocean of sugarcane juice and so forth reached at its very center with the previously mentioned name-mantras.
The specific procedure is that, in order to perform the worship of the *pīṭha*, one should descend from the ship and ascend to the Jewel Island (*ratnadvīpa*).
The method for optional worship (*kāmyapūjā*) is likewise the same; however, the specific details regarding the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) shall be stated later.
The method for worship as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) has also been described exactly as it is, neither deficient nor redundant.
Thus, the fivefold method of Kurukullā worship is twofold: primary (*pradhāna*) and daily (*nitya*), and optional (*kāmya*).

Even as an ancillary (*aṅga*), it is of two kinds: that which is an ancillary to the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of one's own root-mantra, and that which is a preliminary ancillary to the primary daily worship (*pradhānanityapūjā*) of the Pradhānanityā. Furthermore, it serves as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) for one who is unable to perform even the brief supreme worship of the Pradhānanityā. Regarding this, there is the following summary verse:

The ritual for the primary worship consists of two types: the fixed rule (*niyatavidhi*) and the optional rule (*icchāvidhi*). Among these, the former pertains to those who have undergone their own initiation (*nijadīkṣā*). That [initiation] has previously reached the status of being a substitute (*anukalpa*) even for the concise forms of worship. Then follows the measurement of the arrow (*vāṇonmāna*), which constitutes the ritual procedure for the worship of Kurukullā. Thus, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is one who has received initiation and has practiced the obligatory and occasional rites.

Desiring the welfare of oneself and others through the performance of the ritual application (*prayoga*), one should practice the means for attaining knowledge (*vidyāsādhana*). The method for this is precisely as stated in the general introduction to the means for attaining knowledge. In this case, the recitation (*japa*) consists of ten million repetitions;
the fire-oblation (*homa*) is one-tenth of that number, performed with the substances prescribed for the daily oblation (*nityahoma*); and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is likewise.
With water from sacred bathing places and the like, scented with camphor, and in a number equal to one-tenth of the recitation (*japa*),
one should perform worship, infinite praise, recitation, and so forth at all three junctions of the day (*sandhyā*), as well as subsist on a diet of milk.
By means of which the completion of the ritual action for your sake is achieved; thus, having mastered the knowledge, one should perform the applications.
Now follow the applications for the obligatory [rites].

By performing oblations (*homa*) for a period of three nights, seven nights, a fortnight, a month, or a *maṇḍala*— taking into account whether the target is attainable or unattainable— one brings women under one's control by offering mustard seeds smeared with ghee in numbers starting from a thousand. By performing oblations of black pepper smeared with mustard oil, the attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) of women is achieved.

At the time of midnight, by performing oblations of sesame seeds smeared with sesame oil as previously described, women, men, kings, ministers, and others remain under the control of the performer for as long as they live. At midnight, by performing oblations of *vandhūka* flowers smeared with goat’s blood according to the aforementioned method, practitioners become capable of deluding women, even when [the act] has been determined to be an undesirable means.
They become intent upon their desired object.

By performing a *homa* with jasmine flowers that have been smeared with milk and are free from hair, insects, and impurities, one gains mastery over Brahmins. By performing a *homa* with *śatapatra* flowers smeared with milk, one gains mastery over Kṣatriyas.

[These results] come to pass. By offering oblations of *vicakila* flowers of the specific *mallikā* variety, even when smeared with milk, Kṣatriyas become submissive. From an oblation of coconut powder mixed with sugar, smeared with the milk of a white cow that has a white calf, there is the acquisition of gold. [This applies to] those [flowers] soaked in molasses, honey, and ghee.

By performing the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with coconut fruits and honey, in numbers such as a thousand and so forth, according to the previous procedure and for the duration of a *maṇḍala* and so on, one becomes possessed of abundant wealth. For the practitioner who offers plantain fruit, a lotus, or a white water-lily (*kahlāra*) independently [of other substances], there arises an abundance of wealth, grain, and other assets.

The practitioner performing the fire-oblation (havana) with two white and red water-lilies joined together attains everything desired, whether previously mentioned or not. Thus end the applications of the fire-oblation.

In the very same worship previously described, if the act of worship is performed with blue lotuses (*utpala*) in place of flowers, then the destruction of misfortune occurs. By worshipping with white or red lotuses, one attains prosperity; by worshipping with both white and red [lotuses] combined, [the same result is attained].
By worshipping with two *kumuda* flowers, there shall be no deception and one shall obtain fame.

By worshipping with any one of the *japā*, *bandhūka*, or *dāḍima* flowers, there is likewise the attainment of wealth and fame. [One may also worship] with *saugandhika*, *vicakila*, *kuṭaja*, *śatapatra*, *punnāga*, *pāṭala*, or *campaka* flowers.

For the practitioner who worships sequentially on the seven days beginning with Sunday, throughout the duration of the mandala and other rites, there shall be an abundance of wealth, grain, land, clothing, livestock, and so forth. Every day, until the conclusion of the mandala and other rituals, [one should worship] with sandalwood, black agallochum resin, or any other fragrant substance that has been sprinkled upon the site of the fragrance.

For one who worships with saffron consecrated with fragrant substances, there is an abundance of all desired objects; from worship performed with camphor in the aforementioned manner, there is the attainment of good fortune; likewise, from such worship, there is an increase in lifespan, the subjugation of all beings, and the prosperity of wealth consisting of elephants, horses, and the like. [The offering of] musk-scent...

By worshipping for a month or a year with two types of musk, one will attain equality with Kandarpa among women. By worshipping for a year with cardamom, cloves, kaṅkola, and nutmeg according to his own means, the practitioner becomes famous on earth. For one who worships the aforementioned Goddess for a year with pieces of camphor—
A piece of camphor offered to the Goddess becomes truly inexhaustible, and all desired accomplishments come to pass.
Thus conclude the ritual applications for worship.

Having drawn three circles by means of internal and external dimensions, and having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus within them, one should construct the nine-yoni wheel inside the circle of its pericarp according to the previously mentioned method, upon the wheel consisting of the lines of accomplishment (*siddherekhā*).

In the center of the entire [mandala], having written the *māyābīja* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) together with the visarga and bindu— which constitutes the present mantra— and having written within it the name of the practitioner, the words of the rite, and the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should write the first eight syllables of the present mantra in a clockwise direction, starting from the front, upon the eight outer triangles. Then, on each of the eight outer petals, [one should write...]
Having written the sixteen syllables beginning with the ninth [letter], including the *visarga* and excluding *hṛllekhā*, in a double sequence;

having completed the entire present vidyā arranged within the yantra; and having inscribed the *mātṛkā* in forward order along with the *sarmā* on the inner path, [one should inscribe] the *mātṛkā* with the *bindu* on the outer path.

One should write the *mātṛkā* in reverse order; this is the perfected *yantra*. By wearing it on the hands and other limbs, by installing it in one's own house, village, and so forth, by consecrating water in a jar placed within one's own [dwelling], and by worshipping it daily after having installed it in some secluded place—all desired objects are attained for practitioners.

It accomplishes [the goal]. There is also a specific variety within the particular application, such as this: for the attraction of women, one should draw this yantra with *gorocanā* on birch bark or a piece of linen cloth, roll it into a ball, wrap it in wax, and heat it at night with the charcoal of *khadira* wood. Thus, by one who has practiced the rite for a period of time such as a month or a fortnight, [the woman is attracted].

One should draw [the deity] according to one's own desire. For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), having written this very *yantra* on a cloth, on a pedestal made of *palāśa* wood or the like, or with red lead (*darada*), and having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites therein, through the worship of the Goddess in question for a specific period of time, men, women, kings, and others become subjugated.
In short, even lions, tigers, elephants, horses, and so forth, come under one's control. For the purpose of pacification (*śānti*),
having drawn this yantra with red ochre (*agairika*) on a seashore or a riverbank, one should first perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites there for the Goddess in question.

For one who worships throughout the duration of the mandala and other rites, there shall be the destruction of all diseases and the removal of suffering caused by kings, thieves, and others. Regarding gain: having written this very [mantra] with red ochre on either the shore of the ocean or a river, for one who worships there daily throughout the duration of the mandala and other rites—

There shall be the acquisition of cattle, buffaloes, female and male servants, wealth, grain, and so forth. Likewise, by writing this very yantra with sandalwood paste on a seat made of *palāśa* wood or similar materials, and performing the worship of the aforementioned goddess there for the duration of the maṇḍala-day, there will be an abundance of sons, grandsons, wives, wealth, and grain, as well as renown and the destruction of enemies.

If this very yantra is engraved upon a gold leaf or a silver leaf, or if it is written with ink made from *bhūrja* bark, red ochre, and sandalwood, and then— having been consecrated through worship and other rites— it is worn on the hand or elsewhere, then there shall be liberation from all diseases, followed by an increase in wealth, grain, and happiness.
The practitioner shall obtain [the fruit]. Now, we shall demonstrate the yantra of this thirteen-syllable Vidyā:
having drawn six lines each running east-west and north-south on palm leaf with chalk or other materials, such that they are equidistant and intersect one another, one obtains twenty-five squares.

Having completed that, one should construct the vajra-yāntra using the remaining thirteen squares: having set aside the third square from each of the four directions in the outermost row— which serves as the center— and having erased the three squares located between them in each corner, [the yantra is formed].
From each of the single cells in the cardinal directions, one should write downward into the nine cells— specifically in the central cell—
the *māyābīja* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) which constitutes the present vidyā, containing within it the name of the practitioner’s action and the object to be accomplished.
Having written the eight syllables of the Vidyā in a clockwise direction starting from the square below the central square,
and having written the tenth syllable in the western square, the eleventh in the northern square, the twelfth in the eastern square,
and the thirteenth in the southern square, this yantra is perfected. Therein, [one should meditate upon] the Goddess under discussion.

Having worshipped with the thirteen-syllable vidyā, one should then cast balls of thread mixed with mustard seeds, vermilion, salt, *śūraṣi*, long pepper, black pepper, and the milk of the *arka* plant into that yantra. At night, facing the direction of the woman to be summoned, one should draw her forth from the flame of a lamp as she appears there.

One should cause [the target] to suffer by reciting the thirteen-syllable mantra of Kurukullā. By practicing this heating (*tāpana*) throughout the entire mandala, even a young woman who is otherwise impossible to subdue will certainly be attracted.
However, if there is an obstacle due to a particular religious commitment (*dharma-viśeṣa*), she may instead meet with the fire of separation or death. This is the method of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).

Having written the yantra with very clear syllables on either birch bark or palm leaf, and having made a small ball (*gulikā*) from it, one should place this yantra within the heart-region of a doll (*sikekā*) representing the person to be acted upon; then, while reciting the present vidyā, one should heat it at night with the flame of a lamp. By that means, [one subdues] kings, men, and women.

Even lions and other such creatures remain under one's control for as long as life lasts. Now, even if through the application of powerful means they attain a state equal to that of a slave, nevertheless, they shall never perform any contrary action.
Having written this mantra upon a white cloth with a liquid mixture of red ochre combined with sandalwood paste, one should rub this yantra.
For this practitioner who lies upon it after being consecrated by recitation (*japa*) and other rites, [the deities] become submissive as if indifferent.
Thus is *vaśya* (subjugation). Having written this *yantra* on a linen cloth or a birch-bark leaf using ink produced from lampblack—

Therefore, having first performed tactile contact with the mantra written upon the aforementioned yantra and having recited that mantra a thousand times or more, for one who wears the perfected yantra, there shall be the destruction of all diseases and the destruction of suffering caused by kings, thieves, and the like.
Thus ends the section on peace (*śānti*). Now follow the applications of the seven-syllabled mantra-yantra, which constitutes this very vidyā.
Having drawn two circles with an intervening space on a palm leaf, birch bark, arka leaf, or linen cloth using red ochre or similar pigment,
and having drawn a hexagon within that space, one should write the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the center; then,
having written the name of the practitioner and others within its interior, one writes "kurukulle svāhā" in the six corners.

One should write the six syllables one by one in sequence; having consecrated this very yantra with the present seven-syllable vidyā ten thousand times, one should bury it at an anthill. By that means, on that very day, the serpents dwelling in that region will flee far away. This same yantra may also be used for ornaments such as rings, bracelets, and armlets.

Having drawn [the yantra] and performed the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and other rites, one should worship the Goddess therein; then, having placed it in some secluded spot, for the practitioner who daily worships the Goddess present there,
there shall be no fear in his house of ghosts, spirits, *piśācas*, epilepsy, *vetālas*, *rākṣasas*, *gandharvas*, serpents, scorpions, tigers, and the like.

It does not happen. Having cast this very yantra into a water jar, one should consecrate that water with the seven-syllable vidyā one thousand times. Through sprinkling with that water, the affliction of poison is destroyed for one suffering from it;
by drinking such water, there is the destruction of all poisons, even those most terrifying.

Having written this very *yantra* on a coconut leaf using a pen made from a fingernail-tip, one should visualize this written *yantra* in the form of a serpent and consecrate it with the aforementioned *vidyā* ten thousand times.

When that coconut leaf is afflicted by means of thorns, needles, and so forth, the serpent becomes afflicted; when it is split, the serpent is split—this is indeed a great marvel. Having well-inscribed this very same yantra in sand, one should worship the Goddess mentioned therein with the aforementioned vidyā. One should then encircle the seven-fold serpent with yantras that have attained the nature of the sand itself.
Therefore, even though the snake has awakened, it will not be able to move even a single step outside of that place.
Now, the yantras for the complete sciences.
In this Vidyā, there are thirteen letters— ka, u, la, ya, oṃ, ha, ma, sa, va, ja, na, and śa— which do not repeat.
When each of these is joined with the sixteen vowels, they reach a total number of two hundred and eight.

By writing thirty-six syllables on each petal, those transformed letters (vikṛtākṣara) are fully employed across the eight petals. To do so: having first drawn three circles on the outside, then fashioned an eight-petaled lotus within them, and having constructed a nine-yoni wheel in its pericarp (karṇikā), therein—

Having written the two syllables *ka* and *kā* in the central womb-position, both internally and externally; and having written the syllables of the practitioner’s action (*sādhakakriyā*) and the words of the goal (*sādhyapada*) within the half-moon starting from the letter *ka*; then, outside of that, proceeding clockwise from the tip of each corner, one should write the eight letters beginning with the third and ending with the tenth—namely, *ki ki kū kū kṛ kṝ kḷ kḹ*.

Having drawn the form, [one should place] on the petals outside of that, in pairs, the syllables *ke kai* on the eastern petal, *ku kau* on the northwestern petal, and *kaṃ kaḥ* on the northern petal. (p.
On the petal of Īśāna, the vowels ending in the union of vowel and vowel are *a* and *ā*. On the eastern petal are *i* and *ī*; on the southeastern petal, *ū* and *ū*.

On the southern petal are *ṛ* and *ṝ*; on the southwestern petal, *ḷ* and *ḹ*. Having written these two forms and letters, thirty-six spokes are written within the modified syllables (*vikṛtākṣara*). Then, in the two outer circumambulatory paths (*vīthī*), [the following are placed].

Having written the *mātṛkā* with visarga in direct order (*anuloma*) in the inner circle (*vīthī*), and the *mātṛkā* with bindu in reverse order (*pratiloma*) in the outer circle, the first yantra is accomplished. Furthermore, if within that very same line-drawn wheel (*rekhāmaya-cakra*) described previously, one proceeds from each preceding written syllable to each subsequent one according to the method stated before—

The thirty-six syllables are each written seven times. Thus, seven other diagrams and the first one, totaling eight diagrams, are established; and the transformed syllables of the Vidyā are filled in. Among them, regarding the first diagram: it is traditionally taught that the writing of the *sādhya* (the object to be accomplished) and so forth should be done in the middle portion of the leaf, and in that very place...

On Sunday, one should write: "O Devadatta, accomplish [this] on Sunday; subjugate Yajñadatta," or "O Devadatta, accomplish [this] on the day of the Sun; subjugate Yajñadatta. On Monday, however, one should write: "O Devadatta, accomplish [this] on Monday; subjugate Yajñadatta," and so forth. Having written these for each of the seven days, one should perform daily worship and wear [the mantra] on those respective days.

Regarding the *sthāpana* (installation): by means of the sprinkling of water from a flask empowered by that yantra, or by means of a vehicle [conveyed] by water from a flask conjoined with that yantra, the practitioner shall certainly accomplish the summoning [of the desired object], the pacification of disease, and the acquisition of wealth and so forth. As for the second and subsequent seven yantras, they are to be applied respectively on the days of the Sun and the other planets; for each individual day, the name [of the deity] ending in the seventh case is used. Thereafter—

One should accomplish [the rite]; thus, having written the verbal root *sādhayet* (he should accomplish), followed by "therefore necessarily attract" (*tato'vaśyam ākarṣaṇam*) and so forth as previously described, one should employ [these mantras] for those various aforementioned tasks.

Furthermore, one should place the sevenfold array of yantras, composed of their respective protective syllables, in some secluded spot within the midst of the emerged ship; by that means, protection for the ship from water and other dangers will be secured. In all these cases, the application of worship and so forth consists precisely of the maṇḍala and other such forms. One vajra-yantra is composed of all the modified syllables.

For example: having laid down twenty-two threads each extending east-west and twenty-two threads each extending north-south, with equal intervals between them and intersecting one another, and thus forming four hundred and forty-one squares; and therein, in the first row—

In the four directions, having set aside the eleventh square located in the very center, and having erased the group of nineteen squares situated within the intervening space at each corner; then, in the second row,
[one should erase] the square immediately below the previously set-aside square, as well as one on each of its two sides, making a total of three.
Having set aside three squares each in the four directions, and having erased the fifteen squares situated in the interval between them; then, in the third row,
from the square immediately following the previously set-aside square, take three squares and one square on each side of those two.
Having combined [the grids], and having set aside five squares in each of the four directions,
and having erased the eleven squares situated in the intervals between them; then, in the fourth path,
from the previously set-aside square, there are five subsequent squares and one square on each of their two sides.
Having set aside seven squares in each of the four directions to form a combined group of seven squares,
and having erased the seven squares situated in the intervals between them; [one should then erase] the seven lower squares previously set aside in the fifth row.

Having set aside one square on each side of those two, and having cleared away the three squares situated in the intervals between them in each of the four directions, [one obtains] the *koṣṭhanakas*. Together, these constitute the *koṣṭhanakas*.

Fifty-five squares are wiped out at each corner; thus, in total, twenty squares are wiped out. Two hundred and twenty-one squares remain, and in all four of those outermost peripheral squares, one should draw downward-pointing triangles. In all of them—
Having written the seed-syllable *māyā* (hīṃ) with its *visarga*, one should write the name of the practitioner and so forth within it.

In the remaining two hundred and seventeen squares, beginning from the square below the southeast corner and proceeding clockwise in a counter-clockwise direction (*pradakṣiṇya-praveśagatyā*), one should write the *vikṛta* letters all around; thus, only a central group of nine squares remains.

In that [diagram], having written the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ) together with the *visarga* and *bindu* in the very center of all the squares, and having written the name of the practitioner and so forth within it, one should write the twenty-four syllables— excluding the seed-syllable of Māyā with its *visarga*— in the remaining eight squares, starting from the square directly below the central one and proceeding clockwise in groups of three. This is as follows:
Having drawn the Vajra-mechanism (vajrayantra) upon a new, pure white cloth or a linen garment,

and having performed the preliminary rites such as the installation of the vehicle and the consecration of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), one should worship the Goddess present therein. This protects the ship— placed upon the vessel— from the fear of sinking into the great ocean and other dangers.
This yantra, when propitiated for a period such as a month or a lunar cycle, invariably accomplishes all the aforementioned purposes, including subjugation, attraction, and so forth.
Thus end the applications of the yantras.
Vedadatta, whom she intended to bring under her own control, was rendered unconscious by the Goddess’s striking him with a blade of kuśa grass and bound around the neck with a noose.

Having made the bride join her palms in *añjali* and bow down again and again while she says, "Protect me! Protect me!", and drawing her toward his own feet, he should recite the presented mantra a thousand times during the night, beginning from the time of the mandala construction and continuing every day; by this, whether a man or a woman, anyone at all—

One brings [the subject] under control with certainty. Alternatively, while recollecting the Goddess—who, having pierced the subject with Her own goad and pulled him by the hair on his head, drags him by the feet while he repeatedly cries out, "Protect me! Protect me!"—one should recite the present vidyā one thousand times throughout the duration of the maṇḍala and other rites. By that, [the goal is achieved].

Men and women alike come under one's control. Or else, while recollecting the sādhya—who is surrounded on all sides by the splendor of the described vidyā, who stands with palms joined in reverence, and who repeatedly cries out "Protect me! Protect me! as he approaches the feet of the practitioner—one should recite the aforementioned vidyā a thousand times during the night, continuing until the time for the mandala ritual. By that, [the result is achieved].
All beings, beginning with humans, become pure.
Thus end the applications of meditative cultivation.
And this section concerning Kurukullā is completed.

Thus, in order to suggest that— by means of even this independence from other [methods] such as the "eternal" (nitya) and so forth— the various goddesses who fulfill the desires of their practitioners will surely bring about every desired goal, including all forms of initiation (dīkṣā), spiritual practice (sādhana), the eternal (nitya), and the optional (kāmya), within the worship of all these goddesses; [the author], having described [them] both generally and specifically from one perspective, subsequently...
Having completed the *ku-dīkṣā* along with its auxiliary parts, we shall now demonstrate the necessary duties to be performed:

having placed the disciple in the region of his own nostril corresponding to the flowing breath, one should [visualize] the triad of wheels (*cakratraya*) at his three locations— the *brahmarandhra*, the heart, and the *mūlādhāra*.

Having meditated upon the form of the Śrīcakra, and having worshipped the Goddess therein with the five mental offerings (*pañcopacāra*) preceded by invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, one should place the hand of the living being upon its head and impart [the teaching] for the third time into the ear of the living being. Then, on that day...

Having taught the eternal ignorance (*nityāvidyā*), one should teach the collection of fourteen mantras, beginning with the syllables of the *pūrṇamaṇḍala* and ending with the *gurupādukā* mantra. Those mantras are as follows: *a ā i ī*, etc., sixteen; *ka kā ki kī*, etc., sixteen; *kha khā khi khī*, etc., sixteen; *ga gā gi gī*, etc., sixteen; *gha ghā ghi ghī*, etc., sixteen; *ṅa*.
ṅā ṅi ṅī, and so forth—16; ca cā ci cī, and so forth—16; cha chā chi chī, and so forth—16; ja jā ji jī, and so forth—16;

jha jhā jhi jhī, and so forth—16; ña ñā ñi ñī, and so forth—16; ṭa ṭā ṭi ṭī, and so forth—16; ṭha ṭhā ṭhi ṭhī, and so forth—16; ḍa ḍā ḍi ḍī, and so forth—16; ḍha ḍhā ḍhi ḍhī, and so forth—16; ṇa ṇā ṇi ṇī, and so forth—16; ta...

*Tā ti tī* etc. (16); *tha thā thi tī* etc. (16); *da dā di dī* etc. (16); *dha dhā di dhī* etc. (16); *na nā ni nī* etc. (16); *pa pā pi pī* etc. (16); *pha phā phi phī* etc. (16); *va vā vi vī* etc.
(16); *bha bhā bhi bhī* etc. (16); *ma mā mi mī* etc. (16); *ya yā yi yī* etc. (16); *ra rā ri rī* etc. (16).

16 *la lā li lī* and so forth; 16 *va vā vi vī* and so forth; 16 *śa śā śi śī* and so forth; 16 *ṣa ṣā ṣi ṣī* and so forth; 16 *sa sā si sī* and so forth; 16 *ha hā hi hī* and so forth; 16 *la lā li lī* and so forth; 16 *kṣa kṣā kṣi kṣī* and so forth—this is one complete mantra. 1 *ā kā khā gā ghā ṅā cā chā jā jhā ñā ṭā ṭhā*.
Ḍā ḍhā ṇā tā thā dā dhā nā pā phā bā bhā mā yā rā lā vā śā ṣā sā hā lā kṣā— this is the second mantra, designated by the syllables [ending] with long vowels.
Thus ends the third mantra, designated as Kāmakalā. These three syllables constitute the essence of Kālanityā.

The nine groups of lords (*navanāthavargāḥ*) are as follows: *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, o, aṃ*—this is the first group, consisting of the eight short vowels; *ā, ī, ū, ai, au, aḥ*—this is the second group. Each of the consonant groups *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa* consists of five letters each, followed by *ya, ra, la, va, śa*.

The fifth mantra consists of thirty-six *lakṣas* (one hundred thousand) repetitions of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), beginning with *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *e*. The fourth mantra consists of five colors: the eighth group (*varga*) of six thousand repetitions of five colors, and the ninth group of five colors.

[The syllables are: *a*, *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*; *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*; *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *ṇa*; *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*; *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, *bha*, *ma*; *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*; *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*, *la*, *kṣa*. The fifth mantra consists of thirty-six *lakṣas* of the thirty-six principles. [The vowels are: *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *e*.

The sixteenth mantra consists of the sixteen digits (*kalās*): *ai*, *o*, *au*, *aṃ*, *aḥ*. The seventh mantra is the science of the letters of the sixty *ghaṭikās*, beginning with the letters corresponding to the rising of each respective day, starting with "I worship the *pādukā* of the formless *ghaṭikā-nityā*" and so forth; [the sequence begins]: *aṃ*, *āṃ*, *iṃ*, *īṃ*, "I worship the *pādukā* of Aries," *uṃ*, *ūṃ*, *ṛṃ*, *ṝṃ*.

I worship the sandals of Vṛṣa. Ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ, I worship the sandals of the couple (Mithuna). Oṃ auṃ kaṃ khaṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Karkaṭa. Gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Siṃha. Chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Kanyā. Ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Tulā. Ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Kīṭa. Dhaṃ naṃ...

*Paṃ phaṃ*, the sign of Aquarius (*cāpamāsa*); *vaṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ*, the sign of Pisces (*mīnamāsa*); *raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ*, the sign of Aries (*kumbhamāsa*); *ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ*, I worship the sandals of the sign of Pisces (*mīnāpādukāṃ*). These are the mantras of the twelve zodiac signs; this is the eighth mantra. *Moṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ*, salutation to the Sun (*arkāya namaḥ*); *jhaṃ rī ḷṃ*.

Ḷṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aṃḥ, salutation to Soma; koṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ, salutation to Bhauma; coṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ, salutation to Budha; ṭoṃ ṭaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ, salutation to Saura; toṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ...
Dhaṃ naṃ, obeisance to Guru; poṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ, obeisance to Rāhu; yoṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ, obeisance to Śukra; ṣoṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to Ketu. Thus.

The mantras of the nine planets ending with the tenth: *ḷ ḹ aṃ ka ṅa ña ṇa na ma śa ha kha śa ha*, I worship the *śakti-pādukā*. *a ā ekacaṭatapayaṣa prāṇa-śakti-pādukām*. *i ī e kha cha ṭha tha pha rakṣāgni-śakti-pādukām*. *ṛ ṝ au gha jha ḍha dha bha va sāṃbu-śakti-pādukām*. *u ū au*.

"Gajaḍadavalalelā śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi" is the eleventh Bhūta-mantra. Its essential form consists of the vowels: *ā ī ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ*; the consonants: *ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa pha ba bha ma ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha lakṣa*. Thus is its nature.

The fifty-one-letter Mātṛkā, the twelve-syllable mantra, the Māyā-bīja, and the Śrī-bīja—which constitute the crown of all protective mantras—are followed by the thirteen-syllable mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ svāhā*. This eight-syllable mantra serves as the crown for the two seed-syllables that constitute the self-mantra (*ātma-mantra*).

Because they are taught separately, there are fourteen mantras, each consisting of fourteen syllables; these begin with the Vidyās of their respective Lords and include the nine Vidyās of Navanātha, which are to be understood through the nine governing sections (*adhikāra*). Thus, that which is relevant to the present subject matter has been obtained.

The practitioner, possessing all knowledge, should recite the *Nātha-stotra* three times, prostrate three times, and offer three handfuls of flowers at the feet [of the Guru]. Then Guha, appearing in the form of Prakāśānandanātha and others, bestows [the name] in the manner of "You are Vimarsānandanātha," which is the name of the Nātha immediately following him. This is for the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
One should also give him a second name, such as Ananta and so forth, derived from the first syllable of the letters corresponding to the *udaya-ghaṭikās*.
Together with these two, along with his well-known name given by his father and others—(p.

Furthermore, one’s own mention by name should be followed in the ritual declaration (*saṅkalpa*) for the worship of the Guru, in the declaration for the praise of the Guru, and also in the composition of poetic works; thereby, the lineage of Gurus becomes well-known, as does the specific date of one's initiation. Then, having cleansed the Śrīcakra, which serves as the support for the water-pot (*kalaśa*):

Having satisfied the Brahmins and married women with food, ornaments, clothing, and other gifts, he should remain in whatever state is most conducive to his well-being. Then, he should instruct him in the various types of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites. Starting from that day, he should perform the desired daily ritual sequence every single day.
If there is an interruption in the aforementioned daily ritual sequence extending over a month consisting of thirty-six days,

one must again perform for oneself the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) according to the prescribed method— either through one's own master, or through the master of one's master, or through the son of the master, the elder brother of the master, or the younger brother of the master, or through one's own elder brother, or even by oneself alone.

Having stood upon the Śrīcakra and recited the root mantra one thousand times, one should then commence from that point and perform the daily rite as instructed by one's own Guru without interruption.
Thus, this is a summary of the entire purpose of initiation.
On the tenth lunar day, Guha should examine the mantra of Pañcakūṭādinityā and,
according to the prescribed rite, bestow it upon the disciple on the fourteenth lunar day.
The preceptor should instruct [the disciple] in the Vidyā of Jvālāmālinī for the purpose of piercing;
thereafter, that man who has mastered the Vidyā becomes fit for piercing. || 2 ||
Having correctly drawn the Śrīcakra on a ground measuring three cubits,
one should worship Maṅgalā with one water-pot using one's own Śaktis, as was done during the previous initiation.
On the second day, at the prescribed time, he should worship [the deity] along with the Śaktis of the Śrīvidyā after the conclusion of the seating, and then perform the consecration.
First, he performed the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi), followed by the mantras for the seats (āsana);
thereafter, he recited the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅga) and the eight mantras of the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevī).
Having taught the Great Vidyā, he should then himself teach [the following].
Indeed, this first instruction here is for the removal of impurities.

On a wheel measured at nine cubits, one should establish the ground for each successive enclosure; furthermore, having placed the pitchers of that same measure within the three *uṣṭra*s, they should be accompanied by the *śakti*s.
Having fully worshipped Maṅgalā among them while preceded by meditation on that wheel,
one should subsequently dissolve her into oneself and contemplate the Śrīcakra in the center.

Having diligently worshipped the principal deity within the *bindu* situated in the center of the *śrīcakra*, with the fivefold offerings beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, as well as the sun-rituals (*sūryopacāra*).

The powers beginning with *aṇimā*, numbering according to the lunar days (*tithi*), accompanied by their respective individual Śaktis, should each be worshipped at the jars with the five offerings, such as fragrance and the rest, while reciting those hymns.
But there is no further obscuration of the powers beginning with *a*, *ā*, and *ī*;
therefore, through the sequential application of the *aṇimā* [powers] and so forth, starting from the tip of the foremost [finger] to the jar and so on. (11)
Having consecrated [the deity] separately with the jars of the enclosures (āvṛtis), each according to its own inherent power and atomic essence,
one should then [consecrate him] with the water from the central jar situated in the middle of all.
After the consecration with the fifteen *Nityās* by means of the *vidyās*,
one should subsequently consecrate the principal [deity] with sprouts and ripe fruits.
With his head covered by sprouts from which all water has been mostly removed except for a small remainder,
he should bathe his own disciple who stands in the midst of the circle of the Mother-goddesses (mātṛkācakra).
Then, having instructed [the disciple] according to the ritual for the initiation into the mantra of Vārāhī,
the Guru should subsequently pierce [the disciple] who is established within the wheel of the piercing vidyā.

Having performed the worship and the ritual of pleasing the disciples who have entered the Śrīcakra, on a day such as the full moon, or on any other day, lunar mansion, or asterism [as prescribed], [he should perform the initiation]. 16.
Then, the second instruction of the primary science (pradhānavidyā) should be performed;
subsequently, the Guru [should do so] in sequence on the first lunar days (pratipad) and the following tithis. || 17 ||

Having instructed [the disciple] on the vidyās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā according to their respective prescriptions up to the Pūrṇāhuti, he should then instruct Kurukullā according to the rule.
"This instruction, 'one should direct [the self],' is proclaimed as the second;
it concerns the cultivation of the identity of the Guru, the Mantra, and the reality of the Self for human beings. (19)
From this, the destruction of one's own innate birth and the onset of evil latent impressions occurs;
therefore, O ladies, there is always a necessity for this dawn.

This full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), moreover, is threefold; here, in the first [type], there are one thousand five hundred and thirty-nine (1539) jars, while in the middle [type], they are measured at nine hundred and sixty-six (966). (21)
Let her alone move everywhere as the auspicious one;
today, she who bestows powers such as *aṇimā* should be worshipped according to the system of the seven enclosures.
Where the primary Śakti is worshipped, in that very vessel Aṅgalā is likewise worshipped;
the limbs (aṅgas) should be worshipped along with her, and drops from the vessels should be offered into the Śakti-vessel.

In the highest and middle [kalpas], the principal deity, endowed with their respective powers and the [siddhis] such as *aṇimā*, [is placed] in the jar; finally, however, [the deity is placed] upon the jar.
As before, one should worship the goddesses beginning with Aṇimā within the circle,
in their respective places within the wheel itself, which has been constructed beneath the water-pot.
When the primary place for worship is obtained, reflection [on other matters] is without authority;
thus, due to the two prior positions and the lack of any other recourse, [the rite is performed] from the transit of the Sun into Aquarius.
In all these positions, the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, conjoined with their respective veils, are to be worshipped in their clearly visualized locations in due order. (27)
For in whichever case the measurement of the jars would result in a remainder, one should, in brief, divide the measure in khārīs and give [the remainder] to those [remaining jars]. || 28 ||
Furthermore, regarding the consecration (abhiṣeka) mentioned previously,
the wise should join all the power-mantras (śakti-mantra) to the two sides [of the syllables], numbering fifteen hundred and thirty-six.
One should indeed delight in the powers beginning with *aṇimā*;
for while they are to be applied according to the verbal [instruction], *aṇimā* and the others are [further] to be employed through mantra.

Following the consecration, there is then the sprinkling with the mantras of the fifteen Nityās, and the sprinkling with the principal Vidyā; this is the Pūrṇābhiṣecana (the Full Consecration). || 31 ||
The first worship lasts for thirty-one days, the second for five of those [periods],
and the final worship, performed according to the fixed times, lasts for two days.
The consecration (abhimantraṇa) is also prescribed for all three fortnights;
the third is the instruction which bestows the attainment of the identity of one's own self with Lalitā.

Then, from the Lord of the Daily [Ritual] (Dinanityādinātha), the various attendants shall be instructed in succession; the training follows the sequence of the lower [levels], beginning with the obligatory (nitya) and the optional (kāmya).
Instruction in proper conduct and the rules for atonement must be performed prior to the commencement of the initiation rites for the knowledge of the Earth, the Eyes, and the Vidyās.
After the worship, one should perform the rite of covering (the eyes) for the gurus, the yoginīs, and the yogins, using rings, garments, colored powders, ornaments, and so forth.
At the conclusion, one should present sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and others;
having arranged for the feeding of Brahmins, one should bring the rite to completion. || 37 ||
The twenty-one rites are indeed distinct and not one;
therefore, the rites for the subsequent members and the preliminary members should each be performed separately.
Thus [it is said].
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the sixteen Nityās, together with their preliminary and concluding rites.

Now follows the procedure for the practice of the principal Vidyā. During the spring and summer seasons—whether in the primary or secondary sense—one should begin from the full moon day and continue until the subsequent full moon, provided the lunar days increase.
There are thirty-two solar days (*sāvana-dina*). At that time, having bathed with fragrant waters, adorned with two red garments, red sandalwood, coral, garlands, and ornaments,
his mouth scented with camphor, and his teeth and lips reddened by the dye of betel-leaf;

The practitioner, having satisfied the Guru— even if he is far away— with garments, ornaments, ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), and so forth, [should do so] in a pavilion colored with any one of the substances such as vermilion, red lead, lac, or red ochre, perfumed with incense by the Guru and others, illuminated by rows of lamps, and beautifully adorned with canopies and the like; or, if association with him is impossible, [he should satisfy] his representative, such as his son or wife.

Having satisfied [the deity], at the conclusion of one's daily obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, during each of the three periods consisting of morning, midday, and evening, for every instance of the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), [one should offer] substances in the form of plantain fruit, jaggery, sugar, milk, and sweetened milk (*pāyasa*). (p.

Having performed the offering of five-fold forms, oblations, camphor, and the ritual waving of lights (nīrājana), one should perform the constant recitation (japa) a thousand times at the conclusion; and at the end of that,
during each twilight, preceded by silence, one should perform it one thousand forty-one times at the conclusion of the evening worship.

Having recited the root mantra— enclosed by the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), the phoneme placement (*varṇanyāsa*), and the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*)— numbering one thousand forty-three times, and having performed the offering characterized by the contemplation of non-difference with that [mantra],
one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) according to the prescribed rite for the daily sacrifice using a tenth part of the recitation; and from that same tenth part of the recitation, he...

One should perform the libation with camphor-water. In this very manner, it should be performed every day for a period of thirty-two days. This being so, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) reaches the number of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) through a uniform count of three thousand one hundred and twenty-five repetitions each day, beginning from the full moon.

Even if one cannot complete the entire month ending on the full moon, one must perform the worship of the Guru or his representative every day, and likewise, one should feed a large number of Brahmins who are devotees of Śrīvidyā with food consisting mostly of sweets. When this is done:
The completion of one hundred thousand [recitations] occurs within thirty-two days, starting from one full moon and ending with the subsequent full moon; likewise,
the completion of twenty-one hundred thousand occurs in twenty-one months consisting of thirty-two civil (sāvana) days each, and in eighty-four such months.
The completion of the number of primary vidyā-sādhanas—eighty-four hundred thousand in total—as applicable to the present age, becomes possible;
for it is not feasible to perform this continuously over a period of seven years as suggested by some arguments.
Furthermore, even within that timeframe, the continuous occurrence of full-moon months consisting of thirty-two solar days (sāvana-dina) is simply unattainable.
In your view as well, the continuity of those performing *puraścaraṇa*—beginning on the full moon and concluding on the full moon—is indeed contradicted.
If it is argued that this restriction regarding the lunar day (*tithi*) pertains to the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) performed previously, that is equally applicable to me as well.
Nor should it be said that there is a fault of contradiction in the number [of repetitions], just as there is none in the time ending at midday prescribed in another tantra;
for the root text itself establishes the number as three thousand two hundred and twenty-five.

Do not harbor the doubt as to how the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) could be fulfilled; for the means are available through the eighty-four types of Brahmins, their initiation (*dvāra*), and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Furthermore, the methods for accomplishing the mantra even for those devoid of wealth will become clear from the *Kāmyakamalākara*.
For the act of engaging in sexual intercourse more than once with one's own wife during her fertile period,

the following are prohibited for one who causes obstacles: conversing with atheists, longing for another's field, another's house, or another's wealth, anger toward women, striking them, and reviling the maker of one's dwelling.

In dreams, mounting an elephant or a palace, meeting women on a boat, seeing a king, seeing a woman, witnessing festivals such as dancing and singing, and so forth, are indicators of favorable fortune.
Being struck by soldiers with swords or golden weapons, being embraced with affection, sexual union with another's wife, and the discharge of semen [are also significant].

Disturbance in the kingdom, the death of kinsmen caused by fire, wind, or water, affliction with disease among relatives, a disposition toward neglecting one's teacher, and the failure to obtain materials required for spiritual practice— these and similar signs indicate adversity. One should subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya), or consume fruits and roots, or take only milk as food.

The practitioner shall eat once a day the remainder of the oblation, which has been offered to the deity during the eighth part of the day; thus concludes the introduction to the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Furthermore, this recitation (*japa*) must be performed only in a place purified by the *kūrma-cakra*. The method for that is as follows:
[one should draw lines] extending east-west and north-south, with equal intervals between them.
Having divided the maṇḍala for worship and other rites into nine sections by means of four lines intersecting one another,

one should write the letter *ka* in the eastern compartment, the four letters beginning with *kha* in the center, and [the remaining letters] in the directions starting from the east; [then] the lotus for rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*) is in the southeast.
The *Tripurasundarīpaddhati* named *Kamalā*, composed by the venerable and excellent scholar Premanidhi in the form of a manual for the *Śrīvidyā*.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.

May that certain illustrious one— who brings about the fulfillment of his own desired aims without effort, whose praise of the Lord’s image is not even composed by the four classes of people, and who displays mastery in composing commentaries on great texts— be most highly extolled in body and speech.
The lord of the Haihayas.

Having fully relied upon the system of the King of Tantras through devotion to the lotus feet of the King of Kings, and following the instructions of my own true guru, I shall now unfold the lotus of rites for specific desires.

For just as only those devoted to obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) are authorized for occasional duties (*naimittikakarman*), so too only those devoted to occasional duties have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for optional rites (*kāmyakarman*). Likewise, only those who have mastered the mantras have the qualification for optional rites. When even a single mantra has been mastered, other [mantras], though not yet accomplished, become mastered as well.

They too must certainly accept the performance of rites for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*). A preceptor who has correctly mastered the mantras shall accomplish the desired goal even for a patron (*yajamāna*) whose own mantras are not yet perfected. Likewise, a patron whose mantras are more highly perfected may, when in a state of incapacity, follow the ritual procedure through the mediation of a Brahmin whose mantras are not yet perfected. [The same applies to] the preceptor...

Since both sacrificers possess perfected mantras, there is no dispute regarding this; consequently, the successful performance of the rite follows. Thus concludes the determination of those qualified for rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*). There are six types of rites performed for specific desires, distinguished by their purposes: protection (*rakṣā*), pacification (*śānti*), victory (*jaya*), acquisition (*lābha*), subjugation (*nigraha*), and destruction (*nidhana*). Protection refers to [the removal of] fear arising from thieves, tigers, and so forth, among other people.

The continuous absence, in its own locus, of what has been previously established in each successive stage is [the nature of] peace (*śānti*). Peace (*śānti*) is the destruction of afflictions such as diseases and spells that have already arisen. Victory (*jaya*) is the activity that brings about the accomplishment of a specific objective determined by oneself as one's duty toward an enemy—wherein the enemy is to be slain. In this regard, the enemy...

Regarding such matters intended by the king as "the enemy has been brought from Vardhāpura," the common worldly usage that "this king has become victorious" due to the enemy's flight and so forth is merely figurative for those who do not understand the king’s intention. Therefore...

In such a situation, the king considers himself victorious, thinking "I am the winner. Furthermore, "acquisition" (*lābha*) is an activity conducive to the manifestation of one's own ownership (*svasvatva*) with respect to an object that was previously not one's own; this takes the form of the birth of sons, slaves, and so forth, or the form of taking possession of a wife, wealth, and so forth. Even in the case of things like kusha grass or wood found in the forest, which lack the ownership of another, there is [the manifestation of] one's own ownership.
Because it possesses existence, [the author] has stated it in that way, rather than defining it as "an operation conducive to the arising of non-ownership over another's property.

Restraint (*nigraha*) is threefold, distinguished by *stambhana* (paralysis), *uccāṭana* (eradication), and *dveṣaṇa* (inciting hatred). *Stambhana* is an operation conducive to obstructing the anger, exertion, movement, and so forth of kings and others. It is [also] conducive to separation from staying in one place for a long time.

The operation (*vyāpāra*) is *uccāṭana* (eradication). For those who have attained mutual affection or for those who are indifferent, the operation of hatred is death; that very thing is also designated by the term *nidhana*.
The subjugation (*svāyattīkaraṇa*) of a king’s wife and so forth is mentioned therein by the term *vaśya*, which is indeed victory (*jaya*). Therefore, he has been conquered by this knowledge.

The conventional usage among authoritative persons that "this man has been conquered by a woman" occurs in various instances; even enchantment (*mohana*) is indeed a victory. Even attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), because it results in subjugation (*vaśyatva*), is indeed a victory or a specific gain. Furthermore, practices such as *mṛtyuñjaya* (conquering death) are included within protection (*rakṣā*) or pacification (*śānti*). The warding off of enemy armies is also a form of suppression (*stambhana*), which is a type of restraint (*nigraha*).
Thus it is included. This concludes the exposition on the nature of the classification of optional rites (kāmya-karma).
p.

2a) For each of the rites beginning with protection (*rakṣā*), there are seven types of applications, distinguished by worship (*pūjā*), fire-oblation (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), yoga, the purification of the body (*puñjalīkriyā*), and the breaking of diagrams (*yantrabheda*). Regarding the rite of protection:
The earth mandala is used for pacification; the water mandala for pacification; the fire mandala for victory; the wind mandala for gain;
and the space mandala for subjugation and destruction. Regarding the colors of these very elements in these rites:
in pacification they are white; in victory they are red; and in gain, subjugation, and destruction they are black.

All [seasons]. The primary spring (*vasanta*) occurs during the months of Caitra and Vaiśākha. By calculating five *ghaṭikās* each for the thirty *ghaṭikā*-measured days in succession—resulting in six periods of five [days]—the six seasons, beginning with spring, occur in order during the day. During the night as well, when its measure is thirty *ghaṭikās*, [the same applies].
By a sequence of five five-ghaṭikā periods during the day, the six seasons beginning with spring (*vasanta*) occur; and these seasons are secondary (*gauṇa*).

Thus, when the first five ghaṭikās of the day—corresponding to the two months beginning with Caitra—and likewise the first five ghaṭikās of the night, constitute the spring season, protection must be performed therein. [This applies to] Jyeṣṭha and so forth...

In the second pentad of the day and night of the two-month period beginning with [the month of] Mārgaśīrṣa, it is the summer season (*grīṣma-ṛtu*); therein, rites for pacification (*śāntika-karma*) are to be performed. In the third pentad of the day and night of the two-month period beginning with Śrāvaṇa, it is the rainy season (*varṣā-ṛtu*); therein, the rite of victory (*jaya*) is to be performed.
In the fourth pentad of the day and night of the two-month period beginning with Āśvina, it is the autumn season (*śarad-ṛtu*); therein—

The *lābhakarman* (attainment-rite) is to be performed. During the two months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, in every fifth day and night, the winter season (*hemantartu*) occurs; therein, all three types of *nigraha-karma* (subjugation rites) are to be performed.
During the two months beginning with Māgha, in every sixth day and night, the cool season (*śiśirartu*) occurs; therein—

The rite of *nidhana* is to be performed. Even when the primary [time] is unavailable, this must be done during a secondary time— whether for the sake of a desired result or as a mandatory duty— for the purpose of protection and pacification.

In the four rites known as *jaya* (victory) and *lābha* (gain), one should proceed facing any one of the directions—east, north, or northeast. Even therein, for the pacification of disease (*rogaśānti*), one should face the southeast (*āgneyī*); for eradication (*uccāṭa*), the northwest (*vāyavyī*); and for causing enmity (*vidveṣa*)...
Facing the intermediate direction of Nairṛti; in other cases of rites of subjugation (*nigrahakarma*), facing the western direction;

and in the rite of killing (*māraṇakarma*)—which is synonymous with the rite of destruction—facing the southern direction. This is the determination regarding the classification of the application of optional rites (*kāmyakarma*). As for the application, it should be performed on a lunar day (*tithi*), weekday (*vāra*), and asterism (*nakṣatra*) that are favorable to oneself.

In that regard, the worship of the presiding deities of those respective ritual applications must be performed at the beginning of each; therein, the presiding deities of the lunar days (*tithi*) are as follows:

Agni for the first day (*pratipad*), the Aśvins for the second, Umā for the third, Vighna (Gaṇeśa) for the fourth, the serpents for the fifth, Ṣaṇmukha (Kārttikeya) on the sixth, Ravi (the Sun) on the seventh, and the Mothers (*mātṛs*) on the eighth.

On the ninth [tithi], Durgā; on the tenth and subsequent days, the Directions (Diśas); on the eleventh, Dhana-da; on the twelfth, Keśava; on the thirteenth, Yama; on the fourteenth, Hara; and on the new moon and full moon, Śaśin is the presiding deity. Here, one should worship with mantras ending in the dative case and the word *namaḥ*, preceded by the *māyā-bīja* (*hrīṃ*) and the *śrī-bīja* (*śrīṃ*), such as *hrīṃ śrīṃ vahnaye namaḥ*.
