The worship of male deities (*pūṃrūpadevatā*) is to be performed. In the case of a location for dual deities, the application is: *hrīṃ śrīṃ daṃ snābhyāṃ namaḥ*. The mantras are as follows: *hrīṃ śrīṃ umāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ mātṛkāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth, for female deities.
In the rites of worship, one should employ the names as they are stated in this very tantra, and not according to one's own whim.

For example, the lords of the days (*vāreśāḥ*) are as follows: Śiva and Arka are the two masters of Sunday (*ravivāra*); Ambikā and Candra are the masters of Monday (*somavāra*); and Kumāra [is the master of Tuesday].
Āra (Mars) and Bhauma (Mars) are for Mars; Vidhi (Brahmā) and Jña (Mercury) are for Mercury; Viṣṇu and Guru (Jupiter) are for Jupiter; Ramā (Lakṣmī) and Asita (Kṛṣṇa) are for Venus;

and Kubera and Śauri (Viṣṇu) are the two lords for Saturday. Here too, the application of the pair of seed-syllables (*bīja*) is obtained through general rule, but the seven-syllable yoga is obtained through specific rule. Thus: *hrīṃ śrīṃ śivāya*.

*Namaḥ*. *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, salutation to Ravi; thus, for the presiding deities of the day of Śiva and Ravi: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Ambikā. *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, salutation to Candra; thus, for the presiding deities of Ambikā and Candra, these are the worship mantras according to the distinction of male and female. In the same way, this should be understood for the subsequent worship of the lords of the days of the mantras. The lords of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are as follows:

The Aśvins belong to Aśvinī; Yama to Bharaṇī; Vahni (Agni) to Kṛttikā; Dhātṛ to Rohiṇī; Candra (the Moon) to Mṛgaśīrṣa; Śiva to Ārdrā; Aditi to Punarvasu; Guru (Jupiter) to Puṣya; the Sarpas (Serpents) to Aśleṣā;
the Pitṛs (Ancestors) to Maghā; Aryaman to Pūrvaphalgunī; and Bhaga to Uttaraphalgunī.
The Sun is the deity of Hasta; Tvaṣṭṛ of Citrā; the Maruts of Svātī; Indra and Agni of Viśākhā; Mitra of Anurādhā;
Indra of Jyeṣṭhā; Nirṛti of Mūla;
Water of Pūrvāṣāḍhā; the Viśvedevas of Uttarāṣāḍhā; and Hari of Śravaṇa.

To Dhaniṣṭhā belongs Vāsava; to Śatabhiṣā, Varuṇa; to Pūrvabhādrapadā, Ekapād; to Uttarabhādrapadā, Ahirbudhnya; and to Revatī, Pūṣan as the lord. Here too: *hrīṃ śrīṃ* salutation to the Aśvins; *hrīṃ śrīṃ* salutation to Yama; *hrīṃ śrīṃ* salutation to Indra and Agni.
These and other such mantras are to be employed in the worship of the respective lords of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); likewise, daily worship is also essential, and it is of many kinds. (p.

On the day of the daily practice (*dinanityā-prastutaprayoga*), one should count the days starting from the beginning of the Yuga; those [days] that are obtained as part of the *anityā-kāla-nityā* and *avidyā* are to be accepted. Alternatively, on the day of the rising of the letter *A*, the thirty-six deities—beginning with *A Ā Ī A KĀ Ī AKHĀ Ī AGĀ Ī* and ending with *AHĀ Ī AKṢĀ Ī AKṢĀ Ī*—are to be worshipped.
Beginning from the syllable of the sunrise of the day of the current practice, thirty-six deities are presented as objects of worship.

Alternatively, the term *vidyādinanityā* refers to the syllables beginning with the first vowel (*a*) conjoined with the first consonant (*ka*), the second syllable being the first consonant (*ka*) conjoined with the first vowel (*a*), and the third syllable being the third vowel (*i*). These syllables constitute the name of the deity.

"Only this one Vidyā is to be worshipped. Or rather, the meaning of the term *dinanityā* (daily goddess) here refers to Kāmeśvarī and the others who are attained on their respective lunar days (*tithi*) and are indeed constant. In this regard, the mantras for their worship are to be understood as follows: *hrīṃ śrīṃ a ā ī dinanityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth. Thus ends the section on the lunar days (*tithi*).

Description of the Daily Worship of the Lords of the Constellations and the Nityās. Thus, the worship of the Lords of the Sudhātvis—the deities presiding over rites for specific desires—along with their Śaktis, is also essential. The method for this is as follows: having made a circle one cubit in diameter and inscribed a hexagon within it, one should place [the deities] one by one in seven locations: in the center and within the six corners of that hexagon.

Having fashioned a hexagon—that is, having produced a single wheel consisting of seven hexagons—one should worship Nityānityā with her mantra in the pericarp of the central hexagon. Then, in the directions of Īśāna, East, Agni (Southeast), Rakṣas (Southwest), Varuṇa (West), Vāyu (Northwest), one should worship the six Śaktis: Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Sākinī, and Hākinī.
Having performed the worship,
one should worship Sākinī in the center of the hexagon at the front portion, and then [worship] in a clockwise direction starting from its tip.

I worship the sandals of the power Jaḥ; I worship the sandals of the power Hrīṃ; I worship the sandals of the power Śrīṃ; I worship the sandals of the power Aḥ; I worship the sandals of the power Āḥ; I worship the sandals of the power Iṃ; I worship the sandals of the power Uṃ; I worship the sandals of the power Eṃ; I worship the sandals of the power Aiṃ; I worship the sandals of the power Oṃ; I worship the sandals of the power Auṃ; I worship the sandals of the power Aḥ; I worship the sandals of the power Aḥ; I worship the sandals of the power Kaḥ.

Having worshipped the six powers with their respective mantras, and having honored Hākinī in the pericarp of the six-cornered [mandala] located in the northwest direction, one should worship in clockwise order starting from the front petal: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Khaśakti;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Gaśakti; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Ghaśakti."

Having worshipped the six energy-syllables (varṇa-śakti) with the mantras: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandal of the letter *ṅa*-energy; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandal of the letter *ca*-energy; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandal of the letter *cha*-energy," one should worship Ḍākinī in the pericarp of the hexagon in the northeast. Then, starting from the tip of that [petal] and proceeding clockwise:
I worship the sandal of the power of *ja*: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ja-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. I worship the sandal of the power of *jha*: *hrīṃ śrīṃ jha-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.
I worship the sandal of the power of *ña*: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ña-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. I worship the sandal of the power of *ṭa*: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ṭa-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.
I worship the sandal of the power of *ṭha*: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ṭha-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. I worship the sandal of the power of *ḍa*: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ḍa-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having worshipped the sixfold power of the letters with mantras, and having fully worshipped Rākinī in the pericarp of the eastern hexagon, one worships, proceeding clockwise from its tip: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the power of Ḍha;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the power of Ṇa; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the power of Ta."

Having worshipped the six powers (*śakti*) corresponding to the letters of the *vidyā* with: "Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, I worship the *pādukā* of the power of Tha," "Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, I worship the *pādukā* of the power of Da," and "Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, I worship the *pādukā* of the power of Dha"; and having worshipped Lākinī in the pericarp of the southeast hexagon, [one worships] starting from its tip and proceeding clockwise with: "Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Na..."
I worship the sandals of Śakti. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Paśakti. (p. 5a) [blank page]
Having drawn four lines of the length and breadth of one's own hand,
and having thereby produced a wheel consisting of nine squares, [one should draw] four surrounding lines within each of the nine squares.

Having constructed one circle by the method of "touching and not touching," and having further constructed two other circles with equal intervals at its ends, one should produce two paths using all three circles together;
[then] also in the pericarp (karṇikā) of the circle situated in the very center—
Having produced another wheel of compartments by means of drawing two pairs of lines— one extending from east to west and one extending from south to north— dividing the space between them equally;

In this same manner, having fashioned eight squares for each of the eight directions starting from the east— each square being joined with a wheel of nine central squares arranged in two rows by two— the worship-wheel (*pūjā-cakra*) of all nine planets is produced. Therein, in the central square of the wheel of nine squares situated in the very center of everything...
Having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) and having written the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object of practice (*sādhya*) within it;

then, having written the eight vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *l̥* (long-nāsa) one by one in each cell of the eight squares situated outside that [central square], starting from the northeast (Īśāna); and then, in the path situated inside those [outer squares], the solar syllable *ma*.

Having written around [the center] the forms *maṃ*, *māṃ*, *miṃ*, *mīṃ*, *muṃ*, *mūṃ*, *mṛṃ*, *mṝṃ*, *mḷṃ*, *mḹṃ*, *meṃ*, *maiṃ*, *moṃ*, *mauṃ*, *maṃ*, and *maḥ*— thus assuming their respective shapes— in connection with the sixteen nasalized vowels (*savindvaḥ*),
one should write the Mātṛkā alphabet with its nasalizations (*savindu*) in the outer path (*vīthī*) surrounding that; thus is the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*) of the Sun completed.

It occurs as follows: when the Sun has entered the sign of Aries (*meṣa-rāśi*), one should worship the Sun with perfumes and other offerings using the mantra: *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ dhātre namaḥ*. When [the Sun] is situated in Taurus (*vṛṣa*), the mantra is: *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ aryamṇe namaḥ*. When [the Sun] is situated in Gemini (*mithuna*), [the mantra is]: *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ mitrāya*.

*Namaḥ*. This is the mantra. When [the Sun] is in Cancer (*karka*), the mantra is: *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*. When in Leo (*siṃha*), [the mantra is]: *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ...*. When in Virgo (*kanyā*), the mantra is: *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ bhagāya namaḥ*. When in Libra (*tulā*), [the mantra is]: *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ...*

The mantra for [the Sun] in Libra is: *oṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ vivasvate namaḥ*. The mantra when [the Sun] is situated in Scorpio is: *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ indrāya namaḥ*. The mantra when [the Sun] is situated in Sagittarius is: *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ pūṣṇe namaḥ*. Thus is the mantra.
When [the sun] is in Capricorn (makara): *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ parjanyāya namaḥ*—this is the mantra.
When in Aquarius (kumbha): *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ tvaṣṭre namaḥ*—this is the mantra. When in Pisces (mīna): *oṃ...*

The mantra is: *aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. Having written the seed-syllable *jharaṃī* in the center of the wheel starting from the eastern direction, and having written the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth within it; then, in the eight outer compartments starting from the northeast (*īśāna*), one writes: *ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ*.

Having written the eight vowels, one should write the letter *jha* conjoined with the sixteen vowels— namely *jhaṃ jhāṃ jhiṃ jhīṃ jhuṃ jhūṃ jheṃ jhaiṃ jhoṃ jhauṃ jhṛṃ jhṝṃ jḷṃ jhḹṃ jhaṃ jhaḥ*— in the path (vīthī) situated outside of that. Then, in the path situated even further outside, one should write the Mātṛkā letters, each accompanied by the bindu (*m*), for every syllable.
Having prepared the lunar disc, one should worship the Moon with perfumes and other offerings using the fifteen-syllable mantra: *jhara īṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aṃḥ jñoṃ somāya namaḥ*.
Having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) in each of the central sections of the wheel extending from the southeast to the northwest, and having written the letter *ka* within them,
and having written the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the subject (*sādhya*) and so forth within that as well; then, in the eight outer squares starting from the northeast,
one writes the eight syllables *khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ bhaumāvetya*.

Outside of that, on the path (vīthī), having written the letter *ka*—which is associated with the sixteen vowels as follows: *kaṃ kāṃ kiṃ kīṃ kuṃ kūṃ kṛṃ kṝṃ kḷṃ kḹṃ keṃ kaiṃ koṃ kauṃ kaṃ kaṃḥ*—and which is another synonym for emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), and having further written the Mātṛkā along with the *bindu* outside of that, one should prepare the Maṇḍala for the worship of Bhauma. Therein: *oṃ kaṃ*.

One should worship Bhauma with perfumes and other offerings using the eleven-syllable mantra: *khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ bhaumāya namaḥ*. In the central portion of the wheel located in the southern direction, [one should place] the syllable *ca* ending with the *praṇava* (oṃ).

Having written [the syllable] that has *kūrma* as its synonym, and having written the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object of practice (*sādhya*) within it, one should write the eight syllables— *caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ vu dha ā*— in the eight outer compartments for Vudha.

Outside of that, having written the sixteen syllables: *caṃ cāṃ ciṃ cīṃ cuṃ cūṃ cṛṃ cṝṃ cḷṃ cḹṃ ceṃ caiṃ coṃ cauṃ caṃ caṃḥ*, and further outside of that, having inscribed the Mātṛkā with the *bindu* (anusvāra), the worship-yantra for Mercury (*Budha*) is thus prepared. [Then recite]: *oṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ budhāya namaḥ*.
One should worship Mercury with the eleven-syllable mantra using the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*).

Having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the center of the wheel located in the southwest direction, and having written the letter *ṭa* within that, and having further written the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the practitioner (*sādhaka*) within that, one writes outside of that: *oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ sauraye*.

Having written these eight single-syllable [mantras], one should place the sixteen-syllable sequence—*ṭāṃ ṭiṃ ṭīṃ ṭuṃ ṭūṃ ṭṛṃ ṭṝṃ ṭḷṃ ṭḹṃ ṭeṃ ṭaiṃ ṭoṃ ṭauṃ ṭaṃ ṭaṃḥ*—in the path outside of that. Then, having placed the Mātṛkā with the *bindu* outside of that, on the loters of the Yantra for the worship of Śanaiścara: *oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ*.

One should worship Śani with the eleven-syllable mantra "Ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ sauraye namaḥ" using the five offerings beginning with perfume (gandha). Having written the Praṇava (Oṃ) in the wine-square of the wheel starting from the western direction,

having written the letter *ta* within that, and having written the names of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and the practitioner (sādhaka) and so forth within that as well, [one should place them] in the eight squares outside of that.
Having written the eight syllables *taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ* for the Guru,

and having filled the surrounding path with the sixteen syllables *taṃ tāṃ tiṃ tīṃ tuṃ tūṃ tṝṃ tṝṃ tḷṃ tḹṃ teṃ taiṃ toṃ tauṃ taṃ taṃḥ*, one should then write the Mātṛkā along with the *bindu* outside of that as well.
Once the circle of Bṛhaspati has been prepared, one should worship the Guru with offerings such as perfumes and so forth using the eleven-syllable mantra: *oṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ gurave namaḥ*.

Having written the *praṇava* in the center of the wheel whose spokes extend to the intermediate direction of Vāyu, the letter *pa* within it, and the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and so forth within that, one should [place them] in the eight compartments outside of that.

Having written the eight-syllable mantra *oṃ paṃ phaṃ vaṃ bhaṃ maṃ rāhave*, one should place the sixteen-syllable mantra *paṃ pāṃ piṃ pīṃ puṃ pūṃ pṛṃ pṝṃ pḷṃ pḹṃ peṃ paiṃ poṃ pauṃ paṃ paṃḥ* in the surrounding path (*vīthī*). Furthermore, having placed the Mātṛkā with the *bindu* outside of that as well, [the rite] is accomplished.
In the Rāhu-pūjā-maṇḍala: "Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ rāhave namaḥ.
With this eleven-syllable mantra, one should worship Rāhu with the five offerings, beginning with fragrance.

In the center of the wheel of the northern direction, one should write the *praṇava* (oṃ), inside it the letter *ya*, and within that the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Having written the eight-syllable mantra *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ śukrāya* in the eight squares outside of that, one should write *yaṃ yāṃ yiṃ yīṃ yuṃ yūṃ yṛṃ* on the path outside of that.

Having written the sixteen-syllable mantra: *yṝṃ yḷṃ yḹṃ yeṃ yaiṃ yoṃ yauṃ yaṃ yaṃḥ*, and having further written the Mātṛkā alphabet with the *bindu* (anusvāra) around it, within the completed maṇḍala for the worship of Śukra, one should perform worship with perfumes and other offerings using the eleven-syllable mantra: *oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ śukrāya namaḥ*.

One should worship Śukra. In the mantra consisting of nine squares situated in the northeast direction, adorned with two outer corridors, one should write the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) in the central square, the letter *ṣa* at its end, and within that, the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the practitioner (*sādhaka*), etc.
Then, having written the eight-syllable mantra—*saṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ ketave*—in the eight squares situated outside of that, [one should worship].

Outside of that, on the path (vīthī), having written the sixteen-syllable sequence: *ṣaṃ ṣāṃ ṣiṃ ṣīṃ ṣuṃ ṣūṃ ṣṛṃ ṣṝṃ ṣḷṃ ṣḹṃ ṣeṃ ṣaiṃ ṣoṃ ṣauṃ ṣaṃ ṣaṃḥ*, and further outside of that, having written the Mātṛkā with the bindu (*anusvāra*), then, upon the completed wheel for the worship of Ketu, [one recites]: *oṃ ṣaṃ saṃ ha laṃ kṣaṃ ketave namaḥ*.
Thus, one should worship the banner with the eleven-syllable mantra and with offerings such as perfumes and the like.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of the nine planets.
If, however, the Sun is situated in its exaltation sign, Aries (p. 8a),
and one desires to perform a worship of the Sun, or if it is intended to be performed on a Sunday, or else—

When there is a desire to perform the ritual on the new moon festival (amāvāsyā-parvan), one should then proceed to another mandala for the purpose of worshipping the Sun. The method for that is as follows: two circles, each measuring three cubits in both width and length, [should be prepared] in a location such as a palāśa seat or any other suitable place, as previously described.
Having prepared [the ground] with one of red sandalwood, vermilion, or red ochre,

and having drawn nineteen lines each extending east-west and nineteen lines extending north-south, with equal intervals intersecting one another, one should produce a wheel consisting of four hundred squares and provided with a single path; therein—

Having joined each of the twenty-five letters from *ka* to *ma* with the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, and having added the nasal bindu (*m*), one forms the four hundred syllables beginning with *kaṃ kāṃ kiṃ kīm* and ending with *moṃ mauṃ maṃ maḥ*. Starting from Īśāna, these are to be arranged all around in a clockwise direction.
Having drawn [the mandala] according to the method of entry, one should worship the path (vīthī) outside of it as follows: *ka ka a*, *kha ā*, *ga ī*, *gha ī*, *ṅa u*, *ca ū*, *cha ṛ*, *ja ṝ*,
*jha ḷ*, *ña ḹ*, *ṭa e*, *ṭha ai*, *ḍa o*, *ḍha au*, *ṇa aṃ*, *ta aḥ*, *tha ka*, *da kha*, *dha ga*, *na gha*, *pa ṅa*,
*pha ca*, *ba cha*, *bha ja*, *ma jha*, *ma ña*, *mā ṭa*, *mi ṭha*, *mī ḍa*, *mu ḍha*, *bhṛta ṇa*.
*Bhṛ*, *tha*, *mḷda*, *mḷdha*, *mena*, *maipa*, *mopha*, *mauva*, *maṃbha*, *maṃ*, *maṃḥ*, *iya*, *īra*, *aila*, *khava*,

*chaśa*, *ṭhaṣa*, *thasa*, *pha-ha*, *rala*, *jña*, *kṣeya*— by means of these forms, which consist of sixteen consonants (*sparśavarṇa*) connected with vowels (*svara*), and ten syllables representing the Sun and Fire (*sūryavarṇavahnidaśasaṃkhyavarṇaiḥ*), [one should perform the recitation].
When the worship-circle has been prepared, one should place the fifty-one established *mātṛkā* phonemes there, in that path (*vīthī*), arranged all around in a total number of one hundred and one.

One should worship the Sun with perfumes and other offerings using any one of the twelve previously mentioned mantras, which are regulated by the Sun’s position in the zodiac signs beginning with Aries. This is the procedure for the worship of the Sun when situated in its exaltation sign and so forth. However, if the Moon is situated in its exaltation sign in the form of Taurus, or on a Monday, or on the day of the full moon (pūrṇamāsī);

When the worship of Candra is intended, then another mandala must be constructed for that purpose. The procedure for this is as follows: having fashioned two circles with a one-finger interval between them—one inner and one outer—using sandalwood and camphor mixed together at any suitable location such as a pedestal made of *palāśa* wood, [one should proceed] within the center of the inner circle.
Having drawn ten lines each extending east-west and north-south, equally spaced and intersecting one another, one should produce a worship mandala consisting of eighty-one squares; then,
having placed a large letter *U* in the very center square, one should place the seed-syllable *CĀM* within it.

Having written this, and having also written the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object of practice (*sādhya*) within it, one should write, starting from the northeast square (*īśānakoṣṭha*) and proceeding clockwise around the periphery in a counter-clockwise entry-path: *jaḥ jāḥ jiḥ jīḥ juḥ jūḥ jṛḥ jṝḥ jḷḥ jḹḥ jeḥ jaiḥ joḥ jauḥ jaṃḥ jaḥ jhaḥ jhāḥ jiḥ jhīḥ jhuḥ jhūḥ jhṛḥ jhṝḥ jhḷḥ jhḹḥ jheḥ jhaiḥ joḥ jhauḥ*.

jhaṃḥ jhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhāḥ ṭhiḥ ṭhīḥ ṭhuḥ ṭhūḥ ṭhṛḥ ṭhṝḥ ṭhḷḥ ṭhḹḥ ṭheḥ ṭhaiḥ ṭhoḥ ṭhauḥ ṭhaṃḥ ṭhaḥ | vaḥ vāḥ viḥ vīḥ vuḥ vūḥ vṛḥ vṝḥ vḷḥ vḹḥ veḥ vaiḥ voḥ vaṃḥ vaḥ | saḥ sāḥ siḥ sīḥ suḥ sūḥ sṛḥ sṝḥ sḷḥ sḹḥ seḥ saiḥ soḥ sauḥ saṃḥ ||

Having written the sixteen vowels as "saḥ," and having inscribed the letters ja, jha, ṭha, va, and sa— representing the objects of the lotus-heart, the water, the fire, the earth, and the air— each associated with one of the [sixteen] radiances, he then [proceeds] on the path outside of that.
ja jha ṭha va sa a; ja jha ṭha va sa ā; ja jha ṭha va sa i; ja jha ṭha va sa ī; ja jha ṭha va sa u; ja jha ṭha va sa ū;
ja jha ṭha va sa ṛ; ja jha ṭha va sa ṝ; ja jha ṭha va sa ḷ; ja jha va sa ḹ;
ja jha ṭha va sa e; ja jha ṭha va sa ai; ja jha ṭha va sa o; ja jha ṭha va sa au; ja jha ṭha va sa aṃ; ja jha ṭha va sa aḥ.

ja jha ṭha va sa ka | ja jha ṭha va sa kha | ja jha ṭha va sa ga | ja jha ṭha va sa gha | ja jha ṭha va sa ṅa | ja jha ṭha va sa ca | ja jha ṭha va sa cha | ja jha ṭha va sa ja | ja jha ṭha va sa jha | ja jha ṭha va sa ña | ja jha ṭha va sa ṭa | ja jha ṭha va sa ṭha | ja jha ṭha va sa ḍa | ja jha ṭha va sa ḍha | ja jha ṭha va sa ||

sa ṇa ja jha ṭha va sa ta ja jha ṭha va sa tha ja jha ṭha va sa da ja jha ṭha va sa dha ja jha ṭha va sa na ja jha ṭha va sa pa ja jha ṭha va sa pha ja jha ṭha va sa va ja jha ṭha va sa bha ja jha ṭha va sa ma ja jha ṭha va sa ya ja jha ṭha va sa ra ja jha ṭha va sa la ja jha ṭha va sa va ja jha ṭha va sa.

Having written the letters of the Mātṛkā arranged in the form of a diagram consisting of the ocean of nectar on a couch (mañca), according to the sequence *śa ja jha ṭha va sa ṣa ja jha ṭha va sa sa ja jha ṭha va sa ha ja jha ṭha va sa la ja jha ṭha va sa ma ja jha ṭha va sa ya ja jha ṭha va sa ra ja jha ṭha va sa la ja jha ṭha va sa*, one should [place] *hrīṃ ḷ ḹ e ai o* upon the worship-diagram (*pūjāyantra*) thus prepared.

One should worship Soma as before with the fifteen-syllable mantra: *au aṃ aḥ soṃ somāya namaḥ*. Thus ends the procedure for the worship of the Moon to be performed at the time of the Uccā [conjunction] and other such occasions. Regarding the worship of Vāstu:

because its non-performance results in undesirable consequences, it is obligatory; furthermore, it is prescribed as a rite to be performed at the time of constructing a house, a pavilion, or similar structures.
The one-eyed [line], being a subordinate leaf-fragment, does not manifest that [form] as it did before;
and having struck down ten lines and another set of ten lines, which are equidistantly spaced and mutually intersecting.
Having constructed the yantra for the worship of the deities of the eighty-one square plots (*vāstu*),
one [should place] there a single [deity] formed by nine squares consisting of the fourth, fifth, and sixth squares on each side.
Having prepared the *mahākoṣṭha* by erasing eight lines extending toward the four directions from the central square,
one should then form three squares connected to the central *mahākoṣṭha* and three squares extending toward the four directions within the surrounding path consisting of sixteen squares.
Having erased two lines at a time to unify them, one should leave a single square remaining in each corner of that path.
Then, in the path situated outside that [inner] path—which consists of twenty-four squares—one should [leave] four squares in each corner in successive order. In the outermost path...

Of the [mandala] consisting of thirty-two squares, there are four squares in each corner in successive order, making eight squares in total; by drawing two lines across each corner of the horizontal thread, one brings it to sixteen squares.
By drawing horizontal lines through the corner squares of the middle row, each of those squares becomes divided into two;
thus, there are two squares on the left side and two squares on the right side.
By erasing the single dividing line between the central squares, each of them is reduced to a single square. In that very [line]...
In each direction along the street, one should leave a single square remaining. Thus, there is one square in the center;
outside that, a group of four squares in the four cardinal directions; and a group of four squares in the four corners—making eight squares in total.
Outside of those, by drawing horizontal lines at the corners, eight more squares are formed.

On both sides of those [rows], there are two middle squares on each side, making four squares in the four directions; these together constitute twenty squares. Outside of that, by drawing horizontal lines at the corners, eight squares are formed. In the center, in each direction—

Regarding "seven sets of seven squares," this means that when combined, there are thirty-six squares; thus, in total, there are sixty-five squares. In the central great square, one should place Brahmā with the mantra: *oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*.

Having meditated upon [Brahmā] seated on a lotus throne, resembling a golden image, four-faced, and intent upon the study of the Vedas, one should worship him with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and other offerings. Outside of that, in the compartments of the directions starting from the east in sequence:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Āryaka; Oṃ, obeisance to Vivasvat; Oṃ, obeisance to Mitra; Oṃ, obeisance to Mahīdhara."
With the mantras, [place] the group of four beginning with Āryakā. In the southeast corner (Agnikoṇa), in the outermost half-square situated on the left side:
*Oṃ sāviśāya namaḥ*. In the two half-squares below that, in reverse order: *Oṃ savitrenamaḥ*.
In the southwest corner (Nairṛtyakoṇa), in the outermost half-square situated on the left side: *Oṃ indrāya namaḥ*.
In the two half-cells below that, moving counter-clockwise: *oṃ indrajitena namaḥ* in the outermost north-west corner (*vāyavya-koṇa*), in the half-cell situated on the left side;
*oṃ rudrāya namaḥ* in the two half-cells below that, moving counter-clockwise; *rudrajāya namaḥ* in the north-east corner (*īśāna-koṇa*).
In the half-cell situated on the left side at the furthest outer edge, one should worship with "oṃ āyāya namaḥ.
Then, in the two half-cells below that, by repeating [the mantra] twice: "oṃ āpavānsāya namaḥ," one should worship. Thus, seventeen cells have been assigned to thirteen deities.

In the four corners beginning with the southeast (Agni) along the middle row, one should erase the single dividing lines situated on the sides of those squares that have been reduced to half-squares; then, in each resulting square: *oṃ sarvāya namaḥ*, *oṃ guhāya namaḥ*, *oṃ aryamṇe namaḥ*, *oṃ jambhakāya namaḥ*.
Oṃ, homage to Pilipicchā! Oṃ, homage to Carakī! Oṃ, homage to Vidārī! Oṃ, homage to Pūtanā!
Thus one should worship all the deities of the cardinal directions and intermediate points. In this manner, with these twenty-one deities, [one worships] the twenty-five squares.
These are assigned. Then, starting from the half-square situated on the right side of the northeast corner (Īśānī) at the outermost perimeter:
*oṃ īśānāyanamaḥ* (Salutation to Īśāna); *oṃ parjanyāyanamaḥ* (Salutation to Parjanya); *oṃ jayantāyanamaḥ* (Salutation to Jayanta); *oṃ śakrāyanamaḥ* (Salutation to Śakra);
*oṃ bhāskarāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Bhāskara); *oṃ satyāyanamaḥ* (Salutation to Satya); *oṃ vṛṣāyanamaḥ* (Salutation to Vṛṣa); *oṃ antarikṣāyanamaḥ* (Salutation to Antarikṣa).

Having thus worshipped the eight deities, beginning from the half-cell situated on the right side of the southeast corner in the southern direction: *Oṃ agnaye namaḥ*; *Oṃ pūṣṇe namaḥ*; *Oṃ vitathāya namaḥ*;
*Oṃ yamāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ gṛharakṣakāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ gandharvāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ*...

*Oṃ*, salutation to Bhṛṅgarāja; *oṃ*, salutation to Mṛga. Having thus worshipped these eight deities, beginning from the half-square situated on the right side of the southwest corner (nirṛtikoṇa) in the western direction: *oṃ*, salutation to Nirṛti; *oṃ*, salutation to Dauvārika;
*oṃ*, salutation to Sugrīva; *oṃ*, salutation to Varuṇa; *oṃ*, salutation to Varuṇa; *oṃ*, salutation to Puṣpadanta.

Homage! Oṃ, homage to Asura. Oṃ, homage to Śoṣa. Oṃ, homage to Bhoga. Having worshipped these eight deities of the heart, beginning from the half-square situated on the right side in the north-western corner of the northern direction: Oṃ, homage to Vāyu. Oṃ, homage to Nāga. Oṃ, homage to Mukhya. Oṃ, homage to Soma. Oṃ, homage to Bhallāṭaka.
*Namaḥ*. *Oṃ argalāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ dityai namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped these eight deities, thirty-two compartments are assigned to the thirty-two deities. Thus, in total. (p. 11a)
Fifty-seven squares have been assigned to fifty-three deities. Among the sixty-five squares, eight squares remain. Therein, the second row consists of four central squares starting from the east;
by drawing two lines from Īśāna to Nirṛti and from Agni to Vāyu, each [of these]—

Having prepared a four-compartment grid and written the syllables of the current yuga in their respective forms, such as *a*, *am*, and so forth, one should write the successive syllables of the Nityās, beginning with *ā*, *āḥ*, *ī*, and so on. In the four compartments situated on the right side, starting from the east,
one should write the three syllables of the specific day’s Nityā and the syllable for the rising of that specific day.

In the four squares of the western row, one should write the eight syllables—*prācya*, *ādi*, *bhuvam*, *toyam*, *agnim*, and *vāyum*—in pairs according to their sequence. In the four squares of the northern row, one should write the four syllables *pūjaya*, *ami*, *iti*, and *varṇa* one by one. Thus, the four squares are assigned.
The opinion of the ancients is that four squares remain unassigned;

however, in reality, after the outer path has been completed, one should perform the worship of Sāvitra and the others by rotation within the two half-squares situated outside the eight squares (such as those of Agni) located on the third path. And thus, by this path of worship of Sāvitra and the others performed in rotation—

It should be understood that no particular *koṣṭha* (cell) is left unassigned; therefore, having performed the worship of the fifty-three deities beginning with Brahmā according to the previously stated sequence, one should worship the Kali Yuga with the mantra "Obeisance to the Kali Yuga," and then [worship] the *nityāpādukā* with the mantra: "A Ā Ī Paryāīya, I worship the *nityāpādukā*."

Having worshipped [the deity] according to the ritual sequence, one worships the *udayākṣara* with: "Oṃ uṃ, obeisance to the letter of the rising. Then, at the end of the *nityā-vidyā* of that particular day, one worships the *pādukā* of the day's *nityā* with: "I worship the *pādukā* of the day's *nityā*."

Having worshipped Dinanityā with her mantra, he worships the earth with the mantra "I worship the earth," water with the mantra "I worship satisfaction (toṣa)," fire with the mantra "I worship fire," and wind with the mantra "I worship wind. Then, having worshipped them, he stands facing the east in a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

First, using the aforementioned respective worship mantras, each modified by adding "svāhā" at the end, one should offer oblations to each of those local deities (*vāstudevatā*) in a number such as one hundred and eight or twenty-eight, as previously specified.
Having offered oblations of rice soaked in honey, then mung beans soaked in ghee, and then [rice] soaked in cow’s milk;

and having offered oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) soaked in honey, ghee, and milk, using the very same worship mantras previously mentioned, with milk-rice mixed with condiments, sugar, milk, plantains, cakes, and ghee.

One should offer an oblation (*bali*) to the deities beginning with Brahmā. Likewise, on the days of performing the worship of deities, fire-offerings (*homa*), and other rites, widows should feed at least three *brāhmaṇas* who are regular devotees of the Goddess, providing them with gems characterized primarily by sweet flavors according to their means, and satisfy them with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). When [the Sun] has entered the zodiac sign of Leo...

For the practitioner who performs the worship of the Vāstu deity on a full-moon day during the sun’s transit, accompanied by fire-offerings (homa), the feeding of Brahmins, and the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) within his own home,
there shall be no affliction from the death of children, diseases, spirits, ghosts, or ḍākinīs; nor shall there be fear of snakes, mutual strife, or the malevolent magic of others.

Whatever may happen, there shall be no lack of sons, grandsons, wealth, health, cattle, buffaloes, and other livestock, nor an abundance of male and female servants; yet, for a person who performs worship incessantly according to the previously described method even for a single day, there will be the affliction of disease or the death of a child.
The acquisition of afflictions from spirits, ghosts, and the like; the loss of sons, grandsons, wealth, cows, buffaloes, and so forth;
and the arising of misfortune—[these are determined] by means of the previously mentioned wheel of sixty-five squares located in any place made of gold, silver, copper, or stone.

Having written [the syllables], one should write the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīḥ*) in each of those squares, and inside that, the name of Brahmā and the others ending with the first case-suffix (*prathamānta*). Once the yantra is completed, the respective deities such as Brahmā and the others are to be placed in their respective squares on any one of the first, second, third, fifth, or seventh lunar days, [for the protection of] a house, a village, a hamlet, or a district.

Having worshipped in accordance with the requirement for installation before [the deity], or else having worshipped for a short time, a long time, a longer time, or a very long time— according to whether the desired goal is easily accomplished, difficult to accomplish, accomplished with hardship, or accomplished through improper means—
one should place [the image] in some secluded spot within one's own home, preceded by the recollection of the respective deities of the site (vāstudevatā), three times.
One should offer handfuls of flowers into the tantric yantra. Then, for the sake of pacifying all calamities such as the malevolent magic (*parakṛtyā*) directed against one's house and so forth,

and for the attainment of all desired goals, one should dig a pit inside [the house], deposit [the yantra] there at a time favorable to the eleven zodiac signs and other factors, and cover it with excellent earth.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of Vāstu.

Practitioners (*sādhaka*) are of three kinds, based on the distinction between those who are to be accomplished (*sādhya*), those who accomplish (*sādhaka*), and those who have attained accomplishment (*siddha*). Meditation (*dhyāna*) is also of three kinds, based on the distinction between the gross (*sthūla*), the subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the supreme (*para*). Among these, the *sādhya* and the *sādhaka* are the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) for the gross and subtle meditations, respectively; however, only the *siddha* has the qualification for supreme meditation, in which mantras, ritual accomplishments (*siddhi*), worship, and so forth are not required.

One who desires to know that [object] while possessing a specific mode of cognition is the "sādhya" (the object to be accomplished); one who possesses a known mode of cognition but whose accomplishment has not yet arisen is the "sādhaka" (the accomplisher);
and one who possesses a known mode of all accomplishments but whose state of complete perfection is as yet unknown is the "siddha" (the perfected one).
Among these, the coarse meditation (*sthūla-vyāna*) regarding optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) is described in sequence as follows:

Mounted on elephants, horses, and chariots, or standing in various vehicles, or seated upon lions, tigers, and Garuḍas— these [deities] should always be meditated upon for protection, for the attainment of victory in battles, and for the safeguarding of kings, kingdoms, and so forth.

On a path difficult to traverse due to *piśācas*, thieves, serpents, and the like, one should meditate upon all those deities attended by their powers (*śaktis*), whether individually or collectively; it is certain that they will bring about happiness and remove fear. For the sake of protection, there is the visualization of a yellow color and a crescent-moon shape, as well as a white color, which will be described hereafter.

In this context, for the rite of victory, meditation consists of general visualization (*sāmānyadhyāna*). Just as all [the goddesses] are mounted upon Garuḍa, endowed with two hands holding wind and fire, possessing two eyes and one face, having eight arms and a terrifying form, they are to be meditated upon as burning the multitude of enemies by means of their own forms and powers.
Or perhaps you conquered that great army on the summit of the battlefield, which was surrounded on all sides by terrifying roars— whether with four faces, eight faces, or gentle countenances;
or whether with two faces and twice as many arms, you achieved victory through your desired forms and strategic maneuvers.
Visualize them bearing in their left hands a multitude of single-staff bows and other arrows, piercing the entire bodies of the enemy host so that streams of blood flow from them; or else,
visualize them holding shields and swords in their other hands, cleaving the fourfold army of the foe with those blades.
Having meditated upon the eternal [Goddess], one who remembers her as holding maces in nine left hands and likewise other weapons such as claws and arrows in the right,

and as terrifyingly destroying a fourfold army divided into hundreds of parts, shall be victorious; or else, remembering her holding tridents in nine left hands and holding *kurara* birds in nine right hands, one shall be victorious.

Or, having recollected the goddess who causes the enemy army to fall, Ripujaya [attains victory]; or, having meditated upon the leather-shields and daggers, numbering as previously stated, striking down the enemy force, he attains victory.
Or would one achieve victory by contemplating the enemy's army as being bewildered by sleepless nights and handless hands;
or by remembering the hosts of the army as being crushed by the winds from the hands of *piśāca* demons and serpents;
or by remembering the army in battle as being struck down by nooses and razors? Or how else might one attain victory?

Whether one visualizes her tearing apart the army in an instant with a hook and a saw, or whether one remembers her striking the entire force of all enemies with a plow and a pestle—one shall be victorious. In all these ten positions, she possesses eighteen arms and nine faces equally; or alternatively—
From his sixteen faces, thirty-two arms emerge— whether fifty arms or twenty-five mouths [are intended]—
holding fire, wind, bow, arrow, shield, sword, mace, claw, trident, axe, shield, dagger, sleep, darkness,
demon, serpent, noose, and razor.
Visualizing them holding pairs of weapons consisting of a hook, a saw, a plow,
and a pestle in their left and right hands respectively, and striking down the enemy force with those very weapons,
one who follows this application for victory will certainly be victorious; what more need be said?

One should remember the Victorious Ones (Ajitā) as having thirty-six faces and seventy-two hands, bearing the pairs of weapons previously mentioned; by so remembering, one becomes victorious. Alternatively, one should remember them as having forty-nine faces and ninety-eight hands, striking the enemies with the aforementioned weapons; by so remembering, one shall be victorious. Or else, [one may remember them] as having sixty-four faces.

One will be victorious by recollecting [the goddesses] measuring one hundred and twenty-eight cubits, striking the enemy army with the previously mentioned multitudes of weapons; or alternatively, by recollecting those measuring one hundred and sixty-three cubits with eighty-one faces,
endowed with the aforementioned weapons— not only that, but actually slaying the enemy army with them.

One should recollect [this]; by that, victory occurs. Alternatively, one should visualize [the goddesses] with a hundred faces and two hundred hands, striking the enemy army with the pairs of weapons previously mentioned; by this, victory will certainly be attained. And here, victory is of four kinds.
Regarding the application for gain through the destruction, flight, capture, or prostration of the leaders of armies,
the visualization is as follows: [The goddesses] emerge from the single face, having two arms, holding their desired objects,
wearing sandals, adorned with all ornaments, and surrounded on all sides by Śaktis who resemble themselves.

"Adorned with forest garlands while singing and dancing"—by meditating thus, one attains all desired objects. Likewise, by remembering the eternal goddesses as smiling-faced, singing, mounted upon decorated horses, and surrounded by their Śaktis, the power to subjugate the world arises through the practice of subjugation (vaśya). Similarly, [one attains this] by remembering them as adorned and mounted upon elephants. Adorned...

Surrounded by eternal Śaktis mounted on elephants and absorbed in song, one who remembers this practice for attaining Lakṣmī should abide in it; for it brings about fame such as "He is a man of great wealth," "He is a most generous donor," and so forth, bestowing various enjoyments of pleasure that are envied even by kings.

One should attain prosperity, mounted upon an adorned chariot and surrounded by one's own female attendants who are likewise mounted on adorned chariots and engaged in singing. For men who remember her constantly, there is this attainment of wealth;
for kings who remember her in this way, preceded by the aforementioned meditation, there is this attainment of victory over enemies.

If, through the practice for attaining Lakṣmī, the attainment of Lakṣmī should indeed occur, then one should remember the Nityās as they ascend the *vādukā* trees in a solitary plantain grove accompanied by their own powers (*śaktis*), considering the lightness or heaviness of the task at hand,
and whether it is achievable or unachievable.

For one who recites the root-mantra for a mere fortnight or a single month according to the aforementioned method, there shall be the attainment of treasure and the possession of its enjoyment for as long as life lasts, by the practitioner of the rites of Lakṣmī to be described hereafter.

By practicing the previously mentioned application even in groves of betel-nut trees (*pūgīphala*), *dakṣārāma*, and *caṃpaka* trees, one obtains the results previously described; for one who practices the previously mentioned application in mountain thickets, there is the acquisition of wealth, as is the case with a grove of plantains (*kadalīvana*) situated on the seashore.
For one who practices such rites preceded by that same meditation in places such as groves of betel-nut trees or forests of *caṃpaka* trees,

there will certainly be the acquisition of a great many jewels; and for one who performs the rite of Lakṣmī preceded by the aforementioned recollection within garden-groves situated in the middle of rivers flowing to the ocean, such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, [there will be the attainment of] gold.

For one who performs the rite for obtaining a maiden while recollecting Nityā— who is accompanied by Śaktis mounted on sandals and absorbed in song as they proceed to the assembly hall having ascended their sandals— there shall be the attainment of countless maidens of beauty, youth, and virtuous character for as long as life lasts, even in a secluded forest.
If she has come under one's own control, there will be the attainment of a wife;

by remembering the applications for subjugation while mounted on a horse in any of the aforementioned secluded forest locations such as plantain groves, one shall, through mind, speech, and action, bring the king under one's power right there.

For one who remembers [the mantra], kings who pursue others become submissive; even those mounted on chariots become so for one who remembers the liberation from bondage and the attainment of all other goals when joined with the suppression [of the enemy] through meditation.
Indeed, all those [goddesses] of smoky color, of terrifying form and very fierce, are to be meditated upon there for the purpose of eradication (*uccāṭana*).
For the purpose of causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), one should employ the cries of the heron, hawk, curlew, crow, and owl;
furthermore, all those [beings] crowded with terrible weapons—such as the sword, jackal, gayal, porcupine, deer, horse, and boar—are to be used. (p. 14b)
Thus: meditation on the *nidhana* (concluding part) is as follows: one should remember all the *vetālas* and *piśācas* as being black in color. Subtle meditation (*sūkṣma-dhyāna*) is as follows:

while mentally remembering a form of light resembling the filaments of a pomegranate flower located somewhere within the *mūlādhāra* and other centers up to the mouth, one should also visualize within that [light] the form of the object of attainment (*sādhya*), according to one's own desire. Thus.

Alternatively, preceded by subtle meditation, one should contemplate one's own repeated movement back and forth along the path of the *suṣumṇā* from the *mūlādhāra* to the end of the *brahmarandhra*; or, preceded by subtle meditation, through the application of various desired objects, the attainment of those respective desired goals occurs.
Just as in the supreme meditation (*paradhyāna*), gold alone exists within bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and crowns without any difference from them, appearing in their respective forms; even so,
there is only one Supreme Self who possesses the power of manifestation (*prapañca*) as all those various beings— men, animals, birds, and so forth.
Furthermore, when one’s own self perceives its own nature— which is like a lamp sheltered from the wind— through repeated resolute application,
that very state is the supreme meditation (*para-dhyāna*) which, once accomplished, fulfills all desires even without ritual worship.
In brief, he accomplishes ritual applications such as libations (tarpaṇa) and fire-offerings (homa). Thus end the general meditations for specific desires (kāmya).

Thus, relying on this general procedure for all rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), all the ritual applications (*prayoga*) for such desires that will be described hereafter should be followed accordingly. Among those, the ritual applications for worship (*pūjā*) are as follows: in the month of Caitra, having worshipped the Goddess in a yantra, an image, or some other locus with the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Lalitā Nityā," [one should proceed with] rice-grains (*vrīhi*).
As for the substance (dravya),
one should worship Tripurā or the sandals with the mantra "I worship Tripurā," thereby attaining identity with her.

A Brāhmaṇa who knows that [mantra] should contemplate it; having honored that Brāhmaṇa, he should give [the sandals] to that Brāhmaṇa in the month of Vaiśākha with the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the pādukā of Tripureśvarī," using flowers and other offerings produced in that specific month.

Having worshipped with that very mantra, one should give black gram (*māṣa*) rice to the Brāhmaṇa who has been honored. In the month of Jyeṣṭha, having worshipped with flowers and other offerings produced in that month using the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ tripurasundarī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, one should give barley (*yava*) rice to the Brāhmaṇa who is its devotee—meditated upon as non-different from [the Goddess] and fully gratified by that very mantra.

In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should offer [the gift] with the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Tripuravāsinī," having worshipped them with flowers and other offerings produced in that month; then, with this very same mantra, one should offer honey from the *vimāya* (the spiritual state) determined as non-different from the devotee who has been worshipped. In the month of Śrāvaṇa...

Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings produced in that month using the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Tripureśvarī," and having worshipped her with this very mantra while meditating upon her as non-different from the devotee who has thus adored her, one should give ghee to a Brāhmaṇa. In the month of Bhādrapada, [one should worship] with the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Tripuramālinī."

Having worshipped with the flowers and other offerings appropriate to that month, one should offer sesame oil—produced from sesame seeds—to a Brahmin who has been honored with this very mantra and perceived as non-different from the deity and its worshipper. In the month of Āśvina, one should worship with the mantra:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ tripurasiddhāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, using the flowers and other offerings belonging to that month.

Having worshipped with this very mantra, and having meditated upon the cow’s milk as being non-different from the worshipper who has been thus honored, one should give it to a Brahmin in the month of Kārttika. Hrīṃ. (p.

Having worshipped [the deity] with the mantra "I worship the sandals of Śrī Tripurā" using flowers and other offerings appropriate for that month, one should give a garment to a Brahmin who has been worshipped with this very mantra and who is determined to be non-different from the worshipper of that [deity].
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, [one should worship] with the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Śrī Tripurasundarī."

Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings produced in that month, one should give gold to a Brahmin who has been honored with that mantra and who is the object of meditation as non-different from that deity and its worshipper.
In the month of Pauṣa, [one should worship] with the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ lalitāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings produced in that month, and having meditated upon that Vidyā as non-different from the Māsaka, one should give a jewel-like Brahmin who has been honored with its mantra. In the month of Māgha, one should worship with the flowers and other offerings of that month using the mantra: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the wish-fulfilling sandals."
One should offer sesame seeds to a Brahmin who has been worshipped with that very mantra and meditated upon as non-different from the deity;
having worshipped [the deity] in the month of Phālguna with flowers and other offerings produced in that month, using the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ kāmāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

One should offer food to a Brahmin who has been worshipped with that very mantra and whose mind is focused on meditation upon his identity with the deity being worshipped. For the practitioner who worships in this manner,
there shall be the attainment of all desired objects— such as wealth, sons, and so forth— along with the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) of strength, health, and long life.

The first practice: having prepared a pedestal in each of the months beginning with Caitra, using respectively the wood of *śleṣmāntaka*, *karañja*, *vibhītaka*, *nimba*, *pippala*, *kadamba*, *bilva*, *vaṭa*, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *raktacandana*, *karpūra*, and *sahakāra* trees,
one who worships the Goddess there in those respective months receives her command in every case.
The second formulation is that there would be such unimpededness as the state of having an unobstructed command and the possession of faith regarding the subject matter of the treatise.

For the practitioner who constantly worships by means of flowers and other offerings produced during each season— beginning with spring— which are accomplished over two months such as Caitra and Vaiśākha, and who thus pervades the actual time of the seasons,
there arises a collective fivefold fruit: longevity, fame, prosperity, land, and victory.
The third application.
Thus end the monthly applications.

On whichever first lunar day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight one may choose, at the conclusion of the worship consisting of an offering (*naivedya*) of plantains, jaggery, and coconut fruits—each counted individually—one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) once for each item. On the second day, at the conclusion of the worship with these same items doubled, the oblation shall be twice as many; on the third day, [the same applies].

Following the worship with those [substances] tripled, there is a triple oblation; on the fourth day, following the worship with those quadrupled, there is a quadruple oblation; on the fifth day, following the worship with those quintupled, there is a quintuple oblation;
on the sixth day, following the worship with those sextupled, there is a sextuple oblation.
On the seventh [day], after worship with those [substances] multiplied sevenfold, there is a fire-offering (homa) sevenfold;

on the eighth, after worship with those multiplied eightfold, there is a fire-offering eightfold; on the ninth, after worship with those multiplied ninefold, there is a fire-offering ninefold; on the tenth, with those multiplied tenfold.

After worship on the tenth day, there is a fire offering ten times [the number of offerings]; on the eleventh day, after worship, there is a fire offering eleven times with those [offerings] multiplied elevenfold; on the twelfth day, after worship, there is a fire offering twelve times with those [offerings] multiplied twelvefold; on the thirteenth day, [there is a fire offering] thirteen times with those [offerings] multiplied thirteenfold.

After the worship, there is a fire-offering (homa) consisting of thirteen-fold repetitions. On the fourteenth day, after the worship with those [offerings] repeated fourteen times, [the rite is performed]. (p.

The fourteen-fold oblation is performed on the full moon day; following the worship with those [offerings] multiplied fifteen times, there is a fifteen-fold oblation. On the first day of the dark fortnight, following the worship with those multiplied fourteen times, there is a fourteen-fold oblation. On the second day, following the worship with those multiplied thirteen times—

On the third [day], after worship with twelvefold [repetitions] of those [mantras], there is a homa of twelvefold [repetitions]; on the fourth, after worship with elevenfold [repetitions] of those, there is a homa of elevenfold [repetitions]; on the fifth, [there is a homa] with tenfold [repetitions] of those.

After worship, on the tenth day, there is a fire-offering (homa) consisting of ten repetitions; after worship on the sixth day, there is a fire-offering consisting of nine repetitions; after worship on the seventh day, there is a fire-offering consisting of eight repetitions;
and after worship on the eighth day, there is a fire-offering consisting of seven repetitions.

On the ninth day, after worship with those [substances] multiplied sixfold, there is a fire-offering (homa) multiplied sixfold; on the tenth day, after worship with those multiplied fivefold, there is a fire-offering multiplied fivefold; on the eleventh day, after worship with those multiplied fourfold, there is a fire-offering multiplied fourfold; on the twelfth day, after worship with those doubled...

On the thirteenth day, the *homa* is threefold; after worship with those [mantras] doubled, on the fourteenth day, the *homa* is twofold; and after worship with those very same [mantras] single-fold, the *homa* is indeed single-fold. Thus, when the recitation (*japa*) and the *homa* are undertaken according to the increase and decrease of the lunar fortnight, although it follows the logic of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance...
Although on the new moon day (darśa), the general absence of both worship and fire-oblation (homa) is pervaded by the general absence of food-offerings,
nevertheless, due to a specific scriptural injunction, one should perform worship once with plantain fruit, jaggery, and coconut, and likewise perform the homa once with each of these individually.
In this way, through such worship, the practitioner attains prosperity equal to that of a king.
Thus concludes the ritual application for the lunar days (tithi).

On Sunday, having worshipped with red lotuses, milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is the food offering; on Monday, worship with white water-lilies (*kumuda*), with milk as the food offering; on Tuesday, worship with red lotuses (*raktotpala*), with plantain (*kadalī*) as the food offering; on Wednesday, [worship] with *nagara* flowers.

For the practitioner who performs worship continuously for the duration of one full year— offering *navanīta* (fresh butter) as the sacrificial food (*naivedya*) on a Monday with *kahlāra* flowers, offering sugar as the sacrificial food on a Friday with white lotuses, offering sugar as the sacrificial food on a Saturday with blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*), and likewise offering ghee as the sacrificial food— the afflictions of the planets [shall cease].
Preceded by cessation, there shall be the attainment of all happiness.
Thus end the applications of the days of the week.

Standing on the upper ground of a mountain for seven days and nights, he worships the Goddess with perfected substances and wild flowers; [thereby] the siddhi of the *khecarī* [is attained]. Or, staying in a forest banyan tree or in mountain groves for seven days and nights, he worships the Goddess with the two perfected substances and with *kadaṃba* flowers and *jātī* flowers.

For one who worships her, the accomplishment of the yakṣiṇīs is attained; those perfected female deities grant everything desired through the performance of specific rites directed toward those various goals, for the practitioner who worships the Goddess with *ketakī* flowers accompanied by the substances of accomplishment on the seashore for the duration of a month.

The servants of the practitioner, having become accomplished, attract and bestow upon him his desired woman; they grant victory over enemies in battle and provide various kinds of illusions; and they repeatedly bestow upon the practitioner whatever he desires, such as garlands, ornaments, and various kinds of food and drink.

Having drawn the Śrīcakra above the seat of one's own natal asterism, one should then, for a month, every day at night in a cremation ground, perform worship of the Principal Goddess according to the prescribed method with *śālmalī* flowers and the perfected substances (*siddhadravya*).

For one who worships with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), the *piśācas* become accomplished (*siddha*). By means of those stone-hurlings performed by them, victory over enemies occurs in battle. Having gone to the forest alone and becoming fearless, at night [one should worship] the Goddess situated within the *Śrīcakra* with *mālatī* [flowers].

For one who worships for the duration of a month using flowers of the *jāti*, *punnāga*, *ketakī*, and *madhuka* gathered all at once, together with the perfected substances (*siddhadravya*), the accomplishment of the *vetāla* occurs;
having mounted the back of the accomplished *vetāla*, one shall go very swiftly to whatever region one desires to reach.
In a cremation ground, or in the temple of Caṇḍikā, or— in its absence— in a forest devoid of people other than oneself, at the time of midnight; the practitioner,
dressed in black garments, with black unguents and black garlands, and with a mind full of intense wrath,
having rendered the seat black by smearing it with substances such as aguru and the like, [should perform the rite] upon that seat which has attained blackness through substances such as aguru.

Having drawn the Śrīcakra and meditated upon the Goddess who is of an extremely dark complexion, one should worship her with dark-colored perfumes, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), flowers, and so forth. [One should then perform the ritual] using the birth-sign (yoni) of the victim's enemy's natal asterism: for Aśvinī and Bharaṇī, the horse-yoni is prescribed; for Svātī and Ardra, the buffalo-yoni.
Having been instructed by these and other such means, he should offer an oblation (*bali*) consisting of that [victim] after its decapitation as a perfected substance (*siddhadravya*).

By performing this in this very manner for the duration of a month, at the end of the month, various types of sorceresses (*kṛtyā*) emerge from the third eye of the Goddess. To them, he should then offer his own objective as food. Thereafter—

When they return after having devoured their entire faction of enemies, they say, "By your grace, our desired goal has been accomplished; go back as you came," and with this prayer, the eyes of the Goddess once again become invisible right there, while she remains adorned with red coral garlands, garments, perfumes, and ointments.
The practitioner, having remained for one month in a secluded garden, performs [the rite] within the Śrīcakra,
preceded by the invocation, meditation, and other [preliminaries], using *kahlāra*, *campaka*, and *aśoka* [flowers].

For the practitioner who worships with the five flowers consisting of *pāṭalī* and *śatapatra*, together with the perfected substances (*siddhadravya*), the accomplishment of *māyā* arises. Consequently, in whatever way he desires to act, he shall become capable of assuming that very form.
Thus end the applications for the seven siddhis, beginning with Khecarī.

Having meditated upon the Śrīcakra in the center of one lotus among the lotuses located at the sites of the Mūlādhāra, the root of the Liṅga, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the middle of the eyebrows— namely, the four-petaled, six-petaled, ten-petaled, twelve-petaled, sixteen-petaled, and two-petaled lotuses— therein...

Having worshipped with substances of great efficacy—namely camphor, sandalwood, saffron, musk, and other perfected substances—and having meditated on Lohitā, Lalitā, and so forth, if one sees the Goddess endowed with all her limbs and all her weapons, then it is auspicious; however, if she is deficient in even a single limb, one should know it to be inauspicious. In that regard, within the two wheels beginning with the Mūlādhāra:

In that manner, there is knowledge of the auspicious and inauspicious regarding past objects; in the two [positions] beginning with the navel, there is knowledge of the auspicious and inauspicious regarding present objects in that manner; and in the other two, there is knowledge of the auspicious and inauspicious regarding future objects in that manner. This is the application for the knowledge of the auspicious and inauspicious. [Regarding] one's own cupped hand... (culukariṇi).

Having meditated upon the Śrīcakra and worshipped the Goddess there with perfumes and other offerings, one should consecrate that water three times with the root mantra accompanied by the Mātṛkās. Then, having visualized one's own tongue as being shaped like a lamp and consisting of the specific channel named Sarasvatī, [one should perform this] every day for the duration of a year.

For the practitioner who drinks that water in the morning, there shall arise the fourfold scholarship consisting of eloquence, poetic skill, the capacity for discerning the meaning of texts, and the ability to expound them.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for worship intended for the sake of scholarship.

Having meditated on the Śrīcakra in a handful of water and worshipped the Goddess therein with perfumes and other offerings, one should consecrate that water three times with the root mantra accompanied by the Mātṛkās; for one who drinks this every morning throughout their life, [the result is as follows].

Having attained the triad of fruits— namely, the perfection of the eightfold yoga beginning with breath control (prāṇāyāma), the perfection of the performance of rituals prescribed in the Vedas, and the knowledge of the true nature of the Self— one shall attain union with the venerable Śiva.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for worship intended for the attainment of yoga-siddhi.
Having made a large circle according to one's own desire with saffron— or with any one of sindūra, gairika, lac, vermilion, and so forth— or else with white sandalwood and red sandalwood,
and having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus within it, one should draw a hexagon in its pericarp and [the remaining figures] on the outer [petals].

Having determined six hexagons, numbering six, within each of the six corners and having thus completed the Anugraha-cakra, one should invoke the principal Goddess of the present context into the station of Nityānityā throughout the month;
then, having meditated upon her in the center as surrounded by the Nityānityā-śaktis, namely Ḍākinī and the others, each joined with their respective powers.

Having worshipped the principal deity with *campaka* and blue lotus flowers, one should worship the Śaktis— namely Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Śākinī, and Hākinī— in the six corners, located in the directions of the southwest, northwest, east, southeast, northeast, and west. Furthermore, in the outer six corners, the previously mentioned [deities] beginning with the Rākṣasa should be worshipped in sequence.

For the practitioner who worships the thirty-six syllable-energies (*varṇaśakti*) again and again, six by six, within each hexagon, there arises [the cessation] of that which causes fever, of that which causes the mind to become distracted by spirits (*bhūta*), of that which causes the mind to become distracted by seizing spirits (*graha*), and of heart-trembling and so forth.
Specific diseases—such as ear diseases, head diseases, abdominal pains, and so forth—become free from illness.
Furthermore (p. 19a), other diseases arising from any of the [three humors]—wind, bile, or phlegm—also come to subside.
Thus ends the procedure for the destruction of diseases.

In a location near the gateway to the path leading into the netherworld (pātāla), having constructed the Śrīcakra in such a manner— with sixteen triangles drawn in the positions of the principal deities and the subordinate deities of the enclosures according to the method of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka)— one should [perform the rite] in its center during the autumn season, whether in the primary or secondary [period].

Having worshipped the Supreme Goddess, the principal deity, preceded by the rites of invocation and so forth, with fragrant flowers accompanied by the perfected substances (siddhadravya) up to the nose [of the image], and having fully honored the sixty-four attendant powers (śaktis) of the sixteen-fold enclosure, the practitioner [should worship] the daughters of the Nāgas, the daughters of the Yakṣas, and the daughters of the Rākṣasas.

Among the daughters of the Gandharvas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, human Siddhas, Kinnaras, and the exceptionally noble serpent-maidens born of the Nāgas, he shall obtain various kinds of play in their respective worlds together with those maidens, according to his own diverse inclinations. Thus it is said.

The ritual procedure for obtaining the eleven maidens, beginning with the Nāga-maiden: by performing worship with *kiṃśuka* flowers and offering oblations (*naivedya*) of milk, sugar, clarified butter, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) for the duration of a month, one obtains ornaments. By following the previous procedure with *pāṭala* flowers, one obtains an elephant; by following the previous procedure with red lotuses (*raktotpala*), [one obtains a horse].
Success with horses is indicated by *kumuda* flowers; the acquisition of donkeys by *utpala* flowers; success with camels by *tagara* flowers; the acquisition of cattle by *jambīra* flowers;
success with buffaloes by *lakuca* fruits; the acquisition of sheep by *dāḍima* fruits; the discovery of treasure by *madhūka* flowers;
and the attainment of the position of Lord of the Gaṇas by *madhūka* flowers.
By offering *vakula* flowers, one gains a woman; by *kahlāra* flowers, one gains a son; by *śatapatra* flowers, victory is attained;
and by *ketakī* flowers, one achieves success with chariots, palanquins, and the like—even when mixed with any fragrant substances such as camphor and musk.

For one who worships with flowers for the duration of a month and offers milk, sugar, and so forth as the fourfold food offering (*naivedya*), there shall be the attainment of all prosperity (*sarvasaubhāgyasiddhi*). One may perform this practice for two months, three months, or until the completion of the desired task. Thus concludes the ritual procedure that grants fifteen fruits.
Having visualized the Śrīcakra in the waters of some great river, one should invoke the Goddess along with her retinue there;
then, having prepared the *arghya* as before, one should worship her with all or some of the flowers previously mentioned.
One should then perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with that *arghya* water, in either a hundred thousand or another such number. By this, [one wards off] hostile armies and so forth.

There shall be the pacification of all calamities. Thus concludes the ritual application for the pacification of calamities such as foreign invasions. Having drawn the Śrīcakra upon a certain seat and having worshipped the principal deity there along with the enclosures, preceded by invocation and other rites—through consecration with ghee therein, there is fullness of lifespan; through consecration with honey, there is good fortune.
From consecration with milk, one attains health; from consecration with a combination of ghee, honey, and milk, one attains sovereignty;
from consecrations with coconut water and other excellent substances, there is the accomplishment of success along with the favor of kings and others;
from consecration with snow-water, the attainment of kingship occurs; and from consecration with water from sacred fords (śrāddha-tīrtha), the previously mentioned fruits and so forth are obtained.

There shall be the abundant attainment of fruits such as sons and so forth. Thus ends the yoga for attaining long life and other benefits. One who dwells for a day and night in a forest of *pūgī-phala* trees, and for a month uses their flowers and consecrated substances (*siddha-dravya*), [attains the aforementioned results].
One should worship the Goddess together with her retinue within the Śrīcakra;
by means of such qualities as enchanting women and [bestowing] beauty, one shall become equal to Kandarpa (the God of Love). Thus ends the practice for causing delight to women.
Having meditated upon the maiden as non-different from the Goddess throughout the entire month according to the prescribed rules,
and having invoked the Goddess in that manner, they worship Her;
then, the *kṛtyās* instigated by others and the malevolent mantras (*abhicāra-mantra*) instigated by others become averse toward the practitioner, turning back against their own instigators.

They devour their enemies. Thus is the practice for the pacification of *kṛtyā* and other such evils. For one who worships Śrī Lalitā—accompanied by the respective powers residing in the various wheels (*cakra*)—for the duration of a month, preceded by meditation and invocation within the three yantras named Vajra-liṅga, Meru-liṅga, and Mahā-liṅga, there shall be happiness in this world consisting of sons, wife, wealth, and so forth.
And after death, one shall attain the happiness of heaven and so forth. Thus concludes the application for the happiness of both worlds.

For one who worships daily for the duration of a month with flowers— each fashioned from gold weighing one hundred *māṣas* according to their capacity, and made fragrant with camphor, musk, and other aromatic substances—
the destruction of all sins accumulated in previous births shall occur. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the destruction of sin (*pāpakṣayaprayoga*).

For one who worships the Goddess together with her enclosures (*sāvaraṇā*) in the *Śrīcakra* daily for a month using these nine gems gathered together, there shall be the destruction of all sins and the direct visual perception (*akṣuṣapratyakṣa*) of the Principal Goddess.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the direct perception of the Goddess. [One should worship] with fresh garments well-scented with fragrant substances such as camphor and the like.
For those who worship [this] daily for the duration of one month, there shall be the destruction of all sins accumulated in this life,
as well as the pacification of suffering arising from enemies, magical spells, poisons, and the like.

This is the application for the destruction of sins accumulated in this life: having meditated upon one's own body as the Śrīcakra, one should visualize the individual soul (jīvātman) therein in the form of a flame of a lamp as the Principal Goddess; and [one should likewise contemplate] the organs of knowledge and the organs of action situated all around within the body and one's own self.

Having meditated upon the mind, intellect, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and so forth— as well as the powers such as *aṇimā*, the coverings (*āvaraṇa*), and the deities— having offered fragrance as fragrance, non-violence and the like as flowers, touch as incense, form as a lamp, taste as an oblation (*naivedya*), and sound as praise, [one should worship] her together with her coverings.
For the practitioner who worships the Goddess incessantly, liberation while living (jīvanmukti) occurs.
Thus concludes the practice for liberation while living.
Thus are concluded the ritual applications for worship as taught in the sixth chapter.

I shall describe the fruits for one who, having written the Kālanityā-vidyā— measured by six, fire (three), mountain (seven), and one's own arms (two)— upon a leaf that is entirely beautiful with the syllable *ra*, constantly worships it here with fragrant perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; and in whatever country, city,
or house there is the worship of the Kālanityā-vidyā established upon a book.

There shall be no fear of affliction caused by the actions of others incited by enemies, nor fear of hostile armies, drought, excessive rain, spirits, ghosts, untimely death, and so forth; if such results are intended for the country as a whole, it goes without saying that the city will also be connected with such results—what need then to mention the household? However...

One must exert effort with regard to the ritual application (*prayoga*) out of respect for the fruit, respect for the worship, and respect for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). For it is not appropriate that there be equality between a ritual application intended for the protection of a single house and one intended for the protection of an entire region.

For the practitioner who performs such worship, there shall be the accomplishment of all tasks intended for oneself. Thus concludes the procedure for the daily worship of the Kālanityās presiding over the book that grants all desired objects to the practitioner and removes obstacles such as [unfavorable] places and times. [This is to be done] upon a very large and smooth cloth, within the wheels of time (*kālacakra*).

Among the five hundred and seventy-six [years], starting from the first year of each respective yuga until its final year, one should extract the Kālacakra corresponding to that year for which the worship has been performed; then,
having extracted the eight-petalled lotus as prescribed, that extracted Kālacakra falls upon its own pericarp.

Likewise, having extracted and written the eight mantras of the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevī) previously mentioned upon the petals, one should write the Kālacakra within the pericarp situated at the center of all; then, having written the letter *ā*, which is the face-circle of the pericarp, and having written the letter *ī*— which is a synonym for the fourth vowel— in that very same row, one should create three rows within the belly of the letter *ī*.
Therein, having sequentially inscribed the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the verb of action,

one should write the form beginning with the letter *a*— which is synonymous with the "first vowel"— at the initial portion of the two syllables inscribed upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) over the course of one year, and likewise each of the great syllables individually.
Having joined each syllable with a single *tattva*, one should write them; for each individual wheel corresponds to one year.

A year consists of sixteen months, and in each month there are thirty-six days; thus, in total, there are five hundred and seventy-six days in one year. The syllables likewise consist of thirty-six letters of the *tattvas*.
Each [of these] should be written there, having attained a number of five hundred and seventy-six through their conjunction with each of the sixteen vowels.

In the same manner, on whichever day, having written in the center of the pericarp (karṇikā) at the initial position the very syllable that was obtained from the scripture as the foremost syllable to be written in the outer enclosure,
one should join that very syllable with the second facial syllable by means of the euphonic combination known as *savarṇadīrgha*, using those respective unmodified syllables.

One should cause them to be joined. The letter *A* alone is intended for the first year; then, from the beginning up to the end of the alphabet (*Kṣa*), day after day, they are unified as one. Bound to the second face, the third is without modification.
Thus, it is established that one should inscribe the three-syllabled Vidyā within the pericarp (*karṇikā*). When the Yantra has been thus perfected—
