Having fashioned the filaments, which extend from the lines on both sides of each petal by two degrees inward toward the base of the circle, up to the limit of the central circle of filaments, in pairs according to the sequence of petals; [one should proceed as follows].

Having erased the filaments and the portions of the Brahma-thread located within the petals, one should thus produce the second constituent wheel of the Śrīcakra, known as the sixteen-petalled lotus, by means of three circles in this manner. Then, having established six marks on that same side at the measurement of six parts, [one should do so] also on the opposite side.

Having fashioned six marks each according to the measure of one-sixth [of the diameter], and having produced sixteen marks in total upon the circle; then, starting from each pair of inner marks and proceeding to each outer mark,
excluding the circle at the base of the sixteen petals, [one should draw] that which is situated inside it.

Having first conceived a circle at the tip of the eight-petaled lotus as the outer circumference, one should then form the stamen-circle by drawing a circle with a radius of twenty-six parts; then, having formed the base-circle of the petals by drawing a circle within that with a radius of twenty-four parts,
[one should place] the outer circle there.
Having marked four points at the four corners by measuring half the length of the segment situated between the two intermediate points of the intersection of the Brahma-sūtras,
and having marked two points at the two locations of the intersection of the Brahma-sūtras;

There are two marks on the eastern and western sides of the point where that [line] intersects; thus, there are eight marks in total, which constitute the tips of the eight petals. Having divided [the circle] at the tips of the petals, one should [draw lines] from each tip to the points of intersection on both sides of the point where the Brahma-line (the central axis) intersects the circle of the base, using equal intervals throughout.
Having made each individual mark and thus produced eight marks in total,

one should fashion the eight petals by drawing sixteen lines in combination, starting from the two internal marks located on both sides within the inner circle and extending to the outer marks. For each petal—
By means of the sequence of pairs and pairs, from the two side lines, within two parts and two parts [respectively], the root-circles are joined together. (p.

Having fashioned the filaments (kesara) up to the extent of the second circle, which is accepted as the circle of the filaments, and having erased the portions of the Brahma-threads located within the petals, the third constituent wheel of the Śrīcakra, known as the eight-petalled lotus, is accomplished by means of three circles; and thus:

Between the sixteen-petalled and eight-petalled lotuses, there is a single path (vīthī) which, as will be described, concludes here just as it does in the previously mentioned lotus-wheel (*kamalacakra*). In reality, however, since the filaments (*kesara*) are not taught [here], they do not exist in the present context. Furthermore, because of the observation that "by six circles" (*ṣaḍbhir vṛttaiḥ*), it is indeed a circle (*vṛtta*).

The consensus of opinion is that it is indeed expressly stated [in the text]. Since it is not specifically mentioned in the *Amṛtaghaṭayantra*, and because the description of the petals (*kesara*) is given under the name "writing of the letters" (*varṇalikhana*), the petals certainly exist everywhere in this tantra.
For this very reason, the statement "by six verses" (*ṣaḍbhir vṛttaiḥ*) also refers to the solar nature of the *Tithigrantha*.

The venerable teachers [state] that the prohibition found in other tantras does not apply here; therefore, all marks— except for those placed at the positions of six parts, six parts, three parts, four parts, three parts, five parts, and six parts along the Brahma-sūtra extending from east to west— are to be excluded.
Having wiped [the area] according to the instructions of Vasiṣṭha, one should stretch a single thread each upon the third and seventh marks respectively in front of oneself,
forming circular lines. Then, having stretched two threads extending from north to south,
starting from the northern and southern ends of the third thread— which serves as the western thread— one should [draw] those two threads.
Having placed [the thread] with its eastern tip at the end of the Brahma-thread,

and having likewise stretched two other threads starting from both ends of the seventh thread (which serves as the eastern thread) until the western end of the Brahma-thread, one completes the six-cornered wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*).
Starting from the southern tip of the second line up to the point where it intersects the ninth Brahma-line;
and starting from the northern tip of the second line up to the point where it intersects the ninth Brahma-line.

Having drawn two lines with their tips pointing upward to form one triangle; and having drawn another pair of lines starting from the southern tip of the eighth line up to the point where the first line intersects the Brahma-sūtra; and having thus formed another triangle with its tips pointing downward, such that there are four lines in total. In this manner:
One should apply manual skill [as follows]:
starting from the southern tip of the ninth line up to the point where the fourth line intersects the Brahma-thread;
and starting from the northern tip of the ninth line up to the point where it intersects the Brahma-thread at the fourth line.
By drawing two lines downward, a triangle is formed below. Starting from the southern tip of the first line up to the point where it meets the seventh line,
and starting from the northern tip of the first line up to the point where it meets the seventh line at the Brahma-thread intersection—

Having struck another line and formed an upward-pointing triangle, the eight vital points (*marmāṣṭa*) are produced. Starting from the southern tip of the fourth line, up to the point of intersection between the eighth line and the Brahma-thread,
[one proceeds] along the fourth line.

Then, having drawn two lines starting from the northern [point] up to the junction of the eighth line and the Brahma-sūtra, and having formed an upward-pointing triangle, one should likewise [draw] each of the sixth lines with a southern tip and a northern tip.

Having laid down two lines from the starting point up to the intersection with the Brahma-sūtra (the central vertical line), and having thus formed a downward-pointing triangle, a regular tetrahedron is produced. By making each of the fifth lines also point toward the south, the Śrīcakra is completed. And here, starting from the second [line] which points upward—
The third line extends to the point where it intersects with the Brahma-sūtra.
44a) By laying down two lines, one forms a downward-pointing triangle, and thus two equal [triangles] are produced. Thus [it is said].

Having wiped away the Brahma-thread (brahmasūtra) which is contained within everywhere, and having now placed the drop (bindu) inside the extracted *yoni*, the Śrīcakra becomes extracted. And here, the first line of the great triangle (*mahātrikoṇa*) is the downward-pointing second line;
[and there are] upward-going lines at the ends of the first horizontal and south-north lines.
By virtue of the junction, two equal [segments] are established on both sides of the second line. Likewise,
there are the lines starting from the end of the second line and reaching the first line— the Brahma-sūtra—
and the lines starting from the point of intersection of the western circle-line with the Brahma-sūtra.
Due to the junctions on both sides of the third line, there are two equal [segments]. Likewise, the third line is the line originating from the end of the first line;
[this occurs] due to the junctions of the lines originating from the point of junction between the first line and the Brahma-sūtra.

Furthermore, there are two equal [segments] on the two middle sides, which together constitute four equal [segments] for the third line. Likewise, there is an upward line originating from the end of the fourth line. Due to the junction of the lines originating from the point where the second line meets the Brahma-sūtra, there are two equal [segments] on both sides.
Success is achieved on the fourth line; likewise, it occurs by virtue of the junction of the fifth line,
the downward-pointing line originating from the ends of the second and ninth lines,
and the upward-pointing line originating from the end of the first line.
On both sides, at the fifth line, there are two equal [intervals]. Likewise,
due to the junctions of the lines beginning from the end of the fourth line and the lines beginning from the end of the ninth line, there are two equal [intervals] on both sides at the sixth line.
A great triangular line is formed starting from the third terminal point at the upper end of the seventh line;
furthermore, on both sides, there are two equal [triangles] formed by the junctions of lines originating from the terminal points of the eighth line.
On the seventh line, a square is formed; from the ends of the eighth and ninth lines, a downward line is drawn,
and from the ends of the second line, an upward line is drawn— the junction of these two further forms another [square] on both sides.
Regarding "two equal [parts]": by joining together, the seventh line forms two equal [segments].

Due to the junction of the lines—namely, the upward-pointing tip of the [seventh] line, the downward-pointing tip of the great triangle’s [eighth] line, and the line initiated from the end of the ninth line—the two equal [segments] on either side of the eighth line are established. Thus it is said.
When combined, it results in eighteen equal circles.

There are four squares formed by the first and second lines; from the third and fourth [lines], there are three, of which two are facing upward and are synonymous with *vahni* (fire) and *puṇya* (merit), and one—
And here there are two downward-facing compartments (*koṣṭha*) which are synonyms for the *yoni*, *śakti*, and so forth.
Between the second and third [compartments] are seven triangles. Among them, one is upward-facing and four are downward-facing.
Between the fourth and fifth [compartments] are seven triangles; among those, four are [downward-facing].

There are three squares facing upward and four facing downward; between the fifth and sixth [squares], there are four downward-facing triangles; between the sixth and seventh, there are five squares and seven triangles. Among those, six are downward-facing and one is upward-facing, making six squares in total.
In the space between the seventh and eighth [squares], there are five downward-facing triangles;
four squares with one opening facing upward; and four cells with openings facing upward.

In the space between the eighth and ninth [squares], there are three triangles; among them, one faces upward and two face downward. There are also two compartments here, and two triangles here—one in the lower portion and one in the upper portion of all the lines.
In sequence, there are forty-three triangles in total, consisting of upward-facing and downward-facing ones:
nineteen are upward-facing and twenty-four are downward-facing.
This results from the twenty-four intersections formed by the four lines extending upwards and downwards.

The numbers: Within a single Brahma-thread, nine triangles are interconnected. Among them, five are downward-facing and four are upward-facing; in brief, between each of those downward- and upward-facing triangles, there is one intervening square. Thus it is said.

The Extraction of the Śrīcakra. Now, as it occurs subsequent to the worship, the ritual procedure for initiation (*abhiṣeka*) is set forth, having entered the path of memory. On the day prior to the day of initiation, one should [visualize] the Kālacakra as previously described, which has been attained for that year.

Having extracted an eight-petaled lotus joined with the [mudrās] such as Vahirgatavaśinī and others, and having installed it according to the prescribed rite, at the conclusion of the worship— including the [deities] of the lunar day, the weekday, and so forth, which are mentioned for application in rites for specific desires (kāmyakarman)— one should proceed, preceded by the placement of the *arghya* water, after recording the place, time, one's own lineage (*gotra*), zodiac sign (*rāśi*), name, and the desired object, in accordance with the injunctions.
"I shall perform [the rite] without the application of consecration (abhiṣeka). Having thus made the primary formal resolve (pradhāna-saṃkalpa),
one should place there a water-pot (kalaśa) capable of holding a measure of water equal to a khārī,
fill it with water consisting of a decoction of fifty-two medicinal herbs, and [place] gold and other items therein as before.
Having performed the casting [of the deity], the wrapping with a pair of garments, the covering of the face with mango sprouts, and so forth;

and having meditated there upon the Śrīcakra—characterized as described—which is the manifestation of all auspiciousness and the removal of the thoughts of crookedness, p. 45b) ... [the practitioner] should visualize it.

Having worshipped Lalitā, who is the principal deity therein, preceded by the worship of the seat (*pīṭha*), meditation, invocation, and so forth, according to the system of nine enclosures (*navāvaraṇa*); and having performed the consecration of the water-jars (*kalaśābhimantraṇa*) at night with all the *Kālanityās*, numbering three hundred and sixty-seven (20736).

In the morning, having again performed only the worship in that very same water-pot according to the nine-fold arrangement (*navāvaraṇa*)— following the sequence of invocation (*āvāhana*), the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and so forth as before— the preceptor, together with his wife, should seat the disciple for whom the consecration is to be performed upon the throne.

In one's own birth asterism, according to the number twenty-eight and so forth determined by its own configuration; in the tenth asterism from that, and in the nineteenth asterism from that— at the time of one's birth,
whichever planets such as the Sun and others reside in which respective asterisms, and likewise in those same asterisms encountered month by month.

One should perform the consecration every full moon day throughout the entire year. Once consecrated, the disciple should give to the preceptor who performed the consecration a ring fashioned from gold weighing twelve *suvarṇas* and a cow.
By means of this rite of consecrating one's own limbs, the consecrated person shall attain the status of a great king (*mahārāja*). By no other [means].
Even if that [attainment] is impossible due to a powerful obstacle, the status of being honored by the king (*rājamānyatva*) will certainly occur;
or rather, while the princes obtain the kingdom, others attain the status of being honored by the king.
For the entire lineage of one who performs the ritual of consecration (*abhiṣeka-prayoga*) throughout two years in the manner described, [the result follows].
There shall be the possession of great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*). Through initiation (*abhiṣeka*) extending over three years, the accomplishment of a *vidyādhara* shall arise;
through initiation extending over four years, the accomplishment of a *khecarī* shall arise.

From initiation at five years of age, there shall be long life. Through initiation up to six years, one achieves sovereignty equal to that of Indra and the other world-protectors. Through initiation up to seven years, one attains equality with the sun in terms of majesty and so forth. From initiation at eight years... [the state of] equality.

By virtue of gladdening all people and other such qualities, [this state] comes to be. Through consecration (*abhiṣeka*) up to nine years, equality with Śrī Lalitā is attained. However, through consecration at ten years, there is nothing further to be accomplished;
for there is no object of desire superior to equality with the Goddess. Thus.

The Ritual Procedure for the Vase Consecration Based on the Kālacakra. According to the aforementioned method, on the day prior to the intended consecration and so forth, one should prepare the Śrī-cakra on a well-leveled ground or similar surface after having cleared it. Therein, having installed the vessel according to the ritual rules preceded by the consecration of the yantra, one performs the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*).
Having worshipped the Goddess with the nine enclosures (navāvaraṇa) preceded by the offering of vehicles and other items,

one should worship all the mantras of Kālanityā according to the previously mentioned number. On the following day, on the occasion of one's own birth-star (janmanakṣatra), or on the new moon (amāvāsyā), or during a special occasion such as a lunar eclipse, [one should initiate] the disciple.

One should perform the consecration as before. Having been consecrated, one should give the previously mentioned fee and satisfy the guru. By that [act], there will be the removal of the unfavorable influence of the planets, calamities caused by one's own enemies, and the effects of *stambhana*, *dveṣaṇa*, and *uccāṭana* wrought by foes;
furthermore, even direct blows from swords and the like that would otherwise lead to death.
And he desires the pacification of *kṛtyās*, which consist of the practice of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) as prescribed in the mantra-śāstras and other texts with the intent of causing death.

The five afflictions consisting of ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live, as well as the sufferings pertaining to the internal, the celestial, the elemental, and the physical, come to destruction. Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the vase-consecration based on the Śrīcakra. Now follows the ritual procedure for the recitation of the Kālanityā-vidyā.

First, that wheel of worship (*pūjācakra*) is described: having constructed two squares, one within the other, and having fashioned two doors in the eastern and western directions there—just as in the *Śrīcakra*—one should, within that space, fashion an eight-petalled lotus;
and in its pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should arrange the nine-yoni wheel according to the directions specified for the worship-wheel of Kulasundarī. Therein...

Having written the three-syllabled Vidyā—which is either one's own object of worship or that which pertains to the specific day—at the very center of all [the petals], and having inscribed within the interior of its third syllable the names of the person to be accomplished and the practitioner, such as "O Devadatta, grant me your grace! Act! and so forth; then, starting from the fire-born [southern] petal and proceeding up to the left side of the tip of the eighth petal—

In the sixteen locations, one writes the sixteen mantras beginning with *hrīṃ ārūpiṇīśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi* and ending with *hrīṃ aḥrūpiṇīśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. Then, in the path between the two squares within the circle at the tips of the petals, one places the syllable *ha* in the west.

Having written the syllable *la* in the south and the syllable *kṣa* in the east; having written the seed-syllable of Māyā, also known as *Hṛllekhā*, in the northern direction; having written the twelve syllables from *a* to *ai* in the southwest corner;
having written the twelve syllables from *o* to *na* in the southeast corner; [and] in the northeast corner...
Having written the twelve syllables beginning with *jha* and ending with *dhana* (i.e., *jha ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa*),

one should write the twelve syllables beginning with *pa* and ending with *ṣa* (i.e., *pa pha ba bha ma ya ra la va śa ṣa*) in the northwest corner (*vāyavyakoṇa*). This is the ritual application for desired results (*kāmyaprayoga*).
The writing of the aforementioned syllables is not required even in the *nityapūjā* yantra. Having thus extracted the yantra and prepared the materials for worship,

one should perform the rites ending with bathing, sitting on the seat, sipping water (*ācamana*), purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).

Having offered the *bali* with the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā, which takes the form "Kurukullāyai svāhā," and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should prepare the *arghya* as before using the two mantras for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the primary Nityā that are about to be described, and then perform the primary formal resolve (*pradhāna-saṃkalpa*).

Having performed [the rite] preceded by the mention of the fruit intended for oneself, and having performed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa at the end of the six limbs of the Mātṛkā, one should perform it with the Kālanityā-vidyā written in the center, repeated twice:
*A* to the heart, *namas*; *Ā* to the head, *svāhā*; *I* to the tuft, *vaṣaṭ*; *AḤ* to the armor, *hum*.

Having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) in this manner—namely, *ā netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* for the eyes and *ī astrāya phaṭ* for the weapon—upon the thumb and other fingers, as well as upon the heart and other parts of the body; one should meditate, preceded by visualization, according to the following description: "One should contemplate [the deities] who are red and non-red, possessing non-red ornaments, garlands, and unguents, and holding nooses, goads, sugarcane bows, and flower-arrows."

Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, as well as the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and so forth for the *Kālanityās* of the middle womb, and having worshipped them with the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*) beginning with the primary offering and ending with betel (*tāmbūla*), one should worship the Gurus in three rows behind this principal Goddess using the previously mentioned Guru-mantras, proceeding clockwise around the triangle as prescribed.

Having worshipped the six-limbed deities with the aforementioned mantras, and having worshipped the weapons with the mantras previously mentioned at the sides of the central *yoni* and on the flanks of their respective banners, one should worship Hrīṃ Arūpiṇī starting from the front corner according to the order of writing.
Having worshipped the sixteen forms, letters, and powers (varṇa-śaktis) using the mantras written preceded by fourteen syllables, such as "I worship the sandals of Śakti" (śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi),
one should then worship [the goddesses] in the eight directions starting from the front of the square, beginning with: "Hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Brāhmī-śakti," and so forth.

Having worshipped the powers (śaktis) such as Brāhmī with mantras beginning with twelve syllables, and having performed the remaining three services consisting of libation (tarpaṇa), hymn (stotra), and prostration (namaskāra), one should offer an oblation (bali) with the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā, and [conclude] with the hymn consisting of twelve verses shown in the *Nityakamala*.

Having praised the Goddess and having bid farewell to the Goddess within one's own self, one should dismiss the vessel of the *arghya* offering. Then, for the sake of one's own welfare— combining both the aforementioned fruits and immediate results— one should quickly sit upon the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*) that was previously prepared and worship the mantra of Kālanityā.

However, one who desires only the fruit of *āvṛtti* (repetition) should sit down in any pure place and recite those mantras; the method for this has already been shown at the occasion of the *apārāyaṇa*. In that case, by repeating all the *Kālanityā* vidyās fifty times (50), liberation from the shackles and bonds inflicted by enemies occurs.

By a hundred repetitions, there shall be the attainment of eyes... [omitted] ... By one hundred and fifty (150) repetitions, a bridegroom shall obtain a maiden, and a maiden shall obtain a bridegroom. By two hundred (200) repetitions, poverty shall be destroyed. By three hundred (300) repetitions, there shall be the acquisition of land filled with grain. By four hundred (400) repetitions, there shall be the state of great wealth. By five hundred...

By five hundred repetitions, one becomes the lord of the earth; by six hundred (600), there is the attainment of a kingdom; by seven hundred (700), there shall be the Great Fortune (Mahālakṣmī) that pervades the entire lineage of those who practice it.

By reciting this [mantra] eight hundred times (800), all kings shall become obedient to his command; by reciting it nine hundred times (900), there is the fulfillment of unspoken desires for those who chant this collection of vidyās, and through the generation of affection in women, one attains equality with the god of love (Manobhava). Thus end the applications mentioned in connection with worship.

These have been explained in the sections on consecration and recitation. Now, we shall set forth the ritual procedure for the fire sacrifice (homa), which follows in the order of the topical outline.

The daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) is performed either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). Having sprinkled [the area] with the water of the arghya-offering while reciting the root-vidyā, one should fashion a wheel of nine squares by drawing four lines running east-west and four lines running north-south using kusha grass. Having established the fire along with its vessel, one should take a single fragment of charcoal from it.

Having cast [the fire] in the southwest direction with the mantra "kravyādebhyo namaḥ," one should rotate it three times around the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and other such sites in a clockwise direction starting from the northeast; then, having placed it in the center of the nine-square grid and ignited it with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*),
one should perform the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*) by sprinkling water from the *arghya* vessel all around the pit and other areas, unless there is a specific exception.

Having kindled the fire with sacrificial wood, one should worship the seven tongues of flame in the seven central squares, proceeding clockwise with the mantras beginning with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hiraṇyāyai Namaḥ. Then, after meditating on the non-difference between the fire and the five deities under discussion, [one should offer oblations] with the aforementioned fire-mantra ending in "Svāhā."
Having offered nine oblations with each of the previously mentioned mantras ending in "svāhā" for the tongues beginning with Hiraṇyā,
having likewise offered nine oblations for each with clarified butter using either a palāśa or aśvattha leaf,
and having given one oblation each to the principal deities and the attendants such as Aṇimā and the rest;
Preceded by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform oblations with the respective substances and in the respective numbers according to each specific desire.
For instance, [one may offer] leaves, filaments, and so forth, filled with [substances] mixed with insects or hair, combined with the three sweets (trimadhura).

For a year, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (the lunar day *pratipad*) up until the full moon— the period known as the "white" (*śukla*) fortnight— he offered, in uninterrupted succession, hundreds of thousands of various lotuses and other flowers such as red *karavīra* and so forth.

For the practitioner performing oblations, there shall be equality with a king by virtue of possessing wealth such as elephants, horses, and the like, as well as having his commands unimpeded by all people. Even for one who performs oblations with white lotuses during those same fifteen days previously mentioned, equality with a king occurs.
By offering *kahāra* flowers for a full year on those very days previously mentioned, there shall be an abundance of wealth, grain, and so forth.

By performing oblations with blue lotuses (*utpala*) for a full year on those same days, one shall attain great prosperity. By offering red lotuses for a full year on those same days, one shall obtain a maiden; [as well as] red lotuses, *karavīra*, and other such flowers.

For one year, performing oblations every single day during those same five days— with each of the six substances consisting of *puṣpa*, white lotus (*abja*), *kahlāra*, blue lotus (*utpala*), and red lotus (*raktotpala*), each individually saturated with saffron pollen, and offered in a number of either one hundred thousand or one million— one becomes possessed of unwavering Great Fortune (*mahālakṣmī*).
And long life comes about preceded by happiness and self-mastery.
For one who performs the fire-oblation (*homa*) for a full year, as previously described, using the six substances such as lotuses smeared with sandalwood paste, [the result follows].

For the practitioner who performs oblations for one year, using each of the previously mentioned six substances individually— smeared with camphor and dūrvā grass— for the aforementioned period of fifteen days, there shall be long life preceded by the happiness of sons, male servants, and female servants.

In the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), there will be long life accompanied by the happiness of young women, preceded by the attainment of a state equal to Kandarpa through beauty, the enchantment of women, subjugation, and so forth.
For one who, beginning from the first lunar day until the new moon, offers oblations every day in ascending order with sugar-coated in ghee,
numbering either one hundred or one thousand, for the duration of one year, there arises the attainment of prosperity free from rivals.

It may be so: for practitioners who perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) throughout the year using jaggery mixed with honey on those very days—beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa-pratipad*) up to the new moon (*darśa*)—there shall be long life preceded by splendor, fortune, victory, and health. On those very days...

For a practitioner who performs the fire-oblation (*homa*) for one year using grapes smeared with milk and consumes only milk as food, there will always be long life preceded by constant clarity of mind. During those same fifteen days, for one year, [one should perform the oblation] with [grapes] smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).

By performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) with dates (*kharjūra*), one attains long life, health, victory, and great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*). During those same fifteen days of the dark fortnight, for the duration of one year,
[one should offer] plantain fruits (*kadala-phala*) smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*).
By performing one hundred thousand oblations with any one of these, preceded by the honor of all kings, merit, and fame,

the practitioner attains a happy life of a hundred years. This is accomplished by offering coconuts mixed with sugar and honey on the fifteenth days of the dark fortnights throughout the course of a year.

For one performing the fire sacrifice (*homa*), there is the attainment of all desired objects. By performing the *homa* with coconut fruits soaked in sugarcane juice on those very same fifteenth days of the dark fortnight, there shall be the acquisition of many roots and garments of various colors. On those same days, [the results are as stated].
For one year, [one should offer] each of the six substances consisting of sugar, jaggery, grapes, dates, plantains, and coconut fruits, individually smeared with the three sweets (trimadhura). (p.

From this oblation, there is the attainment of even greater prosperity. For one whose cow’s calf is white and who herself is white at that time, by performing the *havana* (offering) for one year on the fifteen days of the dark fortnight with the aforementioned six kinds of substances smeared with the milk of that cow, there is the attainment of even greater prosperity; likewise, by using substances smeared with the milk of a buffalo-cow.
By performing oblations for one year during the fifteen days of the dark fortnight each month with the six substances beginning with sugar,

all desired goals are accomplished; likewise, by performing oblations for one year during the fifteen days of the dark fortnight each month with the six kinds of substances beginning with sugar, saturated either with goat’s milk or sheep’s milk, all desired goals are accomplished.

By performing oblations for one year on the fifteenth days of the dark fortnights with substances such as sugar mixed with coconut pulp and saturated with milk, all desired goals are accomplished; likewise,
by performing them daily throughout both the bright and dark fortnights for one year, using [offerings] smeared with cow’s milk, honey, and ghee.
By performing oblations for twenty-one days with the twelve substances consisting of the group of six beginning with *paṅkaja* and the group of six beginning with sugar (*śarkarā*),

or alternatively, by performing oblations every day for an entire year using the aforementioned twelve substances combined, one experiences the happiness of abundance in cattle, land, gold, and clothing.
The practitioner shall become long-lived. Thus concludes the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) preceded by the lunar days (tithi).
By performing oblations every Saturday for an entire year with white rice cooked in milk, mixed with either ghee, honey, or both, one attains abundance of food.
By performing oblations every Monday for an entire year with coconut fruits combined with sugar, one attains an abundance of grain.
On a Tuesday (Bhauma-vāra), there is the attainment of a prosperous land through the offering of food smeared with honey; there is the acquisition of fortune (śrī).

By performing oblations with those [materials] mixed with earth from the ground intended as the object of one's own acquisition, one hundred thousand times for each respective ground, the acquisition of that ground is attained.
For one who performs an oblation of sesame seeds and rice grains smeared with ghee on Wednesdays throughout the course of a year:
There is the attainment of the glory that bestows all happiness.

For one who offers oblations with the pollen of jackfruit seeds mixed with cow’s milk on every Thursday throughout the year, there will be the attainment of great prosperity and abundance in all things. This should be done every Friday for the duration of one year.

For the practitioner who offers oblations of coconut flower pollen mixed with sugar or mixed with jaggery, there shall be an increase in sons, grandsons, and progeny, preceded by the attainment of great fortune lasting for a period of one year, starting from the very moment of contact [with the deity].
This applies on every Saturday.

For a practitioner who, for the duration of one year, performs oblations with sesame seeds that are free from contact with hair, insects, and the like, and likewise unmixed with substances such as ghee, oil, or the three sweets (*trimadhu*), or alternatively, with sesame seeds smeared with sesame oil— on every day of the week, including those of the Sun, Moon, and others— he shall attain prosperity (*lakṣmī*) desired by all people.

For the practitioner who offers oblations— either one hundred or one thousand times— for each of all the previously mentioned seven substances, such as white rice-porridge and sesame seeds, combined with their respective medicinal ointments,
the attainment of the fruit is Mahālakṣmī herself within a period of seven days, a month, or a year.

There shall be prosperity. In this regard, even for those joined with great poverty and the like, there is a remedy through the specific power of the vidyā; therefore, one should strive in its application in every way.
For there is a remedy for those things whose occurrence is inevitable.

Based on the observation of such passages as "if it should be so," one should remain indifferent. On the days of the performance of the *homa* mentioned or yet to be mentioned, one should feed three or two Brahmins who are devotees of the *Śrīvidyā*, according to one's capacity. Thus it is said.
The ritual procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) preceded by the day of the week: an oblation with *śāli* rice mixed with honey under the asterism Aśvinī;
an oblation with rice grains smeared with ghee under Bharaṇī; an oblation with mung beans smeared with oil under Kṛttikā;
and an oblation with black gram (*māṣa*) food soaked in cow’s milk under Rohiṇī.
An oblation of sesame seeds soaked in coconut water should be performed under the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa; an oblation of black sesame seeds soaked in sugarcane juice under the asterism Ārdrā;
an oblation of white mustard seeds soaked in buffalo milk under the asterism Punarvasu;
and an oblation of black mustard seeds soaked in goat’s milk under the asterism Puṣya.

If a homa is performed by the practitioner under the asterism Āśleṣā using kodrava grains soaked in undiluted milk, he becomes a Mahālakṣmī-kara (one who brings great fortune) within the time required for the preparation of curdled milk. A homa performed under the asterism Maghā with offerings of the three sweets (trimadhu) mixed with raw rice flour is auspicious.
A homa performed under the asterism Pūrvaphalgunī with offerings of the three sweets mixed with cooked rice is likewise effective.
An oblation of *mudga* beans cooked with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) should be performed under Uttaraphalgunī;
an oblation of *kṛśara* rice mixed with the three sweets should be performed under Hasta; an oblation of *māṣa* beans smeared with the three sweets should be performed under Citrā;
and an oblation of boiled rice cooked with turmeric powder and the three sweets should be performed under Svātī.
An oblation of rice mixed with molasses and smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) is performed under Viśākhā;

an oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with the three sweets is performed under Anurādhā; and an oblation of pure boiled rice (*śuddhodana*) smeared with the three sweets is performed under Jyeṣṭhā. When practiced by the adept, this brings about the attainment of victory, prosperity, and fame.
A *homa* performed with broad grains (*pṛthuka*) smeared with cow’s milk under the *Mūla* asterism;

a *homa* with barley meal (*saktu*) smeared with cow’s milk under *Pūrvāṣāḍhā*; a *homa* with parched grain (*lāja*) smeared with cow’s milk under *Uttarāṣāḍhā*; [and a *homa*] with sugarcane stalks smeared with cow’s milk [under the same].

Homa performed during Śravaṇā consists of cakes made from śāli rice, anointed with the three sweets (trimadhu). Homa during Dhaniṣṭhā consists of cakes made from barley, anointed with the three sweets. Homa during Śatabhiṣā consists of cakes made from caru, anointed with the three sweets.
An oblation of cakes made from *mudga* beans soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhura*) performed under Pūrvabhādrapadā;
an oblation of cakes made from *māṣa* beans soaked in the three sweets performed under Uttarabhādrapadā;
and an oblation of cakes produced from sesame paste soaked in the three sweets performed under Revatī—these, when accomplished, bring about victory, fame, fortune, and freedom from disease.
It shall be the bestower of long life, good fortune, world-wide honor, and the fruits of physical form for practitioners.
Thus concludes the ritual application of the *nakṣatra-puraskāra-homa*. There are three kinds of *siddhi-yogas*:

those arising from the conjunction of specific lunar days (*tithi*) and weekdays, those arising from specific lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and weekdays, and those yogas included within other yogas such as *vikumbha* and so forth.

Regarding the "distinction" (*viśeṣa*): in all three of these cases, whatever substance is used for the fire-oblation (*homa*), that substance becomes an abundance for the practitioner. Furthermore, through the conjunction of lunar mansions and weekdays, or lunar days and weekdays, during the "Amṛta-yogas," [one may perform the rite] with *guḍūcī* plants smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), or else with *dūrvā* grass smeared with the three sweets.
A fire sacrifice (homa) performed with sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu) shall pacify all diseases. When the Sun is in the sign of Aries,
the Moon in Taurus, Mars in Capricorn, Mercury in Virgo, Jupiter in Cancer, Venus in Pisces,
and Saturn in Libra, the practitioner performing a homa with red lotuses [attains] for all...

One would be the best among the middling; however, there is not even a trace of possibility for being the best in one's own family. When the Moon has entered Aries, and Jupiter is in Taurus, and Venus has reached Libra, that is the yoga known as Parvata.
"One increases what has been given by oneself to an amount equal to oneself"—this is the definition stated [in the text].
During the *parvata-yoga*, whatever substance is used for the fire-oblation (*homa*), that substance becomes equal in measure to a mountain (*parvata*). Thus it is said.
The ritual procedure for the *yogapuraskāraka-homa*. Now follows the ritual procedure for the *kātyāyanīya-homa* and others, performed for the purpose of satisfying the planets.
When the Sun is in the sign of Leo or Aries; when the Moon is in Cancer or Taurus;
when Mars is in Aries, Scorpio, or Capricorn; when Mercury is in Gemini or Virgo;
when Jupiter is in Sagittarius, Pisces, or Cancer; when Venus is in Taurus, Libra, or Pisces; and when [Saturn] is in Capricorn, Aquarius, or Libra.

Or on a Saturday, for the practitioner who performs a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with ghee and sugar, reciting the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) either one hundred thousand or ten thousand times, the planets, being satisfied,
will not act with hostility, provided that [the rite is performed] under one's own asterism (*svarkṣe*).

At all times during the month of Vaiśākha, an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) smeared with ghee and sugar, performed with the Śrīvidyā mantra, brings prosperity. Furthermore, when that [rite] is completed, there shall be no affliction from the planets within one's own lineage. During all months beginning with Caitra, on the three asterisms of one's own birth, one should perform [the recitation] of dūrvā grass, guḍūcī, and sesame seeds, each by the number of one hundred thousand or another [specified] count.

Through the performance of *homa*, preceded by the perfection of the requisite conditions for removing secondary diseases and bestowing happiness and so forth, that practitioner shall remain happy for as long as he lives. If *homa* is impossible every month during the three lunar mansions of one's own birth, one should recite the primary daily mantra (*nityā-vidyā*) together with the daily mantra of that specific day; by that means, for that practitioner—
At any time, one may encounter some affliction such as being pursued by the royal police, or suffering humiliation, death, imprisonment,

and the like. On every month, at the birth-star (janmanakṣatra), or when such a wife [is present], one should perform [this rite] with water mixed with camphor and saturated with the three sweets (trimadhura), in a number of either one hundred or one thousand [offerings].

One should satisfy [the deity] with the root-vidyā. If such a libation (tarpaṇa) for each month and for the three birth-constellations (*janmanakṣatra*) is impossible, one should worship that Goddess with fragrant flowers. As for the previously mentioned fire-offerings (*homa*), recitations (*japa*), libations, and worship—whosoever...
He who does not practice even a single rule inevitably becomes,

at all times and in every way, overwhelmed by the afflictions of disease, the afflictions of poverty, the afflictions of public humiliation, and so forth. However, for a practitioner, when the Moon is in its own exaltation, in its own sign, or on its own day, [if one recites] a thousand or a hundred [times],...

One should worship Muktavidyā; for such a person, affliction by the planets shall never occur. Therefore, these applications are essential for practitioners. Otherwise, one who does not perform these applications will be afflicted by planetary distress, poverty, disease, and other such misfortunes.

If practitioners are afflicted by disease, poverty, or planetary influences, or likewise tormented by kings and bandits, then they will become objects of ridicule and contempt in the world; this is the summary. Thus concludes the ritual application for oblations and other rites that result in the propitiation of the planets. [Regarding] *palāśa*:

By performing oblations for an entire year with the five-fold components (pañcāṅga) consisting of flowers, fruits, vegetables, leaves, and roots, even one who is mute becomes eloquent. By offering oblations individually with the five-fold components of *arka* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), the attainment of every desired object of the mind occurs one by one; all desired objects are attained.

They are to be offered with a single deity as the intended recipient. Since each individual performance (prayoga) yields a single result, it is precisely this conclusion that applies in all cases of this kind: when there is a distinction between individual performances, multiple results arise from performances belonging to the same class. [One should offer] the five limbs of the bilva tree, each smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu).
By performing oblations until the completion of the mandala, the practitioner shall become Mahālakṣmī, pervading his entire lineage.
By offering lotus seeds smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu) throughout the extent of the mandala, one becomes a source of wonder for all the worlds.

One shall obtain prosperity. By performing oblations of *campaka* flowers mixed with honey until the completion of the mandala, one will possess great wealth. Likewise, for a practitioner who is childless, the birth of a virtuous son occurs through oblations of *campaka* flowers combined with honey until the completion of the mandala.

When the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Capricorn, for the practitioner who— abandoning the uninterrupted sequence— performs the fire-oblation (*homa*) with *caṃpaka* flowers soaked in ghee according to some method for the duration of forty-nine days up to the limit of the mandala,
there is the attainment of the stage of omniscience in its entirety.

And one would possess the power to consume various kinds of meat, non-edibles, foods, and so forth. When the Moon is in the sign of Taurus, for anyone who performs a fire-oblation (*homa*) for twenty-nine days with *campaka* flowers smeared with milk— abandoning the uninterrupted sequence and performing it in whatever manner possible— one will obtain a hundred cows.
By offering oblations with *campaka* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) throughout the previously mentioned period, one attains the state of always remaining at home,

as well as the acquisition of a virtuous son, a land filled with grain, and a hundred cows— these being the three desired fruits. Through the performance of *homa* with *pāṭala* flowers saturated with honey, the practitioner [attains these results].
One shall obtain a maiden as one's own wife through the performance of a *homa* with *tagara*,
flowers, parched grain (*lāja*), and *kuṭaja*, even when these are mixed with honey and offered independently of one another.
[The same result follows] from the *homa* of *mālatī* flowers, *nagara* flowers, parched grain, and *kuṭaja*.
By performing oblations for each of all these substances individually until the end with cow’s milk mixed [with them], filling the entire mandala,

the acquisition of wealth occurs. Furthermore, the acquisition of highly valuable garments of various colors will also result from performing oblations for each of the four items, such as the *pāṭala* flower and others, mixed with cow’s milk.

By performing oblations of *śatapatra* flowers soaked in the "three sweets" until the completion of a mandala, one attains the goddess Lakṣmī; and by offering each of the four types of flowers— namely the *kesara*, *kadaṃba*, *kundamallikā*, and the *vicikila* consisting of its various sub-varieties— one likewise attains her.

Even from performing oblations in a mandala saturated with the three sweets (trimadhura), one attains prosperity; furthermore, beginning from the first lunar day and proceeding through the fifth, one should offer flowers of *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jātī*, *puṇnāga*, and *suraparṇa*— the latter being synonymous with *nameru*— each saturated with honey, one by one in sequence.

Through the performance of *homa* with each of the five substances individually, the attainment of great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*) occurs. However, if the *homa* is performed in sequence, one by one, with the five flowers beginning with *mallikā* soaked in cow’s milk on the five lunar days beginning with the first day (*pratipad*), then there is an abundance of gold. Furthermore, if [the *homa* is performed] with *mallikā* and the others on the five lunar days beginning with the first day...

If an oblation is performed with five substances thoroughly saturated with cow’s ghee, then there will be the attainment of fortune in the form of ornaments such as bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and strings of pearls. By performing a homa with substances saturated with honey and karṇikāra flowers on the five lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad), [the same result follows].
There shall be unshakable prosperity that never departs at any time.

By performing oblations, one by one in sequence from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) to the fifth, with the five forms of the vehicles— namely, the white water-lily (*kahlāra*), the red *mukuḍa*, the white lotus (*utpala*), and the red lotus (*raktakamala*)— there will be many ornaments for each individually.

By offering flowers drenched in the three sweets (trimadhura), one obtains the fortune of Mahālakṣmī. With Ketakī flowers mixed with honey, by performing oblations on the days beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) up to the fifth, the practitioner shall obtain garments of various colors and of great value. By offering white flowers smeared with milk, starting from the first lunar day...
Up to the fifth [day], through the performance of oblations, there is the acquisition of white garments, pearls, and beauty.
By performing oblations with *maruvaka* flowers soaked in honey until the completion of the maṇḍala, all desired goals are accomplished.
Through oblations made with *damanaka* leaves soaked in honey until the completion of the mandala, the attainment of prosperity (*śrī*) occurs.

Whatever colored flowers are offered in oblation with the *Śrīvidyā*, one obtains clothing of that same color. Here too, the time for the oblation consists of the drawing of the mandala and so forth. [With] mustard seeds and black pepper soaked in mustard oil...
By performing oblations until the mandala is completed, and having first cast aside the pride born of natural modesty, one should attract the woman of one's desire.
[One should do so] with each of the following flowers individually: *pāṭalī*, *kunda*, *mandāra*, *śephālī*, *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, and *meru*.
By performing oblations with honey-mixed [substances] up to the limit of a maṇḍala, the subjugation of all women occurs simultaneously.

By offering as an oblation one or another of those very fuels, such as pāṭalī wood and so forth, soaked in ghee, men become subject to one's will. If, among those, one or all of them are offered soaked in ghee...

If the oblation were performed at night, then the practitioner would obtain clarified butter (*ājya*). If an oblation is performed using any one or all of those woods, such as *pāṭala* and others, smeared with sugar, then the entire world will be brought under control. [This is done] with ghee.
From the performance of oblations with *pluta* rice until the completion of the mandala, there is an abundance of food;
from the performance of oblations with rice mixed with sesame seeds smeared with ghee until the completion of the mandala, there is an increase in lifespan;

and from the performance of oblations with salt smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) and finely ground [grains] until the completion of the mandala, [there is success], performed in a continuous sequence every half-night.
By offering [the oblation] with a count of either one hundred or one thousand, the subjugation of all the limbs [of the body] occurs.
By this very ritual application, even courtesans are brought under control.
[This is done] with a circle demarcated during the time of midnight, using salt ground into an extremely fine powder and mixed with the juice of sugarcane from Puṇḍra.
From performing one hundred or more oblations for a period of time practiced according to the directions, kings become submissive.
From performing oblations of clarified butter alone for a period of time practiced during the [auspicious] *maṇḍala* and so forth, the practitioner becomes wealthy for as long as he lives.
By performing the homa with clarified butter alone, practiced in an uninterrupted sequence on the very days of impurity and so forth, one attains enjoyment and the abundance of prosperity.
The practitioner, having bathed in the morning, anointed himself with fragrant unguents, wearing a red garland and white sandalwood paste for the purpose of the *tilaka*, [should proceed].

Wearing white garments and bearing another white garland, having become serene in mind and having worshipped the principal deity, one should [offer] into the fire kindled with *vilva* wood prepared according to the previous method,
milk from a cow whose calf and body are white, measuring one *prastha*.
Having prepared milk-rice (*pāyasa*) from one *prastha* measure of white *śāli* rice grains,
and having taken a large ball of milk-rice mixed with sugar, milk,
and ghee, one should empower it one hundred times with the *Śriyam Me Dehi* mantra while reciting each syllable clearly, over a fire kindled with *vilva* wood.

Having offered oblations with the principal *nityā-vidyā* one hundred times or more into a fire consecrated by the previously mentioned rites, located either in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and having completed the remainder of the worship; then,
having eaten the remnants of the offering consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasānna*), and if desired, having eaten something else as well, [one passes] the remainder of the day.

One should conclude in silence. For the practitioner who performs this practice continuously for one full year, there will be an abundance of great prosperity. For one who performs this application in this manner without interruption throughout their entire life, Great Lakṣmī never abandons them, nor their entire noble lineage.

On the fifth, tenth, and full-moon days— specifically when these occur on Sundays— one should perform worship preceded by an offering of milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Whoever performs a fire-oblation (*homa*) with milk-rice for the duration of one year will become exceedingly prosperous with wealth, grain, and other riches.
If the calf of a cow is reddish and her own body is also reddish, one should extract the fresh butter from her milk and place it upon the pericarp of a white lotus flower.
Having remained until the completion of the *sādhana* days related to that extraction, on the second day, which was a Tuesday (*bhaumavāra*),

the practitioner must certainly [attain] by taking fresh butter (*navanīta*) with flowers in his hand and reciting the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) hundreds of times or more until the mandala is reached, while in the Capricorn ascendant (*makaralagna*).

One shall obtain the fortune of a land endowed with all crops in full abundance. Having placed fresh butter and a white lotus into the milk of a cow that has a white calf and is herself white, and having set it there on the very day of its preparation,
one should, in the morning, offer that white lotus and the fresh butter into the fire with the root-mantra on a Friday, preceded by silence.

Thus, by performing the fire-sacrifice (*homaprayoga*) in the manner described on seven Fridays, the attainment of great prosperity will certainly occur. Likewise, on a Saturday, having placed fresh butter churned from the blood-red milk of a cow whose calf is red, along with a naturally blooming red lotus, upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that lotus; at dawn on a Sunday, one should perform this while observing silence.

One should offer oblations with the root-vidyā. For the practitioner who performs oblations in this manner during the eight solar returns, there will be an abundance of great wealth, grain, and so forth. When Jupiter is situated in the sign of Cancer and the ascendant is Cancer, by offering oblations of Karṇikāra flowers or Campaka flowers smeared with fresh butter, [one gains] the power to employ difficult-to-obtain objects and the like.

By performing this, one shall obtain great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*) that is free from reproach, impossible for kings, thieves, and others to seize, and which extends to one's sons, grandsons, and descendants. By offering oblations of fresh butter mixed with sugar— or even plain butter— one attains long life preceded by splendor, fortune, wealth, health, and victory.
By performing a fire offering (*homa*) of one hundred thousand oblations of *vandhūka*, *palāśa*, and *āmrā* flowers, each smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*),
one shall obtain good fortune, prosperity, victory, splendor, and wisdom. [Offerings of] curd-rice...
A person authorized for the mandala, desiring supreme prosperity, should write his own desired object—
along with the agent, the object of the action, and the ritual procedure— upon pieces of palm leaf that have been moistened. Then,
by means of an oblation accompanied by fresh butter, performed for a hundred or more repetitions until the completion of the mandala, or for a month, or for seven days, [the goal is attained].

All desired objectives are accomplished. [One should write] with vermilion on *palāśa* leaves, with saffron on *āmra* leaves, with sandalwood on *panasa* leaves, and on betel leaves with a paste of saffron, musk, camphor, sandalwood, *gorocanā*, and vermilion— this being the *yakṣakardama* paste.

Having written one's own desired object as before—using musk on the leaves of a *campaka* tree, and combined with cardamom, cloves, *kaṅkola*, and nutmeg along with sugar on a lotus leaf—one should perform a fire-oblation (*havana*) of that [mixture] together with fresh butter, starting at midnight until the completion of the prescribed number of cycles (such as a hundred). From this, the accomplishment of all desires occurs. Now, [the next procedure]:

The Application of Cruel Homas: In all cruel applications, certain specific requirements that must necessarily be performed are first described. These include: the enemy’s ascendant at birth, the enemy’s birth asterisms, the piercing conjunctions (*vedhayoga*) with malefic planets on the days of the application, the unfavorable transit (*gocara*) of the enemy’s planets on those days, and likewise, the unfavorable state of the *aṣṭakavarga*. Thus it is said.
Having ascertained that the enemy lacks strength due to the weakness of his physical form (*rūpa-prakāra*) and that it is a time when suffering has arrived,

one should commence rites such as killing (*māraṇa*), driving away (*uccāṭana*), causing hatred (*dveṣaṇa*), or paralyzing (*stambhana*) the enemy, and not otherwise. Furthermore, one must determine in which deity—
whether a minor (*kṣudra*) or a great (*mahā*) deity— the enemy’s devotion lies, and whether that devotion is firm or trivial.
Indeed, a firm devotee of the Great Deity cannot be overcome even by a clever person through mere deliberation.

In the scriptures of the Guru, both the purity of one's intent and the absence of indolence must be examined; for among the enemies of the world of the Guru, these two are the primary adversaries. (p. 55b)

Even if he is capable of both punishment and favor, he must still be examined in this manner: whether he is pleasing or displeasing to his enemies, to his own distinct kinsmen, to the circle of servants, and to the subjects; furthermore, it must be examined whether those standing by the enemy’s side are well-versed in counsel or ill-versed in counsel. Likewise, one must examine the lifespan and the *dāya* (inheritance/fortune).

When it is certain that the state of being a Guru exists only in connection with the mere presence of pleasure, and when the absence of such a state is determined; and when it is ascertained that even a Guru lacks the power of restraint and grace— which are the very essence of the worship of the Great Deity—
and is devoid of the quality of winning over the world, then those who remain in his proximity will find authority only in the treatises of evil ministers and not in the Guru.

Since there is no certainty regarding the existence [of the enemy], and because there is an absence of even that which would obstruct the accomplishment of the fruit of a cruel deed— due to the absence of its cause—
the ritual application (*prayoga*) in the form of a causal factor for the production of the desired result must be performed;
however, if an adversary who is undesirable acts as an obstacle, then the performance of the *dhāvana-prayoga* (the rite of driving away) should be undertaken.

It should be understood that because each individual limb [of the rite] is unfailing, the result must reside in the agent alone. Furthermore, it is to be performed at a specific time and in a specific place, not at all times nor in all places. The practical meaning is that it should be performed at the time when the eighth sign from the enemy’s birth-ascendant (janmarāśi) is situated in the ascendant (lagna), and in the place where that eighth sign is located.
The method for knowing the positions of such zodiacal signs is as follows: Aries is in the eastern direction; Gemini in the southeast;
Cancer and Leo in the southern direction; Virgo in the southwest; Libra and Scorpio in the western direction; Sagittarius in the northwest;
Capricorn and Aquarius in the north; and Pisces in the northeast. Furthermore, whichever sign is the enemy of a particular zodiac sign [is determined by this].

The practical meaning is that, having stationed oneself in the western direction when Scorpio is the ascendant, the performance of that malevolent ritual (*abhicāra*) should be undertaken; this should be applied similarly for other zodiac signs as well.

In all sixty *ghaṭikā*-constituted solar days (*sāvana-dina*), the twelve signs beginning with Aries occur in a sequence of five *ghaṭikās* each. Thus, from the thirty-sixth *ghaṭikā* up to the fortieth *ghaṭikā* of every day, there is the transit of the sign Scorpio; however, in another system, it is solar.
Due to the division of months beginning with Caitra, this should be inferred in the same way for the enjoyment of other zodiac signs (*rāśi*), such as Scorpio (*vṛścika*), even at different times.

Within the bodies of living beings, which measure ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the zodiac signs beginning with Aries (*meṣa*) reside from the head down to the feet, each occupying a space of eight finger-breadths. And so it is said:

From the fifty-seventh finger-breadth up to the sixty-fourth finger-breadth, the portion of the body occupied by the sign of Scorpio (Vṛścika-rāśi) resides. It is precisely during its transit that injuries from weapons such as swords occur; it is in that very place that the piercing with thorns and so forth should be performed upon its effigy. Likewise, this applies to the region situated in the eighth house.

The conclusion is that when the ascendant is situated in the eighth house from the enemy's sign, and the enemy is situated in the eighth house from the ascendant, the practitioner should strike [the enemy] with a sword, arrows, or other weapons. Furthermore, having identified the "poison-location" (viṣasthāna) of the enemy, one should inflict the blow with arrows and so forth upon that poison-location, not upon the location of water (nāpasthāna). This same principle applies to the effigy (puttalī) as well; it must be at the very spot of the poison-location.
The piercing with thorns and so forth should be performed; its procedure is as follows:

beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the new moon, one should sequentially [pierce] on the right side of men the heart (1), breast (2), throat (3), nose (4), eye (5), ear (6), and the middle of the eyebrows (7) across those thirty lunar days.
In the six [locations] including the middle of the jaw, the middle of the forehead, and the middle of the head; in the nine left-side locations:

the middle of the head (10), the middle of the conch-shell [of the chest] (11), the middle of the eyebrows (12), the ear (13), the eye (14), the nose (15), the throat (16), the breast (17), and the heart (18);
and in the left-side [locations] of the secret place (19), the knee (20), the shank (21), and the back of the foot (22). [And] the back of the foot (23).

In thirty locations—the twenty-four on the right side beginning with the big toe, plus the big toe (25), the back of the foot (26), the calf (27), the knee (28), the secret organ (29), and the navel (30)—the portions of poison reside. (p.

For women, however, during the thirty lunar days beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) and ending with the new moon (amāvāsyā), [the breath] moves in sequence through: 1. the left side of the heart, 2. the left breast, 3. the left side of the throat, 4. the left nostril, 5. the left eye, 6. the left ear, 7. the left side of the space between the eyebrows, 8. the left temple, and 9. the left side of the head.

10. The right side of the head; 11. The right cheek; 12. The right side of the space between the eyebrows; 13. The right ear; 14. The right eye; 15. The right nostril; 16. The right side of the throat; 17. The right shoulder; 18. The right side of the heart; 19. The right side of the navel; 20. The right side of the private parts; 21. The right knee.
21. the right lower leg; 22. the back of the right foot; 23. the big toe of the right foot; 24. the big toe of the left foot;
25. the left foot; 26. the left lower leg; 27. the left knee; 28. the left secret region; 29. the left side of the navel; 30. in these thirty places of form, the portion of poison resides.

Likewise, within the poison-vein (*viṣanāḍī*) itself, the aforementioned rite should be performed; it is of three kinds according to the distinction of the lunar day (*tithi*), weekday (*vāra*), and asterism (*nakṣatra*) poison-vein, as follows: on the first lunar day (*pratipad*), the quartet beginning with the sixteenth *ghaṭikā*; on the second, beginning with the sixth; and on the third, beginning with the ninth.

On the fourth [day], beginning with the eighth; on the fifth, also beginning with the eighth; on the sixth, beginning with the sixth; on the seventh, beginning with the fifth; on the eighth, beginning with the ninth; on the ninth, beginning with the eighth; on the tenth, beginning with the eleventh; on the eleventh, beginning with the fourth;
on the twelfth, beginning with the fourteenth; and on the thirteenth, beginning with the fifteenth.
On the fourteenth day, the four *ghaṭīs* beginning with the eighth; on the fifth day, the four *ghaṭīs* beginning with the eighth;
on Sunday, the twenty-first *ghaṭikā* and so forth; on Monday, the third *ghaṭikā* and so forth; on Tuesday, the thirteenth *ghaṭikā* and so forth.
In Mercury, the four *ghaṭīs* beginning from the eleventh *ghaṭī*; in Jupiter, from the eighth *ghaṭī*; in Venus, from the sixth *ghaṭī*;

and in Saturn, from the twenty-sixth *ghaṭī*, constitute the "poisonous *ghaṭīs*. In Aśvinī, the four *ghaṭīs* beginning from the fifty-first; and in Bharaṇī, the four *ghaṭīs* beginning from the twenty-fifth [are likewise poisonous].

The four *caṭīs* beginning with the thirty-first *ghaṭī* of Kṛttikā, the four [units] beginning with the forty-first *ghaṭī* of Rohiṇī, and the four *ghaṭīs* beginning with the fiftieth *ghaṭī* of Mṛgaśīrṣa.
The four units beginning from the twenty-second ghaṭikā of Ārdrā;
the four units beginning from the thirty-first ghaṭikā of Punarvasu;
and the four units beginning from the thirty-first ghaṭikā of Puṣya.
In Aśleṣā, it begins from the thirty-third ghaṭikā and its following four;
in Maghā, from the thirty-first ghaṭikā; in Pūrvaphalgunī, from the twenty-first ghaṭikā; in Uttaraphalgunī, from the nineteenth ghaṭikā; and in Hasta, from the twenty-second ghaṭikā.

In Citrā, from the twenty-first ghaṭikā onwards; in Svātī, from the eleventh ghaṭikā onwards; in Viśākhā, from the fifteenth ghaṭikā onwards; in Anurādhā, from the eleventh ghaṭikā onwards; in Jyeṣṭhā, from the fifteenth ghaṭikā onwards;
in Mūla, from the fifty-seventh ghaṭikā onwards; and in Pūrvā-phalgunī.

In the twenty-fifth *ghaṭikā* and so forth; in Uttarā, in the twenty-first *ghaṭikā* and so forth; in Śravaṇa, in the eleventh *ghaṭikā* and so forth; in Dhaniṣṭhā, in the eleventh *ghaṭikā* and so forth;
and in Śatabhiṣā, in the nineteenth *ghaṭikā* and so forth.
In Śatabhiṣā, it begins from the nineteenth ghaṭikā;
in Pūrvabhadrapadā, from the seventeenth ghaṭikā; and in Uttarabhadrapadā, from the twenty-fifth ghaṭikā.
In the *revatī* nakṣatra, the four ghaṭīs beginning with the thirty-first ghaṭī constitute the *viṣaghaṭī*. Likewise, this should be observed during the two types of *dagdha-yoga*:
on Sunday, *bharaṇī* and the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) are *dagdha*;
on Monday, *citrā* and the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*); likewise on Tuesday, *uttarāṣāḍhā* and the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*); and on Wednesday, *dhaniṣṭhā*.

Likewise, the third lunar day on a Thursday with Uttaraphalgunī, and the sixth with Śukra (Venus) and Jyeṣṭhā, are burnt; and similarly, the eighth with Saturn and Revatī, and the ninth are also burnt. All four types of Mṛtiyoga (death-constellations) must be considered.
Among them, the first is as follows: Anurādhā on a Sunday, Uttarāṣāḍhā on a Monday, Śatabhiṣā on a Tuesday, and Aśvinī on a Wednesday.

When Jupiter is in Mṛgaśīrṣa, Venus in Āśleṣā, and Saturn in Hasta—this is the second [set]. Furthermore, as with the Sun and Mars, the first, sixth, and eleventh lunar days are auspicious; for the Moon and Venus, the second, seventh, and twelfth;
for Mercury, the third, eighth, and thirteenth; and for Jupiter, the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth.

The fifth, tenth, and fifteenth lunar days [are forbidden] on Saturday. Thus, the third [type of conjunction] is as follows: Anurādhā on Sunday, Svātī on Monday, Jyeṣṭhā on Tuesday, Śravaṇa on Wednesday, Revatī on Thursday, Puṣya on Friday, and Punarvasu on Saturday.
The fourth [type] is as follows: Dhaniṣṭhā and Śatabhiṣaj, Hasta and Citrā, Viśākhā and Anurādhā, and Ārdrā.
In the case of Punarvasu, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Revatī; Aśleṣā and Maghā; Bharaṇī and Kṛttikā;
and Mūla and Pūrvāṣāḍhā—the fourth quarter of the day is known as the *mṛtyuyoga* (death yoga). Furthermore, two types of *nāśayoga* (destruction yoga) are to be observed:
the first is as follows—Maghā on Sunday, Jyeṣṭhā on Monday, Kṛttikā on Tuesday, and Ārdrā on Wednesday.
The root of the Guru [is] Śukra; for Venus, it is Śatabhiṣā; for Saturn, it is the Uttaraphalgunīs. As for the second [method], it is the twenty-third [asterism] from one's own birth asterism. (p.

The twenty-second lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), also known by the synonym *nāśikā*, is observed as the *nāśaka* (destructive), *padanāśa* (loss of position), and *yogapada* (conjunctional state) within the *abhva* (the horse). Likewise, *yamaghaṇṭa*, *kaṇṭaka*, *kulika*, and *kālavelā* must also be taken into account; their nature is such that, for example, from the day of the week under discussion, it is the day of Śani (Saturday).
Having multiplied that [number] by the number of the [specific] darkness (tamas),
the muhūrta characterized by the resulting number produced is designated as *kulika*;
it has a measure equal to the sixteenth part of a solar day (*sāvana-dina*) consisting of sixty *ghaṭikās*, starting from the current weekday.
The muhūrta called Kālavelā, which possesses a number of qualities equal to the count of the weekday [Budhavāra] and has the stated measure,
is this Aghaṇṭa muhūrta; it is distinguished by a number twice that of the count belonging to the current weekday, starting from the present weekday.
The number of Mars days (bhaumavāra) doubled constitutes the specific muhūrta known as Kaṇṭaka. Regarding the Karanas such as Kulika and others for each respective day starting from Saturday (Śani),
one should double the uniform count of the days elapsed since Saturday and add it [to the previous total].
Distinguished by two designations, the Kulikā and others occurring on that day will have a measure equal to one-sixteenth part of that day;
likewise, the Muhūrta known as Ardhayāma is also to be considered. Its nature is as follows:
when the number of the weekday is multiplied by three and divided by eight, if the remainder is added to one, then—

The period of time characterized by that same number of units is known as *muhūrta-ūrdhva-yāma*; it is also called the second *kāla-velā*. It is as follows: on Sunday, *Bharaṇī*; on Monday, *Ārdrā*; on Tuesday, *Maghā*; on Wednesday, *Citrā*; on Thursday, *Jyeṣṭhā*; on Friday, *Abhijit*; and on Saturday, *Pūrvabhādrapadā*. Likewise, there are the conjunctions of *pātāla*, *go*, *viṣaya*, *aṅka*, and *ṛkṣa*.

The yogas are Caṇḍīśa, Caṇḍāyudha, Yaugika, Mahāśūla, Kāṇayoga, Raktasthūṇa, Kaṇṭakasthūṇa, and Pañcārgayoga; this group of yogas is to be followed according to their respective occurrences. Their essential natures are as follows:
Having divided into thirty parts the duration of time taken by the sun to transit through the zodiac sign of Libra, that time [is determined] when the sun stands in its tenth lord.
The one known as Pātāla occurs on the fourth and seventh tithis of the bright fortnight on Monday;
on Tuesday, the sixth, eighth, fourteenth, ninth, and fifth; on Wednesday, the seventh, tenth, and thirteenth;
on Thursday, the fifth, seventh, and eighth; on Friday, the fifth, ninth, and twelfth; and on Saturday.

On the fourth, fourteenth, and eleventh lunar days, there is a conjunction with the Viṣu yoga. From whichever nakṣatra the sun has entered, one counts as many nakṣatras as there are among the six consisting of Maghā, Āśleṣā, Citrā, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, and Revatī;
the nakṣatra reached by counting from the Aśvinī nakṣatra according to that specific number [is the subject of the yoga].
And that [diagram] is named Caṇḍīśacaṇḍāyudha. Having drawn seven lines extending from east to west,
and having established seven lines extending from south to north intersecting the eastern lines— excluding the positions of the four corners—
a wheel is produced with the tips of the seven lines in each of the four directions.
Having written the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) from Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī, including Abhijit, at those twenty-eight line-tips;
and having likewise written each planet in the position of whichever nakṣatra it occupies; and likewise [noting] that which is situated between two line-tips characterized by an unfavorable yoga.

The meaning is that even two asterisms may become auspicious for evil deeds; or else, having drawn three upward-pointing tridents and six lines extending from south to north, and having placed four lines in the corners and two lines at the very bottom—
thus having laid out twenty-eight lines in total.

Having drawn a line through the center of the constellation occupied by the sun, or a central meridian line, and having written the other constellations in the directions starting from that [line] in a clockwise direction; (p.
All nine constellations situated upon the trident— especially the three constellations situated on the central prong—
are givers of death; the six constellations situated on both sides of the middle prong of the trident cause disease.

The triad of asterisms situated below causes defeat in battle; furthermore, it brings about agitation, death, and imprisonment. The remaining sixteen asterisms are auspicious and should be avoided for inauspicious rites. However, the aforementioned twelve asterisms are to be employed for cruel rites. This indeed is [the rule].

The Great Trident Yoga (Mahātriśūlayoga) is like the "One-eyed" Yoga (Kāṇayoga). The seven lunar mansions—Ārdrā, Maghā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Citrā, Jyeṣṭhā, Abhijit, and Bharaṇī—are called the "One-eyed" and are auspicious for the body. They are to be adopted, as in the case of the "Red Pillar" Yoga (Raktasthūṇayoga).

From the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) conjoined with Mars, as many [mansion-intervals] as it takes to reach the Mūla mansion, that same number of mansions likewise constitutes the Kaṃcaka-sthūṇa yoga. From the mansion occupied by the Sun, as many [mansion-intervals] as it takes to reach the Mūla mansion, that same number of mansions likewise [constitutes the yoga]. This is the Pañcārka defect.
When the Sun has entered the thirteenth degree of the sign of Leo, the first solar defect named *dhūma* (smoke) occurs;

when the Sun is in the seventeenth degree of the sign of Scorpio, the second [defect] named *vyatīpāta*; and when the Sun is in the seventeenth degree of the sign of Taurus, the third solar defect named *pariveṣa* (halo) occurs.
When the Sun is in the twenty-ninth degree of the sign of Taurus, there is the fourth solar defect (arkadoṣa) named Dhanurdhara;
when the Sun is in the sixteenth degree of the sign of Libra, there is the fifth solar defect named Kena.
If a marriage, the installation of a Yantra or similar object, or any other rite is performed at a Lagna afflicted by any one of these defects, it results in the destruction of the family.

Death occurs from eating various kinds of food, and the arising of disease occurs during the *cūḍākaraṇa* (tonsure ceremony); however, these defects are certainly to be avoided in the case of cruel rites (*krūrakarman*).
For this very reason, they should not be adopted even in auspicious rites (*maṅgalakarman*) other than those already mentioned.

59b) Furthermore, regarding the *homa* for cruel rites (*krūrakarma*), there is a specific distinction: the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and spoon (*sruva*) should be made with a serpent’s head; one must not use leaves of the *pippala* or *palāśa* trees, nor any other vessel. For the purpose of killing (*māraṇa*), one should follow only the triangular hearth (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*).
The office of the *adhvaryu* priest is fixed to the south; this rite is prescribed for a cremation ground or a desolate place.
When there is no specific instruction regarding the blood of one's own slayer, an enemy, or a birth-star, the oblation is offered with cooked rice mixed with blood.
Here, the preparation of the site and the enclosing are done with arrows, and not with *kuśa* grass as in a peaceful (*saumya*) fire-offering. The visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
