Having two heads, seven hands, three feet, and seven tongues, his form was threefold; with six extremely cruel, reddish eyes, and with four hands, he held a *śakti* and the sacrificial ladles *sruk* and *sruva*, while with the others he held a *tomara* spear,
a palm-leaf fan, clarified butter, and a fine vessel, roaring incessantly.

"One should meditate on the eater of oblations (Agni) with his mouth wide open. When a non-cruel *homa* is performed upon the head, ears, eyes, or the interior of the mouth of the fire, there occurs the destruction of the enemy's very limb. This rite should be performed within one's own territory; however, it may also be done in a foreign land or at a border region, provided that it does not involve the employment of another's command.

It must be guarded by a multitude of one's own soldiers bearing various weapons and missiles, so that enemies such as rival kings, having learned through spies who the practitioner is, will not have him killed by thieves and the like. In this same way, for the sake of self-protection, one should practice the mastery of the *Mṛtyuñjaya* and other *Nityā* vidyās. In this regard:

All the brahmins were devoted to their own duties; the king was impartial toward women and commoners alike; he possessed a firm conviction in the authority of the Vedas and other scriptures; though not harsh, he was generous and kind toward all living beings. (p. 60a)
Even without any connection such as greed or affection, one who desires to remove the suffering [of others] is a compassionate person, another term for which is "merciful.

Thus, there are six types of humans who might at some point become objects of an attempt to kill—even the most wicked nihilists—for by the destruction of a single such person, many virtuous and noble people are saved. Poison, fire...

Those who strike with weapons, those who seize the livelihood of a field, and those who employ means for killing— even those for whom the rite of killing has been taught— should be subjected to the performance of the rite of killing. Having performed an anointing with fragrant oil, one should bathe with that very same vidyā employed for the ritual application.

Having performed worship according to the method of daily worship, one should satisfy one's own guru and the Brahmins with wealth acquired through those rites, or acquired by other means, amounting to half of one's own property, or at least a fourth part thereof; and then, according to the previously described method of consecration, [one should worship] one's own Nityā Goddess.

Having performed the consecration with the water from the flask empowered by the wheel of daily worship, and having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times while subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), the practitioner— who performs the *dūrvā* oblation for a full year and undergoes consecration during the three asterisms of his own birth— becomes free even from the slightest trace of that sin.
One shall attain purification. Thus ends the general method for cruel rites (*krūrakarma*). Now, its specific applications:
by offering oblations (*havana*) into a fire kindled with wood from the *vimītaka* tree, using its fruits smeared with the juice of *dhattūra*, in numbers such as a thousand and so forth; or else—

By performing oblations a thousand times or more with *karañja* wood— known by the synonym *naraktamālā*— which has been anointed with the juice of *dhattūra* leaves; or alternatively, by performing oblations a thousand times with *karañja* fruits in a fire kindled with *karañja* wood-fuel, even a *śatru* (enemy) who is otherwise impossible to conquer shall go to the abode of Yama.
For the practitioner who, for one month, performs oblations into a fire kindled with *dhattūra* wood using *dhattūra* fruits soaked in *dhattūra* juice, [the following occurs].

There shall be the destruction of the enemy: by performing a *homa* until the end of the mandala in a fire kindled with *evadha* wood, using fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *evadha* smeared with a span (*vitasti*) measure of oil, or alternatively, using its fruits smeared with oil, the death of enemies will occur. [This is performed] in a fire kindled with *aruṣkara* fuel-sticks, which is another synonym for *bhallātaka*.

By performing one hundred or one thousand oblations (*homa*) with seeds belonging to that [enemy] which have been smeared with those very substances up to the limit of the mandala, the enemy shall suffer great affliction or even death preceded by fever. This is performed using a single cotton seed smeared with *sauvīra*, which is synonymous with *kāñjika* and *āranāla*.

From performing oblations until the completion of the mandala, the death of enemies caused by mutual strife shall occur for the practitioner who, having saturated ginger, long pepper, and black pepper with mustard oil, continuously offers them in a fire kindled with fuel from the tree corresponding to the birth-constellation of his enemy, at a count of one thousand or more, throughout the entire mandala. The enemy of that practitioner shall suffer from fever.

He shall meet his death. [This occurs] by means of blood from those born under the same birth-star and zodiacal sign as the enemy, or indeed by means of sacrificial fuel-sticks from trees belonging to the birth-star and zodiacal sign of the enemy, all drenched in the blood of those born under the same birth-star and zodiacal sign as the enemy, filling the entire mandala.
By means of the prescribed utterance, in whatever manner, the death of the enemy shall occur in this very birth in every way—
either with *nīvāra* grains soaked in mustard oil, or with neem seeds smeared with mustard oil,
or with cotton seeds drenched in mustard oil, or with *karañja* seeds smeared with mustard oil.
For the practitioner who offers oblations in a continuous sequence numbering one thousand and so forth, up to the limit of the mandala,

the inciting of enmity among enemies occurs. This takes place when the fire is kindled with wood from a tree corresponding to the birth asterism of the enemy, during the previously described yoga known as *kanīcāsaraparyāya-pātāla*.

At midnight, for the practitioner who offers oblations numbering a thousand or more— using fuel-sticks from trees belonging to the enemy’s *nakṣatra* soaked in mustard oil until the completion of the mandala— the enemy shall certainly be eradicated in every way. [This applies to] a poisonous tree...

Whether with leaves, or with fuel-sticks from a poison-tree, or with seeds of a poison-tree— by a practitioner who offers oblations in a fire kindled by the wood of a poison-tree, numbering a thousand or more up to the limit of the mandala,
the elephants and horses of the enemy shall perish after first being afflicted by diseases. Thus.

[This concerns] the cruel applications [of spells] by an enemy situated near oneself. Regarding a sorcerer who is an enemy, one should first perform an application for creating enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*) with that sorcerer, thereby bringing about his lack of assistance; then, according to the method described above, an application such as killing (*māraṇa*) should be performed. However, if even enmity is impossible to create, or if one can endure a delay of that duration, [one may proceed otherwise].

At that time, this ritual procedure for their slaying should be performed for those sixteen Brahmins who possess the established primary *nityā-vidyās* under discussion, and who, being exceedingly fond of themselves, are firmly resolved that they will by all means achieve the fruit from this rite.

Having performed the rite of enclosure (*varaṇa*), one should offer oblations in the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) prescribed for killing with the substances prescribed for killing, two by two, during each watch (*prahara*) in an uninterrupted sequence. Thus, throughout the eight watches,

by means of sixteen Brahmins performing the uninterrupted oblation of the substances prescribed for killing, [the target] is protected in every way even against those who possess mantras, provided they are non-existent [as protectors].

"Among protectors, the enemy surely meets his death. When all these applications for *homa* have been thus stated, for as many times as the *homa* has been performed, for that same number of times the recitation (*japa*) must also be performed at the conclusion of the *homa*. Then, having dissolved the chosen deity into one's own self, one should apply a tilaka with those ashes using the *Śūla-vidyā*. In the case of peaceful rites (*saumya*), [the procedure is as follows].
In the case of cruel *homa* applications, the same [rules] apply.
61b) However, even here, the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the feeding of Brahmins must not be forgotten. Thus end the procedures for *homa*.
Having restrained the breath (prāṇāyāma) and performed the three nyāsas according to the previously mentioned characteristics,

one should prepare the arghya water with pure water using the six-limbed mantra and the root-vidyā; then, having inscribed the place, time, one's own lineage, zodiac sign, name, and body with that water, [one should proceed] according to the application of one's intellect.

One should perform the primary formal resolve (*pradhāna-saṃkalpa*) as follows: "I shall perform the ritual procedure for the libation (*tarpaṇa*) of Śrīvidyā. In that context, the words denoting place and time should be mentioned in the locative case (ending in the seventh case-ending) in the sense of location;

the words beginning with *gotra* and ending with the personal name should be mentioned in the nominative case (ending in the first case-ending); and the words denoting the object of desire [should be mentioned in the dative case].

The mention is made by using the dative case ending; then, having uttered the Śrīvidyā mantra and recited the mantra "I satiate Śrī Tripurasundarī, obeisance," one should perform [the rite] for a number of either one hundred or one thousand repetitions— according to the consideration of ease or difficulty—
extending over seven days, a fortnight, a month, or as long as the time required for the mandala and so forth.

One should satisfy [the deity] with the substances to be described hereafter, according to each specific desire. In that regard, women are brought under control by means of coconut water; with pure water, one should recite for each mantra: "O Devadatta, bring Yajñadatta under my control! Bring him under control! and so forth.

For Devadatta, who performs the libation while reciting the name [of the deity] and throughout the previously mentioned time, all people— who were the objects of his own purposeful action— become submissive. Furthermore, by performing the libation with coconut water scented with *ketakī* flowers and camphor, a woman becomes submissive.
Whatever they may be commanded to do, they will carry it out; moreover, they will offer their own lives and all their possessions.

By performing libations for a longer duration than previously specified with water scented with *nameru*—a synonym for *suraparāpara*—they become submissive. Through libations with water scented with *campaka* flowers, one gains the power to delight the world.
By offering libations with water scented with *pāṭalī* flowers and *śatapatra* flowers,
one shall obtain qualities that cause wonder among all the world.
Libation with water scented with musk fulfills all desires, both those explicitly mentioned and those unmentioned.
Through libation with water scented by sandalwood and camphor, there is the accomplishment of every undertaking.

By performing libations with water mixed with rice-gruel (śaktū), numbering in the thousands or hundreds of millions, extending as far as the ritual mandala, one obtains wealth, grain, clothing, and other such things.

Prosperity that endures for a long time accrues to one who performs the libation (*tarpaṇa*) every night until the completion of the mandala at midnight with water mixed with jaggery; all obstacles are warded off.
By performing the libation with water mixed with *viṃvāra* wood in an uninterrupted sequence until the completion of the mandala, [the destruction] of enemies [is achieved].

Mutual hatred is accomplished when water mixed with powdered [substances] is offered as a libation within the mandala during its prescribed time; by such a libation, the death of enemies occurs. By offering a libation of plain boiled rice-water (ulloda) within the mandala and other settings during the prescribed time, the affliction of fever comes upon the enemies.
Sprinkling [the enemy's dwelling] continuously for as long as it takes to complete a maṇḍala with water mixed with the juice of *nimba* leaves,

preceded by a quarrel, quickly brings about the pacification of enmity among adversaries. By means of water mixed with the juice of *nimba* leaves that has been made to overflow, [this effect is achieved] before long.

Death results from excessive libations (tarpaṇa) extending beyond the limits of the maṇḍala, or from severe abdominal ailments such as dysentery. Here too, the distinctions between auspicious and cruel rites, as well as the preliminary and concluding limbs of the aforementioned optional rites, must not be forgotten.
Thus end the applications of libation. The applications of meditation have already been stated. The applications of the yoga-bhadrās follow.

The statement "having as its agent one who has merely accomplished [the rite]" is not mentioned here because it is of no use for the accomplishment of the goal. Now follow the applications of the *puttalī* (effigy). First among these is the method of constructing the *puttalī*.

The twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), beginning with Aśvinī and ending with Revatī, each have four quarters (*pādas*); these very quarters are intended here by the term "degrees" (*aṃśa*). Thus, taken together, there are one hundred and eight degrees (*aṃśas*).

All the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) have been concluded; and their lords are the twelve planets in successive order. Thus, through nine cycles, the twelve planets attain lordship over all the degrees (aṃśas). It is concluded as follows: Earth (1), Nāgas (8), Viśvas (13), Nasvas (20), Pañcabhujas (25), Dvirāmas (32), Kṣoṇīdharas (7), Agnis (3)... [and so on].
The degrees of Mars in the signs beginning with Aries are: 37, 44, 49, 56, 60, 68, 73, 80, 92, and 97.
The degrees of Venus in the signs beginning with Gemini are, in order: 27, 14, 19, and 28.

The feet [of the meters] are measured by: moon-fire (31), elephant-Rāma (38), Rāma-Vedas (43), Bravāṇa (50), arrow-Bāṇa (55), eye-limb (62), Sītā (67), Vedas-beginning (74), Nanda-mountain (79), six-elephant (86), earth-Nanda (91), eight-mark (98), three-zero-evil-measured (103);
and by Rāma (3), limb (6), fifteen (15), and serpent (18).

The portions assigned to the Moon by Nakṣatrapāda, the leader of the secondary [traditions], are: seventy-two (Śailabāhu), thirty (Vyomāgni), thirty-nine (Nandaguṇa), forty-two (Bāhuyayodharāṃśāḥ), fifty-one (Ekeṣu), fifty-four (Vedaśra),
sixty-three (Rāmarasa), sixty-six (Gaśāstra), seventy-five (Pañcāṅga), seventy-eight (Nāgagiri),
eighty-seven (Saptagaja), ninety (Bhrananda), sixty-nine (Nandāṅka), and one hundred and two (Vāhuviyadeka).
Veda (4), Kṣitīśa (16), Gajabāhu (28), Khavārddhi (40), Saṃkhyadhiṣṭha (52), Abdhiśāstra (64), Rasaparvata (76). (p. 63a)

The parts of the sun (the solar days) in this [cycle] are: Nāga-nāgas (88), Śūnya-abhra (100), Parimitāḥ (70), Śaśalakṣmaṇaḥ (1), Aṃśāḥ (9), Pañca (5), Aṅga-bhūmi (16), Navabāhu (29), Dharā-samudra (41), Trīṣu (53), Smara-ṛtu (65), Naga-parvata (77), Nanda-nāga (89), Bhū-vyoma-bhū-miti (1001), and Nandā (9) and Kaṃ (12).

The degrees for Jupiter are considered to be 21, 24, 33, 36, 45, 48, 57, 60, 69, 72, 61, 84, 93, 96, 95, and 108; these are the values for Jupiter, while for Saturn they are 10, 21, 33, 45, 57, 69, 81, 93, 105, and 117. (10)
Śa (1), Vāhubhuja (22), Rāmabhuja (23); in sequence:

Vedātri (34), Pañcadahana (35), Aṅgavidhi (46), Kṣamādhṛk (47), Vedāṣṭavāṇa (58), Navavāṇa (59), Nasa (70), Kasā (71), Netrāṣṭa (82), Vahnivasu (83), Vedanadve (94), Su (95), Nandāṅga (96), Vyomabhūmiti (107).

It should be made with a measurement of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). There are thirty-six degrees for the nine constellations beginning with Aśvinī; likewise, there are thirty-six degrees for the second group of nine beginning with Maghā and ending with Jyeṣṭhā;
and likewise, there are thirty-six degrees for the third group of nine beginning with Mūla and ending with Revatī. Thus.

There are one hundred and eight divisions (*aṃśas*), which are also known as *vādas*. Among them, for an enemy born in the first group of nine divisions (*navaka*) of the earth-element (*bhauma-aṃśaka*), the effigy (*puttalī*) shall measure fourteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

In the second group of nine, for an enemy born from the portions of the five planets beginning with Mars, a puppet (puttalī) measuring eleven and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas) should be made. In the third group of nine, for an enemy born from the portions of the five planets beginning with Mars, a puppet measuring thirteen finger-breadths should be constructed.

In this context, the lords of the signs starting from Aries are, respectively: Mars, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn; and [the lords] of the eyes and teeth are to be understood as [Mars, Venus, and Jupiter]. [The materials required are:
earth from a cremation ground, ashes, any one of the salts such as *saindhava* (rock salt) or *sauvarcala*, and dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*).

Having combined these eleven substances in equal parts— pippalī, marica, dhūvāra (commonly known in the local dialect as *gṛhadhūma* or house-soot), garlic, *hiṅgu*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and red ochre (*gairika*)—
and having added an equal quantity of clay that has been processed by the hands of a potter at the appropriate time, the total becomes twelve [ingredients].

When no specific materials are prescribed, a doll (puttalī) should be made in all cases. However, in the ritual for killing (māraṇa), it should be made from wood belonging to the tree of the birth-constellation (janmanakṣatra) of the enemy; or else, from rice-flour mixed with the hair, foot-nails, and teeth taken from the enemy's body;
or else, from the flour of black gram (māṣa) mixed with the aforementioned four items beginning with hair.
Alternatively, having divided into eight parts the length of a doll made from beeswax together with the four [substances] beginning with hair—
measuring sixteen finger-breadths— one part, which is two finger-breadths, constitutes the head;
the portion of the body from below that down to the waist consists of all the remaining parts, including the hands, belly, and so forth.
The portion from the waist downwards to the ends of the two feet consists of three parts,
each being six *aṅgulas* in measure. With one part consisting of two *aṅgulas*,
the two hips and the two tips of the feet are each determined to be half a half-*aṅgula* (one-quarter *aṅgula*) in size.
In other tantras or in other sections of this [tantra], in places where specific details are not mentioned, one should perform the rite of the *puttalī* (effigy) according to that same method.

This applies to the six rites (*ṣatkarma*) consisting of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), paralyzing (*stambhana*), expelling (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*).
Furthermore, four small figurines should be made for each [of the four directions].

Among them, one—made of rice flour and endowed with the aforementioned set of four [features] beginning with hair—should be brought to the state of being buried beneath the officiant, the practitioner. The second [figurine] likewise [is endowed with the set] beginning with hairlessness.
The third [line], made from clay by a potter together with the four [other materials], is to be used for the act of burying beneath the seat where the Hotṛ priest places his feet; however,
the one made from the wood of a tree associated with an inimical constellation is to be used for the act of burying beneath the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of the beeswax.

Having fashioned an effigy from a mixture of hair, nails, and so forth—along with the four [substances] beginning with "enmity" (vairi)—bound with its feet upwards and its head downwards in a winnowing basket or similar vessel, one should hang it over a pit. However, the effigy used for rites such as *homa* is distinct; it need not be mentioned in every instance.
Having thus prepared the effigy, one should perform the ritual applications (*prayoga*). For instance:
Having fashioned an effigy (puttalī) out of the aforementioned substances—such as the enemy's birth star (nakṣatra), tree, and so forth—characterized by the specified measurements;

and having performed the ritual installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) of the enemy to be targeted therein; one should [strike] it with a sharp weapon at the forefoot, the ankle, the knee, the thigh, the lower part of the navel, and the region of the heart.
Having divided [the body] into twelve parts— the part from the heart upwards to the throat,

and the head— one should, at the time of midnight, with a mind full of wrath and wearing red garments, perfumes, garlands, and unguents, offer oblations with the root-mantra using those body-parts smeared with mustard oil and *aruṣkara* oil. By that, for whomever...
This doll of the enemy, when offered as an oblation, will certainly bring about his destruction.
Having fashioned a doll from the flour of śāli rice mixed with jaggery, black pepper, and cumin, [one should place it] in the region of its heart.

Having written the name of the person to be acted upon—such as "Devadatta, may he bring Yajñadatta under my control"—and having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (infusion of life) for that target, one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*). Then, having poured the residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*) into the effigy (*puttalī*), one should cook that effigy with that very same clarified butter. Even if one lacks the personal capacity, one should [act] through the medium of the door-guardian (*dvārānāra*) using the tip of one's own hand.

Having touched [the food] a thousand times and worshipped it with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should then eat it while reciting the mantra and meditating that it has the very form of the person to be subdued (*sādhya*) and is permeated with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). By this, women, men, and kings shall become submissive for the duration of their lives. Having fashioned an effigy (*puttalī*) of the enemy out of red chalk (*gairika*),...

When the eighth house from the Ripu (the sixth house) is the Ascendant, this is the period of the *ardhayāma-muhūrta* known as *Yamaghaṇṭā*. It is a time of poison-veins (*viṣanāḍī*) and a place of poison (*viṣasthāna*).

In whichever limb—such as the head or the hands—a wound is inflicted by a needle, a thorn, or the like, in that very limb there will arise, gradually, pain preceded by boils, needles, thorns, and so forth, or else swelling.
Or, by means of wounds from swords and other weapons, death shall come through the power of water and the enemy.

Having fashioned an effigy (*puttalī*) from the wood of a tree belonging to the enemy’s birth-constellation (*vairi-nakṣatra*), and having performed the ritual installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) therein, one should have it mounted upon a female donkey; then, by slowly drinking the decoction of its urine and water, the enemy will gradually be seized by a fever of burning heat (*dāhajvara*).

The practitioner shall lead [the enemy] to the city of Yama: having fashioned an effigy from beeswax at midnight, he should heat it over embers of *khadira* wood and the like; by that means, the enemy, gradually becoming afflicted with madness and fever, shall meet his death. [One should surround] the effigy of the enemy made from beeswax and other materials with thorns...
Having thus prepared one whose limbs have been pierced in this manner, one should bury her at midnight in a cremation ground;
by that means, the enemy will be possessed by a piśāca or similar spirit at that very moment and shall meet his death.
Having fashioned an effigy (*puttalī*) with the twelve previously mentioned substances—beginning with a wheel and clay—along with the four items starting with wool;

having buried it beneath the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); and having kindled a fire upon it with wood from a tree belonging to the enemy’s birth-constellation (*nakṣatra*), one should perform [the rite] at midnight with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from an enemy-tree smeared with serpent-oil, in a number such as a thousand.

For the practitioner who offers oblations with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), the enemy shall gradually be seized by a fever of the *sannipāta* type; consequently, his tongue becoming crooked and his consciousness lost, he shall utter incoherent speech and go to the abode of Yama. Having fashioned an effigy (*puttalī*) from the twelve previously mentioned substances mixed with the four [substances] beginning with hair, during the dark fortnight...
On the ninth lunar day coinciding with a Tuesday, one should bury [the ritual object] beneath the temple of Caṇḍikā. By this means,
the enemy— remaining unknown to spirits and others alike— shall receive a blow to the head like a vajra-strike and fall into flight before the completion of seven days.
Having finely ground four substances— mustard, black gram, sesame, and rice grains— in equal proportions,
one should add an equal amount of finely ground wood-chips from the tree belonging to the *nakṣatra* of one's enemy; having combined these five substances...

Having mixed equal parts of castor seed powder with the six substances and fashioned a doll from them, one should write upon its heart: "Kill, kill Devadatta! Then, touching that doll, one should recite the third-section vidyā in reverse order, beginning with the syllables *halakasīm*.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times by count,

at a nakṣatra that is the seventh, sixteenth, or twenty-fifth from the enemy’s birth-nakṣatra, and when the eighth house or the ascendant (lagna) of the enemy is occupied by the Sun, one should bind that effigy according to the tantra by cutting off its two feet.
Having taken up the doll with the hand that had been placed within the hollow of the flowing stream,
and having again recited the previously mentioned *pratiloma-lalitā-vidyā* one thousand times, [one should perform the rite] there upon that doll.

Having worshipped the principal deity, one should offer oblations into the fire consecrated according to the previously mentioned method by means of the six substances consisting of mustard seeds, black gram, sesame, rice grains, pieces of wood from the tree of the presiding asterism, and castor seeds— until the number reaches one thousand as completed by the performers of the rite.
One should suspend that doll from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) by means of a sling or similar device, with its feet upwards and its head downwards.
When this is done, on the very day of the ritual performance— and not after a delay of time— the person becomes overwhelmed by heat and thirst,
and falls to the ground here and there.
One who is deprived of consciousness, rolling about, with speech faltering like that of a mallet striking a drum, shall quickly meet death.
Having fashioned an effigy from the wood of the tree belonging to the birth-nakṣatra of the enemy,
having smeared it with the milky sap of the *arka* and *sruhī* plants, and having placed within its heart-region a name written on a palm leaf, one should [proceed].
Having bound the effigy with two threads of *arka* at the level of its two feet, making it face downwards with its feet pointing upwards,

and having suspended it above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) over a water-jar or similar vessel, [one should perform the rite] using fuel-sticks from an enemy tree that have been smeared with the milky sap of *arka* and *sruhī*.
One should offer oblations by the thousands at midnight; by that means, within three days, the enemy shall be afflicted with fever.

If, out of fear of the sin of his death, he pacifies his anger and seeks to protect him, then one should remove the effigy from above the sacrificial pit and cast it into the midst of the moss found in a pond. By that [means]...

Gradually, happiness shall arise for him. Having fashioned a doll from the wood of the tree belonging to the birth-constellation of the enemy, and having performed the consecration of its life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should place it inside an unbaked earthen vessel.

On a Saturday, having bathed before the temple of Caṇḍikā, and having offered a *bali* sacrifice near the very spot where one has dug up the earth belonging to an enemy born under an inimical constellation— such as Aja and others—
the practitioner shall kill his own enemy by means of a thunderbolt strike, an earthquake, or other such calamities; likewise, [he shall do so] with an effigy made of that very same [earth].
Having repeatedly placed [the substance] beneath a threshold in one's own house, one should kindle an uninterrupted fire upon it;
then the enemy will suffer from fever, dysentery, and disease.
[Furthermore,] having smeared the enemy’s birth-star with the milk of the *arka* and *sruhī* plants, one should place it inside a small earthen vessel.

Having fashioned a doll joined with the leg-bone of a deer named Ruru, and having bound its feet with a cord of *arka* fibers, one should bury it at night in the house of the enemy during the rising of the eighth zodiac sign (*lagna*). By this means, within a month, he shall be expelled from that place and go elsewhere; thus, enmity arises between the two enemies.

Having fashioned two dolls from wood taken from a tree belonging to the birth-constellation (*nakṣatra*) of those two individuals whose enmity one desires to produce, and having written the names of both—the two subjects (*sādhya*)—on a palm leaf with the mantra "Create mutual hatred between Yajñadatta and Devadatta! Create it! and affixing it to the hearts [of the dolls], one [should wrap] one doll in a cat's skin and the second...

Having wrapped it in the skin of a rat, one should bury two small figurines individually on each of the banks—of whatever type those local shores may be—extending as far as the maximum flood-level of the two boundary rivers. Alternatively, one may bury both in separate locations within a cremation ground;
or else, one may bury them in separate places within the temple of Caṇḍikā. By that means...

There shall be mutual enmity between those two enemies. Having fashioned nine effigies according to the measurements prescribed for the primary enemy’s asterism, tree, and wood, and having written upon palm leaves placed within their hearts, "Devadatta, bring about the destruction of his lineage, bring it about!"—

Having recited the *pratiloma* (reverse-order) *lalitā-vidyā* of the third section one thousand times each, preceded by physical touch, one should bury nine effigies (*puttalī*)— one in the center and eight in the eight directions— in the house of the enemy. By that means, [the enemy's...]

It results in the uprooting, destruction, and eradication of the family. Thus ends the application for the death and other rites concerning an enemy who is nearby. One hundred and eight effigies made from the wood of the tree corresponding to the enemy’s birth asterism should be prepared according to the previously mentioned method, with dimensions determined by the *aṃśaka*.

One should prepare all the effigies by writing the names of the practitioner and the target upon thin leaves and placing them within their respective hearts; these should then be smeared with the milky sap of the *arka* and *tuhī* plants. Then, at midnight, facing the direction of one's enemy, one should offer each effigy individually into the fire. In whichever division (*aṃśaka*) [the rite is performed]...

One should offer each respective effigy into the corresponding part of the fire-pit, which has been constructed according to the prescribed measurements in the form of the feet of those respective constellations (*nakṣatra*). For one performing the rite in this manner, even if the enemy is currently alive, he shall die.

In the same way, one may also accomplish the rite of inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*). However, the distinction in the case of inciting enmity is that, whereas previously [in the case of killing], it was Devadatta... [the text continues].

"Kill! Kill!"—this is the writing [of the mantra]. Here, however, "Make Devadatta and Yajñadatta hate each other! Make them hate each other!"—this is the writing [of the mantra]; such is the application for causing death from a distance and so forth. These are the applications of the *puttalī* (effigy). Now, the applications of the *yantra*:
therein, having drawn the *śrīcakra* and performing the worship of Lalitā with her enclosures according to the previously stated method...
Having enjoyed here in this birth the glorious prosperity desired by the practitioner according to his wish, and having attained knowledge at the end,
he shall achieve the realization of the true nature of Śrī and Śiva. If one is unable to draw the Śrīcakra as previously described, the Kamalacakra should be drawn instead.

The procedure for that is as follows: on a perfectly level surface, having first made a mark in the center, one should place a gnomon with its face toward that point, and then measure twenty-four finger-breadths all around it.
Having produced a circle by means of a "crab-turn" (karkāṭaka-bhrāmaṇa), one should fashion a triangle facing oneself in the exact center of that circle. Outside of that,
one should draw sixteen circles in succession with intervals of two aṅgulas, five aṅgulas, two aṅgulas, and five aṅgulas.
Having fashioned another [mandala] and produced seventeen circuits in combination,
one should proceed in sequence upon the eight paths— numbered eight— that are separated by intermediate paths of two finger-breadths and have intervals of five, four, and three finger-breadths.

Having fashioned lotuses with fifteen, eight, ten, fourteen, eight, sixteen, and eighteen petals, and having fashioned a triangle in the pericarp at the center of all of them along with a bindu within it,
[one should perform] the three-fold breath control (prāṇāyāma), the ritual placements (nyāsa), the offering of arghya, and the primary formal resolve (saṃkalpa).

Having performed the worship of the *pīṭha* (seat) first, and immediately after the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should worship the principal deity within the lotus inside the triangle with twelve offerings (*dvādaśopacāra*). Then, on the rear side, one should worship the nine *Nāthas* in three rows, according to the sequence of three *Nāthas* in each row.

Having worshipped the eight weapons on the two sides, and having worshipped the fifteen Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā in the fifteen petals, proceeding clockwise from the front petal,
and having completed the worship of the deities who are equal in rank to the principal deity, [one proceeds] among the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).

Having worshipped the eighteen powers beginning with *aṇimā*, which constitute the first enclosure, one should also worship the Nityā-kalās, such as Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others, on the sixteen petals— starting from the petal in front of the Goddess and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction from the west, southwest, south, and so on, ending at the northwest.

On the eight petals, having worshipped Anaṅgakusumā and the others in the sequence of the cardinal directions starting from the east, and in the sequence of the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, [one should worship] on the fourteen petals.

Having worshipped the fourteen Śaktis beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī in sequence from the west, southwest, and south; having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā from the west up to the letter *ma* on the ten outer petals; and having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with Sarvajñā according to the previously mentioned sequence on the ten inner petals.
"Within the eight-petaled lotus," and so forth. Having worshipped the eight goddesses of speech in counter-clockwise order (vāmākrama),
and having worshipped the triad beginning with Kāmeśvarī starting from the tip of the central triangle and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction,
one should again worship Lalitā in the center of the *bindu*, followed by the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*), the offering, and so on, as before.

One should perform the rites beginning with the daily fire-oblation (*nityāhoma*) and ending with the dismissal (*udvāsana*). For the practitioner who acts in this manner, the attainment of Great Fortune (*mahālakṣmī*) shall occur in this very life; and at the end, having attained knowledge and taking refuge in Śivā, who is identical with primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there shall be union (*sāyujya*) with Me, the creator of the universe. Thus concludes the fruit of the yantra of the daily worship.
Having marked the center in the middle of a well-prepared site and placed a compass there,

one should construct a circle by rotating it with a measurement of twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and so forth all around. Having drawn another circle outside that with an interval of one finger-breadth, [one should proceed] within the pericarp of the inner circle.

Having laid down two lines— one extending east-west and one extending north-south— intersecting each other, one should produce a wheel consisting of nine squares. Then, within the corridor formed between the two circles,
one should draw seven lines of equal intervals starting from the east.

Having performed [the construction], once the line-diagram (*rekhāmaya-cakra*) has been completed, by virtue of its connection with the preceding square, it serves as the producer of the portion that joins the eastern part belonging to the two circular lines situated above it.
In that same manner, having fashioned a pot-mouth (*ghaṭamukha*) four finger-breadths above that,
one should construct an eight-petalled lotus with its face downward in the upper portion of that [mouth], complete with stalk, petals, filaments, and pericarp, and [draw] two circular lines.

Below the western portion of the relative [structure], which is determined to be the base of the jar, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with its stalk, petals, filaments, and pericarp facing upwards; therein, one should inscribe the syllables. The method for this is as follows:
in the four corner squares of the wheel consisting of nine central compartments, [one should place] the present *vidyā*...
Having written the first section; having written the second section in the four squares located in the cardinal directions;

and having written the third section—containing the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) such as "Devadatta," with the word "puṣpa" and the mantra "dīrghaṃ kurukuru," etc.—in the central square.

Having written, in sequence, the letters *sa*, *ka*, *la*, *ha*, *ra*, the fourth vowel (*ī*), and *ma* in the seven squares starting from the east located in the space between the outer circular path,
one should write the syllable *jaḥ* on the stalk of the upward-facing lotus and the two syllables *jhaṭaṃ* in a fourfold form upon its petals.

One should write the syllable *va* eight times on the filaments (*kesara*), the syllable *sa* in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and the two syllables *jha* and *ṭa* four times on the petals of the downward-facing lotus. Furthermore, one should write the syllable *va* eight times on the filaments and the syllable *sa* in the center of the pericarp; however, in reality, there are two syllables on the filaments and the pericarp just as there are on the petals.
The inscription consists of two syllables, because there is no cause for the non-writing of a single syllable.
And that [inscription] occurs in the yantras by means of the second or third mode, according to the principle of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and the *ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*-assignment.

The third and fourth [syllables] are by way of repetition in the filaments (*kesara*), while the fourth and fifth are combined in the pericarp (*karṇikā*); such is the meaning of the root text. Having placed the jar in the machine named the "Amṛtaghaṭa" (Jar of Nectar) thus constructed, one should perform the consecration during the three lunar mansions of one's own birth.

For the practitioner who performs [the rite] through the medium of a guru and others, there is an increase in lifespan. By performing it without interruption on the days of the new moon (*kuhū*), lunar eclipses, solar eclipses, and the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (*saṃkrānti*), as well as on days afflicted by the influence of malefic planets, there is the complete removal of all misfortunes (*ariṣṭa*) indicated by one’s birth under such astrological configurations as *mūla*, *śleṣā*, and *vyatīpāta*.
There is the warding off of afflictions caused by the planets; there is the destruction of great diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā) and the pacification of epilepsy.

For one who performs the consecration (abhiṣeka) on the nights corresponding to their own birth for a period of three years, there arises a lifespan of one hundred years preceded by liberation from all diseases. However, if...

Having engraved this very same previously described yantra upon a leaf made of gold, silver, or copper, and having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths), one should fashion a vessel in the shape of a *liṅga* out of clay,
place the rolled-up yantra therein, and cast it into a vessel of honey according to the prescribed ritual procedure.

One should worship the principal goddess there; then the pacification of untimely death occurs. However, if one does not write the fourth vowel in the portion of the third seed-syllable situated in the middle part of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth, but instead writes the third seed-syllable at the beginning and end with the name of the person to be accomplished written in the middle, [then it should be worn] on a ring, an armlet, or a necklace.

Or, having cast it down and performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) upon that yantra, if the practitioner carries it, then there will be the attainment of all desired objects and the avoidance of all undesired ones. If...
However, when the previously mentioned yantra is engraved upon a large stone by means of a craftsman,

and after performing the consecration of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and worship, it is deposited in any one of the locations such as a pond, a lake, or a well, then for all men who perform their ablutions with that water, [the benefit] occurs incessantly and not merely occasionally.
There shall be happiness. Thus end the applications of the Amṛtaghaṭa machine.

Having drawn eight lines extending east-west and eight lines extending north-south, intersecting one another with equal intervals, one should produce forty-nine squares; then, five squares each in the four corners of the outermost path (vīthī),
and one square each in every corner of the second path, making a total of...

Having erased twenty-four squares, and within the remaining twenty-five squares, having first constructed triangles facing oneself in the four squares situated in the cardinal directions starting from the east, one should then arrange the twenty-four variations produced by the differentiation of the first four syllables of the third Vidyā in the sequence of the eastern and other squares.

Having written [the letters] in the order of entry— by way of the twenty-fourth, twenty-third, twenty-second, twenty-first, and so on, ending with the third, second, and first *vidyā*s— in the remaining central square situated in the middle of all;

Having written this third section, which contains the names of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth, in its entirety, one should complete this yantra with the name of the perfected one (*siddha*). By first performing the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and then wearing it, victory is attained in battle, in fields, in disputes, and other such situations.
Having drawn this yantra on the ground every month on the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth days,
and having consecrated it, one should place a water-pot there according to the prescribed rite; then, for one desiring a son, [the rite is performed] by means of an ablution with that water.

There is the attainment of a son; for one seeking marriage, the obtaining of a bridegroom; for a maiden seeking a groom, the acquisition of her desired husband; for kings and others seeking land, the gain of territory; for those seeking wealth, the acquisition of riches;
and for those seeking cattle, buffaloes, elephants, horses, and so forth, the attainment of those respective animals. However, if this previously mentioned [result]...
Having written this yantra on birch bark with saffron and other substances, one should wear it on the hand or elsewhere;

then there will certainly be the attainment of subjugation, the attainment of mantric power, the attainment of all scholarly erudition, and the acquisition of a house. This wearing of the yantra is also necessary for the accomplishment of the previously mentioned other tasks. Thus.

The applications of the Siddha-vajra yantra: Having drawn eighteen lines extending east-west and eighteen lines extending north-south, intersecting one another at equal intervals, one produces a wheel consisting of two hundred and sixty-nine (269) squares. Then, in the first row...
Having excluded the ninth square from each of the four directions on the outermost layer surrounding the entire [grid],
and having cleared away the fifteen squares situated in the center,
one should [place] one [deity] below each of the previously excluded squares in the four directions of the second path.
Having set aside three squares in total— namely, the two squares situated at the two sides of that [group] and the three squares combined—
and having erased the eleven squares each located in the middle,
[one should fill] in the third row the three squares situated below the three squares previously set aside, as well as the two squares situated at their sides.
Having combined [the cells] and set aside five cells, and having cleared away the seven cells situated around them; then,
on the fourth row, the cell previously set aside and the five cells below the group of five—

Having set aside seven squares in total—consisting of the two squares adjacent to that [central square] and the three squares situated around it—one should erase them. Thus, at each corner, thirty-six squares are erased;
in total, one hundred and forty-four (144) squares are erased.
One hundred and forty-five (145) squares remain; therein,
three squares from the downward row, three squares from each of the four directions, and one from the first row,
totaling four squares.

By erasing the three lines that divide the compartments—namely, the two side-lines and the vertical line—and thereby unifying them, one forms upward-facing triangles in all directions; thus, one hundred and thirty-nine (139) compartments remain. Therein:
Starting from the central square among the five squares located outside the eastern direction, and proceeding clockwise by way of entry,
there are one hundred and twenty [syllables] (120) arising from the twenty-fold variations of the five letters constituting the entire *hara* of the third section of the Śrīvidyā.

Having written the Vidyā once in the single square, one should write the first segment by rotating it through the three squares located in the southern part of the remaining central nine-square grid; then the second segment by rotating it through the three squares in the left part;
and finally the third segment—containing the names of the practitioner (sādhaka), the person to be acted upon (sādhya), and so forth—by rotating it through the three central squares.

Having thus prepared the yantra and placed the secondary flask (parikalasha) upon it, through consecration with its water, there is the attainment of all previously mentioned and hereafter described fruits.
Thus, by wearing [the yantras], there is the attainment of all fruits; the wearing of all the yantras must be performed as follows:

having first drawn the yantra to be worn upon a piece of ground, having established a water-pot (kumbha) there, having worshipped the deity of that yantra therein, and having caused an ablution with its water to be performed.

Having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one’s means, and having performed the worship of the mantra-deity, the yantra, and the guru— concluding with prostrations and preceded by the offerings of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth—
one should think: "By the wearing of this [yantra], may the fruit intended for me certainly be realized."

It should be followed with the greatest firmness of conviction. However, in the absence of the fourfold rites beginning with consecration (*abhiṣeka*), there is no attainment of results merely from wearing [the yantra].

Likewise, even by worshipping the yantra daily at home, all fruits are attained. Similarly, by burying the yantra in the house or other locations, all goals are accomplished; yet this is provided that one has first established the specific fruit as the intended object.
The drawing of the yantra on that [specific] yantra results in the attainment of that specific fruit at that time, and not of another.

Furthermore, the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—which is of many kinds, such as the Ekādaśa and so forth—should not be written [in such a way] that all fruits might be accomplished simultaneously.
Thus end the applications of the *Koṣṭhavajra* yantra. [The lines] extend from east to west and from south to north.

Having laid down twenty-six lines each, with equal intervals between them and intersecting one another, and having thus produced six hundred and twenty-five (625) squares; therein, one should erase the eight triangular squares located at the corners. The manner of doing so is as follows: here—

In the calculation of the southern and northern rows, there are twenty-five rows in number; in the calculation of the surrounding rows, the first row consists of ninety-six squares, and [the central area] contained within it is— (p.
The second [row] consists of eighty-four squares in the middle, each composed of twenty-five squares;
the fifth consists of sixty-four squares; the sixth consists of fifty-six squares;
the seventh consists of forty-eight squares; and the eighth consists of forty squares.
The ninth [layer] consists of thirty-two squares; the tenth consists of twenty-four squares;

the eleventh consists of sixteen squares surrounding it; and the twelfth is the path (vīthī) consisting of eight squares surrounding that—thus there are twelve paths, with one square located in the very center, according to the manner in which the stated number of squares is established around the paths.
In the outermost row, having set aside the thirteenth square from each side in the center,
and having erased twenty-three squares in each corner by diminishing eight squares from each respective preceding row into the successive inner rows, [one proceeds] in the second row.
Having abandoned three squares in total— namely, one square below the previously abandoned central square and one square on each of its two sides—
in the four directions, and then having erased the remaining nineteen by nineteen squares, [one proceeds] in the third path.
Having abandoned the five squares in total— namely, the three lower squares previously set aside and the two squares at their sides—
and having erased the remaining fifteen squares in each [row], [one proceeds] in the fourth row.
The five lower squares previously abandoned and the two squares situated at their side,
making seven squares in total (p.
Having discarded those situated in the middle, and having erased eleven squares in each corner;

and in the fifth row, having discarded nine squares in total— consisting of the seven lower squares previously mentioned in the four directions and the two squares situated at their sides— in each corner.
Having wiped away seven squares, on the sixth path (vīthī) in the four directions,

one should leave aside eleven squares each— consisting of the nine squares below the previously abandoned nine squares and the two squares situated at their two sides— and [retain] those situated in the middle thereof.
Having wiped away three by three squares in each corner, a total of seventy-eight squares have been wiped away in each of the six rows at every corner; thus, in the *trayantre*,
three hundred and twelve squares have been wiped away, while three hundred and thirteen squares remain.
In that regard, there are four squares in the first row, twelve in the second, twenty in the third,
twenty-eight in the fourth, thirty-six in the fifth, and forty-four in the sixth; thus, the number of squares increases by eight at each successive stage.

In the seventh and subsequent rows, however, the number of squares is as previously shown. In the outermost row, there is one square situated in each of the four directions; together with the three squares located in the row immediately below it—three squares for each direction—there are thus four squares in total for each direction.

By erasing the three respective dividing lines and bringing each section into a single square, one should draw an upward-pointing triangle in the fourth cardinal direction; thus, two hundred and ninety-seven squares (297) remain. Therein, beginning from the outermost western row...
In the enumeration, it is the thirteenth [square] situated within the row; because it is the thirteenth when counting the squares proceeding from south to north,
for that very reason.

Starting from the row situated outside the triangle of this central square— which is the eleventh square when counting from that central square— by merging together three squares on each of the right and left sides through the erasure of the two vertical lines that divide the squares;
Then, having omitted three squares from each of the twelfth and fourteenth rows— namely, the single square situated in the very center of each respective row and one square on each of its two sides—
there are eight squares in total, comprising two squares on each side across both rows.
By erasing one line from each respective divider, the state of four compartments (koṣṭha) should be achieved.
Then, from the eleventh and fifteenth rows respectively, the single central compartment of each,
along with the two compartments on either side of it— making two compartments on each side— thus totaling [four].
Leaving aside five squares for every street (vīthī),
and subsequently two squares on each side of those streets,
one should bring about the state of having two-by-two squares by erasing the single dividing lines between the squares, resulting in four squares per street.
Thus, eight squares have been cleared together. Then, having set aside the respective central square of the tenth and sixteenth rows, as well as the three squares adjacent to each of those two sides—
thus excluding seven squares from each row respectively— from the tenth row extending downwards:
One should erase one square on each of the two sides; thus, in total, two squares of the tenth row are erased.
In the sixteenth row from the top, two squares each situated above and below on every side—
making four squares in total— are erased. In the seventeenth row,
having omitted three squares in total— one located in the very center and one on each of its two sides— [the remaining are filled].
One should erase two adjacent squares—meaning four squares in total—connected to each previously erased row of squares; thus, thirty-two squares become erased.
Thereafter, those [squares] situated on the sides of the rows of the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth consonants (ha-saṇāḥ) [are to be treated].

Having erased ten lines in total— namely, three lines on each of the two sides making six lines situated in the twentieth row, four lines above the triangle formed by the three squares located in the center of the nineteenth row and on both its sides— one should proceed.
Nine squares are wiped away. Thus, in total, forty-one squares are wiped away.
Here, within the three hundred and thirteen squares situated inside the two side-squares that have been wiped away in the tenth row—
The pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) consists of sixteen squares ending with the last square of the row of liquor (the second row).
The base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) consists of fifteen squares above that. The nine central squares are designated as the *liṅga*.
Once the yantra has been thus prepared, one should write the syllables of the mantra. The method for doing so is as follows:

Starting from the tenth row, having written the *māyābīja* (the syllable Hrīṃ) individually in each of all ten central squares located within the nineteenth row, [one should write] the third section of Lalitā within that.
Having written [the mantra], one should write the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth within the interior of the fourth vowel; then,
having written the first *kūṭa* by repetition on the right side of the three cells situated at the very top.
Having written the second *kūṭa* by rotation within the three compartments on the left side,
there remain twenty-four compartments out of the forty compartments of the *liṅga*, sixteen of which have already been assigned to the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) and the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The external vajra-cells consist of two hundred and sixteen cells; thus, in total, two hundred and forty (240) cells remain. Within these, there are one hundred and twenty varieties of the Vidyā arising from the five-syllable permutations of the third section of the Vidyā.

Having written [the syllables] one by one in a clockwise direction, starting from the central square of the five squares located in the eastern direction and proceeding with a circular inward movement, and having again written those same *vidyās* according to the sequence of writing around the perimeter without releasing [the previous ones],
[one should place] the *māyā-bīja*— also known as *hṛllekhā*— in each of the triangles situated at the four directions.

Within that, one should write the third root, the seed-syllable of Vidyā; and within that as well, in the region of the interior of the fourth vowel, one should inscribe the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth, in the form "Devadatta, subdue Yajñadatta" and so on.
This is the Yantra called Siddhakoṣṭhaliṅga. Having installed it, all tasks [are accomplished]. When established here...

Through the sprinkling of water from a ritual jar (*kalaśa*), through recitation and so forth, by wearing [the mantra] written on birch bark or other materials upon one's own drums and such instruments,
by worshipping it daily after having written and installed it in the home, or by [installing it] in stone, copper, or other yantras within the house and so forth with upward lines;
Having engraved it accordingly, the practitioner should accomplish his goal by burying it according to the prescribed ritual in the eight directions and in the center.
In brief, there is no task whatsoever that cannot be achieved through this yantra. Thus [it is said].

The Application of the Koṣṭha-liṅga Yantra: First, having constructed a square with an interval of one *aṅgula*, one should write each subsequent letter starting from the first letter of the *Nityā-vidyā*. In the center, one should write the respective pair of letters (*yugārṇa*) and the hour-letter (*ghaṭikārṇa*), depending on whether they are internal or external. A yantra of this kind [is thus formed].

For the practitioner who worships [the deity] after having it depicted on a cloth and so forth, there is victory, long life, health, and the attainment of wealth, sovereignty, and other such gains. This fruit belongs not only to the act of worship itself, but also to the consecration with water from a jar presided over by that [deity], to carrying it [in procession], and to burying it; through these, one attains all desired fruits.

This is the result. Thus end the applications of the Meruliṅga yantra. Having drawn twenty-one lines each, extending east-west and north-south, intersecting one another with equal intervals, upon some level and smooth ground, there arise four hundred squares.
Having completed that, in the middle of its twenty rows, there are five squares on one side of the very last bottom row;
in the row above that, six; in the row above that, seven; and in the fourth row above that, eight. In the fifth row [from the top], [there are nine].

In the sixty-ninth row there are ten; in the seventh [from the end] eleven; in the eighth ten; in the ninth nine; in the tenth eight; in the eleventh seven; in the twelfth six; and in the thirteenth five.
Thus, in sequence from the first row to the thirteenth row, one hundred and one squares have been erased in total.
They are on the second side.
Having erased not even a single square in the first row, [erase] one in the second row.
In the third [row] there are two squares; in the fourth, three squares;
in the fifth, four squares; in the sixth, five squares; in the seventh, six squares;
in the eighth, five squares; in the ninth, four squares; in the tenth, three squares; and in the eleventh, two squares.
On the twelfth [square] one [cell], on the thirteenth five [cells]; by the side of that, one should erase at least some [cells].
Thus, thirty-six (36) cells have been erased in total.
[This applies to] the group of five rows consisting of the fourteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth [squares].

At the time of wiping the first side, ten squares each from the sides of those respective rows were previously wiped; at the time of wiping the second side, five squares each must be wiped in each of the five rows. Thus, in total, there are seventy-five (75) squares.

The two rows [of squares] should be wiped clean, and likewise nineteen and twenty [squares] should be established; this wiping is according to the instruction and because it is seen in the ritual injunction. In reality, however, nineteen lines should be drawn extending east-west, and twenty-one lines should be drawn extending north-south; by that—

It should be understood that no more than two rows will remain; thus, there are exactly three hundred and sixty (360) squares here. Accordingly, there are fifteen (15) in the first row, thirteen (13) in the second, eleven (11) in the third, nine (9) in the fourth, seven (7) in the fifth, and [seven] in the sixth.
Five on the fifth, three on the seventh,
again five on the eighth, seven on the ninth, nine on the tenth, eleven on the eleventh, and [eleven] on the twelfth.

Thirteen (13) plus fifteen (15) makes twenty-three; together with the one hundred and twenty-three (123) squares [already mentioned], there are one hundred and twenty-six squares in total. Furthermore, in the upper portion, there are five rows, each containing five squares, which together constitute twenty-five (25) squares.
Thus, one hundred and forty-eight (148) remain,
and two hundred and twelve (212) [remain]; these, when combined, result in three hundred and sixty (360) squares.
Here, in the six lower compartments denoted by the term *adhiṣṭhāna* (base), and in the six upper compartments denoted by the term *piṇḍikā* (pedestal),
one should write the one hundred and twenty (120) variations of the five-syllable mantra.
In the three compartments situated between the *adhiṣṭhāna* and the *piṇḍikā*, one should write the three syllables of the daily *Nityā* mantra in each row.

Starting from the fifth square in the top row of the twenty-five squares and proceeding clockwise around the periphery, there are twenty-four varieties produced by the permutations of the four syllables;
having written the names of the practitioner and the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the remaining central square, the yantra is thus established.

In brief, the practitioner should employ the means consisting of worship, consecration, wearing, and burying for the sake of each of their respective various desires. Thus ends the application of the Great Liṅga Yantra. Having constructed a Yoni with three lines facing oneself and a wide interior on some level ground or similar surface, of that—
Having divided each of the three sūtras eleven times respectively, and having made ten marks at each of those respective divisions, [one proceeds] from mark to mark. (p. 75a)

Having cast thirty lines starting from the piercing of the vital points (*marmabhedana*), one should produce the triangles in the following order: first, one hundred and twenty-one [triangles] facing downwards by means of thirty lines; then, one hundred and twenty-one facing upwards, beginning with the [triangle at the] top, and so forth. Then, starting from the tips [of those triangles], proceeding clockwise—

Having inscribed, in sequence and all around, the one hundred and twenty vidyās produced by the variations of the five syllables, one should write the names of the practitioner (sādhaka), the person for whom the rite is performed (sādhya), and so forth, in the remaining single square. This is the Siddha-yantro;
it is effective when preceded by any one of the following methods: worship, wearing [the yantra], consecrating a water-pot (kalaśa) empowered by it, or burying it.

The practitioner should apply [this] to all his respective desires. Thus end the applications of the Yoni Yantra. Having made a mark in the center on some level, smooth ground, and having laid a thread extending north-south and east-west by means of that [mark];

Having marked two signs on both sides of the southern water-line, one should lay down two lines starting from those marks and extending to the eastern end of the Brahma-line; then, starting from the same point,
one should lay down another two lines extending to the western end of the Brahma-line, forming two [intersecting] lines.
Having cleared the area extending from east to west and from south to north,
one should form two triangles joined to each other, with one apex pointing upward and the other downward; then,
for each of these two triangles, one should divide the lines on the left and right into five parts each.
Having placed four marks each at the end of the divisions, there is a first line starting from the left-hand mark of the spokes and ending at the right-hand mark of the *yoni*,
and a second line starting from the right-hand mark of the spokes and ending at the left-hand mark of the *yoni*; thus, these eight marks are mutually [connected].
Having joined [the lines] by drawing the grid-lines and having prepared twenty-five square compartments in the form of vajras,
one should begin from the first peak located at the very top of all of them.

Having arranged the twenty-four vidyās consisting of the four-syllable variations of Śrīvidyā by entering and proceeding in a clockwise direction, one should write the names of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), the practitioner (sādhaka), and so forth, in the central square. Thus, through worship on the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth days in the Siddhayantra, [the desired result is attained].

Through the empowerment by sprinkling from the vase presided over by that [deity], through wearing it, and through burying it in houses, cities, and so forth, all desired accomplishments (*siddhi*) written individually in the center of the practitioner shall come to pass. Thus are the applications of the Vajra-vajra yantra.

As before, having formed a triangular *yonicakra* through mutual conjunction, one should divide it into eleven parts with three lines; at the end of these divisions, having made ten marks each, and by joining the marks to one another as before,
one should produce one hundred and twenty-one squares using ten lines each.
Beginning from the eastern peak and proceeding clockwise by way of entry,

one should write the Śrīvidyā mantras— numbering one hundred and twenty due to the variations of the four-syllabled vidyās— around the periphery; then, having written the names of the practitioner (sādhaka) and the object of attainment (sādhya) in the remaining central square, the yantra is completed.
Through daily worship, dhāraṇī-retention, consecration, and burial, the practitioner shall accomplish all desired goals.

Thus end the applications of the Great Vajra-Vajrayantra. Having fashioned the *astrayonicakra* (the wheel of the source of weapons) by joining together the previous deities with upward-pointing and downward-pointing fierce forms, one should place twenty-six symbols along each line in its center.

Having drawn lines upon them, one should worship the nine and ninety-nine [deities] and offer the three types of services consisting of libation (*tarpaṇa*), recitation of hymns (*stotra-pāṭha*), and prostration (*namaskāra*). In the Kali age,
preceded by the consumption of milk for four hundred thousand [repetitions], [the mantra] should consist of only the word "amuṣya."
Having separately offered forty thousand oblations of that mantra with sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, and *pratyañji*, all soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhura*), twenty thousand times each;

Having completed the fire sacrifice (homa) until it reaches ten times that number, and having gratified [the deity] with four thousand offerings of pure water mixed with fragrant substances such as camphor and musk;
and having fed the Brahmins and satisfied the Guru with sacrificial fees, prostrations, and other honors— with this [mantra] thus accomplished:

One should perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) and others into a doll, a yantra, or similar objects by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra. The procedure for this is as follows:
[one should draw] eight lines intersecting one another, extending east-west and north-south, with their internal spaces mutually joined.

Having prepared a wheel consisting of forty-nine squares, one should write the forty syllables of the present vidyā in a clockwise direction, beginning from the northeast square. Then, having written the letters ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, and sa repeatedly in the remaining nine squares surrounding it, [one should place] [the remaining syllable] in one square.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in another square, followed by the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the verb of action, one should—preceded by the contemplation of the non-difference between the cause and the Supreme Brahman (*para-brahman*)—visualize the seed-syllable of Māyā (*māyā-bīja*) as being red in color, having the nature of a rope for the purpose of attraction; then, touching the effigy (*puttalī*), [one recites] *hrīṃ*... [the sense-faculty].
Having drawn [the vital force] from within Devadatta’s body and placed it into the doll via the portion of the *pratiṣṭhā* channel with one's hand,

and having touched this yantra while reciting the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra a hundred times; then, having placed this yantra— which has been prepared from those substances according to the prescribed directions— among the materials for making the doll, those materials...

Or, having placed [the materials] in a mechanical device (yantra), one should fashion effigies (puttalikā). Once the effigy is perfected, one should install the vital breaths and other faculties of the person to be acted upon (sādhya). The procedure for this is as follows:

At midnight, the practitioner [recites]: "Hrīḥ! I draw forth the entire mantra and the meaning of the mantra from the body of Devadatta and establish the ear-faculty (śrotrendriya) within the effigy. 1. Hrīḥ! I draw forth the skin-faculty (tvagindriya) from within the body of Devadatta and establish it within the effigy. 3. Hrīḥ! The eye-faculty (cakṣurindriya)..."

I draw [the faculty] from within the body of Devadatta and establish it in the effigy. 3. Hrīḥ! I draw the gustatory faculty from within the body of Devadatta and establish it in the effigy. 4. Hrīḥ! I draw the olfactory faculty from within the body of Devadatta and establish it. 5. Hrīḥ! The vocal faculty...

I extract from within the body of Devadatta and establish it in the doll: 6. Hrīḥ! The hand-faculty, I extract from within the body of Devadatta and establish it in the doll. 7. Hrīḥ! The foot-faculty, I extract from within the body of Devadatta and establish it in the doll. 8. Hrīḥ! The anus-faculty...

I draw [the faculty] from within the body of Devadatta and establish it in the effigy. 9. Hrīṃ! I draw the organ of generation from within the body of Devadatta and establish it in the effigy. 10. Hrīṃ! I draw the object of sound from within the body of Devadatta and establish it in the effigy. 11. Hrīṃ! [I draw] the object of touch...

"Devadatta," and so forth, as before. 12. *Hrīṃ*, for the sake of form (*rūpa*); "having drawn [it] from within Devadatta’s body," and so forth, as before. 13. *Hrīṃ*, for the sake of taste (*rasa*); "Devadatta," and so forth. 14. *Hrīṃ*, for the sake of smell (*gandha*); "Devadatta," and so forth. 15. *Hrīṃ*, for the sake of speech (*bhāṣaṇa*); "Devadatta," and so forth. 16. *Hrīṃ*, for the sake of grasping (*grahaṇa*); "Devadatta," and so forth. 17. *Hrīṃ*.
18. *Hrīṃ*, for the purpose of going, Devadatta... and so forth. 19. *Hrīṃ*, for the purpose of the lap, Devadatta... and so forth. 20. *Hrīṃ*, for the purpose of bliss, Devadatta...
and so forth. 21. *Hrīṃ*, from within the body of Devadatta’s mind... and so forth. 22. *Hrīṃ*, the *jīva* from within the body of Devadatta... and so forth.

p. 77a) Hrīṃ! O Devadatta, [I take] the skin, and so forth. 23. Hrīṃ! Raṃ! O Devadatta, [I take] the blood, and so forth. 24. Hrīṃ! Laṃ! O Devadatta, [I take] the flesh, and so forth. 25. Hrīṃ! Vaṃ! O Devadatta, [I take] the marrow, and so forth. 26. Hrīṃ! Śaṃ! O Devadatta, [I take] the bones, and so forth. 27.

*Hrīṃ ṣaṃ*, [I extract] the marrow of Devadatta, and so forth. (28) *Hrīṃ saṃ*, [I extract] the semen of Devadatta, and so forth. (29) *Hrīṃ*, having extracted the vital energy (*ojas*) from within the body of Devadatta, I establish it in the effigy (*puttalī*). Having thus recited these thirty mantras, [one should extract] the thirty objects mentioned, beginning with the faculty of hearing and ending with the faculty of touch, from the person to be acted upon, such as Devadatta.

Having visualized with the mind that the effigy has entered from within the body, and having again touched the effigy at the line situated in the portion of the *pravaha* channel, one should recite the mantra syllable by syllable one thousand times, saying: "May the speech, mind, and vital breaths of this Devadatta come here into this effigy; svāhā!"

Thus, the effigy (pūttalī), in which the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other faculties of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) have been established, shall accomplish all tasks. In the case of a deity’s yantra, however, the name of the deity should be substituted in place of "Devadatta" [in the mantra]. This is the method for the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). For the purpose of pacifying a *kṛtyā* (malevolent rite) performed by enemies with the intent to kill oneself, one should [use] the previously written [mantra] in reverse order (*pratiloma*).

There are eight divisions of the Kālacakra. Following each of these individual signs, one should proceed with any one of the four methods—vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), worship, retention, or burial—preceded by the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Among those, there is the reverse-order wheel (*pratilomacakra*).
Beginning with the *vidyā* inscribed upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*),

one should recite the five hundred and seventy-six syllables of the *vidyā* located at the outer tips and so forth; then, following the sequence of the respective years obtained through the *anuloma* and other methods, one should again recite each of those five hundred and seventy-six *vidyās*.
But where,
by chance, that very year which has reached the forward-moving wheel (anuloma-cakra) becomes a reverse-moving wheel (pratiloma-cakra);

In this context, there is a single method for the mountain-arrow (five hundred and seventy-six). The application of knowledge (*vidyāvṛtti*) occurs as follows: when it is necessary to perform acts such as inciting hatred against enemies through the destruction of their fortune, one must follow the *pratiloma* (reverse) wheel of time. Here, the letters beginning with *kṣa* number thirty-six.

Each [syllable] possesses sixteen forms by virtue of being connected with each of the sixteen vowels; nevertheless, through meditation on those respective letters as connected with their vowels, one should recite the mantra *akṣāī* once. Then, one should recite the mantra *akṣāī* sixteen times, *alāī* sixteen times, *ahāī* sixteen times, *asāī* sixteen times, *aṣāī* sixteen times, and *aśāī* sixteen times, and *avāī* sixteen times.

alāī 16 arāī 16 ayāī 16 amāī 16 abhāī 16 avāī 16 aphāī 16 apāī 16 anāī 16 adhāī 16 adāī 16 athāī 16 atāī 16 aṇāī 16 aṭhāī 16 aḍāī 16 aṭhāī aṭāī 16 ajāī 16 ajhāī 16 ajāī 16 achāī 16 acāī 16 aṅāī 16 aghāī 16 agāī 16 akhāī 16 akāī 16 a-

One should recite sixteen times the Vidyā consisting of the letters written in the thirty-six paths as "Āī 16. This is the sequence of the Vidyā of the forward and reverse wheels (cakras) to be performed by oneself, according to the method taught in the aforementioned *Samaya* for the twelve-cornered wheel [of] sixty-four years.
Because the first year is the *anuloma* (forward-moving) wheel with twelve spokes, which serves as the wheel for the attainment of the year, [the syllables] beginning with *ṭa-āī 16*,
*ṭakāī 16*, *ṭakhāī 16*, and so forth, ending with *ṭahāī 16*, *ṭalāī 16*, and *ṭakṣāī*, are written in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) according to the sequence of the sixteen days starting from the first.
One should recite each of the thirty-six *tattva-vidyās* sixteen times. For the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*) of these *vidyās*,
one should place a water-pot (*kalaśa*) upon this wheel and also perform ablution with its water.

Furthermore, the vidyās for the consecration of the vase (*kumbha-abhimantraṇa*), which is another synonym for the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka-pada*) intended to be performed, should also be recited in this very same sequential order. Thus end the applications of the reverse-order Kālacakra.

For the subjugation of kings and others, one should extract the external *saṃpuṭa* sequence-wheel (*bāhyasaṃpuṭakramacakra*) and follow one of the four methods consisting of worship, ritual practice, consecration, and non-digging.
