For the protection of cities, villages, and so forth, one should extract the internal *saṃpuṭa* sequence-wheel (*ābhyantarasaṃpuṭakramacakra*).

One should follow one of the five methods consisting of its worship, dhāraṇā, consecration, burying, or [other rites]. In that regard, for the practice of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) in the current year, having recited once the *kāī* syllable—the knowledge-mantra (*vidyā*) consisting of the letter *ka*—one should recite:
*u āī ukāī ukhāī chagāī ṭhaghāī ḍaṅāī ḍacāī ḍachāī ṭhajāī ḍajhāī chatrāī ḍaṭhāī*.
Ḍaḍhāī, ḍaḍāī, ḍaḍhāī, ḍaṇāī, chatāī, ṭhathāī, ḍakṣāī, ḍalāī, ḍahāī, ḍhasāī, ḍaṣāī, ḍaśāī, ḍavāī, ḍalāī, ḍarāī, ḍayāī, ḍamāī, ḍabhāī, ḍadhāī, ḍaphāī, ḍapāī, ṭhanāī,
ḍadhāī, ḍadāī— these are the vidyās, each to be recited sixteen times.

One should recite as if remembering the connection with the sixteen vowels for each syllable of the second Vidyā. Thus, following the sequence of the external *saṃpuṭa*, after the recitation of the Vidyā, one should recite according to the forward and reverse order (*anuloma-anuloma*) starting from the first year of the twelve-angled wheel (*dvādaśakoṇaka-cakra*) which has been introduced. Therein, first: *da ā ī*.

Having recited the *karṇikā-vidyā*, one should [recite] the thirty-six *vidyās* beginning with *uāī* and ending with *ukṣāī*, preceded by the recollection of the connection between the second syllables and the sixteen vowels. (p.

One should recite each [syllable] sixteen times. For the purpose of providing protection in the current year, one should recite the *vidyā* employed for the ritual action, beginning with *ḍḷāī ṭḷkāī ḍḷkhāī*, and so forth; *ḷgāī ḷdhāī*, and so forth; *vḷkṣāī kḷkṣāī*; *ṭḷhāī ṭḷsāī*; *dḷṣāī dḷśāī dḷṣāī*, and so forth; ending with *dḷvāī dḷdāī*. These are indeed the previously mentioned *anuloma-vidyās*.
One should recite the mantras associated with the wheel pertaining to this year's application. Thus end the applications of the encapsulated Kālacakra.

In the case of affliction by disease, for one whose external wheel has been overturned, or for the sake of victory over enemies, for one whose internal mechanism has been overturned, one should perform the extraction according to the previously mentioned method; then, one of the means consisting of worship, consecration, wearing [the mantra], or recitation should be practiced. *ḍathāī ḍatāī*.

this is to be done when one desires to obtain enemies, victory, cattle, land, gold, vehicles, clothing, silver, and so forth.

ḍḷhāī 3, ḍḷsāī 4, ḍḷṣāī 5, ḍḷśāī 6, ḍḷvāī 7, ḍḷlāī 8, ḍḷrāī 9, ḍḷvāī 10,

If one desires the eradication (*uccāṭana*) of one's own [enemies], having extracted the wheel scattered externally,

one should follow any one of the four methods consisting of worship, meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*), consecration (*abhiṣecana*), and burial. ṇa-āī 1, ṇakāī 2, ṇakāī 3, ṇalāī 4, ṇakhāī 5, ṇahāī 6, ṇagāī 7, ṇasāī 8, ṇaghāī 9.

When one desires to cause the eradication (*uccāṭana*) of others, the internal interlaced wheel (*ābhyantaravyākīrṇacakra*) should be rotated; therein also:
The pursuit of any one of the four methods consisting of worship, dhāraṇā, consecration, and burial is as before:
ṇlakṣāī 1, ṇa-āī 2, ṇlalāī 3, ṇakāī 4, ṇlahāī 5, ṇlakhāī 6, ṇlasāī 7, ṇlagāī 8, ṇlaṣāī 9, ṇlaghāī 10, ṇalaśāī 11, ṇlaṅāī 12, salavāī 13, ṇlacāī 14, salalāī 15, salarāī 17.

Having recited sixteen times for each of the sixteen vowels by means of connecting them with the second syllables,
one should [recite] the *prakṛtavarṣacakra-anuloma-vidyās* beginning with *ṭha-āī*, *ṭhakāī*, *ṭhakhāī*, and so forth,

One should recite sixteen times for each of the sixteen [syllables]. If one desires to perform an extremely difficult eradication (*uccāṭana*), even in that case, it consists precisely of those connected with the vowels. That is called "invocation" (*āvāhana*) and "intermingling" (*vyākīrṇa*).

Turning the wheel: for those [cases] connected with the essential meaning (*artha-svarasa*) which are otherwise impossible to accomplish, one should perform whichever among the four remedial measures—worship (*pūjana*), consecration (*abhiṣecana*), wearing [the amulet] (*dhāraṇa*), or digging (*khanana*)—is intended, according to the respective order. Among these, in the first case: *ṇṛkṣāī* 1, *ṇṛkṣāī* 2, *ṇṛkāī* 3, *ṇṛlāī* 4.
ṇṛkhāī 5, ṇṛhāī 6, ṇṛgāī 7, ṇṛsāī 8, ṇṛghāī 9, ṇṛṣāī 10, ṇṛṅāī 11, ṇṛśāī 12, ṇṛcāī 13, ṇṛvāī 14, ṇṛchāī 15, ṇṛlāī 16, ṇṛjāī 17, ṇṛrāī 18, ṇṛjhāī 19,
ṇṛyāī 20, ṇṛñāī 21, ṇṛmāī 22, ṇṛṭāī 23, ṇṛbhāī 24, ṇṛṭhāī 25, ṇṛvāī 26, ṇṛḍāī 27.
Ṇṛphāī (28), Ṇṛḍhāī (29), Ṇṛpāī (30), Ṇṛṇāī (31), Ṇṛnāī (32), Ṇṛtāī (33), Ṇṛdhāī (34), Ṇṛthāī (35), Ṇṛdāī (36)— these are the thirty-six vidyās,
preceded by the contemplation of the connection between each of the sixteen vowels and the sixteen consonants of the second syllable.
Having recited [the mantra], one should also recite the *anuloma-vidyās*— such as *ṭhāaī*, *ṭhakāī*, *ṭhakhāī*, and so forth—

which are related to the present year-wheel (*varṣacakra*), sixteen times each; this should be done while contemplating the connection between each individual vowel among the sixteen vowels and its corresponding second syllable.
In the second [case], by means of the letter *ṇa*—which has the form of the letter *eṇa*—in the place of the first syllable, there is this distinction: it is merely the insertion of a *visarga*;

everything else remains entirely as before. Thus end the applications of the *vyākīrṇacakra*. If it is performed with the intent of causing the death of enemies, or if it is performed for the sake of the practitioner’s own death;

Has the ritual procedure consisting of the placement of nooses and so forth been performed? Or has an act such as immobilization (*stambhana*) or inciting hatred (*dveṣaṇa*) been carried out by an enemy against the practitioner, or has an enemy performed [such acts] during the application of a rite for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*)?

Has an enemy employed a protective rite against women? Or has a practitioner performed a rite favorable to a disease that is curable? Or has a rite been performed favorable to the practitioner’s victory? Or has a practitioner...

If the enemy has performed a ritual application for the sake of destroying the land, gold, and so forth belonging to a specific person, or if the enemy has performed a ritual application for the purpose of the eradication of a practitioner, then [this is done] for the sake of nullifying the results of all nine aforementioned ritual applications.

For the purpose of pacifying the results of terrestrial, celestial, and atmospheric portents, as well as for the pacification of the results of birth under the *Mūla* or *Aśleṣā* constellations and so forth, one should perform whichever of the four means—worship, wearing [the yantra], consecration (*abhiṣecana*), or recitation—is appropriate, after having extracted the *Anulomacakra*. In that regard: *a-ā-ī*.

"A-kā-ī-a-khā-ī" are the applications of the *anuloma-cakra*. When one desires to provide protection for a country, city, village, or the like against *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, kings, thieves, and so forth, one should construct a temple (*prāsāda*) dedicated to a deity there; having fashioned a seat (*sattva*) in its central part, that location [should be prepared] with stone powder and other materials.

Having surrounded it and made it inviolable, one should place within it the *Kālacakra* known as the "Inner Casket" (*abhyantara-sampuṭa*), which is composed of any one of the aforementioned materials— gold, silver, copper, or a *śālagrāma* stone— and having performed the consecration of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and worship, [one should install] that wheel. Beyond that wheel...

Having covered it with stone or other materials according to one's experience, and having placed upon the upper part of the hub (karṇikā) of the wheel situated within, an image of the deity of that wheel made of either stone, copper, silver, or gold, one should perform the rite of consecrating the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) therein.

For the practitioner who worships that [deity] every day at each junction of the day, protection of the country and so forth will certainly occur. Alternatively, for one who desires the protection of a village, city, or similar place, there are nine locations: the eight directions and the center.
Having fashioned nine new boxes from stone and the like, having lined their interiors and exteriors with stone powder and other materials,
and having placed within them a wheel called the "inner casket" (abhyantara-sampuṭa) upon which one of the aforementioned forms has been engraved in gold or another precious metal;

Having first performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath), the worship of the principal *Nityā* therein with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) is prescribed according to the method already stated. Then, [worship] is performed individually with each of the thirty-six Vidyās belonging to the *Kālacakra-Nityās*, who reside upon the pericarp of the wheel currently being consecrated.

Having worshipped with [mantras] repeated sixteen times, and having spent three days in this very manner of worship and so forth; then, having covered those pits with stones in such a way that no impact occurs upon the central wheel, and having placed nine stone pedestals upon them, [one should perform worship] at the three junctions of the day on those pedestals.

For the practitioner who worships the principal Nityā with the sixteen types of offerings, protection of the country and so forth will certainly occur. Thus concludes the application of the *Kālacakra* in the sequence of the *sampuṭa* for the purpose of protecting countries, villages, and the like. [This is performed] in sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) whose shapes correspond to the nine wheels beginning with the thirty-six-cornered one, as obtained according to the sequence of their respective years.
Having offered oblations by the hundreds or thousands with the previously mentioned substances according to each specific desire,

one should accomplish all tasks by means of the thirty-six Vidyās inscribed upon those respective wheels. Likewise, by means of those same Vidyās, one may also achieve success through libations (tarpaṇa) using camphor-water, performed in numbers of either a hundred or a thousand.

The accomplishment of all desired aims [is attained]. Likewise, from the worship of each respective *cakra* with its corresponding *vidyās*, there is the accomplishment of all desired aims. Thus, having placed the *kalaśa* within each respective *cakra*.

In that regard, by means of those respective vidyās, one should worship the thirty-six eternal [deities] who are the very forms of those vidyās; having consecrated them as before with water empowered by each of those vidyās repeated sixteen times each,
all desired accomplishments are attained through that sprinkling, at the conclusion of each respective ritual application in every case.

The summary is as follows: one should follow one's capacity regarding the offerings—whether all of them or some individually, such as land, ornaments, cattle, gold, clothing, servants, and so forth, or even one or two of these combined. Thus concludes the ritual applications for oblations and other rites performed with the Vidyā inscribed upon the respective wheels, which grant all desired fruits. Now, [the next section begins].

The applications of the Yantra of Śrīsundarī and others, which have attained a state unique to all eternal [deities]: having laid down five lines each extending east-west and five lines extending north-south, forming a wheel of sixteen squares with very large intervening spaces intersecting one another, [one should place] in each square...

Having laid down two threads extending from east to west and two threads extending from south to north, intersecting at the center, nine squares are produced; thus, one hundred and forty-four (144) squares are completed.

Beginning with the nine-square grid starting from the center (putreśāna) and proceeding in sequence until the end of the nine-square grid located in the intermediate directions (nairṛtya), one should fill it with the mantra syllables that will be described hereafter. Regarding the filling of each individual corner of the nine-square grid: [the order is] east, southeast, south, southwest, west, northwest, north, and northeast.

The middle sequence (*madhyakrama*). This is to be understood everywhere in the diagram under discussion. Furthermore, within each of these squares, there are two circles with an intervening space between them; the outer circle touches the line of the square. (p.

Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus by joining those [lines], one should draw a single circle outside of that; then two further circles, each separated by an interval of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), with their lines touching the tips of the petals. Having thus prepared the two circles with their lines, one should write the syllables of the mantra within them. Those syllables are as follows:

In the first *kūṭa*, which consists of the six consonants forming the essence of the laughter (*hasa*) and the *kalā-harī* of Śrī Tripurasundarī, all the letters of the *pūrṇamaṇḍala* are to be joined one by one in sequence before the letter *ha*, which is synonymous with Vārāhī. In this manner, [the mantra] acquires five hundred and seventy-six names.

At the end of the first *kūṭa*, by joining each of the sixteen vowels in place of the fourth vowel (*caturthasvara*) which has the form of a long *ā*, nine thousand two hundred and sixteen variations of the mantra consisting of the first *kūṭa* are produced; some of these variations are written below for the sake of clarity: *ahasakalaharaṃ* (1).

1. *ahasakalaharaṃ* 2. *ahasakalaharāṃ* 3. *ahasakalahariṃ* 4. *ahasakalaharoṃ* 5. *ahasakalaharuṃ* 6. *ahasakalaharūṃ* 7. *ahasakalaharṛṃ* 8. *ahasakalaharṝṃ* 9. *ahasakalaharḷṃ* 10. *ahasakalaharḹṃ* 11. *ahasakalahareṃ* 12. *ahasakalaharaiṃ* 13. *ahasakalaharoṃ* 14. *ahasakalaharauṃ*
*ahasa-kala-haraṃ* (15) and *ahasa-kala-haraḥ* (16)—thus, sixteen variations have been shown by making the letter *a* the first.

In this same manner, by making each of the fifteen vowels beginning with *ā* the first, there are likewise sixteen variations for each; thus, in total, there are two hundred and fifty-six variations for the *a*-group (*avarga*). Likewise, [there are variations] starting with *ka, kā, ki, kī*, and so forth.

The *ka*-group consists of sixteen phonemes beginning with *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, and so forth; likewise, the *kha*-group consists of sixteen phonemes beginning with *kha*, *khā*, *khi*, *khī*, and so forth.
In this manner, all the phonemes ending in *kṣa* as well as those beginning with *a* are each composed of sixteen phonemes, totaling thirty-six.

At the end of each of those, by joining with the sixteen vowels, there result 9,216 distinct variations. The locations for writing these in the aforementioned yantra are now shown: first, having written the *kūṭa* in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), containing within it the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object of practice (*sādhya*), and so forth; thereafter—

Having written the twenty-four *kūṭa*-syllables, beginning with the first and second and ending with the twenty-fourth, four by four in sequence within the six triangles; and having subsequently written the forty syllables, beginning with the twenty-fifth and ending with the sixty-fourth, five by five in sequence upon the eight yantras.

Having placed the fifty-one Mātṛkās, beginning with the letter *kṣa* joined with the Visarga and ending with the letter *ka*, upon the first path of the outer circuit; and having written the Mātṛkā in reverse order, beginning with *a* with its Bindu and ending with *kṣa*, upon the second path, [one should place them] within the interior of the hexagon.
Having written the group of six syllables corresponding to each of the six permutations of the eternal [syllable],

one completes the yantra by writing it within the nine compartments of the circle located in the northeast direction, specifically in the compartment situated at the end of the nine directions. Then, for the four syllables *a, ā, i, ī*,
which consist of sixteen vowels each joined with the final portion [of the consonants], there are sixty-four [combinations].

Then, having applied the *vidyā*, one should write the sixty-fifth *phūṭa*— which has the form "u ha sa ka la ha ra m"— within the pericarp of the outer wheel (*bahirgata-cakrīya-vṛtta*), with the names of the practitioner, the object of practice, and so forth inserted within it.
Immediately after that, in this same manner...

Starting from the sixty-fifth peak as before, one should perform the writing of the fourfold divisions and the filling of the space between the lines and the paths; thus, sixteen forms each of the letters of the full mandala—namely *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, and *ṝ*—are assigned. In this manner, [they are placed] in the central pericarp situated within the southern square.

Having written the sixty-four variations beginning with the *vidyākūṭa* consisting of one hundred and twenty-nine syllables— namely "la-ha-sa-ka-laṃ ha-ra-m"— starting from [the letter] *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *e*, *ai*, and so forth;

Sixteen forms of sixteen types have been assigned; then, having written the Vidyā-kūṭa consisting of one hundred and ninety-two syllables— namely *oha sa ka la ha ra mi*— in the central pericarp located within the chamber of Nirṛti, and having again internalized that very same [mantra] and written sixty-four other successive kūṭas, [one writes] *o au aṃ a*.

Sixteen forms have been assigned to each of the four castes (*catuvarṇa*). In the western compartment, upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*), the fifty-seventh and two-hundredth *kūṭa*, namely *ka ha sa ka la ha ra m*, is written; beginning from that very *kūṭa*, the sixty-four *vidyā-kūṭas* are written, [representing] the forms *ka ka ā ki*.

At the end of each of the four classes of consonants (*caturvarṇa*), the writing of sixteen forms each— produced through their connection with the sixteen vowels— is accomplished. Having written in the wind-square (*vāyukoṣṭha*) the form *akuhasakalaharam*, which is the thirty-first [letter] after three hundred, in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the syllable-cluster (*rūpakūṭa*), that very same [form] is written in rotation.

Beginning from the first peak (kūṭa) and having written the sixty-four peaks, the sixteen forms each of the four syllables ku, kū, kṛ, and kṝ have been written. Having written the fifty-eighth peak of the Vidyā— namely *kḷ hasakalahara*— in the pericarp of the northern square, that very same [syllable] is written again in the surrounding circle.

Having written the sixty-four *kūṭas* of the *Kūṭamāra*, and having written the sixteen forms each for the four syllables *kḷ kḹ ke kai*, one should place the forty-ninth [syllable] plus four hundred— that is, the forty-ninth *kūṭa*— in the pericarp of the northeast square (*īśānakoṣṭha*) as *kohasakalaharam*.
Having written those [syllables] from that point onward, and having inscribed the subsequent sixty-four *kūṭas* as follows:
*ko kau kaṃ kaḥ*, sixteen forms of each of the four letters are thus written; and in the pericarp of the central square, [the syllables] *kha ha sa ka la ha ra m* are likewise [inscribed].
Having written the first syllable of the present vidyā, composed of seven consonants— the 1,305th [counting from the beginning]— and then returning once more to that same starting point.
Having drawn sixty-four *kūṭas*, sixteen forms of each of the four classes of vowels— namely the *sva*, *svā*, *akhilīru*, and *sāṇa*—
are written; thus, in the wheel of ninety-one squares located in the northeast, one hundred and seventy-six variations of the first *kūṭa* are written.
In this manner, the sixteen variations for each of the two groups of sixteen syllables, as well as the four syllables constituting the third group,
are written out. Following this same direction, [the method applies] to the second through fifteenth wheels consisting of nine squares, obtained in a clockwise sequence.

The completion must be followed accordingly; thus, when this is so, the total number of divisions of the first *kūṭa* of the *vidyā*, amounting to nine thousand two hundred and sixteen (9,216), is fully accounted for. Within these very [divisions], there are one hundred and forty-four (*144*) yantras.
Having omitted the peak-syllable located at the very first pericarp and written the second peak-syllable in its place,

one should then inscribe the first, second, and subsequent peak-syllables as before; thus, there are as many yantras of the Vidyā consisting of various peak-syllables as are measured by the number two, one, two, four, and nine.
They are thus accomplished. Having written each successive peak— from the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and so on,
up to the end of the peaks numbering nine thousand two hundred and sixteen—
omitting each preceding peak in its place by writing it upon the pericarp (karṇikā), [one proceeds].
Having written the sixty-four *kūṭas*— each consisting of the respective [consonant] together with its own medial vowel and the following vowel— in the manner previously described,
[one obtains] the form consisting of one hundred and forty-four.

The number of yantras is determined by multiplying the number of *kūṭas* (syllabic units) by that same factor; thus, from the result, the number of yantras produced is equal to the sum of the numerical value of the *kūṭas* multiplied by the number of yantras, which amounts to 1,327,104 (represented as 4-0-7-1-3). This applies to Sarvamaṅgalā as well as to other [mantras].

The first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of the sciences (*vidyā*), according to the method previously described, [is placed] at the beginning and end of the sixteen vowels which are the colors of the full mandala.

There are as many such mechanical devices (yantras) as there are yojanas, and each of all the eternal [deities] possesses one. Here, two types are intended: those involving the application of *catis* and those involving the application of *nakṣatras*.
Among these, in the application of *nakṣatras*, in every case, the name of that respective *nakṣatra* ending in the seventh case is used.

In the nine-square grid belonging to the great square of Īśāna— beginning from the square located in the first cell of that grid and ending with the central square— one should write the forms beginning with *Aśvinī*, *Bharaṇī*, *Kṛttikā*, and so on, up to *Aśleṣā*.

Having written those respective seed-syllables (*kūṭa*) within their appropriate sections, one should also write the names of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the ritual action (*karman*).
In the nine [squares] of the great treasury located in the east, as before, starting from Mṛgaśirā and so forth;
likewise in the nine squares of the great treasury situated in the south, starting from Āśleṣā and so forth;
thus for all the constellations in five cycles, but in the final nine [squares], starting from Aśvinī and so forth.
In the application of lunar days, one should write the "Navakarma" [yantra] alone;
in all cases and on all lunar days, within the nine scattered yantras located in the northeast (Īśāna) direction, one should write: "O, subdue Devadatta, subdue Jñadatta! (vaśam kuru kuru).

Immediately thereafter, within the fifteen yantras consisting of all nine squares located in the sixteen compartments, one should sequentially write for Devadatta on the first lunar day [the command] "subjugate Yajñadatta," and so forth, up to the fifteenth day, writing "subjugate Yakṣadatta" for Devadatta; this should be done under each respective constellation.
The names of those respective constellations (*nakṣatra*) and lunar days (*tithi*), ending in the seventh case, should be written;

for when one desires the fruits that will be attained through the worship, consecration, wearing, and so forth of a particular yantra on those specific constellations and lunar days, the previously written yantra should be placed in the eastern square for the sake of obtaining knowledge.
The second is for the pacification of all obstacles; the third for the attainment of prosperity (*lakṣmī*); the fourth for the accomplishment of health;
the fifth for the alleviation of the affliction of disease; the sixth for the attainment of victory; the seventh for the cessation of all calamities;
and the eighth for one's own increase in progeny, fame, and so forth.
One should proceed by means of any one of the four methods consisting of the mantra, worship, dhāraṇī, consecration, or burial for the sake of obtaining a son.

Likewise, for the protection of the nine categories of things beginning with ignorance (ajñāna) and ending with sons, the nine treasures and nine machines should be pursued through worship and other rites; similarly, for the increase of goats, the increase of horses,
the increase of cattle, the increase of sheep, the increase of camels, the increase of goats, and the increase of buffaloes.

Following the sequence of the nine-square wheel starting from the first and ending with the seventh, when there is a desire to inflict disease and affliction upon all or some of the seven types of animals— beginning with elephants— belonging to an enemy, one should employ the eighth yantra, whether it arises through another method or is produced by following the eighth mantra.

For the purpose of pacifying any of the seven diseases beginning with *gaja*, one should follow the ninth diagram (*yantra*). By this same method, it is established that for all the diagrams consisting of nine squares written in the second through the fifteenth and sixteenth [sections], there is an option regarding the placement of the Guru and others in their respective stated functions; this applies to everything mentioned in this section.

The summary is that [this occurs] through the connection of the yantras with their respective fruits. Thus end the applications of the various yantras in the nine-square grid for attaining knowledge and so forth. Twenty-four lines, extending east-west and north-south, intersecting one another at equal intervals, [are drawn].
Having drawn twenty-four lines and thus produced five hundred and twenty-nine (529) squares,
one should exclude the twelfth square located at the center of the first outermost row in each of the four directions; furthermore,
in all four corners, [one should exclude] twenty-one squares each situated between the squares of those respective directions.
Having wiped clean the squares, one should omit three squares in each direction within the second path inside that [boundary]: namely, the single square directly below the previously omitted square,
together with the two squares situated on either side of it.
Having erased seventeen squares each within the intermediate spaces at every corner, [one should erase] the three squares below the previously discarded squares in the third row situated therein. (p.
Having set aside five squares in total— two squares situated on each side—
and having erased thirteen squares in each corner located between them,
[one proceeds] in the fourth row within that area.

Without omitting the seven squares consisting of the five squares below the five squares abandoned in the eastern row, plus the two squares situated on either side of that [row]— and having erased the nine-by-nine square grids located in the intervening spaces between them in each corner— [one proceeds] within the fifth row situated therein.

Having abandoned nine squares in each direction— consisting of the seven previously abandoned squares plus two squares situated on either side— and having erased the five squares located within the intermediate corners, one should likewise [abandon] the nine previously abandoned squares in the sixth row within that area.

The two compartments situated on either side of that [central one] make eleven compartments in total; having set aside one compartment from each of the four directions, one should erase the single compartment located between them in each corner,
as well as the four-compartment group situated in each of the two initial rows extending toward all directions.

Having made it a single square, one should draw an upward-pointing triangle therein. This being done, two hundred and forty-nine (249) squares remain; by clearing sixty-six squares for each corner, this is for the purpose of the triangles in the first two rows in the four directions.
By erasing sixteen squares, two hundred and eighty squares are collectively erased.

The method for writing the letters of the Vidyā within these squares is as follows: beginning from the middle square among the five squares situated below the triangle, located in the western row at the very bottom, one writes the final letter of the Vidyā of Citrā.
Having written the letters from the beginning up to the first letter of the end of *Ādisundarī*,
and having filled two hundred and twenty-five squares, [one should place] the third section of *Lalitā* in the remaining twenty-four squares.
Having written the twenty-four varieties of the *vidyā*, beginning from the final variety and ending with the first variety;
and having formed three rows within the interior of the letter *ī* of the cloth (*paṭaka*) across all twenty-four varieties.

Having written the name of the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*)— such as "Devadatta"— in the upper [triangle], the name of the accomplisher (*sādhaka*)— such as "mine" (*mama*), the storehouse of love— and so forth in the lower [triangle], and the name of the action (*karman*)— such as "make him submissive" (*vaśaṃ kuru*)— between the two, one should likewise write [the names] endowed with the words for the object, the accomplisher, the action, and the verb within all four triangles.

One should write the third section of the Lalitā [mantra]. In this manner, the writing of the target (sādhya), the practitioner (sādhaka), and so forth concludes with twenty-two [syllables] in this yantra. Here, the sixteen Nityā-mantras beginning with Lalitā and Citrā are to be written as follows: *hrīṃ tripurasundarīnityāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi* (16).

Hrīṃ! I worship the sandals of the eternal goddess Kāmeśvarī. 14. Hrīṃ! I worship the sandals of the eternal goddess Bhagamālinī. 15. Hrīṃ! I worship the sandals of the eternal goddess Nityaklinnā. 14. Hrīṃ! I worship the sandals of the eternal goddess Bheruṇḍā. 13. Hrīṃ! I worship the sandals of the eternal goddess Vahnivāsinī.

I worship. 15. Hrīṃ! I worship the *pāduka* of Mahāvajreśvarī Nityā. 16. Hrīṃ! I worship the *pāduka* of Dūtī Nityā. 12. Hrīṃ! I worship the *pāduka* of Tvaritā Nityā. 13. Hrīṃ! I worship the *pāduka* of Kulasundarī Nityā. 15. Hrīṃ! I worship the *pāduka* of Nityānityā. 12.
Hrīṃ! I worship the Nityā of the Blue Banner, who is self-manifested. 15. Hrīṃ! I worship the Nityā of Discipline, who is self-manifested.

13. Hrīṃ! I worship the Nityā of All-Auspiciousness, who is self-manifested. 15. Hrīṃ! I worship the Nityā of the Garland of Flames, who is self-manifested. 15. Hrīṃ! I worship the Nityā of the Variegated, who is self-manifested. 13. [This is] the sequence for these Vidyās.
Earth 16, Indra 14, Viśvaka 13, Arrow-Moon 15, King 16, Sun 12, Viśvaka 13, Arrow-Moon 15, Sun 12, Arrow-Moon 15.

The Viśva (13), Vāṇa (5), Vidhu (1), and Sāyaka (5) [make] 15; the Indu (1) [makes] 16. When combined with the Viśva (13), the Samiti (3), the Mita (5), and the Savarṇa (4), [the total is] 35. Combined with the Vāṇa (5), this is the collection of syllables (varṇasaṃgraha). Thus prepared, the Vajrayantra is [drawn] upon stone, copper plate, silver plate, or gold plate—each subsequent one being more excellent—with upward lines.

Having engraved it exactly as described, preceded by the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force), and having placed it at some secluded spot, for one who worships Śrī Lalitā together with the fifteen Nityās in this very yantra using the mantras written in their respective locations, there is the attainment of all desired objects; however, when that which is desired is the specific goal [at hand], then—

That very desired mantra and yantra should be drawn twenty times according to the prescribed method. In whatever region this yantra is installed, there shall be no misfortune for a distance of one yojana. Thus ends the application of the Vajra-yantra.

Having fashioned a circle on level ground with a wide interior space suitable for drawing the desired colors and other features to be described later— this being the extent of that circle— or alternatively, having inscribed the present *vidyā* (mantra) within all twelve spokes and corners of the wheel,
containing the name of the practitioner and others; the fruit [of this] is the installation of the yantra accomplished through such means.
It occurs as follows: having placed a flask upon the previously mentioned Vajrayantra or the twelve-spoked yantra,

and having filled it with the syllables and medicinal herbs of the present vidyā, one should empower it there— after first worshipping the limbs and the goddess Gaṅgā along with her retinue— by reciting the present vidyā itself one thousand times or more.
From the consecration with that water, there is the pacification of all calamities arising from the basis of past lives, the increase of previous prosperity, the alleviation of planetary afflictions,
and the quelling of diseases and other misfortunes. The measurement [of the vessel] is divided twenty-fourfold, starting from half the measure of the rear portion of the verse.
Having fixed a compass at the seventh division from the end of the region and drawn a second circle around it, and then,

counting from that same point, having fixed the tip of the compass at the thirteenth division from the western line of the circle at the sixth division, one should complete a third circle; [this is] of the outermost circle.
Having marked the four sectors situated between the eastern and other directions with signs, (p. 86b) [one should proceed].
Having made eight marks by including two internal marks within those [eight] external marks— thus combining them with the four directional marks—
one should drop one line each from each mark up to the fifth mark respectively;
having thus laid down twelve lines, [one reaches] the third circle-line falling upon the center of the twelve joints.
A circle drawn on the outside, with two twelve-angled triangles joined at their base and apex, constitutes the perfected twelve-spoked wheel (*dvādaśāracakra*).

Within that, inside the pericarp of the circle, the wheel should be rotated. Inside that, in the instrument consisting of the lines of the *siddharekhā*, one should not inscribe the letters; rather, the method for this is as follows: within the central point (*bindu*), one should [place] the *Lalitā-vidyā*.
Having written the previously mentioned form of the sixteen-syllable mantra,

one should arrange three rows connected to the fourth vowel associated with the *māyā-bīja* located in the portion preceding it; then, having written the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in the third row, the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the first row, and the words for the action and the ritual act (*karmapada-kriyāpada*) in the second row.
Having written the vidyās of Kāmeśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Nityaklinnā in the corners of the east,

north-east, and south-east respectively, one should then write the vidyās of the twelve Nityās beginning with Bheruṇḍā and ending with Vicitrā in the twelve outer corners starting from the front and proceeding clockwise.

Having drawn this yantra— which is joined to the outer boundary lines and consists of all the letters of the Mātṛkā— on any one of gold, silver, copper, or stone, and having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force) before placing it in some secluded place such as a house, one who worships it attains all desired objects.

Within a radius of one *yojana*, no inauspiciousness shall ever arise. Thus end the applications of the twelve-spoked wheel (*dvādaśāracakra*). For one who recites daily these mantras numbering nine thousand two hundred and sixteen (*rasacandrabhujāṅka*), there occurs the cutting off of poverty, the destruction of sin, the eradication of suffering and the beginningless succession of evil latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and the attainment of contentment.
One should always know that when the recitation of the vidyā is impossible, there are individual means for each of the 175 syllables of the full maṇḍala.
By giving the first portion of the first *kūṭa* of Tripurasundarī to the recipient of that same number of portions,
and having assigned the sixteen vowels one by one to the positions of the fourth vowel (*svarasthāna*) in the subsequent portion, [the result] becomes one hundred and sixteen.

Among the nine thousand well-known mantras consisting of three syllables each, one should recite sixty-seven hundred and fifty mantras—one for each vowel—on a single day; thus, in sixteen days, the mastery and completion of all the mantras must be accomplished. First, each individual letter of the full mandala is [to be mastered] first.
In this manner, the collection of the *vidyā* and the ointment (*añjana*) constitutes the second syllable; therein, the vowel joined with the internal portion (*antarbhāga*) is the third syllable.

According to this method, there is the *Vidyaiṣajyakṣarī*. By counting this collection of syllables as a single syllable, the *Tripurasundarī-vidyā* possesses the nature of being three-syllabled (*tryakṣarī*). Thus...
Even worship with fragrant flowers and those specific vidyās destroys poverty and other such misfortunes; likewise,

the destruction of poverty and so forth results from the libation (tarpaṇa) performed with the waters of rivers such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, mixed with fragrant substances like camphor, while reciting the aforementioned vidyās.
Through oblations of sesame seeds that are averse to fragrant scents, white rice, and the aforementioned vidyās, poverty and other afflictions are destroyed.

Having prepared a water-pot within the previously described yantras composed of those respective vidyās, one should fill it with the decoction-water of the medicinal herbs corresponding to the syllables of those vidyās.
First, let it be filled with the waters from that jar, consecrated by the vidyās;

through that consecration, there shall be liberation from the sufferings caused by malevolent magic, kṛtyās, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, apasmāras, rākṣasas, yakṣas, guhyakas, ḍākinīs, and so forth. It is said that one should stand up to the neck-deep in the water of rivers flowing to the ocean, such as the Gaṅgā, and [perform this].
Through the recitation of the Vidyā, the destruction of all sins accumulated in previous births occurs.

Through oblations of ghee with these Vidyās, through bathing in the waters of rivers flowing to the ocean, and through libations (tarpaṇa) with these Vidyās, there shall be the destruction of all sins accumulated in previous births. Thus ends the application of the modified Vidyā. Now, [the original Vidyā]:
The applications of all these vidyās are now described, insofar as the powers residing within the nine cakras inside the Śrīcakra are of the very nature of Śrī Lalitā.

In that regard, first is the *uṣpra-stha-vidyā*: initially, there are five hundred and seventy-six (576) syllables, each having the color of a full mandala; furthermore, the second set of syllables consists of thirty-six *tattva*-syllables, which are joined together by forming a junction (*saṃdhi*) with the initial portion.
The letters of the full mandala are indeed the third letters as well; individually,
at the end of the first and second letters whose natures have been described, they possess the visarga and are thus the letters of the full mandala here, belonging to the middle letter.

The middle syllables— having reached a count of twenty thousand seven hundred thirty-six (20,736) through the sequential union of the thirty-six principles beginning with *ākāra*, which themselves have attained a count of sixty-seven (67) by virtue of being the colors of the full mandala of each of the sixty-four sciences (*vidyās*)—
are situated at the end of each of those [syllables].

When combined with the syllables of the full mandala including the visarga, along with the third syllable of the *rus* [group], they total 11,943,936; for each of these, when divided by the initial portion, there is 6,879,707,136,
which is the sum of the syllables of the full mandala combined with six, fire (3), earth (1), mountains (7), zero (0), mountains (7), nine (9), mountains (7), oceans (4), and seasons (6).

Those three mantras, consisting of three syllables each, have been established; and their state of having three syllables is stated with the intention that there is an identity between the two middle syllables— the reality-syllable (*tattvākṣara*) and the syllable of the full maṇḍala—
whereas in fact, they actually consist of four syllables.
In that regard, since the unity of the various sciences (*vidyā*) arranged in a single sequence must be accepted,

the sixty-seven and so forth variations numbering five hundred, which are produced through the conjunction of the syllables of the *akāra* form with reality (*tatva*), are to be excluded from the exterior. Likewise, for the six syllables consisting of *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*, [the variations] connected with the third and fourth vowels [are to be excluded] along with the letter *ha*.

By means of the two *lakāra*s, since each of the six syllables has already been partially traversed, even their thirty-six forms each are not to be repeated; thus, when combined, [this concerns] the middle syllables. (p.

It has been declared that there are one hundred and forty variations to be excluded; furthermore, because the letter *kṣa* is a conjunct, it does not possess its own sixteen variations like the *cakrādi* [group], and thus those [sixteen] must be included within the former. Consequently, [the total is] as follows.
Seven hundred and thirty-six varieties have emerged in connection with the middle vowels. Thus,
twenty thousand (20,000) varieties remain as the remainder,
even within the third types of syllables consisting of the full mandala of vowels together with the visarga, such as *aṃ*, *kaṃ*, *khaṃ*, *gaṃ*, and so forth.
Since the addition of the *visarga* is impossible for the thirty-six letters that already possess the nasal dot (*bindu*), thirty-six variations emerge.
Because the addition of the *visarga* is impossible among the thirty-six letters— such as *aḥ*, *kaḥ*, *khaḥ*, and so forth— even for those six syllables, these thirty-six variations arise.

Of the four [groups], the third and fourth are redundant due to the addition of the *visarga* to the vowels and the *talas*; thus, those four syllables are to be excluded. Consequently, seventy-six *vādās* are excluded in total, and the third set of phonemes (varṇas) is established as exactly five hundred. And so it is.
When each of the five hundred third-syllables is joined with twenty thousand middle-syllables,

there arise one hundred million (10,000,000) distinct combinations; and when each of these is further joined individually with the colors of the full mandala at the preceding stage, they amount to five hundred and seventy-six million.

Having accepted the state of being a single syllable, one should worship [the deity] with the three-syllabled [mantra], or with any other vidyā repeated twice, while applying the six-limbed mantras to one's own thumbs and other fingers as follows: "Oṃ, salutation to the Heart; Ka, svāhā to the Head; Aḥ, vaṣaṭ to the Tuft; Ka, huṃ to the Armor; Ka, vauṣaṭ to the Three Eyes; Aḥ, phaṭ to the Weapon."

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart and other centers, and having likewise placed the syllables upon the previously described yantra consisting of a square, an eight-petaled lotus, and nine triangles, one should perform day and night the meditation, invocation, worship, offering of oblations (*bali*), daily fire-sacrifice (*homa*), and so forth, as prescribed for the worship of Kālanityā.

Through the recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), and other rites pertaining to this vidyā, all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) are accomplished for the practitioner. Thus ends the application of the vidyā of the Ut- Yoginī situated within the Śrīcakra. Now follows the application of the subtle fire-oblation (*sūkṣma-homa*).
In the triangle of the *mūlādhāra*,
there is fire with rays extending upwards; it is present in the heart-lotus, both above and below.
The sun with its rays streaming forth is situated upon the crown of the head; below that, in the lower part of the *brahmarandhra*, is the moon with its rays streaming forth.

Having contemplated the unification of these three luminaries, one should offer oblations into the kindled fire mentally with the mantras to be mentioned hereafter. This is called the "Prāṇāgnihotra" by the Vedas. Those mantras are as follows:

99a) *Satā oṃ* 16. Thus are the ninety-six mantras, arranged in sixteen groups of sixteen, composed of lunar syllables situated within the enclosure of the sun and fire.
Those composed of the letters of fire situated within the cavities of sun and moon; those composed of the letters of fire situated within the cavities of moon and sun;
and those composed of the letters of fire situated within the cavities of sun and moon.

They are formed by the letters of the Sun situated within the enclosure of the Moon and Fire, and they are also formed by the letters of the Sun situated within the enclosure of Fire and the Moon. Among them, the sixteen letters from *ka* to *ta* are solar; the sixteen letters from *tha* to *sa* are lunar; and the vowels are those of Fire.

Regarding the statement "the sixteen colors of the moon": by means of these very mantras, beginning with *oṃ* and following the sequence ending in *khāṣoṃ kasoṃ*, the fire-oblation (*homa*) should also be performed in reverse order. Thus, taken together, this oblation results in a total count of one hundred and ninety-two.

When the oblation into the substratum of the nature of light—preceded by the utterance of these syllables and characterized by the mutual increase of their connection—is performed, and the oblation of the entire universe denoted by those syllables has been accomplished, the Hotṛ priest attains the threefold light that is the very essence of Śrī Śiva; what more, then, could be desired beyond this? Thus.

The Procedure for the Prāṇāgnihotra Homa. Now, the Nityākavaca—which brings about the unimpeded accomplishment of all one’s own ritual applications, fulfills every desired object, and is to be recited and meditated upon during the morning and evening—is herein written. It is for the sake of liberation from all calamities and for the attainment of all prosperity.
For the pacification of afflictions caused by spirits, ghosts, and demons, for the attainment of happiness, for the destruction of all diseases, and for victory in battle;
in terrifying situations involving thieves, lions, tigers, elephants, gavayas, and the like; in the forest, when traveling over mountains, on the road, or likewise during a famine.
In the midst of distress caused by water, fire, or wind, or when there is a confusion such as that involving a boat, one who has recited the *Nityākavaca* even once overcomes all other dangers.

He becomes happy, free from conflict, without rivals, and with his senses conquered. Listen, O Goddess, for I shall speak that armor which is composed of you; by means of which even I was always victorious in battles against the gods and everywhere.

May Sarvadātmānalalitā protect me always. May Āgneyī protect the eastern direction, and Kāmeśī immediately thereafter. May Bhagamālā protect the southern direction, and may she always protect my right side. Then, may Nityaklinnā protect the northern direction, and Īśānī protect as far as the northeast; may Rathabherurāḍā protect that direction always.
May Vāyavī likewise protect my western direction, and may Sāvahnivāsinī protect me from the north.
May Mahāvajreśvarī protect my intermediate direction; may the messenger Dūtī always protect my left side with haste. And may Kulasundarī protect this northern direction for my welfare.

May Nityā protect me always from above; may she who is called Nityā-yavākā protect me from below at all times. May Jayā protect me on all sides. May Sarvamaṅgalā always grant me auspiciousness. [Salutations] to her whose form is joined with the word "Jvālāmālinī," which sets ablaze the body, senses, mind, and vital breaths.

Such is the analysis of the compound. May he who constantly protects from oppressions always protect my variegated mind—from Kālī, from anger, as well as from greed, delusion, pride, and intoxication;
from sin, envy, sorrow, and doubt, from everything, and always from you, O Aśvabha, through praise and through diligent effort.
May the Givers protect me at all times from false actions, cruel thoughts, violence, and likewise from theft;
may they, mounted upon elephants, protect me constantly with their own powers during auspicious and inauspicious moments, and likewise may those mounted upon horses protect me always on every side.
May those mounted on lions protect me, even as they traverse the intermediate space; may those mounted on chariots protect me from all sides at all times in battle;
and likewise, may those mounted on Garuḍas protect me, even as they move through the sky.
May those who dwell in the elements and those who go everywhere protect me always and in all places.
May they drive away the seizing spirits (*graha*s) such as *bhūta*, *preta*, *piśāca*, *apasmāra*, and *kṛtyā*.
Adorned with their own powers and weapons, may they—mounted upon elephants, horses, lions, and Garuḍas, and bearing every kind of armament—protect me.
"May the innumerable goddesses of power protect me always from all sides.

One should recite this *nityā-kavaca*, which provides protection from everything, every evening and morning. "Never shall he who is equal to me behold or hear anything inauspicious. Although the final verse of the preceding five verses does not possess the formal characteristics of a *kavaca*, [it is nonetheless included].

Some maintain that the purpose of reciting [the *Kavaca*] is the very statement of its fruit; however, many hold that since the portion explaining the fruit and so forth is not established as having various recitations (*nānāvṛtti*), it is not necessary to recite it. In various recensions...
The recitation of the *Kavaca* (Armor) together with the introductory and concluding sections, as well as the portions beginning with the "Fruit of Illumination" (*udghoṭaphala*),
is prescribed for the middle recitations; however, some maintain that only the *Kavaca* itself should be recited during those middle recitations and not the other portions—
this being their authoritative view regarding the recitation intended for specific purposes such as honoring teachers, kings, and others.
The phrase beginning with "bhāgam" (the portion) should be understood as referring to my [name], such-and-such sacrificer.

Furthermore, this recitation should be preceded by the mention of place, time, lineage (*gotra*), zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), name, desired object (*kāmanā*), and so forth; for even here in this *tantra*, it is indicated that the performance must be accompanied by a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). And at the end, there is the offering of the remainder (*nivedana*).

One should perform either the meditation on the *japya* (the mantra to be recited) or the meditation on the specific deity to be propitiated by it. The recitation should be neither silent nor loud, but rather in the form of a low-voiced muttering (*upāṃśujapa*).
Furthermore, it should not be preceded by idle chatter, nor should it be performed without first rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) and other preliminary rites.

The recitation of the *kavaca* must be performed after the obligatory twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) at both junctions of the day, and not before; such is the application of the *kavaca*. Now follows the application of the *mṛtyuñjaya-vidyā*.
*Ghaṃhaḥ jjauṃ* is the first division; *vlaṃjyaiṃśaḥ* is the second division; *śaḥ jjhauṃvaṃ* is the third; *śa dvaṃjyaiṃ* is the fourth; *jjhauṃvvaṃ śa* is the fifth; *ktauṃ śaṃvvaṃ*.
Thus, there are various divisions; one may worship any one of these divisions, but there is no restrictive rule that one must worship all the divisions.
Even if one worships all the divisions, there is no loss of the scriptural purpose. Elsewhere it is said: "This is your [instruction].
Following the *mātṛkā-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* and the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, [one performs]: *vvāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *vvīṃ śirase*.

One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the six limb-mantras: "Svāhā vaṃ to the crest-lock," "Vaṣaṭ vāṃ to the head," "Hūṃ raṃ to the armor," "Huṃ laṃ to the eye," "Vauṣaṭ vaḥ to the ear," and "Phaṭ vaḥ to the weapon. This should be done by placing [the mantras] on one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other locations, according to the sixfold division previously described. At the station of the digit of nectar (*amṛtakalā*), one should [place them] individually with the vowels that constitute the lunar digits of nectar.

One should perform the *kūṭanyāsa* conjoined with one's own deity of worship. Regarding the syllable *ṭha*, as in the case of a male practitioner performing the *nyāsa* on his own limbs during the bright fortnight, this is the sequence: on the right big toe on the first lunar day (*pratipad*), the syllable *ṭvaṃ*;
on the back of the right foot, the syllable *ṭvo*; at the ankle, the syllable *ṭviṃ*; and at the knee, the syllable *ṭvīṃ*.

The syllable *ṭuṃ* on the right side of the secret place; the syllable *ṭūṃ* on the right side of the navel; the syllable *ṭvṛṃ* on the right side of the heart; the syllable *ṭṝṃ* on the right breast; the syllable *ṭvṛṃ* on the Yakṣa-nose; the syllable *ṭveṃ* on the right eye;
the syllable *ṭvaiṃ* on the right shoulder; the syllable *ṭvoṃ* on the right eyebrow.
Having placed the syllable *auṃ* on the right side of the head, and the syllable *ṭvaṃ* and the syllable *ṭvaḥ* on the right big toe,
one should again place [the following] from the right big toe up to the end of the right big toe:
*śaḥ*, *śāḥ*, *śiḥ*, *śuḥ*, *śūḥ*, *śṛḥ*, *śṝḥ*, *śḷḥ*, *śḹḥ*, *śeḥ*.

Having placed the sixteen peak-syllables (*kūṭa*)—namely *śaiḥ*, *śoḥ*, *śauḥ*, *śaṃ*, and *śaḥ*—one should again assign [the syllables] *juṃ*, *jūṃ*, *jiṃ*, *jīṃ*, *juṃ*, *jūṃ*, *jṛṃ*, *jṝṃ*, *jḷṃ*, *jḹṃ*, and *jeṃ* from the big toe of the right foot to the end of the big toe of the right foot. (p.

One should place the sixteen *kūṭas*, namely *joṃ jauṃ jaṃ juḥ*. This is the *anyāsa* (alternate placement) based on the lunar day (*tithi*) beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*). On the second [day], one should perform it starting from the back of the right foot up to the big toe of the right foot. On the third [day],...

On the fourth [tithi], starting from the right ankle; on the fifth, starting from the right knee; on the sixth, starting from the right side of the private parts; on the seventh, starting from the right side of the navel;
and on the eighth, starting from the right side of the heart.
On the ninth day, beginning from the right breast; on the tenth day, beginning from the right side of the throat;
on the eleventh day, beginning from the right nostril; on the twelfth day, beginning from the right eye;
on the thirteenth day, beginning from the right ear; and on the fourteenth day, beginning from the right eyebrow.

Starting from the right cheek; on that fifteenth day, beginning from the upper part of the right [side] and extending as far as each respective preceding part, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *kūṭa* associated with the sixteenth vowel of *Rama* is performed everywhere at the very point of commencement. This applies during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
By those who have offered [the oblation], the syllable *vaṃ* is on the left side of the head;
*sāṃ* on the left cheek; *viṃ* on the left eyebrow; *vīṃ* on the left ear; *vuṃ* on the left eye;
*vūṃ* on the left nostril; *vṛṃ* on the left part of the throat; *vṝṃ* on the left shoulder; and *vḷṃ* on the left side of the heart.
Not on the left side of the navel. One should perform the second placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: *ṭve* on the secret left part;

*vāma* on the left knee; *jānu* on the left ankle; *ṭṭhoṃ* on the back of the left foot; *ṣṭhauṃ* on the big toe of the left foot; and *ṣvaṃ* and *ṣvaḥ* should again be placed on the upper left part. Second.

Having sequentially deposited the fifteen peak-syllables (kūṭas)— *śaḥ*, *śāḥ*, *siḥ*, *śīḥ*, *śuḥ*, *śūḥ*, *śṛḥ*, *śṝḥ*, *śḷḥ*, *śḹḥ*, *śeḥ*, *śaiḥ*, *śoḥ*, *śauḥ*, *śaṃ*, *śaḥ*— starting from the upper left portion down to the big toe of the left foot,
one should again deposit the sixteenth peak-syllable, *śaḥ*, at that very same upper left portion.
One should place [the syllables]. Then again, starting from the upper left portion and proceeding to the upper left portion:
jaṃ juṃ jiṃ jīṃ juṃ jūṃ jṛṃ jṝṃ jḷṃ jḹṃ jeṃ jaiṃ joṃ jauṃ juṃ juḥ. Thus.

One should place sixteen *kūṭas*. Thus, in both fortnights, there results the placement of forty-eight *kūṭas* in total. For women, however, [the placement occurs] on the left big toe, or the back of the left foot, or the left ankle, or the region of the left knee, or the region of the left *yoni*, during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).
On the left side of the navel, the left side of the heart, the left hand, the left part of the neck,
the left nostril, the left eye, the left ear, the left eyebrow, the left cheek, the left side of the head,
and again on the upper part of the big toe of the left foot— the aforementioned syllables are to be recited in reverse order during the second and subsequent [recitations].

Alternatively, the aforementioned syllables should be deposited in sequence upon the sixteen locations reached by the counting order beginning from the back of the left foot and ending at the sole of the left foot; however, in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), one begins on the first lunar day with the head, the right side, and the right cheek.
On the right eyebrow, right ear, right eye, right nostril, right cheek, right breast, right portion of the heart, right portion of the navel, right portion of the womb, right portion of the knee,
the back of the right foot, the big toe of the right foot, and the right upper sides, respectively.

In connection with the three previously mentioned *ākūtas*, forty-eight syllables—formed by the conjunction with the vowels—are to be deposited in groups of sixteen each. However, in the second and subsequent [groups], one should deposit them from the respective second position obtained according to the aforementioned sequence of lunar days (tithis) up to their respective ends; such is the method for this deposition (*nyāsa*).
The practitioner, having attained a body of nectar, should perform meditation as follows:

their bodies moistened by nectars flowing from the crescent moon atop a crown resembling pure crystal, they are adorned with garlands and garments of immortality; [they hold] the night-lotus, the white lotus, the red lotus, and the moon, with rays of nectar.

"Smiling-faced and adorned with pearl ornaments, they stand in the midst of ten verses endowed with sixteen meters; thus they are surrounded by those sixty hundred energy-entities (śaktis) whose nature consists of syllables. (p.

Thus, immediately after meditation, one should worship Kamrteśa together with his Śakti within his perpetual circle of worship (*nityapūjācakra*). Regarding that perpetual circle of worship: having first produced a single circle with a pericarp on a level piece of ground of a desired measurement, one should then produce another circle outside of that, with a space of one *tula* between them. Outside of that...

A circle with an interval of five *aṅgulas* [is drawn]; outside that, another circle with an interval of one *aṅgula*; outside that, again a circle with an interval of five *aṅgulas*. Outside that, an interval of one *aṅgula*; outside that, an interval of five *aṅgulas*; outside that, an interval of one *aṅgula*; outside that—
With an interval of five finger-breadths, then outside that an interval of one finger-breadth,
then outside that an interval of five finger-breadths; then outside that an interval of one finger-breadth,
then outside that an interval of five finger-breadths, then outside that an interval of one finger-breadth, then outside that—
With an interval of five finger-breadths, then outside that an interval of one finger-breadth, then outside that an interval of five finger-breadths,
then outside that an interval of one finger-breadth, then outside that an interval of five finger-breadths,
then outside that an interval of one finger-breadth, and then outside that again an interval of five finger-breadths.

Having constructed twenty paths— consisting of eleven circles each one finger-width apart and twenty circles with five-finger-width intervals between them, totaling twenty-two circles amounting to eleven fingers in width—
one should proceed according to the primary ritual resolve (*pradhāna-saṃkalpa*).
Having worshipped the goddess under discussion with the twelve services (upacāras), beginning with water for the feet, upon the pericarp situated within all [the petals],
one should proceed from the tip of the lotus situated on the outermost edge toward the inner lotus portion located in the intermediate directions starting from the northeast (nairṛti).
One should worship the powers of that enclosure up to the edge of the petals (*ājadalāntam*).
Their names, which consist of the forms of their respective syllables, are incorporated into the specific mantras for each of those worships. And they are as follows:

There are fourteen syllables therein: first, one *kūṭākṣara* (cryptic syllable) which serves as the source for each respective modified letter; then each modified letter; then the three-syllable word "rūpāṇi" (forms); then the six-syllable word "śaktīḥ" (powers); and then the seven-syllable phrase "pādukāṃ pūjayāmi" (I worship the sandals). Having clearly extracted these, they are written here. Tejaṃ.
