"Saṃsaḥrūpiṇī," and so forth (80). Having thus worshipped the eighty-four Śaktis in the five lotuses according to this method, one should again worship, as before, starting from the tip of the eastern petal of the sixth sixteen-petaled lotus.
One should worship these eighty powers with the very mantras previously mentioned. However, regarding the distinctions in these [mantras],
one should follow the sequence ending in the *visarga* by removing the *bindu* from the position of the *bindu* within the seed-syllables (*bīja*) that serve as the respective preceding bases.

And thus, the mantras conclude as follows: "I worship the *pādukā* of the power (*śakti*) whose form is *jaḥ*, *jaḥ*; I worship the *pādukā* of the power whose form is *jāḥ*, *jāḥ*. This constitutes the thirteenth [section], consisting of the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*).

Having prepared the three types of ritual services consisting of the remaining stotra, tarpaṇa, and namaskāra, one should offer the bali with the Kurukullā-vidyā at the conclusion of the worship. At the beginning of the worship as well, the offering of the bali with the sixteen-syllable mantra is performed as before. [The offerings] are smeared with the liquid of *śrīkhaṇḍa* and camphor, and consist of fragrant flowers such as *jāti* and others.

In the worship with flowers and leaves, these should be taken in place of flowers; and milk-porridge (pāyasa) accompanied by milk, plantain fruit, and sugar should be offered in place of the sacrificial oblation (naivedya) during the worship. For the attainment of success in this vidyā, forty lakhs of recitations must be performed in the Kali age.

From the day the recitation begins until the completion of one hundred thousand recitations, one should consume only milk and nothing else. Having completed the recitation, a fire sacrifice (*homa*) should be performed with ten parts of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), milk, sugar-coated plantains, and other offerings, according to a tenth part of the number of recitations. Upon completing the fire sacrifice, a libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be performed with water scented with camphor, equal in number to the count of the fire sacrifice.

In this case as well, the feeding of Brahmins and the pleasing of one's guru are required; thus this vidyā becomes accomplished. Indeed, the sign of the accomplishment of the vidyā here is this: having touched with the palm of the hand the water from the salt ocean and consecrated it one hundred times with the aforementioned vidyā, it becomes sweet like milk.
One should not fall into such a state of non-existence; rather, for the sake of establishing that [reality], the methods to be described hereafter should be followed.
Thus, one whose knowledge is perfected should pursue the ritual applications (*prayoga*), as follows:
by means of the previously mentioned worship-mandalas (*yantra*) and according to the sequence of worshiping the powers (*śakti*) of their respective phonemes.

Having written the respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) that constitute the original nature of each letter, and having written one's own first *kūṭa* in the very center, one should write the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth within it.
Having thus consecrated the prepared yantra, the fourfold means consisting of its worship, its wearing, the sprinkling with water from a jar empowered by it, and its burial,
will certainly accomplish all that is desired by the seeker of the goal, even if it was written within another yantra. Another application is as follows:
Having laid down twenty lines each extending east-west and twenty lines each extending north-south, which intersect one another and are equidistantly spaced,
one should produce one hundred and sixty-one squares; then, at each corner...

One should erase the forty-five squares so that the central yantra assumes the form of a vajra. The method for this is as follows: on the outermost path consisting of nineteen squares, one should leave out the tenth square located at the very center in each direction, and likewise in each corner.

Having erased seventeen by seventeen squares situated in the middle of that [grid], one should omit three squares in each direction within the second row— namely, the single square directly below the previously omitted square and one square on each of its two sides—
and thus omit thirteen squares in each corner.

Having swept [the area], in the third path, having abandoned five squares in each direction— namely, the three squares below the previously abandoned square and one square each situated on its two sides—
and having swept the nine central squares in each corner, [one proceeds] in the fourth path.
Having set aside seven squares in each direction— consisting of the five squares situated in that first row and one square on each of its two sides—
and having erased the five central squares in each corner,
[one proceeds] with the fifth path, which is situated in that first row.

Having set aside eleven squares in each direction— consisting of a central group of nine squares and one square on each of its two sides— one should erase the single remaining square in each corner. This applies to those squares situated within the first and second rows.
Having unified the remaining four squares by erasing the three dividing lines of the central square,
one should draw upward-facing triangles in each direction; thus another sixteen-square grid is delineated.
Thus, having combined [the numbers], one hundred and ninety-six (196) squares are erased;

one hundred and sixty-five (165) squares remain. Among these, beginning from the square situated in the middle of the five squares located in the eastern direction, one proceeds in a clockwise manner by way of entry.
Having first written the deformed amṛta-syllables of the vidyā around [the grid], starting from the initial cell and proceeding to the cells on the left side;
and in the same manner, beginning from the cell directly below the initial cell of the grid...
Having written [the syllables] in all the pathways up to the end of each respective left-hand square,

and having inscribed one hundred and fifty-six nectar-oceans (amṛtārṇas), there remains a single square in the very center; surrounding that, there are eight squares on the outside, among which are the squares situated in the directions starting from the east.
Having written the four syllables remaining from the modified [mantra] and the dead syllable,

one should write the five modified three-syllabled vidyās— those distinct vidyās other than the ones already written in the corners and the center of the present yantra— each in the four triangular fields located at the four cardinal directions, and the present vidyā itself.
One should write the names of the goal (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth, repeated four times. This constitutes one completed yantra.

If, however, other mantras (*vidyā*) are written in the triangles, and the remaining mantras are written in the five central squares, then, due to the difference in mantras, there arises a difference in yantras; thus, five other perfected yantras are established.

The six yantras have been produced by combining them; this is the sequence of writing here: *dvaṃjaṃ* 1, *dvaṃjāṃ* 2, *dvaṃjiṃ* 3, *dvaṃjīṃ* 4, *dvaṃjuṃ* 5, *dvaṃjūṃ* 6, and so forth—in this manner, the first *kūṭa* is joined to all the nectar-letters (*amṛtavarṇa*). [The first and second...]
In the first two diagrams, one should employ the sequence beginning with *śaḥjaṃ*, *śaḥjā*, *śaḥjiṃ*,
*śaḥjīṃ*, and so forth. The conjunction of the second *kūṭa* should be employed in the third and fourth diagrams, beginning with *jhajarauṃjaṃ*.

The conjunction of the third *kūṭa*—beginning with "jhajarauṃjāṃ 2 jhajarauṃji" and so forth—should be applied to the fifth and sixth syllables among the *mṛta*-syllables in both the fifth and sixth yantras. For those who worship either of these two yantras, there is never any fear of disease, nor do they suffer from afflictions (*ādhi*). This [is the result] when one of these yantras is buried.

If, preceded by the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and worship, this occurs on a day favorable to one's own [natal] ascendant among the eleven signs, then there shall be no fear of pestilence (*mārī*) in that region, nor shall there be affliction from the planets (*graha*). Even earthquakes and portents (*utpāta*) shall not occur;
such is the summary. Thus end the applications of Amṛteśvarī. Now, regarding the worship of the deities of the Gemini (*mithuna*) sign:

The applications of those yantras and so forth are now described because they were not mentioned previously. Having drawn twelve lines each extending east-west and twelve lines each extending north-south, with equal intervals and intersecting one another, one should produce one hundred and twenty-one squares; then, on the first outermost path surrounding them all...

Having omitted the sixth square in each of the four directions and having erased the nine squares situated in the center of each corner; and having omitted, in each direction, three squares from the second row— namely, the one directly below the previously omitted square and the one on each side of it.

Having cleared the five central squares within that [area], and having omitted five squares in each direction— consisting of the three squares below the previously omitted squares in the third row, plus one square on each side of them; thus, omitting five squares in every direction.
Having erased one square located at the center of each corner,
fifteen squares are erased at each corner in total; thus,
sixty squares are erased in all, leaving sixty-one squares remaining.
Therein,
having written the mantra of the daily *nityā* for that day in the very center of the grid,
one should form three rows within the interior of the fourth vowel, beginning with the name of the practitioner in the genitive case, such as "of Devadatta," and so forth.

Having written the names beginning with "sarvādhaḥstāt" and ending with "dviyāntam," as well as "madhye vaśaṃkuru kuru" and so forth, one should construct downward-pointing triangles within each of the four squares reaching the four directions in the eastern row.

Beginning from the triangle situated in the western direction and proceeding from the square located below it in a clockwise manner by way of entry, one should write the fifty letters starting with the letter corresponding to the rising of that day; having written them as they fit, one should then write ten more letters. Thus, when this is accomplished, the installation of the Yantra containing the deities of the couples is complete.

With the aforementioned Śakti-mantras, such as *hrīṃ śrīṃ arūpiṇī śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi* and *hrīṃ śrīṃ ārūpiṇī śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and with the Kṣetreśa-mantras, such as *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ rūpa-kṣetreśa-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi* and *hrīṃ śrīṃ āṃ rūpa-kṣetreśa-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

One should worship the fifty pairs of deities (*mithunadevatā*) according to the sequence of syllables obtained from the *ghaṭikā* [of the time] during their respective worship, using aloe-wood incense, fragrant flowers, incense smoke, lamps, and food offerings. By this, there shall be the pacification of afflictions caused by the planets, afflictions from various diseases, and afflictions from kings, thieves, and the like. Here, by the mention of the "pairs of deities," [it refers to] each individual Śakti and Kṣetrapāla.
At the conclusion of the worship, the worship of the Parāparā Śakti and the Kṣetrapāla should be performed; this is determined by the sequence.
Having covered the maṇḍala with fragrant white flowers and perfumes, one should worship the deities of the couples (mithuna-devatās);
thus there shall be the attainment of prosperity.

For the practitioner who worships throughout the entire year on the full lunar days, specifically the fifth and the fifteenth, all desired accomplishments are attained; likewise, during the three lunar mansions of one’s own birth, all results are achieved through the mantras previously shown according to the prescribed ritual.
For the practitioner who worships the fifty pairs of deities with a total number of one hundred [offerings], there shall be a lifespan of up to one hundred years,
characterized by the experience of happiness preceded by freedom from mental and physical afflictions.

Even for the purpose of pacifying malevolent magical rites (*abhicāra*) performed by an enemy, the worship of the deity of the couple (*mithunadevatā*) must be practiced. The method for this is as follows:

oneself, until the completion of the mandala, every day without interruption, throughout the watch (*yāma*), if one has the capacity for worship, [one should perform it] for the sake of the two [deities], one's own...

Having invited seven Brāhmaṇas who are friends, who have not eaten regularly [for some time], and who are skilled in the rites of worship; or, in the absence of such capability on one's part, having selected eight Brāhmaṇas, through them, for every watch (prahara) throughout the night— beginning from each respective hour (ghaṭikā)-letter— one should [worship] all the deities of the pairs (mithuna-devatās) within the Vajrayantra.
One should worship during the middle portion [of the day] as specified by the name of the *sādhya* (the deity to be accomplished) and so forth, joined with the daily *nityā*.

In this way, according to the measure of the *ghaṭikās* of each watch (*prahara*), the worship of the deities of the couples results in being performed eightfold for some and sevenfold for others at every watch. Thus, up until the end of the circle of every *ghaṭikā*, [the worship continues].

Having performed the worship of the deity of the *mithuna* (the pair), one should satisfy those Brahmins with gifts of cows, land, gold, and so forth, while avoiding stinginess regarding wealth. By means of this, the application of the *bhicā* rite destroys only the enemy and not oneself; thus, when this is deposited in one's own home, there is the accomplishment of all goals.
Those who know how to protect [the treasure] become free from disease, devoid of enemies, and fearless. As for the method of its concealment:
on a wide tablet made of gold, silver, copper, or stone, one should carve the aforementioned vajra-diagram so that it has upward-pointing lines. Then, in all the squares therein—

Having repeatedly written the *māyāvīja* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*), one should write the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the name of his desired object, and the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*)— each within the interior of the fourth vowel (*au*) of that *Māyāntardinanityā*— in three rows within the central square.
Having duly installed the Vajrayantra, which is endowed with the syllables of the first sixty [verses] within the remaining squares,
and having worshipped the deities of the couples therein, on a day favorable to oneself, at the moment of the ascendant of the eleventh zodiac sign—
"In some secluded spot, one should bury [the yantra] in one's own house or elsewhere. Regarding the *nityapūjā-yantra* of the deities of the *mithuna* (pairs),
if it is impossible for a single person to perform it with that many [required] materials,
it should be performed through various devotees by way of providing food, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth for the ritual enclosures (*āvaraṇa*).
Thus end the ritual procedures for the worship of the divine couple and other rites.
In this context, all ritual applications (*prayoga*) must be performed only after both [the self and the deity] have been accomplished, and not otherwise.

The method for accomplishing that consists of the *puraścaraṇa*—comprising recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), ritual service (*tarpaṇa*), and feeding Brahmins—as described in the respective *kalpas*; this has indeed been stated in those various places. First, regarding one [method]:

Since it is impossible for an individual to perform the required number of recitations (*japa*), this practice should be carried out through various Brahmins who are devotees of him, preceded by the offering of a feast and ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Even so, due to the abundance of widows, there may be obstacles to the commencement of the rite, as in the following example:
The enjoyment of women consists of mental transformations produced by touching or seeing the breasts and hips of women;
however, the enjoyment of one's own wife as prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras—limited to the fertile period (ṛtukāla), non-barren, and occurring only once—is not an obstacle.
[Likewise forbidden are] conversing with atheists and slandering others.

Grief, such as the thought "will there be death? arising from being preoccupied with the preliminary rites for a funeral, is caused by the death of a son or others. Desires directed toward another's field, another's house, or another's wife—such as stealing women, men, or wealth—are signs of evil. For example, in a dream, being struck by dark-complexioned men, being anointed with oil, or [interacting] with the wives of others.

The *saṃbhoga* [result] is as follows: the displacement of even a single sense organ—whether among the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) or the organs of action (*karmendriya*)—from its own respective location; the outbreak of calamities in one's region; and the destruction of one's wife, kin, and relatives.
Indifference toward the guru, failure to acquire the necessary materials for the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), lack of attainment,
the outbreak of diseases such as leprosy among one's kinsmen,
and excessive devotion to the mantras and deities other than the one currently being worshipped— these are the ten obstacles for those who practice daily worship.
The method for achieving success is as follows:
In the previously mentioned wheel of the fifty *mātṛkā* syllables within the fifty squares, using any one of the substances— red sandalwood, saffron, or vermilion—
and following the instructions of the Guru with devotion, in a secluded place free from the disturbances of heat or cold.

In a temple whose interior has been whitened with lime-powder and other substances, one should draw fifty excellent birds— colored with gold, silver, copper, or any other pigment— within the worship pavilion;
having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force) for the wheel, one should there worship the presiding mother-deities, beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*).

One should recite the *mātṛkā* daily, according to tradition, one hundred thousand times or some other such number. As for the tradition: having first recited each letter from *a* to *kṣa*, each accompanied by the nasal bindu (*m*), one should then recite from *kṣa* back to the first vowel (*a*), each with the visarga (*ḥ*). This constitutes one cycle. In this manner, it is taught.

For a practitioner who thus practices the Mātṛkā-mantra for one full year, preceded by worship, his own chosen mantra will certainly become perfected (*siddha*). In all such cases, a rosary (*mālā*) is prescribed for the purpose of counting the recitations (*japa*): [it may be made of] *rudrākṣa*, *putrajīva*, or red sandalwood.

A garland should be fashioned from crystals, corals, pearls, gold, silver, or any of these gems, arranged such that each subsequent one is secondary to the preceding one; this number of gems, totaling one hundred, is the most excellent in all respects and for all desires, unlike [the methods] in other tantras where it is differentiated according to specific desires.

Therein, the garland of the four classes (*caturvarṇamālā*) follows the direct order (*anulomakrama*); each individual class has the form of the letter *ā*, from which the complete mantra of the one situated in the *svāpoṣṭha* arises.

This is the first repetition; then the letter *ā*, then one's own mantra to be worshipped—this is the second repetition; then the letter *ī*, then the mantra—having thus repeated the mantra for each of the fifty letters exactly fifty times, and having meditated upon the letter *kṣa* as determined to be the Meru mountain.
Having uttered the letter *la*, one should then utter the root mantra; then the letter *ha*, then the mantra; then the letter *sa*, then the mantra.
Having thus uttered [the letters] in reverse order up to the end of the first vowel (*a*), one should recite the root mantra at the end of each.
By this method, the recitation of one's own chosen mantra interspersed with the Mātṛkā alphabet, performed one hundred times, becomes perfected. In this manner, by repeating [the cycle] three times—

For one who recites [the mantra], the recitation of the mantra a thousand times becomes perfected; and this recitation of the root mantra interspersed with the *mātṛkā* is not only useful for knowing the count of the recitation, but is rather the bringer of all accomplishments (*siddhi*),
the preventer of [mantras] falling from the hand, the shatterer of the jewel-case (*maṇika*), and [it serves as protection against] fear upon touching the forefinger, or the touch of impurity.
And it possesses the quality of being free from various defects such as being pierced by the arrows of other philosophical systems;

furthermore, in the absence of the previously mentioned names, there are three joints consisting of the middle joint of the nameless finger (*anāmikā*), its root joint, and the root, middle, and tip joints of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*), as well as the tip joint of the nameless finger and the middle and tip joints of the middle finger (*madhyamā*).
Recitation (*japa*) should be performed with a rosary (*mālā*) consisting of ten joints, namely the tip of the index finger and the base joint of the middle finger;
by repeating this [sequence] ten times, a recitation numbering one hundred or more is accomplished.

Furthermore, for a specific desire (*kāmanā*), the recitation must be preceded by the placement (*vinyāsa*) of *yoga-pallava* and other elements; the method for this is as follows: [for example, against an enemy...]

In the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) for a target named Devadatta, one should first recite the mantra to be personally chanted once, saying: "Eradicate, eradicate Devadatta, my enemy! Then, one should also chant the six-syllable mantra, saying: "Eradicate, eradicate Devadatta, my enemy! It is exactly the same [for other rites].
One should recite the mantra a hundred times or more; this is the arrangement known as *yoga* for the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*).
For the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), such as "Kill my enemy Devadatta! Kill him!"—in rites of killing involving the name of the target and so forth—one uses "my" and so on.

At the end of the fourteen-syllable mantra, one should recite the mantra to be muttered by the master once. In this very manner, one should again and again mutter the mantra at the end of the fourteen-syllable mantra. This is the pallava-named placement (vinyāsa) pertaining to the rite of killing: "Paralyze, paralyze the army of my enemy Devadatta!"
In the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*) involving the name of the target (*sādhya*) and so forth, one should place the seven-syllable mantra beginning with *pañcāccama* at the front and the end,

and in the middle, recite the mantra of one's own private recitation (*svābhijapya*). At the conclusion, by reversing the order of the target’s name and so forth, this placement known as "encasement" (*sampuṭa*) is prescribed for the rite of immobilization.

"In this *keśāntika* rite named after the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth— [performed with the thought], 'May you pacify this disease that has arisen in me without harming my body'— first one syllable of the mantra, then one syllable of the *sādhya*,
then one syllable of the mantra."

Having performed the interlacing (*grathana*) of the syllable of the object of attainment (*sādhya*) with the syllables of the mantra— beginning from the first syllable of the *sādhya* up to its conclusion— by means of the repetition of the mantra according to the method of "one syllable of the *sādhya" at a time," one should recite the resulting mantra one hundred times or more for the rite of pacification (*śāntika*). This is as follows:

The arrangement of the name according to the sequence of the *śāntika* rite is as follows: for the purpose of a subjugation rite (*vaśya-karma*) such as "May Yajñadatta bring Devadatta under my control," one begins with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth; then two syllables of the mantra, then one syllable of the *sādhya*, then two syllables of the mantra, then one syllable of the *sādhya*, and so on, in this manner until the completion of all the syllables of the *sādhya*.

Having performed the *vidarbhaṇa*—the interlacing of the syllables of the mantra with the syllables of the object to be accomplished—by means of repetition of the mantra and so forth, one should recite the resulting mantra a hundred times or more. This is the arrangement called *vidarbhaṇa*, which is suitable for rites of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*). Recitation (*japa*) in this manner is intended for those who are capable; however, for those who are incapable:
In all desires whatsoever, one should recite the mantra alone.
And this very point was indicated by the Blessed One himself through both the description of the characteristics of the arrangement of yoga and so forth, and the description of its application.
Thus concludes the second method for attaining mantra-siddhi, consisting of the worship of the Mother (Mātṛkā).

Alternatively, the third method is that all mantras become perfected through the repetition of the syllables of one's own chosen deity, which are strung together one by one from the *āmnāya*-taught eternal vidyās. Or else, [they are perfected] by the combination in one place of the medicinal herbs of the syllables of one's respective mantra.
Having ground [the substance] and made pills the number of which corresponds to the syllables of that mantra, one performs worship with the mantra of the deity to be worshipped (sāṃkhopāsyamantra).

Then follows wearing [the pill], consuming it, smearing it on all limbs, and bathing one's own body with water connected to it— this constitutes the fivefold method, whether performed in its entirety or individually.

The mantra becomes perfected by relying on four modes; thus, there are four types. Furthermore, even for mantras belonging to the virtuous, there is a mode of incorrect arising as follows: through the instruction of that mantra to unsuitable disciples, the mantra—along with its presiding deity—incurs a state of lack of harmony toward that guru. This occurs constantly in the case of rites performed for selfish desires (*kāmyakarman*).
Even for one who possesses a perfected mantra (*siddhamantra*), [the mantra] becomes ineffective toward the preceptor who employs it; that is, toward the one who applies that mantra.

Furthermore, among the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites, if one applies [the mantra] to recitations and so forth at times other than those prescribed as the specific means and time for each particular rite, the mantra’s efficacy toward that [preceptor] likewise passes away.

Due to the doubt as to whether this act prescribed by the Guru is authoritative or not, and due to the doubt as to whether "from this performance, will this fruit accrue to me or not," he asks about its correctness with trepidation; for, in the absence of a certainty regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there remains a doubt with a predominant alternative (*utkaṭakoṭika-saṃśaya*) concerning the failure to achieve correctness.

Even for a matter well-established in the scriptures, there is the fault of disregarding the teacher if one fails to practice it; and even for a matter not mandated as necessarily to be performed by the scriptures, there is the fault of disregarding the teacher if one practices it without the teacher's approval.
The counter-mantra attains incorrectness.
Herein, according to the Tantra, that which consists of serving another’s wife, censuring others, and so forth, is prohibited.
Furthermore, due to the transgression arising from failing to practice that conduct, the mantras become ineffective toward that Guru; and due to "offense against the deity"—
which consists of not contemplating the worshipped deity as the Supreme Brahman— the mantras likewise become ineffective toward Him.

He enters into [the state of] other deities, other humans, and women; even by force, he renders those who revile the mantras ineffective, and he is supreme among the three: the guru, the mantra, and the deity.

The incorrectness of mantras arises from ignorance— either in the form of a failure to maintain the state of Brahman, or in the form of a lack of understanding regarding the methods for performing the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites directed toward their respective deities—
or even from the predominant worship of many deities' mantras that have not become auxiliary limbs [of one's own practice].
The mantra becomes ineffective.
Therefore, these twelve types [of practitioners] must be avoided by those who desire the accomplishment of mantras. This is the section on the improper performers.
Now, the means for the correct performance [of the ritual]:
the cause of all the splendors of fire, sun, and moon; of the powers of will, knowledge, and action; and of the three forms consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.

The determination of the essential nature of that Brahman which is the cause of the entire universe—consisting of the three qualities characterized as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and comprising the knower, the knowledge, and the objects of knowledge—is itself the path of mantra within one's own meditated mantras;
it is this very thing that is called the "living state" (*jīvatva*) by the term *pada*. This alone is declared to be the perfect state inherent in mantra. Thus.

One must also engage in the investigation of the meaning of the mantra. The meanings of the mantra are threefold, distinguished as the supreme (*para*), the gross (*sthūla*), and the subtle (*sūkṣma*). In the *mūlādhāra*, from the will-power (*icchā-śakti*) which is the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) in the form of time, there arises the state of *aparā* (the lower) in the form of the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*).

The primordial power (*ādyāśakti*) is designated by the term "state of emergence" (*udayapada*), and that same power is also what is conveyed by the term "sound" (*nāda*). It is that very state. Of that [same thing]...

As the sound (*nāda*) is led progressively upward through the wheels (*cakras*) known as Svādhiṣṭhāna, Anāhata, and Viśuddha, it undergoes a transformation into the forms of Paśyantī and Vaikharī; through its connection with the articulatory locations (*sthānas*) beginning with the head, there occurs the fulfillment of its complete manifestation in the form of those respective syllables.

This is the second power, which is designated by the term "resting place" (viśrāntipada). In both cases, establishing the stability of the intellect is the supreme meaning of mantra, which should be cultivated by the perfected ones (siddhas) through the study of all [sciences],
such as the lexicons and grammars, by means of the proficiency in words and their meanings derived from the state of the perfected ones.

The object to be meditated upon by the practitioner (*sādhya-bhāvanīya-artha*) is the contemplation of the constituent elements of the mantra, such as its syllables and parts, in their aspect as *śakti*. The object to be meditated upon by the seeker (*sādhaka-bhāvanīya-artha*) is the contemplation of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier—the phenomenal world consisting of the letters and the five elements.
Having meditated upon the object to be meditated upon according to one's own nature...

Even if an object intended to be meditated upon as distinct from oneself is described by another [teacher], there is no harm to any scriptural meaning whatsoever. Furthermore, it is essential to follow the methods for binding the *yonimudrās*; "yoni" refers to the *suṣumṇā* situated in the space between the genitals and the penis.
The Kuṇḍalinī, who is the cause of the three worlds and whose form is a triangle of fire situated at the pericarp of the four-petalled lotus at the base of the stalk of the nāḍīs,
resides below the thousand-petalled *kalā* located at the Brahma-randhra; she is known by the name Mudrā,
and because she bestows supreme bliss upon reaching her own abode, the Suṣumṇā nāḍī— which is situated within the petals— is called "Bondage" (*bandhana*).
The Mātrā residing in the place called the Heart, situated in the Anāhata-cakra; the Sun, whose rays extend upward and downward;

Fire, whose rays extend to half the periphery and resides in the previously shown location; and the Moon, whose rays extend downward as far as the Sun and resides in the previously shown location—the meditative integration (*anusandhāna*) of these three luminaries.
The removal of defects in mantra is essential.
110a) By means of the word "I" (ahaṃ), all phonemes ending in the letters *a* and *ha* are included.
All objects are expressed as being presented through the relation of being denotable by their respective words. Furthermore, one's own self is also the referent of the word "I" (ahaṃ);

thus, there arises a cognition whose qualificandum is the specific mantra and its deity to be meditated upon—which constitute the referent of the word "I"—and whose qualifier is identity with that [self].
Furthermore, even for the purpose of removing defects in the mantra, the Guru should instruct the disciple in such a way that [the mantra] becomes firm within him.

These are the means for the correct accomplishment of the mantra. Now, the signs of the prior absence of the arising of mantra-perfection (*mantrasiddhi*) and the signs immediately following its arising are described. [In this regard,] in dreams, by a group of women...
Whether it be contact, conversation, and so forth; or merely seeing a gathering or a dead body; or merely touching an elephant while walking upon mountains or palace rooftops;
or witnessing a dance, hearing music, or seeing festivals such as weddings; or even merely seeing wine or meat individually—each of these constitutes a transgression.
Whether it be mere contact or both together, these fourteen factors indicate the future attainment of success (*siddhi*).

Even if a certain degree of aversion or anger arises for the sake of maintaining the life of a householder—lasting only for a short time—for one who possesses perfected mantras, there is no excessive hatred nor should there be excessive anger. [This holds true] even in the face of the long-term suffering caused by separation from children, wife, and so forth.

Indeed, even sorrow in the form of recurrence does not occur for them; nor does excessive joy arise in them even upon the cause consisting of the acquisition of wealth and the like; even excessive affection toward sons and others does not occur for them;
and even envy, which is a momentary affliction directed toward the virtues of others, does not occur for them.
Gambling, hunting, and other such vices do not exist for them; even when suffering arises,
because they do not experience it, they always abide as if in constant happiness, and their capacity to obtain the requisites for food is achieved without effort.

They do not experience the hardship of repeated application because their desired goal is not achieved; rather, according to the principle that "what need is there for success through even a single word?",
they attain their desired object without the hardship of repeating those various applications.
In meritorious acts such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, in sacrifices such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*, in gifts such as the gift of a human being,
and at holy sites such as Kāśī and Prayāga, their intellect becomes firm; they attain renown—
which is synonymous with prestige— and the acquisition of highly valuable ornaments, garments, and the like.
They become free from mental fatigue; they attain the company of good disciples; they possess gratitude, characterized by the desire to repay the kindness of others who have rendered them assistance;
and they possess the power to pacify the three types of afflictions—those pertaining to moving beings, stationary objects, and artificial forms.

Even for those who have not yet attained the knowledge of the true nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*), some [signs] occur; and even for one who is healthy, they possess the power to cause possession by spirits and the like. Thus, these few signs mentioned are indicators of partial mantra-attainment (*mantrasiddhi*), whereas all [signs] together are indicators of complete mantra-attainment.

With more than half [of the signs], the accomplishment of the mantra is to be known as middling; it is easily accomplished, whereas the difficult-to-accomplish and the extremely difficult-to-accomplish tasks are for the noble ones. Thus, the three types of accomplishment that initiate the application have been described.
These are the signs of mantra-accomplishment. Alternatively, there is the method of mental cultivation (*āsanā*): on one's own head...

Having contemplated the aforementioned [deities] as Śrī Tripurasundarī in the form of Ārurā and so forth, because they are worthy of worship; and having contemplated Śrī Tripurasundarī herself as the nature of consciousness (cit-rūpa), whose essence is reflective awareness (vimarśa); one should contemplate the triad consisting of the two ears and speech as the divine triad beginning with Prakāśa; and the triad of apertures—the two eyes and the organ of generation—as the three Siddha Gurus.
The two nostrils and the anus—these three should be contemplated by the human guru as the three fires.
Having risen in the morning and observed the offering of oblations, [one should perform] the prayers consisting of mantras and deities. (p.

The *māyās* are the powers that, by producing the cognition of something as being what it is not within the primary deity, cause one to proceed upon a wrong path; through praying to them in the morning, there shall be no engagement in evil paths on that day.
One should contemplate the nature of the boar (*vārāhī*) in the limbs of the deity—namely, the skin, blood, bones, and marrow—and likewise in the skin and flesh.
For those whose nature is blood, these very limbs of the deity Kurukullā should be visualized;

furthermore, in the worship of the sacred seats (*pīṭhapūjā*), the four oceans— the Sughaṭaka, Pīlu, Devatā, and Ikṣusāgara— should be meditated upon as the objects of all human desires consisting of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.

The horses previously mentioned should be contemplated as being of the nature of one's own visual faculty; the elephants previously mentioned should be contemplated as being of the nature of the objects of that [faculty], such as form and so forth; and the Jewel Island should be contemplated as being one's own body. As for the nine jewels, which correspond to the nine divisions [of the island], they should be contemplated in their respective order.
Flesh, hair, skin, blood, semen, marrow, bone, fat, vitality, strength, and the middle [of the body] are to be understood [as the constituents]. In that island, the rivers are proclaimed;

and as for the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpataru*), they are [to be worshipped] preceded by the mention of place, time, lineage, zodiac sign, name, desire, and so forth, along with the performance of their respective rites.

These [rites] are to be visualized as having the nature of a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), characterized by the sprinkling of water containing kuśa grass, sesame seeds, flowers, and unhusked rice grains held in the hand, preceded by the utterance of the statement of the vow (*pratijñāvākya*). By this, it is emphasized that the formal resolve must necessarily be followed, as it grants the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) and the blue lotus (*utpala*). [This occurs] all around the garden of the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadrumodyāna*).

The six seasons previously mentioned should be contemplated as the six *cakras*, beginning with the *mūlādhāra* located within one's own body. One should perform the visualization of the *Cakreśvarīs* as being of the nature of the thirty-six *tattvas*. The moat of the Goddess should be visualized as having the form of the *kuruṇā* [plants], and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) as consisting of jewels, specifically made of rubies (*māṇikya*). Its splendor...

It has already been stated that the nature of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) is one's own essential form (*svarūpatva*). One should meditate upon the four powers (*śakti*) worshipped at the corners as being the essential nature of the principles (*tattva*) such as space (*deśa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consists of the knower, the act of knowing, and the object known.

In that regard, one's own nature as the knower (*jñātṛtva*) is to be meditated upon. The implements of worship, consisting of the *arghya* and so forth, are to be meditated upon as being of the nature of all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñāna*). The *Śrīcakra*, however, is to be meditated upon as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Furthermore, worship is to be understood as the very meditation on the non-difference between the state of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*), which is the subject, and the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*), which is the object. Thus it is said.

Following the meditation on the deities of the *pīṭhas*, one should pursue the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), which consist of the blending and manifestation of the light of the three peaks (*kūṭatraya*); thereafter, the latent impressions of the nine coverings (*navāvaraṇa*) should be pursued: the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the heroic, the furious, and the terrifying.

The ninth rasa is known as the disgusting (*vībhatsa*) and the marvelous (*adbhuta*); thus there are nine rasas. It is observed that "niyati" (destiny) constitutes the ten forms (*daśarūpatva*), by which the ten supernatural powers (*siddhis*), beginning with *aṇimā*, are to be contemplated. Furthermore, hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, death, sin, and merit—this [is the group].

Furthermore, the eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, should be meditated upon as being composed of the eight categories [of the Sāṃkhya system]. Herein are the eight rasas— peaceful, marvelous, compassionate, heroic, humorous, loathsome, furious, and terrifying— as well as the erotic, hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion,
old age, death, the anus, and the genitals.

One should meditate upon the identity with the eighteen [deities] of the first enclosure, beginning with *aṇimā*, in their sequential order; however, this is not established by a rule such as the literal sequence of the text. This is because the terms "merit" (*puṇya*) and "sin" (*pāpa*) are intended to refer to the anus and the generative organ respectively.
Furthermore, since the sense organs and the apertures possess distinct natures, there is no [conflict] in contemplating the identity with the previously mentioned Lords (*nātha*).

There is no tautology with the term *sahana*. There is no tautology with the latent impression (*vāsanā*) to be described by means of the property that pervades the nature of being a faculty (*indriyatva*), because the two subsumed properties (*vyāpyadharma*), namely "being the anus" and "being the generative organ," are distinct. For there is no contradiction in a single substratum (*dharmin*) being the object of various latent impressions through its diverse forms, as in the case of the ear and the skin.

Having meditated upon the sixteen powers constituting the second enclosure—beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others—as being the nature of the eye, nose, tongue, sense of smell, genitals, anus, feet, hands, speech, and mind, which are the playful manifestations of water, wind, fire, and taste.

The eight powers of Anaṅgakusumā and the others, who constitute the third enclosure, are to be meditated upon as the objects of the five organs of action—speech, grasping, excretion, procreation, and enjoyment—and as being of the nature of the three humors (doṣas): wind, bile, and phlegm. [These are] Suṣumṇā, Laṃbuṣā, Kuhu, Vāraṇā, Yaśasvinī, Piṅgalā, Pūṣā, and Payasvinī.

The fourteen powers beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, who constitute the fourth enclosure, are to be meditated upon as being of the nature of the fourteen principal channels (nāḍīs) within one's own body, namely: Sarasvatī, Śaṅkhinī, Gāndhārī, Iḍā, Hastijihvā, Viśvodarā, and so forth. [Likewise] Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, and Udāna...
And likewise Vyāna; as well as Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.

Thus, by means of the nature of the ten internal winds residing within one's own body, the ten powers—beginning with Sarvasiddhi—are to be meditated upon as constituting the fifth enclosure: Agni, Vahni, Śuci, Tejas, Prabhā, Dāva, [Uṣmā, Arcis, Jvālā, and Havyavāhana].

The eleven intermediate fires—Śikhidyuti, Dāha, and Grāsa—are situated respectively in the skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, wind, bile, and phlegm; they are to be meditated upon as being the nature of the ten powers (śaktis), beginning with Sarvajñā. Thus ends the visualization of the deities of the sixth enclosure.

The deities of speech, beginning with Śinī, who constitute the seventh enclosure, are to be visualized as having the nature of cold, heat, pleasure, pain, desire, and the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. One should meditate upon the five arrows made of flowers as being composed of one's own sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, by way of the mind.
One should contemplate the sense-faculty of the mind as being like a bow made of sugarcane; one should contemplate the noose as being the nature of attachment to specific forms;
and the goad should be contemplated as the specific hatred directed toward objects such as those of the rainy season. Thus it is said.
Kāmeśvarī is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the fourfold weapons of worship, due to her equality with *pradhāna*;
Bhagamālinī is [the latent impression] in the form of the principle of *mahat*, and [Nityaklinnā] in the form of *ahaṃkāra*.
Vajreśī is to be meditated upon as having an unmanifest form; this is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the eighth enclosure.
Lalitā, who resides in the central point (*bindu*) in the midst of all things purified by the ninth enclosure, is to be meditated upon as one's very own self (*svātmatva*);
thus, the latent impression of the prior consciousness (*pūrvasaṃvidāsanā*) has been indicated. Kāmeśvarī, however, [is to be meditated upon] as the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
Having meditated upon the graceful movements [of the deities], one should contemplate the red-colored [deity] as being of the nature of passion for the true form of one's own Self.
The firm stability of the contemplation of the Self-nature within all things is alone to be understood as the meaning of the term "worship" (*upāsanā*).
As for the attainment that is the fruit of worship, it consists in nothing other than the realization of one's own Self regarding any object whatsoever.

It should be understood that [the state] consists precisely in the absence of any connection. The contemplation of the attributes and characteristics of the Self, such as existence, consciousness, and bliss, is the very meaning of the term *mudrāvāsanā*.
The five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—in their respective order...
The forms of the little finger, ring finger, middle finger, index finger, thumb, and the [other] fingers arise.
Through the various combinations of those elements, there occurs for the mind the contemplation of the manifold phenomenal form of the principal deity.
Even at a time when one is engaged in the failure to contemplate one's own true nature due to being bound by the nature of worldly objects (*palasvabhāva*),

through the meditation on the state of being composed of the deity whose form is consciousness (*cidrūpadevatāmaya*), non-negligence itself must be contemplated as the very essence of the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) such as water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, which transcend the worship and satiation of the *āvaraṇa* deities. Those situated within the *śrīcakra*...
The sixty-seven quintillion [deities], beginning with Saṃgītayoginī and others,

are to be meditated upon as the cause of the various conceptualizations and mental constructions in the minds of all beings. Whatever deity’s mantra-syllables are installed, one should cultivate the visualization of one's own body as having the very nature of that deity.

The latent impression (*vāsanā*) of all things is the essential nature of the deity of the mantra; the cultivation of that very form within the mantra being recited is precisely the *japa-vāsanā*. It is the setting of the various conceptual constructions—the manifold imaginings of the universe—within one’s own essential nature, which is like the flame of a lamp.

The contemplation of one's own nature (*tvabhāvanā*) is thus the offering of libations (*tarpaṇa*), which consists precisely in the contemplation of one's own nature as being mixed with the triple latent impression (*trikavāsanā*)— namely, the impressions of sacrifice (*homavāsanā*), the installation of the self (*ātmanyāsa*), and recitation and sacrifice (*japahoma*).

The "practice-impulse" (*prayogavāsanā*) is the very destruction within one's own self of greed, delusion, and malice— which are the causes of all conceptual constructions— preceded by their non-arising within that self;

it consists of the stabilization of the contemplation of the non-difference between oneself and the object of both the *yantra* and the *mantra*, [occurring] in the *Bhairava-yantro* (the machine of Bhairava).

The practice of worshiping the three junctions (*sandhyā*) preceded by the continuous contemplation of the state consisting of the destruction of the highest and middle [levels]— attained through the impressions (*vāsanā*) of both mantras— is indeed what is called the "impression of the three junctions" (*trisandhyā-vāsanā*). Delusion (*moha*).

The consecration-impregnation (*abhiṣeka-vāsanā*) consists of the continuous contemplation of one's own nature, preceded by the non-recurrence of those three types of suffering— namely, the suffering of change, the suffering of suffering, and the suffering born of ignorance which is applied to the pillar of suffering obtained through the lack of discernment regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done.

The Self is the form of the entire universe and all-pervading; the contemplation of its non-difference [from oneself] is like the sky being unaffected by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, or by the various transformations of pleasure, pain, greed, delusion, and so forth arising from those elements, just as the sky remains untouched by the cage of the dust of the latent impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*).

The very contemplation of one's own self as being untainted is what is called the impression of instruction; the certain realization of the voidness of the distinction between oneself and the Guru regarding one's own substance and one's own form is the impression of the Guru’s fee (*guru-dakṣiṇā*);
and the stabilization of the inquiry into the true nature of one's own self as taught by the Guru is indeed what is called the impression of service to the Guru.

The fifteen *nityās* exist within the lunar orb as the very nature of time, which consists of the fifteen lunar days (*tithis*)—from the first to the fifteenth—belonging to both the bright and dark fortnights; just as there is knowledge of their existence, so too there are the fifteen *nityā-vāsanās*. Furthermore, these *tithi-nityās* consist of their respective internal, specific temporal aspects.
The time characterized as the lunar orb is being transformed by those respective eternal [powers] which consist of intermediate durations. (p.
Since the Great One is the nature of light itself,
one should contemplate the state of being worshipped by means of the meditation on distinctness for these fifteen Nityās; thus,
[the sequence] of the fifteen Nityā-vāsanās consists of the water-principle, the air-principle, the earth-principle, and the space-principle.

The recitation of the Vidyā should be performed preceded by the contemplation of the non-difference of one's own nature from Śiva—the essence of the fires (vahni-tattva), which are non-dual and the cause of the universe; this is the first latent impression (vāsanā).
By means of the letter *ha* contained within the word *hṛllekhā*, the self-luminosity of one’s own Self is expressed.
By the letter *ra*, the state of devouring is expressed; by the fourth vowel, which is the nature of Śiva and Śakti, the identity (*tādātmya*) of those two forms as described is stated;
and by the *bindu*, the determination of their unity—preceded by the absence of duality—is proclaimed. This is the second [interpretation].

The Impression of Recitation (*japavāsanā*). Thus ends the determination of the impressions (*vāsanā-nirṇaya*). Now, the various types of mantras to be inscribed upon the previously mentioned yantras are described. Among them, first, the varieties of three-syllabled mantras are:
those with sixty, forty-two, and twenty-four [syllables]. 1, 2.
