I shall now describe the ritual procedure for meditating upon the lotus-feet of the Lord of Indirā, known as Haihaya, who fulfills the desires of the world’s mind; he is inconceivable by the heart, the accomplisher of wonders, independent, and whose desired rites are revealed through the atomic power (*aṇu-rāja*). Now, the rites rooted in the Vidyā taught in the thirty-fourth chapter of the *Tantrarāja* are set forth according to the stated sequence. Therein, first:

The Siddhasārasvatavidyā is as follows: Aiṃ Hrīṃ is the Vāgbhava-bīja; Māyā and Śrī-bīja; the letter E joined with the letters Ha, Sa, Kha, and Ra, together with the Bindu; and the letter Au joined with the letters Ha, Sa, two Has, and Ra, together with the Visarga. Thus are the five syllables.

"HASAKHA PHARE HASAHA HARAŪM"—this is the present vidyā consisting of these syllables. As before, one should here also place the water-pot (kalaśa), worship Sarvamaṅgalā upon it, and then, after dismissing her, one should again contemplate the Kulasundarī-cakra within the pot. Furthermore, that which was written there beneath the pot—
Having again visualized that wheel within the vessel, which is itself situated upon the vessel at the location of Vindu,
one should worship the Kulasundarī of the directions— neither deficient nor excessive— with this five-syllabled vidyā. In this regard,
there is a specific distinction concerning the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Having fully uttered the five-syllable vidyā, at its end [say] *hṛdayāya namaḥ*.

Again, at the end of the five syllables, [say] *śirase svāhā*. Again, at the end of the five syllables, [say] *śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*. Again, at the end of the five syllables, [say] *kavacāya huṃ*. Again, at the end of the five syllables, [say] *netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*. Again, at the end of the five syllables, [say] *astrāya* [phaṭ].

Having performed the placement [of the fingers] starting from the thumb with the mantra *phaṭ*, the practitioner should again perform the placement upon his own six locations, beginning with the heart. (p.

Alternatively, one should perform the placement of the limbs and the heart and so forth (*hṛdayādinyāsa*) as before, using the mantras: *athavāhaṃ* for the heart with *namaḥ*, *hrīṃ* for the head with *svāhā*, *hrūṃ* for the tuft (*śikhā*) with *vaṣaṭ*, *hraiṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*) with *huṃ*, *hrauṃ* for the three eyes with *vauṣaṭ*, and *hraḥ* for the weapon (*astra*) with *phaṭ*. Regarding these two options, the determination is according to one's own guru’s tradition.

Then, for the purpose of dispelling all obstacles, one should perform the binding of the ten directions using the nārāca-mudrā, formed by the application of the tips of the index finger and thumb with the sound "Astrāya Phaṭ."

There, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the complete Vidyā consisting of fifteen syllables. As for the recitation (*japa*) as a means of attainment: in the Satya Yuga it is five hundred thousand; since we are currently in the Tretā Yuga, which requires fourfold that amount, it measures twenty hundred thousand.
As before, there is no option regarding the consumption of fruits, roots, and so forth; however—

The rule is that one should subsist on milk alone. Having thus perfected the mantra, one should employ it in all the rites for desired objects (*kāmyakarman*) mentioned in the *Kulasundarīpaṭala*. Furthermore, by means of this perfected vidyā, having consecrated a purified maiden upon her head with a count of a thousand or more [recitations], [one may bestow her].

Having caused [the disciple] to drink water consecrated with mantras a thousand times or more, the practitioner should say the words "Recite the verses," meaning that he should recite the *ślokas*. Then, he should sprinkle [him] with a continuous stream of pure water accompanied by the *abhinava-vṛnda* mantra.

Furthermore, when questioned, she shall provide answers according to the facts regarding all matters—past, present, and future—pertaining to the practitioner's inquiries. This applies even to the *vidyās* mentioned in this chapter, after considering their favorability or unfavorability; it was not previously stated as being restricted solely to the domain of all *mantras*.
"Let the rest be forgotten entirely, O Kulasundarī; thus ends the exposition of the Siddhasārasvata-vidyā."
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with its stalk and pericarp, one should place the *praṇava* (oṃ) on the stalk, the syllables of the mantra in rotation upon the petals,
and [the seed-syllable] in the pericarp.

Having written the letter *sa* together with the *visarga*, and having placed it along with the vessel as before, one should contemplate the wheel of Sarvamaṅgalā; then, at the conclusion of its worship and dismissal (*udvāsana*), one should again contemplate the previously mentioned wheel and worship Mṛtyuñjaya therein. Here too—

The preparation of the *arghya* is performed with the two mantras introduced by the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*). Having joined either the complete present *vidyā* or merely the *praṇava* at the beginning of each [limb], one performs the placement (*nyāsa*) of the respective *mātṛkā* letters in their corresponding locations: *sāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *sīṃ śirase svāhā*.

With the mantras: *sūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *saiṃ kavacāya hūṃ*, *sauṃ netratrāya vauṣaṭ*, and *saḥ astrāya phaṭ*, one performs the *aṅguṣṭādi-nyāsa* (assignment to the thumbs and other fingers) and the *hṛdayādi-nyāsa* (assignment to the heart and other limbs). Then, with the twelve-syllable complete Vidyā, *oṃ juṃ saḥ pālaya pālaya saḥ ju oṃ*, one performs the threefold *vyāpaka-nyāsa* (all-pervading assignment).
The offering of the *bali* before and after the worship is performed with the previously mentioned sixteen-syllable mantra; the remainder is done with the present mantra.

As for the visualization: [He is] seated upon the pericarp in the middle of the petals of the first, middle, and third syllables, his limbs moist with nectar, and his crown joined with the digit of the moon.

They meditate with their own identity upon a lotus that pierces the noose of anxiety— the garland of the deer-marked moon— such that the Lord’s limbs are moistened by the very nectar flowing from the letter *sa*, which is the form of the moon moving within its pericarp at the upper portion.

In the worship of the Lord (*nāthapūjā*), after the words *prakāśānanda* and so forth, one should insert the word *mṛtyuñjaya* and append the seven-syllable mantra at the end. Here, immediately after the worship of the weapons (*āyudha*) and before the secondary enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), during the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*), only these three deities are to be worshipped: "Oṃ *nānā* to the petals, Oṃ *paṃ* to the petals, Oṃ *kaṃ* to the pericarp (*karṇikā*). All else [is omitted].

As before, having thus performed the worship within the water-pot (*kalaśa*) and spent that night with vigils, dancing, singing, and so forth, one should, in the morning, after the worship as previously described and the consecration by the water of the pot, receive the mantra from the venerable Guru following the worship of the Guru and the offering of the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*), preceded by the piercing (*vedha*).

Having perfected this mantra by reciting it one million two hundred thousand times, and while contemplating the state of identity with the previously mentioned *Dhyānakamṛtyuñjaya*, if [one recites it] every day in numbers such as a thousand;

If one recites [the mantra], then even one whose life has reached its end shall become long-lived and become prosperous with wealth, grain, sons, grandsons, and so forth. Thus concludes the exposition of the Mṛtyuñjaya-vidyā. The mantra for the eight-petalled lotus is the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*). Having placed the water-pot (*kalaśa*) right here, all procedures from the meditation on the Sarvamaṅgalā-cakra up to the conclusion of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) are to be performed as before.

One should perform [the ritual]. With the mantras "Śrīṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ," "Hrīṃ Śirase Svāhā," "Klīṃ Śikhāyai Vaṣaṭ," "Śrīṃ Kavacāya Huṃ," "Hrīṃ Netratrayāya Vauṣaṭ," and "Klīṃ Astrāya Phaṭ," one should carry out the placement (nyāsa) on the thumbs and other fingers, as well as the placement on the heart and other limbs. Furthermore, with the complete three-syllable mantra "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ," [one should perform it] three times.
The pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa): [one should meditate on her] as ruddy, seated upon a ruddy lotus, with a face like a serene lotus.
Holding in her six arms a flower-hook, a lotus, a lotus-noose, and a sugarcane bow, she is radiant with ruby-like buds; she carries a water-pot, ornaments, betel, a fly-whisk, a mirror, and sandals.

One should meditate on her as being surrounded by and encompassed by the Śaktis, who stand encircling her while holding [attributes] all around and singing; this is the visualization. Here, the weapons are located precisely upon the pericarp, in the regions near the right and left arms of the Goddess situated in the center: "Oṃ, obeisance to Puṣpeṣu. Aṃ.
*Oṃ aṅkuśāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the goad). *Paṃ padmāya namaḥ* (Salutation again to the lotus). *Pāṃ pāśāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the noose).

*Iṃ ikṣucāpāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the sugarcane bow). Thus, the weapons are worshipped. Then, with the repetition of "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi" (I worship the sandals of the Śakti), the Śaktis are to be worshipped on the eight petals. [One should recite] three hundred thousand times for each syllable in reverse order.

When the practice of the Vidyā is undertaken according to the method described in the context of Lalitā’s recitation-count, the recitation for its accomplishment in the Satya Yuga is established as twenty-five hundred thousand (25 lakṣas) based on the seven syllables of the Vidyā; however,
in the present case, this results in eighty-four [lakṣas].

Thus, this Vidyā named Siddhātripuṭā has been established. However, the authors of the commentaries state that for the purpose of practice (*sādhana*), the recitation (*japa*) should begin at sunrise in the morning and consist of exactly three thousand repetitions; they maintain that if it were otherwise, it would not be the time for [the rite].
The application [of the mantra] follows immediately after its accomplishment (*mantrasiddhi*),

because no specific time limit is prescribed for the conclusion of the application, and it is impossible to assert that it must pervade a period such as a *maṇḍala* and so forth. In my view, however, even the previously mentioned number of means (*sādhana*) is obtained from the very beginning.

This is not untenable. Therefore, if one recites [the mantra] three thousand times every day, beginning from the time of sunrise in the morning, while meditating on the identity of the *tripuṭā-vidyā* with one’s own self, then the attainment of that which is the object of the *vidyā* occurs; and if Lakṣmī is the intended object, the attainment of Lakṣmī occurs.
By recitation aimed at obtaining beauty, one attains beauty;
by recitation aimed at gaining poetic skill, one gains poetic skill; and by recitation aimed at gaining proficiency in singing, one gains proficiency in singing—for men, women, or kings alike.

By reciting with the aim of attaining the status of being a vessel for [the deity’s] abundant affection, one achieves that very status of being a vessel for [their] affection. Whatever remains unstated here should be understood by reference to the general discussion. Thus ends the description of the *tripuṭā-vidyā*.
Since no specific worship-diagram (*pūjā-yantra*) has been mentioned here, the *mātṛkā-cakra* alone is to be employed as the general standard applicable to all.
Having lifted [the vessel] from the ground and placed a *kalaśa* upon it, one should contemplate the wheel of Sarvamaṅgalā within it, together with its enclosures (*āvaraṇas*).

At the conclusion of the previously mentioned ritual sequence ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*), one should again contemplate the *mātṛkā*-wheel and worship Garuḍa with the present *Garuḍa-vidyā*. An offering of sacrificial food (*bali*) should be presented at the beginning and end of the worship.
With the sixteen-syllable mantra itself: *Oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*. *Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ śirase svāhā*.
*Vairimohi śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*. *Garuḍayakṣī kavacāya huṃ*. *Haṃsa haṃsa hiṃsa hiṃsa netrattrayāya vauṣaṭ*.

With the mantras "svāhā astrāya phaṭ," which are associated with the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*), one performs the placement (*nyāsa*) on the thumbs and other fingers, as well as the placement on the heart and other parts of the body. *Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ vairimohigarujyakṣī haṃsa haṃsa hiṃsa hiṃsa*.
With the present root mantra consisting of twenty-three syllables ending in "svāhā," one should perform the threefold pervasive nyāsa (*tridhāvyāpakanyāsa*).
While doing so, one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Meru situated before Tāṇḍava-Śambhu, as being filled with [the deity] devouring the oblations.
This is his visualization (*dhyāna*). There are no weapons, nor any enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), names, mantras, visualizations, worship, or the like.
And this reception of the mantra is accomplished by means of the very act of receiving it preceded by the consecration with the water from the jar prepared at the earlier time;
and as for the practice (*sādhana*) regarding the Sun or the Moon, when there is an eclipse of their feet (*padoparāga*),
then starting from the time of the commencement of the eclipse until the time of its release, whatever number [of recitations] is achieved, that many [are required].

After liberation [from the mantra] through the aforementioned number of recitations, at the conclusion of the bath, or on the following day, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a tenth part of the recitations,

and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) consisting of a hundredth part of the recitations. For the sake of accomplishing the completeness of all those rites, everything previously mentioned— such as the feeding of Brahmins and the offering of fees to the Guru— must be performed.

Having consecrated water one hundred times with the mantra accomplished through sugarcane, he caused even those who had reached the state of being on the verge of death— those fainted by contact with the poison arising from the bite of a hooded serpent— to drink that water; and by the mere sprinkling of that water, [they were restored] instantly.

One should restore those afflicted by disease to health. Even those seized by other [poisons] entirely should be freed from their afflictions by drinking such water. Furthermore, by giving a drop of *pakṣākṣa* seed oil consecrated one hundred times with the aforementioned mantra, the suffering caused by the venom of serpents and other creatures is destroyed. Not only that—
It wards off the affliction of mobile poisons in the form of snakes, scorpions, and the like; moreover,
it brings about the destruction even of stationary poisons such as *kālakūṭa* and artificial poisons produced by the mixing of equal parts of ghee and honey.

Thus ends the exposition on the *garuḍavidyā*. Having extracted the *mātṛkāyantra* from a smooth surface or the sky using vermilion and other substances, and having performed the ritual sequence ending with the meditation on the wheel of Sarvamaṅgalā within the jar placed there as before;

Furthermore, having determined that the *mātṛkā* yantra itself is the yantra for the worship of the Goddess mounted upon the [central] chariot—since no other specific yantra has been mentioned—one should meditate on it as ending with the *kalaśa* (pitcher) and worship it as before. In this regard, there is this distinction: *hrīṃ* to the heart.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) on one's own thumbs and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other body parts, with the following: *namaḥ hrīṃ śirase svāhā*, *hrīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *hraḥ kavacāya huṃ*, *hrauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, *haḥ astrāya phaṭ*.
Then, for the ten-syllable complete vidyā: *oṃ ehi yārameśvari svāhā*.
The pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) should be performed three times using the previously mentioned six-limbed mantras and vidyās;

this is the preparation of the general offering water (sāmānyārghya). As for the visualization: she is mounted on a chariot drawn by red horses, wearing red garments and ornaments, four-armed and three-eyed, with a lotus-face full of grace, holding a skull-bowl and a shield in her right hands, and a sword and a fist [of cloth] in her left.

Blazing brightly, with her neck bound by a golden chain by the other two [goddesses], her own goal accomplished; struck by golden canes, with her pair of hands joined in *añjali*, speaking "I am your slave" at the very feet of the intensely near [deity]; thus, in the midst of the preeminent [deity], at the end of the *vidyā*, [he offers] water for the feet (*pādya*) to the firm one.

Having worshipped according to the manner previously shown with the words "I imagine," one should worship the four weapons in the directions starting from the east, near the arms, with the following mantras: "Bhaṃ, obeisance to the elephant goad (aṅkuśa); Caṃ, obeisance to the shield (carma) held in the fist; Heṃ, obeisance to the golden noose (hemapāśa); Hemaśāya, obeisance to the golden [club]; Heṃ, obeisance to the golden staff (hemavetra). Thus the four weapons are to be worshipped.

Immediately after the consecration with the hundred jars, the disciple who has received initiation from the Guru should perform the recitation (*japa*) for the purpose of accomplishing the *vidyā* forty thousand times during the present age.

Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) ten times that number, and having fed the Brahmins without resorting to stinginess regarding wealth, one should master the *vidyā* by means of a teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*). Once one knows the *vidyā* to be perfected through signs proclaimed in dreams and so forth, one should perform the ritual applications (*prayoga*). They are as follows:
If one performs meditation for a thousand or more repetitions directed toward the attraction or subjugation of a specific person,
and recites this vidyā at night for seven nights, or for three [nights], or for a month, or until a mandala is completed,
that person will certainly be attracted and brought under control; and having become submissive, they shall carry out every command for as long as they live.

Furthermore, for this practitioner, there arises the attainment of Mahālakṣmī, the acquisition of gold, and the attainment of all other desired objects such as sons, grandsons, and so forth. Thus concludes the description of Aśvārūḍhā. [Regarding the practice] on very smooth ground, or specifically on the earth, since no other yantra has been mentioned:

Even if not attained through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), having written down the *mātṛkā* wheel which is attained in common, and having fashioned a jar (*kalaśa*) above it according to the aforementioned method, at the conclusion of the rites beginning with the visualization of the *Sarvamaṅgalā* wheel and ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*):
having visualized the *mātṛkā* wheel written below as being inside the jar, [one should perform] the worship there with sixteen [offerings].
One should perform the worship of the present goddess Annapūrṇā, preceded by the offering of *ācamana* water at the beginning and the end.

In this regard, however, there is this specific distinction: *hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śirase svāhā*, *hrūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *hrauṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *hrauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, *astrāya phaṭ*—this is the *ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*. *Namaḥ*...

With the complete seven-syllable mantra, "Bhagavati Māheśvari Annapūrṇe Svāhā," one performs the threefold pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*). Then: *Oṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *Śiras* to the head, *svāhā*; *Bhagavati* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*;
*Māheśvari* to the armor (*kavaca*), *hum*; *Annapūrṇe* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *Svāhā* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*.
The six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the six words associated with the mantra.
Some maintain that the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) is as before; however, in this system, the six-limbed placement is restricted to the *māyīya* [mantra] alone.

The preparation of the general *arghya* offering is performed by means of the six-limbed mantra and the *vidyā*. Having performed each complete *vidyā* or merely a prostration (*praṇāma*) at the front portion [of the respective limbs], one performs the placement (*nyāsa*) of the corresponding *mātṛkā* letters in those locations.
As for the visualization (*dhyāna*), however, it is of her who gazes while intent on a dance that causes terror to serpents.
One should visualize her with a smiling face, offering water for the feet from a golden vessel.
Then, as before, one should perform daily recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblations (*homa*) in either a number of one hundred or one thousand, and their respective tenth parts (*daśāṃśa*).
Having received the mantra and the status of a teacher (*guru*) preceded by the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the water from such an empowered jar (*kalaśa*), [one should proceed].
One should accomplish the recitation (japa) of sixty-eight lakhs (6,800,000) as desired for this present age, along with its tenth-part oblations (homa) and other rites.

Having accomplished this, one should commence at dawn— preceded by the aforementioned meditation— the practice for a thousand days, while performing the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga), nasal (nāsā), and pervasive (vyāpaka) nyāsas in an interwoven manner (sampuṭita) upon this very *annapūrṇā-vidyā*.
The Japanese practitioner shall not encounter poverty in any way whatsoever.

Even during times of famine or in a great desert region devoid of food, he who performs the recitation of this vidyā at another time shall never suffer from hunger. The rest is as described in the general introduction and applies here as well.
Thus concludes the exposition of the Vidya of Annapūrṇā.

Just as before, because no specific [procedure] has been stated and since this is not a [special] yantra, one should extract the *mātṛkā-cakra* obtained through general rule upon the ground. Having placed the jar there as before,
one should perform the previously described procedure beginning with the visualization of the *sarvamaṅgalā-cakra* within it and ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*).

Following the sequence of the constituent elements arranged in prior and posterior order, and having visualized within the water-pot (kalaśa) the Mātṛkā-cakra— which, although already inscribed upon the ground, is intended for the worship of the deity Śrī Śiva, the embodiment of the Nava-vidyā at its conclusion— one should there worship the ninefold form of the present Vidyā. Herein...

The six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) should be performed by appending the complete Vidyā—preceded by the sixfold Mother-mantra (*mātṛkā*)—to the beginning of each of the mantras, starting with "Hṛdayāya namaḥ" and "Śirase svāhā.
The pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) should be performed three times with the complete mantra *hasakṣamalavayūṃ*.
The conceptualization of the general meaning is accomplished by means of both the previously mentioned six-limbed mantras and this complete mantra.
Having placed this complete mantra at each respective location starting from the beginning, as previously described.

The Mātṛkā-nyāsa: as for the meditation, one should meditate upon [the deity] intent on dancing while causing terror to serpents; this is performed with the constant recitation [of the mantra] and its multiples, such as a thousand times or ten parts thereof. Having thus received the present mantra preceded by the consecration with the water from the jar (kalaśa) which has been so sanctified, [one performs it] nine times.

Having attained the number thirty-six lakhs through the performance of three hundred thousand recitations for each syllable of the perfected phonemes, one should perform the recitation in the Kali Yuga at four times that amount,
totaling one hundred forty-four lakhs.

Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) ten times that number, one should practice the *sādhana* of the nine-fold Śiva-mantra. In the same manner, having drawn another Mātṛkā-yantra and placed a water-pot (*kalaśa*) there,
and after performing the entire worship of Sarvamaṅgalā and the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) as before, one should again meditate upon the Mātṛkā-cakra within the pot.

Having meditated upon the Ninefold One (Navātmikā), one should worship the goddess Navātmikā therein. In this context, the placement of the heart-mantra (*hṛdayanyāsa*) and so forth is as previously described, with this specific distinction: at the end, in place of the sixth vowel, the fourth vowel is to be incorporated into the mantra.
This is the only difference; as for the visualization (*dhyāna*), however, she is the one who causes terror to the serpents.

The specific point is that the Goddess of the present mantra should contemplate Śiva’s dance preceded by the manifestation of forms such as Garuḍa; for during such a dance, the serpents who have become her loincloth flee in terror and take to every direction. Such is [the visualization].
The implied meaning is that the Goddess should be meditated upon out of curiosity while beholding the state of Śiva; thereafter,
at the conclusion of the worship, following the consecration with the water from the empowered jar, [the ritual involves] the ninefold nature pertaining to Śiva here on page 127b.
Immediately upon grasping [the essence], one should grasp the power consisting of nine aspects;

one should also perform the mantra-sādhana for both [mantras] according to the sequence of initiation (dīkṣā). Thus, when the two mantras have been mastered, one should recite both mantras according to the stated sequence and number, such as a thousand times, preceded by the meditation on the two aforementioned deities.
One should recite [the mantra]; by that, the accomplishment of all desired goals occurs once one has made a single wish and performed the recitation.

For that purpose, the accomplishment may arise either as something intended or unintended; it may arise simultaneously for many intended objects, or it may be the accomplishment of an unintended object. However, at all times, [this applies] to everything.

At some time, in that very same place, and not merely in some single location; in every way and with certainty, and not by mere chance (*kākatālīya-nyāya*); for all people, and not for just any random individual;
and as something superior, and not merely equal—such a person shall remain as a worshiper of these two combined mantras. Thus concludes the exposition of the ninefold mantra.
Having drawn the perpetual worship-cakra of Sarvamaṅgalā upon a very smooth ground with vermilion and other pigments, and having placed a water-pot there,
one should visualize within it the worship-cakra of Sarvamaṅgalā as written below. Then,
having performed the worship of Sarvamaṅgalā and so forth according to the previously instructed method— neither deficient nor excessive— one should spend that night [in vigil].

Having dispelled [the night] with festivities such as dance and song and by means of keeping a vigil, in the morning, one who has attained the vidyā through the completion of the previously mentioned rites— including worship, recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), dismissal (udvāsana), consecration with the water from the ritual jar (kalaśa-abhiṣeka), piercing the eye (vekavedha), worship of the guru, the offering of the guru’s fee (dakṣiṇā), and the propitiation of the yoginīs and others— [should proceed].

Furthermore, the practitioner who has correctly mastered the methods for the application and performance of the vidyā-sādhana, having performed the japa for the sake of accomplishing that vidyā according to the method stated in the *Lalitāprastāva*— namely, three hundred thousand repetitions for each syllable in the Satya-yuga, adjusted to a total of forty-eight [thousand] in the present yuga— [attains success].

Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) ten times that number according to the stated method, one should accomplish this *vidyā* by means of feeding Brahmins, giving the preceptor’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*), and so forth.

Here, the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the mantras: *hrāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *hrūṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; *hraiṃ* to the armor, *hum*; *hrauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; and *hraḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*. Then, the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) is performed three times with the four-syllable mantra *oṃ klīṃ namaḥ*, or alternatively, by repeating this same mantra six times.

The six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is also performed. The preparation of the *arghya* offering and the meditation (*dhyāna*)—beginning with "of golden hue, beautiful," and so forth—are exactly as described in the introduction to the *Sarvamaṅgalā*. The worship diagram (*pūjāyantra*) is likewise that very same worship diagram; and those same deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*) belong to this *Devīhṛdayavidyā*.

As for the function of the root mantra, by means of the present four-syllable vidyā, this four-syllable [mantra] should be employed at the very beginning of each of the Mothers even during the mātṛkā-nyāsa; having thus accomplished it through the vidyā, one should perform the ritual applications (*prayoga*). They are as follows: white leprosy [is cured by] these two—the root of *suvarṇapuṣpī* and [the root of another plant]—properly [mixed] with the juice of the leaves of *suvarṇapuṣpī*.

Having purified those flour-pastes through the ritual of elemental purification (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites, the practitioner— having abandoned all other food and consuming only milk-rice (*pāyasa*), devoted to the recitation of the mantra at night, and having subdued his senses—
should apply that medicinal paste to the three locations consisting of the heart of the central point of the earth.

Having written the *māyābīja* (the syllable Hrīḥ) over the three locations as previously described, one should, at the time of midnight, in a secluded place made pure by smearing with cow dung and so forth and free from insects such as those that damage crops, meditate upon the Vidyā residing in the *ājñācakra*, whose color is intensely red, and likewise meditate upon that deity who is also of an intensely red hue.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred or one thousand times, one should go to sleep. Then, in a dream, this Goddess, who is the embodiment of all auspiciousness, will certainly speak a true response regarding the matter of the dream's content. Furthermore, since she is worshipped by women, this Vidyā grants their desired fruits at that very moment.
By this much, even though it is composed with the *praṇava*, it is intimated that the mantras belonging to the present tantra [grant] authority to all three [genders].
Through this *vidyā* being worshipped, women obtain good fortune, as do all others.
The attainment of fortune, fame, long life, health, and victory occurs. Thus concludes the exposition of the Devīhṛdaya-vidyā.
Having extracted the *mātṛkā* wheel upon a smooth surface such as leather and placed a jar there,

one should contemplate the wheel of Sarvamaṅgalā within it; then, having performed its worship together with the seven verses beginning with "caraṇa," at the conclusion of the rites ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*), one should again contemplate the *mātṛkā* wheel and the *pūrṇaśakti*, and worship Gaurī.

The mantras are as follows: *hrāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *hrīṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; *hraiṃ* to the armor, *hraiṃ*; *hrauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *hraḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*. Alternatively, they may be: *oṃ rudradayite yogīśvari svāhā* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *oṃ rudradayite yogīśvari* to the head, *svāhā*, and so forth.

The placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the root-mantra alone; in both cases, the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) is performed three times with the complete twelve-syllable mantra: *oṃ rudradayite yogīśvari svāhā*.
One should perform the preparation of the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*) using the complete mantra of the six-limbed rite, and meditate upon her as red.

She stands upon a red horse, adorned with red garments and ornaments; she has four arms and three eyes, her lotus-face is serene, and in her right and left hands she holds a shield and a brilliantly shining staff.

Having bound the one to be subdued by the neck with the *homapāśa* [cord] using two other [mantras], [the officiant] should worship the principal deity alone in the center— [the deity] struck by a golden staff, with both hands joined in *añjali*, saying "I am your slave," and striving for his own [spiritual] welfare— and having worshipped the *Nāthas* behind him or elsewhere as well.
Around that, on the right and left sides: *bhaṃ* to the one who holds the shield, *namaḥ*; *caṃ* to the one who holds the shield and fist, *namaḥ*; *heṃ* to the golden noose, *namaḥ*.

"Hem Hemavetrāya namaḥ"—thus the four weapons are to be worshipped. The recitation (*japa*) of this vidyā should be four hundred thousand times. With a number equal to one-tenth of that recitation, one should perform daily fire-offerings (*homa*) and libations (*tarpaṇa*). Having thus mastered this Gaurī-vidyā, one may perform its ritual applications (*prayoga*). They are as follows: by means of the heart-mantra, she is the attractor of one's own [beloved] in the middle of the night.

Having drawn the form of a mechanical doll (*yantrī*), and having written the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) in its heart in such a form as "O [Devi], draw Yajñadatta, who has brought about the attraction of Devadatta," if one,
with the mind fixed on that [doll], meditating upon it and likewise meditating upon the Goddess according to the aforementioned method, faces the direction of that [target]...

One should recite the Vidyā according to the prescribed method for a period of time such as seven days, a month, or a *maṇḍala*, starting from a count of one thousand. Then, immediately upon the completion of the ritual application (*prayoga*), at that very moment, one shall attract her. Likewise, this Vidyā brings about the subjugation of the world, the subjugation of kings, and the subjugation of women, provided it is practiced daily throughout the duration of the *maṇḍala* and other such periods.

Having recited it the required number of times, one accomplishes [the rite]; what need is there for much talk? In rites for subjugating women and the like, there are no other vidyās—such as the Aśvārūḍhā-vidyā—that produce results so immediately and with such certainty as the Gaurī-vidyā. Any hope of attaining the certain fruits through the service of others is far off. Thus concludes the exposition of the Gaurī-vidyā. On the ground...
Having drawn the Sarvamaṅgalā-cakra with vermilion and other substances,

and having performed the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) and the visualization of the Sarvamaṅgalā-cakra therein, one should worship Sarvamaṅgalā according to the prescribed directions, neither omitting nor adding anything. Then, one should pass that night preceded by festivities such as dance and song.

In the morning, having received this *vidyā* through instruction preceded by worship and consecration as before, the disciple should practice the present *vidyā*. Therein, the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the *māyābīja* joined with the six long vowels: *hrāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *hrūṃ* to the tuft (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *hraiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *hrauṃ*...

*vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes; *phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*) with *hraḥ*. This should be performed by one who has assumed that form. The pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) is: *careṭi iṭimuṭhikākaṭamuḍi svāhā*.
The rite should be performed with the complete fifteen-syllable vidyā as presented here.

The preparation of the general arghya (offering water) is done by means of the two methods of the six-limbed mantra just mentioned. The visualization is exactly as in the Sarvamaṅgalā-vidhi, beginning with "golden-colored and beautiful," and so forth. That same [visualization] constitutes the worship and the yantra; these are the powers of the seven enclosures.

In this current age, for the purpose of accomplishing this vidyā, there should be six million recitations (japa). The fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa) should each be performed with a tenth part of the number of recitations. Having thus perfected the vidyā through the feeding of Brahmins, the offering of fees to the guru, and so forth, one should perform the ritual application (prayoga). The method for that is as follows:

If, in the space between the plantain groves and the groves of betel-nut trees, one performs daily worship and adoration at the three junctions of the day— observing silence throughout the period prescribed for the mandala and other rites— and recites the present fifteen-syllable mantra a thousand times or more;
Then one should mutter the Vidyā; at that time, one should give a gold coin weighing one hundred thousand units (lakṣa-pramāṇa) according to the description.

Thus ends the exposition on the Vidyā of the Hundred Thousand Offerings (*lakṣadā-vidyā*). Having drawn the Mātṛkā-cakra upon the ground and having placed the water-pot (*kalaśa*) therein, [one performs] all rites beginning with the visualization of the Sarvamaṅgalā-cakra within it and ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*).
Having meditated upon the *mātṛkā* wheel, one should worship the Goddess who bestows the three *niṣkas* there in the center with the present mantra;
then, at the end of that twelve-syllable present mantra, one should worship with mantras such as "I offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to her who bestows the three *niṣkas*," and so forth.
Behind [the central deity] or on all sides, one should worship the bow, arrows, noose, and goad by means of *māyā*.
Combined with the six long vowels— in the form of *hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śirase svāhā*, and so forth—

the six-limbed vidyā (*ṣaḍaṅgavidyā*) is presented here. Having first performed each of the twelve-syllable vidyās in their entirety, the ritual placement of the limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed using the mantras of the deities of the six limbs, beginning with "to the heart, *namaḥ*," and so on.
In both cases as well, the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) is to be performed three times with the twelve-syllable mantra: *oṃ navakeśīkanakaṃ vā svāhā*. (p.

The preparation of the general *arghya* offering is performed by means of these very two aforementioned vidyās with their six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). As for the visualization (*dhyāna*), however: [one should meditate on] Lalitā as red in color, holding an arrow, a bow, a noose, and a goad in her hands, adorned with various kinds of ornaments—thus far.
In this manner, having completed the worship according to the previously stated sequence, ending with the *nīrājana* and the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*).

Without performing the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*), one should perform the rites beginning with worship at dawn and ending with the dismissal (*visarjana*), followed by the consecration with water from the empowered jar (*adhivāsitakalaśajala-abhiṣeka*) up to the instruction of the mantra (*vidyopadeśa*); then,
having sat down at the foot of a banyan tree situated on the peak of any mountain whatsoever.

In the Satya Yuga, by a count of thirty-six lakhs; in the Kali Yuga, by a count of one crore and forty-four lakhs—having performed the recitation (*japa*) for the accomplishment of the mantra (*vidyā-sādhana*), and having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) as a tenth part of that, one should accomplish the *vidyā* through the feeding of Brahmins, the pleasing of the Guru, and so forth. This accomplished *vidyā* [should be recited] every day.

One should give three *niṣkas* of gold. For this very reason, the ownership of that which is given belongs to the deity; such is the direction [of the rule]. This concludes the exposition on the knowledge regarding the gift of three *niṣkas*.
Having drawn the wheel of Sarvamaṅgalā on the ground with *darada* (vermilion) and other substances, and having placed a water-pot (*kalaśa*) therein,

one should again visualize the wheel for the worship of Sarvamaṅgalā within it. There, in every way, one should worship the Goddess who recites the praises of Sarvamaṅgalā, preceded by the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the offering of the *arghya* vessel, the invocation (*āvāhana*), and so forth.
Having spent the night in worship while relying on the sevenfold group of obstructions, and having dispelled [the fatigue] with dance, song, and so forth, at the conclusion of the morning worship—

one who has obtained the vidyā through the consecration by the water from the jar used for its dismissal, the piercing [of the channels], the worship of the Guru, the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and so on— [should proceed].

The practitioner should accomplish the vidyā. Herein, by means of whichever [mantra] joined with the six long vowels—*hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śirase svāhā*, and so forth—according to the stated method, the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed once. For a single desired syllable, or for the complete vidyā, it is repeated six times, beginning with "to the heart, *namaḥ*."

Thus, etc., the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed at the beginning of the six-limbed mantras. The pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) is performed with the joined eight-syllable mantra; the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*) is likewise performed with both the six-limbed mantras and the eight-syllable vidyā.

The *mātṛkānyāsa* and the meditation (*dhyāna*)—beginning with "of golden hue, beautiful," and so forth—are all like those of Sarvamaṅgalā. For this very reason, the circle of deities (*pūjācakra*) entered into that meditation consists of those very same deities as the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇadevatā*).
That same method of worship, consisting of sixty lakhs of recitations (*japa*), brings about the accomplishment of the *vidyā* in the current age. From one-tenth of the recitation...

Having accomplished this vidyā through fire-oblations, libations, feeding Brahmins, pleasing the guru, and so forth, one should employ it in practice. At the time of midnight, having worshipped the goddess Sarvamaṅgalā— who is accompanied by all her retinues and grants desired boons— in the manner described in the introduction using *jātī* flowers, the goddess becomes pleased.

One should speak exactly as it is regarding everything—past, present, and future—that has come of its own accord and become the subject of inquiry. This concludes the description of the *vidyā* known as *iṣṭavādinī*.

Having drawn the *mātṛkācakra* itself upon the ground and placed a jar within it, one should worship Sarvamaṅgalā there along with her attendants (*sāvaraṇā*). At the conclusion of her dismissal (*udvāsana*), having again visualized the *mātṛkācakra* within that very [jar], one should perform the worship of Mātaṅginī, encapsulated by the *kavala* (mouthful) consisting of the sixteen-syllable mantra. Therein—

The six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed according to the stated method: *māyayā hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śirase svāhā*, and so forth. Furthermore, the pervasive assignment (*vyāpakanyāsa*) is performed three times with the twelve-syllable complete *Mātaṅginī* mantra: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ mātaṅginyai svāhā śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ*, along with the aforementioned mantras for the six limbs.
The preparation of the general *arghya* offering: one should place this entire Vidyā, or at least the *vāgbhava* syllable alone, at the beginning of each of the letters of the Mātṛkā.

Having joined the *mātṛkās* in their respective places, one should perform meditation [upon her] as follows: she resembles a sapphire, wears red garments and ornaments, has a long hanging braid, is radiant with blossoming *saugandhika* flowers,
wears a garland of severed heads fashioned from them, and is beautified by clusters of pearls.

One should meditate on the Goddess, whose feet are adorned with rings, hero-bracelets, bangles, and anklets; who is constantly playing the lute (vīṇā) together with female attendants equal to herself; and who is surrounded by women of beautiful form, smiling with wonder. Here, in the middle [of the ritual], at the conclusion of the Vidyā-mantra, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) and so forth with the mantras beginning with "mātaṅginyai pādyaṃ kalpayāmi."

The ritual offerings beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) are set aside; the presentation is performed solely with the present *vidyā*. Following this, the capacity for the worship of the weapons (*āyudha*) is obtained through the general rules of worship for the Nine Lords (*navanātha*) as found in their respective Tantras. Surrounding that [the deity], one says: "Oṃ, obeisance to the attendants (*aṅganājana*)."

Having worshipped the women who have surrounded that [liṅga], the aforementioned ritual items—beginning with the night vigil (*rātrijāgaraṇa*) and ending with the attainment of knowledge (*vidyāprāpti*), occurring in their sequential order—are to be followed as before. In the present age, there are forty-eight hundred thousand recitations (*japa*); by means of the *homa* and *tarpaṇa* consisting of one-tenth of that number, and the feeding of Brahmins, [the goal is attained].

This Vidyā, which brings about the accomplishment of mantras through the offering of the guru’s fee and other means, grants five results— good fortune, poetic talent, wealth, proficiency in the art of song, and superiority over all people— if it is recited every day for a thousand times starting from the time of its rising. All these five objects, which are the respective spheres of one's desire, are thereby attained.

Thus ends the description of the Mātaṅginī-vidyā. Regarding the worship-circle (pūjācakra) of Vijayānityā: having dug out a level ground in some secluded place, one should place a jar there; then, after performing the entire sequence of rites beginning with the visualization of the Sarvamaṅgalā-cakra upon it and ending with its removal, the worship-circle [is established] on the ground.

Even if [the diagram] has been drawn, one should contemplate it within the vase and worship Vijayā and Nityā there, together with their enclosures, in a manner that is neither deficient nor excessive.

The distinction here is as follows: using the *māyā* seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*) conjoined with the six long vowels, one performs the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* (six-limb assignment) in the manner of "hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ," "hrīṃ śirase svāhā," and so forth; or alternatively, "hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ," "aṭ śirase svāhā," "rājyadeśikhāyai vaṣaṭ," "rājyalakṣmī kavacāya huṃ," and "saḥ netratrayāya."

The placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the mantras: *vauṣaṭ kleṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ astrāya phaṭ*. In both cases, the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) is performed three times with the sixteen-syllable mantra under discussion—*hrīṃ śrīṃ kleṃ aiṃ rājyādairājyalakṣmīsaḥ kleṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ*—as well as with the two aforementioned mantras for the six limbs. The preparation of the general offering water (*sāmānyārghyakalpana*) is likewise performed with these.

Having joined either the complete vidyā or merely the seed-syllable of Māyā to the beginning of each of the *mātṛkā* letters, one performs the placement (*nyāsa*) of those respective *mātṛkā* letters in their corresponding locations. The mantra for the worship of the principal deity is the sixteen-syllabled one already presented; here, in the offering of the services such as water for the feet (*pādya*), there is the insertion of other words as before.

The mantras of the Lord, the weapons, the armor, and the deities are as before. For the practitioner who has received initiation through the preceding rites such as the consecration by means of the water from the jar, there is the recitation of the present number, sixty-four lakhs,
along with its tenth part in fire-oblations and libations.

Having propitiated the Vidyā through the feeding of Brāhmaṇas, the offering of teacher’s fees (guru-dakṣiṇā), and so forth, as well as by means of constant recitation (japa) and worship, one shall attain it very quickly. Thus ends the description of the Rājyalakṣmī-vidyā.
Having lifted the Vijayāyantra itself out of the ground, one should place the *kalaśa* there.

At the end, one should perform the rites beginning with the visualization of the wheel of Sarvamaṅgalā and ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*). Finally, having again visualized the Vijayā-cakra within that [vessel], one should worship Mahālakṣmī. In that regard, regarding the portion of the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*), it should be performed neither deficient nor excessive.
Vijayā provides only the primary worship (*pradhānapūjā*) in the manner already mentioned in the introduction:
*oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *śrīṃ śirase svāhā*, *hrīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *oṃ kavacāya huṃ*,
*śrīṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*.

The ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the mantras: *hrīṃ astrāya phaṭ*. Then: *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kamale kamalālaye prasīda prasīda oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ*. Thus.

The pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) is performed three times with the mantra of the twenty-seven leaves. The general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) is also prepared using the two mantras of the Vidyā, as introduced by the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*).
Then, having received initiation preceded by consecration with the water from the vase (*kalaśa*) sanctified according to the stated directions, one [enters] the present age.

Having mastered the vidyā by means of four hundred thousand recitations along with its one-tenth portion of burnt offerings (*homa*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), and the gratification of Brahmins, the practitioner, performing daily worship and reciting the aforementioned vidyā for a number such as a thousand times according to the prescribed rules, will certainly [attain success].

By worshipping on the full moon or the new moon day when the sun is situated in the zodiac sign of Libra (Tulā), one shall obtain fame, fortune, wealth, health, victory, houses, fields, and so forth; indeed, all desired objects are attained by all practitioners through this worship. Thus concludes the description of the Mahālakṣmī-vidyā.

Having drawn eight lines each extending east-west and north-south, intersecting one another with equal intervals, one should exclude the fourth square situated at the very center in every direction on the outer perimeter; then, having erased the five squares located in the spaces between them.
In the second row, having omitted the fourth square in each direction and having erased the three squares situated in the intervals between them, there are twenty squares in total;
twelve squares are thus erased in the outermost row and [the remaining] eight in the inner second row.
All the squares, having been combined, amount to thirty-two;

seventeen squares remain. Among them, there is a group of nine squares in the center, and in the four directions, eight squares arranged in an inner and outer sequence. Therein, in the middle of the squares—that is, in the very central square—
Having written the first *kūṭa* of the present *vidyā*, which contains the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object of the rite (*sādhya*),

one should then write each syllable of the *vidyā* in a clockwise direction starting from the square immediately below it, ending at the *nairṛtya* (southwest) square; then, beginning again from the square immediately below the square where the writing commenced previously...
Proceeding clockwise from the outermost enclosure (vīthī), one places the four syllables in the four squares located at the corners of the four directions within the second inner enclosure.

Having written [the letters] in their sequential order, one should again inscribe the remaining four mantra-syllables in the four squares starting from the western square and proceeding clockwise, which are connected to the outermost path; thus is established the yantra for the worship of the treasure of the present Goddess, along with the jar (*kalaśa*).

Having placed [the vessel] there, and having performed even a single ritual act— beginning with the visualization of the *Sarvamaṅgalā* wheel and ending with its dismissal— one should again visualize the present wheel within the water-pot (*kalaśa*) and worship *Siddhalakṣmī* as before with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*).

In that regard, the specific details are as follows: in the worship that is an ancillary of initiation (*dīkṣā*), [the goddess is visualized]; whereas in the worship that is an ancillary to the ritual applications for pacification (*śānti*) and subjugation (*vaśya*), she is golden-hued and beautiful, adorned with pearls and rubies, wearing a crown of rubies, her two eyes overflowing with the weight of compassion, holding an *ātulaṅga* fruit in her lotus-like right hand and [another] in her left.

The visualization consists simply of [the Goddess] bestowing wealth and other gifts upon her own devotees; however, the portion stating that she is seated upon a lotus endowed with eight, sixteen, or thirty-two petals, and that her seat is a pair of palaces with four doors, must also be included within this visualization. In this context:
Specifically, because the Yantra is the locus [of the deity] and she is seated right there, for this very reason,
the portion stating that she is "surrounded by her own equal Śaktis numbering seventy-six, composed of other syllables," is also included within the visualization (dhyāna).
Because there is no evidence for postulating alternative locations for those respective powers when their own specifically assigned places are absent;
and because the portion concerning the "conclusion of the auspicious rite" is fulfilled by the previously mentioned portion on meditation alone;
[and] from the fears of lions, tigers, elephants, thieves, and so forth that might arise while traveling on paths through battlefields or various forests and mountains.
And regarding the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) within the realm of the first dhyāna, its specific nature has not been explicitly stated.
It is as follows: [she is] hundred-headed, three-eyed, with a terrifying face on each countenance, and endowed with two hundred arms.

[She is] surrounded by many [deities] possessing powers in the form of their own [respective] aspects, holding in their hands the weapons desired by the practitioner. According to the two mantras mentioned in the introduction to the *Dīkṣāṅgādipūjā* and the *Sunāthapūjāsumaṅgalā*,
the worship of the excellent pair of *mātuluṅga* fruits is performed without any intervening enclosure (*anāvaraṇa*).

In the worship of the ancillaries such as battle and recitation (*japa*), following the worship of the Lord (*nātha*): having worshipped each of the weapons— the wheel, trident, and so forth— as described in the chapter on meditation (*dhyānapaṭala*), individually upon two hundred hands,
and having performed meditation upon the ground near each respective hand, one should worship with the mantra *śaṃ śaktibhyo namaḥ*.
One should worship those who are bowed down on all sides of the principal deity being invoked and who possess forms identical to that of the principal deity being invoked:
*jajharāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *jajharīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *jajharūṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*;
*jajharaiṃ* to the armor, *hum*; *jajharauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; and *jajharaḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*.

The six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the mantras: *jajharīṃ*, *mahācaṇḍatejaḥ*, and *saṃkarṣaṇikālamathaneha*. Thus, the threefold pervasive placement (*tridhāvyāpakanyāsa*) is performed with the seventeen-syllable *Siddhalakṣmī* mantra. Furthermore, the preparation of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) is accomplished by means of these two aforementioned mantras and the present Vidyā-mantra alone; this is the method for the current age.

This occurs through the performance of a hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), followed by a tenth-part of that number of burnt offerings (*homa*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), feeding of Brahmins, and giving of fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor. Once this knowledge (*vidyā*) is mastered, one must certainly perform worship according to the prescribed rule every morning for the duration of a year, performing a recitation of one thousand times in addition to the daily obligatory recitation.

One should perform libations (*tarpaṇa*) with one-tenth of that amount. By this, one attains victory in battles, the excellence of all desired things, and an abundance of wealth such as elephants and horses. It should be understood that this brings about the pacification of afflictions caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *apasmāras*, and *kṛtyās*, as well as relief from the hardships of mountains, forests, and arrows for the practitioner. This is the result of this perfected vidyā.
Even for one who has no other refuge, all desired goals are accomplished through grace. Thus concludes the description of the Siddhalakṣmī-vidyā.

On a level piece of ground, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp, one should write each complete mantra, together with the words for the practitioner, the subject of the rite, and the action, within that pericarp.
Having placed the ritual pitcher (*kalaśa*) upon the completed yantra,
and having performed the entire series of rites beginning with the visualization of the wheel of Sarvamaṅgalā within it and ending with its dismissal (*udvāsana*),
one should then [construct] the worship yantra in that place, which takes the form of the aforementioned eight petals composed of the specific mantra for which initiation is desired.

Having meditated upon each respective mantra-deity therein, one should worship them. Thus, for the purpose of the sevenfold initiation (dīkṣā) into the present mantra, the procedure culminates in following the manner described as consisting of seven jars; this applies even when there is a preference for the worship of a single Gopāla-mantra out of the nine.

There is no insistence on employing all the *gopāla* mantras together, for there is no relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*) among these mantras. This is just as there is no such relationship between the *vidyās* of Lalitā, Kāmeśvarī, and so forth, nor between the *mantras* of Nātha and the others; nor is there any requirement for their collective recitation (*samuccaya*).
Just as in the case of the ninefold Self and the ninefold ignorance, both are mentioned in their respective meditative verses (*dhyāna-śloka*),

and even in the statement regarding the fruit (*phala-vākya*), the power of the dual number indicates that the fruit belongs specifically to the worship of both; however, here, from the meditative verse composed in the singular number, each [Self] is independent of the other.

Therefore, we understand that when there is a desire to worship all mantras, one should employ all of them; when there is a desire to worship two or three, two or three; and when there is a desire to worship a single *mātrā*, only one mantra should be adopted according to the prescribed rule.
For all [practitioners], the lotus with eight petals, whose pericarp is composed of the syllables of their respective mantras as taught, is indeed [the seat].

For the worship, one should hold the support-mantra (ādhāra-yantra) of the initiation-pitcher (dīkṣā-kalaśa). Therein, the seven Gopāla mantras are as follows: *Oṃ gnyauṃ oṃ*—this is the first Siddha Gopāla mantra, consisting of three syllables and four syllables respectively. Herein: *Āṃ* is for the heart (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), *Īṃ* is for the head (*śirase svāhā*), *Oṃ* is for the crest-lock (*śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*), *Aiṃ* is for the armor (*kavacāya huṃ*), and *Auṃ* is for the three eyes (*netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*).

"Aḥ astrāya phaṭ"—these are the five limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*). Regarding them, the practitioner performs their placement (*nyāsa*) on the little finger and in the aforementioned locations, excluding the eyes. [The mantra] "hrīṃ glyauṃ hrīṃ" is repeated with these syllables.

The second is the six-syllabled Kāmarāja-Gopāla mantra. Herein, the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is as follows: *hrāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *hrūṃ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *hraṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *hrauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; and *kaḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. [The seed syllables are] *klīṃ*, *glauṃ*, and *hrīṃ*.

The third is the five-syllable Manmatha-Gopāla mantra, which consists of non-repeated syllables: *tryakṣaro'nāvṛttapañcākṣarakaḥ*. Herein are the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantrāḥ*): *kāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *kīṃ śirase svāhā*, *kraṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *kaiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *kauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, *kaḥ astrāya phaṭ*. The three-syllable non-repeated mantra is *aiṃ glauṃ aiṃ*.

The fourth is the four-syllabled mantra of Kandarpa-Gopāla. Here, the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) are as follows: *Āṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *Īṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *Aiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *Auṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *Aḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. The three-syllabled mantra is *vlūṃ glauṃ vlūṃ*.

The fifth is the *Camakara-ketana-gopāla-mantra*, which consists of five syllables not repeated: *atrayāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *vīṃ śirase svāhā*, *vūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *vaiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *vauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, and *vaḥ astrāya phaṭ*; these are the mantras for the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*). [The seed-syllable is] *strī glyauṃ strī*.

The sixth Manobhavagopāla mantra consists of three syllables and seven non-repeated syllables. Here, the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) mantras are: *sāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *sīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *sūṃ* to the tuft (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *saiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *sauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *saḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. [The seed-syllables are: *yāṃ*, *rāṃ*, *lāṃ*, *vāṃ*, *sāṃ*, *glyauṃ*, *drāṃ*.
*Drīṃ klīṃ ṣlūṃ saḥ*—this eleven-syllable mantra, along with the nine-syllable repetition, is the seventh, the *Sammohana-gopāla-mantra*. Herein: *yāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*;
*yīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *yūṃ* to the tuft of hair, *vaṣaṭ*; *yaiṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*; *yauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *yaḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*.
And the mantras of the six limbs:

in the Satya Yuga, for the recitation of three hundred thousand [times] of each of the three [groups of] non-reversed syllables; and when this present Yuga has arrived, for that [recitation] multiplied fourfold.
The recitation for the purpose of the mantra-practice consists of one hundred thousand repetitions, divided into groups numbered by the oceans (4), the mountains (72), the sky-eyes (60),
the elephants-oceans (48), the sky-limbs (60), and the creators-elephants (64). In the seventh [case], there are nine repetitions of the unchanging syllables.

For in the Kṛta age, the recitation is measured by Śambhu as one hundred thousand per syllable; in the Kali age, the recitation amounts to thirty-six lakhs. This concludes [the rule] regarding the general direction for all [rites] such as the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth.

The pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) should be performed three times with each respective mantra to be worshipped. The preparation of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) should be carried out during each respective worship using both the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) and the primary mantra of that [deity].
Each [element] should consist of either the complete mantra or merely the seed-syllable (*bīja*) arising from the beginning of that respective mantra.

Having joined [the seed-syllables] at the beginning of the Mātṛkās, the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkā-nyāsa) should be performed in their respective locations preceded by the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa). As for the meditation on the principal deity: [one should meditate on Him] as ruddy, six-armed, holding a flute, a noose, a goad, a bow made of sugarcane stalks, and a flower-arrow, together with His Śaktis.

The word "smaret" (one should remember/meditate) refers to the visualization for all Gopālas alike. At the end of each respective primary mantra of one's chosen deity, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, using the aforementioned mantras, with the water from the general *arghya* vessel held in the right hand by means of a sacrificial ladle (*darvī*).

Having offered each of the twelve services (*upacāra*), beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*), one should perform the offering at the various locations as before, using the mantra of one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭa*) appropriate for that specific time. In the eastern quarter: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Siddha Gopāla, who abides in Light (*prakāśa*). *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of Siddha Gopāla, who is the bliss of Contemplation (*vimarśa*).

One should worship the Nāthas by substituting the word "Nātha" with the names of Siddha-Gopāla and the others, using the nine mantras beginning with "pūjayāmi," combined with the respective seven Gopāla formulas according to the lineage of one's own Guru, or even without such a sequence.

Having worshipped the five weapons in their respective locations with the mantras: *vaṃ* to the flute, *namaḥ*; *pāṃ* to the noose, *namaḥ*; *aṃ* to the goad, *namaḥ*; *cāṃ* to the bow, *namaḥ*; and *iṃ* to the arrow, *namaḥ*; [one should worship] *śaṃ*.

Having worshipped all the Śaktis with the mantra "Obeisance to the Śaktis," and having honored the principal deity with their respective principal mantras, one should offer a handful of flowers as an oblation for the completion of the worship of the first enclosure (āvaraṇa), saying: "May this first enclosure deity accept the worship. Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa) with the Vasiṣṭha-stotra.
One should perform the three services consisting of prostration. In this context,
since at times the first [service] is performed with the root mantra as "Lalitā in the form of a male, whose body is emaciated," thereby establishing the identity of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Lalitā,
there may also be the recitation of some hymn to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others in place of the fourteenth service in the middle.
At the conclusion of the dismissal (*udvāsana*), the recitation of the original hymn consisting of twelve verses is absolutely necessary.

For just as, despite the existence of various hymns to the Guru, the hymn to the Guru mentioned in this very Tantra consisting of five verses is prescribed as mandatory, so too is this hymn to all the deities mentioned in this Tantra prescribed for the occasion of the praise of all the deities included in the present reality (*tattva*). Indeed, not...
The state of having a sublated meaning is also inherent in all mantras because the deity is praised in the Tantras as being of the nature of the *ākāra* (the letter A);
likewise, by virtue of its etymological derivation (*yoga*), the word *Tripurā* refers to the *mūlādhāra*.

Because it resides in the three locations consisting of the heart and the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), it is common to all and thus cannot be worshipped by everyone. [The ritual] concludes with the constant recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*),

the offering of oblations (*bali*) performed with the sixteen-syllable mantra, the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), the rite of seeking forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*), and so forth, ending with dance, song, and other such acts.

Having removed the name [of the deity], at the time of performing the daily and occasional rites in the morning, one should perform— as previously described— the worship, recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), offering of oblations (*bali*), the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*), dismissal (*udvāsana*),

consecration with the water from the ritual jar (*kalaśajalābhiṣeka*), piercing (*vedha*), worship of the Guru, the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and initiation (*dīkṣā*). By the command of the Guru, the number of recitations, fire-oblations, and libations (*tarpaṇa*) has been prescribed.
One should accomplish this vidyā by means of feeding brahmins, giving honoraria to one's guru, and so forth.
Then, through the wearing of that yantra, [the practitioner becomes] one whose locus is that very yantra.
By means of a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of substances corresponding to one's own desire, performed with this very mantra as the instrument and worshiped by the act of tending cows,
and by the recitation (japa) of that mantra continuously throughout the time of the mandala and other rites, having accomplished one or the other [of the two goals] through the agency of that mantra.

By means of libations performed with the substances and methods mentioned in the *Prastāva*, following the count of one thousand or more repetitions of the *Nityaklinnā* mantra, and by means of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) using water empowered by this yantra and performed with the respective *Gopāla* mantras, every practitioner shall fulfill their own desires.

One should accomplish [the practice]. And in this tantra, it is stated that if there is no success in the accomplishment through one method of practice, the threefold mode of accomplishment should be performed. If there is no success with one, then it should be done three times; if there is still no success after three times, the application should be repeated five times with various [methods], as taught in other tantras. This is the repetition of the ritual application.

Nor is there even a counter-example (*pakṣa*), because the result arises through non-deviation precisely from its occurrence in a single instance. Furthermore, on Sunday, one should perform the worship of any one of the seven Gopālas—beginning with Siddha-Gopāla and ending with Sammohana-Gopāla—as previously described in the Yantra, preceded by an offering of food in the form of milk; and on Monday, an offering of honey (the synonym for *kṣaudra*).
Preceded by an offering of ghee on a Monday, preceded by an offering of cooked rice and other grains on a Wednesday,
preceded by an offering of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) on a Thursday, preceded by an offering of coconut on a Friday,
and preceded by an offering of plantains with sugar on a Saturday— at these times, [one should perform] the maṇḍala and so forth.

For the practitioner who performs worship encompassing all [these days], the accomplishment of every desired object occurs through the sequential attainment of each respective fruit. Others, however, perform the worship of Siddha-Gopāla on Sunday preceded by an offering of milk, and the worship of Kāmarāja-Gopāla on Monday preceded by an offering of honey.
On Tuesday, one should perform the worship of Manmathagopāla preceded by an offering of ghee;
on Wednesday, the worship of Kandarpagopāla preceded by an offering of food such as boiled rice, *gaṭṭaka*, and cakes.
On Thursday, preceded by an offering of milk-pudding (*pāyasa*),

one should perform the worship of Manobhava-Gopāla, preceded by an offering of either coconut water or fruit into the hand of Makaraketana-Gopāla. On Saturday, preceded by an offering of plantain fruit with sugar.

Having received initiation into all the mantras of Gopāla and having performed the complete sādhana of all those Gopāla mantras according to the prescribed rules, he performs the worship of Saṃmohana-Gopāla every single day without interruption, beginning from the time of the maṇḍala-consecration and continuing throughout, according to the aforementioned procedure.

The practitioner, performing the worship in the prescribed yantra with the mantra written in the center according to the stated injunctions, will certainly obtain his own desired object—the name of which was written in the middle of the yantra.
This is the fundamental meaning they teach; for since it is connected to both sides of the root text, it conveys the meaning of both.

Once their authority is established, one should adhere to whichever single school among them is derived from the tradition of one's own respective guru; thus they prescribe this arrangement of those two schools. However, since the worship of Bhāskara and the others within both these schools is said to grant all desired objects only when performed in the proper sequence, the third school would be unnecessary to begin.

Because the procedure for worship at each respective door, preceded by the offering of *naivedya*, can be understood from the verse beginning with "milk and honey" (*dugdhakṣaudra*) and so forth; whereas in the second alternative, it is for the purpose of enjoining the worship of the seven Gopālas in sequence on the days of the week, starting with Sunday, as established by another scriptural statement.

Since such a designation is necessary, its purpose must be established; for in this way, because application in ritual practices is impossible without the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), it follows that the accomplishment of the *sādhana* of all Gopāla mantras is required prior to the practice—this is the meaning intended. Among all the Gopālas, [one may choose] according to one's own will...
Furthermore, the ritual procedure for worshipping each individual Gopāla alone, as structured by specific offerings prescribed for particular days of the week,
has already been demonstrated previously (p.

In the context of worship, substances such as milk are prescribed as offerings; even so, other substances obtained through the inclination or capacity of the practitioner are not prohibited, because there is no evidence that the permission for those [prescribed items] functions to exclude others. Now, one might object: is this not like the restriction to milk in the case of a diet prescribed for a disease?

If various kinds of food offerings (naivedya) are obtained according to one’s own desire, why should there not be a restrictive rule regarding milk and other such items? For the food offering, as prescribed by scripture, is endowed with the six flavors; since milk and other items are obtained therein without restriction, a specific rule (niyama) concerning them fulfills its purpose precisely by that restriction. A specific statement is not capable of subverting a general scripture—thus it is said.
Since the illustrious Śrīkaṇṭha, Brahmā, and the Manus truly produce wonder through the contemplation of these [teachings],
is there not here the emergence of the river of the nectar of wisdom? Do you not perceive with a great heart this subsequent wonder right here?
Thus concludes the exposition of the seven mantras beginning with Siddhagopāla.

He whose mother is the radiant Guṇavatī, whose father is named Umāpati—a treasure-house of love—whose birthplace is Pañchakubhū, whose place of refuge is Kūrma mountain, and who has made the feet of Acyuta (Viṣṇu), born of Kṛtavīrya, his excellent abode; this is our work, and it reveals the means for attaining the desired objects of Kamalā (Lakṣmī). || 1 ||
He whose lamp is easily accessible at the station of the sun, and who is a kinsman to Hari— the crest-jewel of the rising lineage of the Lord of the Moon— is a cowherd among the virtuous.
Or how else could one enter this [work], which is like a dense darkness regarding the meaning of the tantras? Therefore, abandon these various wonders as they appear. || 2 ||

Through the assistance of the compassionate Goddess, the venerable feet of the Lord of the Twice-born, who has drawn forth [this work] from the ocean of the minds of the dull-witted by means of a wish-fulfilling gem that is well-filled [with merit].
Having manifested as the root that fulfills all desires and having cast down the enemy's pride,
may he— who, by destroying my own impurities, reveals the stainless state— display this wonder.

The splendor of the sun, the best of men, does not exist apart from Kamalā; the splendor of the sun, the lord of the lotus-pond, does not exist without Kamalā. Having forcibly entered my heart, which was agitated by various doubts, O beautiful Kārtavīrya, Kamalā has manifested herself here; thus, there is no fault in this.
O wise friends, please forgive these words of mine.

Thus ends the *Śrīvidyākāmyakarmakamalākamalā*, composed by Premanidhi Śarma, born of the illustrious Bhāradvāja lineage, residing on Mount Kūrmācala, and belonging to the tradition of the one named Itoya. May there be auspiciousness!
